items.description: A pure-white, art-filled cliff house above Praiano — minimalist, modern and blissfully quiet.

items.name: Capri Tiberio Palace
items.description: A jewel-box design hotel a short walk from the Piazzetta — colourful, cultured and quietly glamorous.

items.name: Hotel Punta Tragara
items.description: A Le Corbusier-designed terrace hotel gazing straight at the Faraglioni sea stacks — Capri's signature view.

items.name: Caesar Augustus
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A cliff-top former villa 300m above the sea in quiet Anacapri — an infinity terrace over the whole bay of Naples.

items.name: Hotel Le Agavi
items.description: A terraced hillside garden hotel with a private funicular down to its own beach club — Positano without the crush.

items.name: Hotel Marincanto
items.description: A cliffside garden hotel with steps straight down to the beach — classic Positano at a gentler pitch.

items.name: Villa Franca
items.description: A top-of-town house with a rooftop pool looking straight down the length of Positano.

items.name: Hotel Villa Cimbrone
credentials: Gardens rated a top Amalfi sight — MICHELIN Green Guide
items.description: An 11th-century villa built around the Terrace of Infinity — a garden hotel of rare, literary romance.

items.name: Villa Marina Capri Hotel & Spa
items.description: A discreet, family-run villa hotel with a fine spa, a short stroll from the Piazzetta.

items.name: Bellevue Syrene 1820
items.description: A neoclassical villa on the Sorrento cliff-edge since 1820 — frescoed, antique-filled and grandly romantic.

items.name: Don Alfonso 1890 (Relais)
items.description: A tiny Relais above the two gulfs, wrapped around one of the south's most celebrated kitchens.

items.name: Hotel Poseidon
items.description: A family-run Positano institution with a pool terrace and a warmth that keeps guests returning for decades.

items.name: Palazzo Murat
items.description: An 18th-century Bourbon palace around a bougainvillea courtyard, steps from the beach and the Duomo.

items.name: Hotel Miramalfi
items.description: A cliff-clinging Amalfi hotel with a seawater pool cut into the rock — honest comfort with a real sea view.

items.name: The Amalfi Coast Drive (Strada Statale 163)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: The serpentine coast road threads cliff-edge above a cobalt sea, past lemon terraces and pastel villages, and it is deliberately, gloriously slow. Hand it to a private driver so the whole family can watch the view instead of the hairpins, and stop wherever a belvedere catches the light.

items.name: A Private Boat Day Along the Coast
items.description: The coast reads entirely differently from the water — you swim off the boat in hidden coves, glide under the Furore bridge, and reach beaches no road serves. A chartered gozzo or motor yacht with a skipper is the discreet, unhurried way to see it, with a private lunch stop and shade for the elders.

items.name: Positano — Spiaggia Grande
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: The wide crescent of dark pebbles at the foot of the vertical village is the beating heart of Positano, framed by the tumble of pastel houses climbing the cliff. Book sunbeds at a chic beach club for the day and let ferries and water taxis buzz in and out while you watch.

items.name: Fornillo Beach & the Cliffside Path
items.description: A short, immensely pretty cliff walk from Marina Grande leads to Fornillo, a quieter cove with crystal water that feels worlds away from the summer crowds. It is the calmer beach for a slow honeymoon afternoon or families wanting space from the main scene.

items.name: Church of Santa Maria Assunta
items.description: Positano's icon — a majolica dome of yellow, green and blue tiles blazing against the sky and sea, just steps from the beach. Inside is a revered 13th-century Byzantine Black Madonna, and beneath, a medieval crypt worth the quiet detour.

items.name: Path of the Gods (Sentiero degli Dei)
items.description: The legendary ridge traverse runs high above the coast from Bomerano to Nocelle, an ancient mule track with unbroken views to the sea and the silhouette of Capri. Walk it east-to-west so Positano stays in front of you; a private guide can pace it gently and arrange a car at both ends.

items.name: Amalfi — Cathedral of Sant'Andrea
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: A dramatic sweep of steps rises to a striped Arab-Norman-Byzantine facade that crowns the whole town. Inside rest the relics of Saint Andrew, and the adjoining Cloister of Paradise — a Moorish garden of slender white columns — is one of the coast's most serene corners.

items.name: Museo della Carta (Paper Museum)
items.description: Housed in a cave-like 13th-century paper mill — the oldest in Europe — this small museum shows how Amalfi made the handmade cotton paper that built its medieval trading power. The guided tour, with the old water-wheels still turning, delights curious children and grandparents alike.

items.name: Valle delle Ferriere Nature Reserve
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: A cool, green ravine of streams, waterfalls and giant prehistoric Woodwardia ferns — living fossils — with the ivy-clad ruins of 12th-century ironworks emerging from the vegetation. A gentle three-hour escape from the heat and the crowds, a small entry fee, best with a nature guide.

items.name: Ravello — Villa Rufolo & Its Gardens
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: A 13th-century palace whose terraced gardens so moved Wagner that he set Parsifal's magic garden here. During the summer Ravello Festival, concerts play on a stage cantilevered over the cliff with only sea and sky behind the orchestra — pure theatre for a romantic evening.

items.name: Ravello Festival Concerts
items.description: From July into September, Ravello — 'the city of music' — stages classical concerts in Villa Rufolo's gardens, the famous stage floating above the Gulf of Salerno. A sunset chamber recital or grand orchestral night here is one of the coast's most memorable indulgences.

items.name: Villa Cimbrone & the Terrace of Infinity
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: A romantic garden ending in the Terrazza dell'Infinito, a marble-busted belvedere that Gore Vidal called the most beautiful view in the world — the coast falling away 350 metres to the sea below. Go early or late for the light, and for the honeymoon photograph everyone wants.

items.name: Emerald Grotto (Grotta dello Smeraldo)
items.description: A sea cave where sunlight filtering through an underwater fissure turns the whole cavern a glowing emerald green, its floor spiked with stalactites and stalagmites. Reached by lift from the coast road or by boat, it is a short, magical stop — an easy wonder for all ages.

items.name: Fiordo di Furore
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: A slim fjord slicing into the cliffs, spanned high above by the coast-road bridge and hiding a tiny pebble beach and cluster of old fishermen's houses at its foot. Every summer divers leap from the 30-metre bridge in an international championship; best admired from the water on a boat day.

items.name: Atrani — Italy's Smallest Town
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: A single, near-perfect fishing village of stacked houses and a tiny piazza opening onto the sea, just around the headland from Amalfi yet almost untouched by its crowds. Come for a slow, authentic dinner where locals still outnumber visitors.

items.name: Praiano & Marina di Praia
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: Widely called the coast's most romantic village for its sunsets and its double view — the bay of Positano on one side, Capri on the other. Below, the sliver of Marina di Praia beach tucks between cliffs, and the seaside path to Grotta dell'Africana makes a lovely evening walk.

items.name: Vietri sul Mare — the Ceramics Town
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: The 'Capital of Ceramics,' where five centuries of hand-painted majolica spill from every workshop in bold Mediterranean colour. Commission a bespoke dinner service or tiles, and see the Solimene factory's extraordinary curved facade and the tiled Villa Comunale.

items.name: Li Galli Islands
items.description: Three private islets between Positano and Capri, mythologised as the home of Homer's sirens and once owned by dancers Nureyev and Massine. You cannot land, but circling them by boat and swimming in the clear water around Gallo Lungo is a highlight of any coast cruise.

items.name: Lemon Grove & Limoncello Experience
items.description: On terraces cut vertically into the cliff, family farms grow the prized Sfusato Amalfitano lemon — huge, fragrant, PGI-protected. Walk the pergolas, pick your own fruit, distil a bottle of limoncello to take home, and taste lemon cake in the shade; children love the ritual.

items.name: A Private Cooking Class
items.description: Learn to make fresh pasta, seafood or classic Campanian dishes in a hillside kitchen or amid the lemon groves, then eat what you cooked over a long lunch. Hosts happily build a fully vegetarian menu — ideal for multi-generational groups and a warm, hands-on afternoon.

items.name: Capri — The Blue Grotto (Grotta Azzurra)
items.description: Known to the Romans as Tiberius's bath, this sea cave fills with an otherworldly electric-blue light as sun refracts through the water beneath the low entrance. You lie flat in a small rowing boat to slip inside — a brief, unforgettable thrill worth timing carefully for calm sea.

items.name: Capri — The Piazzetta
items.description: The little square under its clock tower is the island's stage, where an aperitivo among the well-dressed is almost obligatory. Sit, order a drink, and watch the parade — the most stylish people-watching in the Mediterranean.

items.name: Capri — The Faraglioni
items.description: Three towering rock stacks rising from the sea off Capri's southern coast, the island's signature silhouette. Boats pass through the natural arch of the middle stack for luck; the Belvedere di Tragara above gives the classic postcard view.

items.name: Anacapri & Villa San Michele
items.description: Quieter, higher and more authentic than Capri town, Anacapri holds the villa built by Swedish doctor Axel Munthe — a house of classical antiquities opening onto a pergola and one of the island's finest sea panoramas. A calmer, cultured half-day away from the glamour.

items.name: Chairlift to Monte Solaro
items.description: A gentle single-seat chairlift floats you up over gardens and orchards to Capri's 589-metre summit in about fifteen minutes, opening a 360-degree panorama over the island, the Faraglioni, the Bay of Naples and Vesuvius. Effortless, and a highlight for those who don't want to hike.

items.name: Sorrento — Marina Grande & Villa Comunale
items.description: The old fishing quarter of Marina Grande lines the quay with characterful seafood trattorie, while up in town the Villa Comunale gardens frame a sunset view across the bay to Vesuvius, with a lift down to the water. An easy, gracious base and gateway between coast and city.

items.name: Bagni della Regina Giovanna
items.description: A natural sea pool ringed by the ruins of a Roman villa, connected to the open sea by a rocky arch — Queen Joanna's legendary bathing spot. A short walk from the road delivers a wild, uncrowded swim far from any beach club, for those who like their luxury raw.

items.name: Pompeii
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Archaeological Areas of Pompei, Herculaneum and Torre Annunziata
items.description: The Roman city frozen mid-life by the eruption of AD 79 — streets, frescoed villas, a forum and plaster casts of its people, all sealed under ash for centuries. Vast and moving; go with a private archaeologist-guide early in the day, and mind the heat for elders and children.

items.name: Herculaneum (Ercolano)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Archaeological Areas of Pompei, Herculaneum and Torre Annunziata
items.description: Smaller than Pompeii but far better preserved — buried by hot mud that carbonised and saved wooden beams, doors, even furniture, so you walk through intact multi-storey Roman houses. The quieter, more intimate ruin, easily paired with Pompeii or done on its own.

items.name: Villa Oplontis (Torre Annunziata)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Archaeological Areas of Pompei, Herculaneum and Torre Annunziata
items.description: A sumptuous seaside villa, likely Empress Poppaea's, with some of the finest Roman wall paintings anywhere yet almost no crowds. The connoisseur's stop on the Vesuvian circuit — vivid trompe-l'oeil frescoes and a garden colonnade, all to yourself.

items.name: Mount Vesuvius
items.description: The volcano that buried Pompeii still broods over the bay, and a short walk from the car park along the crater rim rewards you with a look into its smoking mouth and a sweeping view over Naples and Capri. A driver to the upper gate makes it comfortable for the whole family.

items.name: Paestum — The Greek Temples
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Cilento and Vallo di Diano National Park with the Archaeological Sites of Paestum and Velia
items.description: Three colossal Doric temples of the 6th and 5th centuries BC, standing golden and near-complete in open meadows — among the best-preserved Greek architecture on earth, older than the Parthenon. Deeply calm and uncrowded; pair with the museum's famous Tomb of the Diver fresco.

items.name: Naples — Cappella Sansevero & the Veiled Christ
items.description: In a small Baroque chapel lies Sammartino's Cristo Velato, a marble Christ draped in a veil so translucent it seems impossible carved from stone — one of the world's great sculptures. A short, spellbinding visit at the heart of the old city; book timed tickets ahead.

items.name: Naples — Spaccanapoli & the Historic Centre
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Naples
items.description: The dead-straight ancient street that literally splits old Naples, lined with churches, cloisters and the year-round nativity artisans of Via San Gregorio Armeno. Loud, alive and utterly authentic — the antidote to the coast's polish, best explored on foot with a guide and a pizza stop.

items.name: Naples — Museo Archeologico Nazionale
items.description: The treasury of everything portable dug from Pompeii and Herculaneum — the great mosaics, bronzes and frescoes, plus the Farnese marbles. Seeing it before or after the ruins makes the whole story click; a private guide keeps it to the highlights for a two-hour visit.

items.name: Nocelle Village
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: A tiny car-free hamlet clinging to the mountain above Positano, the eastern end of the Path of the Gods, with a handful of terrace trattorie and a plunging sea view. Descend the 1,700-odd steps to town, or simply lunch here in the hush far above the resort.

items.name: Conca dei Marini & Marina di Conca
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: One of the coast's smallest, most exclusive villages, wrapped around a jewel of a cove below whitewashed houses — long a discreet retreat for the international set. Come by boat for the swimming and the seclusion, and taste the local sfogliatella Santa Rosa where it was invented.

items.name: Furore — The Village That Isn't There
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: A 'painted village' with no real centre, its houses scattered up the mountainside and its walls covered in vivid murals, threaded by the Path of the Love (Sentiero dell'Amore). A quiet, offbeat wander for those who have already ticked the icons.

items.name: Cetara — Fishing Village & Colatura
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: A working tuna and anchovy port that still makes colatura di alici, the amber anchovy essence descended from Roman garum. Eat spaghetti alla colatura at a harbourside table where the fishermen land their catch — the coast's most delicious hidden authenticity.

items.name: Scala — The Oldest Town on the Coast
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: Facing Ravello across the valley, Scala is the coast's most ancient settlement and one of its quietest, with a medieval cathedral and paths down through chestnut woods and terraces. A restorative half-day for walkers and those seeking the coast before tourism.

items.name: Marmorata Waterfalls & the Atrani Valley Walk
items.description: The green Dragone valley behind Atrani hides old mills and small waterfalls on a gentle walk up toward Ravello, an escape into shade and birdsong minutes from the sea. An easy, pretty leg-stretch that few day-trippers ever find.

items.name: Sunset Aperitivo at a Cliff Terrace
items.description: The coast faces west, so its sunsets are a nightly event — best taken with a glass on a hotel or restaurant terrace hung over the sea. Reserve the corner table at a Michelin-starred maison or a Ravello garden bar for the evening the family will remember.

items.name: Marina di Furore & the Sea-Village Frescoes
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: At the mouth of the fjord sits a cluster of old monazeni — fishermen's houses built into the rock — reachable by a stair from the bridge. Photogenic and almost secret, it is the closest thing to a fishing hamlet time forgot on the whole coast.

items.name: Kayak & Swim the Sea Grottoes
items.description: Paddle a sea kayak along the base of the cliffs into little grottoes and arches — Grotta dell'Africana, Grotta del Fico — that no boat or road can reach, stopping to swim in impossibly clear water. A gentle active morning that even novices and teenagers enjoy.

items.name: Torre dello Ziro & the Amalfi–Pontone Ridge
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Costiera Amalfitana
items.description: A short climb to a lone medieval watchtower on a spur between Amalfi and Atrani, with a dizzying double-bay view and a dark Renaissance legend attached. Under an hour up from Pontone, it is the coast's best-value viewpoint for modest effort.

items.name: Sorrento Lemon & Inlaid-Wood Craft
items.description: Beyond limoncello, Sorrento is the home of intarsio — intricate inlaid marquetry — worked in family ateliers for generations. Visit a workshop and museum, commission a piece, and understand the craft heritage behind the souvenirs; a cultured pause between coast and city.

items.name: Quattro Passi
items.description: The Mellino family's cliff-top villa above the Bay of Nerano — the only three-star kitchen in all of southern Italy.

items.name: L'Olivo
items.description: Andrea Migliaccio's light, Mediterranean haute cuisine at the Capri Palace — the island's only two-star.

items.name: Don Alfonso 1890
items.description: The Iaccarino family's landmark above the two gulfs — a founding temple of modern Campanian cooking.

items.name: Torre del Saracino
items.description: Gennaro Esposito's seafront kitchen in a medieval watchtower — the coast's most decorated home-grown chef.

items.name: La Sponda
items.description: Le Sirenuse's candlelit terrace — 400 flames each night, and Positano tumbling to the sea below.

items.name: Zass
items.description: The starred kitchen of Il San Pietro, cut into the same cliff — sea light, seafood and quiet perfection.

items.name: Rossellinis
items.description: Palazzo Avino's fine-dining room high in Ravello — refined cooking with the whole coast spread beneath.

items.name: La Serra
items.description: Chef Annarumma's glass-walled room at Le Agavi, with arguably the best view of the bay in Positano.

items.name: Il Flauto di Pan
items.description: Dinner in the gardens of Villa Cimbrone — starred cooking beside the Terrace of Infinity.

items.name: Alici
items.description: Borgo Santandrea's sea-terrace kitchen — bright, ingredient-led cooking above a private cove.

items.name: Glicine
items.description: Hotel Santa Caterina's flowering-terrace dining room, looking straight out to the Amalfi sea.

items.name: Il Refettorio
items.description: Starred cooking in the old refectory of a cliff-top monastery — hushed, considered and beautifully sourced.

items.name: La Caravella dal 1959
items.description: Southern Italy's first Michelin star, in a 12th-century ducal palace — history you can taste.

items.name: Sensi
items.description: A modern, sea-facing kitchen in Amalfi town doing precise, contemporary Campanian plates.

items.name: Li Galli
items.description: Villa Franca's rooftop kitchen, named for the islands off Positano — a starred table with a panoramic sweep.

items.name: Un Piano nel Cielo
items.description: 'A floor in the sky' — Casa Angelina's white-on-white starred room above quiet Praiano.

items.name: Il Riccio Restaurant & Beach Club
items.description: The world's only Michelin-starred beach club — seafood on the rocks beside the Blue Grotto.

items.name: Le Monzù
items.description: J.K. Place Capri's terrace kitchen — refined island cooking with the harbour laid out below.

items.name: Terrazza Bosquet
items.description: The starred terrace of Sorrento's grande dame, over the citrus gardens and the marina.

items.name: Il Buco
items.description: Giuseppe Aversa's kitchen in a 16th-century cellar — Campanian cooking with real personality, and famous pasta.

items.name: Lorelei
items.description: A newly-starred sea-terrace kitchen on the Sorrento cliffs — modern, bright and beautifully sited.

items.name: Relais Blu
items.description: A hillside starred room at the tip of the peninsula, with Capri floating in the window.

items.name: Antica Osteria Nonna Rosa
items.description: Family cooking of the Sorrentine hills, elevated to a star — soulful, seasonal and generous.

items.name: Next2
items.description: A stylish, sustainability-minded room on Positano's main street — modern Campanian without the grand-hotel price.

items.name: Da Adolfo
credentials: MICHELIN Guide — noted / long-standing coast institution
items.description: A ramshackle beach shack reached only by boat — grilled mozzarella on lemon leaves, and the real coast.

items.name: Lo Scoglio (Da Tommaso)
credentials: A landmark coast institution — celebrated by chefs worldwide
items.description: The beloved Bay of Nerano family trattoria — the original spaghetti alla Nerano, off its own jetty.

items.name: Il Riccio Beach Club
items.description: A white-and-blue rock terrace by the Blue Grotto — Champagne and a starred kitchen where the day slides into evening.

items.name: Franco's Bar
credentials: Part of Le Sirenuse — World's 50 Best Hotels 2025
items.description: Le Sirenuse's open-air bar suspended above Positano — a French 75 at golden hour, and the finest terrace on the coast.

items.name: Champagne & Oyster Bar, Le Sirenuse
credentials: Part of Le Sirenuse — World's 50 Best Hotels 2025
The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A jewel-box bar of vintage Champagne and oysters inside the coast's most storied hotel.

items.name: Anema e Core
credentials: Capri's defining nightlife institution — over 40 years
items.description: Capri's legendary taverna — Neapolitan guitars from midnight to dawn, where politicians, locals and film stars share one dance floor.

items.name: Music on the Rocks
credentials: Positano's landmark nightclub — a long-running institution
items.description: A club carved into the cliff at the end of Positano's beach — the coast's one true late-night dance floor.

items.title: A private gozzo day along the coast
items.description: Your own wooden boat and skipper to swim the Li Galli islets, lunch in a fishing cove, and see the towns from the water.

items.title: Le Sirenuse in Positano
items.description: The Sersale family's cliffside icon — a Champagne-and-oyster bar, a Vespa, and the coast's most photographed pool.

items.title: Chef's table at Quattro Passi or Rossellinis, Ravello
items.description: Michelin-starred Campanian cooking with the whole gulf laid out below the terrace.

items.title: A private concert at Villa Rufolo during the Ravello Festival
items.description: Music on the cliff-edge stage where Wagner found the garden of Klingsor, arranged with the best seats in the house.

plan.heading: 4 days on the Amalfi Coast, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive by private transfer over the coast road and settle into Le Sirenuse, with its view down the tiers of Positano.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A slow afternoon at the hotel's Aldo's bar and pool, then a walk down to the Spiaggia Grande.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at La Sponda at Le Sirenuse, the room lit by hundreds of candles.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A chartered gozzo along the coast to the Li Galli islets and the grottoes below Positano.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at Da Adolfo, reached only by boat, then swimming off the deck.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Aperitivo at Franco's Bar, then dinner at Zass or the seafood at Chez Black on the beach.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive up to Ravello for the gardens of Villa Rufolo and Villa Cimbrone's Terrace of Infinity.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at the Belmond Caruso's cliff-edge pool, then the quiet lanes of the town.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Rossellinis or the Michelin table at Il Flauto di Pan, with a concert if the Ravello Festival is on.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Private launch to Capri and the Blue Grotto before the crowds, then up to the Piazzetta.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at Il Riccio by the Grotta Azzurra, then the chairlift to Monte Solaro above Anacapri.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: An early dinner at Da Paolino under the lemon trees before the crossing back.

items.description: The vertical, glamorous postcard town — for those who want the scene and don't mind the steps and the prices.

items.name: Ravello
items.description: High, cool and cultured above the coast, suited to travellers who prefer gardens and quiet to the beach crowd.

items.name: Amalfi & Atrani
items.description: The historic heart with its cathedral, plus tiny Atrani next door — a good central base with a real town's rhythm.

events.name: Ravello Festival
events.note: A summer-long programme of orchestral concerts and recitals on the Villa Rufolo terrace above the sea.

events.when: late spring (rotates; Amalfi every four years)
events.name: Regatta of the Ancient Maritime Republics
events.note: A costumed rowing race between Amalfi, Genoa, Pisa and Venice, with a medieval procession when Amalfi hosts.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Naples (NAP), then take a private car along the coast road or, far more elegantly, a helicopter or private boat transfer straight to your hotel's jetty at Positano or Ravello.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Travel by private boat for coastal hops and a chauffeured car for the corniche; the cliff road is narrow and slow, so leave the driving to a local and arrive by sea where you can.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Good coverage in the towns with occasional dead spots on the cliffs and at sea; an Italy or EU eSIM plus hotel wifi covers you.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Euro; cards work in hotels and better restaurants, but carry cash for beach clubs, boat crews and smaller trattorie, and round up for good service.

onGround.note: Ravello sits above the crowds for serenity, Positano for the postcard; come May to June or September to avoid August gridlock, and pack flat shoes for the endless steps.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Late May-June and September are the sweet spot: warm sea, long light, before and after the August crush. Avoid August (peak Italian holiday, gridlocked coast road) and November-March, when many hotels and boats close.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No non-stop; the gateway is Naples. Fly one-stop via Gulf hubs (Emirates/Qatar/Etihad) into Naples, or Air India non-stop Delhi-Rome (~8.5h, 4x weekly) then ~1h to Naples. From Naples the coast is best reached by pre-arranged private car (~1.5h to Positano) or, in season, private boat transfer. Qatar Qsuite via Doha is the strongest business cabin on the routing.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required; routine EU standards. Very safe. The genuine hazards are the narrow, vertiginous coast road and boat transfers in rough seas, so plan drivers and timings. Tap water is potable.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Straightforward for vegetarians; Campanian cooking is tomato-, lemon- and vegetable-led. Jain is workable at good hotels with notice. Dedicated Indian dining is scarce on the coast itself, so arrange in-villa/hotel Indian cooking in advance if it matters.

seo.title: Amman & Petra — TripAgent
seo.description: Amman & Petra, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Amman & Petra
hero.tagline: Hills of Roman ruins above the road to Petra.

ourTake.lede: Treat Amman as the base and Petra as the reason. Give the capital a day for the Citadel and the Roman theatre, then drive the King's Highway south rather than the fast desert road — the wadis and Crusader castles are the point. At Petra, arrive at opening and walk past the Treasury to the Monastery; most people never get that far.
ourTake.comeIf: You want Petra, Wadi Rum and the Dead Sea threaded into one unhurried, deeply historic journey.
ourTake.skipIf: You want beaches, shopping or a resort week; this is a trip for the curious traveller.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Amman & Petra. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Amman
items.description: A palatial tower on the highest of the White City's seven hills — Four Seasons polish, the surest hands in Jordan.

items.name: The St. Regis Amman
items.description: Butler service on every floor and Levantine art throughout — the St. Regis ritual, brought to the diplomatic quarter.

items.name: Fairmont Amman
items.description: A glass tower over the new downtown — floor-to-ceiling city views, Le Labo baths, beside the Four Seasons and St. Regis.

items.name: Kempinski Hotel Ishtar Dead Sea
credentials: Travel + Leisure World's Best — among the world's top 500 hotels, best in Jordan
Condé Nast Traveler — Top 5 Middle East resorts
World Luxury Spa Awards / World Travel Awards — Jordan's Best Hotel Spa (2017–2019)
items.description: Nine pools and hanging gardens down to the shore — a Babylon-inspired resort on the longest private beach in Jordan.

items.name: Grand Hyatt Amman
credentials: Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice Awards 2023 — Top 20 Hotels in the Middle East
items.description: A long-standing grand house near Rainbow Street — an in-house art gallery and four restaurants, quietly reliable.

items.name: W Amman
credentials: Marriott Luxury Portfolio — W Hotels flagship, Jordan
items.description: A bold contemporary statement in the new downtown — a canyon-walk entrance inspired by Petra, and W's design energy.

items.name: Mövenpick Resort & Residence Dead Sea
credentials: World Travel Awards — Jordan's Leading Resort (multiple years)
items.description: An Arabic village of low stone buildings and gardens sloping to the sea — the award-winning Zara Spa its centrepiece.

items.name: Mövenpick Resort Petra
credentials: Accor / Mövenpick 5-star — unrivalled position at the Petra entrance
items.description: Fifty metres from the Petra gate — Levantine mosaics and marble, and the shortest walk to the Rose City there is.

items.name: Evason Ma'In Hot Springs
credentials: Six Senses group heritage — spa set beneath a natural hot-spring waterfall
items.description: A canyon oasis 264 m below sea level, a hot-spring waterfall cascading into the pool — the setting is the star.

items.name: Memories Aicha Luxury Camp
credentials: Within the UNESCO World Heritage Wadi Rum Protected Area (2011)
items.description: Glass-domed 'Martian' bubble suites open to the stars, deep in the Valley of the Moon — the desert night, in comfort.

items.name: The Siq, Petra
items.description: The 1.2km sandstone gorge that opens Petra: walls soaring 80 metres, narrowing to a slit, until the Treasury flashes into view at the end. Walk it slowly at first light with a private guide before the coaches arrive, and let the children run the last stretch to the reveal.

items.name: The Treasury (Al-Khazneh), Petra
items.description: The single most recognisable facade on earth, 40 metres of rose-red rock carved straight into the cliff by the Nabataeans. Arrive at dawn for the light on the columns and space for a proper family photograph, then take mint tea at a cliffside spot facing it.

items.name: The Monastery (Ad-Deir), Petra
items.description: Petra's largest monument, wider and taller than the Treasury, reached by roughly 800 rock-cut steps high into the mountains. Well worth a second day; older travellers can ride a donkey up while the fit hike, and the view from the ridge opposite is the reward.

items.name: The Royal Tombs, Petra
items.description: A row of grand mausoleums carved into the cliff below the theatre — the Urn, Silk, Corinthian and Palace tombs — their stone banded in swirls of colour. Climb at late afternoon when the west light sets the whole facade glowing.

items.name: The High Place of Sacrifice, Petra
items.description: A Nabataean altar platform on a summit reached by a stepped trail, with a sweeping view over the entire valley of tombs. A rewarding morning climb for active families; a guide brings the ritual carvings to life.

items.name: The Street of Facades & Colonnaded Street, Petra
items.description: Beyond the Treasury the canyon widens into a whole carved city — rows of tomb facades, a Roman theatre cut from rock, and a colonnaded main street. This is where a full day inside Petra earns its keep, ideally at an unhurried pace with a driver waiting at the gate.

items.name: Petra by Night
items.description: Three or four evenings a week the Siq is lit by some 1,500 candles and you walk in near-silence to the Treasury for music and story under the stars. A quietly magical close to a Petra day; book ahead and go on a night your camp or hotel can arrange transfers.

items.name: Little Petra (Siq al-Barid)
items.description: A miniature Nabataean canyon a short drive north of Petra, far quieter, with a rare painted ceiling in one of its rock-cut halls. A gentle, crowd-free hour that pairs beautifully with a long lunch at one of the boutique lodges nearby.

items.name: The Amman Citadel (Jabal al-Qala'a)
items.description: On the city's highest hill, layered with Roman, Byzantine and Umayyad remains and a grandstand view over the white houses of Amman. The obvious first stop; a private guide turns the scattered stones into a clear story for three generations at once.

items.name: Temple of Hercules, Amman Citadel
items.description: Two towering Roman columns and a giant carved stone hand are all that remain of a 2nd-century temple that would have outsized anything in Rome. Golden hour here, with the city falling away below, is one of Amman's finest photographs.

items.name: The Umayyad Palace, Amman Citadel
items.description: An 8th-century audience hall crowned by a reconstructed dome, the most photogenic corner of the Citadel and cool inside on a hot afternoon. The domed chamber and vast underground cistern reward a slow look with someone who can explain them.

items.name: The Roman Theatre, Amman
items.description: A 6,000-seat theatre cut into the hillside in the 2nd century, still steeply dramatic in the heart of downtown. Climb to the top row for the view; the two small folklore museums flanking it are a quick, worthwhile add.

items.name: The Jordan Museum
items.description: Jordan's flagship museum in Ras al-Ayn, home to the 9,000-year-old Ain Ghazal statues — among the oldest large human figures ever made — and copper-scroll material from the Dead Sea Scrolls. Air-conditioned, beautifully laid out and ideal for a hot midday with children.

items.name: King Abdullah I Mosque
items.description: Amman's landmark mosque, its vast blue mosaic dome visible across the city, built 1982–89 and open to respectful non-Muslim visitors outside prayer times. A serene, cool interior; robes are provided and a discreet guide smooths the visit for a family.

items.name: Rainbow Street & Downtown Souks, Amman
items.description: The city's most walkable stretch — cafes, galleries and rooftop views on Rainbow Street, spice, gold and textile souks tumbling downhill into Al-Balad. Best explored on foot late afternoon; a good private guide knows which lanes are worth the detour.

items.name: The Royal Automobile Museum, Amman
items.description: Some 70-plus cars and motorcycles from the late King Hussein's collection, from a 1916 Cadillac of the Arab Revolt to a Mercedes gullwing, a Ferrari F40 and the Aston Martin. A genuine crowd-pleaser for car-loving teenagers and grandfathers alike, set in King Hussein Park.

items.name: Darat al Funun, Amman
items.description: A hillside compound of restored 1920s houses and a small Byzantine ruin, now Amman's leading home for Arab contemporary art, with gardens, a library and a quiet cafe overlooking the old city. A calm, cultured hour away from the heat and crowds.

items.name: The Jara Souk & Wild Jordan Center, Amman
items.description: The Friday Souk Jara for local craft and the RSCN's Wild Jordan cafe for one of the city's best terrace views and honest Jordanian cooking. Both are easy, characterful stops; Wild Jordan is reliably good for vegetarian and Jain-aware family dining.

items.name: Hashem & Habibah, Downtown Amman
items.description: Two Amman institutions minutes apart: Hashem for 24-hour falafel, hummus and fatteh in a downtown alley, and Habibah since 1951 for the definitive plate of warm kunafa. The most authentic bite in the city — and both are naturally vegetarian-friendly.

items.name: 4x4 Desert Safari, Wadi Rum
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Wadi Rum Protected Area
items.description: A private jeep tour across the red sand of the Valley of the Moon — towering rock walls, dunes, springs and canyons that doubled as Mars on film. The essential Wadi Rum half-day; camel or horse can be added for the children.

items.name: A Night in a Luxury Bedouin Camp, Wadi Rum
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Wadi Rum Protected Area
items.description: Sleep in a domed or Martian-style suite with a private terrace, a zarb dinner cooked underground, and a sky thick with stars. The finest camps offer proper beds, ensuite bathrooms and discreet service — an unforgettable, safe night out for multi-generation families.

items.name: Um Fruth & Burdah Rock Bridges, Wadi Rum
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Wadi Rum Protected Area
items.description: Two natural stone arches — the low, climbable Um Fruth and the lofty Burdah, one of the highest rock bridges anywhere. Um Fruth is an easy scramble for a family photo; Burdah is a guided half-day for the surefooted.

items.name: Khazali Canyon & Lawrence's Spring, Wadi Rum
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Wadi Rum Protected Area
items.description: A cool, shaded slot canyon walled with ancient Thamudic petroglyphs, and the greenery of a spring tied to T.E. Lawrence. Gentle, atmospheric stops on a jeep route — the carvings fascinate children when a Bedouin guide reads them.

items.name: Hot-Air Ballooning over Wadi Rum
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Wadi Rum Protected Area
items.description: A sunrise flight above the desert, drifting over red dunes and sandstone islands as the light turns them gold. The most serene view of Rum there is — a private basket can be arranged for a special morning.

items.name: Stargazing in Wadi Rum
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Wadi Rum Protected Area
items.description: With almost no light pollution, Rum is among the world's great skies; camps run telescope sessions on the Milky Way and planets, best around the new moon. A quiet, wondrous close to a desert day for all ages.

items.name: Floating in the Dead Sea
items.description: Bob effortlessly on the surface of the lowest point on earth, 430-odd metres below sea level, water so salt-dense you cannot sink. A must-do novelty for the whole family; go from a resort beach with fresh-water showers close by.

items.name: Dead Sea Mud & Spa
items.description: Coat yourself in mineral-black mud, let it dry, rinse it off in the sea, then retreat to a world-class spa — the Kempinski Ishtar's is among the largest in the Middle East. A restorative day of pampering for multi-generation travellers.

items.name: Jerash Roman Ruins
items.description: One of the best-preserved Roman provincial cities anywhere — the colonnaded Oval Plaza, an 800-metre chariot-rutted Cardo, the Temple of Artemis, Hadrian's Arch and a hippodrome. A day trip from Amman that astonishes; a guide and an early start make it.

items.name: The Madaba Mosaic Map
items.description: In a working Greek Orthodox church, the oldest surviving map of the Holy Land — a 6th-century floor mosaic of some two million tiles. Small but extraordinary; Madaba's mosaic workshops and stone-set churches fill a rewarding half-day.

items.name: Mount Nebo
items.description: The height from which Moses is said to have seen the Promised Land, with a fine memorial church, ancient mosaics and a view stretching to the Dead Sea and, on a clear day, Jerusalem. A moving, easy stop near Madaba for any family.

items.name: Bethany Beyond the Jordan (The Baptism Site)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Baptism Site (Bethany Beyond the Jordan)
items.description: The believed site of Christ's baptism on the east bank of the Jordan — excavated churches, pools and the riverbank itself. A serene, deeply meaningful visit; access is by official shuttle with a guide, so plan through your concierge.

items.name: Dana Biosphere Reserve
items.description: Jordan's largest reserve, tumbling from cool mountains to desert lowlands across four ecological zones, with over 800 plant species and rare Nubian ibex. Hike the Wadi Dana trail or simply take the sunset view; a wild, restorative counterpoint to the ruins.

items.name: Feynan Ecolodge, Dana
items.description: A candlelit, solar-run lodge at the desert end of Dana, named among the world's top eco-lodges by National Geographic, reached the last stretch by Bedouin 4x4. Star-bathed nights, Bedouin hospitality and slow days — a rare, soulful stay for the curious.

items.name: Diving & Snorkelling in Aqaba
items.description: The Red Sea at Aqaba holds warm, clear water year-round, healthy coral and famous sites like the sunken tank and the Cedar Pride wreck within a protected marine park. Gentle house reefs suit first-time snorkellers and children; private boat dives suit the certified.

items.name: Aqaba Marine Park & Beach Resorts
items.description: Jordan's warm-water resort town on the Gulf of Aqaba, the natural place to unwind after Petra and Wadi Rum with beach clubs, glass-bottom boats and easy family swimming. A relaxed coda to a Jordan itinerary, with views across to three countries.

items.name: Qasr Amra (Qusayr 'Amra)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Quseir Amra
items.description: A small 8th-century Umayyad bath-house whose walls and dome carry the finest surviving early-Islamic frescoes — hunts, musicians and a rare painted zodiac. There is nothing else quite like it in the world; the highlight of the desert-castle loop east of Amman.

items.name: Qasr Kharana
items.description: A square, near-perfect Umayyad building in the open desert, long thought a fort but likely a caravan inn, its rooms ranged around a courtyard. A striking, atmospheric stop on the eastern loop — quick to see and photogenic against empty land.

items.name: Qasr Azraq
items.description: A black-basalt fortress rebuilt in the 13th century and famous as T.E. Lawrence's winter headquarters during the Arab Revolt. History buffs and Lawrence readers relish it; pair with the nearby Azraq wetland reserve.

items.name: Umm Qais (Gadara)
items.description: A Decapolis city on a green plateau in Jordan's far north, its black-and-white theatre and colonnaded street looking out over the Sea of Galilee and the Golan. Panoramic, uncrowded and lovely at sunset, with a well-regarded local restaurant on site.

items.name: Ajloun Castle (Qal'at ar-Rabad)
items.description: A 12th-century Ayyubid fortress raised under Saladin to face the Crusaders, commanding wooded hills and long views over the Jordan Valley. A satisfying stop for children who like castles, often paired with Jerash and Umm Qais on a northern day.

items.name: As-Salt (The Place of Tolerance)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — As-Salt, the Place of Tolerance and Urban Hospitality
items.description: A honey-limestone Ottoman-era town on three hills, famed for its yellow-stone mansions and a lived tradition of Muslim-Christian harmony. A gentle, authentic half-day of stepped lanes and guest-house hospitality, a short drive from Amman.

items.name: Umm ar-Rasas
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Um er-Rasas (Kastrom Mefa'a)
items.description: A quiet archaeological site south of Madaba whose Church of St Stephen holds one of the Byzantine world's great mosaic floors, mapping the cities of the region, alongside a rare 15-metre stylite tower. An off-the-track gem for those who loved the Madaba map.

items.name: The King's Highway Drive
items.description: The ancient road threading Madaba, Wadi Mujib's canyon overlooks, Karak's Crusader castle and Dana on the scenic way south to Petra. With a private driver it turns the transfer into the journey — the slow, storied route rather than the fast desert highway.

items.name: Karak Castle
items.description: A hulking Crusader fortress on a spur above the King's Highway, with vaulted halls and dungeons to explore and enormous valley views. A dramatic break on the drive to Petra that children and history-lovers both enjoy.

items.name: Wadi Mujib Siq Trail
items.description: Jordan's 'Grand Canyon' meeting the Dead Sea — a wet gorge trail where you wade and scramble up a river between soaring walls, run by the RSCN in season. An exhilarating adventure for fit teenagers and adults, minutes from the Dead Sea resorts.

items.name: Ma'in Hot Springs
items.description: Thermal waterfalls tumbling steaming into pools in a desert gorge below sea level, with a spa resort built around them. A relaxing, slightly wild interlude near the Dead Sea, easy for all generations to enjoy.

items.name: Fakhreldin
items.description: Lebanese fine dining in a former prime minister's villa — immaculate mezze and service, the grand Amman institution since 1997.

items.name: Alee
items.description: Chef Ali Ghzawi's modern Levantine cooking — home flavours retold through storytelling and playful texture.

items.name: Dara Dining by Sara Aqel
credentials: MENA's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 — No. 18, Highest New Entry Award
items.description: Season-led cooking with an Italian thread, in a beautifully restored villa — the most talked-about opening in the city.

items.name: Shams El Balad
credentials: MENA's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 — No. 8, Best Restaurant in Jordan
items.description: Farm-to-table Jordanian home cooking in a sunlit old house — the freshest, most honest table in the city.

items.name: Sufra
items.description: Traditional Jordanian cooking in a converted 1950s villa with a garden terrace — the classic Amman lunch.

items.name: Beit Sitti
items.description: 'Grandmother's house' — a hands-on home-cooking experience in a restored family home, cooking then sharing the meal.

items.name: Hashem
credentials: Documented Amman institution — a national landmark of Jordanian cuisine
items.description: The city's iconic falafel-and-hummus house since the 1950s — open all hours, once served the royal family, still unbeatable.

items.name: Sekrab
items.description: A rooftop of found-object 'junk' art and open-air seating — quirky Jordanian plates over the old city's lights.

items.name: 13C, Bar in the Back
credentials: MENA's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 — No. 36 (the only Jordanian venue on the list run as a bar)
items.description: A hidden speakeasy behind an unmarked door — the most serious, most awarded mixology in Jordan.

items.name: Cantaloupe Gastropub
credentials: Widely cited as Amman's landmark Rainbow Street rooftop bar
items.description: The original Rainbow Street rooftop — iconic three-hill views over downtown and a long, easy Amman evening.

items.name: District Urban Rooftop
credentials: Widely cited among Amman's premier cocktail rooftops
items.description: A chic high-rise rooftop in the new downtown — inventive cocktails and a sweeping skyline panorama.

items.name: Sekrab Rooftop
items.description: Open-air, junk-art rooftop that turns from supper to a lively late crowd over the lights of the old city.

items.title: Petra by Night through the candlelit Siq
items.description: Two thousand candles light the gorge to the Treasury for a music-and-projection show, on the evenings it runs.

items.title: A private guide from the Treasury to the Monastery
items.description: The long climb past the tombs to Ad Deir, with an archaeologist to read the Nabataean city for you.

items.title: A night in a luxury camp in Wadi Rum
items.description: Bedouin hospitality and a bubble suite under the desert sky where Lawrence of Arabia rode.

items.title: Floating and a spa evening at the Dead Sea
items.description: The lowest point on earth, with mineral mud and sunset over the West Bank hills.

plan.heading: 5 days in Amman & Petra, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Citadel above Amman with the Temple of Hercules, then the Roman theatre below.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch of mezze at Sufra in a restored villa, then the galleries of Jabal Al Weibdeh.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner and a nightcap at the Four Seasons Amman overlooking the hills.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive to Jerash, one of the best-preserved Roman cities, walking its oval forum and colonnaded street early.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch in the Ajloun hills, then the crusader castle of Qal'at ar-Rabad.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return to Amman for dinner at Fakhreldin, the city's finest Levantine table.

days.title: The desert and the descent south

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive to the Dead Sea, floating in the mineral water and lunch at the shore.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Continue south along the King's Highway, pausing at the Wadi Mujib overlook.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Check into the Petra Marriott or a fine local riad, an early dinner before Petra.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Enter the Siq at first light to reach the Treasury before the crowds, then the Street of Facades.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Climb the 800 steps to the Monastery for lunch and the view, then the Royal Tombs in soft light.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Petra by Candlelight through the lit Siq, then dinner back at the hotel.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive into Wadi Rum, a private 4x4 through the red sands and rock bridges of T.E. Lawrence's desert.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch under an overhang, then the Nabataean inscriptions and Khazali canyon.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Sunset from a dune and dinner at a Bedouin luxury camp beneath the Milky Way.

items.name: Jabal Amman / Rainbow Street
items.description: For the walkable, café-lined old heart of the capital, near the galleries and downtown souks.

items.name: Abdoun
items.description: For the modern, embassy-district polish — the smarter hotels and restaurants, quieter and greener.

items.name: Wadi Musa
items.description: The town at Petra's gate; base here so you can be first through the Siq at opening.

events.name: Jerash Festival
events.note: Jordan's flagship culture festival, staged among the floodlit Roman ruins north of Amman.

events.name: Petra Desert Marathon
events.note: A trail race through the ancient city and surrounding desert, drawing runners from around the world.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Arrive at Queen Alia International (AMM) south of Amman, where a fast-track greeter and private car begin the transfer — about forty minutes to the capital, and roughly three hours south to Petra along the Desert Highway.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver with a good vehicle is the way to cover Jordan's distances; Petra itself is walked, and the fit should keep an early start for the Monastery climb, with horses and carts available for the Siq.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: An eSIM from Zain or Orange Jordan gives dependable 4G in Amman and around Petra; coverage is patchier in the desert, so plan for gaps in Wadi Rum.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Jordanian dinar (JOD) is strong and cash-friendly; cards work in Amman hotels and better restaurants, but carry dinars for Petra, guides and tips, where 10 percent is the norm.

onGround.note: Amman's Abdoun and the Four Seasons area suit a city base; for Petra, stay close to the gate and enter at opening to have the Treasury near-empty. Dress modestly away from hotels, bring proper walking shoes and sun cover, and consider Petra by Night on its scheduled evenings.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Spring (March-May) and autumn (September-November) are ideal: mild 20-25C days for Petra and Wadi Rum. Avoid December-February, when Petra turns cold and wet with desert nights below freezing, and peak summer, when it tops 38C.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi to Amman on Air India, roughly 5.5 hours, or via the Gulf hubs on Emirates, Qatar Airways or Royal Jordanian in business. Routing through Doha or Dubai lets you use a first-class lounge and often improves the cabin over the direct service. Petra is about a three-hour private transfer south of Amman.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: Recommended: hepatitis A and typhoid, with routine vaccinations current. Jordan is safe and welcoming for visitors; normal caution applies. Tap water in Amman is treated but not recommended for drinking, as rooftop storage tanks can harbour contamination, so drink bottled throughout. Petra involves long walks and uneven terrain in strong sun.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Very easy for vegetarians: the Levantine table is largely plant-based, with hummus, mutabbal, falafel and vegetable mezze everywhere. Jain travellers should flag onion and garlic, which are common. Indian food is limited outside Amman, so carry a few provisions for the Petra leg; Amman has a handful of Indian restaurants for a fix.

seo.title: Amritsar — TripAgent
seo.description: Amritsar, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Amritsar
hero.tagline: Spiritual heart of the Sikhs around the Golden Temple.

ourTake.lede: Amritsar is essentially about two things done exceptionally well: the Golden Temple and the food. See the temple at both night and dawn, when it is quietest and most moving, and eat your way through the old city rather than the hotel restaurants. The Wagah border ceremony is a spectacle but heavily touristy; go if it interests you, but the temple and the Partition Museum are the deeper experiences.
ourTake.comeIf: You want the Golden Temple at first light and the finest Punjabi food there is.
ourTake.skipIf: You want beaches, nightlife or a long stay.
