note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Amritsar. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Taj Swarna, Amritsar
items.area: GT Road / near the Old City
credentials: Taj Hotels flagship five-star in Amritsar
157 rooms and suites; J Wellness Circle spa
items.description: The city's flagship five-star — Taj polish and Punjabi warmth, five kilometres from the Golden Temple.

items.name: Hyatt Regency Amritsar Hotel & Spa
credentials: Shanti Spa — the largest spa in Amritsar
items.description: A 248-room Hyatt with the largest spa in the city and twice-daily transfers to the Golden Temple.

items.name: Radisson Blu Hotel, Amritsar
credentials: Largest ballroom in Amritsar; two lawns
items.description: A grounds-set Radisson Blu with the largest ballroom in the city — the wedding address on the airport road.

items.name: Ranjit's SVAASA
items.description: A 200-year-old family haveli reborn as a wellness boutique — the only true heritage stay in Amritsar.

items.name: Holiday Inn Amritsar Ranjit Avenue
credentials: IHG Holiday Inn — international mid-luxury standard
items.description: A dependable IHG house in the leafy Ranjit Avenue district — well-run and central to the newer city.

items.name: Sri Harmandir Sahib (The Golden Temple)
items.description: The gilded sanctum floats at the centre of the Amrit Sarovar, its reflection breaking gently on the water while unbroken kirtan drifts across the marble. For a Sikh-heritage family it is the still point of the whole journey; for anyone it is one of the most moving spaces in India.

items.name: The Parikrama
items.description: The white marble walkway that rings the sarovar, walked barefoot and clockwise, past pilgrims, gilt-edged shrines and the slow ripple of the tank. A private guide who knows where to pause turns a circuit into a reading of five centuries of Sikh history.

items.name: The Akal Takht
items.description: The seat of temporal Sikh authority, facing the Harmandir Sahib across the causeway, where the community's edicts have been issued since 1606. Standing before it explains the Sikh idea that the spiritual and the political are one.

items.name: The Amrit Sarovar (Holy Tank)
items.description: The pool of nectar that gives Amritsar its name, its steps worn smooth by generations who bathe here at dawn. Sitting at the water's edge in the quiet before sunrise is the single most peaceful hour the city offers.

items.name: The Palki Sahib Ceremony (Night)
items.description: Each night the Guru Granth Sahib is carried on a silver-and-gold palanquin from the sanctum to the Akal Takht amid rosewater and shouldered devotion, the Sukhasan ritual ending around 9:30-10 PM. Attending it, then again the Prakash before dawn, bookends a stay in something unforgettable.

items.name: Dawn Darshan & The Prakash Ceremony
items.description: In the dark small hours the Guru Granth Sahib is installed in the sanctum and the first hymns rise as the sky lightens over the gold. Arriving at 3-4 AM with a guide who can move you through the crowd is a rare, unhurried privilege.

items.name: The Langar (Guru Ka Langar)
items.description: The world's largest free community kitchen feeds up to a hundred thousand people a day, everyone seated on the floor as equals. Rolling rotis alongside the sevadars for an hour is a humbling, hands-on experience that stays with multi-generational travellers.

items.name: Central Sikh Museum
items.description: Above the main entrance to the complex, galleries of Guru portraits, martyr paintings, arms and rare manuscripts trace the faith's history and its long line of sacrifice. A quiet, weighty counterpoint to the devotion outside, and free to enter.

items.name: Gurdwara Baba Atal Rai
items.description: A nine-storey octagonal tower beside the Golden Temple, its walls once painted with frescoes of Guru Nanak's life, built in memory of Guru Hargobind's young son. Fewer visitors climb it, and the rooftop gives a rare high view over the sanctum and the old city.

items.name: Jallianwala Bagh
items.description: The walled garden where, in 1919, General Dyer's troops fired on a peaceful gathering; the bullet-marked wall and the martyrs' well remain, now within a renovated memorial complex with galleries and a light-and-sound show. A short walk from the Golden Temple and essential to understanding modern India.

items.name: Partition Museum
items.description: Housed in the restored colonial Town Hall, this is the world's first museum dedicated to the 1947 Partition, told through survivor testimony, personal objects and letters. For Punjabi families whose grandparents crossed the new border, it is often the most personal stop in the city.

items.name: Attari-Wagah Border Beating Retreat
items.description: The daily lowering-of-the-flags ceremony where Indian and Pakistani guards high-kick and posture as the crowd roars, held at the last checkpost before Lahore around 6 PM. Reserve VIP seating near the gate; the patriotism is unabashed and children love it.

items.name: Gobindgarh Fort
items.description: Maharaja Ranjit Singh's military fort, once the treasury of the Koh-i-Noor, reopened as a living-history complex with the Sher-e-Punjab 7D show, the Toshakhana turban museum, artisans and folk performers. A full evening's outing that works well across three generations.

items.name: Kandha Boldiyan Ne (Whispering Walls) Show
items.description: The nightly sound-and-light spectacle projected onto the fort's ramparts, telling the story of the fort and Ranjit Singh's Sikh empire after dark. Book the 8 PM show and pair it with an early dinner inside the fort's dhaba court.

items.name: Durgiana Temple
items.description: A Hindu temple to Durga and Lakshmi built in the 1920s in the very image of the Golden Temple, gilded and set in its own tank. It gives a fuller sense of Amritsar as a shared sacred city, and is far quieter than its famous cousin.

items.name: Ram Tirath Temple
items.description: The reputed hermitage of sage Valmiki, where legend places the birth of Luv and Kush and the writing of the Ramayana, marked by an ancient tank and a colossal Valmiki statue. A peaceful, mythic day-side detour that most tourists miss entirely.

items.name: Maharaja Ranjit Singh Museum & Summer Palace
items.description: The Lion of Punjab's own summer palace, set in the Ram Bagh gardens, now displaying his arms, armour, coins, miniatures and a panorama of the Sikh court. The best single place to meet the man whose empire made Amritsar, and to walk his gardens after.

items.name: Ram Bagh Garden (Company Bagh)
items.description: The formal garden Ranjit Singh laid out on the model of Lahore's Shalimar, with pavilions, a summer palace and old shade trees in the heart of the city. A cool, green interval between the intensity of the shrines.

items.name: Amritsar Heritage Walk (Old City)
items.description: A guided route through the 400-year-old walled city, from the Town Hall through the katras and akharas to the Golden Temple, past frescoed havelis, the old mint and hidden shrines. A private early-morning walk, before the crowds, is the finest way to read the real Amritsar.

items.name: Chitta Akhara
items.description: A monastic complex from 1781 on the heritage walk, prized for its delicate Rajasthani-influenced wall paintings tucked deep in the lanes. The kind of place only a good local guide will open for you.

items.name: Thathera Bazaar (Guru Bazaar Coppersmiths)
credentials: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage (Thatheras of Jandiala Guru)
items.description: The craft of the Thatheras, hand-beating brass and copper utensils in a rhythm unchanged for generations, is inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list. Watching a vessel take shape and taking one home is a genuinely rooted keepsake.

items.name: Kesar Da Dhaba
items.description: Serving since 1916 in a narrow old-city lane, famous for dal makhani slow-cooked overnight in a brass pot over wood flame, lachha parathas and firni. The unshowy, definitive Amritsari meal; a guide can arrange a quiet table away from the queue.

items.name: Bharawan Da Dhaba
items.description: A pre-Partition institution (since 1912) near the Town Hall, turning out tandoor-fresh kulchas, dahi bhalla and chole for the better part of a century. Vegetarian, generous and a fixture of any Amritsari food pilgrimage.

items.name: Amritsari Kulcha (The Dish)
items.description: The city's signature: a potato-and-spice-stuffed flatbread crisped in a tandoor, cracked open with white butter and dark chole. Worth eating at more than one address, kulcha crawl style, to argue over who does it best.

items.name: Ahuja Milk Bhandar (The Lassi)
items.description: The legendary spoon-thick lassi, so dense with malai you scoop rather than sip, poured in a cramped old-city corner. A five-minute detour that becomes a highlight; a private car and guide make the narrow lanes easy.

items.name: Kulcha Land
items.description: A cleaner, sit-down alternative to the old-city dhabas on the newer Lawrence Road, doing crisp stuffed kulchas washed down with lassi. Useful when travelling with elders who want the flavour without the crush.

items.name: Sadda Pind
items.description: A twelve-acre recreation of a 19th-century Punjabi village, with mud homes, artisans, Gatka, Bhangra, bioscope and a full Punjabi buffet. A curated, comfortable way to give children and grandparents the rural Punjab their family came from; overnight stays exist for the fully immersed.

items.name: Khalsa College
items.description: A 300-acre campus of magnificent Indo-Saracenic architecture designed by Bhai Ram Singh in 1892, its main building a favourite of film crews. A short stop for the scale and the beauty of the facade, and for the story of Sikh self-assertion under the Raj.

items.name: Gurdwara Baba Deep Singh Shaheedan Sahib
items.description: The shrine marking where the 75-year-old warrior-scholar Baba Deep Singh fell in 1757 defending the desecrated Golden Temple, one of Sikhism's most revered martyrdom sites. A powerful, less-visited stop for those tracing the faith's history of sacrifice.

items.name: Gurdwara Chheharta Sahib
items.description: Built where Guru Arjan Dev sank a great well fed by six Persian wheels, giving the town its name; the sixth Guru was born nearby. A calm, historic gurdwara on the way to the Wagah border, easy to fold into that afternoon.

items.name: Hall Bazaar
items.description: The oldest, busiest market in the city, entered through a Mughal-style gateway, stacked with phulkari, Punjabi juttis, dry fruit and handicrafts. A guide can steer you to the trusted old houses for embroidery and footwear worth carrying home.

items.name: Katra Jaimal Singh Market
items.description: The textile heart of Amritsar, its lanes lined with shops for suits, sarees and wedding fabric at prices that surprise. Punjabi families still come here to buy trousseaux; a knowledgeable escort makes the bargaining painless.

items.name: Papad-Warian Lanes (Majith Mandi)
items.description: The alleys where sun-dried Amritsari papad and spiced lentil warian are made and sold, the smell of asafoetida hanging in the air. A quick, sensory old-city errand that yields the most authentic edible souvenir of Punjab.

items.name: Punjabi Jutti Shopping
items.description: Amritsar's hand-embroidered leather juttis are among the finest in India, made by families who have stitched them for generations. Commissioning a bespoke pair, or fitting the whole family, is a small, memorable indulgence.

items.name: Pul Kanjari
items.description: A little pleasure-stop Maharaja Ranjit Singh built for his dancer Moran, complete with baoli, temple, mosque and gurdwara side by side as a mark of his secular rule. A poignant, near-empty ruin best paired with the Wagah ceremony the same afternoon.

items.name: Gurdwara Tarn Taran Sahib
items.description: Founded by Guru Arjan Dev, this gurdwara holds the largest sarovar of any Sikh shrine, thronged on the monthly Amavas. A serene, grand day-trip that rewards early arrival, well short of the tourist trail.

items.name: Sri Khadoor Sahib
items.description: The home town of the second Guru, Angad Dev, where he formalised the Gurmukhi script and where Mata Khivi ran an early langar. Part of the classic three-gurdwara heritage circuit south of the city, rich in the faith's formative story.

items.name: Gurdwara Baoli Sahib, Goindwal
items.description: The great stepwell of eighty-four steps built by the third Guru, Amar Das, in the 16th century, a place of deep pilgrimage on the banks of the Beas. The furthest and most atmospheric of the day-trip gurdwaras, open from before dawn.

items.name: Pingalwara
items.description: Bhagat Puran Singh's home for the destitute, sick and abandoned, a byword in Punjab for selfless service. A visit, or a quiet contribution, gives a stay a dimension of seva beyond the shrines and the food.

items.name: Saragarhi Memorial Gurdwara
items.description: A memorial to the 21 Sikh soldiers who fought to the last man at Saragarhi in 1897, one of history's most celebrated last stands. Small but stirring, and close enough to the Golden Temple to see in the same morning.

items.name: Sardar Bhagat Singh Museum, Khatkar Kalan
items.description: The ancestral village and museum of the revolutionary Bhagat Singh, preserving his belongings, letters and family home. A longer day-trip for the patriotic and the historically minded, best done with a driver and a picnic.

items.name: Amritsar Food Trail (Guided)
items.description: A curated crawl through the old-city lanes taking in kulcha, lassi, fish tikka, jalebi and kada prasad in a single morning, led by someone who knows every counter. The most delicious way to understand why food is half the reason to come to Amritsar.

items.name: Makhan Fish & Chicken Corner
items.description: For the non-vegetarians, the city's most famous Amritsari fish tikka, batter-fried in the winter season and eaten hot off the tawa. A savoury counterpoint for families who want more than the vegetarian dhaba canon.

items.name: Jalianwala Bagh Light & Sound Show
items.description: The evening projection within the renovated memorial that narrates the 1919 massacre against the bullet-scarred walls. An emotive way to close a day begun at the Golden Temple, and a chance to sit with the history rather than pass through it.

items.name: Golden Temple Roof & Sunset Views
items.description: As the light softens, the gold catches fire and the reflection in the sarovar deepens; the langar hall roof and the parikrama's far side give the calmest vantage. Timing a slow evening circuit for golden hour is the photograph everyone remembers.

items.name: Qila Ahluwalia & The Old City Gates
items.description: Fragments of the fort of the Ahluwalia misl and the surviving gateways of the walled city, woven into the heritage walk, mark the boundary of eighteenth-century Amritsar. Small architectural clues that make the whole old city legible once a guide points them out.

items.name: Makhan Fish & Chicken Corner
credentials: A recognised Amritsar culinary icon (since the 1960s–90s lineage)
Renowned for Amritsari fish (singhara / sohal) and tandoori chicken
items.description: The definitive Amritsari fried fish — crisp, tender singhara fish that made the city's most famous non-veg name.

items.name: Beera Chicken House
credentials: Renowned for tandoori murga, keema naan and Amritsari fish
items.description: Four decades of smoky tandoori chicken with a dry-rub the city argues over — no colour, no fuss, just fire.

items.name: Surjit Food Plaza
credentials: Renowned for tandoori and Amritsari non-vegetarian classics
items.description: The grand old name of Amritsari non-veg — tandoori meats and fried fish with a fuller sit-down setting.

items.name: Kesar Da Dhaba
items.area: Old City (Chowk Passian, near the Golden Temple)
credentials: The Better India / Slurrp — favoured by Nehru, Indira Gandhi, Lala Lajpat Rai
Condé Nast Traveller India — Amritsar must-visit
items.description: A century-old pure-vegetarian legend — dal makhani cooked overnight in copper, once served to Nehru and Lala Lajpat Rai.

items.name: Bharawan Da Dhaba
items.area: Old City (near Town Hall / Golden Temple)
credentials: YourStory / Slurrp — a century-old Amritsar institution
A ten-minute walk from the Golden Temple
items.description: Amritsar's oldest dhaba — pure-veg Punjabi cooking slow-simmered in desi ghee since a tent in 1912.

items.name: Kanha Sweets
credentials: A landmark Amritsar sweet shop & breakfast institution
items.description: The city's morning ritual — puri chole and halwa, plus a sweet counter of pinni, kaju katli and motichoor.

items.name: All India Famous Amritsari Kulcha
credentials: Outlook Traveller — among Amritsar's best kulcha
items.description: The kulcha the city sends you to — crisp, many-layered, butter-soaked, praised by chef Vikas Khanna.

items.name: Gian Chand Lassi Wale (Gian Di Lassi)
credentials: A landmark Hall Bazaar milk bhandar
Renowned for thick peda lassi (makhan, malai, curd)
items.description: A kulhad of peda lassi so rich it doubles as a meal — Hall Bazaar's most famous glass.

items.name: Golden Temple Langar (Guru Ka Langar)
items.area: Old City (within the Golden Temple complex)
credentials: The World Book of Records — world's largest free kitchen
Instituted in the 15th–16th century; a UNESCO-recognised living tradition
items.description: The world's largest free kitchen — a simple vegetarian meal served to around 100,000 people a day, to anyone, for free.

items.name: The bar at Taj Swarna
credentials: Inside Taj Swarna — Taj Hotels' Amritsar flagship
items.description: The most composed evening drink in a modest city — Taj service, well-kept spirits and quiet.

items.name: Rooftop cafés overlooking the Golden Temple
credentials: Rooftop cafés on the Golden Temple heritage plaza
The definitive Amritsar evening view — the lit temple after dark
items.description: Not a bar but the city's real night view — chai or a cold coffee above the illuminated temple, mirrored in its pool.

items.title: Pre-dawn darshan at the Golden Temple
items.description: Arrive before first light for the palki ceremony, when the marble is empty and the recitation carries across the water.

items.title: Volunteer or private visit to the langar kitchen
items.description: A guided look inside the world's largest free community kitchen, which feeds tens of thousands daily.

items.title: Old-city food walk with a specialist
items.description: A private crawl through the century-old kulcha, lassi and dhaba institutions of the walled city.

items.title: Private curator visit to the Partition Museum
items.description: A considered, guided visit to the moving museum of 1947, best done with context and time.

plan.heading: 2 days in Amritsar, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

days.title: The Golden Temple, at its two best hours

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive at Harmandir Sahib soon after dawn, when the marble is cool and the kirtan carries across the sarovar, with a guide who explains the seva rather than rushing you through.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Walk the restored Heritage Street and the Partition Museum at Town Hall, then rest through the afternoon heat.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return to the Golden Temple after dark for the Palki Sahib ceremony, then dinner of Amritsari kulcha and dal at the old-city institution Kesar Da Dhaba.

days.title: The border and the food streets

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A langar visit to see the world's largest community kitchen at work, then the sober, well-told Jallianwala Bagh memorial next door.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Drive out to the Wagah border early enough to be seated properly for the evening Beating Retreat ceremony.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Back in the city for Amritsari fish and kulchas along Lawrence Road, or a quiet dinner at your hotel if the day has been full.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Heritage Street / near the Golden Temple
items.description: Steps from the temple and the food lanes; best for dawn and night visits on foot.

items.name: Ranjit Avenue
items.description: The newer, calmer part of town with modern hotels; for comfort a short drive from the old city.

items.name: Lawrence Road / Mall area
items.description: Central and lively with dining; suits those wanting a mix of the old and the new.

events.name: Baisakhi
events.note: The Sikh new year and harvest festival, celebrated with great fervour at the Golden Temple; the peak time to witness the faith.

events.name: Guru Nanak Gurpurab
events.note: The birth anniversary of the founder of Sikhism, when the temple is spectacularly illuminated at night.

events.name: Diwali / Bandi Chhor Divas
events.note: The temple and city are lit with lamps and fireworks reflected in the sacred tank; a beautiful night here.

events.name: Lohri
events.note: The Punjabi winter bonfire festival, marked warmly across the city with music and food.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Sri Guru Ram Dass Jee International Airport (ATQ), about a 40-minute chauffeured drive to the walled city and the Golden Temple precinct.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with driver for the city and the Wagah border, and slow walking through the old-city lanes, which are best explored on foot.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Strong Jio and Airtel 4G/5G across the city; a local SIM from the airport is the simplest option.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Indian rupee; cards are accepted at hotels and larger restaurants, but carry cash for the old bazaars and street food; tipping is modest and appreciated.

onGround.note: The Golden Temple asks for covered heads and bare feet, with scarves and a cloakroom provided at the entrance; go at dawn or after dark for the quietest, most luminous darshan, and time the Wagah border ceremony for late afternoon.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: October to March is the window, with 10-25C days ideal for the Golden Temple and Wagah; avoid May-June, when heat nears 40C, and the humid July-August monsoon.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Amritsar (Sri Guru Ram Dass Jee International, ATQ) takes direct flights: Delhi (about 1 hr 15 min), Mumbai (about 2.5 hrs), Bengaluru. Air India and IndiGo fly it in business/premium; for a first-class feel, connect through Delhi's T3 and use the Air India Maharaja lounge before the short hop up.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No special vaccinations beyond routine Hepatitis A/Typhoid. Very safe, welcoming city, even around the temple at night. Stick to bottled or filtered water; the langar food at the Golden Temple is famously clean.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Amritsar is a vegetarian's home ground, from Punjabi thalis to the free langar at the Golden Temple. Jain requests are well understood. Kesar Da Dhaba and Bharawan Da Dhaba are institutions for pure-veg Punjabi cooking.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Amritsar, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Amsterdam — TripAgent
seo.description: Amsterdam, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Amsterdam
hero.tagline: Golden Age canals, gabled houses and easy sophistication.

ourTake.lede: Amsterdam rewards slowness and punishes the checklist. Base yourself in the canal belt, walk or cycle everywhere, and give the big museums their first opening hour rather than the crowded middle of the day. The Jordaan and the quieter southern canals are where the city actually lives; the Red Light District and the coffee-shop trail are what everyone else came for, and you can happily skip both.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a walkable, cultured European city of canals and world-class museums taken at an unhurried pace.
ourTake.skipIf: You are chasing sun, beaches, or dramatic landscape; Amsterdam is a compact, urban, weather-dependent city.

firstLook.heroCaption: grand neo-gothic brick hotel facade under blue sky

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: April to June for long light and the tulips, September for calm and mild days. Avoid the grey, wet, dark November-to-February stretch.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jun, Jul, Aug and Sep

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: De L'Europe Amsterdam
items.area: Canal Ring — on the Amstel, by Muntplein
credentials: MICHELIN Three Keys (2025 — the Netherlands' highest)
The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The city's original grand dame, on the Amstel since 1896 — a classic European grand hotel, family-owned and freshly renovated.

items.name: Waldorf Astoria Amsterdam
items.description: Six adjoining 17th-century canal mansions on the Herengracht — the only Forbes Five-Star hotel in the Netherlands, with a garden courtyard rare for the centre.

items.name: Rosewood Amsterdam
items.area: Canal Ring — former Palace of Justice, Prinsengracht
items.description: Rosewood's first Dutch house, in the 1665 former Palace of Justice on the Prinsengracht — 134 rooms, an Asaya spa and a 12-metre pool.

items.name: Conservatorium Hotel
items.area: Oud-Zuid — Museum Quarter, facing the Rijksmuseum side
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A former music conservatory turned soaring glass-roofed design hotel, opposite Museumplein — the city's most architectural luxury stay.

items.name: Hotel Okura Amsterdam
items.area: De Pijp — south of the centre
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A serene Japanese-run grand hotel with the city's greatest concentration of stars under one roof — three MICHELIN stars across its restaurants.

items.name: Anantara Grand Hotel Krasnapolsky Amsterdam
items.description: An 1865 landmark on Dam Square, reborn under Anantara — grand scale, a famous glass-roofed Winter Garden, and a Michelin kitchen within.

items.name: The Dylan Amsterdam
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: An intimate canal-house hotel on the Keizersgracht around a hidden courtyard — home to one of the city's two-star kitchens.

items.name: Pulitzer Amsterdam
items.description: Twenty-five interlinked 17th- and 18th-century canal houses between two canals — a whole block of the Grachtengordel turned into one characterful hotel.

items.name: Hotel TwentySeven
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: A jewel-box, all-suite hotel of just sixteen suites on Dam Square — intensely private, with a one-star kitchen on the top floor.

items.name: Pillows Grand Boutique Hotel Maurits at the Park
items.area: Centre — by the Hortus Botanicus / Artis
items.description: A restored 19th-century mansion by the botanical garden — a polished, art-filled boutique house on the calmer eastern edge of the centre.

items.name: Tivoli Doelen Amsterdam
items.area: Canal Ring — on the Amstel, by Muntplein
items.description: One of the city's oldest hotel sites on the Amstel, reborn as a contemporary Tivoli — a classic Dutch address with fresh polish.

items.name: Rijksmuseum
items.description: The nation's treasure house, built for the Dutch Golden Age: Rembrandt's colossal Night Watch, Vermeer's quiet interiors, Delftware and ship models across eighty galleries. A private early-access tour before the doors open lets a family stand alone with the great canvases; the garden and the airy atrium café make an easy pause for younger children.

items.name: Van Gogh Museum
items.description: The largest Van Gogh collection on earth, roughly 200 paintings and 500 drawings hung to trace his life from Nuenen to Auvers — Sunflowers, Almond Blossom, The Bedroom in one place. Book a timed slot and go at opening; the multimedia guide is a gentle way to keep teenagers engaged.

items.name: Anne Frank House
items.description: The canal-side house on the Prinsengracht where Anne Frank, her family and four others hid for two years behind a bookcase, and where she wrote the diary. Tickets are timed and sell out weeks ahead — book the moment they release. A quiet, sobering hour that older children carry with them; the annex is steep and unsuitable for very young ones.

items.name: Stedelijk Museum
items.description: The Netherlands' museum of modern and contemporary art, from Malevich, Mondrian and Matisse through Warhol and Dutch design, in the landmark 'bathtub' extension on Museumplein. A natural third stop once the Rijksmuseum and Van Gogh are done, and rarely as crowded.

items.name: The Canal Ring (Grachtengordel)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Seventeenth-century canal ring
items.description: The seventeenth-century belt of three grand canals — Herengracht, Keizersgracht, Prinsengracht — lined with gabled merchant houses, hump-backed bridges and houseboats. Simply wander the towpaths at golden hour; the 'Golden Bend' on the Herengracht holds the grandest of the old mansions.

items.name: Private canal cruise
items.description: See the city the way it was meant to be seen — from the water. A chartered open saloon boat with a skipper glides under the low bridges of the canal belt at dusk; arrange a private vessel with your own catering and a discreet crew rather than the packed public boats. The most relaxed way for multiple generations to take in the city together.

items.name: Jordaan
items.description: The former working-class quarter turned Amsterdam's most charming neighbourhood: narrow lanes, hidden courtyards (hofjes), independent galleries, brown cafés and antique shops along the Elandsgracht. Best enjoyed slowly on foot with no fixed plan, stopping wherever the window looks good.

items.name: The Nine Streets (De Negen Straatjes)
items.description: Nine little cross-streets threading between the main canals, packed with concept boutiques, vintage dealers, jewellers and specialist cafés — the best browsing in the old city. Compact enough to cover in an afternoon, with plenty of veg-friendly cafés and patisseries for a break.

items.name: De Pijp
items.description: Amsterdam's most vibrant food-and-drink district, built around the Albert Cuyp market and Sarphatipark. Bakeries, wine bars, and an unusually deep bench of Indian, Surinamese, Middle Eastern and vegetarian kitchens make it the easy choice when the family wants variety at dinner.

items.name: Albert Cuyp Market
items.description: The largest open-air market in the Netherlands, running since 1905 with 260-odd stalls of cheese, flowers, fabric, street food and stroopwafels pressed fresh. A lively morning stroll; watch the pockets and go early before the crowds thicken.

items.name: Amsterdam-Noord & NDSM Wharf
items.description: A two-minute free ferry across the IJ from Centraal delivers you to the city's creative frontier — a former shipyard of street-art hangars, design studios, waterfront restaurants and flea markets. A refreshing half-day away from the tourist core.

items.name: A'DAM Lookout
items.description: The highest public viewpoint in central Amsterdam, atop the 100-metre A'DAM Tower, with a 360-degree skydeck and 'Over the Edge' — Europe's highest swing, out over the water. Cap it at the revolving Moon restaurant or the rooftop bar; the thrill-swing is a hit with teenagers.

items.name: EYE Filmmuseum
items.description: A sculptural white building on the northern bank of the IJ devoted to cinema — exhibitions, restored classics, and a waterfront terrace with one of the best views back across the water to the old city. Reachable on the same free ferry as A'DAM Lookout.

items.name: Vondelpark
items.description: Amsterdam's great green lung, opened in 1865: 47 hectares of ponds, lawns, rose garden and an open-air theatre, minutes from the museums. Rent bikes for the family, picnic on the grass, or take an early-morning run before the galleries open.

items.name: Hortus Botanicus
items.description: One of the world's oldest botanical gardens, laid out in 1638 as a physic garden for the city's doctors, with a butterfly house, a three-climate palm glasshouse and an ancient cycad collection among the finest in Europe. A calm, shaded green pause and lovely with children.

items.name: Begijnhof
items.description: A hushed medieval courtyard of almshouses hidden behind an unmarked door off the Spui, home to one of the city's oldest wooden houses and a clandestine chapel. Free, tranquil and easily missed — a moment of stillness a step off the busiest streets.

items.name: Museum Van Loon
items.description: A perfectly preserved patrician canal house on the Keizersgracht, still furnished as the Van Loon family (co-founders of the Dutch East India Company) kept it, with a formal French garden and coach house behind. An intimate, uncrowded glimpse of how the merchant elite actually lived.

items.name: Museum Willet-Holthuysen
items.description: The only fully furnished Amsterdam canal house open daily, a lavish Herengracht mansion redone in Louis XIV style with a rare surviving eighteenth-century garden. A quick, elegant complement to Museum Van Loon just around the corner.

items.name: Rembrandt House Museum
items.description: The house on the Jodenbreestraat where Rembrandt lived and worked for nearly twenty years at the height of his fame, reconstructed with his studio, cabinet of curiosities and printing press — with live etching demonstrations. A vivid, human counterpoint to seeing his masterworks at the Rijksmuseum.

items.name: Moco Museum
items.description: A townhouse on Museumplein showing crowd-pleasing modern and street art — Banksy, Basquiat, Warhol, KAWS, Haring — plus immersive digital rooms. Fast, fun and photogenic; the natural pick when the family wants contemporary energy between the old masters.

items.name: Royal Palace of Amsterdam
items.description: The seventeenth-century town hall on Dam Square, built to trumpet Amsterdam's Golden Age wealth and now one of the King's official palaces — marble halls, Empire furniture and a grand Citizens' Hall mapped with the heavens. Open to the public when no state functions are on; check the calendar first.

items.name: Nieuwe Kerk
items.description: The late-Gothic 'New Church' beside the Royal Palace, no longer a parish church but the setting for royal coronations and weddings and now a hall for major art and photography exhibitions. Worth stepping in to see what is showing beneath the soaring vaults.

items.name: Oude Kerk
items.description: The oldest building in Amsterdam, a 1300s church with a painted wooden ceiling and Rembrandt's wife buried beneath the floor, now doubling as a bold contemporary-art space in the heart of the old quarter. An arresting collision of the medieval and the modern.

items.name: Westerkerk
items.description: The tallest church tower in the city, finished in 1638, standing over the Prinsengracht beside the Anne Frank House — climb the Westertoren on a guided ascent for a rooftop panorama of the canal belt. Rembrandt is buried here in an unmarked grave.

items.name: Concertgebouw
items.description: A concert hall of near-mythic acoustics, ranked with Vienna's Musikverein and Boston's Symphony Hall, home to the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra since 1888. Book ahead for an evening concert, or catch the free Wednesday lunchtime rehearsal-concert — a cultured, dress-up night out.

items.name: Ons' Lieve Heer op Solder (Our Lord in the Attic)
items.description: A complete Catholic church hidden in the attic of a seventeenth-century canal house, built when public Catholic worship was banned — the second-oldest museum in Amsterdam and utterly unexpected. A remarkable, little-known secret in the heart of the old town.

items.name: Portuguese Synagogue (Esnoga)
items.description: A vast, candlelit 1675 synagogue — among the grandest of its era — still lit only by hundreds of candles, with hidden treasure chambers open to visitors. Part of the Jewish Cultural Quarter alongside the Jewish Museum and National Holocaust Museum.

items.name: Bloemenmarkt (Floating Flower Market)
items.description: The world's only floating flower market, a line of stalls on barges along the Singel selling tulip bulbs, seeds and blooms since 1862. A quick, colourful stroll near the Munttoren — a pretty stop rather than a destination in itself.

items.name: Foam Photography Museum
items.description: A serious yet intimate photography museum in a Keizersgracht canal house, rotating its shows every few months across documentary, fashion and emerging talent. Small enough to enjoy in an hour and always current.

items.name: STRAAT Museum
items.description: A colossal shipyard warehouse at NDSM filled with more than 180 monumental street-art and graffiti works by 170-plus artists from around the world. Bold, immersive and a hit with older kids and teenagers; pairs naturally with the NDSM ferry outing.

items.name: H'ART Museum
items.description: A grand former almshouse on the Amstel, once the Hermitage Amsterdam, now hosting blockbuster loan exhibitions from major museums such as the British Museum and Smithsonian. A generously scaled space for a single, well-curated show.

items.name: NEMO Science Museum
items.description: A green copper Renzo Piano building shaped like a ship's prow, five floors of hands-on physics, chemistry and space experiments aimed squarely at children. The stepped rooftop is a free public terrace with a fine city view even if you skip the exhibits.

items.name: ARTIS Amsterdam Royal Zoo
items.description: The oldest zoo in the Netherlands and one of the oldest still running in the world, set in a leafy nineteenth-century park with an aquarium, planetarium, butterfly pavilion and the Micropia microbe museum on site. A full, easy family day among fine old architecture.

items.name: Micropia
items.description: The only museum in the world devoted entirely to microbes, part of the ARTIS complex — living microorganisms under microscopes, a body-scanner that maps your own flora, and cheese-cultures explained. Genuinely novel and surprisingly gripping for curious teenagers.

items.name: Het Scheepvaartmuseum (National Maritime Museum)
items.description: The story of Dutch seafaring housed in a monumental 1656 admiralty warehouse, with a full-scale replica of the East India Company ship Amsterdam moored alongside to climb aboard. The replica ship makes it especially good with children.

items.name: Tropenmuseum
items.description: A grand ethnographic museum in a monumental building by the Oosterpark, telling the story of world cultures and the Dutch colonial past through immersive, thoughtfully reframed galleries. Of particular resonance for Indian visitors given the shared colonial and trade history.

items.name: Heineken Experience
items.description: An interactive tour of the original 1867 Heineken brewery on the Stadhouderskade — brewing history, a stable of dray horses, tastings and a rooftop bar. Slick and fun for a mixed group; the tasting can be skipped for younger travellers.

items.name: House of Bols
items.description: An interactive genever and cocktail experience opposite the Van Gogh Museum, telling the story of Lucas Bols, the world's oldest distilled-spirits brand (1575), and ending with a made-to-order cocktail at the mirror bar. A grown-ups' interlude between the galleries.

items.name: Gassan Diamonds
items.description: A working diamond polishing house in a former steam-powered factory, offering free guided tours of the cutting and grading process — and a discreet showroom for those who wish to buy. A natural fit for UHNI travellers with an eye for stones; private viewings can be arranged.

items.name: Cycling the city
items.description: Amsterdam runs on the bicycle, and there is no more authentic way to move through it — quiet residential canals, the Vondelpark, and the flat greenway north of the IJ. Hire from a reputable shop, or take a guided family ride to learn the etiquette before setting off alone.

items.name: Zaanse Schans (day trip)
items.description: An open-air village of working windmills, wooden houses, a clog workshop and a cheese farm on the Zaan river, about twenty minutes by train. The classic postcard-Holland half-day; go early to have the mills before the tour buses.

items.name: Haarlem (day trip)
items.description: A refined small city just fifteen minutes by train, with a splendid market square, the Grote Kerk, the Frans Hals Museum and the Teylers — the oldest museum in the country. A calmer, elegant alternative to a busy Amsterdam afternoon.

items.name: Utrecht (day trip)
items.description: A handsome canal city half an hour away, its wharves lined with waterside cafés below street level, the Dom Tower climbable for wide views, and Miffy's museum for younger children. Less crowded than Amsterdam and easy to reach by frequent train.

items.name: Keukenhof (seasonal day trip)
items.description: The world's grandest spring bulb garden, seven million tulips, daffodils and hyacinths in bloom across 32 hectares, open only from mid-March to mid-May. A dazzling seasonal excursion; a chauffeured car or helicopter avoids the peak crowds and coach queues.

items.name: Giethoorn (day trip)
items.description: The 'Venice of the North', a car-free village of thatched farmhouses linked only by canals and wooden footbridges, reached by whisper-quiet electric boat. About two hours out — best as a full-day escape, ideally with a private driver, for a wholly peaceful day on the water.

items.name: Spectrum
items.description: Sidney Schutte's precise, layered cooking in the Waldorf Astoria — two stars and one of the city's benchmark tasting tables.

items.name: Ciel Bleu
items.description: A two-star institution on the 23rd floor of the Okura — refined contemporary cooking with the finest dining view in the city.

items.name: Flore
items.area: Canal Ring — Nieuwe Doelenstraat, by the Amstel
items.description: Bas van Kranen's near-vegetarian, hyper-seasonal cooking — two stars and a Green Star, one of the most forward kitchens in the Netherlands.

items.name: Vinkeles
items.description: Two-star French cooking in an atmospheric 18th-century former bakery within The Dylan — one of the city's great romantic rooms.

items.name: Restaurant 212
items.description: An open-kitchen counter on the Amstel where you watch two-star cooking up close — theatrical, precise and personal.

items.name: RIJKS
items.description: A one-star kitchen inside the Rijksmuseum — locally sourced Dutch cooking beside the world's great Rembrandts.

items.name: The White Room
items.description: Refined cooking under an ornate 1885 ceiling on Dam Square — a one-star room of real grandeur inside the Krasnapolsky.

items.name: Bougainville
items.description: Tim Golsteijn's elegant one-star cooking with panoramic views over Dam Square — a jewel-box room above the square.

items.name: De Kas
items.description: A daily-changing menu grown in the restaurant's own 1926 greenhouse — the original farm-to-table Amsterdam, now with a star and a Green Star.

items.name: Bolenius
items.description: Vegetables and herbs from its own kitchen garden drive this one-star, Green-Star kitchen in the Zuidas — quietly one of the city's most sustainable tables.

items.name: Yamazato
items.description: Authentic Japanese kaiseki that earned a MICHELIN star — a rare traditional Japanese room outside Japan, inside the Okura.

items.name: Daalder
items.description: Relaxed but serious one-star cooking in the west of the city — casual fine dining that quietly punches above its room.

items.name: Wils
items.description: Live-fire, wood-fired cooking with a great wine list — a one-star grill that does open flame beautifully.

items.name: Sinne
items.description: A neighbourhood one-star in De Pijp doing refined French–Mediterranean menus at a friendlier price than the grand rooms.

items.name: MOS
items.area: Eastern Docklands — IJdok, on the IJ
items.description: A small one-star room on the IJ waterfront — precise French-and-international cooking with water on three sides.

items.name: De Juwelier
items.description: Richard van Oostenbrugge and Thomas Groot's Franco-inspired seafood room — a stylish, contemporary one-star on Utrechtsestraat.

items.name: Bistro de la Mer
items.description: A refined French seafood bistro that earned a star — classic technique, beautifully sourced fish, unfussy elegance.

items.name: Zoldering
items.description: An intimate one-star with a serious wine focus — considered French cooking in a small, personal room.

items.name: Freddy's Bar
items.area: Canal Ring — De L'Europe, on the Amstel
credentials: Inside De L'Europe — a MICHELIN Three-Key hotel
items.description: The clubby, panelled bar of the De L'Europe grand hotel — named for Freddy Heineken, and a classic Amsterdam institution.

items.name: Pulitzer's Bar
credentials: Inside the Pulitzer — a MICHELIN One-Key hotel
items.description: A stylish gentleman's-club-style bar across three rooms inside the Pulitzer — over fifty cocktails and real canal-house character.

items.name: Tales & Spirits
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — 50 Best Discovery
items.description: A long-running Amsterdam favourite in an ancient building — an inventive, humour-filled list and warm, expert hospitality.

items.name: Door 74
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — 50 Best Discovery
items.description: The Netherlands' first true speakeasy — unmarked, reservation-only, and still one of the city's best cocktail rooms.

items.name: Flying Dutchmen Cocktails
items.area: Canal Ring — Singel, in the Odeon
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — 50 Best Discovery
items.description: Tess Posthumus and Timo Janse's bar in the 1662 Odeon — over 900 spirits, the biggest selection in the country, and a classics-first ethos.

items.name: Rosalia's Menagerie
items.area: De Wallen — on one of the oldest canals
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — 50 Best Discovery
items.description: A temple to Dutch spirits in a townhouse in the Old Town — thought to hold the largest genever selection in the Netherlands.

items.name: Advocatuur
credentials: Inside Rosewood Amsterdam — a MICHELIN Two-Key hotel
items.description: The signature bar of Rosewood Amsterdam in the former Palace of Justice — a polished, contemporary drinking room in the city's newest grand hotel.

items.name: Twenty Third Bar
credentials: Alongside Ciel Bleu — a two-MICHELIN-star restaurant
items.description: A high, glass-walled bar beside Ciel Bleu on the 23rd floor of the Okura — the best skyline view for a drink in the city.

items.title: Private morning at the Rijksmuseum before opening
items.description: The museum arranges guided early access to the Gallery of Honour, so the Vermeers and the Night Watch are yours before the doors open to the public.

items.title: A saloon boat with a skipper through the small canals
items.description: A classic wooden boat with your own captain threads the narrow inner canals that the big tour boats cannot enter, ending wherever you like for dinner.

items.title: After-hours viewing at the Van Gogh Museum
items.description: A curator-led evening walk through the collection once the day crowds have gone, arranged through the museum's private-visit office.

items.title: A day trip by classic car to the tulip fields and Keukenhof
items.description: In April a private driver runs you out to the bulb fields and the gardens early, well ahead of the coach traffic from the city.

plan.heading: 3 days in Amsterdam, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive at the Waldorf Astoria on the Herengracht, then the Rijksmuseum, guided, for the Vermeers and the Night Watch.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A private saloon boat through the canal ring, the merchants' houses from the water.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Spectrum at the Waldorf, two Michelin stars, canal-side.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Van Gogh Museum from opening, the letters and the late fields.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Anne Frank House by timed entry, then the Jordaan's quiet courtyards and galleries.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Rijks or Bougainville, refined and rooted in the season.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A car to Delft for the old town, the Nieuwe Kerk, and the Royal Delft workshop.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Mauritshuis in The Hague for Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A final dinner back in Amsterdam at Ciel Bleu, high over the city.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Grachtengordel (Canal Belt)
items.description: The postcard heart; suits a first visit that wants to walk out of the door and into the Amsterdam of the imagination.

items.name: Jordaan
items.description: Former working-class lanes turned quietly chic; for those who prefer neighbourhood cafés and small galleries to landmarks.

items.name: Oud-Zuid (Old South)
items.description: Leafy, residential and moneyed, beside the museum quarter and Vondelpark; suits families and anyone wanting calm and space.

events.name: King's Day (Koningsdag)
events.note: The whole city turns orange and takes to the streets and canals for the country's biggest party; book rooms far ahead.

events.name: Amsterdam Light Festival
events.note: Illuminated artworks along the canals, best seen from a heated boat on a cold winter evening.

events.name: Tulip season and Keukenhof
events.note: The bulb fields and the gardens outside the city are at their peak; the single reason many travellers time spring here.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Schiphol; a chauffeured car covers the 20-minute run into the canal belt, and the airport's own rail link is fast if preferred.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Walking is the joy of the old centre, complemented by a private car or a chartered saloon boat along the canals.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Excellent everywhere; a KPN or Vodafone eSIM works well, and wifi is fast and widespread.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Euro; the Dutch are a near-cashless society and cards work everywhere, so tipping is light — rounding up or a few percent.

onGround.note: Stay along the Grachtengordel canal ring or in the Museum Quarter for calm and proximity; the city is understated rather than showy, so dress is relaxed, and private after-hours viewings at the major museums can be arranged.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: May-June brings tulip season's tail, long light and mild, dry-ish days; September is calm and golden. Avoid November-February for short, damp, grey days, and note April's tulip peak draws heavy crowds.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Nonstop from Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru in roughly 9-10 hours. KLM flies it most frequently with a solid World Business Class; Air India also serves it direct. Schiphol is compact and efficient, and KLM's Crown Lounge and single-terminal layout make onward European connections painless.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations beyond routine; very safe and orderly. Ordinary care against bicycle traffic and canal-side edges. Tap water is excellent and safe.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian is easy; Jain and strict no-onion-garlic want advance notice. A strong Surinamese-Indian and Indian scene means good roti and thali houses; the city's fine-dining kitchens cater to vegetarians readily when briefed ahead.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Amsterdam, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Andaman Islands — TripAgent
seo.description: Andaman Islands, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Andaman Islands
hero.tagline: Coral seas, white sands and dense tropical island calm.

ourTake.lede: The Andamans are about the water and a small number of exceptional beaches, not a packed island-hopping schedule, so pick one or two islands and stay put rather than churning through ferries. Havelock (Swaraj Dweep) has the famous sand and diving; Neil (Shaheed Dweep) is the quieter one. Do the diving or snorkelling properly with a good operator, and treat the historical Cellular Jail in Port Blair as a meaningful half-day, not an afterthought.
ourTake.comeIf: You want white sand and clear water without leaving the country or arranging a visa.
ourTake.skipIf: You want cities, culture or nightlife.

firstLook.heroCaption: Modern pool villa with palms and umbrella

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: Come in the dry season, November to April, for calm seas and clear diving; time it to turtle nesting December-March or the January Island Tourism Festival, and avoid the May-to-September monsoon.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Andaman Islands. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Taj Exotica Resort & Spa, Andamans
credentials: Taj Hotels (IHCL) flagship luxury resort — the Andamans' only internationally-branded five-star
Set on Radhanagar Beach, long ranked among Asia's finest (TIME, 'Best Beach in Asia', 2004)
items.description: Seventy-two thatched villas on stilts across 46 acres of rainforest above Radhanagar — the one true icon of the islands, and reason enough to make the crossing.

items.name: Jalakara
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller — Gold List 2020 ("by far the loveliest place to stay" in the Andamans)
Mr & Mrs Smith — personally-visited member hotel
items.description: Seven singular rooms hidden in virgin rainforest on a hillside inland — a British-built jungle villa-hotel that feels wholly private and quietly perfect.

items.name: Barefoot at Havelock
credentials: The first sustainably designed and operated resort in the Andamans (eco-pioneer standing)
Closest quality stay to Radhanagar Beach
items.description: The resort that opened Havelock in 2002 — Nicobari-inspired cottages of cane, thatch and wood in 25 acres of forest, a hundred metres from Radhanagar.

items.name: Symphony Palms Beach Resort & Spa
credentials: Official five-star beach resort, Havelock — among the island's largest full-service properties
Extensive in-house dive centre and water-sports operation
items.description: A large, capable five-star on Govind Nagar beach — sunrise views, an ocean spa and beach candlelight dinners, run at scale.

items.name: Sea Shell Resort & Spa, Havelock
credentials: Sea Shell Group — one of the longest-running quality hotel operators across the Andamans (Havelock, Neil and Port Blair)
items.description: A well-established seaside chalet resort with a spa — a dependable, comfortable Havelock stay close to the jetty and the beaches.

items.name: Sea Shell, Neil
credentials: Sea Shell Group — Neil Island's leading quality resort
items.description: The most comfortable base on quiet Neil — the slow, uncrowded island for members who want stillness over scene.

items.name: The Cellular Jail National Memorial — the Kala Pani
items.description: The colonial 'Kala Pani' prison where Veer Savarkar and hundreds of freedom fighters were exiled and tortured — seven radiating wings of solitary cells built so no prisoner could see or signal another. For an Indian family this is not sightseeing but pilgrimage; walk the surviving three wings, stand in Savarkar's cell, and let the gallows and the flogging yard land in silence.

items.name: The Light-and-Sound Show at the Cellular Jail
items.description: As dusk falls over the prison courtyard, an old peepal tree 'narrates' the story of the jail across forty-five minutes of light, music and voice — the most moving hour on the islands and best in the original Hindi. Have your advisor book the front rows; younger children and grandparents alike leave shaken and proud.

items.name: Radhanagar Beach (Beach No. 7) at sunset
credentials: Ranked 'Best Beach in Asia' by TIME magazine (2004); among the world's top-rated beaches
items.description: A kilometre of powder-white sand backed by rainforest and lapped by glass-clear turquoise — routinely called one of Asia's finest beaches and the postcard image of the Andamans. Come for the late afternoon when day-trippers thin out, wade into the warm shallows, and watch the sun drop straight into the Bay of Bengal.

items.name: Scuba diving the Havelock reefs — Nemo Reef & Barracuda City
items.description: Havelock is India's premier dive base — twenty-plus sites with soft and hard coral gardens, 20–30m visibility in season, and reliable sightings of turtles, rays, reef sharks and clouds of fish. Gentle sites like Nemo Reef and Barracuda City suit first dives and children over ten, while PADI 5-Star centres certify you from Discover-Scuba to Open Water in a few unhurried days.

items.name: Snorkelling & the coral gardens of Elephant Beach
items.description: Reached by a short boat hop or a forest walk, Elephant Beach has live coral just off the sand — the easiest, most rewarding snorkel on Havelock, with guides holding your hand in shin-deep water if needed. It is the family water-sports hub too: glass-bottom boats, sea-walking and jet-skis, so non-swimmers and teenagers are equally occupied.

items.name: Kalapathar Beach at sunrise
items.description: Named for the black rocks that punctuate its white sand, this quiet east-facing crescent is where you watch the first light spill over the sea while most of the island still sleeps. A short, contemplative stop with a coffee flask — beautiful, uncrowded and photogenic in the low morning sun.

items.name: Vijaynagar Beach (Beach No. 5) morning walk
items.description: The long, tree-lined stretch fronting Havelock's older resorts — shallow, calm and famous for its sunrise, a short walk from Kalapathar. One of the island's genuinely peaceful corners for an early stroll before the day's activities begin.

items.name: Bioluminescence & mangrove night kayaking
items.description: On a moonless night you paddle silent creeks where every stroke ignites the water into blue-green sparks — dinoflagellates that glow at the touch. Led by a guide in a stable double kayak, it needs no paddling experience and is the single most magical thing couples and families do here; the darker the moon, the brighter the sea.

items.name: Game fishing charter off Havelock
items.description: The reefs, drop-offs and channels minutes from Havelock are world-class sport-fishing grounds — popping and jigging for giant trevally, and trolling for sailfish, wahoo and tuna in the December-to-February peak. Private AC charters run catch-and-release with professional crews; a marquee half- or full-day for the anglers in a multi-generational group.

items.name: Private-boat island-hopping & sunset cruise
items.description: Charter a speedboat, catamaran or small yacht and string together the quiet corners — a snorkel stop, a deserted sandbar, a beach picnic, Neil Island — entirely on your own clock, skipping the public-ferry crush. A sunset cruise off Havelock, with the crew laying on drinks and privacy, is the natural centrepiece for an anniversary or honeymoon.

items.name: Ross Island (Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Dweep) — the ruins
items.description: A fifteen-minute boat from Aberdeen Jetty lands you on the old British capital — once the 'Paris of the East' — now a haunting garden of ballrooms, a church and a bakery being swallowed whole by strangler-fig roots. Netaji hoisted the tricolour here in 1943; deer and peacocks now wander the colonial bones, making it the islands' most atmospheric short excursion.

items.name: North Bay Island — sea-walking & snorkelling
items.description: The reef pictured on the ₹20 note sits just off North Bay, and here even non-swimmers can 'sea-walk' the seabed inside a fed-air helmet, entirely dry-haired and calm. Snorkelling, glass-bottom boats and scuba round it out — the ideal soft introduction to the underwater Andamans on your first day out of Port Blair.

items.name: Corbyn's Cove Beach
items.description: Port Blair's own coconut-fringed town beach, a short drive from the jetty and lined with palms — an easy sunset-and-a-drink stop when you are based in the capital rather than a swim-all-day destination. Convenient, relaxed and pleasantly close to the airport for the first or last afternoon of a trip.

items.name: Samudrika Naval Marine Museum
items.description: Run by the Indian Navy, this well-kept museum walks you through the islands' geography, tribes and reef ecology, with a small aquarium and the skeleton of a blue whale washed ashore in Nicobar. A cool, air-conditioned hour that sets up everything you will later see underwater — good for curious children before a snorkelling day.

items.name: Anthropological Museum
items.description: A thoughtful, small museum on the indigenous peoples of the archipelago — the Great Andamanese, Onge, Jarawa and the uncontacted Sentinelese — with tools, dwellings and photographs that give respectful context to communities whose reserves are rightly off-limits. The quiet, essential grounding for understanding these islands beyond their beaches.

items.name: Chatham Saw Mill & Forest Museum
items.description: On a small island linked to Port Blair by a bridge, one of Asia's oldest sawmills still cuts island timber, with a forest museum of carved teak and padauk and a war-scarred bomb pit from the Japanese occupation. A short, offbeat stop for those drawn to industrial and wartime history.

items.name: Chidiya Tapu — sunset point & Munda Pahad trek
items.description: The southern tip of South Andaman, a short drive from town, where the mangroves and birdlife give way to the best sunset near Port Blair. A gentle trek up Munda Pahad opens panoramic sea views on both sides — a rewarding late-afternoon escape without leaving the main island.

items.name: Mount Harriet National Park (Mount Manipur)
items.description: The highest hill on South Andaman, wrapped in tropical forest and butterflies, with a lookout over the harbour and Ross Island — the very view once engraved on the ₹20 note. A cool, green half-day drive-and-walk for those who want forest and vantage over sand.

items.name: The Natural Bridge (Howrah Bridge), Neil Island
items.description: A wave-carved coral-rock arch beside Laxmanpur, reachable on foot only at low tide across pools full of starfish, sea cucumbers and small fish — locals nicknamed it the 'Howrah Bridge'. Time it with your guide for the receding tide, then stay for the sunset that follows: Neil's signature hour.

items.name: Laxmanpur Beach sunset, Neil Island
items.description: A long, west-facing sweep of shell-strewn sand that is the finest sunset perch on sleepy Neil — the Natural Bridge sits at its far end, so you pair the two into one unhurried evening. Neil's slower pace and empty beaches make it the antidote to busier Havelock.

items.name: Bharatpur Beach, Neil Island
items.description: Neil's shallow, swimmer-friendly lagoon right by the jetty, with soft coral close in and calm water — the island's water-sports beach for glass-bottom boats, snorkelling and easy swims. The gentlest sea in the region, well suited to children and nervous swimmers.

items.name: Sitapur Beach (Beach No. 1) sunrise, Neil Island
items.description: The easternmost beach on Neil, a natural little cove that catches the sunrise while the island is still asleep. Pair it with the Laxmanpur sunset and you bookend a full Neil day with the sea's two best moments.

items.name: Baratang — the limestone caves
items.description: A dawn convoy along the Andaman Trunk Road, then a speedboat through primeval mangrove creeks and a short forest walk to caves hung with stalactites and stalagmites — a proper adventure day out of Port Blair. The road crosses the protected Jarawa reserve in escorted convoy, where stopping, photography and any contact are strictly forbidden, and rightly so.

items.name: Baratang — the mud volcanoes
items.description: Small, bubbling cones of grey mud pushed up by natural gas — a rare geological curiosity and the other half of the classic Baratang day. Modest to look at but genuinely unusual, and a hit with children collecting oddities of nature.

items.name: Jolly Buoy Island — the marine national park
credentials: Within the Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park (est. 1983)
Open seasonally (roughly Nov–Apr) on rotation with Red Skin to protect the reef
items.description: Inside the protected Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park off Wandoor, Jolly Buoy is a strictly plastic-free island of untouched coral gardens seen by glass-bottom boat and snorkel. It opens only part of the year to let the reef recover — some of the most pristine, best-protected coral you can still swim over in India.

items.name: Red Skin Island — the marine national park
credentials: Within the Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park
Open seasonally (roughly Mar–Sep) on rotation with Jolly Buoy
items.description: Jolly Buoy's counterpart in the same marine park, opening on the alternate season so the reefs are always rested — the same clear coral gardens, glass-bottom boats and snorkelling from a permit-controlled, single-use-plastic-free island. Whichever is open when you visit is the day-trip to book from Port Blair.

items.name: Diglipur — Ross & Smith twin islands
items.description: Far in the wild north, two islands joined by a dazzling white sandbar that appears and vanishes with the tide, so you can walk from one to the other across the sea. Remote, barely developed and staggeringly beautiful — the reward for those who go beyond the standard three-island circuit.

items.name: Saddle Peak — the archipelago's highest point
items.description: At 732 metres, the highest summit in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, reached by a demanding 8km forest trek through evergreen jungle to panoramic views over the north coast. A serious half-day hike for the fit and adventurous, and the roof of the islands.

items.name: Turtle nesting at Kalipur & Ramnagar beaches
items.description: The dark-sand beaches around Diglipur are among the few places on earth where four species of sea turtle — including the giant leatherback — come ashore to nest between roughly October and March. Guided night walks let you witness turtles laying and, later in the season, hatchlings scrambling to the sea: a quiet, unforgettable wildlife privilege.

items.name: Barren Island — India's only active volcano
items.description: A conical, smoking island rising from the sea 135km east of Port Blair — the only confirmed active volcano in South Asia, where black lava slopes meet electric-blue water. Landing is forbidden, but scenic boat and seaplane approaches, and world-class liveaboard dives over lava-formed reefs teeming with sharks and manta rays, make it a bucket-list expedition for serious divers.

items.name: Long Island & Guitar Island — the hidden Andamans
items.description: Reached by boat from Havelock, Long Island keeps its jungle village pace with barely a road, and a short hop away Guitar Island is a guitar-shaped sliver of sand that becomes a floating sandbar at high tide. This is the Andamans before tourism — empty beaches, silence, and the pleasure of a private-boat picnic with nobody else in sight.

items.name: Radhanagar Beach — Beach No. 5 sandbar walk
items.description: Just before Radhanagar proper, a natural lagoon and sandbar (locally 'Beach No. 5' or Neil's Cove) offers calm, shallow water ideal for a gentle swim away from the main beach's crowds. A quiet companion stop that most day-trippers miss.

items.name: The stilt-luxury of Taj Exotica, Radhanagar
items.description: The islands' flagship resort — 72 stilt villas with private plunge pools spread across rainforest and a private stretch by Radhanagar, styled on Nicobari and Jarawa architecture and built without felling a tree. Even non-guests can dine at a private beach table or spa at the J Wellness Circle; for a honeymoon or multi-gen escape it sets the bar for what tropical India can offer.

items.name: The Rajiv Gandhi Water Sports Complex, Aberdeen
items.description: On the Marina Park waterfront by Aberdeen Jetty, this is the launch point for Ross Island and North Bay and a cluster of jet-ski, banana-boat and speedboat rides over the harbour. A convenient, family-friendly first taste of the water before the outer islands — and the gateway jetty you will pass through more than once.

items.name: Discover-Scuba & the shore reef at Nemo Reef
items.description: For those who have never dived, a supervised Discover-Scuba session on Havelock takes complete beginners — no certification, minimum age around ten — down to shallow, sheltered coral to breathe underwater for the first time among clownfish and anemones. The gentle, hand-held introduction that turns a nervous first-timer into a diver by lunchtime.

items.name: Glass-bottom boat over the reef
items.description: The dry, effortless way for grandparents and small children to see live coral, fish and the occasional turtle — a flat-bottomed boat with a glass floor gliding over the reefs off North Bay or Elephant Beach. The inclusive option that lets a whole multi-generational group share the underwater world at once.

items.name: Jetty-hopping Havelock → Neil by private ferry
items.description: The two showcase islands sit a short catamaran-ferry apart, so a well-planned itinerary pairs Havelock's diving and Radhanagar with Neil's slower beaches and Natural Bridge in one seamless arc. A concierge who pre-books the fast ferries (they sell out in season) turns the region's fiddliest logistics into a smooth ribbon of island days.

items.name: The Settlers, Taj Exotica
credentials: Within Taj Exotica Resort & Spa, Andamans — the islands' only internationally-branded five-star kitchen
items.description: The resort's signature table, telling the Andamans' history through local ingredients — the most considered dinner on the islands.

items.name: Jalakara Restaurant
credentials: Within Jalakara — Condé Nast Traveller Gold List 2020 & Mr & Mrs Smith member hotel
items.description: A small, changing menu cooked with real intent in the jungle — dinner as a quiet, personal event rather than a service.

items.name: Barefoot Bar & Brasserie
credentials: Within Barefoot at Havelock — the Andamans' pioneering eco-resort
items.description: A thatched-hut dining room in the eco-original's forest — honest island cooking and fresh catch, barefoot and unhurried.

items.name: Full Moon Café
credentials: Long-standing Havelock traveller favourite — consistently among the island's highest-rated independent restaurants
items.description: A beach-facing bistro that has been Havelock's most-recommended independent table for years — fresh seafood, Indian and continental, done well.

items.name: Anju-Coco Resto
credentials: Well-known Havelock traveller favourite — noted for grilled tuna and attentive, personal service
items.description: A warm, family-run island favourite known for its grilled tuna and genuinely personal service — the honest heart of Havelock eating.

items.name: Something Different — A Beachside Café
credentials: Popular Havelock beachside café — a long-standing traveller favourite for its setting and seafood
items.description: Fusion seafood plates and a picture-perfect beach setting — the most scenic casual meal on the island.

items.name: Resort sundowner bars (Taj Exotica / Barefoot)
credentials: Within Taj Exotica Resort & Spa and Barefoot at Havelock — the islands' best-run bars
items.description: The most polished drink on the islands — a proper cocktail at sunset from the resort bars, which is as refined as an Andaman evening gets.

items.name: Beach-shack sundowners, Havelock
credentials: Havelock's informal beach-shack bars — the island's only real evening scene
items.description: The islands' idea of a night out — a cold drink and fresh grill at a beach shack as the sun goes down. That is the extent of it, honestly, and that is the point.

items.title: Private diving or snorkelling off Havelock
items.description: Some of the clearest water and best reefs in India, with a top dive centre and a private boat away from the crowds.

items.title: Dawn at Radhanagar Beach
items.description: The famous wide white beach at first light, empty before the day boats arrive, for the best of its light.

items.title: Sea-kayaking through the bioluminescent mangroves
items.description: A guided night paddle where the water lights up with plankton, one of the islands' rarest experiences.

items.title: Private visit to the Cellular Jail and its history
items.description: A considered, guided visit to the colonial prison and its sound-and-light story of India's freedom struggle.

plan.heading: 5 days in the Andaman Islands, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.text: Fly into Port Blair, then transfer by private launch across the water to Havelock (Swaraj Dweep).

slots.label: Afternoon

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Sundowners on Radhanagar Beach as the light goes, then dinner at the resort's overwater table.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A guided dive or first-time discovery dive off Havelock's house reefs with a PADI instructor, the water warm and clear.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Rest through the heat of the day, then a slow swim and reading hours on Radhanagar.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Grilled catch of the day and a cold bottle of white on the sand.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Private boat to Neil (Shaheed Dweep), calmer and greener, with a stop at the natural coral bridge at Laxmanpur.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Snorkel the shallows off Bharatpur, then lunch under the casuarinas.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return to Havelock at dusk, an easy dinner at the villa.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A dawn kayak through the mangrove creeks before the wind picks up, guide leading the way.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A spa afternoon, or simply the hammock and the tide.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A private dinner set on the beach, lanterns and the sound of the reef.

slots.label: Morning

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Havelock (Swaraj Dweep)
items.description: The main island for beaches and diving with the better resorts; best for most travellers.

items.name: Neil (Shaheed Dweep)
items.description: The smaller, slower island of quiet coves; suits those wanting seclusion and calm.

items.name: Port Blair
items.description: The capital and transit hub with the historical sites; practical for arrival, less for a beach stay.

events.name: Island Tourism Festival
events.note: The islands' main cultural festival in Port Blair, with music, dance and craft from the archipelago's communities.

events.name: Peak diving & clear-water season
events.note: The dry season with the calmest seas and best visibility; the window to time a trip around the reefs.

events.name: Subhash Mela
events.note: A festival at the Cellular Jail marking Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose's birthday, tied to the islands' freedom history.

events.name: Monsoon (to avoid)
events.note: Heavy rain and rough seas disrupt ferries and diving; worth planning around by staying away.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Port Blair (IXZ) via Chennai, Kolkata or Delhi, then a chauffeured car and, for Havelock, a private or premium ferry (or a seaplane-style charter) carries you on to the island resort.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver covers Port Blair, while on Havelock and Neil islands a resort car or hired jeep serves; boats handle all inter-island movement.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Mobile data is slow and patchy beyond Port Blair; the better resorts on Havelock offer wifi, but treat the islands as a place to disconnect.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Indian rupee; carry ample cash as cards and ATMs are unreliable outside Port Blair; tipping boat crews and dive guides is customary.

onGround.note: No permit is needed for Indian passport holders, though restricted tribal areas are strictly off-limits; base yourself on Havelock (Taj or a private beach villa), factor ferry timings and monsoon season (May-September), and book diving at Radhanagar and Elephant Beach in advance.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: November to April is the window — calm seas, 25 to 30°C, and the clearest water for diving, with January the settled peak. Avoid June to September, when the southwest monsoon roughens the sea, disrupts ferries and closes the outer islands.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Fly into Port Blair (IXZ, Veer Savarkar). Delhi has direct services (~3h40m) on Air India and IndiGo; from Mumbai and Bengaluru it is usually one connection via Chennai, Bengaluru or Kolkata (~5 to 6 hours total). No lie-flat first on the sector, so we arrange the Chennai/Bengaluru leg in business and a fast-track meet-and-greet at Port Blair, then a private seaplane or chartered boat onward to Havelock.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: Domestic — no vaccinations required, though routine cover should be current. Islands are safe and calm; the real notes are practical — the sea, not crime. It is tropical, so mosquito-borne dengue/chikungunya rise in the wetter months; use repellent. Drink only bottled or filtered water, never the tap.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian is easy and Jain requests are honoured, but this is a remote island chain — Indian food leans simple South-Indian and Bengali rather than refined. The best kitchens are inside the resorts: Taj Exotica and Jalakara on Havelock both do a considered vegetarian and Jain menu with notice, which is the way to eat well here.
