seo.title: Athens — TripAgent
seo.description: Athens, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Athens
hero.tagline: The ancient cradle of democracy beneath the Acropolis.

ourTake.lede: Athens is a summer-evening city, not a midday one. Do the Acropolis at opening or in the last hour before close, then spend the heat of the day indoors at the Acropolis Museum and the National Archaeological Museum, and let the city come alive after dark in Koukaki and Pangrati. Most people give Athens a rushed day and run for the islands; two unhurried nights and a rooftop with a Parthenon view will change their mind.
ourTake.comeIf: You want to walk through the birthplace of Western civilisation, then eat and drink well in a city that has quietly become one of Europe's most exciting.
ourTake.skipIf: You are chasing beaches or resort calm — Athens is a dense, layered city, best paired with the islands for that.

firstLook.heroCaption: Modern pool villa with palms and umbrella

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: April to June and September into October bring warm, clear days, ancient-theatre nights and Orthodox Easter's drama; skip a half-empty, oppressive July-August when the city decamps to the islands.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Mar, Apr, May, Jun, Sep, Oct and Nov

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Hotel Grande Bretagne, a Luxury Collection Hotel
items.description: Athens' grand address since 1874 — a neo-classical landmark on Syntagma with the definitive Acropolis view from its rooftop, host to royalty and heads of state for 150 years.

items.name: King George, a Luxury Collection Hotel
items.description: The discreet, jewel-box palace beside its sister Grande Bretagne — smaller, more private, with a legendary Penthouse Suite and its own private pool facing the Acropolis.

items.name: Four Seasons Astir Palace Hotel Athens
credentials: MICHELIN Guide — Three Keys (2025), the only Three-Key hotel in Athens
items.description: The Riviera icon — a pine-covered peninsula on the Saronic Gulf with three private beaches, half an hour from the centre, and the city's most complete resort experience.

items.name: One&Only Aesthesis
items.description: One&Only's first European resort — a mid-century Riviera revival on a preserved seafront in Glyfada, with airy bungalows and villas, a private beach and a Guerlain spa.

items.name: The Dolli at Acropolis
items.description: A restored neo-classical mansion on Mitropoleos, between old-town Plaka and Monastiraki, with a rooftop pool set against an unobstructed Parthenon.

items.name: Xenodocheio Milos
items.description: The hotel from the family behind the Estiatorio Milos restaurant empire — a refined, food-forward house on the elegant Vasilissis Sofias avenue near the Benaki and Cycladic museums.

items.name: Electra Metropolis Athens
credentials: Electra Hotels & Resorts — Greek luxury group
items.description: A polished, well-run city hotel in a Karantinos-designed modernist building, minutes from Syntagma, best known for its 10th-floor rooftop pool and M Bar with sweeping Acropolis views.

items.name: Ergon House Athens
items.description: A food-and-design hotel built around a working Greek agora — market, deli and restaurant on the ground floor, warm modern rooms above, in the heart of the centre.

items.name: Perianth Hotel
items.description: A contemporary art-and-design hotel in a restored 1930s modernist building near Kotzia Square, with a serious Greek-art collection and a rooftop over the old town.

items.name: The Acropolis — Parthenon, Erechtheion & Propylaea
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Acropolis of Athens
items.description: The sacred rock above the city and the reason most travellers come. Enter through the monumental Propylaea gateway to reach the Parthenon (447-432 BC), the Erechtheion with its Porch of the Caryatids, and the elegant little Temple of Athena Nike. Take a licensed private guide and go at opening or in the last two hours before close to avoid the heat and cruise crowds; the marble reflects fierce midday sun.

items.name: Temple of Athena Nike
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Acropolis of Athens
items.description: The smallest and most graceful temple on the Acropolis, perched on the bastion beside the Propylaea, built 427-424 BC to the goddess of victory. Its Ionic delicacy is a quiet counterpoint to the Parthenon's scale, and the spot gives a clean view down to the Saronic Gulf.

items.name: Odeon of Herodes Atticus
items.description: The stone Roman theatre of 161 AD tucked into the Acropolis's south slope, still used for the Athens Epidaurus Festival on summer nights. Attending a performance here — opera, orchestra or Greek tragedy under the lit Parthenon — is one of the most atmospheric evenings in the city; a concierge can arrange the best-placed seats.

items.name: The Acropolis Museum
items.description: Bernard Tschumi's glass-and-concrete museum at the foot of the rock, built over an excavated ancient neighbourhood you walk above on glass floors. The top-floor Parthenon Gallery is rotated to align with the temple itself, framing it through floor-to-ceiling glass. The restaurant terrace has a fine Acropolis view and a calm, veg-friendly menu — good for a multi-generation lunch.

items.name: Ancient Agora & Temple of Hephaestus
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Acropolis of Athens (associated monuments)
items.description: The civic heart of classical Athens, where Socrates argued and democracy took shape, spread across a green archaeological park below the Acropolis. It holds the Temple of Hephaestus — the best-preserved ancient Greek temple anywhere — and the reconstructed Stoa of Attalos, now a museum. Shaded, walkable and far less crowded than the rock above.

items.name: Roman Agora & Tower of the Winds
items.description: The Roman-era marketplace built under Caesar and Augustus, a short walk from the Ancient Agora. Its highlight is the octagonal Tower of the Winds, an ingenious 1st-century BC timepiece and weather station combining sundials, a water clock and carved wind gods — an easy, engaging stop with children.

items.name: Plaka
items.description: The oldest continuously inhabited quarter, a warren of neoclassical houses, bougainvillea and pedestrian lanes under the Acropolis. Best explored slowly on foot with a private guide who can steer you off the tourist strip to the quieter courtyards, tavernas and small churches — a gentle, multi-generation walk.

items.name: Anafiotika
items.description: A tiny pocket of whitewashed, blue-doored houses clinging to the north slope of the Acropolis, built in the 1830s by island craftsmen from Anafi who wanted a piece of home. Stepping into these silent, flowering lanes feels like being teleported to a Cycladic island in the middle of the city — a hidden gem most visitors miss.

items.name: Monastiraki & the Flea Market
items.description: The buzzing square where ancient, Byzantine and Ottoman Athens overlap, with a mosque, a library and Roman ruins in view of the Acropolis. The flea market spills through Avissinias Square and the surrounding lanes — antiques, coins, vintage and bric-a-brac — reaching full energy on Sunday mornings. A knowledgeable dealer can find genuine pieces amid the clutter.

items.name: Syntagma Square & the Changing of the Guard
items.description: The city's central square in front of the Hellenic Parliament, where the Evzones in their pleated foustanella and pom-pom shoes guard the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The guard changes on the hour; the grand ceremony with the full detachment and band is Sunday at 11am. A stately, photogenic ritual the whole family enjoys.

items.name: National Archaeological Museum
items.description: The finest collection of ancient Greek art in the world — the gold Mask of Agamemnon, the bronze Artemision Zeus/Poseidon, the intricate Antikythera Mechanism and rooms of Cycladic and classical sculpture. Vast enough to warrant a private guide who curates a focused two-hour route rather than trying to see everything.

items.name: Panathenaic (Kallimarmaro) Stadium
items.description: The only stadium in the world built entirely of marble, on the site of the ancient Panathenaic games and restored to host the first modern Olympics in 1896. You can run a lap on the track, climb to the top tier for a photo, and see original Olympic torches in the tunnel museum. An early-morning visit is best.

items.name: Temple of Olympian Zeus & Hadrian's Arch
items.description: The largest temple in ancient Greece, begun in the 6th century BC and finished by Hadrian 638 years later; fifteen colossal columns still stand against the Acropolis backdrop. Beside it, Hadrian's Arch marks the old boundary between the classical city and the Roman one — a quick, dramatic stop between Plaka and the National Garden.

items.name: Lycabettus Hill
items.description: The highest point in central Athens, crowned by a whitewashed chapel and a terrace cafe. Ride the funicular up from Kolonaki near sunset for a 360-degree sweep — the Acropolis below, the city, and the sea and islands beyond as the lights come on. Book a table on the summit for sundowners.

items.name: Filopappou Hill (Hill of the Muses)
items.description: A pine-covered hill directly across from the Acropolis, laced with landscaped stone paths by the modernist architect Dimitris Pikionis. The summit monument gives the classic postcard view of the Parthenon at eye level — the best free vantage in the city, and gloriously quiet at golden hour.

items.name: Benaki Museum of Greek Culture
items.description: A private collection in a neoclassical mansion opposite the National Garden, sweeping across Greek civilisation from prehistory through Byzantium to the War of Independence, with dazzling gold, icons and folk art. Elegant, manageable in an hour or two, with a rooftop cafe overlooking the greenery.

items.name: Museum of Cycladic Art
items.description: Home to the serene, minimalist marble figurines of the Bronze Age Cyclades that so influenced modern sculptors like Brancusi and Modigliani. A refined, beautifully lit museum with a lovely glass-roofed cafe — a natural pairing with the nearby Benaki, both in chic Kolonaki.

items.name: Byzantine and Christian Museum
items.description: One of the world's great collections of Byzantine art — icons, mosaics, frescoes, textiles and liturgical treasures — set in a garden villa on Vasilissis Sofias avenue. A quiet, uncrowded counterpoint to the classical sites, and a revelation for anyone who thinks of Greece as only ancient.

items.name: Kerameikos
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Acropolis of Athens (associated monuments)
items.description: The ancient cemetery and potters' quarter that gave us the word 'ceramic', with sculpted grave monuments lining the Street of Tombs and the old Sacred and Dipylon gates. Green, tranquil and rarely busy — a contemplative site with an excellent small on-site museum, minutes from the buzz of Gazi.

items.name: Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Centre (SNFCC)
items.description: Renzo Piano's landmark cultural complex — the National Library, National Opera and a vast sloping park — gifted to the city by the Niarchos Foundation. Walk up to the green roof for sea-to-Acropolis views, take in an opera, or simply let the family roam the fountains, canal and gardens. Superb contemporary architecture.

items.name: Cape Sounion & the Temple of Poseidon
items.description: A Doric temple to the sea-god on a cliff at the tip of Attica, its white columns catching the last light over the Aegean. The 70km coastal drive down the Athens Riviera is half the pleasure; time the private car to arrive for sunset, with dinner at a seafront taverna on the way back.

items.name: The Athens Riviera (Vouliagmeni & Astir)
items.description: The string of upscale coastal suburbs south of the city — Glyfada, Vouliagmeni, Kavouri — with sheltered coves, marinas and beach clubs. Astir Beach and the Four Seasons at Astir Palace are the fashionable set's playground; a half-day here balances the archaeology with sea, seafood and sun.

items.name: Lake Vouliagmeni
items.description: A rare brackish thermal lake — a flooded limestone cave ringed by cliffs, fed by underground mineral springs that hold a steady, spa-like 24°C year round. Float in the mineral water beneath the rock face, with the little doctor-fish nibbling at your feet; part of the protected Natura 2000 network.

items.name: Kolonaki Shopping
items.description: The city's most elegant quarter, climbing the slope of Lycabettus around leafy Kolonaki Square. This is where the Greek designers, international luxury houses, jewellers and galleries cluster, alongside intimate cafes for people-watching. The place for discreet, unhurried luxury shopping with a personal shopper.

items.name: Psyrri
items.description: A former workshop district turned into the city's most vibrant nightlife and dining quarter — street art, meze tavernas, cocktail dens and live rebetiko music behind unassuming doors. Atmospheric and slightly rough-edged; a private guide unlocks the best mezedopolia and the after-dark energy.

items.name: Koukaki
items.description: A leafy, residential neighbourhood on the Acropolis's southern flank, repeatedly ranked among the world's coolest districts. Its pedestrianised lanes off Dionysiou Areopagitou are lined with third-wave coffee, natural-wine bars and neighbourhood tavernas — a calm, local base a short walk from the ancient sites.

items.name: Varvakios Central Market
items.description: The thundering 19th-century covered market between Monastiraki and Omonia — the meat and fish halls, spice and olive stalls, and the herb and cheese shops of the surrounding streets. A sensory plunge into everyday Athens; go with a food guide for the freshest bites and to navigate the crowds.

items.name: Rooftop Sundowners with an Acropolis View
items.description: Athens does the illuminated-Acropolis rooftop like nowhere else — bars such as A for Athens and the terraces of Plaka and Psyrri hotels look straight at the lit rock across the tiled sea of the old town. Reserve a front-row table for dusk, when the Parthenon glows gold then floodlit against the dark.

items.name: National Garden & Zappeion
items.description: A shaded royal garden behind Parliament — palm avenues, ponds, a small menagerie and hidden ancient fragments — opening onto the elegant Zappeion hall built for the 1896 Olympics. A green, restful pause in the centre, ideal for a slow morning stroll with elders and children.

items.name: Delphi
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Archaeological Site of Delphi
items.description: The 'navel of the world', where the ancient Greeks came to consult the Oracle of Apollo, set on the dramatic slopes of Mount Parnassus above a sea of olive trees. The Sanctuary, theatre, stadium and a superb museum (the bronze Charioteer) reward a full day; roughly three hours each way, best done with a private car and guide.

items.name: Mycenae
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Archaeological Sites of Mycenae and Tiryns
items.description: The citadel of Agamemnon and heart of the Bronze Age Mycenaean world — the monumental Lion Gate, the beehive Treasury of Atreus tomb, and the shaft graves that yielded the gold funerary masks. Often combined with Nafplio and Epidaurus on a full-day Argolis loop through the Peloponnese.

items.name: Epidaurus
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Sanctuary of Asklepios at Epidaurus
items.description: The ancient healing sanctuary of Asclepius, famed for its perfectly preserved 4th-century BC theatre whose acoustics carry a whisper from the stage to the topmost of 14,000 seats. Standing at its centre to test the sound is a genuine wonder; pairs with Mycenae and Nafplio.

items.name: Nafplio
items.description: Greece's first modern capital and its most romantic small town — Venetian and neoclassical mansions, waterfront cafes, the island fortress of Bourtzi and the Palamidi castle above with its long stone stair. A graceful lunch stop on the Argolis day, or an overnight for a slower Peloponnesian escape.

items.name: Hydra
items.description: A car-free island roughly two hours by fast ferry, where stone captains' mansions rise in an amphitheatre above a perfect harbour and the only traffic is donkeys and water taxis. Long an artists' and celebrities' bolt-hole, it is chic, timeless and utterly calm — a magical day away from the mainland.

items.name: Aegina
items.description: The nearest island escape — about 40 minutes by hydrofoil from Piraeus — known for its pistachios, fishing harbour and the beautifully preserved hilltop Temple of Aphaia, part of a 'sacred triangle' with the Parthenon and Sounion. An easy, relaxed day trip when time is short.

items.name: Little Kook
items.description: A wildly over-the-top fantasy cafe on Pittaki Street that redecorates its entire lane for each season — Alice in Wonderland, Christmas, Halloween — into an immersive fairy-tale set. Kitsch to the core and a favourite with children and Instagram; a fun, whimsical stop for younger family members.

items.name: Areopagus & Pnyx Hills
items.description: Two low rock outcrops beside the Acropolis heavy with history — the Areopagus where the ancient council met and St Paul preached, and the Pnyx where the citizens' assembly invented democratic debate. Both are free, open and give lovely Acropolis and city views; the Areopagus is a popular, if slippery, sunset perch.

items.name: Panagia Kapnikarea & Byzantine Churches
items.description: The 11th-century Kapnikarea sits marooned in the middle of Ermou shopping street, a tiny domed Byzantine jewel among the fashion stores; nearby stand the Holy Apostles in the Agora and the little Metropolis. A quiet thread of medieval Athens running beneath the classical and the modern.

items.name: Piraeus & the Marinas
items.description: The great port of Athens since antiquity, its pretty Mikrolimano and Zea marina harbours ringed with seafood tavernas and yachts. Beyond the ferry bustle it has a fine Archaeological Museum and a growing dining scene; the departure point for any Saronic island run and for private-yacht charters.

items.name: Dionysiou Areopagitou Promenade
items.description: The grand pedestrian boulevard that curves around the base of the Acropolis, linking the Acropolis Museum, Herodes Atticus theatre and Thissio — marble-paved, tree-lined and closed to cars. The single loveliest walk in the city, especially in the early evening with street musicians and the rock lit above.

items.name: Theatre of Dionysus
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Acropolis of Athens (associated monuments)
items.description: The birthplace of Western theatre, carved into the Acropolis's south slope, where the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides were first staged. The carved marble front-row thrones for priests and dignitaries survive; included with the Acropolis ticket and easily missed on the way up.

items.name: Benaki Museum of Islamic Art
items.description: A specialist offshoot of the Benaki in a neoclassical building above Kerameikos, holding one of the world's most important collections of Islamic art — ceramics, metalwork, textiles and a reconstructed 17th-century Cairo reception room. Its rooftop cafe overlooks the ancient cemetery and the Acropolis beyond.

items.name: Meteora
items.description: Byzantine monasteries perched impossibly atop sheer sandstone pillars rising from the Thessalian plain, one of the most surreal landscapes in Greece. It is genuinely far — around four to five hours each way — so it is best as an overnight or a private-plane/train excursion rather than a same-day trip from Athens.

items.name: Wine Tasting in Attica & Nemea
items.description: Attica's old vineyards and the nearby Nemea region — Greece's most celebrated red-wine appellation, built on the indigenous Agiorgitiko grape — sit within an easy private drive of the city. A curated cellar-door day with a sommelier introduces Assyrtiko, Malagousia and Agiorgitiko away from the crowds.

items.name: Private Athens Cooking Experience
items.description: A hands-on afternoon with a Greek home cook or chef — market shopping at Varvakios, then working through mezze, dolmades, moussaka and honey-soaked sweets in a private kitchen or garden. Easily tailored for vegetarian and Jain-friendly menus, and a warm, involving activity across generations.

items.name: Delta
items.description: Athens' only two-star table — a modern-Greek tasting menu inside the Renzo Piano-designed Stavros Niarchos cultural centre, cooking that reads the whole country through one seasonal lens.

items.name: Spondi
items.description: The house that started it all — Athens' first Michelin star, awarded in 2002 and held ever since, French-rooted haute cuisine in a romantic Pangrati courtyard.

items.name: Hytra
items.description: Imaginative, Greek-ingredient tasting menus perched above the Onassis Stegi cultural centre, under young chef Yiorgos Felemegas — cerebral cooking with a rooftop bar to match.

items.name: Pelagos
items.description: Refined Greek seafood on the Riviera inside the Four Seasons Astir Palace — pristine fish and shellfish in a gardened, sea-facing setting.

items.name: CTC Urban Gastronomy
items.description: Chef Alexandros Tsiotinis' personal, ingredient-driven cooking in a low-lit Kerameikos room — one of the most creative one-star kitchens in the city.

items.name: Soil
items.description: Chef Tasos Mantis' farm-to-table kitchen fusing Greek produce with Nordic technique — a serious, sustainability-led one-star with a Green Star to prove it.

items.name: Makris Athens
items.description: A one-star newcomer set opposite the Agora ruins, where chef Petros Dimas plates Greece's regional heritage with real technique — history on the plate and out the window.

items.name: Hervé
items.description: An intimate, modern one-star in low-key Petralona — precise, personal cooking away from the tourist circuit.

items.name: The Zillers
items.description: A one-star rooftop restaurant on Mitropoleos with the cathedral and Acropolis framed above the table, under chef Pavlos Kyriakis — refined Greek cooking with the city's best backdrop.

items.name: Botrini's
items.description: Hector Botrini's long-held one-star in the northern suburbs — contemporary Mediterranean-Italian cooking from one of Greece's best-known chefs.

items.name: Tudor Hall
items.description: A one-star rooftop inside the King George, with a direct Parthenon view and elegant Greek-forward cooking — old-world glamour and a Michelin star in one.

items.name: Patio
items.description: A one-star Riviera kitchen at Vouliagmeni, plating modern Greek cooking a step from the sea.

items.name: Nolan
items.description: A Greek-Japanese bistro from chef Sotiris Kontizas, fusing his two heritages with French classics — a Bib Gourmand favourite and one of the most fun tables in the centre.

items.name: Pharaoh
items.description: Chef Manolis Papoutsakis' modern take on Greek tradition — a recent Bib Gourmand entry with generous, confident cooking.

items.name: Akra
items.description: A barbecue-inspired, laid-back Bib Gourmand kitchen doing fire and Greek produce with a relaxed hand.

items.name: Cerdo Negro 1985
items.description: A Bib Gourmand mainstay built around Iberian pork and honest, good-value cooking.

items.name: Jerár
items.description: A long-running Bib Gourmand address prized for quality-to-price — the kind of table Athenians return to.

items.name: Fine Mess Smokehouse
items.description: A Bib Gourmand smokehouse doing serious low-and-slow barbecue — relaxed, generous and very good value.

items.name: The Clumsies
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — peaked at No. 3 (2020), listed every year since 2015
items.description: The bar that put Athens on the world map — a three-storey all-day-into-late space from Kyritsis and Bakoulis, on The World's 50 Best Bars list every year since 2015, as high as No. 3 in the world.

items.name: GB Roof Garden Bar
credentials: Atop the Two-Key MICHELIN Hotel Grande Bretagne; a historic Athens rooftop institution
items.description: The rooftop of the Grande Bretagne — the grande-dame terrace for a Champagne or a Negroni with the Acropolis and Lycabettus laid out below. The classic grown-up Athens aperitivo.

items.name: Alexander's Bar
credentials: Long regarded among Europe's finest hotel bars, inside the MICHELIN Two-Key Grande Bretagne
items.description: A wood-panelled, hushed hotel bar named for its 18th-century tapestry of Alexander the Great — deep spirits, live piano, the old-world Athens nightcap.

items.name: Line
credentials: Europe's 50 Best Bars 2026 — No. 1 (The Best Bar in Europe)
items.description: The city's — and now Europe's — most celebrated bar, a fermentation-led room in a former Petralona art gallery from Vasilis Kyritsis and Nikos Bakoulis, making its own wines, beers and ingredients on site.

items.name: Baba au Rum
items.description: A rum temple beloved by bartenders worldwide — an encyclopaedic rum and tiki-leaning list in a tiny, buzzy room off the old town.

items.name: A for Athens
credentials: The definitive Monastiraki-square Acropolis-view rooftop; widely listed among Athens' best rooftop bars
items.description: The rooftop everyone names first — two levels directly over Monastiraki Square with a dead-centre Acropolis view, cocktails and a young crowd at sunset.

items.name: 360 Cocktail Bar
credentials: One of the most iconic Acropolis-view rooftop bars in the historic centre
items.description: Perched above Monastiraki with one of the most photographed Acropolis panoramas in Athens, a long cocktail list and an all-day menu — reserve for the sunset seating.

items.name: Metropolis Roof Garden & M Bar
credentials: Rooftop of the MICHELIN-selected Electra Metropolis; a benchmark Athens hotel rooftop
items.description: The 10th-floor rooftop of the Electra Metropolis — a pool, Mediterranean plates and signature cocktails against a full-frame Acropolis, the most polished hotel rooftop in the centre.

items.title: Private out-of-hours visit to the Acropolis
items.description: Arranged with a licensed archaeologist, an early or late slot lets you stand on the rock with the Parthenon almost to yourself.

items.title: A performance at the Odeon of Herodes Atticus
items.description: A summer evening of music or drama in the 2nd-century stone theatre beneath the Acropolis, one of the great live settings anywhere.

items.title: Curator-led evening at the Acropolis Museum
items.description: A private walk through the Parthenon Gallery after closing, the marbles lit against the floodlit temple across the glass.

items.title: A day sail from Athens to the Saronic islands
items.description: A crewed yacht from the marina to Hydra or Aegina and back, swimming off the boat and lunching where no ferry crowd reaches.

plan.heading: 3 days in Athens, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: First entry to the Acropolis, up through the Propylaea to the Parthenon before the sun climbs.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Acropolis Museum, ending at the top-floor gallery framing the temple you just walked.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Spondi, the city's long-held two-star, in a courtyard in Pangrati.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Ancient Agora and the Temple of Hephaestus, then the lanes of Anafiotika above Plaka.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Benaki Museum, then coffee in the Kolonaki squares among the antique dealers.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Modern Greek tasting at Delta, inside the Stavros Niarchos centre, two stars and the harbour beyond.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A driver down the Apollo Coast to the Temple of Poseidon at Sounion, on its headland over the Aegean.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at a seaside taverna in Vouliagmeni, then the warm spring lake for a swim.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Rooftop dinner at the Hotel Grande Bretagne with the lit Acropolis in view.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Plaka & Monastiraki
items.description: The old town under the Acropolis; charming and central but touristy, best for a first stay that wants everything on foot.

items.name: Koukaki
items.description: Quiet, well-fed streets a short walk south of the Acropolis; suits those who want neighbourhood tavernas over souvenir lanes.

items.name: Pangrati
items.description: Residential and unhurried around the old stadium; for a second visit that wants to live as Athenians do.

events.name: Athens Epidaurus Festival
events.note: The city's great summer season of theatre, music and dance, staged at the Odeon of Herodes Atticus and the ancient theatre of Epidaurus.

events.name: Athens Marathon, the Authentic
events.note: The original marathon route from the plain of Marathon into the marble Panathenaic Stadium; the classic reason to visit in autumn.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Athens International (ATH); a private car covers the forty-minute run into the centre, meeting you as you clear the terminal.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver is simplest for the city and Cape Sounion; the Plaka, Monastiraki and the Acropolis slopes are walked, on marble that turns slick in rain.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Networks are quick and an eSIM (Cosmote or Vodafone) works on landing; wifi is standard in hotels and cafés.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The euro; cards are widely accepted, keep some cash for tavernas and kiosks, and leaving five to ten percent is appreciated but not expected.

onGround.note: Stay in Kolonaki for refinement or a rooftop in Plaka for the Acropolis at night; visit the Parthenon at opening or in the last hour before close to avoid both heat and crowds, and dress modestly if you enter any church.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: April-May and late September-October are ideal — warm, dry, the ruins comfortable to walk; July-August is fierce, dry heat (often 38C+) that makes midday Acropolis visits punishing.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Now nonstop from Delhi and Mumbai — IndiGo flies it year-round on the A321XLR (roughly 9 hours), with Aegean adding its own Delhi/Mumbai service from spring 2026. For a full business/first cabin, connect via Emirates/Etihad (Dubai/Abu Dhabi) or Turkish (Istanbul); the Gulf carriers give the strongest lounge and onward island connections.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required; tap water is safe to drink. Athens is generally safe — normal caution for pickpockets around Omonia, Monastiraki and the metro. No altitude concern.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Easy — Greek cuisine is rich in vegetable, legume and grain dishes (fava, gigantes, dolmades), and Jain needs are manageable with clear instruction. Indian restaurants are present; Avocado and Nolan offer strong modern vegetarian cooking.

seo.title: Auckland — TripAgent
seo.description: Auckland, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Auckland
hero.tagline: City of sails between two harbours and green volcanoes.

ourTake.lede: Auckland is a jumping-off point as much as a destination, and its best hours are spent on or across the water. Give the museum and the Sky Tower a morning, then get out to Waiheke's vineyards or the black-sand west coast, which is where the region actually earns its reputation. The mistake is treating it as a city break; treat it as a base for the Hauraki Gulf and the wine islands instead.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a gentle, green gateway to New Zealand with harbour sailing, island vineyards and easy day-trips.
ourTake.skipIf: You are chasing the dramatic alpine scenery and adrenaline that live on the South Island, not the North.

whenToGo.blurb: February to March and November to December give warm, settled harbour days, the crimson pōhutukawa bloom and the sailing calendar; skip the wet, cool June-August winter that belongs indoors.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Auckland. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Park Hyatt Auckland
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller Readers' Choice Awards 2023 — Top hotels in Australia & New Zealand
Park Hyatt — Hyatt's maison flagship tier
items.description: The country's most polished five-star house — a low, calm waterfront landmark on the Viaduct edge, with a 25-metre pool and the acclaimed Onemata dining room.

items.name: Cordis, Auckland
credentials: Langham Hospitality Group — Cordis luxury collection
Forbes Travel Guide Recommended — a landmark Auckland five-star
items.description: A large, gracious five-star hotel by Langham Hospitality Group — a heated rooftop infinity pool, a serious spa and the celebrated Chef's dining.

items.name: The Grand by SkyCity
credentials: Home to Metita — Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025 Hotel Restaurant of the Year
A landmark five-star hotel of the City Centre
items.description: A grand five-star tower in the SkyCity precinct — home to Metita, the country's Hotel Restaurant of the Year, with a lap pool and spa.

items.name: Sofitel Auckland Viaduct Harbour
credentials: Sofitel — Accor's French luxury maison brand
A landmark Viaduct Harbour five-star hotel
items.description: A French-accented five-star on the marina's edge — waterfront suites, a heated pool and a graceful spa on the Viaduct.

items.name: The Hotel Britomart
credentials: World's first 5 Green Star-rated hotel (New Zealand Green Building Council)
Condé Nast Traveller Hot List — the only New Zealand hotel listed
items.description: New Zealand's first 5 Green Star hotel — a warm, timber-lined design house in the heart of the Britomart dining and shopping precinct.

items.name: SO/ Auckland
credentials: SO/ by Accor — the group's design-led luxury maison brand
Formerly The Grand by SkyCity heritage building — a landmark City Centre address
items.description: Accor's fashion-led SO/ maison brand in a heritage tower — bold design, a rooftop bar and harbour views over the city edge.

items.name: QT Auckland
credentials: QT Hotels — a landmark design hotel brand
A landmark Viaduct Harbour design hotel
items.description: A playful, art-filled design hotel on the Viaduct waterfront — colour, character and one of the city's liveliest rooftop bars.

items.name: Hotel DeBrett
credentials: A landmark heritage boutique hotel (1925 Art Deco building)
Condé Nast Traveller — recognised Auckland boutique stay
items.description: A beloved boutique hotel in a restored 1925 Art Deco building — individually designed rooms and a buzzing courtyard bar in the heart of the city.

items.name: Sky Tower
items.description: Auckland's 328-metre spire and the tallest structure in the Southern Hemisphere, with three observation decks and glass floor panels that drop the eye straight to the street 186 metres below. On a clear day the view runs 80 kilometres over the Waitematā, the Hauraki Gulf islands and the ring of volcanic cones; take the family up at dusk for the city lighting up, then dine at the revolving Orbit 360 one floor down.

items.name: SkyWalk & SkyJump at the Sky Tower
items.description: For the thrill-seeker in the family: a harnessed walk on a 1.2-metre ledge around the tower's rim at 192 metres with no handrails, or a wire-guided base-jump-style plunge at up to 85 km/h. Grandparents can watch in comfort from the observation deck while the teenagers step off the edge; both run on private timed slots.

items.name: Auckland War Memorial Museum (Tāmaki Paenga Hira)
items.description: A neoclassical temple crowning the Domain, holding the world's finest collection of Māori and Pacific treasures alongside a carved meeting house and a full-sized war canoe. Book the twice-daily Māori cultural performance of song, haka and story for a dignified, multi-generational introduction to the culture of the land, then take tea on the terrace over the harbour.

items.name: Auckland Art Gallery Toi o Tāmaki
credentials: World Building of the Year 2013 (World Architecture Festival)
items.description: New Zealand's oldest and largest art institution, with a soaring kauri-canopy roof over 17,000 works spanning European masters, contemporary New Zealand painting and a moving room of Māori ancestral portraits by Goldie and Lindauer. Entry to the permanent collection is free and it sits at the edge of Albert Park, an easy, cultured hour for any age.

items.name: Viaduct Harbour
items.description: The former America's Cup basin, now a ring of superyachts, waterside restaurants and champagne bars where Auckland comes to be seen. It is the natural place to base an evening on the water and the departure point for private charters and the America's Cup sailing yachts.

items.name: Wynyard Quarter & Silo Park
items.description: A reclaimed industrial waterfront turned promenade of playgrounds, seafood restaurants and the landmark red Silo Park, with summer outdoor cinema and night markets among the old cement silos. A relaxed, stroller-friendly stretch to walk off dinner as the harbour lights come on.

items.name: America's Cup Sailing on the Waitematā
items.description: Take the helm or simply recline on the rail of a genuine former America's Cup grand-prix racing yacht as it heels across the harbour past the Harbour Bridge and skyline. No experience needed and the whole family can crew or watch; private full-boat charters make it a discreet, unforgettable two hours on the City of Sails.

items.name: Auckland Harbour Bridge Climb
items.description: A guided harnessed walk up the arch of the 1959 road bridge to the summit at 65 metres, with the Waitematā, the yachts and Rangitoto laid out beneath you. There is also a bungy off a purpose-built pod for the daring; the climb itself is a gentle, steady ascent suitable for confident older children and grandparents alike.

items.name: Mission Bay & Tamaki Drive
items.description: Auckland's most beloved seaside promenade, a golden crescent of beach with an Art Deco fountain, gelato and waterfront cafés looking straight across to Rangitoto. Drive or cycle the full sweep of Tamaki Drive past the yacht basins for the classic City of Sails afternoon; easy and safe for all ages.

items.name: Bastion Point & the Michael Joseph Savage Memorial
items.description: A clifftop of consecrated ground above Tamaki Drive, its Art Deco obelisk and formal gardens giving a sweeping panorama over the harbour to Rangitoto. It is also one of the most significant sites in modern Māori history, scene of the 506-day 1977–78 land occupation; a quiet, contemplative stop with a story worth a guide.

items.name: Maungawhau / Mount Eden
items.description: Auckland's highest volcanic cone at 196 metres, with a perfect grassy crater at the top and a full 360-degree sweep of the isthmus and both harbours. Walking to the summit is protected as an ancestral maunga, but the reward is the definitive view of the volcanic city; keep to the paths as the crater is sacred.

items.name: Maungakiekie / One Tree Hill & Cornwall Park
items.description: A 182-metre cone crowned by an obelisk and ringed by the largest pre-European earthwork fortifications on earth, set in the gifted parkland of Cornwall Park with grazing sheep and centenarian oaks. A gentle drive or walk to the summit and a picnic under the trees make an idyllic, unhurried family morning.

items.name: Auckland Domain & the Wintergardens
items.description: The city's oldest park, spread over an ancient volcano, with the Wintergardens' twin Edwardian glasshouses of tropical and cool-climate blooms and a fern-filled sunken quarry. A serene, shaded stroll that pairs naturally with the Museum on the same hill.

items.name: Karangahape Road (K' Road)
items.description: Auckland's most characterful strip, a mile of vintage stores, galleries, tiny wine bars and cuisines from Malaysian to modern Brazilian, named among the world's coolest streets by Time Out. Go for the atmosphere and the food rather than luxury shopping; it is bohemian, alive and refreshingly unpolished.

items.name: Ponsonby Road
items.description: Nicknamed 'the dining room of Auckland', a village high street of Victorian villas turned into the city's densest run of good restaurants, cafés and design boutiques, anchored by the food-hall energy of Ponsonby Central. The place to spend a leisurely lunch and afternoon; several kitchens handle vegetarian and Indian palates well.

items.name: Britomart Precinct
items.description: The sleekest quarter of the central city, a cluster of restored heritage warehouses now holding New Zealand designer boutiques, top restaurants and the design-led Hotel Britomart, steps from the ferry terminal. The natural base for a stylish, walkable stay and a Saturday morning market.

items.name: SEA LIFE Kelly Tarlton's Aquarium
items.description: Built into old harbourside sewage tanks by a New Zealand diving pioneer, with curved underwater tunnels of sharks and stingrays and an Antarctic ice enclosure of penguins. A reliable, weather-proof couple of hours that delights younger children on Tamaki Drive.

items.name: New Zealand Maritime Museum (Hui Te Ananui a Tangaroa)
items.description: On Hobson Wharf beside the Viaduct, tracing the ocean story from the first Polynesian voyagers to America's Cup glory, with heritage vessels moored outside that still sail the harbour. A short guided sail on a classic scow or steamer is the highlight for a maritime-minded family.

items.name: Waiheke Island — vineyards, beaches & Oneroa
items.description: A 40-minute ferry to a warmer, sunnier island of forty white-sand beaches and world-class vineyards, where cellar doors like Mudbrick, Cable Bay and Stonyridge serve Bordeaux-style reds over Hauraki Gulf views back to the skyline. The essential Auckland day trip; a private driver-guide or helicopter transfer lets multi-generational groups linger over long lunches without watching the clock.

items.name: Mudbrick Vineyard
items.description: On Waiheke's northern tip, a rose-garden estate with sweeping Hauraki Gulf views to the Auckland skyline, a celebrated restaurant and cottages for those who want to stay the night. The most photographed cellar door on the island and a favourite for a special-occasion lunch.

items.name: Man O' War Vineyards
items.description: At the wild eastern end of Waiheke, a beachfront tasting room reached by a scenic drive through the island's largest private estate, pouring single-vineyard wines feet from the sand. Remote and unhurried; charter a boat or helicopter in for the most discreet arrival.

items.name: Rangitoto Island Summit Track
items.description: The perfect volcanic cone that frames every Auckland postcard, a 600-year-old island reached by a 25-minute ferry, climbed in about an hour through the world's largest pōhutukawa forest and black lava fields to a 259-metre crater rim. The summit view over the gulf and city is superb; bring a torch for the lava caves and sun protection for the exposed scoria.

items.name: Tiritiri Matangi Island Open Sanctuary
items.description: One of the world's great conservation successes, a predator-free island where you walk among some of New Zealand's rarest birds in the wild — takahē, kōkako, saddleback and stitchbird — that exist almost nowhere else so freely. A guided day with an island volunteer is a quiet privilege for nature-lovers; the ferry runs only Wednesday to Sunday, so book ahead.

items.name: Devonport & Mount Victoria
items.description: A 12-minute ferry to a genteel Victorian seaside village of bookshops, cafés and colonial villas, with the little cone of Mount Victoria offering a postcard view straight back to the city skyline. An effortless, charming half-day that even the least mobile of the party can enjoy from the waterfront.

items.name: North Head (Maungauika)
items.description: A headland cone above Devonport honeycombed with Victorian coastal-defence tunnels and gun emplacements, guarding the harbour entrance with commanding views over the gulf. A gentle walk-up with just enough history and dark passages to intrigue children.

items.name: Waitākere Ranges Regional Park
items.description: Sixteen thousand hectares of native rainforest, kauri stands and waterfalls dropping to the wild west coast, half an hour from the city. Note that a kauri-dieback protection programme has closed many forest tracks — go with a guide who knows what is open, and always use the boot-cleaning stations to protect the ancient trees.

items.name: Piha Beach
items.description: The most famous of Auckland's black-sand surf beaches, a dramatic ironsand crescent guarded by the great hulk of Lion Rock and pounded by Tasman swell. Wild, cinematic and beautiful — but the rips are serious, so swim only between the summer patrol flags and consider it a place to watch the surf rather than brave it.

items.name: Karekare Beach
items.description: The most secluded of the west-coast beaches, reached through rainforest and a stream crossing, its vast empty ironsand made famous as the setting of the Oscar-winning film The Piano. Utterly atmospheric and almost always deserted; there are no facilities, so come prepared.

items.name: Muriwai Beach & the Gannet Colony
items.description: A rugged black-sand coast where, from August to March, some 1,200 Australasian gannets nest on the clifftop at Ōtakamiro Point within metres of easy viewing platforms — an extraordinary wildlife spectacle with no effort required. Pair it with lunch at the nearby winery for a full west-coast morning.

items.name: Hunua Falls
items.description: A 30-metre waterfall spilling into a bush-fringed pool in the Hūnua Ranges, under an hour southeast of the city and far quieter than the western beaches. A short, easy path and a picnic make it a gentle escape into native forest; check current track status before you go.

items.name: Matakana Village & Wine Country
items.description: An hour north, a village of boutique galleries, a beloved Saturday farmers' market and a cluster of small wineries such as Brick Bay, whose sculpture trail winds through native bush and ponds. A civilised, low-key alternative to Waiheke for a day among vines, art and artisan food.

items.name: Tāwharanui Regional Park
items.description: An open sanctuary on a peninsula north of the city, ringing white-sand Anchor Bay with predator-proof fencing so that takahē roam the grassland and kiwi call at night. Among the finest beaches in the Auckland region and blissfully uncrowded on a weekday.

items.name: Goat Island Marine Reserve
items.description: New Zealand's first no-take marine reserve, established in 1975 near Leigh, where snapper, crayfish and rays crowd the shallows for snorkellers and a glass-bottomed boat. A rewarding half-day for families who want to see the sea life without diving; go on a calm, offshore-wind day for clear water.

items.name: Te Hana Te Ao Marama Cultural Centre
items.description: An hour north, Auckland's leading Māori cultural centre, where a traditional welcome, a guided walk through a replica fortified pā, a kapa haka performance and a hāngī earth-oven feast give a genuine, unhurried immersion. Arranged as a private group visit it is a dignified highlight for multi-generational travellers.

items.name: Waka Voyaging Experience
items.description: Paddle a waka hourua — a Māori ocean-going canoe — on the Waitematā with the Te Toki Voyaging Trust, learning traditional star-and-swell navigation from the descendants of the Pacific's greatest wayfinders. A rare, hands-on cultural encounter on the water rather than a staged show.

items.name: Waitomo Glowworm Caves (day trip)
items.description: About 2.5 hours south, a limestone cavern where you glide by boat beneath a ceiling of thousands of glowworms glimmering like a private galaxy — one of New Zealand's singular natural wonders. Best done as a private full-day drive, often combined with Hobbiton; the black-water rafting option is for the adventurous.

items.name: Hobbiton Movie Set, Matamata (day trip)
items.description: Two hours south, the immaculately kept Shire from the Lord of the Rings and Hobbit films, forty-four hobbit holes set in green Waikato farmland, ending with a drink at the Green Dragon Inn. A joyful, easy day for film-lovers and children; a private car and guide beats the coach tours for pace.

items.name: Coromandel Peninsula & Cathedral Cove (day trip)
items.description: About two hours east, a coast of pōhutukawa-fringed coves crowned by the great natural rock arch of Cathedral Cove and the geothermal quirk of Hot Water Beach, where you dig your own warm spa in the sand. A long but rewarding day; helicopter transfer turns it into an effortless outing and avoids the winding roads.

items.name: Rotorua Geothermal & Māori Culture (long day trip)
items.description: Around three hours south, the heart of Māori tourism and geothermal drama — bubbling mud, geysers, thermal spas and the living village of Whakarewarewa. It is a stretch as a single day, so most travellers stay a night; a helicopter or charter flight makes a day visit civilised.

items.name: Bay of Islands (overnight-worthy trip)
items.description: Roughly three hours north, a sub-tropical seascape of 144 islands, dolphin cruises, big-game fishing and the founding site of the nation at Waitangi. Truly it deserves an overnight, but a scenic flight or helicopter from Auckland can deliver a memorable single day of sailing and history.

items.name: Scenic Helicopter Flight over the Hauraki Gulf
items.description: Lift off from the waterfront or Ardmore for a private flight over the skyline, Rangitoto's crater and the vineyards of Waiheke, landing for a cellar-door lunch or a remote beach. The most discreet and time-efficient way for a family to see the City of Sails and reach the gulf islands in style.

items.name: Auckland Fish Market & Wynyard dining
items.description: A working fish market turned food destination on the waterfront, with oyster bars, a sushi counter and cooking classes celebrating the day's catch from the Hauraki Gulf. A lively, casual counterpoint to the fine-dining rooms and a good place to understand New Zealand seafood.

items.name: Paris Butter
items.description: One of Auckland's most refined tables, French technique applied to the best New Zealand produce across an ever-changing tasting menu in an elegant Herne Bay villa. The kind of hushed, special-occasion dinner discerning travellers seek; advise the kitchen of any vegetarian or Jain needs when booking.

items.name: Sidart
items.description: Chef Sid Sahrawat's flagship degustation room above Ponsonby, a long-running standard-bearer for creative fine dining in the city with polished wine pairings and warm service. Sahrawat's Indian heritage runs through his kitchens, so it is a considered choice for Indian palates seeking a tasting-menu evening.

items.name: Cassia
items.description: Sid Sahrawat's celebrated modern Indian restaurant, refined, contemporary cooking rooted in the subcontinent that has long topped Auckland's lists — a rare fine-dining Indian table of genuine ambition. Confirm the current location when booking, as the restaurant has relocated from its long-time SkyCity home.

items.name: Auckland Zoo
items.description: A well-regarded conservation zoo beside Western Springs park, with a night-time kiwi house where families can finally see New Zealand's shy national bird, plus native tuatara and a strong Australasian collection. An easy, shaded day for younger children.

items.name: Albert Park & the University Quarter
items.description: A formal Victorian park of fountains, statues and flowerbeds set between the Art Gallery and the university, a green pause in the heart of the city. A pretty, unhurried stroll to link a museum morning with lunch on High Street.

items.name: Motuihe & Motutapu Islands
items.description: Quieter neighbours to Rangitoto and Waiheke, predator-free islands of white-sand bays and gentle walking tracks that see a fraction of the crowds. Ideal for a private boat picnic day when you want the gulf to yourselves.

items.name: Ahi
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025 — Three Hats
items.description: Chef Ben Bayly's celebration of New Zealand producers — a refined, land-and-sea tasting menu that sits at the very top of the national game.

items.name: Cocoro
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025 — Three Hats
items.description: Chef Makoto Tokuyama's serene Japanese degustation — precise, seasonal and deeply personal, a perennial three-hat kitchen.

items.name: Paris Butter
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025 — Three Hats
items.description: French technique met with native New Zealand produce in a handsome villa — one of the most assured kitchens in the country.

items.name: Tala
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025 — Three Hats
items.description: A modern Pacific and Middle-Eastern-inflected tasting menu that vaulted to the top tier — bold, generous and unmistakably its own.

items.name: Sidart
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards — Three Hats (long-standing)
items.description: Sid Sahrawat's long-running degustation temple — inventive, technically dazzling cooking that has anchored the city's fine-dining scene for years.

items.name: Kazuya
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025 — Two Hats
items.description: A unique fine-dining fusion marrying French technique with Japanese precision — intimate, exacting and quietly one of the city's best.

items.name: Metita
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025 — Hotel Restaurant of the Year
items.description: Chef Michael Meredith's Pacific dining room in The Grand by SkyCity — the country's Hotel Restaurant of the Year, celebrating island flavours with polish.

items.name: Farina
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025 — Greenstone Creek Metropolitan Restaurant of the Year
items.description: Chef-owner Sergio Maglione's love letter to seafood, handmade pasta and Neapolitan pizza — Auckland's Metropolitan Restaurant of the Year.

items.name: Culprit
credentials: Viva Top 50 Restaurants, Auckland 2025 — Supreme Winner
items.description: Kyle Street and Jordan MacDonald's inventive, produce-driven room — the supreme winner of the Viva Top 50, doing something entirely its own.

items.name: Onslow
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025 — Two Hats
items.description: Josh Emett's elegant all-day dining room in a heritage building — refined, seasonal cooking with impeccable service.

items.name: Forest
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025 — Innovation Award (Plabita Florence)
items.description: A tiny 17-seat room open just four evenings a week — Plabita Florence's intimate, personal cooking, named Metro's Restaurant of the Year.

items.name: Amano
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Guide 2025 — recognised (Savor Group flagship)
items.description: A vast, buzzing Italian brasserie and bakery in Britomart — house-made pasta, wood-fired cooking and all-day energy.

items.name: Kingi
credentials: A landmark Britomart seafood dining room
items.description: A sustainability-minded seafood room inside The Hotel Britomart — line-caught fish and shellfish, cooked simply and beautifully.

items.name: Cazador
items.description: A long-loved family-run room celebrating wild game and nose-to-tail cooking — characterful, honest and quietly excellent.

items.name: Tempero
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025 — Specialist Restaurant of the Year
items.description: A vibrant Brazilian-rooted room celebrating live-fire and bold flavour — the country's Specialist Restaurant of the Year.

items.name: Apéro
credentials: Lewisham Awards 2025 — Best Wine List & Best Chef
items.description: A cult natural-wine bar and bistro on K' Road — small, seasonal plates and one of the city's finest cellars.

items.name: Caretaker
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars — 50 Best Discovery listed
items.description: A New York-inspired basement speakeasy beneath Britomart — no menu, just a host who reads you and pours the perfect drink, with live jazz early in the week.

items.name: Deadshot
credentials: From the Caretaker stable — a benchmark Auckland cocktail lineage
items.description: Caretaker's cooler, moodier sibling — effortlessly stylish, seated-only and welcoming, where you are led in once a table is free.

items.name: Panacea
items.description: An inner-city cocktail kitchen and whisky bar with a sustainability ethos — inventive drinks and a serious spirits collection.

items.name: Annabel's
credentials: Editorially recognised — Urban List / Denizen Auckland
items.description: A relaxed, characterful Ponsonby bar with a chilled vibe — live music, wine launches and guest-chef pop-ups in a much-loved neighbourhood room.

items.name: The Rooftop at QT
credentials: Atop QT Auckland — a landmark Viaduct rooftop bar
items.description: A glamorous rooftop terrace over the Viaduct marina — cocktails, colour and one of the best harbour views in the city.

items.title: Helicopter to a Waiheke Island vineyard lunch
items.description: A short flight over the gulf lands you among the island's cellar doors for a long table lunch with the harbour below.

items.title: Sail an America's Cup yacht on the Waitematā
items.description: Take the helm or grind a winch on a genuine former Cup boat out on the harbour that made Auckland the City of Sails.

items.title: A private day on the Hauraki Gulf
items.description: A skippered launch to swim, fish and watch for dolphins and whales among the gulf's islands, lunch cooked aboard.

items.title: Bespoke tasting on Waiheke with a winemaker
items.description: A private cellar session across two or three of the island's small estates, walking the vines with the person who made the wine.

plan.heading: 3 days in Auckland, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.text: Check into the Hotel Britomart in the waterfront quarter, then the Auckland Art Gallery Toi o Tāmaki.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Wynyard and Viaduct harbours, and the volcanic cone of Maungawhau / Mount Eden for the view.

slots.label: Evening

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The ferry to Waiheke Island and a morning among the vineyards.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A cellar lunch at Mudbrick or Man O' War overlooking the Hauraki Gulf.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return on the evening ferry for a quiet dinner at Amano.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive west to the Waitākere Ranges and the black sand of Piha or Karekare.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Back through the bush, then the Maritime Museum and the harbour edge.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at Paris Butter or Sidart before departure.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Viaduct Harbour & Wynyard Quarter
items.description: Waterfront dining and marinas at the centre of the action; suits those who want the harbour on their doorstep.

items.name: Ponsonby
items.description: Villa-lined, café-heavy and stylish just west of the centre; for travellers who prefer neighbourhood restaurants to the tourist strip.

items.name: Waiheke Island
items.description: A 40-minute ferry to vineyards and beaches; suits a slower base that treats the city as an occasional day trip.

events.name: Auckland Anniversary Regatta
events.note: One of the world's largest one-day sailing regattas fills the harbour, the clearest expression of the City of Sails.

events.name: Pasifika Festival
events.note: The largest Pacific-culture festival in the world, with village stages, food and performance at Western Springs.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Land at Auckland International (AKL), a 30 to 45-minute chauffeured transfer into the city or to the waterfront; a helicopter can lift you straight to a Waiheke Island vineyard.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car suits the city and its edges, walking works around the Viaduct and Wynyard Quarter, and a short ferry carries you to Waiheke's vineyards and beaches.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM (One NZ, Spark or 2degrees) gives reliable 4G/5G in and around the city; wifi is standard in hotels.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Currency is the New Zealand dollar; cards and contactless are accepted everywhere and cash is rarely needed; tipping is not expected.

onGround.note: Indian passport holders need an NZeTA plus a visitor visa arranged before travel; make Waiheke Island a day or overnight for its wineries, and use Auckland as the gateway to a wider New Zealand itinerary rather than a destination in itself.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Summer Dec-Mar is warm, long-lit and best for the harbour and islands; winter Jun-Aug is mild but wet and windy, and shoulder months Nov and Apr are pleasant and quieter.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No reliable nonstop from India (a direct route is planned but not yet flying); the best one-stop is Singapore Airlines / Air New Zealand via Singapore, ~14h SIN-AKL plus the India-Singapore leg, roughly 20-22h total. Fly Singapore Airlines business to Changi, then Air New Zealand's Business Premier; both partners expanded India-NZ capacity for the 2026-27 season, so connections are good.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations; strict biosecurity as in Australia — declare all food, and note NZ can bar undeclared items. Tap water is safe and healthcare is excellent. Auckland is very safe. No altitude concern.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Strong for vegetarians and Jain travellers; a sizeable Indian community means authentic Indian food and pure-veg options across the city, and mainstream restaurants handle vegetarian well. Sandringham is Auckland's Indian food street and worth a dedicated visit.

seo.title: Bali — TripAgent
seo.description: Bali, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Bali
hero.tagline: Temple-strewn rice terraces, surf coasts and spiritual calm.

ourTake.lede: Bali is really several islands in one, and the mistake is trying to do all of it; pick two bases and stay put. Ubud for culture and rice terraces, and a southern beach or the Bukit for the coast, is the classic pairing that still works. Avoid the traffic-choked Kuta-Seminyak strip if you can, and if your dates land on Nyepi, embrace it, the whole island shuts in silence and it's extraordinary.
ourTake.comeIf: You want cliff-edge villas, ricefield calm and a honeymoon that balances beach with real culture.
ourTake.skipIf: You want a short, easy hop; the flight is long and the south can be crowded.
