Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: May, June and September are the balm — warm days, thermal baths, café terraces; come August for Sziget or December for the Christmas markets, and avoid the cold, dark heart of winter.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jun, Jul, Aug and Sep

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Gresham Palace Budapest
items.area: District V / Széchenyi tér, Chain Bridge
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The city's definitive address — a restored Art Nouveau palace at the Pest foot of the Chain Bridge, looking straight across the Danube to Buda Castle.

items.name: Matild Palace, a Luxury Collection Hotel
items.area: District V / by Elisabeth Bridge, the Danube
items.description: A Belle Époque palace on the Pest riverfront, reborn as a jewel-box hotel — gilded, marbled and unmistakably grand.

items.name: Anantara New York Palace Budapest
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A history-rich palace hotel wrapped around the legendary New York Café — old-world Habsburg grandeur, restored with a light modern hand.

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton, Budapest
items.description: A dignified 1918 former insurance palace off Erzsébet tér — understated, classical and impeccably run, with a stained-glass cupola over afternoon tea.

items.name: Párisi Udvar Hotel Budapest
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller Readers' Choice Awards 2025
items.description: One of Budapest's most breathtaking interiors — a neo-Gothic-Moorish 1913 arcade with a soaring glass-domed atrium, now a hotel of rare drama.

items.name: W Budapest
items.description: A bold reinvention of the 19th-century Drechsler Palace on Andrássy, opposite the Opera House — design-forward, energetic and beautifully restored.

items.name: Aria Hotel Budapest
items.area: District V / near St. Stephen's Basilica
items.description: A music-themed boutique house steps from the Basilica, crowned by the High Note SkyBar — playful, polished and superbly placed.

items.name: Kozmo Hotel Suites & Spa
items.description: An intimate, contemporary suites hotel with a serious spa — a quieter, design-led alternative to the grand palaces.

items.name: Buda Castle (Budavári Palota)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Budapest, the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
items.description: The vast Baroque royal palace crowning Castle Hill, first raised in the 13th century and rebuilt through sieges and centuries — today it holds the Hungarian National Gallery, the Budapest History Museum and the National Széchényi Library. The cobbled courtyards and terraces give a commanding sweep over the Danube and Pest; a private guide turns the layered history into a single unhurried morning for the family.

items.name: Fisherman's Bastion (Halászbástya)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Budapest, the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
items.description: A fairytale neo-Romanesque terrace of white stone with seven pointed turrets — one for each of the Magyar tribes that settled the Carpathian Basin in 895 — framing the single most photographed panorama in Budapest, straight across to the Parliament. The lower terraces are free; come at first light or dusk to have the arcades and the golden view almost to yourselves.

items.name: Matthias Church (Mátyás-templom)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Budapest, the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
items.description: The coronation church of Hungarian kings, its Gothic spire and dazzling diamond-patterned Zsolnay-tiled roof standing at the heart of Castle Hill. Inside, richly painted walls and folk-inspired frescoes make it unlike any church in Europe; the last Habsburg emperor was crowned here in 1916.

items.name: Castle Hill Funicular (Budavári Sikló)
items.description: A charming 1870 wooden cable railway that climbs the steep 48% incline from Clark Ádám Square at the foot of the Chain Bridge to the castle in about 90 seconds. A gentle, characterful way up for grandparents and children who would rather not walk the hill — with a fine view over the river opening as you rise.

items.name: Hungarian Parliament Building (Országház)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Budapest, the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
items.description: The riverside icon of Budapest — a soaring neo-Gothic palace of 691 rooms built 1885–1902, its red dome and lace-like spires mirrored in the Danube. Guided tours climb the gilded grand staircase to the Holy Crown of Hungary beneath the central dome; book a timed English tour in advance, as entry is by escorted slot only.

items.name: The Holy Crown of Hungary & Crown Jewels
items.description: The thousand-year-old coronation crown, orb and sceptre — with the famously bent cross atop the crown — displayed beneath the Parliament's central dome as the enduring symbol of Hungarian sovereignty. Seen only on the guided Parliament tour, guarded by ceremonial soldiers; a quietly moving centrepiece of any visit.

items.name: St. Stephen's Basilica (Szent István-bazilika)
items.description: The grandest church in Budapest, its 96-metre dome deliberately matching the Parliament's to equal Buda and Pest in height. Inside, the mummified right hand of St Stephen, the first king, rests in a jewelled reliquary; the panoramic rooftop gallery gives a 360-degree sweep over the whole city. Summer evening organ and orchestral concerts are a lovely, discreet outing.

items.name: Széchenyi Chain Bridge (Széchenyi lánchíd)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Budapest, the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
items.description: The first permanent bridge to join Buda and Pest, opened in 1849, its great stone lions and iron chains the emblem of the city. A recently restored evening stroll across, lit up over the black river between the castle and the basilica, is the classic first-night walk — unhurried, romantic and free.

items.name: The Danube Embankments & Promenade
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Budapest, the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
items.description: The stretch of quays and terraces on both banks — the Pest side lined with grand hotels and cafés, the Buda side rising to the castle — is the reason UNESCO listed the riverscape itself. A slow evening walk, or a private car pause at a lookout, delivers the bridges and floodlit monuments in one uninterrupted panorama.

items.name: Széchenyi Thermal Bath (Széchenyi Gyógyfürdő)
items.description: Europe's grandest bath complex — a canary-yellow neo-Baroque palace in City Park with 18 pools, the famous steaming outdoor thermal pools where locals play chess in the water, saunas and medicinal springs. The mother of all Budapest baths; book a private cabin and a massage for a serene multi-generational wellness afternoon.

items.name: Gellért Thermal Bath (Gellért Gyógyfürdő)
items.description: The most beautiful of the baths — an Art Nouveau temple of Zsolnay tiles, mosaics and stained glass beside the Danube in the Gellért Hotel. Note: it is closed for a full restoration and is expected to reopen around 2028, so admire the exterior for now and choose Rudas or Széchenyi to bathe.

items.name: Rudas Thermal Bath (Rudas Gyógyfürdő)
items.description: A 16th-century Ottoman bath — an octagonal pool under a domed ceiling pierced with coloured light shafts — paired with a modern rooftop hot tub open to a 360-degree view of the Danube, Parliament and the bridges. The most atmospheric soak in the city, and glorious at night; check the schedule, as the historic Turkish section still keeps single-sex days.

items.name: Lukács Thermal Bath (Lukács Gyógyfürdő)
items.description: The locals' bath — genuinely medicinal springs used since medieval times, its garden walls lined with marble plaques of thanks from cured bathers. Calmer and less touristy than the grand halls, it is the discreet choice for travellers who want the healing waters without the crowds.

items.name: Gellért Hill & the Citadella
items.description: A 235-metre rock rising sheer above the Danube, crowned by the 19th-century Citadella fortress — the finest single viewpoint over the whole city, both bridges and the river bend. A private car can take older travellers most of the way up; sunset here is the classic panoramic reward.

items.name: Liberty Statue (Szabadság-szobor)
items.description: The 14-metre bronze woman holding a palm leaf aloft above the Citadella, visible from across the city — raised in 1947 and long a symbol of the city's freedom. A brief, worthwhile stop woven into the Gellért Hill climb for the view she presides over.

items.name: Cave Church (Sziklatemplom)
items.description: A working Pauline monastery carved into the rock of Gellért Hill, its chapels set inside natural caves opposite the Gellért Baths. An unexpected, hushed and atmospheric detour on the way up or down the hill.

items.name: Great Market Hall (Nagyvásárcsarnok)
items.description: Budapest's grandest indoor market — a soaring 1897 hall of iron and Zsolnay-tiled roof at the Pest end of the Liberty Bridge, stacked with paprika, salami, Tokaji wine and honey below, and food stalls with lángos and paprikás above. A vivid, family-friendly stop for gifts and grazing; the vegetables, cheeses and sweets suit vegetarian palates well.

items.name: Heroes' Square (Hősök tere)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Budapest, the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
items.description: The monumental plaza closing Andrássy Avenue — a sweeping colonnade of Hungary's chieftains and kings around the Millennium Monument, flanked by two great art museums. The grandest ceremonial space in the city and an essential photo stop before entering City Park.

items.name: City Park & Vajdahunyad Castle (Városliget)
items.description: Budapest's great green playground behind Heroes' Square, holding a boating lake, the Széchenyi Baths and the storybook Vajdahunyad Castle — a fantasy of Transylvanian Gothic, Romanesque and Baroque built for the 1896 millennium and now the Agricultural Museum. A relaxed, pram-friendly afternoon for all ages.

items.name: Andrássy Avenue (Andrássy út)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Budapest, the Banks of the Danube, the Buda Castle Quarter and Andrássy Avenue
items.description: The elegant tree-lined boulevard running from downtown to Heroes' Square — Budapest's Champs-Élysées, lined with neo-Renaissance mansions, the Opera House and the flagship stores of Gucci, Louis Vuitton and the maisons. A UNESCO-listed avenue best strolled slowly, with a café stop and some discreet luxury shopping.

items.name: Hungarian State Opera House (Magyar Állami Operaház)
items.description: A neo-Renaissance jewel of the 1880s, built to rival Vienna and Paris, gilded and frescoed within and blessed with famously fine acoustics. Take the guided tour of the interiors, or better, attend a performance in one of Europe's most beautiful auditoriums for an unforgettable evening.

items.name: Dohány Street Synagogue (Great Synagogue)
items.description: The largest synagogue in Europe and second largest in the world, a Moorish-Byzantine masterpiece of 1859 with twin onion-domed towers. The complex holds the Hungarian Jewish Museum, the Holocaust memorial garden and the silver weeping-willow Tree of Life — a moving, essential half-day with a guide.

items.name: The Jewish Quarter (District VII)
items.description: The historic Jewish district, now the city's most fashionable quarter — courtyard synagogues, street art, kosher bakeries, designer boutiques and buzzing cafés threaded through handsome old tenements. A rich, walkable afternoon best explored with a private guide who can open its hidden courtyards and history.

items.name: Szimpla Kert (the original ruin bar)
items.description: The mother of Budapest's 'ruin bars' — a derelict pre-war building filled with mismatched furniture, fairy lights, art and greenery around an open courtyard. More a cultural landmark than a pub; worth a daytime look at its famous farmers' market and interiors even if late-night crowds aren't your scene.

items.name: House of Terror (Terror Háza)
items.description: A powerful museum in the former secret-police headquarters at Andrássy 60, documenting Hungary's fascist and communist terror and honouring their victims — the very cells where prisoners were held survive in the basement. Sombre and unforgettable; a serious counterweight to the city's grandeur, best for older children and adults.

items.name: Shoes on the Danube Bank
items.description: Sixty pairs of iron shoes cast into the embankment just south of the Parliament — a stark memorial to the Jews shot into the river here in 1944–45, their shoes left on the bank. A brief, deeply affecting pause on the riverside walk.

items.name: Hungarian National Gallery
items.description: The definitive collection of Hungarian art from the Gothic altarpieces to the Impressionist Munkácsy and Csontváry, housed within Buda Castle. The upper-floor terrace and cupola add a fine castle-view bonus; a rewarding indoor morning when the weather turns.

items.name: Museum of Fine Arts (Szépművészeti Múzeum)
items.description: Hungary's finest art museum, on Heroes' Square, with over 100,000 works spanning European masters — El Greco, Raphael, Goya and a superb Egyptian and antiquities collection — reopened after a full restoration. A world-class rainy-day option for art-loving travellers.

items.name: Hospital in the Rock (Sziklakórház)
items.description: A secret WWII and Cold War emergency hospital and nuclear bunker hidden in the caves beneath Castle Hill, preserved with wax figures and original equipment and seen only on a guided tour. A gripping, unusual counterpoint to the palaces above — best for older children and adults.

items.name: Memento Park (Szoborpark)
items.description: An open-air museum on the city's edge where the giant Lenin, Marx and Soviet statues torn from Budapest's squares after 1989 now stand together. A thought-provoking, slightly surreal half-day; a private car makes the out-of-town trip easy.

items.name: Margaret Island (Margitsziget)
items.description: A long green island in the middle of the Danube — car-free gardens, a rose garden, medieval convent ruins, a running track and a musical dancing fountain. The city's favourite retreat for a slow morning; hire a family pedal-carriage or simply walk under the plane trees away from the traffic.

items.name: Danube evening cruise
items.description: The classic way to take in the UNESCO riverscape — the Parliament, castle, bridges and basilica all floodlit gold as you glide past after dark. Charter a private boat with dinner or a glass of Tokaji for a serene, celebratory evening the whole family remembers.

items.name: New York Café
items.description: Long billed as 'the most beautiful café in the world' — a riot of gilt, marble columns, frescoed ceilings and chandeliers, once the haunt of Budapest's writers. Reserve for coffee, cake or a grand afternoon tea; go for the astonishing interior as much as the pastries.

items.name: Gül Baba's Tomb & Rose Garden
items.description: The octagonal mausoleum of an Ottoman dervish poet, set in a beautifully restored terraced rose garden high on Rose Hill — the northernmost Islamic pilgrimage site in the world and a place of great calm. A serene, little-visited hideaway with a lovely view over Pest.

items.name: Elisabeth Lookout Tower (Erzsébet-kilátó), Normafa & János Hill
items.description: A neo-Romanesque stone tower atop János Hill — at 527 metres the highest point in Budapest — reached via the scenic Normafa woods and the beloved little Children's Railway or the chairlift. A breezy escape into the green hills with the widest panorama of all; free to climb.

items.name: Bálna (the Whale) & the Danube riverwalk
items.description: A striking glass-and-steel 'whale' of contemporary architecture fusing old brick warehouses on the Pest quay — galleries, cafés and design shops beside the river. A relaxed, modern contrast to the grand old city and a pleasant riverside stop near the Great Market Hall.

items.name: Central Market & artisan food shopping
items.description: Beyond the Great Market Hall, the streets around it hold Budapest's best delicatessens and paprika, foie gras and Tokaji specialists — the place to assemble a hamper of Hungarian gifts. Vegetarian travellers will find superb cheeses, sweet pastries and pickles; a private guide can point you to the finest producers.

items.name: The Danube Bend day trip — Szentendre, Visegrád & Esztergom
items.description: The classic full-day loop north of the city: the cobbled artists' town of Szentendre with its galleries and Orthodox churches, the royal hilltop citadel of Visegrád over a dramatic river curve, and Esztergom with the largest basilica in Central Europe. A private car and guide make it an easy, scenic day for the whole family.

items.name: Szentendre
items.description: A pretty riverside town of pastel houses, artists' studios, Serbian Orthodox churches and marzipan shops, 25 km north of Budapest and reachable in 45 minutes by suburban train. The most relaxed and photogenic half-day escape; charming for a leisurely lunch and a gentle wander.

items.name: Esztergom Basilica
items.description: The largest church in Hungary and one of the tallest in Central Europe, its vast dome rising over the Danube at the Slovak border in the ancient royal city of Esztergom. Climb to the cupola for a sweeping river panorama; a fitting grand finale to the Danube Bend loop.

items.name: Lake Balaton
items.description: Central Europe's largest lake, about 90 minutes from Budapest — the Hungarian 'sea' of vineyards, the Tihany peninsula with its Benedictine abbey and lavender fields, and elegant lakeside villas. A refreshing summer day or an overnight for water, wine and calm; lovely for multi-generational groups.

items.name: Eger & the Valley of the Beautiful Women
items.description: A handsome Baroque town with a famous castle that repelled the Ottomans in 1552, a fine basilica and thermal baths — followed by wine tasting in the cellar-lined Valley of the Beautiful Women, home of the robust 'Bull's Blood' red. A rewarding full day of history, wine and a restorative soak.

items.name: Tokaj wine region
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Tokaj Wine Region Historic Cultural Landscape
items.description: The historic hillside vineyards that gave the world Tokaji Aszú, the golden botrytised dessert wine once 'the wine of kings, the king of wines'. Private cellar tastings among the ancient tunnels reward the longer drive; best combined with an overnight for the full estate experience.

items.name: Vörösmarty Square & the coffeehouse tradition
items.description: The genteel heart of downtown Pest, home to the legendary Café Gerbeaud with its century-old cakes and the Christmas market in winter. A civilised stop for the storied Hungarian coffeehouse ritual — Dobos torte, Eszterházy cake and a slow hour watching the square.

items.name: Fashion Street & luxury shopping (Deák Ferenc utca)
items.description: Budapest's smartest shopping run, a short pedestrian street off Vörösmarty Square lined with international luxury houses, complemented by the maison boutiques along Andrássy Avenue. Discreet, unhurried shopping between sightseeing, with cafés and the grand hotels close at hand.

items.name: Stand
items.description: Szabina Szulló and Tamás Széll's flagship — refined modern Hungarian cooking around a glass-walled kitchen, and the city's most decorated table.

items.name: Babel
items.description: Kornél Kaszás's hushed, elegant room of barely a dozen tables — tasting menus rooted in Austro-Hungarian and Transylvanian tradition, chasing purity of flavour.

items.name: Costes
items.description: The restaurant that won Hungary's first Michelin star in 2010 — polished, classical fine dining that set the modern Budapest standard.

items.name: essência
items.description: A love story on a plate — Portuguese chef Tiago Sabarigo and Éva Jenei let you lead each course Portuguese or Hungarian, or weave the two together.

items.name: Rumour by Jenő Rácz
items.description: Jenő Rácz's confident, contemporary tasting menu — technically sharp, produce-led cooking from one of the country's most talked-about chefs.

items.name: Salt
items.description: A single tasting menu built almost entirely on Hungarian produce and craft — foraged, fermented and fiercely seasonal, in the Nordic spirit.

items.name: Borkonyha Winekitchen
items.area: District V / near St. Stephen's Basilica
items.description: 'Wine Kitchen' — Ákos Sárközi's relaxed, Hungarian-rooted bistro with a serious, wine-led list, holding its star for over a decade.

items.name: New York Café
items.area: District VII / inside Anantara New York Palace
credentials: Inside a Leading Hotels of the World / MICHELIN One-Key hotel
items.description: Often called the most beautiful café in the world — a gilded, frescoed 1894 palace room of marble columns and Venetian chandeliers.

items.name: Gundel
items.area: District XIV / City Park, by the Zoo
items.description: Hungary's most famous restaurant since 1894 — the grand, palatial home of Gundel palacsinta and old-world Magyar ceremony, in the City Park.

items.name: Stand25 Bisztró
items.area: District I / Hold utca market & Várkerület
items.description: The Stand team's casual sibling — hearty, refined Hungarian classics done properly, at a fraction of the flagship's price.

items.name: Goli
items.description: An easygoing modern bistro of small plates and natural wines — inventive, seasonal and squarely the kind of good-value cooking the Bib rewards.

items.name: N28 Wine & Kitchen
items.description: A wine-focused kitchen near the Opera House — considered small plates paired with a deep, characterful list.

items.name: Cabrio
items.description: A natural-wine bar with vintage flair and a leafy terrace — bold, seasonal small plates paired with a 100% natural list.

items.name: 94' Konyha & Bár
items.description: Vibrant, Vietnamese-rooted cooking — fragrant pho and the signature 94' Gohan — bringing real Asian craft to the city.

items.name: Boutiq'Bar
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — 50 Best Discovery
items.description: A serious, buzzy cocktail bar just off Andrássy — classics and inventive drinks made with real craft against a bold red interior.

items.name: High Note SkyBar
items.area: District V / Aria Hotel, by St. Stephen's Basilica
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller — among the world's top rooftop bars
items.description: The rooftop of the Aria Hotel — a front-row seat to St. Stephen's Basilica, floodlit and close enough to touch, over polished cocktails.

items.name: 360 Bar
credentials: A landmark Budapest rooftop, on Andrássy Avenue
items.description: A long-running rooftop on Andrássy with a genuine 360-degree panorama of the city — igloo domes in winter, open terrace in summer.

items.name: Szimpla Kert
credentials: Budapest's original and most famous ruin bar (est. 2002)
items.description: The original ruin bar — a derelict apartment block stripped to the brick and filled with fairy lights, salvaged junk, street art and a disused Trabant.

items.title: Private early session at a thermal bath
items.description: A reserved morning at Gellért or Rudas before the public, in the art-nouveau or Ottoman pools.

items.title: Private cruise on the Danube at night
items.description: A small boat with dinner as the Parliament and Chain Bridge light up along both banks.

items.title: Tokaji tasting with a sommelier
items.description: A private vertical of Hungary's legendary sweet wines, or a day out to the Tokaj cellars.

items.title: Concert at the restored Liszt Academy
items.description: An evening in one of Europe's finest art-nouveau concert halls.

plan.heading: 3 days in Budapest, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

days.title: The Buda hill and the river

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle into Matild Palace, then cross the Chain Bridge and take the funicular up to Buda Castle and the Fisherman's Bastion before the coaches arrive.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Walk the Castle District to Matthias Church, then a quiet lunch and coffee at the terrace of the Hilton overlooking the Danube.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Onyx-successor Salt or, for the classic, the tasting menu at Stand, one of the city's two-star tables.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private morning at the Hungarian Parliament, then the Great Synagogue and a walk through the old Jewish Quarter.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Soak and rest at the Széchenyi thermal baths, arranged with a cabin before the afternoon crowds.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Costes Downtown or the wine-led Borkonyha, followed by a nightcap at the Boutiq'Bar.

days.title: Art, market, and the leafy hills

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Museum of Fine Arts on Heroes' Square, then a stroll down leafy Andrássy Avenue.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Central Market Hall for paprika and Tokaji, then a drive up to the Buda hills for the view.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A final dinner at Babel or the riverside Spago, ending with pálinka.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Castle District (Buda)
items.description: Cobbled hilltop streets and river views — quiet and grand.

items.name: District V / Belváros
items.description: The downtown Pest core near Parliament — central and walkable.

items.name: District VI (Terézváros)
items.description: The Andrássy avenue quarter with the opera and cafés — elegant and lively.

events.name: Sziget Festival
events.note: One of Europe's largest music festivals, held on an island in the Danube.

events.name: Budapest Wine Festival
events.note: Hungarian winemakers gather in the Castle District for the harvest-season tasting.

events.name: St Stephen's Day
events.note: The national holiday, marked by a grand fireworks display over the Danube.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Budapest Ferenc Liszt International (BUD); a private chauffeur meets you inside the terminal and drives the 30–40 minutes into the city.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver on standby suits the sprawl between Buda and Pest, though the historic core around the Danube and Castle District is best walked.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM (Airalo, Yesim) activates on landing; 5G is strong and hotel wifi is reliable throughout the city.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Hungarian forint (HUF) rules despite EU membership; cards are accepted almost everywhere, keep light cash, and 10–12% for good service is customary.

onGround.note: Stay in District V (Belváros) or the Castle District for the finest addresses; the thermal baths (Széchenyi, Gellért) reward a discreet early-morning private session before crowds arrive.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Late spring and early autumn are kind — warm days, cool evenings, the Danube at its best; July-August turns humid and crowded, and January-February is grey and near-freezing.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No nonstop from India; the clean routing is one stop via Istanbul on Turkish Airlines (strong business cabin) or via a Gulf hub on Emirates/Qatar, roughly 11-13 hours total. Turkish's IST connection is the smoothest for onward Central Europe; use the Turkish Airlines lounge at Istanbul, among the best in the network.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No special vaccinations beyond routine; hepatitis A worth being current on. Tap water is safe to drink. Very safe city; ordinary care against pickpockets in tourist crush and around nightlife.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Easy for vegetarians in central Budapest; Jain is workable if you brief the kitchen (Hungarian cooking leans meat and lard, so specify). Indian food is available — Tandoori Palace and Bombay Express are reliable, and upscale hotels handle veg requests well.

seo.title: Buenos Aires — TripAgent
seo.description: Buenos Aires, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Buenos Aires
hero.tagline: A European-grand capital of tango, beef and late nights.

ourTake.lede: Buenos Aires keeps late hours, and fighting that rhythm is the surest way to miss it. Eat at ten, take the milonga after midnight, and reserve mornings for slow walks through Recoleta and Palermo rather than early starts. Skip the staged dinner-tango shows aimed at tour groups; a neighbourhood milonga, even just to watch, is the real thing.
ourTake.comeIf: You want tango, exceptional steak and Malbec, and a European-feeling city at the far edge of the map.
ourTake.skipIf: You keep strictly vegetarian or want a short flight; this is a long haul into a meat-and-wine city.

Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: Autumn in March-April and spring in October-November are finest, with jacaranda purple in November. Avoid the humid January heat.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, May, Jun, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Buenos Aires
items.description: A modern tower and a restored 1916 Belle Époque mansion (La Mansión) side by side in Recoleta — the city's most complete grand hotel, and its most decorated.

items.name: Palacio Duhau — Park Hyatt Buenos Aires
items.description: A 1930s French-style palace joined to a modern wing by an art-lined garden tunnel — terraced gardens, a cheese room and quietly impeccable Recoleta grandeur.

items.name: Alvear Palace Hotel
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The 1932 gilded grande dame of Avenida Alvear — Louis XV and XVI furnishings, white-gloved butlers and a century of Argentine high-society ceremony.

items.name: Palacio Duhau — Park Hyatt (Palacio-wing suites)
items.description: The palace-wing suites of the Duhau — grand proportions, French mouldings and garden or Avenida Alvear views, with the full Park Hyatt service.

items.name: Four Seasons Buenos Aires — La Mansión suites
items.description: The seven suites within the restored 1916 mansion — the most exclusive rooms in the city, with private grandeur and the full Four Seasons hand.

items.name: Faena Hotel Buenos Aires
items.description: Philippe Starck's theatrical red-and-white fantasy inside a converted 1902 grain mill — unicorn statues, a cabaret hall and pure Argentine drama on the docks.

items.name: Casa Lucía
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: A 1929 Bencich-family building on Avenida Santa Fe reborn as a warm, art-filled modern house — timber, brass and a rooftop pool over the city.

items.name: Alvear Icon Hotel
credentials: Alvear maison (sister to The Leading Hotels of the World Alvear Palace)
items.description: The Alvear group's sleek modern tower on the Puerto Madero waterfront — high floors, river and city views and a rooftop pool and spa.

items.name: Hotel Madero
items.description: A polished contemporary hotel on the Puerto Madero docks — a rooftop pool, a spa and a quiet, well-run calm a short walk from the old town.

items.name: La Recoleta Cemetery
items.description: A hushed marble city of the dead where 4,691 above-ground vaults — Evita Perón's among them — line avenues of angels and domes. A private guide turns the sprawl into an hour of storytelling that even restless teenagers fall quiet for; go early, before the coach groups arrive.

items.name: Teatro Colón
credentials: Rated among the world's top three opera houses for acoustics by National Geographic
items.description: Argentina's grand opera house, ranked among the world's finest for acoustics — Pavarotti said its perfection made him nervous. A box for the evening, or a private daytime tour of the golden horseshoe auditorium and marble Salón Dorado, is the city at its most refined.

items.name: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes
items.description: The finest art collection in Latin America — Goya, Rembrandt, Rodin, Monet, Van Gogh and the deepest holding of Argentine masters — all with free entry. A civilised, air-conditioned hour between lunch and the cemetery, easily paced for grandparents.

items.name: Plaza de Mayo
items.description: The historic heart of the nation, framed by the pink Casa Rosada, the colonial Cabildo and the Cathedral — the square where Evita addressed the masses and the Mothers still march on Thursdays. A guide unpacks two centuries of Argentine drama in one walkable block.

items.name: Casa Rosada
items.description: The rose-pink presidential palace whose famous balcony framed Evita — and, for many, the ghost of the Broadway song. Free weekend tours reveal the halls of power, or simply admire the facade from the plaza on a private history walk.

items.name: Buenos Aires Metropolitan Cathedral
items.description: Behind a Greek-temple facade lies the country's principal church, where Jorge Bergoglio said mass before becoming Pope Francis, and where General San Martín's remains rest under permanent guard. Quietly moving even for non-Catholic visitors.

items.name: El Ateneo Grand Splendid
credentials: Named the world's most beautiful bookstore by National Geographic (2019)
items.description: A 1919 theatre — frescoed ceiling, crimson stage curtain, opera boxes intact — reborn as a bookshop where you browse novels from the old balcony seats. A magical, unhurried stop the whole family enjoys, coffee served on the former stage.

items.name: Avenida 9 de Julio & the Obelisco
items.description: The city's Champs-Élysées and Eiffel Tower in one — reputedly the world's widest avenue, crowned by the 67-metre Obelisco. Best seen at dusk from a private car as the traffic-light rivers begin to glow.

items.name: Don Julio
items.description: The parrilla that turned the Argentine steak into world-class theatre — Angus and Hereford dry-aged in its own butchery, poured with a wall of Malbec. Book weeks ahead and let the maître d' arrange a private table; the kitchen handles vegetarians and grilled-vegetable feasts with real care when told in advance.

items.name: San Telmo Sunday Market
items.description: Every Sunday, Defensa Street becomes ten blocks of antiques, silver, leather and buskers, converging on cobbled Plaza Dorrego where couples still dance tango as the light fades. A guide keeps the crowd manageable and steers you to the genuine dealers, not the trinket stalls.

items.name: Caminito & La Boca
items.description: The postcard lane of tin houses painted in leftover shipyard colours, where tango was born among Genoese dockworkers. Best enjoyed mid-morning with a private guide who keeps you within the safe tourist blocks and adds the real immigrant history behind the pretty facades.

items.name: Puente de la Mujer & Puerto Madero
items.description: Calatrava's white 'Woman's Bridge' — a stylised tango dancer in steel — arcs over the old docks, now the city's polished riverside quarter of glass towers and terraced restaurants. An easy, flat evening stroll before a waterside dinner, safe and pram-friendly.

items.name: MALBA (Museo de Arte Latinoamericano)
items.description: Costantini's private collection turned public: Frida Kahlo, Diego Rivera, Tarsila do Amaral and the giants of Latin American modernism in a cool, light-filled building. Compact enough for an afternoon, with an excellent café for a pause.

items.name: Bosques de Palermo (Parque Tres de Febrero)
items.description: The city's green lungs — 400 hectares of lakes, jacaranda and rowing boats, laid out by landscape master Carlos Thays. A gentle morning for multi-generational groups: pedal boats for the children, shaded benches for the elders.

items.name: El Rosedal (Palermo Rose Garden)
credentials: Protected as part of Buenos Aires' Cultural Heritage
items.description: More than 8,000 roses across 90-odd species, pergolas and a poets' garden inside the Bosques — the park's most beloved corner and a florid backdrop for family photographs. Free, serene, and at its peak in the southern spring (October–November).

items.name: Jardín Japonés
items.description: One of the largest Japanese gardens outside Japan, gifted for a royal visit — koi ponds, red bridges, a teahouse and clipped calm minutes from the city rush. A restful, veg-friendly lunch stop that particularly delights grandparents.

items.name: Basílica de Nuestra Señora del Pilar
items.description: The whitewashed colonial jewel beside the cemetery, its original 18th-century Peruvian silver altars still intact, with a small cloister museum upstairs. A five-minute, deeply atmospheric pairing with a Recoleta cemetery visit.

items.name: Floralis Genérica
items.description: A 20-metre steel-and-aluminium flower that opens its petals at dawn and closes them at dusk, mirrored in a reflecting pool — the city's modern icon. A free, photogenic pause on the way between the Fine Arts museum and the law faculty.

items.name: Centro Cultural Recoleta
items.description: A former convent turned contemporary-arts complex — rotating exhibitions, design shows and a rooftop that catches the afternoon light, right beside the cemetery and basilica. A cool, unhurried counterpoint to the neighbourhood's grand history.

items.name: Rojo Tango at Faena
items.description: Tango's most exclusive show: a red-velvet cabaret for barely a hundred guests inside Philippe Starck's Faena Hotel, so close you feel the bandoneón. The discreet, luxurious choice for couples and small parties who want spectacle without a tourist crowd.

items.name: Café de los Angelitos tango show
items.description: A grand dinner-and-show in an 1890 café once frequented by Carlos Gardel himself — the most complete traditional tango experience, with a full orchestra and a Malbec-paired menu. Vegetarian courses available on request; ideal for a first, immersive night of tango.

items.name: Café Tortoni
credentials: Designated a Notable Bar of Buenos Aires
items.description: The city's oldest café, founded in 1858, where Borges and Gardel once sat beneath stained glass and marble columns. A living relic — order a submarino (hot milk with a bar of chocolate) and soak up a slower Buenos Aires.

items.name: Argentine Open Polo Championship (Palermo)
items.description: The world's most prestigious polo tournament, played each November–December at the 'Cathedral of Polo' since 1928, where 40-goal teams draw crowds of 30,000. Box seats, an asado and a chilled Malbec make it the season's grand social occasion for Indian polo enthusiasts.

items.name: Estancia day trip, San Antonio de Areco
items.description: Ninety minutes onto the pampas to a working estancia — gaucho horsemanship, folk music, an open-fire asado and optional polo lessons in the birthplace of Argentine gaucho tradition. A private full-day escape that lands beautifully with families and riders.

items.name: Colonia del Sacramento day trip (Uruguay)
items.description: A one-hour fast ferry across the Río de la Plata to Uruguay's oldest town — cobbled Portuguese-Spanish lanes, a lighthouse and riverside cafés, walkable in an afternoon. Passports and a private transfer make for an effortless second-country stamp.

items.name: Tigre Delta
items.description: An hour north, the Paraná fans into a maze of green islands, stilt houses and rowing clubs best explored by private launch, with the Puerto de Frutos market to browse afterwards. A cooling, scenic day on the water for all ages.

items.name: El Zanjón de Granados
items.description: Beneath an 1830 mansion lies a restored labyrinth of brick tunnels and cisterns tracing 400 years of the city's foundations — a private, atmospheric hour few tourists know. The most rewarding hidden gem in San Telmo.

items.name: Museo Nacional de Arte Decorativo (Palacio Errázuriz)
items.description: A French Beaux-Arts palace by the architect of Buenos Aires' grandest mansions, its rooms hung with El Greco, Manet and Rodin — the only such house that opens regularly to the public. A jewel-box afternoon for lovers of design and la belle époque.

items.name: Palacio Paz (Círculo Militar)
items.description: The largest private house ever built in Argentina — 140 rooms of Louvre-inspired grandeur, a soaring domed rotunda and marble halls, now open by guided tour. Occasional evening tours pair the palace with a lyrical concert or wine tasting.

items.name: Fundación Proa
items.description: La Boca's serious side: a sleek glass-and-steel contemporary art centre with world-class temporary shows and a rooftop café overlooking the Riachuelo. A refined, safe anchor before or after the colourful chaos of Caminito.

items.name: Palermo Soho
items.description: The city's most stylish quarter — independent designers, leather ateliers, art galleries and pavement cafés radiating from leafy Plaza Serrano. The place to shop for one-off pieces and graze between boutiques; a personal shopper smooths the way.

items.name: Palermo Hollywood
items.description: Palermo's cooler, more grown-up cousin, threaded with acclaimed restaurants, cocktail bars and cinema-studio history, coming alive after 10pm as Argentines do. Ideal for a long, late dinner and a nightcap without the backpacker throng.

items.name: Vinoteca at Palacio Duhau – Park Hyatt
items.description: A cellar of 500-plus labels inside a restored palace, where a sommelier walks you through blind Malbec flights paired with the kitchen's small plates. A discreet, luxurious way to learn Argentine wine without leaving the city.

items.name: Puerta cerrada (closed-door) dinner
items.description: Argentina's intimate answer to fine dining — a home turned private restaurant seating a handful of guests, with sommelier hosts and a multi-course, wine-paired menu. Bookable exclusively for your party, and happy to build a vegetarian tasting when asked.

items.name: Avenida de Mayo & Palacio Barolo
items.description: The stately Parisian boulevard linking the Casa Rosada to Congress, crowned by the Palacio Barolo — a 1923 tower designed as a stone homage to Dante's Divine Comedy, with a lighthouse-topped viewpoint. A guided climb rewards you with one of the city's best panoramas.

items.name: Congreso de la Nación
items.description: The green-domed national Congress closing Avenida de Mayo, a Greco-Roman monument to Argentine democracy with free guided tours of its chambers and library. A grand architectural bookend to a historic-centre walk.

items.name: Galerías Pacífico
items.description: A belle-époque shopping arcade under a frescoed cupola painted by Argentina's leading muralists — luxury boutiques below fine art above, on pedestrian Calle Florida. Elegant browsing and a cultural centre make it a rainy-afternoon refuge.

items.name: Milonga at Salón Canning / La Catedral
items.description: Not a show but the real thing — a social dance hall where porteños of every age dance tango until dawn, from grand parquet salons to bohemian converted warehouses. A guide or private teacher lets you watch (or step in) with the etiquette right.

items.name: Feria de Mataderos
items.description: A weekend fair on the city's edge where gauchos ride, folk musicians play and the pampas comes to town — crafts, empanadas and a horseback skill game called the sortija. The most authentic, least touristy folk experience in Buenos Aires, best reached by private car.

items.name: Museo Evita
items.description: Set in a 1920s mansion Evita once ran as a shelter, this intimate museum traces her extraordinary rise through gowns, film and photographs. Essential context for anyone moved by her story at Recoleta, and easily paired with a Palermo lunch.

items.name: Planetario Galileo Galilei
items.description: A striking modernist sphere on three arches inside the Bosques, with immersive dome shows and lakeside lawns around it. A fun, air-conditioned hour for families with children, and a photogenic landmark at dusk.

items.name: Chacarita's La Chacra & the parrilla circuit
items.description: Beyond Don Julio, a private steak-and-wine crawl through the city's best asadores — La Cabrera, Parrilla Peña, Niño Gordo — is a delicious education in cuts, chimichurri and provoleta. A knowledgeable guide secures the tables and translates the grill.

items.name: Aramburu
items.description: Gonzalo Aramburu's precise, artful tasting menu — the highest gastronomic reference in the country, and Argentina's only two-Michelin-star table.

items.name: Don Julio
items.description: Pablo Rivero's parrilla — the definitive Argentine steakhouse, No. 1 in all of Latin America and a one-star table where the grill is treated as an art.

items.name: Trescha
credentials: Latin America's 50 Best Restaurants 2024 — No. 33 (Highest New Entry)
items.description: Tomás Treschanski's 14-course counter for just ten diners — a young, virtuosic kitchen and the city's most exciting fine-dining seat.

items.name: Chila
items.description: A long-standing fine-dining room on the Puerto Madero docks — a tasting-menu celebration of Argentina's regions and its wines.

items.name: Crizia
items.description: Gabriel Oggero's oyster bar and seafood-driven kitchen in a leafy Palermo townhouse — the newest of the city's Michelin stars.

items.name: El Preferido de Palermo
items.description: A restored 1952 corner bodegón reborn under the Don Julio family — Spanish-Argentine classics, house-cured hams and a joyful, buzzing room.

items.name: Mishiguene
items.description: Tomás Kalika's reimagining of Jewish diaspora cooking — pastrami, babka and shakshuka elevated to a celebrated, soulful fine-dining table.

items.name: Niño Gordo
items.description: A neon-lit, theatrical 'Asian parrilla' — Argentine fire cooking crossed with Southeast and East Asian flavours, loud and hugely fun.

items.name: Julia
items.description: A tiny, produce-obsessed neighbourhood kitchen — a short, changing menu of quietly brilliant contemporary cooking from chef Julio Martín Báez.

items.name: Anchoíta
items.description: A farm-to-table kitchen with its own organic plot — Guaraní-inspired sharing plates, house charcuterie, river fish and superb pasta.

items.name: Sacro
items.description: Buenos Aires' most ambitious plant-based kitchen — gourmet vegan cooking, a serious cocktail list and a sleek, grown-up room.

items.name: Elena
credentials: Within Four Seasons Hotel Buenos Aires
items.description: The Four Seasons' dry-aging steakhouse and all-day room — polished Argentine grilling and one of the best Sunday brunches in the city.

items.name: Gran Dabbang
items.description: Mariano Ramón's tiny, riotous storefront where Indian and Southeast Asian spice meets Argentine produce — one of the most loved kitchens in the city.

items.name: Anafe
items.description: A small, chef-led corner bistro celebrated for inventive, produce-driven cooking at an accessible price.

items.name: Café Tortoni
credentials: Historic landmark (est. 1858); a founding member of the world's historic cafés
items.description: The city's most storied café since 1858 — stained glass, marble and mirrors, and the ghosts of Borges and Gardel over coffee and churros.

items.name: El Cuartito
credentials: Historic landmark (est. 1934); a Buenos Aires institution
items.description: A beloved 1934 pizzeria plastered in football and boxing memorabilia — thick porteño pizza and fugazzeta the way the city has always eaten it.

items.name: Florería Atlántico
credentials: Rémy Martin Legend Award (pioneer of the scene)
items.description: A flower shop and wine cellar hiding a legendary basement bar — the pioneer of the modern Buenos Aires scene, and a former World's No. 1.

items.name: L'Orangerie (Alvear Palace)
credentials: Within Alvear Palace Hotel — The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The Alvear Palace's glass-roofed salon — crystal chandeliers, monogrammed china and the most ceremonial afternoon tea or aperitif in the city.

items.name: Tres Monos
items.description: A high-energy, no-menu cocktail den with a social conscience — the highest-ranked bar in South America and a genuine world-beater.

items.name: CoChinChina
items.description: Inés de los Santos's theatrical bar where Vietnam and France meet an Argentine accent — polished, glamorous and one of the world's best.

items.name: Presidente Bar
items.description: The grand end of Buenos Aires cocktail culture — chandeliers over a long bar, a winter garden and a library-styled private room.

items.name: Piano Nobile / Oak Bar (Palacio Duhau)
credentials: Within Palacio Duhau — Park Hyatt (MICHELIN Key, 2025)
items.description: The Park Hyatt palace's clubby wood-panelled bar and garden terrace — impeccable classics, a whisky and cognac library and quiet Recoleta calm.

items.name: Trade Sky Bar
items.description: A Gatsby-styled rooftop with 360-degree views over the Obelisk, Puerto Madero and downtown — the city's most glamorous high-up drink.

items.name: Nicky Harrison
credentials: Widely cited Buenos Aires speakeasy (goop; press)
items.description: A Prohibition-era speakeasy hidden behind a sushi counter — password entry, live jazz and a 1920s-with-an-Argentine-twist theatre.

items.title: A private milonga lesson and a real neighbourhood dance
items.description: A one-to-one session with a maestro, then an escorted evening at an authentic milonga rather than a dinner show.

items.title: Box at the Teatro Colón
items.description: Opera or ballet from a private box in one of the world's great acoustic houses, with a backstage tour arranged around it.

items.title: Asado and horses at a historic estancia
items.description: A day on a private pampas ranch outside the city with gauchos, riding and a full open-fire asado lunch.

items.title: A private cellar dinner with an Argentine winemaker
items.description: A guided vertical of top Mendoza Malbecs paired course by course, hosted in a private room in Palermo or Recoleta.

plan.heading: 4 days in Buenos Aires, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle into Palacio Duhau – Park Hyatt, then walk the Recoleta Cemetery and the French-quarter mansions around Avenida Alvear.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: See the Malba's Latin American collection, then take an unhurried coffee at the Palacio Duhau's garden terrace.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Elena inside the Four Seasons, the city's finest dry-aged beef and a serious cellar.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Wander the leafy streets of Palermo Chico and the botanical garden before the heat.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A private tasting of Argentine Malbec and Cabernet Franc, then browse the ateliers of Palermo Soho.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Don Julio, the Palermo parrilla on the World's 50 Best list; book well ahead.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Explore San Telmo's cobbles and antique arcades, quiet before the Sunday crowds.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Cross to the Costanera and Puerto Madero for the river light and the Fortabat art collection.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A tasting menu at Aramburu, the city's refined modern Argentine kitchen, followed by a late private tango.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive out to a working estancia on the pampas for horses and open country.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A slow asado lunch under the trees, then unhurried return to the city.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A quiet final dinner at Chila in Puerto Madero, overlooking the docks.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Recoleta
items.description: Belle Époque grandeur, the famous cemetery and old money; suits a classic, elegant first stay.

items.name: Palermo (Soho & Chico)
items.description: Leafy, design-led and dense with restaurants and bars; for travellers who want the city's best eating on their doorstep.

items.name: San Telmo
items.description: Cobblestones, antique markets and tango history; atmospheric and bohemian, best for those who like their charm a little rough-edged.

events.name: Tango BA Festival y Mundial
events.note: The world's largest tango gathering, culminating in the World Championship finals at the Gran Rex; free events fill the city.

events.name: Carnaval Porteño
events.note: Neighbourhood murga troupes and free street corsos across more than twenty barrios; a local, unglossed carnival.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Ministro Pistarini (Ezeiza, EZE) for long-haul; a private chauffeur meets you airside and it is a 45-minute run into Recoleta or Palermo, while domestic and regional flights use the closer-in Aeroparque Jorge Newbery (AEP).

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Keep a private car and driver on call for the sprawl, but walk the leafy grids of Recoleta, Palermo and San Telmo, which reward it.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Buy an eSIM (Claro, Movistar or Personal) before landing; 4G is strong across the city and hotel wifi is reliable.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Currency is the Argentine peso; carry some US dollars cash for the favourable informal rate, but cards work in better restaurants and hotels; tip around 10 percent.

onGround.note: Dinner starts late, from 21:00 onward, so plan accordingly; base yourself in Recoleta for grace or Palermo for energy, and a good concierge can secure a table at the hard-to-book parrillas and a private tango salon rather than a tourist show.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Southern-hemisphere seasons are flipped: Oct-Nov (spring) and Mar-Apr (autumn) are mild and dry; Dec-Feb is hot and humid with much of the city on holiday, and Jun-Jul can be grey and damp.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No nonstop from India; the cleanest one-stop is Doha with Qatar Airways (DOH-EZE nonstop, ~18h in the air plus the India-Doha leg, roughly 24h door to door). Ethiopian via Addis Ababa is the alternative. Fly Qatar Qsuite in business; use the Al Mourjan lounge at Doha and keep a 3-4h buffer on the outbound to absorb the long southern leg.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations for India-origin travellers; routine cover plus Hepatitis A is sensible. Tap water is safe in the city. Buenos Aires is generally safe in Recoleta, Palermo and Puerto Madero; use registered cars, avoid displaying valuables, and be alert to distraction thefts.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Argentina is meat-heavy, but Palermo has strong vegetarian and vegan kitchens; pure-veg is workable, strict Jain (no onion/garlic/root) needs briefing ahead. Indian food is limited but present. Sacro (fine-dining vegan) and the Palermo vegetarian scene are reliable.

seo.title: Cairo — TripAgent
seo.description: Cairo, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Cairo
hero.tagline: Pyramids, the Nile and a thousand years of empire.

ourTake.lede: Cairo rewards patience and an early alarm. See the Pyramids at Giza the moment the site opens, before the heat and the crowds, and give a full unhurried half-day to the Grand Egyptian Museum, which finally does the collection justice. Don't try to cram Islamic Cairo, the Egyptian Museum and Giza into one day; the city is dense and the traffic is real, so slow down and let a good fixer smooth the edges.
ourTake.comeIf: You want the Pyramids, the new Grand Egyptian Museum and a Nile-led week of deep history.
ourTake.skipIf: You need calm, orderly streets or a pure relaxation trip; Cairo is dense and chaotic.
