seo.title: Darjeeling — TripAgent
seo.description: Darjeeling, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Darjeeling
hero.tagline: Tea gardens, the toy train and Kanchenjunga at dawn.

ourTake.lede: Darjeeling is about the tea, the toy train and that one clear dawn view of Kanchenjunga, and the honest truth is the mountain hides behind cloud more often than not, so build in enough mornings to catch it. Stay on a working tea estate below the town rather than in the busy Mall area. Come in the clear post-monsoon autumn or the spring; the monsoon buries the views entirely.
ourTake.comeIf: You want tea gardens, the toy train and Kanchenjunga on a cool hill escape.
ourTake.skipIf: You need a fast, direct journey; getting up the hill takes patience.

firstLook.heroCaption: Modern pool villa with palms and umbrella

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: Spring and autumn give the clearest Kanchenjunga views and the prized tea flushes; skip the June-September monsoon of mist and landslides.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Apr, May, Jun, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Darjeeling. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Glenburn Tea Estate & Boutique Hotel
items.area: Glenburn Tea Estate (~1 hr from Darjeeling town)
credentials: A restored 150-year-old colonial tea-planter's bungalow on a working Darjeeling estate
Named among Tatler's '101 Best Hotels of the World'
A signature India property for Scott Dunn, Kuoni, Abercrombie & Kent and Enchanting Travels
All-inclusive stays with estate walks, tea tastings and butler-hosted meals
items.description: The tea-estate stay India is known for — a restored 150-year colonial planter's bungalow on a working estate above the River Rungeet, Kanchenjunga filling the sky.

items.name: Windamere Hotel
credentials: The oldest heritage hotel in the Himalayas
Est. as Ada Villa in 1841; a planters' boarding house from the 1880s; Windamere Hotel since 1939
Set on historic Observatory Hill, overlooking Chowrasta and the peaks
The 1939 Windamere Bar and celebrated colonial afternoon tea
items.description: A time-capsule of the British Raj on the hill where Darjeeling began — coal fires, hot-water bottles, afternoon tea and the oldest heritage hotel in the Himalayas.

items.name: Mayfair Darjeeling
credentials: A heritage resort in the early-1900s summer palace of the Raja of Nazargunj
Prime setting opposite Raj Bhawan (the Governor's House)
British-colonial architecture — grand fireplaces, carved wood, lofty ceilings
Wellness spa, gardens and the Douglas Lounge Bar
items.description: A hilltop heritage resort in the former summer palace of the Raja of Nazargunj — colonial fireplaces and carved wood, gardens, and a spa, opposite the Governor's House.

items.name: Taj Chia Kutir Resort & Spa, Darjeeling
credentials: A Taj Hotels resort within the historic Makaibari Tea Estate (est. 1859), the world's first permaculture tea estate
A 22-acre estate resort, 72 keys including villas and suites
J Wellness Circle spa and a heated indoor pool
Tea-estate walks, nature trails and tastings
items.description: Taj's tea-country resort inside the historic Makaibari estate — bamboo, timber and stone in the mist, with a spa, indoor pool and guided estate walks.

items.name: The Elgin, Darjeeling
credentials: Heritage resort & spa 'since 1887' — built as a manor house for the Maharaja of Cooch Behar
Bought and run for decades by the Oberoi family (from 1965)
Five-star heritage property with a spa
Period Burma-teak furniture, oak panelling and fireplaces
items.description: A 19th-century manor house turned five-star heritage hotel — Burma-teak floors, crackling fireplaces and a grand piano, once an Oberoi-family home.

items.name: Cochrane Place, Kurseong
credentials: A restored colonial-era residence (the 'Hermitage' of magistrate P. J. Cochrane), once owned by the Maharajas of Burdwan
French-style heritage architecture, Burma-teak furnishings and antiques
Perched over the Ambootia, Makaibari and Castleton tea estates
Chai Country restaurant, celebrating regional tea and Anglo-Indian cuisine
items.description: A colonial-era boutique hideaway on a Kurseong ridge — a British magistrate's old house restored, with unobstructed Kanchenjunga views and an Anglo-Indian tea kitchen.

items.name: Tiger Hill Sunrise
items.description: Before dawn you climb to 2,590 m and wait in the cold dark until the first light strikes Kanchenjunga's summit and it turns rose, then gold, over the sleeping range; on the clearest mornings Everest itself is a faint tooth on the far horizon. A private car and a flask of first-flush tea turn the pre-4am pilgrimage into something you will still talk about years later.

items.name: Darjeeling Himalayan Railway Toy Train Joy Ride
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site (Mountain Railways of India)
items.description: The little blue steam engine of 1881 pulls you up through the town's rooftops, around the spiralling Batasia Loop and up to Ghum, India's highest station, at a walking pace that lets you lean out and be handed marigolds. It is pure Raj-era romance, and a joy that spans generations from a five-year-old to a grandfather who rode it as a boy.

items.name: Batasia Loop & War Memorial
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site (Mountain Railways of India)
items.description: The toy train coils through a full circle here around a landscaped garden while Kanchenjunga fills the sky behind the Gorkha soldiers' memorial. The train pauses ten minutes so you can walk the flower beds and take in the panorama; it is the single most photographed spot on the line.

items.name: Ghum Railway Station & DHR Museum
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site (Mountain Railways of India)
items.description: At 2,258 m this is the highest railway station in India, its little first-floor museum lined with the brass fittings, old photographs and a vintage engine that tell the story of how the line was built. A short, atmospheric stop that gives the toy train its historical weight.

items.name: Yiga Choeling Monastery (Ghum Monastery)
items.description: Founded in 1850, the oldest Tibetan monastery of the region shelters a serene fifteen-foot Maitreya Buddha in gold and vermilion, butter lamps glowing against ancient manuscripts. Quiet, incense-scented and deeply atmospheric, it rewards an unhurried private visit away from the town crowds.

items.name: Happy Valley Tea Estate
items.description: Darjeeling's second-oldest garden, planted in 1854 on slopes just below the town, where you walk between the bushes with the pluckers and then sit for a proper tasting of the estate's organic first and second flush. It is the most accessible way to understand why Darjeeling tea is spoken of like a fine wine.

items.name: Padmaja Naidu Himalayan Zoological Park
items.description: India's largest high-altitude zoo runs the country's flagship breeding programmes for the red panda and the snow leopard, and here you can actually watch a red panda curled in a fir tree at eye level. A genuine conservation landmark that captivates children and grandparents alike.

items.name: Himalayan Mountaineering Institute
items.description: Founded after Tenzing Norgay's 1953 Everest summit and long led by him, the institute's museum displays the ropes, ice-axes and expedition relics of Himalayan climbing history, with a viewing telescope trained on Kanchenjunga. For anyone stirred by the mountains outside the window, it is the emotional heart of Darjeeling.

items.name: Chowrasta & The Mall
items.description: The flat, traffic-free promenade at the town's crown is where Darjeeling has always come to stroll, sit on the benches and watch the light change on the ridge. Ringed by Nathmull's tea shop and Glenary's, it is the town's living room and the natural place to begin and end a day.

items.name: Observatory Hill & Mahakal Temple
items.description: A short climb through prayer-flag-draped pines leads to a shrine sacred to both Hindus and Buddhists, where a Shiva lingam and Buddhist bells share the same rock and the views open on all sides. It is the town's oldest sacred spot and quietly moving at any hour.

items.name: St Andrew's Church
items.description: Darjeeling's oldest church, established in 1843, is a plain grey-stone Scottish kirk with memorial tablets to the planters and soldiers of the Raj still on its walls. A short, evocative stop for anyone drawn to the town's colonial thread.

items.name: Japanese Peace Pagoda & Temple
items.description: A gleaming white 28-metre stupa built by the Nipponzan-Myohoji order and inaugurated in 1992, its four golden Buddhas facing out over the valley; at dawn and dusk the resident monks beat the drum and chant in a rhythm you feel in your chest. Serene, uncrowded and unexpectedly powerful.

items.name: Rock Garden & Ganga Maya Park
items.description: About ten kilometres below town a mountain stream is terraced into landscaped falls, stone steps and flower beds, with a boating pond and picnic lawns at the lower Ganga Maya Park. A relaxed half-day in the deep valley, especially lovely for a multi-generation outing.

items.name: Rangeet Valley Passenger Ropeway
items.description: India's first passenger cable car floats you out over tiers of tea gardens dropping to the Little Rangeet river, the whole Rangeet valley unfolding beneath your feet. A short, scenic glide that gives you the tea country from the air.

items.name: Nightingale Park
items.description: A terraced hillside garden crowned by a large Shiva statue, with musical-fountain evenings and one of the town's best framed views of Kanchenjunga across the rooftops. A gentle, well-kept stop a short walk from the heritage hotels.

items.name: Bengal Natural History Museum
items.description: Opened in 1903, this old collection of Himalayan birds, butterflies and mammals is a curiosity of the Raj-naturalist era, dusty cabinets and all. A quiet, quick detour for the curious, close to the Mall.

items.name: Windamere Hotel
items.description: The only truly authentic British-Raj heritage property in Darjeeling, a rambling white bungalow of hot-water bottles, coal fires, four-o'clock tea and a music room where time has genuinely stopped. Even for a High Tea or a nightcap it is an experience the town cannot repeat.

items.name: The Elgin, Darjeeling
items.description: Once the summer residence of the Maharaja of Cooch Behar and hotelier since 1887, the Elgin keeps its wood-panelled lounges, manicured lawns and afternoon-tea ritual immaculate. A heritage stay or a leisurely tea here is the polished, comfortable face of old Darjeeling.

items.name: Glenary's & Keventer's
items.description: Two Raj-era institutions on the same lane: Glenary's for its bakery and the tea room with a valley view, Keventer's for the rooftop breakfast and cold cuts that generations of families have queued for. This is where you taste Darjeeling's colonial-cafe nostalgia over a slow morning.

items.name: Nathmull's Tea Room
items.description: The town's most respected tea merchant since 1931, where you sit and cup single-estate first and second flushes side by side and learn to tell a Castleton from a Margaret's Hope. The most rewarding way to buy Darjeeling tea properly, with real guidance.

items.name: Glenburn Tea Estate
items.description: A working colonial-era garden on a promontory above the Rungeet river where the planter's bungalows have become one of India's most romantic tea retreats, with private guided plucking, factory walks and tastings looking straight at Kanchenjunga. The definitive tea-planter fantasy for a discerning couple or family.

items.name: Makaibari Tea Estate
items.description: The world's first biodynamic and one of the oldest tea gardens, famous for its moonlight-plucked silver-tips and its immersive tours through the factory and the forest that shades the bushes. A pilgrimage for anyone serious about where great tea comes from.

items.name: Goodricke Thurbo & Castleton Estates
items.description: Goodricke's storied gardens produce some of the most sought-after and record-priced Darjeeling lots, and a private tasting arranged through the group shows you the top of the pyramid. For the collector-minded traveller, this is Darjeeling tea at its most exclusive.

items.name: Lloyd's Botanical Garden
items.description: A steeply terraced Victorian garden of 1878 with orchid houses, a fernery and towering Himalayan conifers, a green pocket of calm just below the bustle of the Mall. An easy, restful walk for a slow afternoon.

items.name: Tenzing & Gombu Rock
items.description: A natural rock face used by the mountaineering institute for training and named for Everest's first summiteers, where you can watch aspiring climbers rope up or try a supervised scramble yourself. A short, spirited stop tied to Darjeeling's climbing legend.

items.name: Kalimpong Flower Nurseries
items.description: The hill town's temperate slopes are one of India's great centres for orchids, gladioli, cacti and gerbera, and the terraced nurseries are a riot of colour and scent you can wander through freely. A gentle, unexpectedly captivating side of the eastern Himalayas.

items.name: Pine View Cactus Nursery
items.description: One of Asia's finest private collections of cacti and succulents, more than fifteen hundred varieties bristling under glass on Atisha Road. A quirky, memorable stop that surprises everyone who thinks they don't care about plants.

items.name: Durpin Monastery (Zang Dhok Palri Phodang)
items.description: Consecrated by the Dalai Lama in 1976, this hilltop gompa holds rare Buddhist scriptures and 108 volumes brought from Tibet, its upper terrace opening on the Teesta and Rangeet rivers and the snows of west Sikkim. The most rewarding single sight in Kalimpong.

items.name: Deolo Hill
items.description: The highest point above Kalimpong, a breezy landscaped park where the Teesta winds far below and the whole west-Sikkim snow line stands clear on a good day. A relaxed, panoramic high point that families love for the space and the views.

items.name: Morgan House
items.description: A 1930s English country mansion, once a jute baron's home and now a heritage bungalow wrapped in pine and rhododendron, thick with Raj-era atmosphere and mist. Worth the visit for its faded colonial romance and the grounds alone.

items.name: Dr Graham's Homes & Chapel
items.description: A sprawling 1900 school campus of stone Scottish-mission buildings and a beautiful chapel spread across the hillside, a serene and storied slice of Kalimpong's missionary heritage. A quiet, atmospheric walk through living history.

items.name: Mirik Lake (Sumendu Lake)
items.description: A slender lake ringed by pines and orange orchards where you can row a boat, walk the arched footbridge and ride a pony along the water in cool, gentle air. An easy, pretty day trip that suits every generation of a family.

items.name: Kurseong & Eagle's Craig
items.description: The quieter tea town on the toy-train line, its Eagle's Craig viewpoint looking down over the plains and the Cochrane Place heritage bungalow serving a fine tea. A restful, uncommercialised base deep in the tea country.

items.name: Pelling & Kanchenjunga Viewpoints
items.description: Perched at 2,150 m, Pelling gives arguably the closest full-face view of Kanchenjunga anywhere accessible, the whole massif filling your hotel window at first light. The classic base for the west-Sikkim monastery circuit and the mountain romance at its purest.

items.name: Pemayangtse Monastery
items.description: One of Sikkim's oldest and most important Nyingma monasteries, founded in the 1700s, keeping an extraordinary seven-tiered wooden model of the Buddhist heavens carved by a single monk. A profound, beautifully sited stop with Kanchenjunga as backdrop.

items.name: Rabdentse Ruins
items.description: A short forest walk from Pemayangtse leads to the moss-covered ruins of Sikkim's second royal capital, its stone thrones and chortens standing on a ridge above a vast Himalayan drop. Quiet, evocative and beautifully atmospheric.

items.name: Khecheopalri Lake
items.description: A sacred wish-fulfilling lake hidden in the forest, so revered that birds are said to lift any leaf that falls on its mirror surface, its shores hung with prayer flags. A serene, spiritual detour on the west-Sikkim loop.

items.name: Yuksom
items.description: The sleepy first capital of Sikkim, where the coronation throne of the first Chogyal still stands under the pines and the great Kanchenjunga treks begin. A gentle, history-laden village at the foot of the high mountains.

items.name: Rumtek Monastery (Dharmachakra Centre)
items.description: The largest monastery in Sikkim and the seat of the Karmapa's Kagyu lineage, its golden-roofed shrine hall glowing with murals, a jewelled reliquary and rows of chanting monks. The single most important spiritual sight of the Gangtok region.

items.name: Tsomgo (Changu) Lake
items.description: A high glacial lake at 3,750 m that stays frozen much of the year, ringed by snow with yaks in their festive harness on the shore, an hour and a half's drive from Gangtok on a permit. A dramatic, high-altitude excursion that thrills first-time mountain visitors.

items.name: Nathula Pass
items.description: A historic Silk-Road pass on the India-China border at 4,310 m, where you can stand at the frontier fence in the thin cold air with the army post beside you. A stirring, bucket-list drive that needs a special permit and a clear day.

items.name: MG Marg, Gangtok
items.description: Sikkim's spotless, traffic-free and litter-free central promenade, lined with cafes, tea shops and flower beds and made for an evening stroll. The relaxed social heart of the capital and the natural base for the wider Sikkim circuit.

items.name: Khangchendzonga National Park
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site (Khangchendzonga National Park)
items.description: A vast wilderness of glaciers, alpine lakes and the sacred slopes of Kanchenjunga itself, revered by Sikkimese as a living deity and the setting for the great high treks. Sikkim's crowning wild landscape, entered on permit through Yuksom.

items.name: Singalila Ridge & Sandakphu
items.description: The ridge trek to Sandakphu, West Bengal's highest point at 3,636 m, delivers the fabled 'Sleeping Buddha' line-up of Kanchenjunga with Everest, Lhotse and Makalu ranged beside it. For the adventurous, it is the greatest mountain panorama the region offers, drivable in a rugged Land Rover or walked over days.

items.name: Tinchuley & Takdah Heritage Bungalows
items.description: A cluster of restored British planter and forest bungalows on a quiet ridge among orange orchards and tea, with sweeping Kanchenjunga views and near-total silence. An intimate, off-the-beaten-track base for travellers who want the hills without the crowds.

items.name: Lamahatta Eco Park & Monastery
items.description: A forested, prayer-flag-lined park terraced up to a small sacred pond and monastery, with a Kanchenjunga viewpoint through the pines. A peaceful, uncommercialised stop that breaks the drive between Darjeeling and Kalimpong beautifully.

items.name: Glenburn — the estate table
credentials: Dining within Glenburn Tea Estate, a Tatler '101 Best Hotels of the World' property
Full-board, butler-hosted meals with estate-grown produce
Verandah and riverside picnic settings above the Rungeet
items.description: The finest meals in the hills are served at Glenburn — butler-hosted, produce from the estate, laid out on the verandah with Kanchenjunga in view.

items.name: The Elgin dining room
credentials: Signature dining of The Elgin, heritage resort 'since 1887'
Period Raj-era dining room with grand piano
items.description: A candle-lit heritage dining room with a grand piano — considered Anglo-Indian and regional cooking under oak panelling and old etchings.

items.name: Windamere — afternoon tea & dining
credentials: Dining within the oldest heritage hotel in the Himalayas (Windamere, est. 1939)
items.description: The great colonial afternoon tea of the Himalayas — cucumber sandwiches, scones and Darjeeling tea by the fire, in the oldest heritage hotel in the hills.

items.name: Glenary's
credentials: A Darjeeling institution, confectionery since c.1885
One of the oldest eateries in the hill station
Landmark Nehru Road bakery, restaurant and Buzz Bar
items.description: Darjeeling's grand old café-bakery since the 1880s — a first-floor restaurant, a famous ground-floor bakery, and Kanchenjunga through the windows.

items.name: Keventer's
credentials: Serving since 1911 — a Swedish-founded colonial dairy institution
Rooftop terrace with Kanchenjunga and Mall views
items.description: The 1911 rooftop breakfast institution — sausages, ham and eggs above the Mall, Kanchenjunga on the skyline, immortalised in Satyajit Ray's films.

items.name: Kunga Restaurant
credentials: Consistently ranked among Darjeeling's best for Tibetan food (Tripadvisor)
items.description: The town's most-loved Tibetan kitchen — steaming momos and thukpa in a tiny, family-run room where you may have to wait for a seat.

items.name: Sonam's Kitchen
items.area: Dr Zakir Hussain Road, Darjeeling town
credentials: A cult-favourite small café among Darjeeling's best-loved eateries
Known for hand-roasted coffee and hearty breakfasts
Home-style thukpa, momos and Nepali thali
items.description: A tiny café with a cult following — proper coffee, big breakfasts, and honest thukpa and momos, run by a local family.

items.name: The Windamere Bar
credentials: The Windamere Bar, in continuous character since 1939
Set within the oldest heritage hotel in the Himalayas
Colonial lounge bar — historic photos, fireside sofas
items.description: A single-room Raj-era bar unchanged since 1939 — wood, sofas, old photographs and a whisky by the fire in the oldest heritage hotel in the Himalayas.

items.name: Joey's Pub
items.area: Dr S. M. Das Road, Darjeeling town
credentials: A legendary British-style pub, a Darjeeling institution
Long a fixture of the town's small nightlife (since the early 1990s; rebuilt and reopened 2021)
items.description: Darjeeling's legendary British-style pub — beer, banter and a fire, a fixture of the town's evenings for decades and much-loved by travellers.

items.name: Glenary's Buzz Bar
credentials: The bar of Glenary's, a Darjeeling institution since c.1885
A rare dedicated evening bar on Nehru Road / the Mall
items.description: The basement bar of the town's grand old café — the go-to for a drink and live music beneath the famous 1880s bakery.

items.title: Dawn at Tiger Hill for Kanchenjunga
items.description: An early drive to catch the first light striking the world's third-highest peak; go on a clear morning and go early.

items.title: Heritage ride on the Darjeeling toy train
items.description: The UNESCO-listed steam narrow-gauge line, ideally the Batasia Loop joyride behind a heritage locomotive.

items.title: Private stay and tasting on a first-flush tea estate
items.description: A planter's bungalow among the gardens with a guided walk and a cupping of the celebrated Darjeeling leaf.

items.title: Guided walk to a Himalayan monastery at first light
items.description: An early visit to Ghoom or a hillside gompa before the day's visitors.

plan.heading: 3 days in Darjeeling, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive and settle into Glenburn Tea Estate's Water Lily house in town, or the estate bungalow itself if you want the plantation to yourself.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Walk the Mall and Chowrasta at an unhurried pace, then take tea and toast at Glenary's, the old confectioner on Nehru Road.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dine in on the estate's set Anglo-Bengali dinner, or at Glenburn's town table, with the lights of the valley below.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Leave before dawn for Tiger Hill to watch the sun reach Kanchenjunga, then stop at Ghum monastery and the Batasia Loop on the way down.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Ride a section of the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway toy train, then tour a working tea garden and taste the first-flush lots.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Quiet dinner back at the estate, an early night before the drive out to the tea country.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A full morning at Glenburn: walk the slopes with a planter, follow a basket of leaf from bush to withering loft, and cup the day's teas.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Picnic lunch by the Rungeet river at the foot of the estate, feet in the water, before the climb back up.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Last dinner on the bungalow verandah, then depart the next morning for Bagdogra.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Tea-estate belt (below town)
items.description: Planter's bungalows among the gardens; best for views, calm and the tea experience.

items.name: The Mall / Chowrasta
items.description: The colonial town centre with the promenade and cafes; convenient but crowded in season.

items.name: Jalapahar / upper ridges
items.description: Quieter, higher and forested with the best long views; for those prioritising the mountain.

events.name: Clear-view autumn season
events.note: The most reliable window for cloud-free Kanchenjunga views after the monsoon clears.

events.name: Darjeeling Tea & Tourism Festival
events.note: A festival celebrating the region's tea, culture and music, timed to the clear season.

events.name: Losar (Tibetan New Year)
events.note: The Buddhist new year, marked with masked dances at the town's Tibetan monasteries.

events.name: First-flush tea season
events.note: The prized spring plucking, the best time to experience the estates at work.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Bagdogra (IXB), then a private chauffeured SUV climbs the roughly three-hour, 70km road up to Darjeeling; a helicopter transfer from Bagdogra to Darjeeling is also arranged when weather permits.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with a hill-experienced driver is essential on the steep, narrow lanes, with the Mall and Chowrasta best explored on foot.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Airtel and Jio give reliable 4G in town; signal thins on ridge roads and at remote tea estates, so download maps before setting out.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Indian rupee; cards work at hotels and better restaurants but keep cash for tea gardens, monasteries and the toy train; tipping is 5-10 percent and always welcome.

onGround.note: Stay at a colonial-era estate such as Glenburn or a heritage hill property for the finest views; layer up as evenings are cold year-round, and rise early for the Tiger Hill sunrise over Kanchenjunga before the cloud closes in.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Mid-March to May is kind — mild days, rhododendrons, and clear Kanchenjunga at dawn; October to November brings the sharpest post-monsoon visibility. Avoid July to September, when monsoon closes the views and triggers hill-road landslides.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No airport at Darjeeling itself; fly into Bagdogra (IXB), then a 3 to 3.5 hour car up the hill. Bagdogra takes daily jets from Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru — best served by Vistara/Air India and IndiGo; there is no true business cabin on most sectors, so charter a private helicopter transfer from Bagdogra to Darjeeling (weather-permitting, ~15 min) to skip the road.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: Domestic — no vaccinations needed. Very safe, low crime; the main caution is the winding mountain road and occasional monsoon landslides. Darjeeling sits near 2,000m, so a first day can bring mild breathlessness — pace the arrival. Stick to bottled or filtered water.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Effortless for vegetarian and Jain guests — this is an Indian hill town, so pure-veg and Jain-adaptable food is everywhere. Glenary's for a classic bakery breakfast; Keventer's for the view; and heritage estate stays like Glenburn set an excellent private vegetarian table on request.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Darjeeling, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: New Delhi — TripAgent
seo.description: New Delhi, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: New Delhi
hero.tagline: Mughal grandeur and leafy avenues at India's imperial capital.

ourTake.lede: Delhi is two cities — the Mughal old town and the leafy colonial capital — and you need a day for each. Do Humayun's Tomb over the Red Fort if you have to choose; it's calmer and, many think, more beautiful. Go to Old Delhi early with a guide for the food and the Jama Masjid, and avoid the touts around the big monuments by having a driver and a plan.
ourTake.comeIf: You want Mughal monuments, layered history and the gateway to the Golden Triangle.
ourTake.skipIf: You want calm, clean air or a beach.

firstLook.heroCaption: Woman walking poolside royal tent courtyard

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: October to March is the pleasant season, crowned by the Republic Day parade and Diwali; avoid the May-June furnace and January's smog and fog.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Oct, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to New Delhi. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: The Oberoi, New Delhi
items.area: Lutyens' / Central Delhi (Dr Zakir Hussain Marg)
credentials: Travel + Leisure World's Best Awards — recognised (Oberoi group, service excellence)
items.description: Delhi's flagship Oberoi, reborn after a top-to-toe rebuild — serene rooms above the golf course and Humayun's Tomb.

items.name: The Leela Palace New Delhi
credentials: Travel + Leisure World's Best Awards 2025 — Top 3 city hotels in India
items.description: A gold-domed modern palace in the Diplomatic Enclave — the grandest new-build luxury house in the capital.

items.name: The Imperial
items.description: 1936 Lutyens grandeur — colonnades, palm court and one of India's great art collections on the walls.

items.name: Taj Mahal, New Delhi
items.description: The Taj's Lutyens address — discreet, well-placed and home to the legendary Wasabi and House of Ming.

items.name: The Lodhi
items.description: Big, contemporary rooms — many with private plunge pools — in a green, low-rise pocket of central Delhi.

items.name: ITC Maurya, a Luxury Collection Hotel
items.area: Lutyens' / Central Delhi (Sardar Patel Marg, Diplomatic Enclave)
credentials: Houses Bukhara & Dum Pukht — The World's 50 Best Discovery restaurants
items.description: The capital's power house — home to Bukhara and Dum Pukht, two of the most decorated Indian kitchens on earth.

items.name: Andaz Delhi
items.description: Design-led Hyatt Andaz minutes from the terminals — the sharpest of the airport-side luxury houses.

items.name: Taj Palace, New Delhi
items.area: Lutyens' / Central Delhi (Sardar Patel Marg, Diplomatic Enclave)
credentials: Houses Masala Art & Blue Ginger — Taj signature dining; Condé Nast Traveller India — recognised group
items.description: A vast garden-set Taj in the Diplomatic Enclave — built for scale, conferences and big Indian celebrations.

items.name: Qutub Minar & the Qutub Complex
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Qutub Minar and its Monuments
items.description: The 73-metre fluted victory tower of 1193 is the tallest brick minaret in the world, ringed by the ruins of India's first mosque and the uncorroded 4th-century Iron Pillar. Come at opening hour with a private ASI-trained guide before the coach crowds arrive; it is a short drive from the Mehrauli boutique hotels and the perfect first read of Delhi's layered history.

items.name: Humayun's Tomb
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Humayun's Tomb
items.description: The garden-tomb that rehearsed the Taj Mahal a century early — a red-sandstone and marble mausoleum floating in a formal charbagh, exquisitely restored by the Aga Khan Trust. Go in the low gold of late afternoon; it is the single most composed piece of Mughal architecture in the city and pairs naturally with an adjoining visit to Sunder Nursery and Nizamuddin.

items.name: Red Fort (Lal Qila)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Red Fort Complex
items.description: Shah Jahan's walled palace-city in red sandstone, from whose ramparts the Prime Minister addresses the nation each Independence Day. Walk the Diwan-i-Khas where the Peacock Throne once stood and the marble pavilions of the imperial harem; a good guide makes the faded splendour legible. Enter early to beat the heat and the queues at the Lahori Gate.

items.name: Jama Masjid
items.description: India's largest mosque, Shah Jahan's final architectural flourish, its red-and-white courtyard holding twenty-five thousand worshippers beneath three marble domes. Climb the southern minaret for the definitive rooftop view over Old Delhi's sea of terraces. Dress modestly, remove shoes, and time a visit to fold into a Chandni Chowk food walk next door.

items.name: Chandni Chowk
items.description: The 17th-century spine of Mughal Delhi — a delirium of jewellers, wedding-card printers, saree wholesalers and legendary food, laid out by Shah Jahan's daughter around a moonlit canal that is long gone. The civilised way to see it is a private morning walk or a cycle-rickshaw through the lanes, ending at Karim's or Paranthe Wali Gali; almost everything worth eating here is vegetarian-friendly.

items.name: Khari Baoli Spice Market
items.description: Asia's largest wholesale spice market, trading in cardamom, saffron, dried fruit and chilli from sack-piled shopfronts since the 17th century — the air itself makes you sneeze. Go with a guide who can walk you up to a rooftop godown for the panorama and translate the grading of the saffron and the pistachios, then buy a kilo of the good stuff to carry home.

items.name: Old Delhi Haveli Heritage Walk (Haveli Dharampura)
credentials: UNESCO Asia-Pacific Award of Merit for Cultural Heritage Conservation — Haveli Dharampura
items.description: A meticulously restored late-Mughal mansion in the Shahjahanabad lanes, brought back from ruin over six years and now an award-winning heritage hotel with kathak evenings in its sandstone courtyard. A guided haveli walk decodes the vanishing domestic architecture of Old Delhi — jharokha balconies, carved brackets, hidden courtyards — best ended over a rooftop dinner above the rooftops.

items.name: Lodhi Gardens
items.description: Ninety acres of landscaped calm scattered with the domed tombs of the 15th-century Sayyid and Lodhi sultans — Delhi's most beloved green room, where the city's elite walk their dogs at dawn. Come early for the birdsong and the light through the Bara Gumbad; it sits within a short walk of the Lodhi Hotel, Khan Market and the India International Centre.

items.name: India Gate & Kartavya Path
items.description: Lutyens' 42-metre war memorial arch anchoring the grand ceremonial vista of the redesigned Kartavya Path (formerly Rajpath), sweeping up to Rashtrapati Bhavan. The lawns come alive on winter evenings with families and ice-cream carts; drive the axis after dark when the whole processional way is floodlit, or stroll it at dusk from a Lutyens' Delhi hotel.

items.name: Rashtrapati Bhavan
items.description: Lutyens' colossal presidential palace — 340 rooms crowning Raisina Hill, a fusion of classical and Indian idioms that is arguably the grandest work of the Raj. Book ahead for the guided circuit of the state rooms and the Rashtrapati Bhavan Museum; the whole imperial city of New Delhi radiates from here, and it reads best with a historian at your side.

items.name: Amrit Udyan (the Mughal Gardens)
items.description: The formal terraced gardens behind Rashtrapati Bhavan — Persian charbagh geometry, a rose garden and a bonsai collection — thrown open to the public only in spring, when the tulips and the flowerbeds peak. Entry is free but slotted, from roughly February to March; book online, go on a weekday morning, and treat it as a seasonal event rather than a year-round stop.

items.name: Swaminarayan Akshardham
credentials: Guinness World Record — World's Largest Comprehensive Hindu Temple
items.description: A staggering pink-sandstone and marble temple carved by eleven thousand artisans without structural steel, ringed by a musical fountain, boat ride and manicured gardens on the Yamuna's east bank. Recognised by Guinness as the world's largest comprehensive Hindu temple. Allow half a day, note that phones and bags are barred inside, and know the vegetarian food court is genuinely good.

items.name: Lotus Temple (Bahá'í House of Worship)
items.description: Twenty-seven marble 'petals' folding into a serene lotus, one of the most-visited buildings on earth and a modern architectural landmark open to all faiths for silent meditation. Come near closing for the softest light on the white shell and the quietest hall; it sits a short hop from the Kalkaji temples and Nehru Place, and asks only stillness of its visitors.

items.name: Gurudwara Bangla Sahib
items.description: The most visited Sikh shrine in Delhi, its golden dome mirrored in a vast holy tank, with round-the-clock hymns and a langar kitchen that feeds tens of thousands free every day. Cover your head, walk through the sarovar, and if you can, step into the community kitchen to watch the sheer scale of the seva — it is one of the city's most moving sights, and entirely vegetarian.

items.name: Hazrat Nizamuddin Dargah
items.description: The 14th-century Sufi shrine of Nizamuddin Auliya, still the beating spiritual heart of a warren of medieval lanes — and on Thursday evenings the setting for live qawwali that has run in an unbroken tradition for centuries. Go with a knowledgeable guide, cover your head, and sit for the Thursday qawwali; the intensity of the devotion here is unlike anywhere else in Delhi.

items.name: Safdarjung's Tomb
items.description: The last great garden-tomb of the Mughals, built in 1754 in a slightly overblown late style that historians call the empire's 'last flicker' — a domed marble mausoleum in a quiet charbagh that most visitors skip. That is exactly its charm: a serene, uncrowded stop minutes from Lodhi Gardens, ideal for a photographer or anyone who wants the Mughal aesthetic without the queues.

items.name: National Museum
items.description: India's premier collection — Harappan artefacts including the 4,500-year-old bronze Dancing Girl, Chola bronzes, Mughal miniatures, and relics of the Buddha. It is under long-term redevelopment, so check current access, but a private curator-led tour of the highlights gives the deepest single grounding in the subcontinent's art you can get in one building.

items.name: National Gallery of Modern Art
items.description: Housed in the former palace of the Maharaja of Jaipur near India Gate, this is the country's foremost collection of modern Indian art — Raja Ravi Varma, the Bengal School, Amrita Sher-Gil, the Progressives. A calm, well-lit couple of hours that maps the arc of Indian modernism, and an easy pairing with Bikaner House across the hexagon.

items.name: Sunder Nursery
credentials: Part of the Humayun's Tomb UNESCO World Heritage buffer; UNESCO Asia-Pacific Award-winning conservation by the Aga Khan Trust
items.description: A 90-acre 16th-century heritage park beside Humayun's Tomb, restored by the Aga Khan Trust into Delhi's first arboretum, with Mughal-era monuments, lily pools, a rose garden and over three hundred tree species. It is the most beautifully kept green space in the city — come for a slow morning, a picnic on the lawns, and the Sunday farmers' market when it runs.

items.name: National Crafts Museum (Crafts Museum)
items.description: A living museum of Indian folk and tribal craft — terracotta shrines, a full carved Gujarati haveli facade, textiles and votive art — with resident master artisans demonstrating and selling their work in the courtyards. It is a discreet, deeply rewarding stop for anyone who collects, and the on-site Café Lota is one of the best regional-Indian lunches in the city.

items.name: Hauz Khas Village & Lake
items.description: A 13th-century royal reservoir and the ruins of Firoz Shah's madrasa and tomb, wrapped by a deer park — and abutting an urban village of design boutiques, galleries and rooftop restaurants. Come late afternoon: the medieval monuments glow over the lake, then the lanes turn to shopping and cocktails. A rare place where deep history and contemporary Delhi sit side by side.

items.name: Dilli Haat (INA)
items.description: A permanent open-air crafts and food bazaar where artisans from every state rotate through the stalls, so you can buy Kashmiri pashmina, Channapatna toys or Odisha ikat direct from the maker without the tout-heavy chaos of a street market. Regional food stalls let you eat your way across India in an afternoon; good for gifts and for a relaxed, curated shop.

items.name: Khan Market
items.description: Reputedly among the most expensive retail streets in the world, this compact Lutyens' market is Delhi's most civilised shopping enclave — Good Earth and Anokhi for home and textiles, Full Circle bookshop, Fabindia, artisanal patisseries and quietly excellent restaurants above the shopfronts. The default afternoon for well-heeled Delhi, walkable from the Lodhi and Sujan hotels.

items.name: Mehrauli Archaeological Park
items.description: A sprawling, semi-wild park layering a thousand years of ruins — the Jamali-Kamali mosque and tomb, Balban's tomb, stepwells and Metcalfe's colonial folly — almost none of it ticketed or crowded. Go with a heritage guide and stout shoes; it is the connoisseur's counterpoint to the polished Qutub complex next door, best for a cool-season morning.

items.name: Agrasen ki Baoli
items.description: A dramatic 60-metre stepwell of 108 stone steps descending into shadow, hidden among the high-rises off Connaught Place — atmospheric, faintly eerie and beloved of photographers and film crews. A quick, striking stop between Lutyens' sights; go early before the Instagram crowd fills the steps, and let the sheer geometry of the descent do its work.

items.name: Bikaner House
items.description: The restored Delhi residence of the Maharaja of Bikaner at the India Gate hexagon, now a serious contemporary-arts venue hosting the city's best rotating gallery shows, design fairs and a satellite programme during India Art Fair week. Time a visit to whatever exhibition is up, then lunch at Chor Bizarre or L'Opéra on the premises; entry to the galleries is free.

items.name: Kiran Nadar Museum of Art (KNMA)
items.description: India's leading private art museum, holding one of the finest collections of modern and contemporary Indian art — Husain, Gaitonde, Sher-Gil and a strong contemporary program — with free entry and ambitious curation. A polished, air-conditioned hour or two for serious art-lovers; a landmark new building near the airport is in the works, so the Saket galleries are the current home.

items.name: Chhatarpur Temple (Shri Adya Katyayani Shakti Peeth)
items.description: One of India's largest temple complexes, a sprawling white confection of carved marble and pink sandstone shrines set in gardens on Delhi's southern edge, thronged especially during Navratri. It is a study in the exuberance of modern Hindu temple-building rather than antiquity — a striking, uncrowded-by-tourist stop en route to or from the Qutub and Mehrauli.

items.name: Purana Qila (Old Fort)
items.description: The massive walls of the sixteenth-century citadel of Sher Shah Suri and Humayun, said to sit on the legendary site of Indraprastha of the Mahabharata — with a graceful mosque, an octagonal library tower, and archaeological digs that keep pushing Delhi's history deeper. Quiet, monumental, and beside the Delhi Zoo; go early and let the ramparts and the boating lake set the mood.

items.name: Jantar Mantar
items.description: Maharaja Jai Singh II's masterful astronomical instruments of 1724 — giant masonry sundials and celestial dials built to chart the heavens with the naked eye — standing in a garden minutes from Connaught Place. A short, cerebral stop that rewards a guide who can explain how each surreal red structure actually measures time and the stars.

items.name: Gandhi Smriti (Birla House)
items.description: The house where Mahatma Gandhi spent his last 144 days and was assassinated in 1948, preserved as a moving memorial with his spartan room left as it was and his final footsteps marked across the garden. A quiet, essential half-hour of modern Indian history, close to the Lutyens' hotels and often paired with the National Gandhi Museum near Raj Ghat.

items.name: Raj Ghat
items.description: The riverside memorial marking Gandhi's cremation — a simple black marble platform, an eternal flame and a lawn where visiting heads of state come to lay wreaths. Understated and contemplative; slip your shoes off, and pair it with the nearby memorials to India's other prime ministers along the Yamuna if the mood is reflective.

items.name: Old Delhi Food Walk
items.description: A guided crawl through the alleys around Chandni Chowk and Jama Masjid — Mughlai kebabs and nihari, jalebis fried in ghee, kachoris, kulfi and Karim's — is the tastiest single day in Delhi. Book a reputable private walk that curates the hygienic legends; vegetarian and Jain-friendly itineraries are easy to arrange, from Paranthe Wali Gali to the sweet shops of Ghantewala's heirs.

items.name: Nizamuddin & Nizamuddin East Walk
items.description: A single walkable knot holds the Dargah, the tomb of the poet Amir Khusrau, Ghalib's memorial, Chausath Khamba and the exquisite Barapula-era monuments — seven centuries of Sufi Delhi in a few hundred metres. The Aga Khan Trust's neighbourhood renewal has made it navigable; a specialist guide turns the tangle into one of the richest heritage walks in India.

items.name: Jama Masjid to Feroz Shah Kotla
items.description: The ruined fourteenth-century citadel of Feroz Shah Tughlaq, crowned by a polished Ashokan pillar the sultan hauled from Ambala and re-erected — and famous today for the crowds who leave letters to the djinns in its cellars every Thursday. An offbeat, atmospheric ruin for those who have done the headline forts and want the stranger Delhi.

items.name: Sulabh International Museum of Toilets
items.description: One of the world's genuinely unusual museums, tracing 4,500 years of sanitation from Harappan drains to ornate Victorian commodes — quirky, oddly fascinating, and regularly listed among the strangest museums on earth. A short, memorable detour with children or the incurably curious; not everyone's stop, but nobody forgets it.

items.name: Garden of Five Senses
items.description: A twenty-acre landscaped park near Mehrauli threaded with sculpture, themed gardens, terraced rockeries and an evening food-and-shopping plaza — designed for wandering rather than monument-ticking. A relaxed sunset stroll, popular with Delhi families, and an easy add-on when you are already out at the Qutub or Chhatarpur.

items.name: Sarojini Nagar & Janpath Markets
items.description: The city's great bargain bazaars — Sarojini for export-surplus fashion at a fraction of retail, Janpath for Rajasthani textiles, silver and trinkets. Not luxury, but a gleefully local thing to do: send an assistant or go with a savvy friend, haggle hard, and come away with a bag of finds. A fun counterweight to a Khan Market afternoon.

items.name: Kingsway Camp & Coronation Park
items.description: The forlorn field where the 1911 Delhi Durbar crowned George V, now a haunting open-air graveyard of exiled Raj statues — a colossal George V, viceroys and generals — banished from the city centre after Independence. Utterly offbeat and a little melancholy; a stop for history obsessives and photographers rather than the casual visitor.

items.name: Taj Mahal & Agra Day Trip
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Taj Mahal; UNESCO — Agra Fort
items.description: The obvious and unimpeachable day trip: Shah Jahan's marble tomb to Mumtaz Mahal, plus Agra Fort and the jewel-like 'Baby Taj', roughly three hours down the Yamuna Expressway or under two by the Gatimaan Express. Do it with a private car and guide, start before dawn for the Taj at sunrise, and consider a night at the Oberoi Amarvilas with its every-room Taj view rather than rushing back.

items.name: Neemrana Fort-Palace Day Trip
items.description: A restored 15th-century Aravalli hill-fort turned India's first heritage hotel, about two hours from Delhi on the Jaipur road — terraced ramparts, hanging gardens, a spa and a Flying Fox zipline off the battlements. A civilised lunch-and-walk day, or a serene overnight to break the Delhi–Jaipur drive; non-residents can book the palace lunch and tour.

items.name: Mathura & Vrindavan Day Trip
items.description: The birthplace of Krishna and the town of his youth, a cluster of thousands of temples and ghats about three to four hours south of Delhi — most intense during the Holi celebrations, which are legendary here. A private car and a temple-savvy guide make the crowds manageable; go for the living devotion, the Banke Bihari temple and the evening aarti on the Yamuna.

items.name: Sultanpur National Park & Bird Sanctuary
items.description: A compact wetland reserve about an hour from central Delhi that draws migratory flamingos, pelicans, storks and hundreds of species through the winter months. An easy, gentle morning with binoculars and a naturalist for birders and multi-generational groups wanting green quiet near the city; best from November to March.

items.name: Cycle Tour of New Delhi at Dawn
items.description: Before the city wakes, a guided cycle through the empty avenues of Lutyens' Delhi and the sleeping lanes of Old Delhi — past Rashtrapati Bhavan, the war memorial and the wholesale bazaars stirring to life — is the most magical way to feel the two Delhis. Operators provide good bikes and small groups; the cool air and empty roads make it worth the early alarm.

items.name: Indian Accent
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India Top Restaurant Awards — Top 3 in India
items.description: India's most celebrated modern-Indian table — inventive, vegetable-forward cooking that reads the country back to itself.

items.name: Bukhara
credentials: NDTV Food Awards 2026 — Legendary Restaurant of India
items.description: The legendary North-West Frontier grill since 1979 — dal Bukhara and tandoori meats that have fed presidents and champions.

items.name: Dum Pukht
items.description: Regal Awadhi slow-cooking — the sealed-handi biryani and kakori kebabs that define Lucknowi grandeur in Delhi.

items.name: Le Cirque
items.area: Lutyens' / Central Delhi (The Leela Palace New Delhi)
credentials: Travel + Leisure India — Delicious Dining Awards nominee (2026)
items.description: The reimagined Franco-Italian icon atop The Leela Palace — the most polished European fine-dining room in the capital.

items.name: INJA
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 14
items.description: India-meets-Japan on the plate — a confident, playful fusion that has won both the lists and the room.

items.name: Comorin
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 26
items.description: Manish Mehrotra's all-day Indian comfort table — regional classics and unexpected combinations, with a serious bar.

items.name: Megu
items.area: Lutyens' / Central Delhi (The Leela Palace New Delhi)
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 18
items.description: Refined contemporary Japanese in The Leela Palace — sushi, robata and a hushed, grown-up room.

items.name: Olive Bar & Kitchen
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 6
items.description: Whitewashed Mediterranean courtyards beside the Qutub Minar — Delhi's original see-and-be-seen garden restaurant.

items.name: Tres
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 29
items.description: A long-running European bistro that quietly keeps its standards — honest, seasonal, unfussy cooking.

items.name: Nisaba
credentials: NDTV Food Awards 2026 — Best Opening of the Year
items.description: Manish Mehrotra's first restaurant under his own name — a much-anticipated table set within the Humayun's Tomb complex.

items.name: Bhawan
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 49
items.description: A spirited take on regional Indian street and home cooking — bold, affordable and genuinely fun.

items.name: Karim's
credentials: Time Out Delhi — landmark Old Delhi institution
110+ years; recognised heritage restaurant of the capital
items.description: Since 1913 — the definitive Old Delhi Mughlai kitchen, from a family that once cooked for the last Mughal court.

items.name: 1911 Bar
credentials: Inside The Imperial — MICHELIN Two Keys (2025)
items.description: The colonnaded colonial-era bar at The Imperial — rare whiskies beneath 1930s Lutyens grandeur.

items.name: Lair
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Bars 2025 — No. 8 (Best Bar in India)
items.description: A moody basement speakeasy with a Funktion-One system and a tiered menu — India's best bar, in Asia's top ten.

items.name: Sidecar
items.area: South Delhi (Greater Kailash II, M-Block Market)
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — former list member
items.description: Yangdup Lama and Minakshi Singh's modern classic — the first Indian bar to make both Asia's and the World's 50 Best.

items.name: Home
items.description: A multi-room drinking den that helped put Delhi on the regional bar map — inventive, homey and full of ideas.

items.name: PCO (Pass Code Only)
credentials: The World's 50 Best Discovery — recognised bar
items.description: The faux phone-booth speakeasy that started Delhi's hidden-bar movement in 2012 — still one of its most stylish rooms.

items.name: Cirrus 9
items.area: Lutyens' / Central Delhi (The Oberoi, New Delhi)
credentials: Inside The Oberoi, New Delhi — MICHELIN One Key (2025)
items.description: The Oberoi's rooftop bar — city-light views, careful cocktails and the calm precision of the house.

items.title: Private dawn at Humayun's Tomb
items.description: The great Mughal garden-tomb before the gates open properly, with a historian.

items.title: Old Delhi food walk through Chandni Chowk
items.description: A private crawl through the lanes for parathas, kebabs and sweets most visitors miss.

items.title: Heritage haveli dinner
items.description: A private table in a restored old-city mansion, cooking the refined dishes of the Mughal court.

items.title: Private tour of Lutyens' Delhi
items.description: A drive through the colonial capital's avenues and India Gate with a guide who knows the history.

plan.heading: 3 days in New Delhi, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Check into The Oberoi, New Delhi, overlooking the golf course and Humayun's Tomb.

slots.label: Afternoon

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Indian Accent at The Lodhi, Manish Mehrotra's inventive Indian tasting menu.

slots.label: Morning

slots.label: Afternoon

slots.label: Evening

slots.label: Afternoon

slots.label: Evening

items.description: Broad green avenues and the grand hotels — calm and well-connected.

items.name: Old Delhi (Shahjahanabad)
items.description: The Mughal walled city of lanes and mosques — intense and unmissable by day.

items.name: South Delhi (Hauz Khas / Mehrauli)
items.description: Village ruins, boutiques and restaurants — for a younger, greener stay.

events.name: Republic Day parade
events.note: The nation's grand military and cultural parade down Kartavya Path.

events.name: Diwali
events.note: The festival of lights transforms the city with lamps and fireworks; date follows the lunar calendar.

events.name: Qutub / India Art Fair season
events.note: India's leading art fair draws collectors, alongside heritage festivals in the cooler months.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Arrive at Indira Gandhi International Airport (DEL) Terminal 3, where a chauffeured car and, on request, fast-track immigration meet you at the aerobridge.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with driver is essential across Delhi's distances; the metro is efficient but not how a UHNI traveller moves here.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Excellent 5G and hotel wifi; an Indian eSIM or Airtel/Jio SIM is simple, though most arrivals rely on their concierge's device.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Indian rupee (INR); cards work everywhere formal, keep cash for markets and drivers, and tipping around ten percent is customary.

onGround.note: Stay in Lutyens' Delhi (Aman, The Oberoi, The Imperial) for calm and proximity; air quality dips sharply October to January, so plan indoor mornings then.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Oct-Mar is the kind window, crisp and clear for the monuments; Nov-Jan can bring heavy morning fog and hazardous air. Avoid Apr-Jun, when heat pushes past 40C, and the Jul-Sep monsoon humidity.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Home hub: Indira Gandhi International (DEL) is a primary origin, so no connection needed from Delhi and a short 2-2.5 hour hop from Mumbai or Bengaluru on Vistara or IndiGo. Terminal 3 is the premium terminal; use the Air India or Plaza Premium lounges, and pre-arrange chauffeur pickup to skip the arrivals crush.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: Routine vaccines plus Hepatitis A and typhoid advised; drink only sealed or filtered water. Delhi is generally safe in the central and diplomatic areas with sensible discretion; the genuine concern is winter air quality (Nov-Jan), which can be severe for anyone sensitive.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Effortless for vegetarian and Jain travellers; most fine kitchens keep dedicated Jain preparations. This is Indian food at its source, from Bukhara and Dum Pukht to Indian Accent for a modern vegetarian tasting menu.
