seo.title: Doha — TripAgent
seo.description: Doha, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Doha
hero.tagline: Gulf capital of bold museums and desert sea.

ourTake.lede: Doha has become a genuinely serious cultural stop, not just a stopover. Give it two full days: the Museum of Islamic Art is world-class, and the restored Msheireb quarter and the Souq Waqif are best walked in the evening cool. Time a visit around National Day if you can — the waterfront comes alive.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a compact, refined Gulf stay built around world-class museums and a short, easy flight.
ourTake.skipIf: You want a week of variety; Doha rewards a focused few days more than a long stay.

firstLook.heroCaption: Palm-flanked pool with sculpture toward sea

grid.caption: Modern pool villa with palms and umbrella
purple allium blooms in soft focus

whenToGo.blurb: November to March is the only real window, warm days for the corniche, museums and desert; the jewellery and film weeks and National Day cluster here, and summer is best avoided entirely.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental, Doha
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide 5-Star (2025, sixth consecutive year)
items.description: The group's quiet precision, dropped into the restored heart of the old city.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Doha
items.description: The surest hands in the city — service you never have to think about, on its own beach.

items.name: Raffles Doha
items.description: Qatar's first all-suite house, inside the crossed-sabre towers — theatre with Raffles butlers.

items.name: Rosewood Doha
items.description: A soaring twin-tower newcomer that took a Forbes Five-Star in its first year.

items.name: Four Seasons Resort and Residences at The Pearl-Qatar
items.description: A marina-side resort address on the man-made island, with Four Seasons ease throughout.

items.name: Sharq Village & Spa, a Ritz-Carlton Hotel
items.description: A low-slung Qatari 'village' by the sea — the calm, traditional counterpoint to the towers.

items.name: The Chedi Katara Hotel & Resort, Doha
items.description: GHM's understated design ideal beside the cultural village and its private beach.

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton, Doha
items.description: A grand marina resort with its own beach and yacht berths — classic Ritz-Carlton scale.

items.name: The St. Regis Doha
items.description: A palatial Gulf-front retreat with the signature St. Regis butler on every floor.

items.name: Waldorf Astoria Doha Lusail
items.description: New-city grandeur on the Lusail waterfront — polished, spacious, of the moment.

items.name: Marsa Malaz Kempinski, The Pearl-Doha
items.description: A palace-scaled island house at the gateway to The Pearl — unabashedly grand.

items.name: Fairmont Doha
items.description: The second of the crossed-sabre towers — gold-leaf glamour on a grand scale.

items.name: The Ned Doha
items.description: A landmark government building reborn as a members'-club-and-hotel with real buzz.

items.name: Mondrian Doha
items.description: Maximalist, design-forward drama for the member who wants the volume turned up.

items.name: W Doha
items.description: A high-energy design house in the business district — for celebrations, not quiet nights.

items.name: Banyan Tree Doha
items.description: A spa-led vertical retreat with a sky-high pool over the downtown skyline.

items.name: Banana Island Resort Doha by Anantara
items.description: A ferry-only island escape with over-water villas — the closest thing to a beach holiday off Doha.

items.name: The Plaza Doha, LXR Hotels & Resorts
items.description: A jewel-box LXR house in the walkable downtown quarter, all quiet polish.

items.name: InterContinental Doha Beach & Spa
items.description: A long-established beach resort with the city's largest private stretch of sand.

items.name: Waldorf Astoria Doha West Bay
items.description: A polished business-district tower with Waldorf Astoria service at a gentler price.

items.name: Museum of Islamic Art
credentials: Designed by I.M. Pei — his final museum commission
items.description: I.M. Pei's last great building rises out of the bay like a stack of cubes, holding one of the world's finest collections of Islamic art across three continents and 1,400 years. A private curator-led morning suits multi-generational families, and the fifth-floor IDAM restaurant makes an unhurried lunch with skyline views.

items.name: National Museum of Qatar
items.description: Jean Nouvel's 'desert rose' of 600 interlocking sand-coloured discs wraps around the restored 20th-century royal palace, telling Qatar's story through vast 360-degree film galleries. It is visual, walkable and captivating for children and grandparents alike, and the on-site Jiwan restaurant does an elegant Qatari tasting menu.

items.name: Souq Waqif
items.description: The beating heart of old Doha — restored mud-rendered lanes of spice stalls, oud perfumers, textile and gold merchants, and open-air cafes where families linger over mint tea and shisha. A private guide can time an evening visit around the cooler air and steer you to the best vegetarian mezze houses.

items.name: Katara Cultural Village
items.description: A purpose-built seafront village of galleries, an open-air amphitheatre for 5,000, and two jewel-box mosques — the blue-tiled Katara Mosque and the shimmering Golden Mosque. Free to enter, easy to wander, and lined with restaurants that make it a relaxed multi-generational half-day.

items.name: The Pearl-Qatar
items.description: A man-made island of Riviera-style marinas, superyachts and flagship boutiques, with the Venice-inspired Qanat Quartier and its pastel canals. Ideal for an evening stroll, waterfront dining and discreet luxury shopping, with the Marsa Malaz Kempinski palace hotel anchoring one end.

items.name: Msheireb Downtown Doha
items.description: One of the world's first smart, sustainable regenerated city centres — cool pale-stone streets, wind-tower shade and contemporary Qatari architecture, walking distance from Souq Waqif. A calm, cerebral counterpoint to the souq for slower afternoons.

items.name: Msheireb Museums
items.description: Four restored 1900s heritage houses — Bin Jelmood, Company House, Mohammed Bin Jassim and Radwani — trace Qatar's oil story, community life and a candid history of slavery in the Gulf. Thoughtful, air-conditioned and free, and a meaningful stop for older children and grandparents.

items.name: Doha Corniche
items.description: A seven-kilometre crescent promenade curving around the bay, framing the West Bay skyline on one side and traditional dhows on the other. Best walked at dusk or early morning; a private car can drop and collect at either end for older travellers.

items.name: West Bay skyline & viewpoints
items.description: Doha's cluster of futuristic towers — the twisting Tornado Tower, the Doha Tower and their neighbours — is the postcard image of the city, best seen from a dhow on the bay or a high sky-bar at golden hour. A discreet way to bookend a day of culture with a drink and a view.

items.name: MIA Park & '7' by Richard Serra
credentials: '7' — Richard Serra's tallest sculpture and first public work in the Middle East
items.description: The landscaped park behind the Museum of Islamic Art runs out to a 24-metre steel monument by Richard Serra — his tallest work and first public sculpture in the Middle East, echoing the number seven's meaning in Islam. Space for children to run and one of the finest skyline photo spots in Doha.

items.name: Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art
credentials: World's largest collection of modern and contemporary Arab art
items.description: The world's largest collection of modern and contemporary Arab art — over 9,000 works from the 1840s to today — housed in a converted school in Education City. A serious, quieter museum for guests who want depth beyond the headline icons.

items.name: 3-2-1 Qatar Olympic and Sports Museum
items.description: A vivid, interactive sports museum shaped like the five Olympic rings, tracing global sporting history alongside Qatar's own. Hands-on challenges and simulators make it a genuine hit with children and teenagers.

items.name: Falcon Souq
items.description: A dedicated corner of Souq Waqif where prized hunting falcons perch hooded on gloved stands and are traded for eye-watering sums — a living window into Qatari heritage. Guides can arrange a respectful, unhurried visit that fascinates all ages.

items.name: Souq Waqif Falcon Hospital
items.description: A state-of-the-art three-storey hospital, subsidised by the Emir, that treats up to 150 birds a day in falconry season — from chipped talons to feather transplants. An unexpected, memorable stop that a private guide can slot in beside the Falcon Souq.

items.name: Qatar National Library
items.description: Rem Koolhaas's angular concrete-and-glass hall folds down into a sunken travertine 'heritage' pit holding 4,000 rare manuscripts and a 1478 Ptolemaic map. A design pilgrimage for the architecturally curious, and a serene, cool space to pause.

items.name: Dhow cruise on Doha Bay
items.description: A traditional wooden dhow gliding across the bay is the classic way to take in the West Bay skyline, day or night. Charter one privately for the family, with a table set for a sunset meal and the option to keep it fully vegetarian.

items.name: Khor Al Adaid (the Inland Sea)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List — Khor Al-Adaid Natural Reserve
items.description: A UNESCO-tentative natural reserve where towering dunes tumble straight into a tidal sea lagoon — one of very few places on earth this happens. Reachable only by 4x4 with an expert driver; a private convoy with a chef-catered majlis camp turns it into an unforgettable desert day.

items.name: Sealine desert & dunes
items.description: Under an hour south of Doha, the Sealine dunes are the launch point for dune bashing, sandboarding, quad biking and camel rides across rolling golden sand. A private guide can tailor the intensity — gentle camel rides for grandparents, adrenaline runs for teenagers.

items.name: Al Zubarah Archaeological Site
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Al Zubarah Archaeological Site
items.description: Roughly 105 km northwest of Doha, this walled 18th-19th-century pearling and trading town is the best-preserved of its kind in the Gulf, paired with a handsome restored fort. A rewarding half-day drive for history-minded families with a knowledgeable guide.

items.name: Aspire Park & the Torch
items.description: Doha's largest park — 88 hectares of lawns, a lake and shaded walks — sits beneath the 300-metre Torch tower with its revolving restaurant and vertiginous observation deck. Green space for children by day, skyline dining by night.

items.name: Villaggio Mall
items.description: A Venetian-themed mall with a painted-sky ceiling and real gondola rides along an indoor canal, packed with luxury and family brands and connected to the Torch by covered walkway. A cool, playful afternoon that keeps children entertained while adults shop.

items.name: Place Vendôme Mall
credentials: Home to the largest Louis Vuitton store in the Middle East
items.description: A $1.3bn French-classical mega-mall in Lusail — home to the Middle East's largest Louis Vuitton, flagship Cartier and Bvlgari, and an hourly dancing-fountain show over a 7,400 sqm canal. The pinnacle of discreet Doha luxury shopping and evening dining.

items.name: Banana Island Resort by Anantara
items.description: A crescent-shaped private island a 30-minute catamaran ride from the city, with a long private beach, over-water villas, a surf pool, bowling and cinema — and it is entirely alcohol-free. A day pass or overnight makes a serene multi-generational escape.

items.name: Camel racing at Al Shahaniya
items.description: About an hour from Doha, thoroughbred racing camels thunder down the track steered by robot jockeys while owners follow in 4x4s alongside — a genuinely surreal Qatari spectacle. Early-morning training runs are the atmospheric time to watch with a guide.

items.name: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum
items.description: A private collector's 'cabinet of curiosities' of over 30,000 objects — from Jurassic fossils and Islamic art to vintage cars and the world's largest private sword collection. Endlessly surprising, and a favourite of curious children on the drive out to the desert.

items.name: Katara Towers (Raffles & Fairmont)
items.description: The crescent-shaped twin towers, modelled on the crossed sabres of Qatar's coat of arms, house the Raffles and Fairmont hotels and the city's largest ballroom. Even for non-guests it is a striking architectural stop and a polished spot for afternoon tea.

items.name: Lusail Boulevard & Marina
items.description: Qatar's 'city of the future' laid out along a grand pedestrian boulevard of cafes, boutiques and seasonal drone light shows, running down to a yacht-lined marina promenade. A relaxed evening for families once the desert heat lifts.

items.name: Al Wakrah Souq & dhow harbour
items.description: A beautifully restored fishing-village souq south of Doha, with its own beach, boutique heritage hotels and a harbour full of traditional dhows. Quieter and more atmospheric than the main souq — lovely for an unhurried lunch by the water.

items.name: Purple Island (Bin Ghannam) mangroves
items.description: A peaceful peninsula near Al Khor named for its ancient purple-dye industry, threaded with mangrove creeks best explored by kayak among wading birds. A gentle nature outing that guides can arrange with stable double kayaks for mixed-ability groups.

items.name: Barzan Towers
items.description: A pair of restored late-19th-century watchtowers about 15 km north of Doha, once used to guard water and to sight the moon for the Islamic calendar. A quick, free, atmospheric stop that pairs well with a northern day-trip.

items.name: Fire Station: Artists in Residence
items.description: A former civil-defence fire station near central Doha reborn as a contemporary art complex — studios, changing exhibitions, a cinema and a well-regarded cafe. A cool, low-key stop for guests who like their culture current rather than curated.

items.name: Al Thuraya Planetarium
items.description: A modern planetarium within Katara Cultural Village blending astronomy with the history of Arab celestial navigation under a full-dome sky. A charming, air-conditioned option that delights younger children on a Katara afternoon.

items.name: Al Bidda Park
items.description: A large, gently landscaped park hugging the Corniche with shaded walks, play areas and easy skyline views. A convenient green breather between the museums and the waterfront for families with small children.

items.name: Aspire Zone & Khalifa International Stadium
items.description: Qatar's flagship sports precinct, home to the historic Khalifa International Stadium and world-class facilities from the 2022 World Cup era. Stadium tours and the surrounding parkland make an easy outing for sport-minded travellers and teenagers.

items.name: Galeries Lafayette Doha (Katara Plaza)
items.description: The French department-store landmark reimagined at Katara, gathering luxury fashion, beauty and a gourmet food hall under one elegant roof. A refined, unhurried shopping stop steps from the cultural village.

items.name: Gold Souq
items.description: A dedicated lane within the souq district where cases glitter with 21- and 22-karat gold and intricate Gulf jewellery, prices set largely by weight. A guide who knows the trusted merchants makes buying — or simply marvelling — a comfortable experience.

items.name: Doha Oyster & Pearl Monument
items.description: The much-photographed sculpture of an oyster cradling a giant pearl, honouring Qatar's pre-oil pearling heritage on the West Bay waterfront. A quick, iconic photo stop woven into a Corniche drive.

items.name: Doha Metro (Msheireb station)
items.description: A driverless, marble-and-vaulted metro that is a design attraction in its own right, with Msheireb the palatial central interchange. A cool, novel way to hop between museums and Education City that even luxury travellers enjoy for a stop or two.

items.name: Qatar National Convention Centre (Sidra Tree)
items.description: A dramatic Arata Isozaki building whose facade branches like the sidra tree that shelters poets and scholars in Qatari lore. Worth a photo pass on any Education City visit for the architecture alone.

items.name: Education City public art & mosque
credentials: Features Damien Hirst's 'The Miraculous Journey' sculptures
items.description: The Qatar Foundation campus doubles as an open-air gallery — Damien Hirst's monumental 'Miraculous Journey' bronzes outside Sidra Medicine and the striking calligraphy-clad Education City Mosque. A quiet, cultured drive-through with a knowledgeable guide.

items.name: Souq Al Wakra beach & heritage hotels
items.description: The restored waterfront at Al Wakra pairs a golden public beach with boutique heritage stays built into the old souq's coral-stone houses. A restful seaside afternoon away from the city's pace, easily private-guided.

items.name: Doha's public art trail
items.description: Beyond Serra's '7', Doha has seeded world-class art across the city — from airport and Hamad hospital commissions to sculptures dotting parks and roundabouts. A curator-led art drive stitches the highlights into a single, cultured half-day.

items.name: Katara Beach & Katara Hills
items.description: A 1.5-kilometre family-friendly beach with watersports and parasailing sits beside the cultural village, backed by the twin Katara Hills for sea views. An easy way to add a little sun and sand to a culture-heavy Katara day.

items.name: IDAM by Alain Ducasse
credentials: MENA's 50 Best #44 (2026, Best Restaurant in Qatar)
items.description: Ducasse's French-Mediterranean, on the museum's top floor, with Doha Bay filling the glass.

items.name: Alba
items.description: Piedmontese cooking of real refinement inside the crossed-sabre towers — Doha's newest star.

items.name: Nobu Doha
items.area: Four Seasons Hotel Doha, West Bay
items.description: The largest Nobu in the world, floating over the Gulf — the black cod that conquered the planet.

items.name: Carbone Doha
items.description: The New York Italian-American theatre — tableside Caesar, veal parm and red sauce, done grandly.

items.name: Curiosa by Jean-Georges
items.description: Jean-Georges Vongerichten's playful, produce-led cooking in a jewel-box island room.

items.name: Jamavar
items.description: The Leela's grand pan-Indian house — the first Indian restaurant to win a Doha star.

items.name: Jiwan
items.description: Modern Qatari cooking under the museum's desert-rose roof — heritage, elevated.

items.name: Zuma Doha
items.description: The izakaya benchmark that never empties — precise, buzzy, endlessly reliable.

items.name: Hakkasan Doha
items.description: The Cantonese standard-bearer — dim sum and lacquered duck in a low-lit lattice room.

items.name: Morimoto Doha
items.description: Iron Chef Masaharu Morimoto's Japanese, staged with Mondrian theatre.

items.name: COYA Doha
items.description: Peruvian colour and pisco energy — ceviche, anticuchos and a room that never quiets.

items.name: La Mar Doha by Gastón Acurio
items.area: InterContinental Doha Beach & Spa, West Bay
items.description: Gastón Acurio's seaside Peruvian — bright cebiches and a long beachfront terrace.

items.name: La Petite Maison (LPM) Doha
items.description: Riviera cooking and a room that has never gone out of fashion — the Niçoise classic.

items.name: Gymkhana Doha
items.description: The Sethi family's colonial-club Indian — smoke, spice and swagger, carried from Mayfair.

items.name: Masala Library Doha
items.description: Jiggs Kalra's progressive Indian — familiar flavours, reimagined with a light modern hand.

items.name: Em Sherif Doha
items.description: Beirut's grand Lebanese table — an endless, generous procession of mezze.

items.name: Shanghai Me Doha
items.description: 1930s-Shanghai glamour and pan-Asian cooking with real intent.

items.name: Hoppers
items.description: Sri Lankan and South Indian home cooking — hoppers, kari and roti done with real soul.

items.name: Isaan
items.description: Northeastern Thai cooking with genuine fire and fragrance — a Bib-listed favourite.

items.name: Argan
items.description: Generous, aromatic Moroccan cooking — tagines and pastilla with a proper hand.

items.name: Mila
items.description: Bright Mediterranean and Levantine sharing plates in the Rosewood's newest room.

items.name: Berenjak Al Maha Island
items.description: Tehran's back-street kebab houses recreated over coals — hearty, smoky, generous.

items.name: Baron
items.description: Characterful, generous Mediterranean cooking — a Beirut name that earned its Bib in Doha.

items.name: Dalchini
items.description: Indian-Chinese and pan-Asian comfort cooking with a devoted local following.

items.name: Dar Yema
items.description: Qatari home cooking preserved and served with pride — a rare taste of the real thing.

items.name: Fenyal
items.description: Vibrant, pocket-friendly Khaleeji cooking — falafel, lamb kofta and proper Arabic coffee.

items.name: The lounge bar at Rosewood Doha
credentials: Within Rosewood Doha (Forbes 5-Star, MICHELIN One Key)
items.description: A polished sky-lounge in the twin-tower newcomer that took a Forbes Five-Star in its first year — a smart, contemporary place to begin the evening.

items.name: Ambar, Mandarin Oriental
credentials: Within Mandarin Oriental, Doha (Forbes 5-Star, MICHELIN One Key)
items.description: The quietly assured lounge in the group's Msheireb house — considered cocktails and artisanal bites, in the calmest, most central address in the city.

items.name: Nobu Doha rooftop lounge
credentials: Within Four Seasons Hotel Doha (Forbes 5-Star, MICHELIN One Key)
items.description: The bar level of the largest Nobu in the world — a three-storey pavilion over the Gulf, cocktails and tapas with the West Bay skyline in the glass.

items.name: The rooftop bar at Raffles Doha
credentials: Within Raffles Doha (Forbes 5-Star, MICHELIN Two Keys)
items.description: Live soul and jazz and 360-degree views from inside the crossed-sabre towers — the highest, most theatrical drink in the new city.

items.title: Private view at the Museum of Islamic Art
items.description: I.M. Pei's final major building, with one of the finest Islamic-art collections anywhere, seen before opening.

items.title: A traditional dhow sailing at sunset
items.description: Out on the bay with the West Bay skyline behind you, the way Doha was crossed for generations.

items.title: Falcon souq and desert to the Inland Sea
items.description: A 4x4 run to Khor Al Adaid, the rare place where the dunes meet the sea, on the Saudi border.

items.title: Private tour of the National Museum of Qatar
items.description: Jean Nouvel's desert-rose structure, walked with a guide who unpacks the country's story.

plan.heading: 3 days in Doha, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Walk I.M. Pei's Museum of Islamic Art at opening, then the sculpture park on the water.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Check into the Mandarin Oriental in Msheireb, lunch, then the restored lanes of Msheireb Downtown.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at IDAM, Alain Ducasse's room atop the Museum of Islamic Art, with the skyline across the bay.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Coffee and the falcon souq at Souq Waqif while the morning is cool.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Drive south to the Khor Al Adaid inland sea, where the dunes meet the Gulf, with a private guide.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return for dinner at Jiwan by Alain Ducasse at the National Museum of Qatar, Jean Nouvel's desert-rose building.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The collections at Mathaf and the National Museum of Qatar, then the boutiques of Place Vendôme.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A dhow out to the old pearl banks off Al Wakrah, lunch aboard.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at Toro Toro, then drinks high over West Bay.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: West Bay
items.description: For skyline hotels and the corporate polish; convenient but glassy and car-dependent.

items.name: Msheireb Downtown
items.description: For the walkable, restored heart of old Doha — low-rise, cultured, and near the souq.

items.name: The Pearl
items.description: For marina living, waterfront dining and a resort feel a short drive from the centre.

events.name: Qatar National Day
events.note: A waterfront parade, air and sea displays and fireworks marking the country's unification.

events.name: Ajyal Film Festival
events.note: The Doha Film Institute's week-long festival at Katara, screenings and culture for all ages.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Land at Hamad International (DOH), consistently rated among the world's finest airports, where Al Maha meet-and-assist walks you through immigration to a waiting chauffeured car for the short run into the city.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car covers the distances; the Corniche, Msheireb and Souq Waqif are best explored on foot, and a traditional dhow makes an elegant way to see the West Bay skyline from the water.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: An eSIM from Ooredoo or Vodafone Qatar gives fast 5G on arrival; wifi is excellent throughout hotels and the airport.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Qatari riyal (QAR), pegged to the dollar; cards are standard, cash is handy in the souq, and tipping is appreciated but not expected as service charges apply.

onGround.note: The Pearl and West Bay are the polished places to stay; Qatar is more conservative than the UAE, so dress modestly in public, and alcohol is confined to licensed hotel venues. The National Museum and Museum of Islamic Art are unmissable and never crowded.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: November to March is the kind season: mild 22-27C days, clear skies for the Corniche and desert. Avoid June-September, when heat exceeds 42C with heavy humidity off the Gulf.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru, roughly 4 hours. Qatar Airways flies it best; its Qsuite business product is class-leading, with first-class comfort in a business cabin. Al Mourjan and the Al Safwa first lounge at Hamad International are outstanding for onward connections across Qatar's global network.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required beyond routine; hepatitis A and typhoid advisable. Extremely safe and orderly. Tap water is desalinated and safe, bottled is customary. Summer heat is the main concern.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Straightforward for vegetarian and Jain travellers. Indian cuisine is abundant and pure-veg is easily arranged. Saffron Lounge and the Indian kitchens across West Bay are dependable; luxury hotels handle Jain requirements on notice.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Doha, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Dubai — TripAgent
seo.description: Dubai, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Dubai
hero.tagline: Desert spectacle and skyline glamour at full throttle.

ourTake.lede: Dubai rewards travellers who look past the record-breaking numbers and treat the desert and the older creek city as seriously as the towers. Do the marquee sights (Burj Khalifa, the fountains) early or late to dodge both the crowds and the heat, and spend real time in a private desert camp and the Al Fahidi lanes, which is where the place actually breathes. Come between November and March; the summer is genuinely punishing and most outdoor pleasures shut down.
ourTake.comeIf: You want polished five-star ease, tax-free shopping and a beach-and-brunch rhythm three hours from home.
ourTake.skipIf: You are drawn to old-world texture, deep history or quiet, unmanicured places.

items.name: Four Seasons Resort Dubai at Jumeirah Beach

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Dubai International Financial Centre

items.name: Jumeirah Mina A'Salam

items.name: Raffles The Palm Dubai

items.name: Anantara The Palm Dubai Resort

items.name: Taj Dubai

items.name: Palazzo Versace Dubai

items.name: Atlantis The Palm

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton Dubai International Financial Centre

items.name: Waldorf Astoria Dubai Palm Jumeirah

items.area: Dubai Creek Harbour / Ras Al Khor
items.description: A serene creek-side address away from the strip, looking to the flamingos.

items.name: Le Royal Méridien Beach Resort & Spa
items.description: An established beach resort with gardens that have had time to grow.

items.name: FIVE Palm Jumeirah
items.description: The city's loudest pool party, for members who came to celebrate.

items.name: JW Marriott Marquis Hotel Dubai
items.description: Twin towers on the canal — big, capable, and easy on the wallet.

items.name: Shangri-La Dubai
items.description: A calm Asian-service tower on the main road, understated by Dubai standards.

items.name: Burj Khalifa — At the Top
credentials: Guinness World Record — tallest building in the world
items.description: The world's tallest building at 828m. Ride to the Level 124/125 deck, or book the quieter, pricier At the Top SKY (148) or a private table at The Lounge on 152-154 for canapés and champagne well above the crowds. Time it for late afternoon so you catch the city in daylight and then lit up at dusk.

items.name: The Dubai Fountain
items.description: The choreographed fountain on Burj Lake shoots water up to 150m to Arabic and world music, on the half-hour every evening. Free to watch from the Waterfront promenade; for a calmer view, book a lakeside table at a Souk Al Bahar restaurant or a short abra ride across the lake.

items.name: The Dubai Mall
items.description: One of the world's largest and most-visited malls, and the anchor of Downtown. Beyond 1,200 stores it holds the aquarium, an Olympic-size ice rink, and the fashion-avenue luxury wing. A practical base for a multi-generation family: air-conditioned, endless dining including plentiful Indian and vegetarian options, and direct access to the Burj and fountain.

items.name: Museum of the Future
items.description: The torus-shaped building wrapped in Arabic calligraphy is a landmark in its own right, and inside it is Dubai's most imaginative attraction — immersive, theatrical exhibits on space, ecology and wellbeing. Book a timed slot well ahead; it sells out. Genuinely engaging for teenagers and curious adults.

items.name: Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque (day trip)
credentials: Guinness World Record — largest hand-knotted carpet
items.description: About 90 minutes from Dubai, and the single most beautiful building in the UAE — 82 white-marble domes, the world's largest hand-knotted carpet, and reflecting pools that mirror the whole structure at dusk. Free to enter; modest dress required and abayas are lent to women at the gate. Go late afternoon for the light.

items.name: Old Dubai by abra across the Creek
items.description: Cross Dubai Creek on a wooden abra for a single dirham — the oldest, most atmospheric way to move through the city. It links the Deira souks with Bur Dubai's heritage quarter, and shows you the trading port the whole city grew from. Do it early morning or golden hour.

items.name: Gold Souk
items.description: Hundreds of shops in covered lanes with windows stacked in gold — one of the largest gold markets in the world, and a rite of passage for Indian visitors who know their carat and their making-charges. Prices track the daily rate, so bargain hard on the workmanship. Best in the cooler evening.

items.name: Spice Souk
items.description: A short walk from the Gold Souk, narrow alleys heaped with saffron, dried limes, frankincense, cardamom and chillies. More about the smell and colour than serious shopping, though the saffron and oud are worth buying. Pairs naturally with the abra and the gold market for a half-day in old Deira.

items.name: Al Fahidi Historical Neighbourhood
items.description: Dubai's best-preserved old quarter — coral-and-gypsum houses, wind-tower coolers and quiet sikkas (lanes) from the late 1800s. Wander the galleries, the Coffee Museum, and courtyard cafés, then join the cultural centre's guided walk. A rare slow, shaded corner of the city.

items.name: Al Shindagha Museum
items.description: The UAE's largest heritage museum — a stretch of restored waterfront houses telling the story of the Creek, pearling, perfume and the ruling family, with modern interactive displays. More substantial and better curated than the old Dubai Museum, and an easy, cool, family-friendly cultural afternoon.

items.name: Atlantis Aquaventure & The Lost Chambers
items.description: One of the world's largest waterparks, with record-height slides, a shark-and-ray lagoon and a private beach, plus the adjoining Lost Chambers aquarium of 65,000 marine animals. The standout family day on the Palm; stay at Atlantis The Palm or Atlantis The Royal for direct access and skip-the-queue ease.

items.name: The View at The Palm
items.description: An observation deck 240m up in the Palm Tower, giving the one photo everyone wants — the whole palm-shaped island laid out below with the sea and skyline beyond. Quieter and cheaper than the Burj Khalifa deck, and the best place to actually grasp the scale of the Palm. Book a sunset slot.

items.name: Burj Al Arab afternoon tea or dinner
items.description: The sail-shaped hotel is off-limits unless you have a reservation, so book afternoon tea in the atrium's Sahn Eddar or a table at the Skyview Bar to actually get inside the icon. The gold-leaf interiors are deliberately over the top; go for the experience and the view, not restraint.

items.name: Platinum Heritage luxury desert safari
items.description: The discerning way to do the desert — vintage 1950s Land Rovers in a protected reserve, falconry, camel treks and a private Bedouin-camp dinner, run by one of the few licensed conservation operators. Choose a private vehicle to skip the dune-bashing party crowds; excellent for families and multi-gen groups.

items.name: Louvre Abu Dhabi (day trip)
items.description: Jean Nouvel's museum under a vast latticed dome that scatters a 'rain of light' — a genuinely world-class collection spanning civilisations, from Da Vinci to regional antiquities. The building alone justifies the drive from Dubai. Pair with Qasr Al Watan or the Grand Mosque for a full Abu Dhabi day.

items.name: Qasr Al Watan (day trip)
items.description: The working presidential palace, opened to the public — a staggering display of domes, chandeliers and a mirrored Great Hall, plus a library and a genuinely good evening light-and-sound show on the façade. Dress smartly; it is a state building, not a theme park.

items.name: Jumeirah Mosque
items.description: One of the few Dubai mosques open to non-Muslims, via the Sheikh Mohammed Centre's 'Open Doors, Open Minds' guided tours where you can ask anything over Emirati coffee and dates. The most approachable window into local faith and custom, and beautifully lit at night from the outside.

items.name: Alserkal Avenue
items.description: A warehouse district turned contemporary-art hub — Dubai's serious galleries, artist studios, indie cinema, specialty coffee and concept stores, all in raw industrial units. Where the city's real creative scene lives, far from the malls. Check what's showing before you go; openings are the moment.

items.name: Jameel Arts Centre
items.description: A calm, well-funded contemporary-art museum on the Creek with rotating exhibitions, an art library, sculpture gardens and a rooftop. Free entry, rarely crowded, and a thoughtful counterpoint to Dubai's louder attractions. A good rainy-heat-of-day cultural stop.

items.name: Etihad Museum
items.description: Built on the spot where the UAE was founded in 1971, an elegant modern museum telling the story of unification through the original documents, films and the founding fathers. Compact, well-designed and the clearest explanation of how this country came to be.

items.name: Ras Al Khor Wildlife Sanctuary
items.description: A protected wetland minutes from Downtown where thousands of pink flamingos wade against a backdrop of skyscrapers. Free hides with binoculars look out over the lagoon; best in the cool winter months when migratory birds arrive. A surprising, peaceful hour for families and photographers.

items.name: Dubai Frame
items.description: A 150m golden picture-frame you ride to the top of, with a glass-floor skywalk and Old Dubai on one side, New Dubai on the other — the city's past-and-future divide made literal. Quick, cheap and photogenic; set inside Zabeel Park for a walk afterward.

items.name: Dubai Miracle Garden
credentials: Guinness World Record — largest vertical garden
items.description: The world's largest natural flower garden — over 150 million blooms shaped into arches, hearts and a flower-covered Emirates A380. Open only in the cool season (roughly November to May) and heaving with families; go on a weekday morning. Pure spectacle, and a hit with children.

items.name: Global Village
items.description: A seasonal cultural theme park where 90-plus countries set up pavilions of crafts, street food and shows — a lively bazaar-meets-carnival. Open winter only. Chaotic and fun for families and groups; a low-cost, high-energy evening with a strong South-Asian food presence.

items.name: Hatta (day trip)
items.description: A mountain enclave 90 minutes east — kayak the turquoise Hatta Dam, walk the 3,000-year-old Heritage Village, and drive the Hajar-mountain wadis. A complete change of scene from the city, cooler in the hills, and the closest real nature escape. Best October to April.

items.name: Ski Dubai
items.description: A full indoor snow resort inside a mall — real snow, ski and toboggan runs, and a colony of king and gentoo penguins you can meet. Absurd, and exactly why it delights children in the desert heat. Book the penguin encounter separately if that's the draw.

items.name: The Green Planet
items.description: An indoor tropical rainforest under a glass biodome — one of the region's largest indoor trees, sloths, snakes and free-flying birds across four humid levels. Compact, cool and hands-on; an easy 90 minutes that younger children love.

items.name: Ferrari World (day trip)
credentials: Guinness World Record — fastest rollercoaster (Formula Rossa)
items.description: The world's first Ferrari theme park, home to Formula Rossa — the fastest rollercoaster on the planet at 240 km/h. On Yas Island alongside Warner Bros. World and Yas Waterworld, so it anchors a full theme-park day for families with older kids and thrill-seekers.

items.name: Al Seef
items.description: A 1.8km stretch of Creek-front rebuilt in old-Dubai style — wind towers, sandstone lanes, floating market, cafés and abra stations — that flows straight into the historic quarter. A pleasant, walkable evening by the water with dhows drifting past. Family-friendly and easy.

items.name: Kite Beach
items.description: The best free public beach for activity — kitesurfing, paddleboarding, a running track and casual beach cafés, all with a clean sweep of Burj Al Arab views. More energetic and local than the resort strips; good for an active family morning before the heat.

items.name: J1 Beach
items.description: The Riviera-style beach-club strip that replaced La Mer — 13 upscale dining and beach-club concepts arriving from St-Tropez, Cannes and Tulum along a 500m shoreline. Book a daybed at one of the clubs for a polished, licensed beach day. The current centre of gravity for Dubai's beach scene.

items.name: Dubai Marina & JBR walk
items.description: Stroll the Marina promenade past superyachts and glass towers, then the buzzing beachfront of The Walk at JBR — full of cafés, street performers and people-watching. The most Miami-like part of the city; lovely in the evening. Add a short yacht or dhow cruise from the Marina to see it from the water.

items.name: Sunset yacht or dhow cruise from the Marina
items.description: Charter a private yacht (or join a smaller shared cruise) out past the Marina towers, Bluewaters, JBR and the Palm crescent as the skyline lights up. The private charter is the discreet, family-friendly choice — your own deck, catering and swim stop, away from the party boats.

items.name: Bluewaters Island & Ain Dubai
credentials: Guinness World Record — tallest observation wheel (Ain Dubai)
items.description: A polished dining-and-leisure island connected to JBR, dominated by Ain Dubai, the world's tallest observation wheel at 250m — a striking skyline landmark even when ride operations are paused, so check its status before counting on a spin. Come for the waterfront restaurants and the view of it either way.

items.name: Coffee Museum
items.description: A small, characterful museum in a heritage house tracing coffee across cultures, with antique roasters and a majlis serving traditional Emirati gahwa. A charming, quiet stop while wandering Al Fahidi — the kind of hidden gem that rewards the curious.

items.name: XVA Gallery
items.description: A leading contemporary gallery of Arab and Iranian art tucked into a courtyard heritage house, with a shaded vegetarian café and a tiny boutique hotel. An unhurried, cultured pause in the old town — art, mint lemonade and wind-tower shade.

items.name: Textile Souk
items.description: The covered fabric market on the Bur Dubai side of the Creek — bolts of silk, pashmina and embroidered cloth, and the landing point for the abra from Deira. Bring your bargaining; it's a lively, old-world stretch that pairs with Al Fahidi next door.

items.name: Al Qudra Lakes & Love Lake
items.description: Man-made desert lakes on the edge of the city — a cycling and picnic spot where you'll spot swans, oryx and migratory birds, plus the two intertwined heart-shaped Love Lakes. Cool, quiet and best at dawn or dusk; bring a car and your own supplies.

items.name: Deep Dive Dubai
credentials: Guinness World Record — deepest swimming pool for diving
items.description: The world's deepest swimming pool at 60m, built as a sunken city you dive or freedive through, with an underwater restaurant window. A genuinely unusual, bookable experience for divers and confident swimmers; sessions are limited, so reserve ahead.

items.name: Dubai Opera
items.description: A dhow-shaped venue at the foot of the Burj Khalifa staging opera, ballet, orchestras, musicals and big-name concerts. The most refined night out in the city, and a rare chance to dress up; check the season's programme and book a box for the fountain-side arrival.

items.name: La Perle by Dragone
items.description: Dubai's resident aqua-theatre spectacular — acrobatics, high dives and stunts in a purpose-built theatre with a stage that floods with water. Slick, wordless and family-friendly; the closest thing to a Cirque-style show in the city. Book weekend seats early.

items.name: City Walk & Coca-Cola Arena
items.description: A low-rise, European-style dining-and-shopping district that's pleasant to stroll on cooler evenings, anchored by the region's largest indoor arena for concerts and comedy. A relaxed alternative to the mega-malls, with wide pavements and good restaurants for families.

items.name: Sharjah Arts & Heritage Areas (day trip)
credentials: UNESCO — Sharjah named Cultural Capital of the Arab World (1998)
items.description: Twenty minutes north, the UAE's cultural capital — the Sharjah Art Foundation spaces, the excellent Museum of Islamic Civilization, and the restored Heart of Sharjah heritage quarter. A dry emirate and a serious, uncommercial contrast to Dubai's glitter. Half a day well spent for culture-minded travellers.

items.name: Dubai Aquarium & Underwater Zoo
items.description: One of the world's largest suspended aquarium tanks, viewable free from the mall or up close via the walk-through tunnel, glass-bottom boat and cage-snorkelling. An easy, reliable crowd-pleaser for children when you need an air-conditioned hour inside The Dubai Mall.

items.name: Skydive Dubai — Palm drop zone
items.description: A tandem jump over the Palm, freefalling with the whole island and coastline unfurling beneath you — arguably the most spectacular urban skydive on earth. No experience needed; book weeks ahead as slots go fast. The bucket-list thrill for adventurous visitors.

items.name: Mall of the Emirates & indoor entertainment
items.description: Beyond Ski Dubai, this is a genuinely upscale mall with a strong luxury wing, a cinema and VOX gold-class screens, and Magic Planet for kids. A cool-weather-independent day when the heat is punishing, with plentiful vegetarian and Indian dining nearby.

items.name: Palm Jumeirah Boardwalk & The Pointe
items.description: An 11km promenade along the Palm's crescent for a sea-air walk with Atlantis and the skyline in view, ending at waterfront dining. A calmer, free way to experience the Palm on foot — best at sunset when the light is soft and the heat lifts.

items.name: Emirates Palace & Presidential views (day trip)
items.description: The famously opulent palace-hotel where you can take the gold-flecked cappuccino and afternoon tea in the grand atrium, set in vast gardens on the corniche. A serene, monumental stop that rounds out an Abu Dhabi day alongside the Grand Mosque and Louvre.

items.name: FZN by Björn Frantzén
items.description: The Swedish master's Middle East debut, and one of only two three-stars in the city.

items.name: Trèsind Studio
items.description: The first Indian restaurant in the world to hold three Michelin stars — a matter of national pride.

items.name: Il Ristorante – Niko Romito
items.description: Romito's pared-back Italian ideal, on Bvlgari's island.

items.name: STAY by Yannick Alléno
items.description: Grand French dining, dessert library and all, in a garden setting.

items.name: Row on 45
items.description: A high, intimate counter where French technique meets Japanese omakase.

items.name: Ossiano
items.description: Dinner beside the aquarium wall — theatre that happens to be very good.

items.name: Moonrise
items.description: A rooftop counter for eight — the hardest, and warmest, seat in town.

items.name: Dinner by Heston Blumenthal
items.description: Heston's history-of-British-food, restaged with a Dubai view.

items.name: Al Muntaha
items.description: French cooking 200 metres up, inside the sail.

items.name: La Dame de Pic Dubai
items.description: Anne-Sophie Pic's delicate, aromatic French, translated to Dubai.

items.name: Smoked Room
items.description: Dani García's fire-and-smoke counter — Spanish, primal, precise.

items.name: Hoseki
items.description: A nine-seat omakase in a jewel-box room — the quietest luxury in town.

items.name: Jun's
items.description: Chef Kelvin Cheung's memory-cooking — Asian-American, personal, packed.

items.name: Orfali Bros Bistro
items.description: Three Syrian brothers and the most-talked-about kitchen in the Middle East.

items.name: Tasca by José Avillez
items.description: Portugal's finest, brought seaside — bright, generous, sunlit.

items.name: Hakkasan
items.description: The Cantonese standard-bearer, still holding its star after all these years.

items.name: Avatāra
items.description: A vegetarian Indian tasting menu that earned a star on its own terms.

items.name: Jamavar
items.description: The Leela's grand Indian house, newly starred in Dubai.

items.name: Manāo
items.description: A newly-starred Thai kitchen doing quiet, exacting regional cooking.

items.name: 11 Woodfire
items.description: Everything touched by fire — a chef's-counter ode to the flame.

items.name: Zuma
items.description: The izakaya that set the template for the whole city — still full every night.

items.name: LPM Restaurant & Bar
items.description: Riviera cooking and a room that has never gone out of fashion.

items.name: Gaia
items.description: Greek cooking with a designer's eye — as much scene as supper.

items.name: Boca
items.description: Sustainable Spanish cooking that quietly outclasses the district's louder rooms.

items.name: Mimi Kakushi
items.description: 1920s-Osaka glamour and Japanese cooking with real intent.

items.name: Bombay Brasserie
items.description: Grand Indian dining under the Taj's own roof — nostalgic and assured.

items.name: Bait Maryam
items.description: A Levantine home kitchen, run like family — because it is.

items.name: Lowe
items.description: Zero-waste, market-led cooking with a conscience and a sense of humour.

items.name: 3Fils
items.description: A tiny harbour-side counter that outranks half the city's grand rooms.

items.name: Kinoya
items.description: Soulful Japanese comfort food — ramen and izakaya done properly.

items.name: REIF Japanese Kushiyaki
items.description: Skewers over charcoal from a chef who made small food a big deal.

items.name: 21 Grams
items.description: Balkan home cooking with heart — the antidote to Dubai gloss.

items.name: Indya by Vineet
items.description: Vineet Bhatia's contemporary Indian, at a price that flatters the cooking.

items.name: Berenjak
items.description: Tehran's back-street kebab houses, recreated with real fire and flatbread.

items.name: Shabestan
items.description: Old-Dubai Persian dining on the creek, saffron and all.

items.name: Teible
items.description: Farm-to-table restraint in a design-museum setting.

items.name: Aamara
items.description: Indian cooking with a light, modern hand — Bib-listed and easy to love.

items.name: Revelry
items.description: A gastro-room that punches above its price — Bib-approved.

items.name: Hawkerboi
items.description: Southeast-Asian hawker flavours with real fire and swagger.

items.name: Sufret Maryam
items.description: Bait Maryam's sister — the same Levantine warmth, a lighter setting.

items.name: DUO Gastrobar
items.description: A neighbourhood gastrobar that keeps earning its Bib across outlets.

items.name: Bombay Bungalow
items.description: Beach-side Indian street food and curries — bright, fresh, unpretentious.

items.name: Konjiki Hototogisu
items.description: A Tokyo ramen name that earned its Bib on the bowl alone.

items.name: Hoe Lee Kow
items.description: Unfussy Asian comfort food with a devoted local following.

items.name: Al Khayma Heritage Restaurant
items.description: Emirati home cooking in a wind-tower courtyard house — the real old Dubai.

items.name: Goldfish
items.description: Sushi and seafood done cleanly and without fuss — a neighbourhood gem.

items.name: Khadak
items.description: Indian street-food energy, credentialed by the Michelin inspectors.

items.name: Harummanis
items.description: Malaysian home cooking, gently spiced, quietly excellent.

items.name: Skyview Bar, Burj Al Arab
credentials: Inside Burj Al Arab — global landmark venue
items.description: A drink 200 metres up inside the sail — the view most first visits are chasing.

items.name: Gold on 27, Burj Al Arab
credentials: Inside Burj Al Arab — signature high-concept cocktail bar
items.description: A gilded, theatrical cocktail room high in the sail — indulgence taken entirely seriously.

items.name: Mimi Kakushi
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars 2025 (No. 36) — Best Bar in the Middle East
items.description: 1920s Osaka glamour and serious mixology — the most decorated bar in the region, and it shows.

items.name: Galaxy Bar
items.description: An intimate, constellation-lit room in the financial district — cocktails made with real intent.

items.name: La Petite Maison (LPM) — bar
items.description: The Riviera room the city never tires of — a pre-dinner drink here is a Dubai ritual.

items.name: CÉ LA VI Dubai
credentials: Internationally recognised rooftop group — Address Sky View, 54th floor
items.description: The Burj Khalifa filling the glass, 54 floors up — the rooftop that best frames Downtown.

items.name: Above Eleven
credentials: World Luxury Restaurant Awards — recognised rooftop; established international name
items.description: A neon-lit rooftop with Peruvian-Japanese plates and skyline views — Bangkok's cult name, restaged.

items.name: Zuma bar
credentials: Zuma — MENA's 50 Best Restaurants; the district's benchmark bar-and-dining room
items.description: The bar that set the template for grown-up Dubai nights — still full, still faultless.

items.name: Gaia
credentials: MENA's 50 Best Restaurants (No. 35, 2024) — DIFC's dressed-up late room
items.description: Greek glamour and a dressed-up crowd — as much a scene as a supper, well past midnight.

items.title: Private after-hours At.mosphere and Burj Khalifa top-floor access
items.description: Arrange a private evening on the 148th-floor observation level with a butler and dinner high in the tower, away from the daytime queues.

items.title: Dawn hot-air balloon over the Dubai desert with falconry
items.description: Lift off at first light over the Al Marmoom conservation reserve, then land to a Bedouin breakfast and a private falconry display.

items.title: Private seaplane transfer with an aerial loop over the Palm and World Islands
items.description: A Seawings charter gives you the only genuinely good view of the archipelago and a scenic arrival at your hotel jetty.

items.title: Chef's table at Row on 45 or a private majlis dinner in the desert dunes
items.description: Either a tasting-menu counter seat with the kitchen in view, or a candle-lit private table set among the dunes with an Emirati chef cooking over coals.

plan.heading: 4 days in Dubai, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Cross Dubai Creek by abra to the Al Fahidi quarter, then coffee and cardamom at the Arabian Tea House.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Wander the gold and spice souks of Deira before the afternoon heat, then retreat to your suite at the Bulgari Resort on Jumeira Bay.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Ossiano beneath the aquarium at Atlantis, then a quiet nightcap on the terrace.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: An early, private ascent of the Burj Khalifa before the crowds, followed by the Dubai Fountain from the boardwalk.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Slow lunch and the collections at Jameel Arts Centre, then browsing the galleries of Alserkal Avenue.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Trèsind Studio, the city's three-Michelin tasting room, booked well ahead.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive into the Dubai Desert Conservation Reserve for a private falconry session at first light.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch and a long afternoon by the pool at Al Maha, a Luxury Collection Desert Resort.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A candlelit dinner in the dunes, then stargazing with an astronomer.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private yacht along the Palm and the Marina, swimming off the boat while the city is still cool.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at Nobu, then the Ottomans-to-orientalism rooms of the Etihad Museum.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at Row on 45, and drinks watching the skyline from Aura Skypool.

items.name: Downtown Dubai
items.description: For first-timers who want the Burj Khalifa, the fountains and the Dubai Mall on their doorstep; central but busy.

items.name: Palm Jumeirah
items.description: Beach-resort seclusion on the fronds, best for a slower, water-facing stay away from the city grind.

items.name: Al Fahidi and the Creek (Bur Dubai / Deira)
items.description: The old city of wind-towers, souks and abras, for travellers who want texture and history over gloss.

events.name: Dubai Shopping Festival
events.note: The city's biggest retail and entertainment season, with nightly fireworks, concerts and citywide sales.

events.name: Taste of Dubai
events.note: The city's flagship food festival, with restaurant showcases, chef demos and tastings across a weekend.

events.name: Dubai World Cup
events.note: The world's richest race day at Meydan on the last Saturday of March, a full dress-code social occasion.

events.name: Art Dubai
events.note: The region's leading contemporary and modern art fair at Madinat Jumeirah, anchor of Dubai's art season.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Dubai International (DXB) — most premium carriers use Terminal 1 or the Emirates hub at Terminal 3 — where a Marhaba greeter can meet you airside and clear you through fast-track immigration before a chauffeured car handles the transfer.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Keep a private car and driver on call; the city is built around long air-conditioned drives, though Downtown, DIFC and the marina reward short walks after dark when the heat lifts.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Buy an eSIM (Etisalat/e& or du) before landing for instant 5G; hotel and mall wifi is fast and ubiquitous, and WhatsApp calling now works normally.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The dirham (AED) is pegged to the dollar; cards are taken everywhere, cash is rarely needed, and a 10 percent service charge is usual so tipping beyond a rounding-up gesture is optional.

onGround.note: For a first stay, Downtown or DIFC keeps you central; dress is relaxed but cover shoulders and knees in older districts and mosques. Alcohol is served freely in licensed hotels and restaurants, and Friday is the quiet day, with the working week running Monday to Friday.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: November to March is kind: warm days near 25-28C, cool evenings, low humidity. Avoid June-September, when heat tops 45C with punishing humidity that shuts down anything outdoors.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru, roughly 3.5 hours. Emirates flies it best in business and first, with complimentary chauffeur-drive at both ends; the A380 business bar is worth requesting on the wider-body rotations. Emirates First lounge at DXB is a destination in itself for onward connections.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required beyond routine; hepatitis A and typhoid sensible for any Gulf trip. Very safe, low street crime. Tap water is desalinated and safe, though bottled is the norm. Summer heat is the real hazard, not people.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Effortless for vegetarian and Jain travellers. Pure-veg and Jain menus are widely understood, and Indian food is everywhere. Rasoi by Vineet and the Jain-friendly kitchens across Bur Dubai are dependable; most fine-dining hotels will prepare Jain on notice.

seo.title: Dublin — TripAgent
seo.description: Dublin, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Dublin
hero.tagline: Georgian grace, literary spirit and warm convivial pubs.

ourTake.lede: Dublin is compact and conversational — its pleasures are literary, musical and social rather than architectural, so the best hours are spent in its bookshops, pubs and along the coast. Do the Book of Kells and a serious literary walk, but resist spending your nights in the Temple Bar crush; the good sessions and pints are in the older pubs the locals actually use. Give a day to the DART line out to Howth or Dalkey — the sea and the walking are half of why people love this city.
ourTake.comeIf: You want literary pubs, warm company and a base for Ireland's green coast.
ourTake.skipIf: You want sunshine and grand monuments; Dublin's charm is human, not spectacular.
