guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: The Merrion
items.area: Merrion Square — Upper Merrion Street, opposite Government Buildings
credentials: MICHELIN Two Keys (2025 — Ireland's highest tier)
items.description: Four restored Georgian townhouses facing the government buildings — Dublin's definitive grand hotel, with the country's only two-star kitchen downstairs.

items.name: The Shelbourne, Autograph Collection
items.area: St Stephen's Green — Grafton Street quarter
items.description: The 'Grande Dame' of Dublin, open since 1824 on St Stephen's Green — where the Irish Constitution was drafted, and still the city's most storied address.

items.name: The Westbury
items.area: Grafton Street — Balfe Street, off the main shopping street
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The Doyle Collection's Dublin flagship, tucked just off Grafton Street — a polished, art-filled house at the very centre of the city's shopping and dining.

items.name: Anantara The Marker Dublin
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A striking checkerboard-faced design hotel on Grand Canal Square, run by Anantara — the city's best rooftop bar and a genuine spa with infinity pool.

items.name: The Dylan
items.area: Ballsbridge — Eastmoreland Place, a quiet Georgian lane
items.description: A flamboyant boutique house in a red-brick Victorian former nurses' home, on a leafy lane near the canal — the most characterful small luxury stay in the city.

items.name: Conrad Dublin
items.area: St Stephen's Green — Earlsfort Terrace, by the National Concert Hall
items.description: A polished, well-run Hilton-luxury house opposite the National Concert Hall — dependable five-star comfort a moment from St Stephen's Green.

items.name: InterContinental Dublin
items.area: Ballsbridge — Simmonscourt Road, in two acres of gardens
items.description: A calm, generously scaled hotel set in two acres of private gardens in leafy Ballsbridge — the most spacious luxury stay, with a proper pool and spa.

items.name: The Wilder Townhouse
items.area: Dublin 2 — Adelaide Road, by the Iveagh Gardens
items.description: A restored red-brick Victorian townhouse of forty-odd rooms near the Iveagh Gardens — an intimate, characterful boutique with a lovely gin-and-tea parlour.

items.name: Trinity College & the Book of Kells Experience
items.description: Ireland's oldest university, its cobbled squares reached through an arch that has stood since 1592. The 9th-century Book of Kells sits at the heart of a reimagined digital experience, after which you climb into the barrel-vaulted Old Library. A private early-access guide spares multi-generational groups the queue and the crush.

items.name: The Long Room, Old Library
items.description: A 65-metre corridor of oak and marble busts, the most photographed library chamber in the world. Its books are being carefully removed in a conservation project running to 2027, and Luke Jerram's illuminated seven-metre Gaia globe currently floats at its centre. See it now, in this rare transitional state.

items.name: Dublin Castle & the State Apartments
items.description: Seven centuries of power on one site, from a Viking-age fortress to the Georgian State Apartments where Irish presidents are still inaugurated. A private guided tour takes in the medieval undercroft and the ornate St Patrick's Hall, an easy, cultured morning for a family.

items.name: Chester Beatty
items.description: Ireland's museum of world cultures, and one of Europe's finest, gifted by an American mining magnate. Illuminated Qurans, the oldest known fragments of the New Testament, Chinese jade and Japanese scrolls sit side by side. Free to enter, blissfully uncrowded, with a rooftop garden and a good vegetarian-friendly café.

items.name: Christ Church Cathedral
items.description: Dublin's oldest building, founded around 1030 by the Viking king Sitric, with a vast medieval crypt beneath the nave, the largest in Britain or Ireland. The mummified cat and rat found in an organ pipe, nicknamed Tom and Jerry, are an oddly charming detail for children.

items.name: St Patrick's Cathedral
items.description: The largest church in Ireland, built beside the well where St Patrick is said to have baptised converts. Jonathan Swift, author of Gulliver's Travels, was dean here and lies buried in the nave. Time your visit for choral evensong, sung by a choir that has performed here for over 500 years.

items.name: Guinness Storehouse & the Gravity Bar
items.description: Seven floors rising through a glass atrium shaped like a giant pint, ending at the Gravity Bar, 46 metres up with a 360-degree sweep of the city. Arthur Guinness signed a 9,000-year lease here in 1759. A private tasting and a table at the top can be arranged away from the tour crowds.

items.name: Jameson Distillery Bow St.
items.description: The original 1780 distillery, now a slick whiskey experience with guided tastings and blend-your-own sessions. For serious collectors, private premium tastings pour rare and cask-strength expressions rarely seen outside Ireland.

items.name: Kilmainham Gaol
items.description: The prison where the leaders of the 1916 Easter Rising were held and executed, a place that shaped modern Ireland. The vast Victorian East Wing, ringed by tiered iron galleries, is unforgettable. Tickets sell out weeks ahead, so a guide who secures timed entry is invaluable.

items.name: National Museum of Ireland – Archaeology
items.description: Bronze Age gold hoards, the eerily preserved Iron Age bog bodies, and the Ardagh Chalice and Tara Brooch, the finest surviving Celtic metalwork. A short, well-curated visit that gives real depth to everything else you see in Ireland.

items.name: National Gallery of Ireland
items.description: A serene collection running from Fra Angelico and Vermeer to a whole room of Jack B. Yeats, brother of the poet. Caravaggio's The Taking of Christ, lost for centuries and rediscovered in a Dublin Jesuit house, is the quiet showstopper. Free entry, elegant galleries, unhurried.

items.name: EPIC The Irish Emigration Museum
credentials: Europe's Leading Tourist Attraction (World Travel Awards, multiple years)
items.description: A fully interactive museum in the vaults of a old bonded warehouse, tracing how ten million Irish emigrants shaped the world. Engaging and high-tech, it is a favourite with teenagers and works beautifully for a curious family.

items.name: The Little Museum of Dublin
items.description: A jewel-box townhouse museum of 20th-century Dublin, reopened in 2025 after a €4m restoration, including a whole room devoted to U2. Its guided storytelling tours, capped at small groups, are among the most charming hours in the city.

items.name: St Stephen's Green
items.description: A perfectly kept Victorian park at the head of Grafton Street, with a lake, a bandstand and Yeats and Joyce memorials among the flowerbeds. The ideal breather between shopping and museums, and a green lung for children to run in.

items.name: Merrion Square & the Georgian doors
items.description: The finest Georgian square in the city, ringed by red-brick townhouses with their famous rainbow of front doors and delicate fanlights. Oscar Wilde grew up here, and his reclining statue lounges in the garden opposite. A gentle, photogenic walk through Dublin's most refined quarter.

items.name: Grafton Street & Brown Thomas
items.description: Dublin's pedestrianised shopping spine, lined with buskers and the grand Brown Thomas department store for luxury houses and Irish designers. Nearby Powerscourt Townhouse, a converted Georgian mansion, hides boutiques and cafés under its glass roof.

items.name: Temple Bar (by day)
items.description: The cobbled cultural quarter is genuinely charming in daylight, for the Saturday food market, galleries, and independent shops, and best avoided as a boisterous, overpriced pub scene after dark. Come mid-morning for the atmosphere without the stag parties.

items.name: The Ha'penny Bridge & the quays
items.description: The cast-iron pedestrian bridge of 1816, once charged a halfpenny to cross, is the Liffey's most-loved landmark. A slow riverside walk along the quays, past the Custom House and the Famine memorial statues, threads the city's history together.

items.name: Phoenix Park
items.description: One of Europe's largest enclosed city parks, seven times the size of London's Hyde Park, with herds of wild fallow deer roaming freely. It holds the President's residence, the towering Papal Cross, and open space that feels a world away from the city.

items.name: Dublin Zoo
items.description: One of the world's oldest zoos, dating to 1831, now a spacious modern conservation park with an African savanna and an Asian elephant herd. A reliable, well-run day out for younger children within the greenery of Phoenix Park.

items.name: Áras an Uachtaráin
items.description: The President of Ireland's official residence, a white Georgian mansion open for free guided tours on Saturdays by ticketed lottery. A rare glimpse inside a working head-of-state house for those who plan ahead.

items.name: Glasnevin Cemetery Museum
items.description: The world's first cemetery museum, set in a Victorian garden cemetery where Michael Collins, Daniel O'Connell and Éamon de Valera lie. Superb guided tours bring the 1916 Rising and Civil War alive, and the restored O'Connell Tower gives a 222-step view over the city.

items.name: Irish Museum of Modern Art (IMMA)
items.description: Ireland's leading modern-art museum, housed in the magnificent 17th-century Royal Hospital Kilmainham with formal gardens. Contemporary shows in a serene classical setting, an easy pairing with the neighbouring Kilmainham Gaol.

items.name: National Museum of Ireland – Decorative Arts & History (Collins Barracks)
items.description: A former army barracks now filled with Irish silver, furniture, fashion and a moving exhibition on the events of 1916. Quieter than the Kildare Street museum, and a fine complement to it.

items.name: GPO Museum & O'Connell Street
items.description: The General Post Office was the headquarters of the 1916 Rising, its pillars still pocked with bullet marks. The immersive witness-history museum inside explains the birth of the Republic, on the city's grand central boulevard beneath the soaring Spire.

items.name: Dublinia
items.description: A hands-on recreation of Viking and medieval Dublin, right beside Christ Church. Light, playful and genuinely educational, it is one of the best stops in the city for families with younger children.

items.name: St Patrick's Cathedral & Marsh's Library
items.description: Beside the cathedral sits Ireland's first public library, opened in 1707 and almost unchanged since, with dark oak stacks and rare volumes in wired reading cages. A hushed, scholarly secret loved by bibliophiles.

items.name: Traditional music at The Cobblestone
items.description: A genuine spit-and-sawdust pub where musicians gather for informal trad sessions, fiercely protected from the tourist circuit by its owners. This is the real thing, warm, unpolished and unforgettable, best experienced with a local who knows the room.

items.name: Howth
items.description: A fishing village on a rugged headland, thirty minutes by coastal train, with a cliff walk over the Irish Sea, seals in the harbour, and some of the freshest seafood near Dublin. A superb half-day escape, with a private car easily arranged for those who prefer not to take the train.

items.name: Dalkey & Killiney
items.description: Dublin's Beverly Hills, a genteel seaside village of a medieval castle, artisan cafés and celebrity residents, with the Vico Road viewpoint often likened to the Bay of Naples. Discreet, moneyed and lovely, exactly the sort of place a member might quietly settle.

items.name: Dún Laoghaire
items.description: An elegant Victorian harbour town with two grand granite piers made for a bracing seafront stroll and famous ice cream. The James Joyce Tower at nearby Sandycove, where Ulysses opens, is a literary pilgrimage.

items.name: Bray & Bray Head
items.description: A traditional seaside resort at the foot of the Wicklow Mountains, with a long promenade and a cliff walk on to the pretty village of Greystones. The end of the line, and the gateway to the mountains beyond.

items.name: Glendalough & the Wicklow Mountains
items.description: A 6th-century monastic city set in a glacial valley of two dark lakes and a near-perfect round tower, an hour's drive south through the Wicklow Mountains National Park. The most beautiful day trip from Dublin, best done privately with a guide and a picnic.

items.name: Brú na Bóinne – Newgrange & Knowth
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Brú na Bóinne
items.description: A 5,200-year-old passage tomb older than Stonehenge and the Pyramids, aligned so the rising sun floods its inner chamber at the winter solstice. Access is only by guided tour from the visitor centre, best pre-booked, and easily paired with a private driver from the city.

items.name: Malahide Castle & Gardens
items.description: An 800-year-old castle lived in by one family for nearly all that time, set in parkland with a walled botanic garden and butterfly house. A short trip from the city that suits multi-generational groups, castle for the elders, gardens and playground for the young.

items.name: Powerscourt Estate & Gardens
items.description: A Palladian mansion above one of the world's great gardens, all Italianate terraces, statuary and a lake framed by the Sugarloaf Mountain. Ireland's highest waterfall sits within the estate. A refined half-day, with lunch in the terrace café.

items.name: Kilkenny
items.description: Ireland's finest medieval city, an easy drive or train south, crowned by a great Norman castle and a walkable 'Medieval Mile' of narrow lanes, craft studios and the black-marble St Canice's Cathedral. A full, rewarding day with genuine character.

items.name: Hugh Lane Gallery
items.description: A gracious Georgian gallery holding Impressionist masterpieces and, extraordinarily, the entire reconstructed studio of Francis Bacon, moved brick by brick from London. A cultured, uncrowded hour off the tourist trail.

items.name: MoLI – Museum of Literature Ireland
items.description: A beautiful museum in a pair of Georgian houses celebrating Ireland's literary giants, holding the first copy of Joyce's Ulysses. Elegant, contemplative, with a lovely garden café, it makes the city's UNESCO literary status tangible.

items.name: 14 Henrietta Street
items.description: A single Georgian townhouse that tells the whole social history of Dublin, from grand aristocratic home to overcrowded tenement, through the stories of those who lived in each room. A genuinely moving, small-group experience unlike anything else in the city.

items.name: Iveagh Gardens
items.description: Dublin's 'secret garden', a hidden Victorian pleasure ground of a cascade, fountains, a maze and rose garden, tucked behind the National Concert Hall. Locals treasure it precisely because so few tourists find it.

items.name: Grafton Street pubs — a curated evening
items.description: The snug Victorian rooms of Kehoe's, the literary ghosts of Davy Byrnes from Ulysses, and the tiled beauty of The Long Hall. A guided literary-pub crawl, or a discreet advisor-arranged route, gives the atmosphere of Dublin's pub culture without the tourist bustle.

items.name: St Michan's Church & the mummies
items.description: Beneath a 17th-century church lie limestone vaults whose dry air has naturally mummified bodies for centuries, including a figure said to be a Crusader. A macabre, memorable curiosity for the adventurous, by guided tour only.

items.name: Croke Park & the GAA Museum
items.description: The 82,000-seat home of Gaelic games, Ireland's fiercely amateur national sports, with a museum and an exhilarating rooftop Skyline walk around the stadium rim. A window into a passion no visitor sees coming, and thrilling for older children.

items.name: Teeling Whiskey Distillery
items.description: The first new distillery to open in Dublin in over 125 years, in the historic whiskey district, with hands-on tours and inventive small-batch bottlings. A more intimate, craft-led counterpoint to the big-name distilleries.

items.name: Number Twenty Nine Georgian House
items.description: A meticulously restored middle-class Georgian home of the 1790s, laid out room by room from cellar to attic exactly as it would have been lived in. The most intimate way to understand the elegance behind those famous Dublin doors.

items.name: Trim Castle
items.description: The largest Anglo-Norman castle in Ireland, a mighty 12th-century keep on the River Boyne where Braveheart was filmed. Often combined with Newgrange on a Boyne Valley day, it rewards those who love history with room to roam.

items.name: Restaurant Patrick Guilbaud
items.area: Merrion Square — within The Merrion, Upper Merrion Street
items.description: Ireland's most celebrated restaurant — over forty years at the top, and the country's only two-star table for most of that time, inside The Merrion.

items.name: Chapter One by Mickael Viljanen
items.area: Dublin 1 — Parnell Square, by the Writers Museum
items.description: Finnish chef Mickael Viljanen's precise, luxurious cooking in a Georgian basement north of the Liffey — a benchmark two-star table.

items.name: Liath
items.area: Blackrock — inside Blackrock Market, south county Dublin
items.description: A tiny, surprise tasting-menu room hidden in Blackrock Market — deeply personal cooking built around the five tastes, and now two stars.

items.name: Variety Jones
items.description: Fire-fed, fiercely seasonal sharing plates cooked over open flame in full view — a relaxed, tablecloth-free one-star that feels like a great neighbourhood room.

items.name: Forest Avenue
items.area: Ballsbridge — Sussex Terrace, by the canal
items.description: John and Sandy Wyer's pared-back, ingredient-led cooking near the canal — a likeable, quietly excellent room newly promoted to one star.

items.name: Bastible
items.description: A stylish, understated neighbourhood one-star run with real conviction — seasonal Irish cooking that balances contrasting flavours beautifully.

items.name: Glovers Alley
items.area: St Stephen's Green — first floor of The Fitzwilliam, over the Green
items.description: Andy McFadden's refined French-rooted cooking on the first floor of The Fitzwilliam — a graceful one-star room overlooking St Stephen's Green.

items.name: D'Olier Street
items.area: Dublin 2 — D'Olier Street, by Trinity College
items.description: A stylish, buzzy one-star from a well-known Dublin kitchen partnership — considered, contemporary cooking a step from Trinity.

items.name: Pichet
items.area: Grafton Street quarter — Trinity Street, Dublin 2
items.description: A modern brasserie blending French influences with contemporary Irish cooking — a Bib Gourmand for well over a decade running, and a reliable Dublin favourite.

items.name: Uno Mas
items.description: A stripped-back, Mediterranean-leaning bistro from the team behind Etto — small plates, a smart wine list and a Bib Gourmand for real value.

items.name: Clanbrassil House
items.description: A warm neighbourhood room built around a charcoal grill and family-style sharing plates — a long-standing Bib Gourmand in Dublin 8.

items.name: Bigfan
items.description: Chinese and Taiwanese sharing plates that won a Bib Gourmand in 2026 — the inspectors singled out the pulled-beef wu ya bao as 'lip-smackingly delicious'.

items.name: Borgo
items.description: An osteria-style Italian built around informality and honest pricing — ingredient-led, simple pleasures, and a new Bib Gourmand for 2026.

items.name: Forêt
items.area: Ballsbridge — above M. O'Brien's pub, Sussex Terrace
items.description: The Wyers' rustic little bistro above a Dublin pub — pâté de campagne, coq au vin and other French comforts done beautifully, with a 2026 Bib Gourmand.

items.name: The Horseshoe Bar
items.area: St Stephen's Green — inside The Shelbourne
credentials: Inside The Shelbourne — a Marriott Autograph Collection hotel
items.description: The horseshoe-shaped bar of The Shelbourne — for generations the room where Irish politics, journalism and society have met over a drink.

items.name: The Long Hall
items.area: City centre — South Great George's Street
credentials: A protected Victorian public house, interior substantially intact from the 1880s
items.description: One of the most beautiful pub interiors in Dublin — Victorian mirrors, gas-era lamps and a long mahogany bar, largely unchanged for a century and a half.

items.name: The Palace Bar
credentials: Trading since 1823; a documented literary and journalistic institution
items.description: A Georgian-fronted, Victorian-interior pub that was the mid-century headquarters of Dublin's writers and journalists — and one of the city's great whiskey bars.

items.name: Doheny & Nesbitt
credentials: A Victorian public house dating to the 1840s, with original snugs
items.description: A fine example of Victorian pub architecture near the government buildings — its snugs long the unofficial debating chamber of Irish politics and finance.

items.name: The Sidecar at The Westbury
credentials: Inside The Westbury — a Leading Hotels of the World hotel
items.description: The glamorous, 1920s-inspired cocktail bar of The Westbury, just off Grafton Street — polished service and beautifully balanced classics.

items.name: Bar 1661
items.area: Dublin 1 — Green Street, near the Four Courts
credentials: Featured on the World's 50 Best Bars' Top 50 Cocktail Menu list (2025)
items.description: A warm, community-minded bar dedicated to reviving poitín — the once-banned Irish spirit — from Dave Mulligan, founder of the Bán poitín brand.

items.name: Vintage Cocktail Club
items.description: An unmarked, three-storey speakeasy in the heart of Temple Bar — 1920s decor, low light and one of the most acclaimed cocktail lists in the country.

items.name: The Rooftop Bar at Anantara The Marker
credentials: Inside Anantara The Marker Dublin — a Leading Hotels of the World hotel
items.description: The best true rooftop in the city, atop Anantara The Marker — 360° views over the Docklands to the Dublin mountains and the sea.

items.name: Kehoe's
items.area: Grafton Street quarter — South Anne Street
credentials: A Victorian pub-grocer trading since 1803, interior largely intact
items.description: The pub photographers seek out when they want to show a real Dublin bar — an intact Victorian pub-grocer with original snugs and mahogany drawers.

items.title: The Book of Kells and Trinity's Long Room
items.description: The illuminated ninth-century gospels beneath the great barrel-vaulted library hall.

items.title: A traditional music session
items.description: Find a genuine session in a pub like The Cobblestone in Smithfield rather than the tourist strip.

items.title: A coastal walk from Howth
items.description: Take the DART north for cliff paths, seafood and views back across Dublin Bay.

items.title: The National Museum and a literary walk
items.description: Pair the Iron Age gold and bog bodies with a stroll through Joyce and Beckett's Dublin.

plan.heading: 2 days in Dublin, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Book of Kells and the Long Room at Trinity College at opening, then the Georgian squares on foot.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The National Gallery of Ireland for the Yeats and Caravaggio rooms, then tea at the Merrion hotel.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Chapter One by Mickael Viljanen, the two-Michelin-star room on Parnell Square.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Christ Church and the Chester Beatty library within Dublin Castle, quiet and rarely crowded.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at the Winding Stair over the Liffey, then browse the makers on the streets off Grafton.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A final dinner at Liath in Blackrock, or a Guinness at the counter of Kehoe's if the mood is lighter.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Georgian Dublin / around St Stephen's Green
items.description: Elegant squares and the best hotels — central and refined.

items.name: Temple Bar
items.description: The cobbled cultural quarter — lively and central, but rowdy and pricey at night.

items.name: Ranelagh / Portobello
items.description: Canalside neighbourhoods with good restaurants and a local feel, a short walk south of the centre.

events.name: TradFest
events.note: Traditional and folk music across Dublin Castle, cathedrals and Temple Bar venues.

events.name: St. Patrick's Festival
events.note: Several days of events around the 17 March parade through the city.

events.name: Bloomsday
events.note: The city retraces Joyce's Ulysses in Edwardian dress.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: You arrive at Dublin Airport (DUB), roughly 25 minutes by private car into the city, with a chauffeur meeting you on arrival.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The centre is easily walked and a private driver covers evenings and the drive out to the coast at Howth or the Wicklow hills.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Connectivity is good; an EU eSIM works as Ireland is within EU roaming, and wifi is widely available.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The euro (Ireland uses it, unlike the UK); cards and contactless are accepted everywhere, and tipping around 10 to 15 percent is appreciated but not obligatory.

onGround.note: Stay around Merrion Square or St Stephen's Green for the best of Georgian Dublin; the Irish welcome is genuinely warm and conversation is expected, and reserve ahead at the better tables as the city is smaller than it feels.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: May to September is the kindest window, mild and green with long evenings; rain is possible any day. November-February are dark, wet and often windy, best avoided for touring.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No non-stop from India at present; route via London Heathrow (BA), Frankfurt (Lufthansa) or a Gulf hub on Emirates/Qatar, roughly 12-13h total in business/first. A London or Gulf connection is smoothest; Dublin also offers US pre-clearance if onward to America.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations needed; tap water is safe to drink. Dublin is generally safe; use booked cars at night and keep normal city awareness in the centre.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian food is easy and the Indian scene is strong. Well-regarded Indian kitchens such as Konkan and Ananda handle vegetarian well; Jain requests should be flagged ahead.

seo.title: Dubrovnik — TripAgent
seo.description: Dubrovnik, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Dubrovnik
hero.tagline: The walled Adriatic city of marble streets and sea.

ourTake.lede: Dubrovnik is astonishing and completely overrun by midday cruise crowds, so the whole game is timing — walk the walls at opening or after 6pm and have the Old Town almost to yourself. Don't sleep inside the walls unless you love hauling luggage up stone steps; base yourself just outside and walk in. Give it two nights, then take a boat to the quieter islands, which is where the real Dalmatia lives.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a walled old town, Adriatic swims, and boat days combined into one unhurried week.
ourTake.skipIf: You need direct flights, plentiful Indian food, or a lively city that runs late.

whenToGo.blurb: Come late spring or September for warm seas without the July–August crush; the summer festival is glorious but crowds and cruise ships peak then.
whenToGo.bestMonths: May, Jun, Jul, Aug and Sep

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Villa Dubrovnik
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
Forbes Travel Guide — Global Partner (first hotel in Croatia)
Home to Pjerin — MICHELIN Guide Selected (2025)
items.description: The city's defining luxury address — a serene cliffside villa terraced above the Adriatic, every room facing Lokrum island and the walled city beyond.

items.name: Hotel Excelsior
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: A 1913 grande dame on the Ploče waterfront, five minutes' walk from the city walls — the most enviable address in Dubrovnik proper.

items.name: Sun Gardens Dubrovnik
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A full seafront resort in Mediterranean gardens — three pools, a private beach and a large spa, the region's most complete address for families.

items.name: Hotel Bellevue
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World
Home to Vapor — MICHELIN Guide Selected (2025)
items.description: A boutique house cut into a 30-metre cliff over Miramare Bay — a small hotel with its own beach and some of the finest sea panoramas in the city.

items.name: Rixos Premium Dubrovnik
items.description: A polished cliffside five-star cascading down terraced slopes to the water, about a mile from the walled city — sleek rooms, sea views and a large spa.

items.name: Villa Orsula
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: A restored 1930s villa of just thirteen rooms above the Adriatic — art-filled, intimate and steps from the Old Town, with a private bathing platform below.

items.name: Walk the City Walls
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old City of Dubrovnik
items.description: The essential Dubrovnik experience: a near-2km circuit atop 13th-century ramparts, 25 metres above the sea, looking down on the terracotta rooftops and out to Lokrum. Go early or at golden hour when the crowds thin and the light turns the stone honey-gold; a private guide can pace it for grandparents and children alike.

items.name: Stroll the Stradun (Placa)
items.description: The limestone-paved main promenade, polished to a mirror shine by centuries of footsteps, runs the length of the walled city from Pile to Ploče. It is where Dubrovnik takes its evening passeggiata — a glass of wine at a pavement table as the marble glows under the lamps.

items.name: Pile Gate & Ploče Gate
items.description: The two grand fortified entrances to the walled city, each with a wooden drawbridge and a niche holding a statue of St Blaise, the city's patron. Passing through Pile onto the Stradun is the classic first-arrival moment — arrange to enter on foot with a guide rather than in the cruise-crowd crush.

items.name: Big Onofrio's Fountain
items.description: A great domed 16th-century fountain just inside Pile Gate, the endpoint of a 12km aqueduct built in 1438 — water still runs from its sixteen carved mascarons. A cool, shaded meeting point and a lovely first landmark for children to spot.

items.name: Franciscan Monastery & the Old Pharmacy
items.description: Home to one of the oldest working pharmacies in Europe, founded in 1317, alongside a serene Romanesque cloister of double columns and a museum of medieval apothecary jars. The pharmacy still compounds creams to centuries-old Franciscan recipes — a quiet, cultured pause off the busy Stradun.

items.name: Rector's Palace
items.description: The Gothic-Renaissance seat of the Ragusan Republic, whose rector governed for a single month and could not leave the building during his term. Now the Cultural History Museum, its courtyard has flawless acoustics and hosts summer chamber concerts — a refined evening for a multi-generational party.

items.name: Dubrovnik Cathedral & the Treasury
items.description: A serene Baroque cathedral built after the 1667 earthquake, holding paintings by Italian and Dalmatian masters. Its Treasury is the draw — reliquaries of gold and silver, including the jewelled skull-reliquary of St Blaise and a relic said to be a fragment of the True Cross.

items.name: Dominican Monastery & Museum
items.description: Tucked by the Ploče gate, a fortress-like 14th-century monastery with a luminous late-Gothic cloister and a museum of Dubrovnik-school painting, including an altarpiece attributed to Titian. Calmer than the Franciscan cloister and a favourite for those who like art without the crowds.

items.name: Sponza Palace
items.description: The finest surviving pre-earthquake palace, a Gothic-Renaissance jewel on Luža Square that served as the Republic's mint and customs house. It now guards the State Archives, and its arcaded courtyard is one of the coolest, most photogenic spots to step out of the sun.

items.name: Luža Square, Orlando's Column & the Bell Tower
items.description: The ceremonial heart of the old city: the medieval Orlando's Column (its forearm was the Republic's official measure of length), the 15th-century Bell Tower with its bronze 'green men' who strike the hour, and the Church of St Blaise. The natural place to sit with a coffee and watch the city move.

items.name: Ethnographic Museum Rupe
items.description: A 16th-century grain silo whose vast underground pits ('rupe' means holes) kept the Republic fed through any siege, now a folk-life museum of Konavle costume and craft. Cool, quiet and unusual — and a Game of Thrones location for those who care to know it stood in for a King's Landing street.

items.name: War Photo Limited
items.description: A powerful, world-class photojournalism gallery on Antuninska street, just off the Stradun, founded to show the human reality of conflict — the Balkan wars and beyond. Sobering and beautifully curated; a serious counterpoint to the city's beauty, best for adults and older teens.

items.name: Maritime Museum & Aquarium at Fort St John
items.description: Inside the sea-facing Fort St John, the Maritime Museum tells Dubrovnik's story as a great trading republic through ship models and charts, with a small aquarium of Adriatic sea life on the ground floor. An easy, engaging stop that works well for children.

items.name: Jesuit Stairs & St Ignatius Church
items.description: A sweeping Baroque staircase — Dubrovnik's own 'Spanish Steps' — climbing to the elegant Jesuit church of St Ignatius on the city's highest terrace. A quiet, handsome corner of the old town, and famous as the site of Cersei's walk of shame.

items.name: The Old Port (Stara Luka)
items.description: The intimate historic harbour beneath the eastern walls, ringed by the arsenal arches where the Republic once built its galleys. Wooden boats bob against the stone; it is the departure point for Lokrum and island trips, and a lovely spot for an early-evening aperitivo.

items.name: Fort Lovrijenac
items.description: The dramatic 'Gibraltar of Dubrovnik', a triangular fortress perched on a 37-metre sea-cliff just outside the walls, inscribed above its gate: 'Freedom is not sold for all the gold in the world.' Fans will know it as the Red Keep; everyone else comes for the finest view back onto the walled city.

items.name: Cable car up Mount Srđ & Fort Imperial
items.description: A four-minute glide 412 metres up to the ridge behind the city, where the whole walled town, Lokrum and the Elaphiti Islands lay spread below. Time it for sunset with a table at the summit restaurant — one of the great panoramas of the Adriatic, effortless for grandparents.

items.name: Museum of the Homeland War, Fort Imperial
items.description: Inside Napoleon's hilltop Fort Imperial — the first line of defence during the 1991–95 siege — an exhibition of documents, weapons and film that explains how the city held. Moving and important context, paired naturally with the cable-car ascent and the summit views.

items.name: Sunset drinks at a Buža bar
items.description: Slip through a literal hole in the sea walls ('buža' means hole) to bare tables set on the bare rock, a cold drink in hand and nothing between you and Lokrum but the Adriatic. Unpretentious and unforgettable — the city's best-loved sundowner, cash only and worth every minute.

items.name: Banje Beach
items.description: The pretty pebble beach just outside the Ploče gate, with the walled city as its backdrop — a beach club with loungers and a restaurant on one side, free shingle on the other. Convenient for a swim between sightseeing, with cabana service for those who prefer their sun shaded.

items.name: Sea-kayak to Lokrum Island
items.description: Paddle out from beneath Fort Lovrijenac around the walls and across to Lokrum, slipping into sea caves and a quiet cove for a swim along the way. A genuinely memorable half-day on the water — private guided outings can be arranged for families and set to an easy pace.

items.name: Lokrum Island — botanical garden & peacocks
items.description: A ten-minute boat hop to a forested island of holm oak and cypress, with a botanical garden, a ruined Benedictine monastery, roaming peacocks and rabbits, and the salt 'Dead Sea' lagoon for a warm, buoyant swim. Car-free and shaded — a blissful, unhurried escape for all ages.

items.name: Fort Royal viewpoint, Lokrum
items.description: A short climb through Lokrum's woods to a star-shaped Napoleonic fort crowning the island, with a 360-degree panorama back to Dubrovnik's walls and out over the open Adriatic. A rewarding little adventure to pair with a lazy island afternoon.

items.name: Private boat to the Elaphiti Islands
items.description: A day on the water to the car-free trio of Koločep, Lopud and Šipan — swimming from a chartered yacht, lunching on grilled fish, wandering Lopud's Sunj sand beach and Šipan's olive groves and old sea-captains' mansions. The relaxed, glamorous way to see the archipelago, on your own schedule.

items.name: Lopud & Šunj Beach
items.description: The most polished of the Elaphiti islands, car-free and green, ending in Šunj — one of the few genuine sand beaches near Dubrovnik, shallow and warm for children. A leafy promenade, a few good tavernas and a Renaissance monastery-turned-hotel make it a serene day out.

items.name: Šipan — the island of olives
items.description: The largest and quietest Elaphiti island, where Ragusan nobles built summer villas among the olive groves and vineyards. Two sleepy harbour hamlets, a scattering of ruined palaces, and long lunches of just-caught fish — deep calm within an hour of the old town.

items.name: Koločep & the sea caves
items.description: The nearest and greenest Elaphiti island, laced with pine paths and famous for its sea caves and the luminous Blue Cave, best entered by small boat or kayak. A gentle, unhurried spot for a swim and a seafood lunch far from the crowds.

items.name: Trsteno Arboretum
items.description: A Renaissance nobleman's garden 20 minutes up the coast, the oldest arboretum in this part of the world, with a stone aqueduct, a Neptune fountain and 500-year-old plane trees framing Adriatic views. Fans will recognise it as the Red Keep gardens; gardeners simply love its serene terraces.

items.name: Game of Thrones locations tour
items.description: For the many who came to King's Landing before they came to Dubrovnik: the Jesuit Stairs of the walk of shame, Fort Lovrijenac as the Red Keep, the Ethnographic Museum Rupe, and the harbour and walls that framed a hundred scenes. A fun, well-guided way to read the old city through a different lens.

items.name: Day trip: Ston walls & oysters, Pelješac
items.description: An hour north, the little town of Ston guards Europe's longest medieval fortification — a 5km wall climbing the hillside — beside ancient salt pans still worked by hand. Then to neighbouring Mali Ston to shuck oysters straight from the beds where they grow; a perfect gourmet half-day, wine included.

items.name: Day trip: Pelješac wine country
items.description: The peninsula's steep, sun-baked slopes produce Croatia's boldest reds — the celebrated Dingač and Postup from the Plavac Mali grape. Private tastings at family cellars, long lunches with a sea view, and quiet coves for a swim; a grown-up, unhurried counterpoint to the walled city.

items.name: Day trip: Cavtat
items.description: A gentle 20-minute boat south to a palm-lined Riviera town of yacht-filled harbour and easy waterfront tavernas — Dubrovnik's calmer, more elegant neighbour. Climb to the Račić family mausoleum, a masterpiece in white stone by the sculptor Ivan Meštrović, above the cypress cemetery.

items.name: Day trip: Konavle valley
items.description: The green, spring-fed valley south of the city, a patchwork of vineyards, water-mills and villages keeping the old crafts of silk embroidery and folk dance alive. A day of farm-table feasts, horse-riding and quiet back-roads — the authentic, rural Dalmatia most visitors never see.

items.name: Day trip: Bay of Kotor, Montenegro
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Natural and Culturo-Historical Region of Kotor
items.description: Two hours south into the Mediterranean's only true fjord, its cliffs plunging to still water dotted with medieval towns. Wander walled Kotor, sail out to the man-made islet of Our Lady of the Rocks off Perast, and take in one of Europe's most dramatic coastlines — passports and a private driver make it seamless.

items.name: Day trip: Mostar, Bosnia & Herzegovina
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old Bridge Area of the Old City of Mostar
items.description: A longer day inland to the Ottoman crossroads of Mostar, where the soaring 16th-century Stari Most arches over the emerald Neretva — reconstructed stone by stone after the war, and still where local divers plunge from its parapet. A vivid, moving glimpse of a wholly different culture, bazaars and coppersmiths included.

items.name: Red History Museum
items.description: In a converted graphite factory in the port district, Croatia's first museum of the socialist Yugoslav era — a recreated 1980s apartment, propaganda, design and everyday objects, told with wit rather than nostalgia. An offbeat, thought-provoking hour for the curious traveller.

items.name: Gruž market & harbour
items.description: The working port where locals actually shop — a morning market of Konavle figs, lavender, olive oil and just-landed fish along the quay. A refreshingly real, un-touristed corner, and the departure point for many island boats and yacht charters.

items.name: Cooking or oyster-shucking experience
items.description: Learn to make Dalmatian classics — black risotto, peka slow-cooked under embers, fresh olive oil tasting — in a private class or at a Konavle farmstead. Chefs happily build vegetarian menus for Indian palates; a hands-on afternoon the whole family can share.

items.name: Sunset cruise on a traditional gulet
items.description: Charter a classic wooden gulet for the golden hour, gliding beneath the floodlit walls and around Lokrum with drinks and canapés on deck. Discreet, glamorous and easy — the quintessential Adriatic evening, tailored to a private group.

items.name: Cabrio Sports Car & Buggy safari, Srđ
items.description: For families with restless teenagers, a guided buggy or vintage-car run through the hills behind Dubrovnik, off the tourist grid to hidden viewpoints and old fortifications. A dose of adventure and open air with the whole city laid out below.

items.name: Cathedral of the Assumption Bell & the Rupe views
items.description: Climb to the upper lanes above the Stradun where washing lines stretch between shuttered houses and cats doze on warm stone — the lived-in Dubrovnik behind the monuments. A short, atmospheric wander that rewards those who leave the main drag for the steep side-streets.

items.name: Homeland War & siege walking tour
items.description: A guided walk led by a Dubrovnik local who lived through the 1991–92 siege, reading the shell scars still visible on the paving and rooftops. Deeply human and quietly powerful — the story that turns a beautiful backdrop into a living city.

items.name: Private evening in the Rector's Palace atrium
items.description: During the summer festival the palace courtyard becomes a candlelit concert hall of near-perfect acoustics, staging chamber music and opera under the Adriatic stars. A rare, refined experience — arrange seats and a late dinner afterwards for a special-occasion night.

items.name: Restaurant 360
items.area: Old Town (Stari Grad, on the ramparts)
items.description: Dubrovnik's only MICHELIN star — chef Marijo Curić's refined Mediterranean cooking on a terrace built into the medieval walls above the old harbour.

items.name: Nautika
items.description: Dubrovnik's grand classic — traditional Dalmatian cooking on French and Italian foundations, on terraces facing the illuminated Lovrijenac and Bokar fortresses.

items.name: Pjerin
items.description: The elegant table at Villa Dubrovnik — chef Robert Račić's regional, seasonal cooking with Adriatic seafood at its heart, on a cliffside terrace.

items.name: Stara Loza
credentials: MICHELIN Guide Selected (2025) — listed annually since 2017
items.description: A rooftop room atop a 500-year-old palace on Prijeko street — modern Mediterranean cooking above the terracotta roofs of the walled city.

items.name: Restaurant Dubrovnik
items.description: A romantic rooftop hidden above the old town's lanes — refined, contemporary cooking and one of the quieter fine-dining rooms inside the walls.

items.name: Proto
items.description: A Dubrovnik institution since 1886 — fresh Adriatic fish and shellfish done simply and well, with a leafy first-floor terrace above the old town.

items.name: Kopun
items.area: Old Town (Bošković Square, by St Ignatius)
items.description: A quiet square-side table reviving old Dubrovnik recipes — the signature is capon (kopun), slow-baked in the traditional way.

items.name: Pantarul
items.description: A relaxed modern bistro in Lapad — slow-cooked, market-led Dalmatian cooking (the name means 'fork' in the local dialect) at honest value.

items.name: Azur
items.description: A small room in a quiet corner of the walled city marrying Mediterranean produce with Asian technique — Dubrovnik's most distinctive fusion table.

items.name: Bota Oyster & Sushi Bar
items.area: Old Town (by Buža Gate, behind the Cathedral)
items.description: Dalmatian–Japanese fusion from a family that farms its own oysters in Mali Ston — the freshest raw bar inside the walls.

items.name: Taj Mahal
items.description: Not Indian despite the name — a warm, unpretentious room serving Bosnian home cooking and grilled meats in the heart of the walls.

items.name: Buža Bar
credentials: An iconic Old-Town landmark — the clifftop bar cut into the seaward city walls
items.description: Dubrovnik's most famous drink — a cliff-ledge bar reached through a literal hole ('buža') in the city wall, with nothing between your table and the Adriatic.

items.name: D'vino Wine Bar
credentials: A long-established, well-regarded Old-Town wine bar specialising in Croatian wines
items.description: The Old Town's best-loved wine bar — a knowledgeable, welcoming room pouring Croatian wines by the glass, ideal before or after dinner.

items.name: Cave Bar More
credentials: A well-known Dubrovnik landmark bar set inside a natural cave at Hotel More
items.description: A cocktail bar set inside a natural sea cave — drinks under a floodlit limestone cavern with a glass floor over a pool of Adriatic water.

items.name: Bar at Villa Dubrovnik
credentials: Terrace of Villa Dubrovnik — MICHELIN One Key hotel, The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A cocktail on the terrace of Croatia's most decorated hotel — the walled city, Lokrum and the open Adriatic laid out below.

items.title: Private sea-kayak circuit of the city walls at sunset
items.description: Paddle beneath the ramparts and into the Betina cave as the stone turns gold, ending with a swim off Lokrum.

items.title: After-hours private walk of the city walls
items.description: Arrange a guided circuit of the 2km ramparts once the cruise crowds have sailed, with the Adriatic emptying below you.

items.title: Chartered day to the Elaphiti Islands
items.description: A private skipper to Šipan and Lopud for lunch at a family konoba and a swim off an empty cove.

items.title: Private tasting on Pelješac at Grgić Vina
items.description: The peninsula that supplies Croatia's best reds; taste Plavac Mali at the winery the late Napa legend Miljenko Grgić founded.

plan.heading: 3 days in Dubrovnik, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

days.title: The walls and the old town

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The city walls at opening, the full circuit above the terracotta roofs before the heat.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Rector's Palace and the Franciscan pharmacy, then coffee off the Stradun's side lanes.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Restaurant 360, one star, on the ramparts above the old harbour.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private boat to Lopud and the Elaphiti islands, quiet coves and no cars.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at anchor, then a swim off Šunj's shallow bay before the return.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Seafood and Pošip at Nautika, on the point below the Pile gate, the fort lit across the water.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The cable car up Mount Srđ for the coastline laid out below, then the old fort at the top.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A driver up the coast to the Konavle valley for a family winery and lunch among the vines.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A last dinner at Restaurant Stara Loza's rooftop, the old town roofs falling away below.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Ploče
items.description: The quiet cliffside just east of the walls, home to Villa Dubrovnik and Hotel Excelsior — sea views and a five-minute walk in.

items.name: Lapad
items.description: Leafier, calmer, with swimmable bays and a promenade — best for families and longer, slower stays.

items.name: Old Town (within the walls)
items.description: For those who want to live inside the stone; atmospheric but steep, noisy and crowded by day.

events.name: Dubrovnik Summer Festival
events.note: Six weeks of theatre and classical concerts staged on the ramparts and in courtyards across the Old Town since 1950.

events.name: Feast of St Blaise (Sveti Vlaho)
events.note: The patron saint's day, a UNESCO-listed procession — the Old Town at its most local, with no cruise ships in sight.

events.name: Good Food Festival
events.note: A week of tastings, oyster and wine events across the city as the season quietens.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Dubrovnik (DBV), a scenic thirty-minute drive down the coast; a private car meets you, or arrive by private boat into the old harbour.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver for the coast and Konavle valley; the walled old town is entirely pedestrian and walked, its steep stone stairways worth comfortable shoes.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Coverage is reliable and an eSIM works on arrival; wifi is standard in hotels and restaurants.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Croatia uses the euro since 2023; cards are widely accepted, keep a little cash for smaller konobas, and rounding up the bill is the usual tip.

onGround.note: Walk the city walls at opening or near closing to avoid both the heat and the cruise-ship crowds; stay just outside the walls at Ploče or on the Lapad peninsula for quiet, and take a private boat to the Elaphiti islands for a day away from the crowds.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: May-June and September offer warm Adriatic swimming and walkable city walls without the crush; July-August is hot and cruise-crowded through the Old Town, and winters are mild but wet and quiet.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No India nonstop; connect via Istanbul (Turkish Airlines, the most efficient single-stop), Vienna (Austrian) or Dubai (a flydubai leg onward), roughly 12-14 hours total. Turkish through Istanbul gives the best business cabin and lounge; Dubrovnik (DBV) itself is seasonal, so confirm the onward flight operates on your dates.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations beyond routine; tap water is safe to drink. Croatia is very safe; the main issue is heat and cruise-day congestion, plus steep steps and city-wall stairs. No altitude concern.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Workable for vegetarians though Dalmatian cooking leans to fish and meat; Jain diners should brief restaurants directly. Indian food is limited, so ask hotels in advance — Nishta is a genuinely good vegetarian/vegan option inside the Old Town.

closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Edinburgh — TripAgent
seo.description: Edinburgh, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Edinburgh
hero.tagline: A dramatic stone capital of castle, crag and Enlightenment.

ourTake.lede: Edinburgh is a city to walk and climb — the pleasure is in its ridges, closes and sudden views, so pack good shoes and give yourself time to wander off the Royal Mile. August turns the whole place into one vast festival, which is exhilarating but crowded and dear; if you want the city calm and the light long, come in late spring or early autumn instead. Climb Arthur's Seat, drink good whisky, and treat the Old Town's tourist tartan shops as scenery, not shopping.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a walkable, literary old city with castle views, whisky, and easy reach into the Highlands.
ourTake.skipIf: You are chasing sun, beaches or reliably warm weather.

Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: Late spring through early autumn is kindest; August brings the Fringe, International Festival and Tattoo but heaving crowds, and Hogmanay lights up New Year.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jun, Jul, Aug and Sep

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: The Balmoral, a Rocco Forte Hotel
items.area: New Town / Old Town line — 1 Princes Street, above Waverley
items.description: The city's landmark grand hotel beneath its famous clock tower — Rocco Forte's Edinburgh flagship, and the first hotel in Scotland to earn Forbes Five Stars.

items.name: Gleneagles Townhouse
items.description: The city outpost of Scotland's iconic Gleneagles estate — a former bank on St Andrew Square, part hotel, part members' club, with a glass-domed dining room.

items.name: 100 Princes Street
items.area: New Town — 100 Princes Street, facing the Castle
items.description: An intimate 30-room house on Princes Street from Red Carnation, in the former home of a Scottish explorers' club — two staff to every guest, and full-on castle views.

items.name: Prestonfield House
items.area: Newington — under Arthur's Seat, 10 minutes from the centre
items.description: A theatrical 17th-century mansion in 20 acres of parkland with peacocks on the lawn — the most opulent, romantic country house within the city bounds.

items.name: The Witchery by the Castle
items.area: Old Town — Castlehill, at the gates of Edinburgh Castle
items.description: Nine gothic, theatrical suites in 16th-century buildings at the very top of the Royal Mile — the most singular, atmospheric stay in Edinburgh.

items.name: Waldorf Astoria Edinburgh — The Caledonian
items.area: West End — Princes Street, by the Castle
items.description: The grand former railway hotel at the west end of Princes Street — a Victorian landmark of red sandstone with a great spa and Castle views.

items.name: Kimpton Charlotte Square
items.area: New Town — Charlotte Square, West End
items.description: Seven Georgian townhouses on the New Town's most elegant square, wrapped around a glass-roofed courtyard garden — polished, warm and unstuffy.

items.name: The Glasshouse, Autograph Collection
items.description: A design hotel behind a preserved 1846 church façade, crowned by a two-acre rooftop garden with views to Calton Hill and the Firth.

items.name: W Edinburgh
items.area: St James Quarter — Calton Hill edge
items.description: Scotland's first W — a bold, high-design hotel in the St James Quarter with a rooftop bar and 'ribbon' architecture, for members who want the new and the loud.

items.name: Edinburgh Castle
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old and New Towns of Edinburgh
items.description: The fortress on the black volcanic rock is the city's beating heart — crown jewels, the Stone of Destiny, and the one-o'clock gun fired daily since 1861. A private early-access or after-hours guide lets a multi-generation family have the Great Hall and battlements almost to themselves before the crowds and the coaches arrive.

items.name: The Royal Mile
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old and New Towns of Edinburgh
items.description: The mile-long spine of the Old Town runs downhill from the Castle to Holyrood, past closes, kirks, tartan windows and the High Kirk of St Giles. Walk it with a storyteller-guide who peels back the wynds and hidden courtyards the guidebook crowds stream straight past.

items.name: Palace of Holyroodhouse
items.description: The King's official residence in Scotland, at the foot of the Royal Mile — Mary, Queen of Scots' chambers, the ruined abbey, and state apartments still used for royal ceremony. A quiet, richly historic counterpoint to the Castle, and rarely rushed.

items.name: Arthur's Seat & Holyrood Park
items.description: An extinct volcano rising 251 metres straight out of the city, ringed by a royal park of crags, lochs and grazing land. The summit gives the finest panorama of Edinburgh; a private guide can pick the gentler Dunsapie approach so grandparents and grandchildren reach the top together.

items.name: Calton Hill
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old and New Towns of Edinburgh
items.description: The easy-to-reach hill crowned with the half-finished National Monument, the Nelson Monument and the Dugald Stewart Monument — the postcard view of the city and the Firth of Forth. Golden hour here is the single best photograph you'll take in Edinburgh.

items.name: National Museum of Scotland
items.description: A soaring Victorian glasshouse joined to a modern gallery, holding everything from Dolly the cloned sheep to Lewis chessmen and Scottish design. Free, vast and genuinely all-ages — the roof terrace view is a quiet local secret, and there's easy veg-friendly dining in the grand hall.

items.name: Scottish National Gallery
items.description: The nation's great collection sits between the two halves of Princes Street Gardens — Titian, Vermeer, Raeburn's skating minister, and a superb room of Scottish colourists. Compact enough for an unhurried hour with a private art guide before lunch.

items.name: Scottish National Portrait Gallery
items.description: A red-sandstone neo-Gothic palace on Queen Street, its arcaded entrance hall a frieze of Scottish history, its rooms full of the faces that made the nation — from Mary, Queen of Scots to Sean Connery. Beautiful, calm and free.

items.name: New Town & the Georgian House
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old and New Towns of Edinburgh
items.description: The 18th-century planned New Town — Charlotte Square, Georgian terraces, ordered elegance that reshaped European city-building. The restored Georgian House on the square shows exactly how the merchant aristocracy lived; a walking guide reads the whole ensemble.

items.name: Princes Street Gardens
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old and New Towns of Edinburgh
items.description: The green valley below the Castle, where a railway once was and a loch before that — lawns, the Ross Fountain, and the finest ground-level view of the Old Town skyline. An easy, restful pause between shopping and sightseeing.

items.name: The Scott Monument
credentials: Largest monument to a writer in the world
items.description: The soaring Gothic rocket built to honour Sir Walter Scott — the largest monument to a writer in the world — with a marble statue of the author at its base. The fit can climb its 287 narrow steps for a caged panorama; the view from the gardens below is glorious without the climb.

items.name: Dean Village & the Water of Leith
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old and New Towns of Edinburgh
items.description: A hidden former milling hamlet of Tudor-esque buildings tucked in a river gorge minutes from Princes Street — improbably picturesque and blissfully quiet. Follow the Water of Leith walkway past St Bernard's Well; a photographer's and stroller's delight.

items.name: Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh
credentials: One of the world's leading botanic gardens
items.description: Seventy acres of one of the world's great botanic gardens — Victorian glasshouses, a Chinese hillside, the largest cultivated collection of rhododendrons anywhere, and a skyline view back to the city. Peaceful, pram-friendly, and lovely for three generations at an easy pace.

items.name: Camera Obscura & World of Illusions
items.description: A Victorian 'camera obscura' at the top of the Royal Mile that projects a live moving image of the city onto a dish, plus five floors of mirror mazes and optical trickery. A guaranteed winner with children and the young-at-heart, and the rooftop gives a free Castle view.

items.name: The Real Mary King's Close
items.description: A warren of genuine 17th-century streets and homes sealed and buried beneath the Royal Mile, now brought alive by costumed character-guides. Atmospheric, a little spooky, and unlike anything else in the city — best booked as a private timed tour.

items.name: Greyfriars Kirkyard
items.description: The evocative old graveyard behind the National Museum — resting place of city grandees, birthplace of the loyal-dog legend Greyfriars Bobby, and, some say, the source of names J.K. Rowling borrowed for Harry Potter. A gentle, literary detour.

items.name: The Writers' Museum
items.description: A tucked-away 17th-century townhouse in Lady Stair's Close devoted to Scotland's literary giants — Robert Burns, Sir Walter Scott and Robert Louis Stevenson. Small, free, and a fitting stop in the world's first UNESCO City of Literature.

items.name: St Giles' Cathedral
items.description: The great High Kirk on the Royal Mile, its crown-shaped spire a city landmark — inside, the jewel-like Thistle Chapel with its intricately carved stalls is one of Scotland's finest interiors. A guided visit reads the stained glass and 900 years of turbulent history.

items.name: Victoria Street
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old and New Towns of Edinburgh
items.description: The curving, rainbow-fronted Old Town street of independent shops widely thought to have inspired Harry Potter's Diagon Alley. Photogenic from the Bow above and full of small pleasures — a bookseller of magic, a cheesemonger, a joke shop — for a leisurely browse.

items.name: Grassmarket
items.description: A wide, cobbled square in the Castle's shadow that was once a livestock market and place of execution, now lined with pubs, boutiques and independent shops. A lively spot for people-watching with the fortress rearing above you.

items.name: Stockbridge
items.description: The village-within-the-city — a genteel neighbourhood of independent delis, antique shops and the colonnaded Sunday market, beside the Water of Leith. A refined, unhurried morning away from the tourist track, with strong cafe and veg-friendly dining options.

items.name: The Scotch Whisky Experience
credentials: Home to the world's largest collection of Scotch whisky
items.description: Right beside the Castle, an introduction to Scotland's regions and distilling, home to the world's largest collection of Scotch whisky — nearly 3,500 bottles. The tasting tours suit both a first-timer and a connoisseur, and the shop can source rarities.

items.name: Johnnie Walker Princes Street
items.description: Eight floors of interactive whisky storytelling in a landmarked Art Deco former department store, topped by the 1820 rooftop bars looking straight across to the Castle. Personalised tastings and a superb rooftop cocktail-and-view finish make it a polished flagship experience.

items.name: The Royal Yacht Britannia
credentials: Repeatedly rated Tripadvisor's No.1 Attraction in the World
items.description: The late Queen's floating royal home for over 40 years, berthed at Leith — five decks of state apartments, the royal bedrooms and the Rolls-Royce garage, all frozen as they were. Repeatedly rated among the world's very best attractions; end with tea and cake in the Royal Deck Tea Room.

items.name: Leith & The Shore
items.description: Edinburgh's revitalised historic port — cobbled quaysides, converted warehouses and the city's densest cluster of fine dining, including its Michelin-starred kitchens. Arrive by the modern tram and make an evening of it on the waterfront.

items.name: Dynamic Earth
items.description: An immersive science attraction beneath Arthur's Seat that travels from the Big Bang through ice ages to the present, with a full-dome planetarium. The most engaging rainy-day option for families with curious children.

items.name: Scottish National Gallery of Modern Art (Modern One & Two)
items.description: Two neoclassical buildings in landscaped grounds — a Charles Jencks landform, a Paolozzi studio recreation, and Dada and Surrealist treasures. A calm, cultured half-day reached along the Water of Leith, and free to enter.

items.name: Museum of Edinburgh & the Canongate
items.description: In the lower, quieter reach of the Royal Mile, a rambling 16th-century townhouse telling the story of the city itself, near the handsome Canongate Kirk. A pleasant, low-key stop between the Palace and the Parliament.

items.name: Scottish Parliament
items.description: Enric Miralles' bold, controversial 2004 building at the foot of the Royal Mile — a much-awarded piece of modern architecture that rewards a guided tour of its debating chamber and inventive detail. A striking contrast to the ancient stone all around it.

items.name: The Meadows & Bruntsfield Links
items.description: A broad, tree-lined common south of the Old Town, framed by the cherry-blossom avenue that draws the whole city each spring. An easy, green stroll where local Edinburgh unwinds, well away from the crowds.

items.name: Victoria Terrace & the Vennel viewpoint
items.description: Two of the city's best free photographs — the balcony walkway above Victoria Street, and the stepped Vennel closes off the Grassmarket that frame the Castle perfectly between old tenement walls. A guide who knows the light will time them for you.

items.name: Blackford Hill & the Royal Observatory
items.description: A quiet suburban hill giving a full panorama over the city to the Castle and the Forth, crowned by the Victorian Royal Observatory. A local's viewpoint, easily worked into a private half-day by car.

items.name: Craigmillar Castle
items.description: One of Scotland's best-preserved medieval castles, where Mary, Queen of Scots once sheltered — dramatic, atmospheric and, remarkably for its quality, almost tourist-free. A rewarding short drive for those who want history without the queues.

items.name: Edinburgh International Festival & the Fringe
items.description: Every August the whole city becomes a stage — the International Festival's world-class opera, theatre and orchestras alongside the Fringe, the largest arts festival on earth. Book premium tickets and a hotel far in advance; a concierge is close to essential in peak season.

items.name: The Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo
items.description: Massed pipes and drums and international performers on the Castle esplanade each August, floodlit against the ramparts — one of the great spectacles in the world calendar. Reserved premium seating and a private car for the departure crush make the night effortless.

items.name: Edinburgh's Christmas & Hogmanay
credentials: One of the world's most famous New Year celebrations
items.description: The winter city glows — a Christmas market and rink in Princes Street Gardens, and the world-famous three-day Hogmanay street party and fireworks over the Castle. Hospitality packages and a guide turn a heaving crowd into a warm, easy celebration.

items.name: Rosslyn Chapel
items.description: Seven miles south, the astonishingly carved 15th-century chapel of 'The Da Vinci Code' fame — every surface a riot of angels, greenery and enigmatic symbols. Small, richly atmospheric, and best reached by private car with a guide who can decode the stonework.

items.name: Stirling Castle
items.description: Under an hour away, one of Scotland's grandest and most important castles, magnificently sited on its crag with the restored golden-stone Renaissance palace of the Stuart kings. Pair it with the nearby Wallace Monument and the Kelpies for a full, cinematic day out.

items.name: The Forth Bridges & South Queensferry
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — The Forth Bridge
items.description: Just west of the city, the mighty red cantilever Forth Bridge — a UNESCO World Heritage Site — spans the firth beside its two road bridges. Lunch in pretty South Queensferry and take a cruise out to Inchcolm Abbey for the best perspective of all three.

items.name: Glasgow
items.description: Under an hour by train or car, Scotland's confident second city — the free Kelvingrove and Burrell Collection, Charles Rennie Mackintosh's architecture, and the country's best shopping and dining. A vivid, characterful contrast to genteel Edinburgh.

items.name: Loch Lomond & The Trossachs
items.description: Scotland's first national park, and the gateway to Highland scenery — the largest loch in Britain by surface area, framed by mountains, with lochside cruises and grand hotels. A gentle, spectacular taste of the Highlands within easy day-trip reach.

items.name: The Highlands — Glencoe & the West
items.description: For those with a full day and a chauffeur, the road north opens onto Rannoch Moor and the brooding grandeur of Glencoe — arguably Scotland's most dramatic glen — with the Glenfinnan viaduct and Loch Ness within reach on longer runs. Best done privately, at your own pace.

items.name: The Kelpies & Falkirk Wheel
credentials: The Kelpies — world's largest equine sculptures
Falkirk Wheel — world's only rotating boat lift
items.description: Half an hour west, two feats of engineering-as-art — Andy Scott's 30-metre steel horse-heads, the largest equine sculptures in the world, and the only rotating boat lift on earth. A short, memorable stop that delights children and design lovers alike.

items.name: North Berwick & the Scottish Seabird Centre
credentials: Bass Rock — world's largest Northern gannet colony
items.description: A genteel seaside town under 40 minutes east, with golden beaches, a five-star wildlife centre and boat trips to the Bass Rock — the world's largest colony of Northern gannets. A breezy, family-friendly counterpoint to the city, with fine golf on the coast.

items.name: Restaurant Martin Wishart
items.description: Scotland's longest-held Michelin star — refined modern French cooking on the Leith waterfront, a star for a quarter of a century.

items.name: The Kitchin
items.description: Tom Kitchin's 'from nature to plate' cooking on the Leith shore — Scottish seasonal produce and French technique, starred since 2007.

items.name: Condita
items.description: A candle-lit, six-table room doing a single no-choice tasting menu — the city's most intimate and personal Michelin experience.

items.name: Heron
items.area: Leith — Bonnington Road, on the Water of Leith
items.description: Tomás Gormley and Sam Yorke's calm canal-side room — precise, produce-led tasting menus that won a star and hold it.

items.name: Timberyard
items.area: Old Town — Lady Lawson Street, near the Castle
items.description: A family-run former timber warehouse doing wild, foraged, live-fire Scottish cooking — a Michelin star and, latterly, a Green Star for its sustainability.

items.name: Lyla
items.area: New Town — Royal Terrace, Calton Hill
items.description: Stuart Ralston's seafood-focused tasting-menu room on Royal Terrace — a 'nature to plate' journey through Scottish produce, starred in 2025.

items.name: Avery

events.name: Edinburgh Festival Fringe
events.note: Roughly the first three weeks of the month; the city's defining event.

events.name: Edinburgh International Festival
events.note: The curated classical, opera and theatre programme that runs alongside the Fringe.

events.name: Edinburgh's Hogmanay
events.note: Scotland's landmark New Year celebration, with a torchlight procession and street party.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: You land at Edinburgh Airport (EDI), around 25 minutes by private car to the New Town, with a chauffeur meeting you as you clear.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The city is walkable and handsome on foot, though the Old Town's hills and setts are steep; a private driver is worth keeping for excursions to the Highlands or a whisky estate.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Coverage is reliable; a UK eSIM or roaming plan works well, and note the UK sits outside EU roaming so confirm your plan covers Britain.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The pound sterling; cards and contactless are near-universal, Scottish banknotes circulate alongside Bank of England ones, and a 10 to 12 percent tip is standard.

onGround.note: Stay in the New Town around the Balmoral or on a Georgian crescent for elegance and calm; weather turns quickly, so pack layers and something waterproof even in summer, and book Highland day trips or castle access well ahead.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: May to September is mildest and driest with very long daylight; August adds the Festival and Fringe (book far ahead). November-February are dark, wet and windy; the city is beautiful but bleak then.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No non-stop from India; fastest is via London Heathrow on British Airways (about 12-13h total) with a quick connection, or via a Gulf hub on Emirates/Qatar in strong business/first. The Heathrow routing is smoothest; allow buffer time for the T5 transfer.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required; tap water is safe. Very safe, walkable city; ordinary care at night around the Old Town nightlife and expect changeable, wet weather year-round.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian dining is easy and Indian food is well established. Ask kitchens for Jain-appropriate dishes; several Indian restaurants will adapt with notice, and veg-forward fine dining is common.

seo.title: Florence — TripAgent
seo.description: Florence, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Florence
hero.tagline: The cradle of the Renaissance, set in Tuscan hills.

ourTake.lede: Florence is small enough to exhaust in a weekend and rich enough to return to for a lifetime — the trick is to book the Uffizi and Accademia the moment you have dates, and to see them first thing so the rest of the day is yours. Everyone climbs the Duomo; fewer walk up to Piazzale Michelangelo or San Miniato at sunset, which is the better view and half the crowd. Cross the river to the Oltrarno for the artisans' workshops, and treat lunch as the meal that matters here.
ourTake.comeIf: You want to live inside the Renaissance for a few days, with long lunches, quiet churches and world-class galleries.
ourTake.skipIf: You are after beaches, nightlife or nature; Florence is a walkable art city, not a resort.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Firenze
credentials: World's 50 Best Hotels 2025 (No. 9, highest in Florence)
items.description: A restored 15th-century Medici palace wrapped around the city's largest private garden — the finest address in Florence, without argument.

items.name: Hotel Savoy, a Rocco Forte Hotel
items.description: The grande dame of the city centre, on Florence's grandest square — pure Rocco Forte polish, steps from the Duomo.

items.name: The St. Regis Florence
items.description: A Brunelleschi-designed Renaissance palace on the Arno — St. Regis butler service inside a piece of the city's history.

items.name: Villa San Michele, A Belmond Hotel, Florence
items.description: A former monastery with a façade attributed to Michelangelo's school, looking down on the whole of Florence from Fiesole.

items.name: Portrait Firenze, Lungarno Collection
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The Ferragamo family's jewel steps from the Ponte Vecchio — a small, exacting house with the best river address in the city.

items.name: Collegio alla Querce, Auberge Resorts Collection
credentials: Architectural Digest — Great Design Hotel Award (2025)
MICHELIN Guide — Best New Hotels in the World
items.description: A 16th-century former boarding school on the hillside, reborn as Auberge's first Italian house — the city's newest icon.

items.name: Helvetia & Bristol Firenze, Starhotels Collezione
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The first grand hotel in the historic centre — a 19th-century townhouse on the fashion street, run with quiet Florentine grace.

items.name: Palazzo Portinari Salviati, Residenza d'Epoca
items.description: Frescoed rooms in the 15th-century home of Dante's Beatrice — later Cosimo I de' Medici's own residence.

items.name: Villa Cora
items.description: A 19th-century aristocratic villa above the Boboli Gardens — belle-époque grandeur with a pool and its own park.

items.name: Villa La Massa
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A 16th-century Medici villa on the Arno just beyond the city — Villa d'Este's Tuscan sister, riverside and serene.

items.name: Il Salviatino Firenze
items.description: A converted 15th-century villa high in the Fiesole hills, with frescoes, terraced gardens and the city laid out below.

items.name: Hotel Lungarno, Lungarno Collection
items.description: The Ferragamos' riverside house on the Oltrarno bank, hung with a private art collection and looking to the Ponte Vecchio.

items.name: COMO Castello del Nero
items.description: A restored Renaissance castle in the Chianti hills — the COMO group's Tuscan estate, a short drive from the city.

items.name: Brunelleschi Hotel
items.description: Built into a 6th-century Byzantine tower and medieval church, in a hidden square a lane from the Duomo.

items.name: The Place Firenze
items.description: A discreet, residence-like boutique by Santa Maria Novella — more private home than hotel, and all the better for it.

items.name: Palazzo Vecchietti
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: A 16th-century palace turned all-suite house — Michele Bonan interiors, each room named for a Florentine artist.

items.name: Grand Hotel Minerva
items.description: The only rooftop pool with a Duomo view in the centre, above a 13th-century palazzo on Santa Maria Novella square.

items.name: Riva Lofts Florence
