items.description: A 19th-century factory turned green, sleepy retreat on the quiet bank of the Arno, gently removed from the crowds.

items.name: Velona's Jungle Luxury Suites
items.description: A jewel-box of maximalist design in the historic centre — small, bold and full of personality.

items.name: Torre di Bellosguardo
items.description: A medieval tower and Renaissance villa on the Bellosguardo hill, with the most storied private view of Florence.

items.name: Hotel Calimala
items.description: A polished contemporary boutique metres from the Duomo, with a rooftop terrace over the rooftops.

items.name: Ad Astra
items.description: A quiet villa-hotel set in Europe's largest privately owned walled garden, on the Oltrarno bank.

items.name: NH Collection Firenze Porta Rossa
items.description: One of Italy's oldest hotels, in a medieval tower a lane from the Ponte Vecchio — history at a sensible price.

items.name: Florence Cathedral (Cattedrale di Santa Maria del Fiore)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: The green, pink and white marble bulk of Florence's cathedral is the city's beating heart, its nave vast enough to swallow a crowd yet hushed under Brunelleschi's dome. Entry to the cathedral floor is free, so a multi-generational group can step inside together at their own pace, and a private early guide sidesteps the queues that ring the piazza by mid-morning.

items.name: Brunelleschi's Dome (Cupola del Duomo)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: Still the largest masonry dome ever raised, built between 1420 and 1436 without scaffolding by a technique Brunelleschi kept secret. The 463-step climb between its double shells rewards you with the Vasari-Zuccari Last Judgement frescoes at eye level and all of Florence at your feet — timed-entry only, best booked well ahead through your advisor for a first slot.

items.name: Florence Baptistery (Battistero di San Giovanni)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: The octagonal Romanesque baptistery is among the oldest buildings in the city, its ceiling a shimmering gold-ground mosaic of the Last Judgement that reduces most visitors to silence. Ghiberti's bronze 'Gates of Paradise' face the cathedral — the originals now protected in the Opera del Duomo museum, with faithful casts in place here.

items.name: Giotto's Campanile (Campanile di Giotto)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: Giotto's slender bell tower, sheathed in the same white, green and red marble as the cathedral, is widely held to be the most beautiful in Italy. Its 414 steps open onto terraces that frame the dome itself — the one climb in Florence that puts Brunelleschi's cupola in your photograph rather than under your feet.

items.name: Museo dell'Opera del Duomo
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: The quietest and most rewarding stop of the whole cathedral complex, holding the original sculptures moved indoors for safekeeping — Ghiberti's real Gates of Paradise, Donatello's gaunt Magdalene, and Michelangelo's unfinished Bandini Pietà. A full-scale reconstruction of the cathedral's medieval facade fills a light-filled hall, making this an air-conditioned, unhurried refuge for older travellers.

items.name: Uffizi Gallery (Le Gallerie degli Uffizi)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: The single greatest concentration of Renaissance painting on earth, from Botticelli's Birth of Venus and Primavera to Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael and Caravaggio, hung in Vasari's Medici office block above the Arno. It rewards a private early-access or after-hours guide who can walk you to the essentials in two focused hours rather than three exhausting ones.

items.name: Galleria dell'Accademia (Michelangelo's David)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: You come for one thing — Michelangelo's David, luminous under his purpose-built skylight — and stay for the unfinished 'Prisoners' straining out of their marble blocks nearby, a lesson in genius no photograph conveys. Small enough for a short, comfortable visit with children or grandparents; reserved timed entry is essential year-round.

items.name: Bargello National Museum (Museo Nazionale del Bargello)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: Florence's finest sculpture collection sits in a 13th-century fortress-palace and is almost always calm — Donatello's bronze David, his St. George, works by Michelangelo, Verrocchio and Cellini, and the two competing baptistery-door panels that launched the Renaissance. The connoisseur's alternative to the crowds, and blessedly cool in summer.

items.name: Palazzo Vecchio
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: Florence's fortress town hall still governs the city, its Salone dei Cinquecento a golden hall of Vasari battle frescoes and a Michelangelo 'Genius of Victory'. Family-friendly 'secret passages' tours climb into hidden staircases and the roof timbers, and the tower gives a view that is pure medieval Florence — a rare place where children and adults are equally gripped.

items.name: Piazza della Signoria & Loggia dei Lanzi
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: Florence's open-air sculpture court and its living room for seven centuries, ringed by Cellini's bronze Perseus, Giambologna's Rape of the Sabine Women and a copy of David on the spot the original once stood. Ideal for an unhurried evening passeggiata, with Rivoire's historic cafe on the square for hot chocolate after dark.

items.name: Ponte Vecchio
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: The last of Florence's bridges to survive the war, lined since the 1590s with goldsmiths and jewellers whose little shuttered shops overhang the Arno. Cross it at dawn or after the day-trippers leave for the honeyed light the painters loved; the goldsmiths remain a discreet place to commission a bespoke piece.

items.name: Vasari Corridor (Corridoio Vasariano)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: The Medici's private elevated passage, built by Vasari in 1565 so the family could walk from the Uffizi to the Pitti Palace above the crowds and over the Ponte Vecchio. Reopened to the public in December 2024 after long restoration, it is one of the most exclusive walks in Italy — best arranged as a small-group or private slot through your advisor.

items.name: Pitti Palace (Palazzo Pitti)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: The Medici and later Savoy grand-ducal residence across the river, now a cluster of museums — the Palatine Gallery hangs Raphaels and Titians three-deep in gilded state rooms, alongside the Treasury, costume and modern-art collections. A single palace that can absorb a whole leisurely day, with plenty of seating for those who tire of walking.

items.name: Boboli Gardens (Giardino di Boboli)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: The Medici's monumental hillside garden behind the Pitti, a 16th-century blueprint for the formal gardens of Europe, terraced with fountains, statue-lined avenues and the grotto of Buontalenti. Green, shaded and expansive — the natural place to rest a multi-generational group between museums, with panoramas back over the city.

items.name: Bardini Garden (Giardino Bardini)
items.description: A steep, little-known garden whose Baroque staircase and springtime wisteria tunnel frame one of the most beautiful and least crowded views of the Florence skyline. The villa's terrace cafe is a serene, discreet spot for lunch or an aperitivo away from the centre's bustle.

items.name: Piazzale Michelangelo
items.description: The classic panorama of Florence — the whole terracotta city and its dome laid out across the Arno — from a 19th-century terrace by Giuseppe Poggi. Best at sunset or, for a group who prefers calm, at first light; a private car up the hill spares elderly travellers the climb.

items.name: Basilica of San Miniato al Monte
items.description: One of the oldest and most atmospheric churches in Tuscany, its green-and-white Romanesque facade crowning the hill just above Piazzale Michelangelo. The Benedictine monks still sing Gregorian chant at vespers — a quietly moving experience, and the terrace view rivals the piazzale below with a fraction of the crowd.

items.name: Basilica of Santa Croce
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: The great Franciscan church and the pantheon of Italian genius, holding the tombs of Michelangelo, Galileo, Machiavelli and Rossini, with Giotto frescoes in the chapels and Brunelleschi's serene Pazzi Chapel in the cloister. The leather school behind the apse (below) makes this a natural pairing of art and craft.

items.name: Basilica of San Lorenzo & Medici Chapels
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: The Medici's parish church, its facade left raw but its interior a Brunelleschi masterpiece, with Michelangelo's Laurentian Library staircase alongside. The attached Medici Chapels hold the dynasty's marble tombs carved by Michelangelo himself — Dawn, Dusk, Night and Day — beneath a chapel of inlaid semiprecious stone.

items.name: Basilica of Santa Maria Novella
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: The Dominicans' church, with Alberti's mathematically perfect marble facade and Masaccio's revolutionary 'Trinity', the first true painting in Renaissance perspective. Steps away sits its ancient pharmacy (below), making the quarter around the station a surprisingly rich pocket of the city.

items.name: Officina Profumo-Farmaceutica di Santa Maria Novella
items.description: The world's oldest pharmacy, founded by Dominican friars in 1221 and still compounding fragrances, tonics and rosewater in frescoed, chandeliered salons off Via della Scala. Part museum, part boutique — a discreet, unhurried place to choose gifts, with private appointments and shipping easily arranged.

items.name: Brancacci Chapel (Cappella Brancacci)
items.description: A small chapel inside Santa Maria del Carmine holding Masaccio's frescoes of St Peter — the cycle that taught the entire Renaissance how to paint volume and emotion, studied by Michelangelo as a young man. Timed, small-group entry keeps it intimate; an art-historian guide turns a ten-minute stop into the highlight of a trip.

items.name: Basilica of Santo Spirito
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: Brunelleschi's last and purest church, its plain 18th-century facade hiding a sublime, perfectly proportioned interior — and a small wooden crucifix carved by a teenage Michelangelo. The tree-lined piazza outside is the social heart of the Oltrarno, ringed with wine bars and trattorie that fill at aperitivo hour.

items.name: Palazzo Davanzati (Museum of the Old Florentine House)
items.description: A rare intact 14th-century merchant's palace, its frescoed 'Hall of Parrots' and 'Peacock Room' showing exactly how a wealthy Florentine family lived between the medieval tower and the Renaissance palazzo. Small, calm and endlessly atmospheric — a hidden gem that lets a family picture daily life behind all the marble grandeur.

items.name: Medici Riccardi Palace & Gozzoli Chapel
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: The Medici's first family palace, its tiny private chapel entirely wrapped in Benozzo Gozzoli's jewel-like 'Procession of the Magi', a fresco parade of the family themselves in Renaissance finery. Timed entry keeps the chapel serene — one of the most dazzling small rooms in all of Florence.

items.name: San Marco Museum (Museo di San Marco)
items.description: A Dominican convent where Fra Angelico painted a devotional fresco in every monk's cell, including the ethereal 'Annunciation' at the top of the stairs. Quiet, contemplative and rarely crowded — many consider it the most spiritually affecting museum in the city, and Savonarola's own cell survives here.

items.name: Mercato Centrale & San Lorenzo Market
items.description: A soaring 19th-century iron market hall whose ground floor is Florence's larder and whose upper floor is a bustling gourmet food court open late — pasta, gelato, wine and, importantly, several genuinely good vegetarian and produce-forward stalls for veg-aware travellers. The leather stalls of the surrounding streets are the city's classic shopping scrum.

items.name: Sant'Ambrogio Market
items.description: The neighbourhood market where Florentines actually shop, far calmer than San Lorenzo, with a covered hall of cheese, produce and flowers and a beloved cluster of no-frills lunch spots outside. The authentic, unstaged side of the city for anyone who has already seen the sights and wants to feel the daily rhythm.

items.name: Scuola del Cuoio (Leather School of Santa Croce)
items.description: Founded after the war by Franciscan friars and Florentine leather families inside the monastery behind Santa Croce, still the city's largest working leather workshop where you watch artisans cut, tool and gild by hand. Bespoke bags and small goods can be commissioned and monogrammed on the spot — a memorable, hands-on stop that engages every generation.

items.name: Oltrarno Artisan Quarter (San Frediano & Santo Spirito)
items.description: The 'other side of the Arno' where Florence's craft still lives — book-binders, gilders, silversmiths, frame-makers and cobblers in tiny street-level botteghe along Via Maggio, Via dei Serragli and Borgo San Frediano. A private artisan walk arranges introductions inside the workshops that don't advertise, the quiet luxury of being let behind the door.

items.name: Gucci Garden (Gucci Museum) & Piazza della Signoria fashion houses
items.description: Florence is the birthplace of Italian fashion, and the Gucci Garden on the Piazza della Signoria pairs an archive-museum of the house's Florentine roots with a Massimo Bottura restaurant. A civilised pause for design-minded travellers between the Uffizi and Palazzo Vecchio, moments from the Ferragamo museum across the river.

items.name: Museo Ferragamo (Palazzo Spini Feroni)
items.description: Inside Salvatore Ferragamo's medieval-palace flagship on Via de' Tornabuoni, a museum of the shoemaker-to-the-stars' inventions and Hollywood commissions. Set on Florence's most elegant shopping street — the natural base for a discreet afternoon among the maisons of Via de' Tornabuoni.

items.name: Rose Garden & Iris Garden (Giardino delle Rose)
items.description: A free, gently terraced garden just below Piazzale Michelangelo with a thousand rose varieties, Folon bronze sculptures and the same city view without the tour-bus crowd. The adjacent Iris Garden blooms only in May, when Florence's emblem flower fills the hillside — a serene, romantic spot to catch your breath.

items.name: Basilica of Santissima Annunziata & Piazza SS. Annunziata
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: Florence's most harmonious Renaissance square, framed by Brunelleschi's Ospedale degli Innocenti — Europe's first orphanage and the first truly Renaissance building — with its Della Robbia roundels of swaddled infants. A moving, under-visited corner with a small museum, and the square's arcades give welcome shade.

items.name: Santa Trinita & the Sassetti Chapel
items.description: An easily missed church at the foot of Via de' Tornabuoni holding Ghirlandaio's fresco cycle of St Francis, painted against a recognisable 15th-century Florentine skyline peopled with real Medici-era faces. A quick, rich stop that rewards the shopper detouring off Tornabuoni.

items.name: Galileo Museum (Museo Galileo)
items.description: A dazzling collection of Renaissance and Medici scientific instruments — antique globes, astrolabes, telescopes and, disarmingly, Galileo's own preserved finger. A refreshing change of register from the paintings, and a genuine hit with curious children and grandchildren, right by the Uffizi on the river.

items.name: Stibbert Museum (Museo Stibbert)
items.description: The eccentric hilltop villa of a Victorian collector, its halls filled with a life-size cavalcade of European and Japanese armour and a romantic English garden. Well off the tourist track and reachable by a short private drive — an unexpected, atmospheric outing for a group that has done the Renaissance headliners.

items.name: Fiesole (Roman theatre & hilltop views)
items.description: The Etruscan-Roman town on the ridge above Florence, with a preserved Roman theatre, an archaeological area and cool, cypress-lined lanes that the Florentine nobility retreated to in summer. Twenty minutes by car, it makes an easy half-day escape with the finest long view back over the city — ideal for a leisurely lunch on a hot afternoon.

items.name: Chianti Classico wine estates (Greve, Radda, Castellina)
items.description: The rolling cypress-and-vine country between Florence and Siena, where historic family estates and Antinori's cathedral-like modern winery pour Chianti Classico and Super Tuscans over long lunches. A private-driver day with a pre-arranged cellar visit and estate meal is the discreet way to do it — the kitchens will happily cook Tuscan vegetarian on notice.

items.name: Antinori nel Chianti Classico (winery & estate)
items.description: The Antinori family's architecturally striking headquarters, a spiralling glass-and-terracotta winery buried in the hillside with a rooftop of vines, a museum and a restaurant over the barrel halls. Just 30 minutes from the city — the most polished single wine visit near Florence, and easily booked as a private experience.

items.name: Siena (Piazza del Campo & Duomo)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Siena
items.description: The great medieval rival to Florence, built in warm brick around the shell-shaped Piazza del Campo and crowned by a zebra-striped cathedral of astonishing marble floors. A private day-trip lets an older group tour the Campo and Duomo unhurried and lunch well before the return — Tuscan cuisine here is generous to vegetarians.

items.name: San Gimignano (the towers)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of San Gimignano
items.description: The 'medieval Manhattan', a tiny hill town bristling with fourteen surviving stone tower-houses and famed for its crisp Vernaccia white wine and the world-champion Dondoli gelateria on the main square. Compact enough for a short, comfortable visit and beautifully paired with a Chianti estate lunch on the same private drive.

items.name: Pisa (Piazza dei Miracoli & Leaning Tower)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Piazza del Duomo, Pisa
items.description: The Field of Miracles — the Leaning Tower, the Duomo and the Baptistery gleaming white on a green lawn — is one of the most photographed ensembles in the world and a rite of passage for a first Tuscan trip. Easily combined with Lucca in a single private day; a guide arranges the timed tower climb for those who want it.

items.name: Lucca (walled city & Renaissance ramparts)
items.description: An unspoiled walled town whose intact tree-topped Renaissance ramparts you can cycle in a leisurely loop, with the oval Piazza dell'Anfiteatro, Puccini's birthplace and a genuinely elegant, uncrowded feel. The refined alternative to Pisa's crush — often the day-trip guests remember most fondly.

items.name: Chianti hot-air balloon & vineyard sunrise
items.description: A dawn balloon flight over the vine-striped Chianti hills, drifting silently above castles and cypress avenues before a Champagne-and-Tuscan breakfast on landing. A rare, once-in-a-trip experience arranged privately for a family or couple — weather-dependent, so build flexibility into the itinerary.

items.name: Cooking class & market experience in a Tuscan villa
items.description: A private chef-led class — often paired with a morning at Sant'Ambrogio market — turning fresh Tuscan produce into handmade pasta, ribollita and dolci in a countryside kitchen. Fully adaptable to vegetarian and Jain-friendly requests with advance notice, and a warm, hands-on afternoon that brings multiple generations together around one table.

items.name: Cathedral rooftop & 'Terraces' guided walk
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Florence
items.description: A small-group guided route across the cathedral's usually-closed exterior terraces and galleries, walking around the base of the dome at rooftop height among the marble sculpture up close. An exclusive, vertigo-light alternative for those who'd rather not climb 463 steps but still want the intimacy of Brunelleschi's masterpiece.

items.name: Enoteca Pinchiorri
items.description: Florence's only three-star, in a 17th-century palazzo — three stars held since 2004, and one of Europe's great wine cellars.

items.name: Santa Elisabetta
items.description: A jewel-box two-star inside a Byzantine tower at the Brunelleschi Hotel — Tuscan produce, exactingly rendered.

items.name: Gucci Osteria da Massimo Bottura
items.description: Bottura's playful, worldly kitchen on the city's grandest square — Karime Lopez and Takahiko Kondo cooking with real wit.

items.name: Il Palagio
items.description: Refined, produce-led cooking in the Four Seasons' neoclassical rooms, opening onto the great garden.

items.name: Borgo San Jacopo
items.description: A star with two balcony tables over the Arno, looking straight at the Ponte Vecchio — the finest river view in the city.

items.name: Atto di Vito Mollica
items.description: Vito Mollica's frescoed room behind the cathedral — sea-led, considered cooking in a Medici palace.

items.name: Saporium Firenze
items.description: Ariel Hagen's sustainable, garden-to-plate cooking on the Arno's quieter bank — Tuscany at its most seasonal.

items.name: Serrae Villa Fiesole
items.description: Vito Mollica's second star in the Fiesole hills — modern, refined cooking with the whole valley below.

items.name: Luca's by Paulo Airaudo
items.description: Airaudo's newly-starred kitchen at Hotel La Gemma — inventive, precise cooking in the heart of the city.

items.name: Ora d'Aria
items.description: Marco Stabile's long-standing modern-Tuscan room near the Ponte Vecchio — a Florence fixture of real craft.

items.name: Cibrèo Ristorante
items.description: The elegant flagship of the Cibrèo family — Florence's iconic dishes, cooked with warmth and no pretence.

items.name: La Torre — COMO Castello del Nero
items.description: Refined Tuscan cooking inside a Renaissance castle in the Chianti hills — a destination in its own right.

items.name: Trattoria Cibrèo — Il Cibrèino
items.description: The trattoria sibling of Cibrèo — the same iconic cooking, a fraction of the ceremony, and no reservations.

items.name: Il Santo Bevitore
items.description: A convivial Oltrarno room of cured meats, ribollita and roast pigeon — Tuscan classics done exactly right.

items.name: Il Latini
items.description: A fourth-generation fiaschetteria from 1911 — hams from the ceiling, communal tables, and Tuscany on every plate.

items.name: Zeb
items.description: A tiny mother-and-son counter in San Niccolò serving creative Tuscan cooking to a handful of stools.

items.name: Trattoria Cammillo
items.description: A beloved 1945 trattoria near the Ponte Vecchio — Tuscan classics with a worldly twist, run by the same family for decades.

items.name: Buca Lapi
items.description: The oldest cellar restaurant in Florence, since 1880 — the home of a proper bistecca alla fiorentina.

items.name: La Giostra
items.description: A theatrical, candlelit Santa Croce trattoria of great generosity — pasta, pici and a famous warmth of welcome.

items.name: Trattoria Sostanza
items.description: A working trattoria since 1869 — no reservations, shared tables, and the butter chicken Florence queues for.

items.name: Cibrèo Caffè
items.description: The Cibrèo family's café — modern, reimagined local cooking in a relaxed, all-day setting.

items.name: L'Ortone
items.description: Contemporary cooking on traditional Tuscan foundations, beside the city's oldest food market.

items.name: Podere 39
items.description: A secret-garden trattoria on the city's southern edge — meat, fish and vegetables cooked with real care.

items.name: Trattoria da Burde
items.description: A love-letter-to-Tuscany trattoria on the outskirts — old-fashioned, generous, and worth the short trip.

items.name: Trattoria da Bibe
items.description: A countryside family trattoria south of the city — Tuscan home cooking exactly as it should be.

items.name: Caffè Rivoire
items.description: An 1872 institution on Piazza della Signoria — the grand aperitivo, and the city's most famous hot chocolate.

items.name: Locale Firenze
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars 2025 (No. 22, highest in Italy)
items.description: A 16th-century palace turned world-class cocktail bar — Renaissance rooms, cutting-edge mixology, and Italy's highest-ranked bar.

items.name: Gucci Giardino 25
items.description: A stylish Gucci-designed bar on the city's grandest square — aperitivo and classics with real polish.

items.name: Manifattura
items.area: Centro Storico / near Piazza della Repubblica
credentials: A noted Florence cocktail bar — all-Italian spirits
items.description: A retro bar serving only Italian spirits — vermouth, amari and gin, in a proper mid-century Florentine mood.

items.name: Empireo — Plaza Hotel Lucchesi
credentials: A landmark rooftop bar, atop the Plaza Hotel Lucchesi
items.description: A rooftop with a near-360° sweep of the city — the Duomo, the Arno and the domes, cocktail in hand.

items.name: La Terrazza — Hotel Continentale (Lungarno Collection)
credentials: A landmark rooftop bar, Lungarno Collection
items.description: The Ferragamos' rooftop over the Ponte Vecchio — the most romantic aperitivo terrace in the city.

items.name: Rasputin
credentials: A noted Florence speakeasy cocktail bar
items.description: A hidden 1920s-style speakeasy behind an unmarked door — Florence's cult after-dark cocktail den.

items.title: Private opening of the Uffizi or Accademia
items.description: Stand before Botticelli's Venus, or Michelangelo's David, in a gallery emptied of everyone but your guide.

items.title: The Vasari Corridor with private access
items.description: Walk Medici's secret elevated passage from the Palazzo Vecchio over the Ponte Vecchio to the Pitti Palace.

items.title: Chef's table at Enoteca Pinchiorri
items.description: Three Michelin stars and one of Europe's deepest cellars, in a Renaissance palazzo courtyard.

items.title: A private artisan afternoon in the Oltrarno
items.description: Time in the leather, gilding and mosaic workshops that have supplied Florence's craft for centuries, by introduction.

plan.heading: 3 days in Florence, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private early-access tour of the Uffizi before public opening, ending at the Botticelli rooms.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Duomo complex and Brunelleschi's dome, then a quiet walk to Piazza della Signoria and the Loggia dei Lanzi.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Enoteca Pinchiorri, Florence's three-Michelin-starred table, with a cellar of extraordinary depth.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Galleria dell'Accademia for the David at opening, then the Medici Chapels.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Cross the Ponte Vecchio into the Oltrarno for the Pitti Palace and Boboli Gardens, then the artisan workshops of Santo Spirito.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Aperitivo on the terrace at Portrait Firenze over the Arno, then dinner at Trattoria Sostanza for the classic butter chicken.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive south into Chianti Classico for a private estate tour and tasting at Antinori nel Chianti Classico.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch among the vines, then the medieval hill town of Greve or a stop at Castello di Ama for its wine and art.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return to Florence for a quiet dinner at Il Palagio in the Four Seasons garden.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Duomo / Centro Storico
items.description: The historic core with the great galleries at hand — for first-timers who want it all on foot.

items.name: Oltrarno / San Niccolò
items.description: The artisan left bank, quieter and more local, suited to those who've seen the icons and want the city's soul.

items.name: San Marco / Santissima Annunziata
items.description: A calm, scholarly quarter near the Accademia, good for a restful base a few minutes from everything.

events.name: Calcio Storico Fiorentino
events.note: A brutal, costumed 16th-century football tournament in Piazza Santa Croce, climaxing on the feast of San Giovanni.

events.name: Palio di Siena (nearby)
events.note: An easy excursion to Siena for the bareback horse race around the Piazza del Campo, the great spectacle of Tuscany.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Florence Peretola (FLR) for a fifteen-minute chauffeured car to the centre, or into Pisa/Bologna with a private transfer if your schedule needs a wider jet window.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The historic core is compact and best walked; keep a private driver on call for day trips into Chianti and the hill towns, as most of the centre is a restricted (ZTL) zone.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Excellent 4G/5G throughout; an Italy or EU eSIM is seamless and hotels offer fast wifi.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Euro; cards are near-universal, carry modest cash for artisan workshops and cafes, and rounding up covers the tip since coperto and service are typically on the bill.

onGround.note: Base yourself around the Duomo or across the Arno in Oltrarno for artisan quiet; book the Uffizi and Accademia with a private guide well ahead, and dress covered for the churches.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Late April-June and September-October are ideal: mild, clear, and before the heat. Avoid July-August, when the Arno valley traps heat (mid-30s C) and the city is at its most crowded.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No non-stop. Best routing is Air India non-stop Delhi-Milan Malpensa (~7.5h) then a ~1.5h train to Florence SMN, or one-stop via Gulf hubs into Florence/Pisa/Bologna. Air India's new Delhi-Rome non-stop (~8.5h, 4x weekly) plus a 1.5h train is also clean. Lufthansa/Swiss First via Frankfurt or Zurich gives the best forward cabin.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required; routine EU standards. Very safe; petty theft around the Duomo and Ponte Vecchio is the only concern. Tap water is potable.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Good for vegetarians; Tuscan cooking is bean- and vegetable-rich. Jain needs briefing (garlic is common). Indian options exist, e.g. Ristorante Indian near Santa Maria Novella; ribollita and pappa al pomodoro are naturally vegetarian staples worth knowing.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Florence, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Galle — TripAgent
seo.description: Galle, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Galle
hero.tagline: A ramparted Dutch fort town, gem of Sri Lanka's south coast.

ourTake.lede: Galle is a walled Dutch fort you stay inside, not a beach town you drive through — book a room within the ramparts and give it two nights minimum. The pleasure is aimless: the fort walls at sunset, the lighthouse, the antique dealers and small cafés in the old mansions. Skip the packed midday ramparts near the flag; walk the far northern wall instead.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a Dutch-fort town, boutique villas and a slow coast an hour's flight away.
ourTake.skipIf: You want big resorts, nightlife or a packed sightseeing agenda.

firstLook.heroCaption: Modern pool villa with palms and umbrella

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: December to March is the south coast at its finest, opening with the Literary Festival in January; avoid the May to September monsoon, when the sea turns rough.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Oct, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Galle. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Amangalla
credentials: Set within UNESCO World Heritage Old Town of Galle and its Fortifications (inscribed 1988)
items.description: Aman inside the ramparts — a 1684 Dutch house kept as the most serene address within the walls of the Fort.

items.name: Amanwella
items.description: Aman on a crescent of southern sand — thirty suites in a coconut grove above a private beach, spare and quiet.

items.name: Cape Weligama
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller Gold List 2026 (the only Sri Lankan resort listed)
items.description: A clifftop headland of villas above a 60-metre crescent pool — the south coast's most decorated beach resort, relaunched to reclaim the crown.

items.name: Wild Coast Tented Lodge
credentials: MICHELIN Key hotel selection — the only property in Sri Lanka with two MICHELIN Keys
items.description: Vaulted safari cocoons where the jungle meets the sea on the edge of Yala — the island's only two-Michelin-Key stay.

items.name: Anantara Peace Haven Tangalle Resort
credentials: Condé Nast Traveler Hot List 2017 (best new hotels in the world)
items.description: A polished headland resort on a private cove — coconut plantation, long pools and the reliable Anantara hand.

items.name: Fort Bazaar by Teardrop Hotels
credentials: Set within UNESCO World Heritage Old Town of Galle and its Fortifications (inscribed 1988)
items.description: A restored 17th-century spice-merchant's townhouse in the heart of the Fort — eighteen rooms around a sunlit courtyard.

items.name: Le Grand Galle by Asia Leisure
items.description: A contemporary five-star on the cliff edge, looking straight across the water to the ramparts of the Fort.

items.name: The Galle Fort Ramparts Walk at Golden Hour
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old Town of Galle and its Fortifications
items.description: The great Dutch sea walls loop the whole peninsula, and the ritual is to walk them as the light softens — families flying kites, boys leaping from Flag Rock into the sea, the Indian Ocean going molten to the horizon. It is the loveliest, most unhurried hour of a Galle day, and a private guide can time it so you arrive at the lighthouse for the last of the sun.

items.name: Galle Lighthouse
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old Town of Galle and its Fortifications
items.description: Sri Lanka's oldest light station, whitewashed with a red-tipped crown, stands framed by leaning coconut palms at the Fort's southern tip — the single most photographed spot in the south. It anchors the ramparts walk and glows against the sky at dusk, an easy, iconic stop between the boutiques and the sea wall.

items.name: Dutch Reformed Church (Groote Kerk)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old Town of Galle and its Fortifications
items.description: The 1755 church floor is paved with Dutch tombstones and its cool interior holds antique pews, an organ loft and memorial stones carved with skulls and coats of arms — a quiet, atmospheric window into the Fort's colonial past. It sits a short stroll from the lighthouse and the Old Gate, an unmissable pause on any walking tour.

items.name: National Maritime Museum
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old Town of Galle and its Fortifications
items.description: Housed in a vast 1671 Dutch warehouse built into the ramparts above the Old Gate, the museum tells Galle's story as an Indian Ocean trading port through models of dhows, marine life and archaeological finds pulled from the harbour. A cool, thick-walled retreat from the midday heat and a genuine sense of why this bay mattered for centuries.

items.name: The Old Gate & the Dutch VOC Coat of Arms
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old Town of Galle and its Fortifications
items.description: The original sea-facing entrance still carries the British crest on the outer face and the Dutch VOC monogram within — the two empires that ruled this bay, stacked on one arch. Walk through it toward the harbour and you feel the Fort exactly as arriving merchants once did.

items.name: The Galle Clock Tower & Moon Bastion
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old Town of Galle and its Fortifications
items.description: The 1882 clock tower rises over the landward ramparts, a Victorian landmark marking the highest of the bastions and the best vantage back over the town and the cricket ground below. A short climb rewards you with the classic overview of red-tiled roofs enclosed by the walls.

items.name: Flag Rock Bastion at Sunset
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old Town of Galle and its Fortifications
items.description: The southernmost bastion, where local daredevils dive into the surf and vendors sell spiced fruit as the sun drops into the ocean. It is the Fort's great sunset gathering point — arrive early, take the sea wall slowly, and let the whole scene unfold in the last warm light.

items.name: Meeran Jumma Mosque
items.description: The Fort's only mosque, serving the community since the 1750s, is an unexpected marvel — Victorian and Baroque lines, a European-style atrium and stained glass that could belong to a church, all facing the lighthouse across the lane. A quiet, telling emblem of Galle's layered Muslim trading heritage.

items.name: The Historical Mansion Museum
items.description: A restored merchant's house crammed with one family's lifetime of Galle antiques — lacework, colonial furniture, gems and curios — with artisans still cutting stones and making jewellery in the courtyard. A small, characterful private-feeling museum tucked off Leyn Baan Street, free to enter.

items.name: The Boutique, Gem & Gallery Lanes of the Fort
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old Town of Galle and its Fortifications
items.description: Within the walls, cool colonnaded houses have become the south's most refined shopping — Stick No Bills for vintage Ceylon prints, Barefoot for hand-loomed cotton, and reputable gem houses cutting Sri Lankan sapphires to order. An afternoon drifting Church and Pedlar Streets, gem-buying with a trusted dealer your advisor vets, then coffee in a courtyard café.

items.name: Amangalla — The Grand Colonial Address
items.description: The former New Oriental Hotel, run since 1865 for the age of steamship travel and now Aman's discreet 31-room house within the ramparts, with four-poster beds, teak floors and a serene Ayurvedic spa. Even non-residents can take the ceremonial afternoon tea or a slow lunch — the most elegant way to feel the Fort's history from inside.

items.name: Unawatuna Beach
items.description: A sheltered golden crescent just minutes from the Fort, calm enough for gentle swimming and lined with palm shade and easy beach restaurants — the classic first beach day of a south-coast trip. Family-friendly and safe, with the temple-topped headland at one end and reef snorkelling offshore.

items.name: Jungle Beach
items.description: A hidden cove reached down a jungle path on the Rumassala headland, with clear water, coral to snorkel and far fewer crowds than Unawatuna. The reward-for-effort feel makes it a lovely private-ish morning; a guide with a tuk-tuk or car can drop you at the trailhead and time it before the day-trippers.

items.name: Dalawella Beach & the Palm-Tree Rope Swing
items.description: The Instagram-famous rope swing hangs from a leaning palm over turquoise shallows in front of a small guesthouse, on a quieter, prettier beach than its neighbours. A fun, photogenic stop for honeymooners and families — arrive early for the light and the empty sand.

items.name: Rumassala Hill & the Japanese Peace Pagoda
items.description: A biodiverse headland woven into the Ramayana — legend says Hanuman dropped a Himalayan fragment here carrying healing herbs — crowned by a gleaming white peace pagoda built by Japanese monks in 2004, with sweeping views over Galle bay. A short, meaningful drive up for the myth, the birdlife and the panorama, especially resonant for Indian travellers.

items.name: Yatagala Raja Maha Viharaya
items.description: An ancient rock temple believed to be over 2,000 years old, with a serene cave shrine, a large reclining Buddha and murals, all set on a quiet hillside away from the coastal bustle. A calm, authentic half-hour of the living Buddhist Sri Lanka most beach visitors miss.

items.name: Handunugoda Tea Estate — Virgin White Tea
items.description: The estate of tea legend Herman Gunaratne, famous for 'virgin white tea' plucked so no human hand touches the leaf, offering a tour, a walk through cinnamon and pepper, and a gracious tasting of rare teas with cake. A refined, story-rich morning inland — one of the south's most civilised experiences and easily done privately.

items.name: Koggala Lake & Cinnamon Island Boat Safari
items.description: A wide freshwater lake dotted with islets and mangroves, where a boat glides you past birdlife and monkeys to a temple island and to Cinnamon Island, where one family still peels true Ceylon cinnamon by hand for you to watch. A gentle, scenic half-day blending nature, spice heritage and calm.

items.name: Martin Wickramasinghe Folk Museum
items.description: Set in the ancestral home and gardens of Sri Lanka's most beloved novelist, this beautifully kept folk museum gathers the crafts, tools, masks and everyday objects of old rural Ceylon. A quiet, cultured counterpoint to the beaches, and an easy pairing with Koggala Lake or the tea estate.

items.name: The Stilt Fishermen of the South Coast
items.description: The image that defines Sri Lanka — lone fishermen perched on slender poles above the surf, silhouetted at dawn. Genuine stilt fishing still happens quietly at first light; a good guide takes you to the real thing rather than the posed roadside performers, ideally with breakfast waiting after.

items.name: Mirissa Whale Watching — Blue Whales
items.description: Off Mirissa the continental shelf runs closest to shore, making it one of the world's most reliable places to see the blue whale — the largest animal that has ever lived — along with sperm whales and spinner dolphins. Go on a private, unhurried early boat in the December-to-April season; a bucket-list morning for a family or a honeymoon.

items.name: Mirissa Beach & Coconut Tree Hill
items.description: A long palm-backed bay with a photogenic palm-crowned headland (Coconut Tree Hill) at one end and Parrot Rock to climb at the other, plus easy sunset dining on the sand. The relaxed heart of the south's beach scene, and the natural base for whale watching.

items.name: Weligama Bay — Surf & the Stilt Coast
items.description: A vast gentle bay with soft, forgiving waves that make it the south's best place to learn to surf, framed by fishing boats and the little island temple of Taprobane offshore. Book a private lesson with a patient instructor, or simply watch the sea from a bay-view terrace as the fishermen return.

items.name: Kabalana Beach & Ahangama Surf
items.description: A clean beach break with no rocks and forgiving whitewater, backed by the south's hippest cluster of design cafés and boutique villas — the surf-and-slow-mornings capital of the coast. Beginner lessons on the sand, or just excellent coffee and a swim while the surfers work the point.

items.name: Hiriketiya Beach
items.description: A near-perfect horseshoe bay, small and green-fringed, with beginner waves inside and a bohemian scatter of yoga decks, boutique hotels and good cafés. The fashionable quiet-luxe corner of the deep south — ideal for a honeymoon retreat or a couple of slow, screen-free days.

items.name: Talalla Beach
items.description: A long, gently curving stretch of soft sand with barely a soul on it — the south coast as it was, calm water for swimming and a single serene retreat behind the palms. The place to come for privacy and stillness when the busier bays feel too full.

items.name: Tangalle & the Wild Eastern Beaches
items.description: Where the south turns quieter and grander — long empty beaches, dramatic rocky coves, and the coast's most secluded luxury villas and resorts. The base for the leopards of Yala and turtle-nesting beaches, and the natural finale for travellers who want space, nature and privacy.

items.name: Hikkaduwa Coral Sanctuary & Sea Turtles
items.description: The shallow reef here is a protected marine sanctuary where green turtles glide right up to the shore, viewable by snorkel or glass-bottomed boat. An easy, joyful stop for families on the way south or north — gentle water, bright fish and turtles at close range.

items.name: Kosgoda Turtle Hatchery & Conservation
items.description: A long-running conservation hatchery on a coast where five of the world's seven marine turtle species nest, caring for eggs, injured and rare albino turtles and releasing millions of hatchlings. A meaningful, hands-on hour for children and grandparents alike; go to a genuine conservation project your advisor vets, not a roadside tank.

items.name: Madu River Boat Safari
credentials: Ramsar Wetland of International Importance — Madu Ganga
items.description: A Ramsar-protected estuary of pristine mangrove, threaded by boat past 900 hectares of waterways, tiny islands, a cinnamon islet, a temple island and dazzling kingfishers. A serene, cooling nature morning — beautiful for photography and gentle enough for every generation.

items.name: Lunuganga — Geoffrey Bawa's Country Estate
items.description: The masterwork garden that Sri Lanka's greatest architect built over half a century on a lakeside former cinnamon plantation — outdoor rooms, framed vistas and sculpture that defined 'tropical modernism'. Take the guided tour, or better, lunch or stay in the small country house; essential for anyone who cares about design, and pure calm.

items.name: Brief Garden — Bevis Bawa's Eden
items.description: The romantic, jungly garden and art-filled home of Bevis Bawa — the elder brother whose creation inspired Geoffrey's Lunuganga — full of quirky sculpture, follies and lush planting. A wonderfully personal, lesser-known counterpart to Lunuganga, best paired with it on a single Bawa-legacy day.

items.name: Cape Weligama — The Clifftop Maison
items.description: A collection of freestanding suites and villas ranged along a headland high above the Indian Ocean, with a dramatic crescent infinity pool and whale watching almost from your terrace in season. Even for a long lunch or sundowner it is one of the south's most beautiful perches — discreet, unhurried luxury with the whole ocean below.

items.name: Ayurvedic Wellness & Spa Retreat
items.description: The south is Sri Lanka's heartland of Ayurveda — from the Aman spa's hydrotherapy suites within the Fort to dedicated coastal retreats offering physician-led programmes, herbal treatments and daily yoga. Build in a treatment or a multi-day cleanse; a natural, deeply restorative thread for a wellness-minded honeymoon or family stay.

items.name: Yala National Park Leopard Safari
items.description: Yala holds one of the highest leopard densities on earth, alongside elephants, sloth bears, crocodiles and hundreds of bird species across scrub, lagoon and jungle. Go in a private jeep with a top tracker at dawn — a genuine bucket-list game drive, and best reached from a Tangalle base.

items.name: Udawalawe National Park Elephant Safari
items.description: Open grassland and a reservoir make Udawalawe the surest place in Sri Lanka to see wild Asian elephants — often large herds with calves — in a single unhurried afternoon. Gentler and more reliable than Yala for young children and grandparents, with the elephant transit home nearby.

items.name: Sinharaja Rainforest Walk
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Sinharaja Forest Reserve
items.description: The island's last great tract of primary tropical rainforest, a living cathedral of endemic birds, butterflies, orchids and towering trees, explored slowly on foot with a naturalist. A cool, green, soul-quieting contrast to the beaches — the wild counterpoint to a coastal stay.

items.name: A Private Cinnamon Peeling Experience
items.description: Sri Lanka is the birthplace of true cinnamon, and on the smallholdings inland a family will show you the whole craft — cutting, peeling and rolling the fragrant quills by hand, then a cup of cinnamon tea. A short, sensory, surprisingly moving stop that connects the spice on your table to this exact coast.

items.name: A South-Coast Rice & Curry Cooking Class
items.description: Sri Lankan cooking is a revelation of coconut, curry leaf and gentle spice — and profoundly veg-friendly, with dhal, jackfruit, gotu kola and a dozen little curries per plate. A home or villa cooking session, market visit included, is a warm, hands-on afternoon that Indian palates take to instantly.

items.name: The Galle Fort Food & Café Scene
items.description: Within the walls the old merchant houses now hold some of the island's best eating — from refined Sri Lankan tasting menus to airy courtyard cafés and rooftop sundowners over the ramparts. An evening of slow dining inside the lamplit Fort is one of Galle's quiet pleasures; your advisor can secure the tables that book out.

items.name: A Private Villa & Guide on the South Coast
items.description: The south's signature stay is the private walled villa — a Bawa-influenced house with pool, cook and staff, set among palms or over the sea. With a dedicated car and guide it turns beaches, temples and safaris into an effortless, screen-free rhythm; the ideal frame for a multi-generational trip a short flight from India.

items.name: Turtle-Nesting Watch at Rekawa
items.description: On this dark, protected beach, giant sea turtles heave ashore at night to lay their eggs, watched under strict conservation guidance during the season. A hushed, unforgettable after-dark experience for older children and adults, arranged responsibly from a Tangalle base.

items.name: The Galle International Cricket Stadium
items.description: One of the most beautiful grounds in world cricket, ringed by the sea on one side and the Fort ramparts on the other — you can watch a Test match, in part, for free from the walls above. A vivid, atmospheric stop for cricket-loving Indian families, whether a match is on or not.

items.name: A Sunset Sail or Fishing Trip off Galle
items.description: A private boat out of the bay at dusk turns the Fort's silhouette and lighthouse into the perfect farewell postcard, with the option of light-tackle fishing or simply drinks on deck. A romantic, low-key way to see Galle from the water — the vantage from which it was always meant to be admired.

items.name: Kande Vihara & the Coastal Temples
items.description: On the road north sits Kande Vihara, home to one of Asia's tallest seated Buddha statues, a serene and photogenic stop among mango and frangipani. An easy cultural pause when travelling between Colombo airport and the beaches, and a gentle introduction to the island's devotional life.

items.name: The Fort Printers
credentials: Long-established Galle Fort landmark restaurant (opened 2005) within the boutique Fort Printers hotel
39 Bistro & Wine Bar by The Fort Printers — the Fort's noted wine-led table
items.description: An 18th-century mansion turned the Fort's most established table — antique-hung dining hall and a frangipani courtyard.

items.name: Church Street Social
credentials: Restaurant of Fort Bazaar by Teardrop Hotels (credentialed boutique hotel within UNESCO Galle Fort)
items.description: The kitchen of Fort Bazaar — a sociable dining room running Moroccan, Turkish and Middle-Eastern plates alongside Sri Lankan.

items.name: Wijaya Beach
credentials: Long-standing south-coast institution (established 1980); Tripadvisor Travellers' Choice
items.description: A family-run beach kitchen since 1980, widely held to serve the best wood-fired pizza on the island.

items.name: Poonie's Kitchen
credentials: Widely cited best-of-Galle-Fort vegetarian and healthy-eating destination (Galle Fort restaurant guides)
items.description: A hidden blue-walled courtyard café — salads, smoothie bowls and honest, locally sourced vegetarian cooking.

items.name: Galle Fort ramparts at sunset
credentials: The UNESCO-listed Galle Fort ramparts (inscribed 1988) — the coast's defining sunset gathering
items.description: The sundowner ritual of the south coast — a slow walk along the Dutch sea wall as the light goes and the town gathers on the stones.

items.name: Church Street Social bar, Fort Bazaar
credentials: Bar of Fort Bazaar by Teardrop Hotels (credentialed boutique hotel within UNESCO Galle Fort)
items.description: The most polished bar inside the walls — a courtyard house pouring proper cocktails after dinner.

items.name: Cape Weligama bar terraces
credentials: Bars of Cape Weligama (Relais & Châteaux; Condé Nast Traveller Gold List 2026)
items.description: Drinks on a clifftop above the crescent pool — the most scenic evening bar on the coast, ocean on three sides.

items.name: Rooftop bar, Le Grand Galle
credentials: Rooftop bar of Le Grand Galle (Asia Leisure five-star hotel)
items.description: A rooftop over the Indian Ocean with the Fort ramparts across the water — the best elevated sundowner near Galle.

items.title: Private villa stay inside the ramparts
items.description: A restored Dutch-era merchant house within the fort walls, staffed and entirely your own.

items.title: Sunset walk of the full fort wall with a historian
items.description: A guided circuit tracing the Portuguese, Dutch and British layers most visitors miss.

items.title: Private whale watching off Mirissa
items.description: An early charter to see blue whales without the crowded commercial boats, in season.

items.title: Chef's dinner in a fort courtyard
items.description: A private table in one of the fort's heritage houses, cooking Sri Lankan with estate produce.

plan.heading: 3 days in Galle, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Walk the full circuit of the Dutch fort walls at first light, then the Maritime Museum and the old Dutch Reformed Church.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Wander Pedlar and Church Streets — the jewellers, the Stick No Bills gallery — and take tea at Amangalla's veranda.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at the Fort Bazaar's Church Street Social, then the ramparts again as the lighthouse turns.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive out to Handunugoda tea estate for a private virgin-white-tea tasting under the palms.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The turtle hatchery at Habaraduwa or a quiet swim at Wijaya Beach, then an afternoon by the pool.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Sunset and dinner at Wijaya Beach, wood-fired and barefoot on the sand.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A morning at Lunuganga, Geoffrey Bawa's country garden estate near Bentota, walked slowly with a guide.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Return along the coast with a stop at Brief Garden, then rest within the fort walls.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at Amangalla, the old New Oriental Hotel, in its high-ceilinged colonial dining room.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Galle Fort (inside the walls)
items.description: Cobbled lanes and boutique heritage stays — the only place to base yourself.

items.name: Unawatuna
items.description: A sheltered bay just south — for those who want beach time alongside the fort.

items.name: Ahangama / Talpe
items.description: Quieter coast east of town — villas and surf, for a slower stay.

events.name: Galle Literary Festival
events.note: South Asia's leading literary gathering, staged in the fort's colonial buildings — the 2026 edition runs 22–25 January.

events.name: Esala Perahera season (island-wide)
events.note: The great Kandy procession draws travellers up-country during Galle's dry, bright months.

events.name: Sinhala & Tamil New Year
events.note: Traditional games, sweets and rituals fill the villages around the fort.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: There is no airport at Galle; arrive by private car from Colombo (about two hours on the southern expressway) or, more elegantly, by Cinnamon Air seaplane onto the coast near the Fort.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The Fort itself is best walked — ramparts, lanes and cafés are all within it — with a private driver held for excursions to beaches and tea country inland.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: A Dialog or Mobitel eSIM gives solid 4G across the south coast; villa and boutique-hotel wifi is generally good.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Sri Lankan rupee (LKR); boutiques and restaurants inside the Fort take cards, but keep cash for tuk-tuks, markets and tips of around 10 percent.

onGround.note: Base yourself inside the Dutch Fort for atmosphere or at a private villa on the Habaraduwa/Ahangama coast for seclusion; the walled Fort is a UNESCO site, so evenings on the ramparts at sunset are the local ritual — dress is resort-casual and unfussy.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Same southern-coast rhythm as Colombo but drier: December to March is idyllic on the Fort ramparts, while the southwest monsoon (May to September) brings heavy surf and rain, and October to November sees inter-monsoon storms.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No airport at Galle; fly into Colombo (Bandaranaike/CMB) direct from Delhi or Mumbai on SriLankan or Air India, then a ~2h private car south along the coastal expressway. A chauffeur transfer arranged by the hotel is the discreet way; helicopter transfers can be booked for those who prefer.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: As Sri Lanka generally: no mandatory vaccinations, routine jabs plus Hep A and Typhoid advisable, bottled water only. Calm and safe, favoured by discerning travellers; the Fort is walkable and low-key. No altitude issues.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian and Jain needs are met easily; villa chefs and Fort hotels cook to request. Strong Sri Lankan vegetable curries and rice-and-curry; the boutique Fort kitchens and private villa cooks will tailor pure-veg or Jain menus without fuss.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Galle, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Geneva — TripAgent
seo.description: Geneva, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Geneva
hero.tagline: Diplomacy, watchmaking and a lake framed by Mont Blanc

ourTake.lede: Geneva is a working international city more than a holiday town, and it repays travellers who lean into the lake, the watchmaking and the surrounding Alps rather than expecting Old-World charm on every corner. Do the old town and a lake crossing, use the city as a base for Mont Blanc and the vineyards of Lavaux, and time a serious meal or a watch appointment if that's your interest. It is expensive and reserved, so keep the pace unhurried.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a calm, polished lakeside base for watches, wellness and easy Alpine day-trips.
ourTake.skipIf: You want buzz, nightlife or a bargain; Geneva is quiet and expensive.

firstLook.heroCaption: Riverside hotel at dusk reflected in water

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: May to September is the season for the lake and the Alps; come in April for Watches and Wonders or mid-December for L'Escalade, and skip the cold, grey heart of winter.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jun, Jul, Aug and Sep

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Beau-Rivage Genève
items.description: The city's grande dame since 1865 — fifth-generation family-owned, lake-facing, and quite simply the Geneva address.

items.name: The Woodward, Auberge Resorts Collection
items.description: Geneva's only all-suite palace — a Belle Époque landmark reimagined by Pierre-Yves Rochon, facing the lake and Mont Blanc.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel des Bergues Genève
items.area: Rive Droite / Les Bergues (Quai des Bergues)
items.description: Geneva's oldest grand hotel, open since 1834 — a neoclassical house on the Rhône with Four Seasons polish.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental, Geneva
items.area: Rive Droite / on the Rhône (Quai Turrettini)
items.description: Mandarin Oriental precision on the riverbank — one of only two Forbes Five-Star houses in the city.

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton Hotel de la Paix, Geneva
items.description: An 1865 lakefront landmark reborn under The Ritz-Carlton — grand, contemporary and squarely on the water.

items.name: La Réserve Genève Hotel & Spa
items.area: Bellevue / lakefront, just north of the city
items.description: A Jacques Garcia-designed lakeside resort in its own park — a colonial-safari fantasy a short drive from the centre.

items.name: Hôtel President Wilson, a Luxury Collection Hotel
items.description: A diplomat's favourite on the lake — home to the Royal Penthouse, long reputed the most expensive hotel suite in the world.

items.name: Hôtel d'Angleterre
items.description: An intimate Red Carnation townhouse on the lake — English warmth and a famous piano bar, at a gentler scale than the palaces.

items.name: Hôtel Métropole Genève
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A family-owned Belle Époque house on the left-bank lakefront — dignified, discreet and quietly grand.

items.name: Hôtel Les Armures
items.description: A 17th-century house at the very heart of the medieval Old Town — history, stone and quiet a step from the cathedral.

items.name: InterContinental Genève
items.area: Grand-Saconnex / near the UN and airport
items.description: The city's diplomatic-summit hotel — large, capable and close to the Palais des Nations and the airport.

items.name: The Jet d'Eau
items.description: Geneva's signature: a 140-metre plume of lake water shooting up from the harbour, visible from across the city and lit at night. Ask your driver to time an evening lakeside walk along the Quai Gustave-Ador so the children see it catch the last light.

items.name: CGN Belle Époque paddle-steamer cruise
items.description: Board one of the fleet of restored 1900s-era steamers at the Jardin Anglais or Mont-Blanc landing and glide past vineyards, châteaux and the Alps with a private table for lunch. The unhurried pace and top-deck views suit a multi-generational family, and the galley will manage vegetarian requests with notice.

items.name: Bains des Pâquis
items.description: The beloved public bathing pier reaching into the lake beside the Jet d'Eau, with wooden decks, a sauna and hammam in winter, and a famously good fondue in the little buvette. Unpretentious and thoroughly local, it is where Geneva actually relaxes.

items.name: Jardin Anglais & the Flower Clock
items.description: The lakeside promenade where Geneva's most photographed emblem, the Horloge Fleurie, is planted in thousands of live blooms that change with the season, its second hand the longest in the world. A gentle, pram-friendly stroll right by the Jet d'Eau.

items.name: Île Rousseau
items.description: A leafy islet in the middle of the Rhône, reached by a short footbridge, with the seated statue of philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau under old trees and swans on the water. A quiet green pause in the very heart of the city.

items.name: St Pierre Cathedral & its towers
items.description: The Old Town's Reformation-era cathedral where John Calvin preached, its climbable towers rewarding the effort with the finest rooftop panorama of the lake, the Alps and the tiled roofs below. Beneath it, the archaeological site reveals Roman and early-Christian layers.

items.name: Place du Bourg-de-Four
items.description: Geneva's oldest square, a sloping cobbled space of cafés, a central fountain and antique shops that has been a marketplace since Roman times. The natural spot to sit with a coffee and watch Old Town life unfold.

items.name: Maison Tavel
items.description: The oldest private house in Geneva, a 12th-century stone mansion now a museum of the city's history, whose highlight is the vast Magnin relief model of 1850s Geneva before its ramparts fell. A calm, uncrowded window into how the city grew.

items.name: The Reformation Wall
items.description: A 100-metre monument set into the old ramparts of Parc des Bastions, its five-metre statues of Calvin, Farel, Bèze and Knox marking Geneva's role as the 'Protestant Rome'. The surrounding park has giant chess boards the children can play on.

items.name: Parc des Bastions
items.description: The elegant park at the foot of the Old Town, home to the Reformation Wall, the University of Geneva's founding buildings and rows of giant open-air chess sets. Shaded, central and made for an easy afternoon.

items.name: Patek Philippe Museum
items.description: A private, hushed temple to watchmaking assembled by the Stern family, spanning five centuries of timepieces, enamels and automata across four floors, with Patek's own masterpieces on the top. Essential for the collector and a discreet, world-class hour for anyone with an interest in horology.

items.name: Rue du Rhône watch and jewellery boutiques
items.description: Geneva's golden mile: the flagship maisons of Patek Philippe, Rolex, Vacheron Constantin, Cartier and their peers line the Rue du Rhône and adjacent lanes. Private appointments and after-hours viewings are the norm for serious clients, arranged discreetly.

items.name: Cité du Temps
items.description: A free exhibition space on a bridge over the Rhône dedicated to time and Swiss watchmaking, with the Planet Swatch collection and rotating horological shows. A light, engaging counterpoint to the grand watch museums, right in the centre.

items.name: International Red Cross & Red Crescent Museum
items.description: A moving, superbly designed museum opposite the UN telling the story of humanitarian action through three chambers on defending dignity, restoring family links and reducing natural risks. Sober and powerful, and a reminder of why Geneva matters to the world.

items.name: Palais des Nations (UN Geneva)
items.description: The European headquarters of the United Nations, its grand halls and the ceiling of the Human Rights room open to guided visits set within a park roamed by peacocks. Bring passports; a private guide smooths the security and brings the diplomacy alive.

items.name: The Broken Chair
items.description: A 12-metre wooden chair with a shattered leg standing before the UN, a stark monument against landmines and cluster bombs. It stops every visitor for a moment and photographs beautifully against the flags.

items.name: CERN Science Gateway
items.description: The Renzo Piano-designed visitor centre of the world's great particle-physics laboratory, with free interactive exhibitions on the universe, the quantum world and the Large Hadron Collider. Genuinely thrilling for curious teenagers and science-minded travellers; registration is free but required.

items.name: Musée d'art et d'histoire (MAH)
items.description: One of Switzerland's largest museums, an encyclopaedic collection of fine art, antiquities and armour from Hodler and Corot to Egyptian and Roman treasures. Vast and serene, with an inflatable art installation currently animating its courtyard.

items.name: Conservatoire et Jardin botaniques (Botanical Garden)
items.description: Twenty-eight free hectares of themed gardens, greenhouses, an arboretum and a small animal park on the lake's edge, kept to a high standard. An easy, restful outing that works for grandparents and small children alike.

items.name: Carouge
items.description: Geneva's 'little Italy', a Sardinian-built quarter of low pastel houses, leafy inner courtyards, artisan workshops and independent cafés often called the city's Greenwich Village. The place to browse jewellers and design studios far from the tourist run, then linger over lunch on a shaded square.

items.name: Parc La Grange & its rose garden
items.description: The city's most beautiful park, an 18th-century estate above the lake whose historic Roseraie holds thousands of rose bushes in hundreds of varieties, at their peak in June. Free summer concerts play in the grounds.

items.name: Parc des Eaux-Vives
items.description: An elegant lakeside park adjoining La Grange, with sweeping lawns, old trees and long views to the Jet d'Eau and Mont Blanc. Its 18th-century villa houses a fine restaurant, making it a natural pairing with a garden walk.

items.name: Mont Salève cable car
items.description: A five-minute cable-car ride up 'Geneva's balcony' on the French side to 1,100 metres, with the whole city, the lake and, on clear days, Mont Blanc laid out below. Passports needed; the summit has walking trails and a viewpoint restaurant.

items.name: Plainpalais flea market
items.description: One of Europe's largest flea markets, sprawling across the great open plaza every Wednesday and Saturday, from watch parts and vintage Swiss enamel to furniture and curiosities. A treasure hunt for the collector's eye, best in the morning.

items.name: Villa Diodati (exterior)
items.description: The lakeside mansion above Geneva where Mary Shelley conceived Frankenstein during the stormy summer of 1816 with Byron. Privately owned so only the exterior and surrounding paths can be seen, but the literary aura and Cologny's grand villas make it a rewarding detour by car.

items.name: Auer chocolatier
items.description: A family chocolate house since 1939, tucked in the shopping streets and famed for its amandes princesses and delicate pralines. A small, authentic institution for a discreet gift or a private tasting.

items.name: Favarger chocolate
items.description: Geneva's historic chocolate maker, run by the same family since 1826, whose Avelines and Nougalines are local legends; its lakeside Carouge factory can be visited. An easy, crowd-pleasing stop for the family that travels with a sweet tooth.

items.name: Le Chat-Botté
items.description: The Michelin-starred dining room of the grand Beau-Rivage hotel, refined French cuisine with a lake terrace and a dedicated vegetarian tasting menu. The natural choice for a formal family dinner where the setting matters as much as the plate.

items.name: Old Town antiquarian and gallery lanes
items.description: The steep cobbled streets around Grand-Rue and Rue des Granges hide antiquarian booksellers, art galleries and Rousseau's birthplace at No. 40. A slow, elegant amble through the city's most historic quarter.

items.name: Quai du Mont-Blanc grand-hotel promenade
items.description: The stately waterfront where Geneva's palace hotels line up facing the Jet d'Eau and the Brunswick Monument, with the flower-lined Bains-Anglais steps and lake views. A classic evening stroll from the Beau-Rivage and the Four Seasons doorsteps.

items.name: Lausanne & the Olympic Museum
items.description: The Olympic capital across the lake, its lakeside Olympic Museum set in sculpture gardens tracing the Games from antiquity to now, a hit with children. Pair it with Ouchy's waterfront and the medieval cathedral in the upper town.

items.name: Lavaux vineyard terraces
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Lavaux, Vineyard Terraces
items.description: Steep, ancient stone-walled vineyards cascading to the lake between Lausanne and Montreux, monk-built from the 11th century and among the most beautiful winescapes in Europe. Arrange a private cellar tasting of the rare Chasselas whites, or ride the little Lavaux Express train through the rows.

items.name: Montreux & Chillon Castle
items.description: The Riviera-like resort town on the lake's east end, its promenade lined with palms and the Freddie Mercury statue, leading to the storybook Château de Chillon rising straight from the water. The 1,000-year-old castle that inspired Byron is a highlight for every generation.

items.name: Annecy
items.description: The 'Venice of the Alps' across the border, a jewel of flower-draped canals, a lakeside old town and turquoise water framed by peaks. A relaxed, walkable day of markets, gelato and boat rides; passports required for the border.

items.name: Chamonix & Aiguille du Midi
items.description: The legendary alpine town at the foot of Mont Blanc, from where the Aiguille du Midi cable car climbs to 3,842 metres and a glass 'Step into the Void' box over the glaciers. Unforgettable high-mountain drama within a day of Geneva; a private driver makes the border and timings effortless.

items.name: Gruyères
items.description: A perfectly preserved medieval hilltop village with a hilltop castle, famous for its AOP cheese dairy and the nearby Cailler chocolate factory at Broc. Cheese, chocolate and a fairy-tale walled town in one outing that delights children and adults.

items.name: Salève and lakeside private helicopter flight
items.description: A scenic helicopter transfer or flightseeing loop over the lake, the vineyards and the Mont Blanc massif, arranged from Geneva airport. The most spectacular way to grasp the geography, and a memorable treat for a family celebration.

items.name: MEG — Musée d'ethnographie de Genève
credentials: European Museum of the Year Award winner (2017)
items.description: An award-winning ethnography museum in striking modern architecture, showing world cultures through a collection of over 70,000 objects. Thoughtful, uncrowded and a strong wet-weather alternative to the lake.

items.name: Fondation Baur — Museum of Far Eastern Art
items.description: A discreet town-mansion museum of Chinese and Japanese art, jades, ceramics and Samurai swords, one of Europe's finest such collections. A serene, little-known gem for a quiet cultured hour.

items.name: Ariana Museum (ceramics & glass)
items.description: A palatial 19th-century villa in the UN's park devoted to a thousand years of glass and ceramics, from Sèvres porcelain to contemporary work. Beautiful architecture, free entry to the permanent collection and a peaceful park setting.

items.name: Barbier-Mueller Museum
items.description: A small, exquisite private museum of tribal and ancient art from Africa, Oceania and the Americas, superbly lit and curated in the heart of the Old Town. For the connoisseur, one of the world's great collections of its kind.

items.name: Bodmer Foundation library & museum
credentials: UNESCO Memory of the World collection
items.description: A jaw-dropping private library above the lake at Cologny holding a Gutenberg Bible, Shakespeare folios and papyrus fragments among world literature's treasures. A cultural pilgrimage for bibliophiles, in one of Geneva's grandest residential enclaves.

items.name: L'Atelier Robuchon
items.description: Geneva's only two-star table — the late Joël Robuchon's counter concept, exact and theatrical, around an open kitchen.

items.name: Domaine de Châteauvieux
items.description: Philippe Chevrier's country auberge among the vineyards — a Geneva institution, and GaultMillau's highest-scored table in the region.

items.name: Bayview by Michel Roth
items.area: Hôtel President Wilson, Rive Droite / lakefront
items.description: Refined French cooking under Michel Roth and Danny Khezzar, the lake and the Alps filling the windows.

items.name: Il Lago
items.area: Four Seasons Hotel des Bergues, Rive Droite / Les Bergues
items.description: Refined northern-Italian cooking in the Four Seasons' gilded room — classical, generous and beautifully served.

items.name: Fiskebar
items.area: The Ritz-Carlton Hotel de la Paix, Rive Droite / lakefront
items.description: A Nordic seafood enclave inside the Ritz-Carlton — clean, precise, sea-led cooking with a Scandinavian hand.

items.name: Rasoi by Vineet
items.area: Mandarin Oriental, Rive Droite / on the Rhône
items.description: Vineet Bhatia's evolved, refined Indian cooking — a rare starred Indian table, on the riverbank at the Mandarin Oriental.

items.name: Tsé Fung
items.description: Switzerland's only Michelin-starred Chinese restaurant — Cantonese refinement in Jacques Garcia's lakeside resort.

items.name: Le Cigalon
items.description: The Bessire family's seafood room — first-class fish flown from Roscoff and Audierne, cooked with flawless craft for nearly thirty years.

items.name: La Chaumière
items.description: Serge Labrosse's creative, modern cooking in a converted farmhouse — refined food in an easy country setting.

items.name: L'Aparté
items.description: Armel Bedouet's tiny fifteen-seat room — intimate, precise, produce-led fine dining for a handful of guests.

items.name: La Micheline
items.description: Andres Arocena's bright, seasonal bistronomy — a young star at the new Eaux-Vives station quarter.

items.name: Tosca
items.description: Ivan Baretti's precise Tuscan cooking — Arpège-trained technique in an intimate Eaux-Vives room.

items.name: Windows
items.description: Well-crafted French cooking with the Jet d'Eau and Mont Blanc framed in the window — a lovely lakefront room.

items.name: Osteria della Bottega
items.description: Seasonal Italian with handmade pasta at its heart — an open kitchen and chic industrial room in the Old Town.

items.name: Le Dorian
items.description: A well-priced newcomer with real flavour and craft — the kind of honest, refined cooking the Bib rewards.

items.name: Natürlich
items.description: Sustainable, produce-led cooking on the river — fresh, local ingredients handled with a light, honest touch.

items.name: Leopard Bar, Hôtel d'Angleterre
credentials: Inside a MICHELIN One-Key, Forbes 4-Star hotel — a Geneva institution
items.description: A clubby, low-lit lakefront piano bar — live jazz most nights and one of the city's most characterful drinks.

items.name: Le Bar des Bergues, Four Seasons
credentials: Inside a MICHELIN Two-Key, Forbes 5-Star hotel
