items.description: The Four Seasons' elegant bar — a considered cocktail in one of the city's most polished rooms.

items.name: Atrium Bar, Mandarin Oriental
credentials: Inside a MICHELIN One-Key, Forbes 5-Star hotel
items.description: A stylish riverside bar at the Mandarin Oriental — accomplished cocktails with the group's signature service.

items.name: Le Bar, The Woodward
credentials: Inside a MICHELIN Three-Key hotel (Auberge Resorts Collection)
items.description: An intimate, jewel-box bar inside the city's most exclusive hotel — discreet, dressed-up and beautifully made.

items.title: A boat across the lake to the Jet d'Eau and beyond
items.description: See the fountain from the water, then continue along the Riviera shore toward Lausanne if you have the day.

items.title: A watchmaking maison visit or the Patek Philippe Museum
items.description: The museum's collection of watches and automata is world-class; private house appointments are the deeper draw for collectors.

items.title: A day trip to Chamonix and Mont Blanc
items.description: An hour by road delivers you to the Aiguille du Midi cable car and the high Alps for an afternoon.

items.title: Lunch among the Lavaux terraced vineyards
items.description: The UNESCO-listed slopes above the lake pair Chasselas whites with long views; an easy excursion east.

plan.heading: 3 days in Geneva, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

days.title: The lake and the old town

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Jet d'Eau and the flower clock, then up into the Vieille Ville to St. Pierre Cathedral and the quiet Place du Bourg-de-Four.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The watchmaking rooms of the Patek Philippe Museum, then the Grand Rue for antiquarian bookshops.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at the Hôtel Beau-Rivage's Le Chat-Botté, a Geneva institution overlooking the lake.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Palais des Nations and the Red Cross Museum for the humanitarian city.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Cross into the Genevois vineyards for a tasting at a Dardagny or Satigny domaine.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Bayview by Michel Roth in the Hôtel President Wilson, two Michelin stars on the water.

days.title: The far shore and the mountain

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A morning at the Fondation Baur for its Chinese and Japanese collections, or the CERN visit if science calls.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The cable car up the Salève on the French side for lunch and the view back across the lake to Mont Blanc.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A quieter last dinner at the Domaine de Châteauvieux in Satigny, a two-star inn among the vines.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Vieille Ville (Old Town)
items.description: The hilltop historic core around the cathedral, cobbled and calm; suits those wanting the most characterful base.

items.name: Rive Gauche / Eaux-Vives
items.description: The lakeside left bank of parks, boutiques and good tables; suits travellers who want the water and the shopping close.

items.name: Pâquis
items.description: The lively, mixed quarter near the lake baths with the best-value eating; suits those wanting energy and range over polish.

events.name: Fête de l'Escalade
events.note: Geneva's beloved festival marking the 1602 defeat of Savoy, with torch-lit processions in period dress and chocolate cauldrons.

events.name: Fête de la Musique
events.note: Three days of free concerts across squares and courtyards throughout the old town for the summer solstice.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Geneva Airport (GVA) sits minutes from the city and lake, and a private car handles the short, discreet transfer to your hotel or lakeside residence.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver is the natural choice; the quais and old town reward walking, and a private boat is the elegant way to cross or explore Lac Léman.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Excellent throughout; an eSIM works on arrival and covers the wider Lake Geneva region including nearby France.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Swiss francs (CHF), though euros are often accepted near the border; cards work everywhere and tipping is light — round up or leave a little for good service.

onGround.note: The Right Bank (Rive Droite), near the Beau-Rivage and Four Seasons, puts you on the lake and by the finest maisons; Geneva is quiet and private by nature, which suits a discreet stay.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: May to September is mild and green along the lake with long evenings; winters are damp, foggy and cold, and November is the flattest month to avoid.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No direct flights from India; the cleanest routing is via Zurich on SWISS, or via a European or Gulf hub, roughly 11-13 hours door to door with one stop. Fly SWISS through Zurich for the smoothest connection and a single-carrier baggage handover.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations needed beyond routine; safety is excellent, on par with the rest of Switzerland. Tap water is clean and drinkable throughout the city.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian and Jain needs are well understood in a cosmopolitan, diplomatic city. Good Indian and pure-vegetarian options exist, and most kitchens will adapt for Jain diners with notice.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Geneva, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Goa — TripAgent
seo.description: Goa, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Goa
hero.tagline: Sun-bleached beaches, Portuguese churches and a barefoot pulse.

ourTake.lede: There are two Goas, and the mistake is trying to do both in one trip; pick the quiet, characterful south for beaches and villages, or the livelier north for nightlife and markets. The real Goa beyond the beach is Portuguese-Catholic and Hindu heritage, riverine and green, best seen in the inland villages and the old churches of Panjim and Old Goa. Come in the shoulder weeks either side of peak season for the best of it.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a home-turf beach break that flexes from quiet North Goa villas to full-tilt nights with no visa or long-haul.
ourTake.skipIf: You want somewhere far from home or free of crowds in peak season; December Goa is busy and priced for it.

firstLook.heroCaption: Woman walking poolside royal tent courtyard

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: November to February is golden and dry, the season of Carnival and Sunburn; skip the June to September monsoon unless you want the green, empty version.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Goa. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Taj Exotica Resort & Spa, Goa
credentials: World Travel Awards 2025 — India's Leading Family Resort
World Travel Awards 2024 — India's Leading Family Resort (also 2022 & 2023)
items.description: Fifty-six acres of Mediterranean-village calm above a quiet southern beach — the surest grand address in Goa.

items.name: The St. Regis Goa Resort
credentials: World Travel Awards 2025 — Goa's Leading Resort
World Travel Awards 2024 — Goa's Leading Resort
items.description: Butler service and three pools on a long, empty Cavelossim beach — the most polished stay in the south.

items.name: ITC Grand Goa, a Luxury Collection Resort & Spa
credentials: World Travel Awards 2025 — India's Leading Beach Resort & India's Leading Resort
World Travel Awards 2024 — India's Leading Beach Resort & India's Leading Resort
items.description: An Indo-Portuguese 'grand mansion' of lagoons and courtyards on Arossim beach — big, gracious and wedding-grade.

items.name: JW Marriott Goa
credentials: Travel + Leisure India's Best Awards 2024 — Best Staycation Hotel/Resort (Domestic)
items.description: A cliff-top newcomer above Vagator, looking down the coast to Chapora Fort — the north's most decorated recent opening.

items.name: The Postcard Hideaway, Netravali
credentials: World Travel Awards 2024 — Goa's Leading Boutique Hotel (also 2022 & 2023)
World Travel Awards 2024 — India's Leading Boutique Hotel
items.description: A forest hideaway on the edge of a wildlife sanctuary — Goa with no beach and no crowd, only birdsong and river.

items.name: The Postcard Saligao
credentials: Within The Postcard Hotel — World Travel Awards 2025 & 2024, Asia's Leading Boutique Hotel Brand
items.description: A restored 19th-century Portuguese manor among the paddy fields — village Goa, done with real taste.

items.name: The Postcard Velha Goa
credentials: Within The Postcard Hotel — World Travel Awards 2025 & 2024, Asia's Leading Boutique Hotel Brand
items.description: A riverside colonial house beside the old Portuguese capital — a rare place to sleep within the heritage.

items.name: The Postcard Cuelim
credentials: Within The Postcard Hotel — World Travel Awards 2025 & 2024, Asia's Leading Boutique Hotel Brand
items.description: A 17th-century Portuguese estate with a chapel of its own — quiet, gracious and gently grand.

items.name: Basilica of Bom Jesus
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Churches and Convents of Goa
Built 1594-1605; holds the relics of St. Francis Xavier
items.description: The most revered church in Goa, its weathered laterite facade holding the mortal remains of St. Francis Xavier in a silver casket above a Florentine-marble mausoleum. Go early, before the coaches arrive, when the light through the high windows falls on gilded Baroque woodwork and the nave is nearly your own.

items.name: Sé Cathedral (Cathedral of Santa Catarina)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Churches and Convents of Goa
Among the largest churches in Asia
items.description: One of the largest churches in Asia, built to mark the Portuguese capture of Goa, with a cavernous whitewashed interior and the famous Golden Bell whose toll once carried across the old city. A few minutes' stroll from Bom Jesus, so pair the two in a single unhurried morning.

items.name: Church of St. Francis of Assisi & Convent
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Churches and Convents of Goa
items.description: The quietest and arguably most beautiful of the Old Goa churches, its interior a riot of gilded carving, frescoed panels and painted floral columns. The adjoining convent houses the Archaeological Survey museum, worth a slow half-hour for its portraits of the Portuguese viceroys.

items.name: Church of St. Cajetan & Chapel of St. Catherine
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Churches and Convents of Goa
items.description: St. Cajetan is modelled on St. Peter's in Rome, an unexpected domed silhouette rising from the palms; the tiny Chapel of St. Catherine nearby is one of the oldest Christian structures in Goa. Both are steps from the main churches and let you complete the UNESCO ensemble without the crowds.

items.name: Fontainhas — the Latin Quarter
items.description: Panjim's old Portuguese quarter, a warren of narrow lanes lined with ochre, indigo and green villas, wrought-iron balconies and hand-painted azulejo tiles at every doorway. The single most romantic walk in Goa; do it at golden hour with a guide who can knock on the right doors, then settle in for a slow lunch.

items.name: Fontainhas heritage food & culture walk
items.description: A curated walk through the Latin Quarter that opens private heritage homes, a working bakery and a Goan-Catholic kitchen, with tastings of poee bread, bebinca and feni along the way. The best short cultural experience in the city, easily arranged privately for a family and paced to your interest.

items.name: Fort Aguada & lighthouse
credentials: Built 1612; its 1864 lighthouse is the oldest of its kind in Asia
items.description: A commanding 17th-century Portuguese sea fort above Sinquerim, its ramparts and the oldest lighthouse in Asia looking straight down the coastline. Come near sunset for the light on the Arabian Sea, an easy detour from the Candolim and Sinquerim luxury resorts below.

items.name: Reis Magos Fort
credentials: One of the oldest forts in Goa, built 1551; restored and reopened 2012
items.description: A beautifully restored little fort on the Mandovi's north bank, now a cultural centre with Mario Miranda cartoons, exhibitions and one of the finest river-and-Panjim panoramas in Goa. Refined, uncrowded and genuinely interesting — a rewarding stop en route between the beaches and the capital.

items.name: Chapora Fort
items.description: The ruined hilltop fort made famous by the film Dil Chahta Hai, its crumbling laterite walls framing a sweeping view over Vagator beach and the Chapora river mouth. A short climb rewarded by one of North Goa's great sunset outlooks.

items.name: Ashwem Beach
items.description: A long, calm, casuarina-fringed stretch that is the quiet, upscale face of North Goa, its handful of design-led beach shacks and boutique stays a world away from the Baga crowds. The default choice for a discreet villa or resort day on the sand.

items.name: Mandrem Beach
items.description: Perhaps the most serene of the fashionable northern beaches, a wide soft-sand ribbon crossed by little tidal creeks and backed by upscale restaurants and yoga retreats. Ideal for families and multi-generational stays wanting space and calm rather than a scene.

items.name: Morjim Beach
credentials: Protected Olive Ridley sea-turtle nesting beach
items.description: A broad, breezy beach at the mouth of the Chapora, known both for its Olive Ridley turtle nesting season and its cluster of stylish Mediterranean and Russian-influenced beach clubs. Come for a long lazy lunch by the water and the sense of an easy, cosmopolitan crowd.

items.name: Vagator & Ozran (Little Vagator) Beach
items.description: Twin coves set beneath red laterite cliffs, with a famous carved stone Shiva face on the sand and the ruins of Chapora Fort on the headland above. The dramatic cliff-and-sunset scenery makes it the most photogenic of the northern beaches.

items.name: Anjuna Beach & Wednesday Flea Market
credentials: Anjuna Flea Market, held Wednesdays since the 1970s
items.description: The rocky, boho beach where Goa's counterculture began, and home to the legendary Wednesday flea market that grew out of the 1970s hippie gatherings. Come for the market's handicrafts, jewellery and colour, and for the sense of the Goa that first drew the world.

items.name: Saturday Night Market, Arpora
items.description: Ingo's Saturday Night Market is the polished evening bazaar of the north — global street food, live music, designer stalls and lamps strung through the trees, running only in season. A lively, family-friendly evening out; go with a driver and browse without hurry.

items.name: Palolem Beach
items.description: A near-perfect crescent of calm, palm-backed sand, the postcard image of South Goa and its most beautiful bay. Kayak out to Butterfly Island, watch for dolphins at dawn, and enjoy the gentler, more scenic south — though it is now the busiest beach in the region.

items.name: Agonda Beach
items.description: The quieter, classier neighbour to Palolem — a long, tranquil sweep with excellent eco-conscious beach restaurants and a genuinely unhurried pace. Widely rated the nicest calm beach in Goa, and a fine base for a private villa away from any scene.

items.name: Cavelossim & Mobor Beach
items.description: The heart of luxury South Goa, a broad, clean beach between the Arabian Sea and the Sal river where the region's five-star resorts sit. Sundowner river cruises leave from the Sal, and the wide sands stay uncrowded even in season — the polished-resort choice.

items.name: Colva & Benaulim Beach
items.description: Long, gently shelving beaches that are the traditional face of South Goa, backed by whitewashed churches and quiet fishing hamlets. Benaulim in particular stays low-key and local — a slower, more Goan-Catholic counterpoint to the north.

items.name: Dudhsagar Falls
credentials: One of India's tallest waterfalls, dropping over 300 m
items.description: Goa's spectacular 'sea of milk' — a four-tiered cascade plunging over 300 metres down the Western Ghats, thundering white after the monsoon. Reached by a hired jeep safari through Bhagwan Mahaveer sanctuary; a full and worthwhile day trip inland from the coast.

items.name: Bhagwan Mahaveer Sanctuary & Mollem National Park
credentials: Part of the Western Ghats — a UNESCO World Heritage biodiversity hotspot
items.description: Goa's largest protected forest, 240 sq km of Western Ghats jungle sheltering black panther, Malabar giant squirrel and king cobra, with the Tambdi Surla temple and Dudhsagar within it. The wild, green counterweight to the beaches, for those who want to see the Ghats.

items.name: Spice plantation visit (Sahakari / Savoi / Tropical)
items.description: A shaded walk through cardamom, vanilla, nutmeg and betel groves in the Ponda hills, ending with a traditional Goan thali served on banana leaf. An easy, family-pleasing half-day that pairs naturally with the Ponda temples, and readily arranged as a private, unhurried visit.

items.name: Shri Mangeshi Temple
credentials: Among the oldest and most important temples of Goa
items.description: The largest and most graceful of Goa's Hindu temples, its white lamp-tower rising above green hills — the god shifted here in the 16th century to escape Portuguese destruction on the coast. A serene, beautifully kept shrine that anchors any temple circuit in the Ponda interior.

items.name: Shri Shantadurga Temple, Kavlem
credentials: Over 450 years at Kavlem; among Goa's principal temples
items.description: A luminous hillside temple to the goddess who mediates between Shiva and Vishnu, its worship carried inland from the coast over 450 years ago. Set among wooded hills a short drive from Mangeshi, it completes a calm and moving morning of Goa's living Hindu heritage.

items.name: Tambdi Surla Mahadev Temple
credentials: The oldest surviving temple in Goa, c. 12th century (Kadamba dynasty)
items.description: A tiny 12th-century Kadamba-era Shiva temple of black basalt, tucked in a forest clearing at the foot of the Ghats — the oldest surviving temple in Goa and the only one to escape the Portuguese entirely. Remote, atmospheric and utterly unlike the coast, for the traveller who wants the deep past.

items.name: Salim Ali Bird Sanctuary, Chorão Island
items.description: Goa's only bird sanctuary, a mangrove estuary on Chorão reached by a short car-ferry across the Mandovi, laced with boardwalks over the tidal creeks. A peaceful morning of herons, kingfishers, mudskippers and fiddler crabs — best by small boat at high tide with a naturalist.

items.name: Divar Island
items.description: A time-capsule island of empty lanes, old Portuguese mansions and the hilltop Our Lady of Compassion church, reached only by ferry and blissfully free of traffic. Rent bicycles or drive slowly for an afternoon; it is the Goa that has quietly stayed still.

items.name: Museum of Goa (MOG)
items.description: Artist Subodh Kerkar's three-storey contemporary-art space near Calangute, where large, playful installations engage Goan history, migration and the sea. The one truly serious cultural stop between the northern beaches, and a welcome hour indoors on a bright day.

items.name: Houses of Goa Museum
credentials: Conceived by architect Gerard da Cunha, opened 1997
items.description: A quirky ship-shaped museum built by architect Gerard da Cunha as an ode to Indo-Portuguese domestic architecture — balcões, oyster-shell windows, tiled roofs and Mario Miranda drawings. A charming, brief stop that decodes the very houses you admire across Goa.

items.name: Palácio do Deão, Quepem
credentials: Built 1787 by the Dean and founder of Quepem
items.description: A lovingly restored 1787 mansion built by the priest who founded Quepem town, its garden running down to the Kushavati river and its rooms full of period detail. Book ahead for a private Goan lunch here — one of the most gracious heritage experiences in the south.

items.name: Figueiredo House, Loutolim
credentials: Family mansion dating to the 1590s, one of Goa's oldest Indo-Portuguese houses
items.description: A vast 400-year-old Indo-Portuguese mansion still lived in by the same family, its rooms crowded with Chinese porcelain, Belgian chandeliers, family portraits and a private chapel. A guided visit is a rare, intimate window into old Goan-Catman aristocratic life.

items.name: Braganza House, Chandor
credentials: One of the largest and grandest ancestral homes in Goa (17th century)
items.description: The grandest of Goa's ancestral homes, a mansion whose ballroom-length gallery and rosewood salons run the length of Chandor's square, still occupied by two branches of the Braganza family. The definitive Indo-Portuguese heritage-house visit, unmatched for scale and story.

items.name: Mandovi river sunset & dolphin cruise
items.description: A private evening cruise on the Mandovi, gliding past Old Goa's churches and Reis Magos fort as the light softens over the water, with dolphins often surfacing near the mouth. Charter a quiet boat rather than the party boats for a graceful sundowner on the river.

items.name: Sal River backwater cruise, South Goa
items.description: A serene glide through the mangrove-lined Sal near the southern resorts, watching for kingfishers and dolphins in the calmer, greener waters away from the north's bustle. A gentle, scenic outing that suits the South Goa villa-and-resort pace.

items.name: Goan culinary experience & home dining
items.description: From a chef-led kitchen table on Catholic classics — sorpotel, xacuti, prawn balchão — to a Saraswat vegetarian thali or a seafood spread by the water, Goan cuisine rewards going beyond the shack menu. A private in-villa Goan meal or a curated tasting is the most memorable way in.

items.name: Feni & cashew heritage tasting
credentials: Feni holds a Geographical Indication (GI) tag as a Goa-exclusive spirit
items.description: Feni, Goa's fiery cashew or coconut spirit, is a Geographical-Indication product with a distilling tradition older than the resorts; a small-distillery tasting reveals it as a craft, not a cliché. A distinctive, only-in-Goa experience for the curious drinker.

items.name: Serendipity Arts Festival
items.description: India's largest multidisciplinary arts festival takes over Panjim's riverfront each December with curated visual art, music, theatre and food across historic venues. If your visit aligns, it turns the city into a serious cultural destination for a week.

items.name: Panjim — Church of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception
items.description: The gleaming white church with its dramatic zigzag staircase presiding over old Panjim's main square, floodlit and lovely after dark. A five-minute stop that anchors any wander through the capital, moments from Fontainhas.

items.name: Wellness & yoga retreat (Ashram / beachfront)
items.description: The quiet northern beaches are Goa's yoga and Ayurveda heartland, from serious teacher-training shalas to discreet beachfront spa retreats. Book a private teacher to your villa or a bespoke Ayurvedic programme for a restorative counterpoint to the coast.

items.name: Casino gaming on the Mandovi
items.description: Goa is one of the few places in India with legal casinos, several of them aboard permanently moored floating vessels on the Mandovi off Panjim. A brief, novel evening out for those who want it — go for the setting on the river rather than the stakes.

items.name: Sunburn Festival
items.description: Asia's largest electronic-dance-music festival descends on Goa around the New Year, a defining fixture of the state's party calendar. Framed here for the record — an enormous, high-energy event that draws a young international crowd, best planned around rather than into for a quiet stay.

items.name: Netravali & the bubbling lake, deep South
credentials: Wildlife sanctuary within the Western Ghats
items.description: A little-visited wildlife sanctuary in the far southeast, with the curious 'bubbling lake' at Budbudyachi Tali, waterfalls and dense Ghat forest. A genuine off-map day for travellers who have done the coast and want Goa's wild interior.

items.name: Bomra's
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller (India) x District Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 5 (highest-placed Goa restaurant)
items.description: Burmese-Kachin cooking that has quietly been Goa's most serious restaurant for years — precise, personal, unforgettable.

items.name: Cavatina by Avinash Martins
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller (India) x District Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 8
items.description: A Goan chef reimagining his own Saraswat and Catholic heritage — the most exciting cooking in the south.

items.name: Izumi
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller (India) x District Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 10
items.description: Japanese cooking — sushi, ramen and robata — done with real rigour in a leafy Assagao garden.

items.name: Hosa
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller (India) x District Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 15
items.description: A love letter to South Indian coastal cooking — heritage recipes, plated with real ambition.

items.name: Praça Prazeres
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller (India) x District Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 33
items.description: Chef Ralph Prazeres reworking Goan-Portuguese classics with modern finesse — a rising Goan name.

items.name: Petisco
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller (India) x District Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 11 (as Petisco Kitchen & Bar)
items.description: Small plates and sharing dishes that read the room perfectly — the north's easy, excellent everyday table.

items.name: Avo's Kitchen
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller (India) x District Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 16
items.description: Home-style Goan cooking, the way a Goan grandmother would make it — honest, warm and rooted.

items.name: The Second House
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller (India) x District Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 34
items.description: A quietly confident kitchen doing seasonal, produce-led plates away from the noise — a locals' favourite.

items.name: Slow Tide
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller (India) x District Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 37
items.description: A bar-restaurant of inventive cocktails and easy small plates, named for the slow Goa of the Sixties.

items.name: For the Record — Vinyl Bar
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller (India) x District Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 42
items.description: Records, cocktails and a short, sharp plate list — the north's most stylish listening-and-eating room.

items.name: Boilermaker
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Bars 2025 — No. 30 (highest-ranked bar in Goa)
items.description: A garage-bar reborn as the most internationally-ranked cocktail room in Goa — feni, cashew beer and serious technique.

items.name: Bar Outrigger
items.description: A rum-forward tiki bar by the sea in a tiny fishing village — Arijit Bose's inventive, playful drinks with a view.

items.name: Hideaway
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Bars 2025 — No. 94 (51–100 extended list)
items.description: Live jazz and inventive cocktails under the Vagator trees — the warmest music-and-drinks room in Goa.

items.title: Private heritage-home lunch in a Portuguese mansion
items.description: A meal in a centuries-old Indo-Portuguese house with the family, in the villages of Chandor or Loutolim.

items.title: Sunrise dolphin and estuary boat charter
items.description: A private boat along the quiet backwaters and river mouths before the day-trippers set out.

items.title: Spice plantation and Old Goa churches with a historian
items.description: A guided morning among the Baroque churches of Old Goa followed by an inland plantation lunch.

items.title: Private chef's seafood table on a south Goa beach
items.description: A curated Goan-Saraswat and Catholic seafood menu set up privately at the shore's edge.

plan.heading: 4 days in Goa, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Check into a villa at the Park Hyatt or Alila Diwa in the quieter south, away from the crowds.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Settle by the pool, then a slow walk along Cavelossim or Betul beach at low tide.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at the resort's coastal kitchen — Goan fish curry, prawn balchão, feni to close.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Basilica of Bom Jesus and Sé Cathedral in Old Goa, Portuguese Baroque in the morning cool.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A private boat down the Mandovi or Sal backwaters, watching for kingfishers and river dolphins.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Mustard in Sernabatim for Bengali-French cooking, or Fisherman's Wharf on the water.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Portuguese-era mansions of Chandor — Menezes Braganza House — with a family guide.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A working spice plantation lunch inland at Sahakari, then a swim back at the villa.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Sundowner at the villa, then dinner at Bomra's in Candolim for Burmese cooking.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Fontainhas, the Latin Quarter of Panjim, its ochre houses and small galleries on foot.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Long lunch at Vinayak or a beach club in Ashwem before packing.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A last feni sundowner at Thalassa above Vagator, then the drive to depart.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Assagao / North Goa hinterland
items.description: Chic villas and design-led restaurants inland of the north beaches; for style-seekers who want dinner and buzz.

items.name: South Goa (Assolna, Cavelossim, Palolem)
items.description: Quiet, wide beaches and low-key luxury; best for those who want calm and space.

items.name: Fontainhas, Panjim
items.description: The pastel Latin Quarter of the capital; suits travellers who want heritage lanes over sand.

events.name: Goa Carnival
events.note: A Portuguese-legacy street carnival with floats and parades in the days before Lent, centred on Panjim.

events.name: Sunburn Festival
events.note: India's largest electronic-music festival draws a big year-end crowd to the north; plan around it either way.

events.name: Feast of St Francis Xavier
events.note: A major pilgrimage to Old Goa honouring the state's patron saint, with the relics on rare display in exposition years.

events.name: Shigmo
events.note: Goa's Hindu spring festival, a colourful procession of folk dancers and floats, the local counterpart to Holi.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Manohar International Airport (GOX) at Mopa in the north or Dabolim (GOI) in the south; a chauffeured car, or a helicopter to a private villa, completes the arrival.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with driver is the way to reach beaches and villas; distances between north and south Goa are longer than they look.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Good 4G/5G along the coast, thinner inland; an Indian eSIM or Jio/Airtel SIM covers you.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Indian rupee (INR); cards work at hotels and better restaurants, cash for shacks and markets, tipping around ten percent.

onGround.note: The quiet luxury is in the south (around Cavelossim and Assagao's villa belt) rather than the northern party strip; the season runs November to February, and the monsoon closes much of it June to September.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Nov-Feb is the prime season, dry and warm with calm seas; Mar-May turns hot and humid. Avoid Jun-Sep, when the monsoon brings heavy rain and most beach and water activity pauses, though the greenery is spectacular.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: From India: a short 1-2.5 hour hop from Mumbai, Delhi or Bengaluru into Goa. Use the newer Manohar International (GOX) at Mopa in the north for its better facilities, or Dabolim (GOI) if your villa sits in the south; pre-arrange a private transfer, as both airports are a fair drive from the beach belts.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: Routine vaccines plus Hepatitis A and typhoid advised; drink sealed or filtered water. Goa is safe and easygoing; the honest cautions are strong monsoon sea currents (heed red flags) and ordinary care with belongings in the busier northern beach areas.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Easy for vegetarian travellers, though Goan cuisine leans coastal and non-veg, so Jain diners should confirm ahead; luxury resorts handle both without fuss. Beyond the resorts, Vaibhav and a handful of pure-veg kitchens cover Indian vegetarian and thalis well.

seo.title: Hanoi — TripAgent
seo.description: Hanoi, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Hanoi
hero.tagline: Lakeside temples, French boulevards and old-quarter bustle.

ourTake.lede: Give Hanoi more time than people assume — its pleasures are slow and best taken on foot, ideally at dawn when the lakes belong to tai chi practitioners and the pho stalls are at their sharpest. Skip the packaged water-puppet show and the frantic Old Quarter shopping; the real city is in the crumbling French villas of Ba Dinh, the egg-coffee balconies, and a long lunch of bun cha where Obama once sat. The weather makes or breaks a trip: come in autumn (October–November) for dry, cool days, and avoid the grey drizzle of February and March.
ourTake.comeIf: You want old-quarter atmosphere, brilliant street food and Halong Bay a short drive away.
ourTake.skipIf: You want beaches and resorts; Hanoi is a city of culture, not a place to lie still.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Capella Hanoi
items.area: French Quarter / near the Opera House (Hoan Kiem)
items.description: Bill Bensley's 1920s opera fantasy — 47 rooms, each a jewel-box, and the finest address in the city.

items.name: Sofitel Legend Metropole Hanoi
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide Five-Star (2025, fifth consecutive year)
Condé Nast Traveler Gold List 2025 (only hotel in Vietnam)
items.description: The city's grande dame since 1901 — colonial white-and-green, and the address every visitor of consequence has passed through.

items.name: InterContinental Hanoi Westlake
items.description: Over-water pavilions on stilts above West Lake — a resort calm rare this close to the centre.

items.name: JW Marriott Hotel Hanoi
items.area: Nam Tu Liem / Convention district (west Hanoi)
items.description: Carlos Zapata's dragon-inspired curve — the capital's grand modern house, chosen for heads of state.

items.name: Meliá Hanoi
items.description: A dependable, well-placed international tower in the heart of the city.

items.name: Apricot Hotel
items.description: An art-filled boutique house facing Hoan Kiem Lake — Vietnamese paintings on every wall.

items.name: Peridot Grand Luxury Boutique Hotel
items.description: A polished, urbane boutique tower in the thick of the Old Quarter.

items.name: The Old Quarter — the 36 guild streets
items.description: A thousand years of commerce still hums through this warren north of the lake, where each lane once served a single trade — Hang Bac for silver, Hang Ma for votive paper, Hang Dao for silk. Best walked slowly with a private guide who can read the layers a map cannot.

items.name: A cyclo ride through the old lanes
items.description: The gentlest way to take in the crush of the 36 streets — reclined in a pedalled cyclo while the city flows around you, unhurried and eye-level with the shophouses. An easy, charming loop for elders and children alike before the walking begins.

items.name: Hoan Kiem Lake
items.description: The green heart of Hanoi and the city's favourite gathering place, its still water wrapped in willows and the legend of the returned sword. A dawn circuit past the red Turtle Tower, when locals practise tai chi, is one of the quietest luxuries the city offers.

items.name: Ngoc Son Temple & The Huc Bridge
items.description: A small island temple honouring the general Tran Hung Dao, reached across the vivid vermilion arc of The Huc Bridge. The postcard image of Hanoi — and a serene ten-minute pause in the middle of the old city.

items.name: Temple of Literature
items.description: Vietnam's first university, founded in 1070, a series of tranquil walled courtyards, lotus ponds and stelae carried on the backs of stone tortoises. The most composed and contemplative site in the city, and one that resonates with multi-generation families who prize learning.

items.name: Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum & Ba Dinh Square
items.description: The solemn granite mausoleum on the vast ceremonial square where independence was declared in 1945, its changing of the guard a study in precision. A window into the nation's founding story — go early, and dress modestly.

items.name: One Pillar Pagoda
items.description: A tiny wooden shrine built in 1049 to resemble a lotus rising on a single stone stem from its pond, tucked within the Ho Chi Minh complex. Small in scale but singular in form — worth the short walk from the mausoleum.

items.name: Presidential Palace & Ho Chi Minh's stilt house
items.description: The mustard-yellow French colonial palace with its formal gardens, and behind it the modest teak stilt house where Ho Chi Minh chose to live instead. The contrast between grandeur and simplicity is the whole point.

items.name: Ho Chi Minh Museum
items.description: A striking modernist white building beside the mausoleum, its exhibits tracing the life of the leader and the century that shaped modern Vietnam. A cool, orderly stop that completes the Ba Dinh circuit.

items.name: Imperial Citadel of Thang Long
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Central Sector of the Imperial Citadel of Thang Long
items.description: A thousand years of Vietnamese power layered in one place — Ly dynasty palace foundations, colonial gates and the underground command bunker of the American war, all in a single vast enclosure. The archaeological dig alone rewards a private, well-guided morning.

items.name: The Old French Quarter
items.description: Wide tree-lined boulevards, ochre villas and grand hotels laid out during the colonial decades, a world away from the tangle of the Old Quarter. Best explored on foot or by private car, ending with tea at the Metropole where egg coffee was born.

items.name: Hanoi Opera House
items.description: A 1911 belle-epoque theatre modelled on the Palais Garnier in Paris, all marble stairs and gilt, still staging opera, ballet and Vietnamese folk concerts. Attend a performance, or simply admire the finest colonial facade in the city.

items.name: St Joseph's Cathedral
items.description: A weathered neo-Gothic cathedral from 1886, its twin towers echoing Notre-Dame, presiding over a lively square ringed with cafes. The lanes around it — Nha Tho and Nha Chung — are among the best in the city for a slow coffee and boutique browsing.

items.name: Vietnam Museum of Ethnology
items.description: The finest museum in Hanoi — a thoughtful, superbly labelled survey of Vietnam's 54 ethnic groups, with full-scale traditional houses reconstructed in the garden. Genuinely engaging for children and the most rewarding cultural stop in the city.

items.name: Vietnamese Women's Museum
items.description: A moving, beautifully curated museum on women in Vietnamese life — marriage, motherhood, war and the street vendors who still carry the city on shoulder poles. Compact, powerful and a short walk south of the lake.

items.name: Vietnam National Fine Arts Museum
items.description: Set in an elegant three-storey colonial building, a well-chosen collection running from ancient Buddhist sculpture and lacquer to modern silk painting. Quiet, uncrowded and close to the Temple of Literature.

items.name: Hoa Lo Prison
items.description: The remnant of the French colonial prison, later the wartime 'Hanoi Hilton', with unflinching exhibits on both eras. Sobering and well-presented — a serious counterweight to the city's gentler sights.

items.name: Train Street
items.description: A famously narrow residential lane where a working train passes within arm's reach of the trackside cafes. Access has been repeatedly restricted for safety and opens and closes without notice — go only with a local guide who knows the day's rules.

items.name: West Lake (Ho Tay)
items.description: The city's largest lake, ringed by 17 km of quieter, leafier streets, lakeside villas and the best independent dining in Hanoi. A calm base for a slower stay, with sunset the moment to be on the water's edge.

items.name: Tran Quoc Pagoda
items.description: The oldest Buddhist temple in Hanoi, its red brick stupa rising from a slender causeway into West Lake, dating in origin to the 6th century. Loveliest in late afternoon when the light catches the water and incense drifts from the shrine.

items.name: Quan Thanh Temple
items.description: A serene 11th-century Taoist temple beside West Lake, guarded by a nearly four-metre bronze statue cast in the 17th century. An easy, atmospheric pairing with Tran Quoc just along the shore.

items.name: Dong Xuan Market
items.description: Hanoi's largest covered market, a French-built hall of narrow aisles selling everything from silk and spices to household goods. Chaotic and colourful — a photographer's paradise and a plunge into the working city.

items.name: Thang Long Water Puppet Theatre
items.description: A thousand-year-old northern art form performed on a pool of water, lacquered puppets dancing to live traditional music and folk tales of rice farming and dragons. Short, delightful and a sure hit across three generations.

items.name: Egg coffee (ca phe trung)
items.description: Hanoi's signature indulgence — whipped egg yolk beaten into a rich sweet cream over strong coffee, invented here in 1946. Cafe Giang, run by the inventor's family, is the original; a hidden upstairs table watching the street is part of the ritual.

items.name: Old Quarter street-food trail
items.description: Hanoi is a world capital of street food — pho, bun cha over charcoal, banh cuon, egg coffee — each often mastered by a single family stall. A private evening food guide navigates the crowds, the hygiene and the vegetarian options with ease.

items.name: Bat Trang ceramics village
items.description: A 15th-century pottery village 15 km from the centre, its lanes lined with kilns and workshops where you can throw and paint your own piece to be fired and shipped home. A hands-on half-day that delights families and design lovers alike.

items.name: Long Bien Bridge
items.description: The great 1902 Eiffel-era iron bridge across the Red River, scarred by war and still carrying trains and cyclists over the water and the banana fields below. A quietly poignant walk at golden hour, away from the tour crowds.

items.name: Hang Ma & the craft lanes at festival time
items.description: The lane of votive paper and decorations erupts into colour before Tet and the Mid-Autumn Festival, lanterns and offerings spilling across the street. Timed right, it is one of the most joyous corners of the city.

items.name: Ba Dinh & the diplomatic quarter by car
items.description: Beyond the mausoleum, the leafy avenues of embassies, ministries and grand villas make a graceful private drive between the citadel and West Lake. A restful way to link the morning's monuments.

items.name: Ha Long Bay overnight cruise
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Ha Long Bay
items.description: Nearly 2,000 limestone karsts rising from jade water, best seen from the balcony cabin of a small luxury junk on an overnight sailing — sunset on the sundeck, kayaking hidden lagoons, dawn tai chi. The single most romantic escape from Hanoi, roughly a 2.5-hour transfer away.

items.name: Lan Ha Bay cruise
items.description: The quieter, less-visited neighbour of Ha Long off Cat Ba Island — the same soaring karsts and secret beaches, with a fraction of the boats. The connoisseur's choice for an overnight cruise, reached in about three hours.

items.name: Ninh Binh & Trang An
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Trang An Landscape Complex
items.description: 'Ha Long Bay on land' — rowed in a sampan through flooded caves between towering karsts and rice paddies, past ancient temples and the old capital of Hoa Lu. Utterly cinematic, doable as a long day trip or, better, an overnight from Hanoi.

items.name: Tam Coc & Mua Cave
items.description: The Tam Coc river boats drift through three caves and golden paddies, while a climb of some 500 steps to the Mua Cave viewpoint delivers the definitive panorama over the karst valley. The signature photograph of northern Vietnam.

items.name: Bai Dinh Pagoda
items.description: The largest Buddhist temple complex in Vietnam, a vast modern hillside of halls, a corridor lined with 500 stone arhats and the tallest bronze Buddha in Southeast Asia. Often paired with Trang An on the same Ninh Binh circuit.

items.name: Perfume Pagoda
items.description: A revered pilgrimage of shrines set in a limestone massif, reached by a rowed boat along the Yen stream and then a cable car or hike to the sacred Huong Tich grotto. Loveliest and busiest during the spring festival; serene the rest of the year, about two hours from the city.

items.name: Duong Lam ancient village
items.description: A cluster of hamlets 50 km from Hanoi where 300- to 400-year-old laterite houses, communal halls and banyan-shaded gates preserve the northern delta village of another century. The first village in Vietnam granted national heritage status — a gentle, authentic day in the countryside.

items.name: Mai Chau valley
items.description: A wide green valley of rice terraces and White Thai stilt-house villages, ideal for cycling between hamlets and an overnight stay among the ethnic-minority communities. A soft, scenic introduction to the northern highlands, about four hours out.

items.name: Sapa & Fansipan
items.description: The terraced mountains of the far north, home to Hmong and Dao communities, with Fansipan — the 'Roof of Indochina' at 3,143 m — reached by a modern cable car to summit shrines. A five-hour journey best given two or three days, ideally with a private guide and mountain lodge.

items.name: Ancient House at 87 Ma May
items.description: A restored 19th-century merchant's tube-house open to visitors, its dim rooms and inner courtyard showing exactly how the Old Quarter's traders lived and worked. A five-minute masterclass in vernacular architecture in the heart of the lanes.

items.name: Bach Ma Temple
items.description: The oldest temple in the Old Quarter, dedicated to the white horse spirit said to have guided the founding of the citadel, hushed and incense-dark amid the market bustle. A quiet detour most visitors miss.

items.name: Vietnam Military History Museum
items.description: The nation's flagship military museum, reopened in 2024 in a vast new campus, tracing centuries of resistance through aircraft, tanks and a soaring victory tower. Sweeping, modern and thorough for those drawn to the war years.

items.name: Hanoi cooking class
items.description: A guided morning at the market followed by a private hands-on class in pho, fresh spring rolls and bun cha — with vegetarian menus arranged in advance. A hands-on souvenir the whole family carries home.

items.name: Ceramic Mosaic Mural along the Red River dyke
items.description: A record-holding ceramic mural running several kilometres along the dyke road, telling Vietnamese history in tiny tiles. A colourful, offbeat stop en route to the Long Bien Bridge or Bat Trang.

items.name: Tay Ho lakeside dining & sunset drinks
items.description: West Lake's shore holds Hanoi's most relaxed fine dining and rooftop bars, the water turning gold as the city lights come up. The natural place for a slow, elegant evening away from Old Quarter's clamour.

items.name: Hibana by Koki
items.description: An intimate teppanyaki counter inside Capella — Japanese precision and premium produce, one of the hardest seats in town.

items.name: Gia
items.area: Van Mieu / Dong Da (near the Temple of Literature)
items.description: A modern love letter to Northern Vietnamese heritage, in an Indochine house opposite the Temple of Literature.

items.name: Tầm Vị
items.description: Northern Vietnamese home cooking, kept exact and unhurried — the food a Hanoi grandmother would cook, raised to a star.

items.name: ONVIT
items.area: Yen Hoa / Cau Giay (Grand Plaza Hanoi)
items.description: Korean fine dining told through Vietnam's finest ingredients — the country's first starred Korean kitchen.

items.name: Lamai Garden
items.description: Farm-to-table plant-based cooking with more than half its herbs and vegetables grown on site — a rare green star.

items.name: Chả Cá Thăng Long
items.description: Hanoi's signature turmeric-and-dill fish, sizzled at your table over a charcoal brazier — a single, perfect dish.

items.name: Hà Thành Mansion
items.description: Classic Hanoi cooking in a handsome heritage setting — the old recipes, comfortably staged.

items.name: Ưu Đàm Chay
items.description: Refined vegetarian Vietnamese cooking in a calm, tea-house setting — meat-free without compromise.

items.name: 1946 Cửa Bắc
items.description: Authentic regional Vietnamese dishes in an old villa — quiet, generous, of another era.

items.name: Bún Chả Ta
items.description: Grilled pork and rice noodles in smoky broth — Hanoi's defining lunch, done properly.

items.name: Phở Bò Lâm
items.description: A bowl of beef phở with real conviction — the broth that makes the pilgrimage worth it.

items.name: Miến Lươn Đông Thịnh
items.description: Crisp eel and glass noodles — a Hanoi speciality guarded by a single family.

items.name: Mậu Dịch Số 37
items.description: Vietnamese comfort food in a nostalgic subsidy-era canteen — a warm plate of the country's recent past.

items.name: Bún Chả Hương Liên
items.description: The bún chả joint where Obama and Anthony Bourdain shared a plate and a beer — since immortalised.

items.name: Phở Gia Truyền Bát Đàn
items.description: The queue-out-the-door phở the locals line up for at dawn — a legendary bowl and no ceremony.

items.name: Bamboo Bar, Sofitel Legend Metropole
credentials: Inside the Metropole — a MICHELIN One-Key, Forbes Five-Star landmark hotel
items.description: A poolside Indochine bar in the city's grande dame — a rediscovered wartime air-raid shelter lies just beneath it.

items.name: Workshop14
items.description: The city's most exciting new bar — local ingredients, serious technique, and a place on Asia's list within months of opening.

items.name: The Hudson Rooms
items.description: A dazzling bar inside the Three-Key Capella — 1920s glamour and cocktails to match the setting.

items.name: The Haflington
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Bars 2024 (No. 50) — Vietnam's first top-50 bar
items.description: A cocktail bar staged like a night in a European museum — the first Vietnamese bar ever to break Asia's top 50.

items.name: Nê Cocktail Bar
items.description: The bar that put Hanoi on the map — birthplace of the celebrated 'Phở' cocktail, distilling the city into a glass.

items.name: Top of Hanoi, Lotte Hotel
credentials: Hanoi's highest rooftop bar, atop the 65-storey Lotte Tower
items.description: An open-air perch on the 67th floor of the Lotte Tower — the highest, widest view over the whole city.

items.title: Private seaplane transfer to Ha Long Bay
items.description: A 45-minute Hai Au seaplane flight from Hanoi lands you on the water at Ha Long, turning a four-hour road slog into an aerial reading of the karst-studded gulf.

items.title: After-hours dinner at a restored French villa
items.description: Chefs at addresses like La Badiane and Home Hanoi open private dining rooms in colonial villas for tasting menus that trace northern Vietnamese cooking away from the crowds.

items.title: Dawn on Hoan Kiem Lake before the city wakes
items.description: Arrive at first light to have the red Huc Bridge and Ngoc Son Temple to yourself as the neighbourhood's tai chi and badminton games unfold along the water.

items.title: Private overnight junk in a quiet Bai Tu Long corner
items.description: Charter a small wooden junk into Bai Tu Long, the emptier arm of the bay, for kayaking through hidden lagoons and a night at anchor far from the day-tripper fleet.

plan.heading: 3 days in Hanoi, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle into the Sofitel Legend Metropole, then walk the shaded lanes around Hoan Kiem Lake to the Ngoc Son Temple before the day warms.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Cross into the Old Quarter's guild streets — Hang Bac, Hang Gai — for lacquer and raw silk, ending with tea at a rooftop above St. Joseph's Cathedral.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Gia by chef Sam Tran, whose tasting menu reads Hanoi through the seasons; a quiet nightcap back at the Metropole's Bamboo Bar.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Early visit to the Temple of Literature, then the Ho Chi Minh complex and the stilt house while the grounds are still cool.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Coffee and lacquerware at the Vietnamese Women's Museum, then a slow afternoon at the Sofitel spa.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Bun cha done properly at a family house, then Michelin-listed T.U.N.G by Hoang Tung for a modern Vietnamese tasting.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Private car to Bat Trang, the eight-century pottery village, to watch the wheels and choose a few pieces to ship home.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Return for a leisurely lunch, then the Thang Long water puppet theatre — an old art, done with real care.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at La Verticale in a French villa, chef Didier Corlou's take on Vietnamese spice.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Old Quarter (Hoan Kiem)
items.description: The dense, motorbike-loud heart of the city — best for first-timers who want to walk everywhere and don't mind noise.

items.name: French Quarter
items.description: Wide boulevards, the opera house and the grand old Metropole; suits travellers wanting quiet, space and the classic colonial hotels.

items.name: Tay Ho (West Lake)
items.description: Leafy, lakeside and expat-favoured, with the best cafes and slower mornings — ideal for a longer, more residential stay.

events.name: Tet (Vietnamese Lunar New Year)
events.note: The country's biggest holiday; Hanoi empties of traffic and fills with kumquat trees and peach blossom, though many shops close for several days.

events.name: Dong Da Festival
events.note: Held on the 5th day of the lunar new year at Dong Da mound, it commemorates Emperor Quang Trung's 1789 rout of the invading Qing army.

events.name: Perfume Pagoda Festival
events.note: A months-long pilgrimage southwest of Hanoi where over a million make the boat-and-climb journey to the sacred cave temple.

events.name: Mid-Autumn Festival
events.note: A children's festival that turns Hang Ma street and the Old Quarter into a lantern market with lion dances and mooncakes.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Noi Bai International (HAN); a pre-arranged private car with a fast-track greeter clears you through immigration and covers the 45-minute run into the Old Quarter or West Lake.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Keep a private car and driver on call; the Old Quarter itself is best on foot, as its lanes are too narrow and chaotic for a vehicle.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM (Viettel or Vinaphone) activates on landing and is the cleanest option; hotel and restaurant wifi is fast and widespread.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Vietnamese dong (VND); cards are accepted at hotels and finer restaurants but carry cash for markets and small vendors, and tipping is modest and appreciated rather than expected.

onGround.note: Base yourself around Hoan Kiem Lake or West Lake for calm; dress lightly but cover shoulders and knees at the Temple of Literature and pagodas, and note that traffic crossing is done slowly and steadily rather than by waiting for a gap.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: October to April is dry, cool and clear — October is the pick. Skip June to August: 35C-plus with humidity over 80% makes it feel like 40, and September brings the wettest, typhoon-remnant rain.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi in about 4h30m on Air India, Vietnam Airlines, IndiGo or Vietjet into Noi Bai (HAN); from Mumbai and Bengaluru it is usually one stop via a Vietnamese or Southeast Asian hub. Vietnam Airlines flies it well in business; the DEL service is an overnight departure, so plan to arrive and rest rather than schedule the morning.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations for arrivals from India; hepatitis A, typhoid and routine boosters are sensible. Vietnam is very safe for travellers — petty theft in the Old Quarter is the main watch-out. Drink bottled or filtered water only; tap is not potable.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian is easy and Buddhist 'chay' cooking is a genuine cuisine here, so pure-veg and near-Jain (no onion/garlic on request) is workable at temple-style restaurants. Indian food is available but limited; Namaste Hanoi and Foodshop 45 are the reliable names for a proper Indian meal.

seo.title: Ho Chi Minh City — TripAgent
seo.description: Ho Chi Minh City, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Ho Chi Minh City
hero.tagline: French colonial relics meet frenetic, neon-lit energy.

ourTake.lede: Saigon rewards appetite and energy more than sightseeing — the War Remnants Museum and the Reunification Palace are worth a serious half-day, but the city's real pleasure is at the table and on the street after dark. Base yourself in District 1 for a first visit, then cross into District 3 or Binh Thanh for the food locals actually queue for. Don't try to see it from a bus; the heat and the traffic mean the best moves are short, deliberate, and broken up by a good rooftop.
ourTake.comeIf: You want energy, history and superb food, with the Mekong Delta within easy reach.
ourTake.skipIf: You want calm and space; the city is fast, dense and relentless in its traffic.

whenToGo.blurb: Come December to April for dry, bright days; time it with Tet in February for the city at its most festive, and brace for daily downpours from May to October.
