closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Jodhpur — TripAgent
seo.description: Jodhpur, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Jodhpur
hero.tagline: The blue city beneath Rajasthan's mightiest hill fort.

ourTake.lede: Jodhpur is really about one extraordinary fort and the blue city beneath it, so give the mornings to Mehrangarh and the late afternoons to wandering the indigo lanes of the old town. The rooftop-cafe view of the fort is worth chasing, but the fort itself, seen early, is the reason to come. Pair it with a night at a heritage palace and, if you have time, a village safari into the Bishnoi country.
ourTake.comeIf: You want the blue city, a mighty fort and a palace hotel that once housed a maharaja.
ourTake.skipIf: You want greenery or a beach; this is desert Rajasthan, dry and monumental.

firstLook.heroCaption: Woman walking poolside royal tent courtyard

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: Come in the cool winter, October to February, for clear desert light and the great fort festivals; avoid the fierce April-June heat entirely.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Oct, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Jodhpur. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Umaid Bhawan Palace
credentials: TripAdvisor Travellers' Choice — first Indian hotel named World's Best Hotel (2016); India's Best in subsequent years
items.description: One of the world's largest private residences, half still the Maharaja's home — the first Indian hotel ever judged the best on earth.

items.name: RAAS Jodhpur
items.area: Old Blue City (near the Clock Tower, at the fort's foot)
credentials: World Architecture Festival (WAF) Barcelona 2011 — World's Best Holiday Building
Aga Khan Award for Architecture — nominee (2013)
items.description: A 250-year-old haveli reborn in red sandstone and glass — Mehrangarh filling every window, the most design-led room in the city.

items.name: Ajit Bhawan
credentials: Recognised as India's first heritage hotel — Outlook Traveller
Former residence of Maharaj Ajit Singh of Jodhpur
items.description: India's very first heritage hotel — a 1920s royal residence, leafy and lived-in, where the palace idea began.

items.name: WelcomHeritage Bal Samand Lake Palace
credentials: Heritage palace of the Marwar royal house (Maharaja Jaswant Singh I)
items.description: A 17th-century red-stone summer palace on a 12th-century lake — 60 acres of orchards and birdsong, the city left behind.

items.name: Taj Hari Mahal
credentials: Palace-style heritage 5-star — Heritage Hotels of India
items.description: A Taj palace-style hotel on six acres of gardens — Rajput-Mughal grandeur, big-hotel polish, and the group's assured service.

items.name: Ranbanka Palace
credentials: Recognised heritage palace-hotel — Heritage Hotels of India
Erstwhile palace of the Jodhpur royal family
items.description: A 1920s Rajput palace between Mehrangarh and Umaid Bhawan — solid, characterful heritage without the icon's price.

items.name: Mehrangarh Fort
items.area: Fort hill, above the old city
items.description: The great Rathore stronghold Rao Jodha raised in 1459, rising 400 feet of sheer sandstone above the Blue City, its walls up to 36 metres high. Come at opening with a Mehrangarh Museum Trust historian and let the crowds arrive after you; the fort is a full unhurried morning, not a photo stop.

items.name: The Mehrangarh Museum galleries
items.description: One of India's finest private royal collections, kept by the Mehrangarh Museum Trust: palanquins and elephant howdahs, jewelled arms, Marwar miniatures, and the mirror-and-gold state rooms of Phool Mahal and Moti Mahal. The audio-guide is genuinely good, but a curator-led walk is what turns objects into your family's history.

items.name: The ramparts and cannon terraces
items.description: The high battlements where the old cannon still point out over a sea of blue rooftops, the desert horizon on one side and Jaswant Thada's white marble on the other. This is the view that made the Blue City famous; catch it in the soft light just after opening or before closing.

items.name: Flying Fox zip-line over Mehrangarh
items.area: Mehrangarh Fort ramparts and Rao Jodha Park
items.description: India's first heritage zip-line, six lines that launch off the battlements and fly over Ranisar and Padamsar lakes and deep into the desert park below the walls. A properly thrilling ninety minutes with a serious safety brief; a rare shot of adrenaline the older children and grandchildren will not forget.

items.name: Chamunda Mata Temple
items.description: The kuldevi shrine Rao Jodha carried from Mandore and installed at the fort in 1460, still the family deity of the Rathores and thronged at Dussehra. Its terrace is one of the best free viewpoints in Jodhpur, the Blue City falling away below and the fort walls rising gold behind you.

items.name: Jaswant Thada
items.area: Just east of Mehrangarh, above Devkund lake
items.description: The 1899 royal cenotaph of translucent Makrana marble, so finely cut the sheets glow amber in the sun; still the cremation ground of the Rathore rulers, set above a tiered garden and a small lake. Quieter than the fort and often golden at day's end, with resident musicians in the forecourt.

items.name: Umaid Bhawan Palace Museum
items.description: The public wing of one of the largest private residences on earth, the Maharaja's own Art-Deco palace, with clocks, arms, portraits and the family's story of the twentieth century. The lawns hold the royal vintage cars, Rolls-Royces and Cadillacs among them, a treat for anyone who loves great motoring.

items.name: Stay at Taj Umaid Bhawan Palace
items.description: Still part-home to the Jodhpur royal family, the Taj-run wing is regularly named among the world's finest hotels, all Art-Deco grandeur, private butlers and 26 acres of gardens. The definitive multi-generational Jodhpur address; even non-residents can arrange high tea beneath the great dome.

items.name: Ghanta Ghar (the Clock Tower)
items.area: Heart of the old walled city
items.description: Maharaja Sardar Singh's landmark tower, its clock brought from England, standing at the centre of the old city as the fixed point everyone navigates by. Best seen in the last hour of daylight when the bazaar around it wakes up and the tower catches the low sun.

items.name: Sardar Market
items.area: Around the Clock Tower, old city
items.description: The great bazaar ringing the Clock Tower, alleys of spice, textiles, silver, lac bangles and antiques under the fort's gaze. Go early with a guide who can take you past the tourist stalls to the real merchants; the famed Mathania red-chilli mounds and mounds of saffron and dry fruit are a sensory event in themselves.

items.name: Old spice and textile shops of Nai Sarak
items.description: The lane where Jodhpur's families still buy their bandhej tie-dye, block-print and turban cloth, and where the old spice merchants blend and package to order. Ask a trusted shop to make up a personal masala box or a length of hand-dyed silk; a far better souvenir than anything airport-bought.

items.name: Toorji Ka Jhalra stepwell
items.description: A beautifully restored 18th-century royal stepwell, its carved sandstone tiers plunging into cool green water, built by a queen of Maharaja Abhay Singh. Free and open all day; the surrounding lanes have become the city's most charming little quarter of design shops and cafés.

items.name: The Stepwell Café and rooftop
items.description: The rooftop café looking straight down onto the stepwell and up at the fort, a relaxed spot for a long lunch or a coffee between the fort and the bazaar. Wood-fired pizza and cold drinks in a courtyard-and-terrace setting; the prettiest easy pause in the old city.

items.name: Blue City walk through Navchokiya
items.description: The oldest, bluest tangle of lanes, painted indigo since the Brahmin families first set their houses apart; every doorway and wall a frame. Walk it early with a local guide who is welcomed into the courtyards, and you see a living neighbourhood rather than a backdrop.

items.name: Brahmpuri lanes and rooftops
items.description: The Brahmin quarter climbing up toward the fort walls, its blue houses stacked steeply for the best rooftop views back at Mehrangarh. Time it for the golden hour, when the indigo deepens and the fort glows above the rooftops, then take chai on a family terrace.

items.name: Pachetia Hill viewpoint
items.description: A short climb from the blue lanes to a 360-degree panorama, the patchwork of indigo rooftops on one side and the fort crowning the ridge on the other. A quiet, local sunrise or sunset spot, well away from the tour buses.

items.name: Rao Jodha Desert Rock Park
items.area: Below the fort walls, around Devkund
items.description: Seventy-plus hectares of rocky desert ecology painstakingly restored beneath the fort, laced with walking trails past hidden lakes and 80-odd native plant species. Take a naturalist at opening for the birds and the cool of the volcanic-rock ravines; a serene counterpoint to the fort above.

items.name: Mandore Gardens
items.area: Mandore, 9 km north of the city
items.description: The old Marwar capital before Jodhpur, its temple-like red-sandstone royal cenotaphs rising out of green gardens, with the carved Hall of Heroes and shady walks. A leafy, atmospheric half-morning steeped in the dynasty's earliest history, with resident monkeys and far fewer visitors than the fort.

items.name: Kaylana Lake
items.area: 8 km west of the city, on the Jaisalmer road
items.description: A 19th-century royal-built lake ringed by low hills, best at sunset when the water turns to fire and, in winter, migratory birds gather. Boating and a quiet picnic; a soft, unhurried evening away from the old-city bustle.

items.name: Machia Biological Park
items.area: Near Kaylana Lake, west of the city
items.description: A well-run desert wildlife park beside Kaylana, jeep trails past Asiatic lions, leopards, blackbuck and gharial, with a good clifftop viewpoint over the lake. An easy, engaging couple of hours for families travelling with children.

items.name: Balsamand Lake and Palace
items.description: A 12th-century royal lake with a 17th-century red-sandstone summer palace on its bank, now a heritage hotel in sixty acres of fruit orchards and lawns. Come for a garden lunch or a lakeside dinner; a graceful, tranquil retreat that suits an unhurried afternoon.

items.name: RAAS Jodhpur rooftop and Baradari
items.area: Northeastern old city, below the fort
items.description: The city's original design hotel, built around an 18th-century haveli with every terrace framing Mehrangarh; the rooftop bar has the best fort-at-night view in town. Dine at Baradari in the old twelve-pillared pavilion, then watch the floodlit fort over a nightcap even if you are not staying.

items.name: Rajasthani thali at Gypsy
items.description: Jodhpur's beloved unlimited vegetarian thali, dal-baati-churma, gatte, ker sangri and a dozen Marwari dishes served till you wave the servers away. A generous, entirely veg feast, the honest, festive heart of Marwari home cooking.

items.name: Mirchi bada and mawa kachori at Janta Sweet Home
items.description: The institution for Jodhpur's own street sweets and snacks, the fiery mirchi bada, the rich mawa kachori, ghevar and rabri laddu, all pure-veg and made fresh through the day. Send someone ahead to bring a box back, or sit in for the full sugar-and-chilli education.

items.name: Makhaniya lassi and saffron at the Clock Tower
items.description: Jodhpur's famously thick, saffron-and-pistachio makhaniya lassi, served in clay cups at the old shops by the tower. A five-minute ritual that locals will tell you is non-negotiable; pair it with the market walk.

items.name: High tea at Umaid Bhawan
items.description: Afternoon tea beneath the palace's great Art-Deco dome or on the terraces over the gardens, open to non-residents by reservation. A slice of royal grandeur without an overnight stay; a memorable pause with children or elders who want the palace without the pace of sightseeing.

items.name: Jodhpur RIFF folk festival
items.description: The Rajasthan International Folk Festival, a UNESCO-backed roots-music gathering staged inside the fort under the brightest full moon of the year, dawn ragas on the ramparts and all-night concerts in the courtyards. Book fort accommodation and passes months ahead; the setting alone is worth the trip.

items.name: World Sacred Spirit Festival
items.description: A February festival of Sufi and sacred music split between Mehrangarh and the great Nagaur fort, an intimate, curated affair for those staying inside the forts. Access is limited and must be booked far ahead; deeply atmospheric for travellers who want the rarefied end of Rajasthan's culture.

items.name: Umaid Gardens and Sardar Government Museum
items.description: The city's leafy 82-acre public gardens below Umaid Bhawan, with a museum of Marwar sculpture, miniatures, arms and coins, and a small zoo. A gentle, shaded stroll and a cross-section of regional history; pleasant with grandparents and children in the cooler hours.

items.name: Bishnoi village safari
items.description: A jeep morning among the Bishnoi, the community who have protected the desert's blackbuck, chinkara and khejri trees for 500 years, and whose 363 martyrs died to save a grove. You meet potters, weavers and dhurrie-makers at work, and see herds of blackbuck grazing unafraid; the most moving cultural half-day near the city.

items.name: Kankani, the potters' village
items.description: A Bishnoi village where a master potter still turns a heavy stone wheel by hand to throw the region's clay vessels, often a stop on the safari. A quiet, genuine encounter with a craft that has not changed in centuries; children can try the wheel.

items.name: Salawas dhurrie weavers
items.description: The village famous for its handwoven cotton and camel-hair dhurries, made on pit looms by families who will weave a rug to your colours and size. Buy direct from the weaver and have it shipped; a craft purchase with a story attached.

items.name: Guda Bishnoi lake and blackbuck
items.description: A tranquil desert reservoir where blackbuck, chinkara and, in winter, demoiselle cranes and flamingos come to drink at dawn and dusk. A patient, beautiful wildlife hour, often paired with the Bishnoi safari, best with a good local naturalist.

items.name: Osian temples and desert
items.description: The 'Khajuraho of Rajasthan', a cluster of exquisitely carved 8th-to-12th-century Hindu and Jain temples, crowned by the hilltop Sachiya Mata shrine and the serene Mahavira temple. Pair the temples with a camel ride or sundowner on the dunes just beyond; a full, rewarding day-trip.

items.name: Marwari horses and riding at Rohet Garh
items.description: The 16th-century Rathore thikana of Rohet keeps one of India's finest stables of the ear-curled Marwari horse and runs everything from a dawn hack to multi-day riding safaris across Marwar. For riders, the definitive way to feel the region the way the Rathores did; Rohet Garh is a fine heritage stay in its own right.

items.name: Chandelao Garh and the women's craft cooperative
items.description: A restored village fort-hotel where the Sundar Rang women's cooperative produces hand-embroidered textiles and homeware, and guests learn block-printing and share village meals. A warm, grounded rural day that puts your spending straight into local hands.

items.name: Khejarla Fort day-trip or stay
items.description: A 400-year-old red-sandstone Rajput fort with carved jharokhas and lattice-work, now a characterful heritage hotel amid open countryside. Ideal as a leisurely lunch-and-village stop en route to Jaipur, or a quiet overnight with folk music under the stars.

items.name: Ahhichatragarh Fort, Nagaur
items.description: A vast, superbly restored 12th-century Rajput-Mughal fort of palaces, painted pavilions and ingenious water gardens, an Aga Khan award-winning conservation and the setting for the Sufi festival. A rewarding longer day-trip for those who want a great fort without the crowds, best paired with a stay at Ranvas within the walls.

items.name: Antique and curio hunting in the old city
items.area: Umaid Bhawan Palace road and old-city lanes
items.description: Jodhpur is one of India's great sources for antique and reproduction furniture, doors, silver and colonial curios, shipped worldwide by long-established dealers. Go with an eye and a trusted name; the city's dealers furnish collectors and designers around the world.

items.name: Lac-bangle and silver workshops
items.description: The tiny workshops where artisans still soften and shape coloured lac into bangles and set silver in the old Marwar way, tucked into the bazaar behind the Clock Tower. Watch a bangle made to order in minutes; a small, living craft you can buy at the source.

items.name: Cooking a Marwari meal with a local family
items.description: Several heritage homes and havelis host hands-on classes in the strictly vegetarian Marwari kitchen, ker sangri, gatte, bajra rotla and the sweets, followed by the meal you have made. An intimate way to understand a desert cuisine built without fresh vegetables; a favourite with families.

items.name: Hot-air balloon over the Blue City
items.area: Launch sites on the city's outskirts
items.description: Seasonal dawn balloon flights that drift over the sea of blue rooftops with the fort and desert spread below, a growing fixture in Jodhpur's cooler months. A once-in-a-trip aerial view; weather-dependent, so keep the morning flexible.

items.name: Ranisar and Padamsar lakes
items.description: Two linked medieval reservoirs tucked against the fort ramparts, built to water the citadel and now a peaceful pocket of green and birdlife glimpsed from the walls and the zip-line. A quiet detail most visitors miss; ask at the fort about access on the walking trails.

items.name: Jodhpur polo and the Rathore legacy
items.description: Jodhpur gave the world the jodhpur breech and a proud polo tradition, and the Rathore family still fields celebrated players; the winter season brings matches and the game is woven into estate life at Rohet and beyond. Arranged through the right hosts, a chukka or a match-day is a distinctively Marwari afternoon.

items.name: Risala
credentials: Inside Umaid Bhawan Palace — first Indian hotel named World's Best (TripAdvisor Travellers' Choice 2016); MICHELIN Guide Hotel
items.description: Royal Marwari and Indian cooking from the Maharajas' own recipes, hung with martial portraits, the fort framed beyond the gardens — the grandest table in Jodhpur.

items.name: Baradari
credentials: Inside RAAS Jodhpur — World Architecture Festival 2011, World's Best Holiday Building; MICHELIN Guide Hotel
items.description: Contemporary and Rajasthani plates in an 1850s twelve-pillared pavilion, the floodlit fort towering above the courtyard — Jodhpur's most beautiful dinner.

items.name: Gypsy
credentials: Long-standing Jodhpur institution for the traditional Rajasthani thali
items.description: The definitive unlimited Marwari thali — dal-baati-churma, gatte, ker sangri — carried to the table till you surrender.

items.name: Janta Sweet Home
items.area: Old Blue City (near the Clock Tower / Sardar Market)
items.description: Jodhpur's kachori legend — pyaaz and mawa kachoris, ghewar and mirchi vada, a bazaar rite of passage.

items.name: Shri Mishrilal Hotel
items.area: Old Blue City (Sardar Market, by the Clock Tower)
credentials: Established 1927 — the original makhaniya lassi house (Sardar Market)
items.description: The makhaniya lassi that made Jodhpur famous — saffron, cardamom and a cap of clotted cream, poured here since the 1920s.

items.name: Trophy Bar
credentials: Inside Umaid Bhawan Palace — first Indian hotel named World's Best (TripAdvisor Travellers' Choice 2016); MICHELIN Guide Hotel
items.description: A cabinet of colonial curiosities and hunting trophies — rare whiskies, cigars and quiet royal elegance, the grandest nightcap in the city.

items.name: Stepwell Café at RAAS
credentials: Inside RAAS Jodhpur — World Architecture Festival 2011, World's Best Holiday Building; MICHELIN Guide Hotel
items.description: Three tiers above the floodlit Toorji stepwell, Mehrangarh looming behind — an evening cocktail with the best view in the old city.

items.title: Private early access to Mehrangarh Fort
items.description: One of India's most complete forts, best walked before opening when the ramparts are still and cool.

items.title: Stay or dine at Umaid Bhawan Palace
items.description: A night in one of the last great palace-residences, part working royal home, part Art Deco masterpiece.

items.title: Bishnoi village safari with a naturalist
items.description: A private drive into the desert villages to see the community famed for protecting the blackbuck and khejri trees.

items.title: Zip-line flight across the fort's ramparts
items.description: A rare aerial pass over the walls and lakes below Mehrangarh, for a different view of the citadel.

plan.heading: 3 days in Jodhpur, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive at Umaid Bhawan Palace, the Taj-run Art Deco residence still home to the royal family, and settle before the heat.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A curator-led afternoon at Mehrangarh Fort, ending on the ramparts as the blue city glows below.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Cocktails at the Umaid Bhawan bar, then dinner at Risala over the palace gardens.

days.title: The old city and its makers

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A guided walk through the Sardar Market lanes and the blue houses of the Brahmpuri quarter with a local historian.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Visit the marble Jaswant Thada cenotaph, then an afternoon at the RAAS Jodhpur pool beneath the fort.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Baradari at RAAS on the terrace, with Mehrangarh floodlit above you.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive into the Bishnoi villages for block-printing, pottery and a tea with a farming family, arranged privately.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at Rohet Garh heritage house, then a slow return across the scrub.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A last dinner under the stars at Umaid Bhawan, or a quiet in-suite meal before departure.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Old Blue City (below the fort)
items.description: The indigo lanes and rooftop cafes; best for atmosphere and the classic fort views.

items.name: Umaid Bhawan / palace side
items.description: Grand and secluded on the ridge; suits those wanting palace grandeur and calm.

items.name: Ratanada / newer town
items.description: Quieter and residential with mid-range comforts; for a practical, less touristy base.

events.name: Rajasthan International Folk Festival (RIFF)
events.note: A superb roots-music festival staged inside Mehrangarh Fort on the October full moon.

events.name: Marwar Festival
events.note: A two-day celebration of Marwari folk music and dance honouring the region's heroes.

events.name: World Sacred Spirit Festival
events.note: An intimate festival of devotional and Sufi music held within the fort.

events.name: Diwali
events.note: The blue city glows with lamps beneath the floodlit fort, a striking sight from the rooftops.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Jodhpur Airport (JDH), a civil enclave about 15 minutes from the old city, and take a chauffeured car; Raas, the Taj Umaid Bhawan and the Raas Devigarh set-ups will send a car to meet you.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with driver for the fort and the desert edge, and slow walking through the blue lanes of the old town beneath Mehrangarh.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: 4G is solid in the city and hotel wifi is good; an Airtel or Jio eSIM before you land is the cleanest option.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Indian rupee (INR); cards work at hotels and established shops, cash for the bazaars, tipping around 10 percent.

onGround.note: Mehrangarh Fort is the anchor — go early and take a guide. Stay in the old blue city for atmosphere or at Umaid Bhawan for grandeur; summer heat is severe, so plan sightseeing for morning and evening.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: October to March is the good stretch: warm days, cool nights, the blue city sharp under clear skies. Avoid April to June, when desert heat pushes past 42C, and the July-September rains.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi (approx 1h20m), Mumbai (approx 1h45m) and Bengaluru (under 2.5h) into Jodhpur Airport (JDH); IndiGo flies all three, Air India and Akasa on Delhi. A compact civil-enclave airport, so keep connections generous and let the hotel handle the pickup rather than expecting a lounge.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required beyond routine Hep A/typhoid cover. Safe, relaxed city. Sealed or filtered water; the desert air is dry, so drink more than you think.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Simple for vegetarian and Jain guests; Marwari food is vegetarian by tradition and no-onion-no-garlic cooking is standard. The dining rooms at Umaid Bhawan Palace and RAAS do polished vegetarian Rajasthani; dal-baati-churma is the local staple.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Kathmandu — TripAgent
seo.description: Kathmandu, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Kathmandu
hero.tagline: A Himalayan valley of gilded temples, stupas and living heritage.

ourTake.lede: Base yourself in Patan, not touristy Thamel — the Durbar Square there is the most intact of the three and you'll sleep better. Give the valley its due: Bhaktapur, Boudhanath and Pashupatinath each deserve half a day, and the drive out to Nagarkot for a Himalayan sunrise is worth the early start. The city rewards patience over ticking sights, so slow down and let the courtyards find you.
ourTake.comeIf: You want ancient temple squares, Himalayan air and a gateway to the mountains without a long-haul flight or any visa paperwork.
ourTake.skipIf: You are after beaches, polished resorts or a seamless big-city experience; Kathmandu is dusty, chaotic and low on luxury infrastructure.

whenToGo.blurb: Come October-November or March-April for clear skies, mountain views and the great autumn festivals of Dashain and Tihar; skip the June-September monsoon and January's cold.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Mar, Apr, May, Jun, Oct, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Kathmandu. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: The Dwarika's Hotel
credentials: Travel + Leisure Asia's Best Awards 2024 — Best Luxury Boutique Hotel
Robb Report — The 50 Greatest Luxury Hotel Suites in the World 2025
items.description: Nepal's heritage-luxury landmark — a living museum of carved Newari courtyards, and the country's most decorated address.

items.name: Hyatt Regency Kathmandu
credentials: World Travel Awards — Nepal's Leading Hotel (multiple years, 2016–2023)
items.description: A pagoda-styled resort in its own gardens beside the great stupa — the city's long-standing grand hotel.

items.name: Aloft Kathmandu Thamel
credentials: World Travel Awards — Nepal's Leading Hotel 2025 & 2024
World Luxury Hotel Awards — Country Winner 2025
items.description: A crisp, contemporary Marriott house in the heart of Thamel — lately voted the country's leading hotel.

items.name: The Soaltee Kathmandu
credentials: Safari India South Asia Travel Awards 2019 — Best Resort Hotel for Luxury
items.description: Nepal's first international five-star house — a large, established hotel set in mature gardens.

items.name: Pashupatinath Temple & the Bagmati aarti
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Kathmandu Valley
items.description: One of the most sacred Shiva shrines in the Hindu world, its gilded pagoda roof rising over the Bagmati where the smoke of the cremation ghats never quite settles. For an Indian family the pull is instant and deep — the same Shiva of Kashi, the same river-and-fire theology — and at dusk the Bagmati Aarti of lamps and conch on the far bank is one of the most moving rituals in South Asia. Only Hindus enter the inner sanctum; a knowledgeable guide reads the ghats and the sadhus without intruding.

items.name: Boudhanath Stupa & the evening kora
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Kathmandu Valley
items.description: One of the largest stupas on earth, a vast white dome crowned by the all-seeing Buddha eyes, ringed by red-robed monks, butter lamps and the murmur of Om Mani Padme Hum. At dusk the whole Tibetan quarter walks the kora clockwise around it, prayer wheels spinning — a slow, hypnotic circuit that multi-generational families can join at their own pace. Take a rooftop café table on the circle for the finest seat in Kathmandu.

items.name: The Tibetan quarter around Boudha
items.description: The lanes radiating off the stupa are the heart of the Tibetan diaspora in Nepal — monasteries (gompas) of every lineage, thangka ateliers, incense and singing-bowl workshops, and the scent of Tibetan bread and butter tea. A guided morning here, timed to a monastery's puja with its horns and chanting, gives context the stupa alone cannot.

items.name: Swayambhunath (the Monkey Temple)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Kathmandu Valley
items.description: The valley's oldest and most iconic stupa, crowning a wooded hill reached by a steep flight of 365 stone steps guarded by troops of rhesus monkeys. The painted Buddha eyes gaze out over the whole of Kathmandu, and the fluttering prayer flags, the vajra and the mixed Hindu-Buddhist shrines make it a living crossroads of both faiths. For those who prefer not to climb, a private car reaches a side entrance near the top.

items.name: Kathmandu Durbar Square & Hanuman Dhoka
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Kathmandu Valley
items.description: The medieval royal heart of the city — the old Hanuman Dhoka palace, a dense huddle of pagoda temples, the tall Kasthamandap and the coronation courtyards of the Malla and Shah kings. Some of it is still braced and rebuilding after 2015, which a good guide turns into a lesson in Newari craft rather than a caveat. Best walked slowly in early morning light before the square fills.

items.name: The Kumari Ghar & the living goddess
items.description: A superbly carved Newari courtyard house that is home to the Royal Kumari — a young girl worshipped as a living goddess, an incarnation of the goddess Taleju, who appears briefly at an upper window to those gathered below. It is one of the most singular living traditions on the subcontinent, and being present when she looks out is a quiet, unforgettable moment for a family. Photography of the goddess is forbidden.

items.name: Patan Durbar Square & the Krishna Mandir
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Kathmandu Valley
items.description: The most refined of the valley's three royal squares, an open-air museum of Newari architecture where the stone Krishna Mandir — 21 gilded spires carved entirely from stone in 1637 — stands among a forest of struts, courtyards and shrines. Just across the river from Kathmandu, it is calmer, greener and more intact than the capital's square, and instantly legible to Hindu visitors through its Krishna and Vishnu iconography.

items.name: The Patan Museum
items.description: Widely called one of the most beautiful museums in South Asia, set inside the restored Keshav Narayan Chowk palace and showing gilt-copper and cast-bronze Hindu and Buddhist deities at the very pinnacle of Newari metalwork. Around 300 masterpieces are displayed with rare restraint; the brick-and-timber galleries and the courtyard café make it a cultured, cool-of-the-day pause for all ages.

items.name: The Patan metalwork & Newari craft workshops
items.description: Patan is the valley's city of artisans — in the lanes around the Durbar Square, families still cast bronze and gilt-copper deities by the ancient lost-wax method, exactly as their ancestors did for the Malla kings. A private atelier visit lets a collector watch a statue take shape and commission a piece, a far more meaningful acquisition than anything on a shop shelf.

items.name: Bhaktapur Durbar Square & the 55-Window Palace
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Kathmandu Valley
items.description: The best-preserved of the three royal cities, a car-free warren of ochre-brick lanes where the 55-Window Palace, the Golden Gate and the Lion Gate frame a square that feels frozen in the Malla age. Give it half a day with a guide; it rewards slow wandering more than any single monument in the valley, and children love its open, traffic-free stage.

items.name: The Nyatapola Temple, Bhaktapur
items.description: Nepal's tallest pagoda — five soaring tiers guarded by a stone stairway of wrestlers, elephants, lions and griffins, each pair ten times stronger than the one below. Built in 1702, it survived the great earthquakes untouched, and its silhouette against the morning sky over Taumadhi Square is one of the definitive images of the valley.

items.name: Bhaktapur Pottery Square
items.description: An open square where potters still throw and sun-dry rows of clay pots and figurines in the traditional Prajapati way, as they have for centuries. Hands-on for children and quietly photogenic for everyone; a rare living-craft scene that has not been staged for visitors.

items.name: Bhaktapur juju dhau — the King's Curd
items.description: Bhaktapur's own delicacy: juju dhau, literally 'king of curds' — a rich, faintly caramel yoghurt set in shallow clay bowls that give it its texture. Deeply vegetarian and utterly local, it is the perfect sweet pause between temples, and a taste that stays with you long after the trip.

items.name: Changu Narayan Temple
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Kathmandu Valley
items.description: The oldest Hindu temple still in use in the valley, a double-roofed Vishnu shrine on a quiet wooded ridge, wrapped in some of the finest ancient stone and metal sculpture in Nepal — including a fifth-century Licchavi inscription, the country's oldest. Far less visited than the durbar squares, it pairs beautifully with Bhaktapur and speaks directly to Vaishnavite Hindu travellers.

items.name: Budhanilkantha — the Sleeping Vishnu
items.description: Nepal's largest stone carving: a five-metre Vishnu reclining on the coils of the cosmic serpent Shesha, floating in a recessed pool that stands for the primordial ocean. For Hindus it is one of the valley's most powerful darshan, carved from a single block of black basalt in the Licchavi era; the early-morning ritual bathing of the deity is especially moving. A short drive north of the city, at the foot of the green Shivapuri hills.

items.name: Kopan Monastery
items.description: A serene Tibetan Buddhist monastery on a garden hill just above Boudhanath, famous worldwide for its meditation retreats and its calm, flower-filled courtyards looking out over the valley. Drop in for the free short guided meditation, watch the young monks debate, or arrange a private introduction to Buddhist practice — a restorative half-day that balances the intensity of the temples below.

items.name: The Garden of Dreams
items.description: A jewel-box neoclassical garden built in the 1920s by a Rana field marshal and lovingly restored with Austrian help — six pavilions for Nepal's six seasons, fountains, pergolas and lawns walled off from the roar of Thamel just outside. The most elegant place in central Kathmandu for a quiet coffee or a book; a genuine oasis for grandparents and children alike.

items.name: Thamel — the buzz, and beyond it
items.description: The pulsing tourist heart of Kathmandu: a lantern-lit maze of trekking-gear shops, pashmina and singing-bowl stores, rooftop cafés and live music. It is loud and energetic rather than luxurious, but an hour with a guide turns it into a rich hunt for the good — hand-knotted carpets, cashmere, thangkas and the best momos in town — while the rest is easily skipped.

items.name: Asan & Indra Chowk bazaars
items.description: The spice-and-textile soul of the old city — Asan is a six-way crossroads market trading everything from saffron and lentils to brass gods, while nearby Indra Chowk is the street of the bead sellers (pote), their stalls a river of coloured glass. Chaotic, fragrant and utterly authentic; walked with a guide it is the finest street-life theatre in the valley, and deeply familiar in rhythm to any Indian eye.

items.name: Narayanhiti Palace Museum
items.description: The former royal palace of the Shah kings, opened to the public after the monarchy fell in 2008 — state rooms, thrones and, most hauntingly, the garden site of the 2001 royal massacre, marked and preserved. A sober, fascinating window into modern Nepal's history, a short walk from the smart shops of Durbar Marg. Photography is not permitted inside; closed Tuesdays and Wednesdays.

items.name: Kirtipur old town
items.area: Kirtipur hill, southwest of the city
items.description: A time-warp Newari hill town of steep brick lanes, weavers at their looms and the twin temples of Bagh Bhairab and Uma Maheshwar, looking out over the whole valley to the Himalaya beyond. Barely touched by mass tourism, it offers the medieval texture of Bhaktapur without the crowds — a quiet favourite for travellers who have already seen the headline squares.

items.name: Pharping & the Asura Cave
items.description: A deeply sacred hillside on the valley's southern edge where the Hindu Dakshinkali temple and a cluster of Tibetan monasteries share the same ridge, centred on the Asura Cave associated with Guru Rinpoche (Padmasambhava). A self-arising Tara image and a self-arising Ganesh draw pilgrims of both faiths; peaceful, powerful and far off the standard circuit.

items.name: Everest mountain flight
items.description: A one-hour dawn flight along the length of the eastern Himalaya, every passenger guaranteed a window seat, that curls up to Everest itself and back — twenty peaks above the wing, the cockpit opened for a photograph of the summit. The single easiest way for grandparents and young children to stand eye-to-eye with the roof of the world. Best booked for clear-sky winter mornings (September to April); operated by Buddha Air and Yeti Airlines.

items.name: Everest helicopter to Kala Patthar
items.description: The ultimate valley-to-mountain day: a private helicopter northeast over Lukla and Tengboche to touch down on Kala Patthar (5,545m) beside Everest Base Camp, then breakfast on the terrace of the Hotel Everest View — the world's highest luxury hotel — with Everest, Lhotse, Nuptse and Ama Dablam filling the sky. Four to five hours door to door; altitude means it suits fit adults rather than the very young or elderly.

items.name: Nagarkot Himalayan sunrise
items.area: Nagarkot ridge, east of the valley
items.description: A ridgetop hill station on the valley's eastern rim famous for its sunrise, when a clear dawn unrolls a long Himalayan panorama — on the finest mornings from Annapurna to Everest — over a sea of cloud. Stay overnight at a view-facing lodge and wake to the whole range turning gold; an easy, high-reward escape barely an hour and a half from the city.

items.name: Dhulikhel & the valley rim villages
items.description: A handsome Newari town on the eastern rim with its own well-preserved temples and one of the best all-round Himalayan viewpoints near the capital, a favourite base for gentle rim walks. Quieter and more lived-in than Nagarkot, it makes a serene overnight for travellers wanting mountains, old streets and a slower pace in one place.

items.name: Namobuddha Monastery
items.description: One of the three holiest Buddhist sites in Nepal, on a hilltop where legend says a prince offered his body to a starving tigress — now crowned by the vast Thrangu Tashi Yangtse monastery and college, home to hundreds of monks. The drive out through terraced hills and a Newari village, and the 360-degree ridgetop view, make it a soulful day-trip, often walked as a gentle hike from Dhulikhel.

items.name: Chandragiri Hills cable car
items.description: A smooth ten-minute cable car glides up to a 2,551m ridge for a sweeping panorama of the valley and, on clear days, the Himalaya from Annapurna toward Everest — no trek required, ideal for multi-generational groups. At the top sit the Bhaleshwor Mahadev Shiva temple, cafés and a resort; a soft-adventure half-day that even the least mobile grandparent can share.

items.name: Krishnarpan at Dwarika's — the Newari feast
items.description: The valley's definitive fine-dining experience: a ceremonial Newari banquet of six to as many as twenty-two courses, served on painted earthenware and brass, opening with the traditional Samaya Baji platter. Set inside Dwarika's — a heritage hotel that is itself a living museum of rescued Newari woodcarving and a UNESCO conservation-award winner — it is deeply vegetarian-friendly and the single most refined table in Kathmandu.

items.name: Momos & the Newari table
items.description: No visit is complete without momos — the steamed dumpling that is Kathmandu's true street food — alongside a proper Newari spread of bara, chatamari (the 'Newari pizza'), yomari and the tang of aloo achar. Almost every dish has a rich vegetarian version, and a guided food walk through the old city, or a private Newari cooking session, is a warm, hands-on window into the valley for the whole family.

items.name: Singing bowls & sound healing
items.description: The valley is the world's home of the Himalayan singing bowl, and the best ateliers around Thamel and Boudha will teach you to read a bowl by its tone or lead a private sound-healing session — resonance you feel in the chest rather than merely hear. A restorative, characterful souvenir and experience in one, and a gentle counterpoint to days of temples.

items.name: Thangka painting ateliers
items.description: In the studios around Boudhanath and Patan, master painters still create thangkas — sacred scroll paintings of deities and mandalas — with single-hair brushes and mineral pigments, some pieces taking months of meditative work. A private studio visit lets a collector understand the iconography and commission a genuinely museum-grade piece, not a tourist print.

items.name: Boudhanath butter-lamp dusk & rooftop dinner
items.description: As evening falls the stupa is ringed with hundreds of flickering butter lamps and the low hum of prayer, and the smart move is a candlelit table on one of the circle's rooftop restaurants looking straight down onto the dome. Among the most atmospheric — and calmest — dinners in the valley, and a fitting close to a day of monasteries.

items.name: Private heritage walk of the old city
items.description: The medieval fabric of Kathmandu lives in the lanes and hidden courtyards (bahals and bahis) between the durbar square and Asan — carved windows, forgotten shrines, artisan alleys that no map quite captures. Walked at dawn with a specialist Newari-culture guide, before the traffic wakes, it is the richest and most personal way to read the city's thousand years.

items.name: Panauti — the hidden Newari town
items.description: A serene, little-visited medieval Newari town at the confluence of two rivers (and a mythical third), its Indreshwar Mahadev temple among the oldest and finest pagodas in Nepal. Untouristed and beautifully intact, with community homestays and gentle riverside walks, it rewards travellers who want the valley's soul away from the crowds.

items.name: Sankhu & the Vajrayogini temple
items.description: One of the valley's oldest Newari towns, at the foot of a forested hill crowned by the golden-roofed Vajrayogini temple, a serene and important tantric shrine reached by a stone stairway through the trees. Deeply atmospheric and almost entirely free of visitors, it is a rewarding half-day for those who have already done the headline sites.

items.name: Shivapuri Nagarjun National Park walk
items.description: A green forested reserve on the valley's northern edge, laced with walking trails to the Shivapuri peak, hidden gompas and viewpoints over the whole basin — birdsong, waterfalls and cool air minutes from the city's dust. A gentle guided nature morning that suits families wanting movement and quiet between the temple days.

items.name: Seto Machhendranath & the old-city processions
items.description: Tucked in a courtyard off the Asan-Indra Chowk axis, this white Avalokiteshvara/Machhendranath temple is one of the most revered in the old city and the focus of a great annual chariot procession beloved of both Hindus and Buddhists. Timed with a guide to a puja or festival, it shows the living, shared devotion that still animates Kathmandu's lanes.

items.name: Boudha & Patan by dawn light for photography
items.description: The valley's monuments are transformed in the first hour of light — the Boudha kora nearly empty, Patan's struts and spires gilded, monks sweeping the courtyards. A private photography-led morning with an expert, before the tour groups arrive, yields both the images and the stillness that the middle of the day cannot.

items.name: Pashupatinath Bagmati Aarti at dusk
items.description: Each evening on the Bagmati's terraces, robed priests perform the aarti — a choreography of fire, lamps, bells and conch, echoing the great river rituals of Varanasi and Haridwar. Watched from the far bank as the ghats glow and the chants rise, it is among the most spiritually charged half-hours in the Himalaya, and speaks straight to the Hindu heart.

items.name: Traditional pashmina & carpet houses
items.description: Nepal is a serious source for hand-knotted Tibetan carpets and genuine pashmina, and the established ateliers — many run by Tibetan refugee cooperatives in Jawalakhel and Patan — let you watch the weaving and buy at the source. A guided visit sorts the real cashmere and hand-knots from the mass-market pashmina of the tourist lanes, a purchase that lasts a generation.

items.name: Krishnarpan
items.description: A ceremonial Nepali feast of six to twenty-two courses, served on brass in Dwarika's carved courtyards — the country's definitive dining occasion.

items.name: Restaurant Tusa
credentials: The New York Times — editorial feature
items.description: Nepal's most ambitious kitchen — a Noma-trained team turning the valley's biodiversity into a seven-course tasting menu.

items.name: The Old House
items.description: Newari heritage cooking given a stylish, contemporary turn, off the city's smartest street.

items.name: Le Sherpa
items.description: A long-running farm-to-table favourite with a leafy garden and a Saturday market that draws the whole city.

items.name: The Dwarika's bar
credentials: Genuine standing — the bar at The Dwarika's Hotel, holder of Nepal's first MICHELIN Key (2025)
items.description: A quiet drink within the carved Newari courtyards of Nepal's most decorated house — the calmest, most considered evening in the city.

items.name: Barc
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Bars 2025 — No. 35 (the first Nepalese bar ever to make the list)
Michter's Art of Hospitality Award 2025 — Asia's 50 Best Bars
items.description: An intimate speakeasy hidden inside an office block — Nepali ingredients, world-class technique, and the finest bar in the country.

items.name: Bitters & Co.
items.description: An airy, high-ceilinged room bringing international cocktail culture to the city — an Old Fashioned served in a smoke-filled box, a clarified milk punch worth the visit.

items.title: Dawn kora at Boudhanath Stupa
items.description: Circle one of the largest stupas in the world with Tibetan pilgrims before the crowds arrive.

items.title: Aarti at Pashupatinath
items.description: The evening river ceremony at Nepal's holiest Shiva temple, on the banks of the Bagmati.

items.title: Mountain flight along the Himalaya
items.description: A one-hour dawn flight brings you eye-level with Everest without a single step of trekking.

items.title: Bhaktapur at first light
items.description: The best-preserved medieval city in the valley, quiet and golden before the day-trippers.

plan.heading: 3 days in Kathmandu, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Kathmandu Durbar Square with a scholar guide — the Hanuman Dhoka palace and the Kumari's house.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Climb to Swayambhunath at a gentle hour for the valley view, then the quiet courtyards of Patan on the way back.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Newari tasting menu at Krishnarpan in Dwarika's Hotel, served across many small ritual courses.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Boudhanath stupa early, walking the kora with pilgrims before the shops open, then tea on a rooftop above it.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Pashupatinath along the Bagmati with a guide, unhurried and respectful, then rest.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Dwarika's courtyard among its salvaged Newari woodwork, or a quiet table at the Hyatt Regency.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Bhaktapur's Durbar Square and potters' square, the best-preserved of the three medieval cities.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A thangka studio and a Mustang-wool workshop, choosing pieces with time to talk to the makers.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A last dinner at Bhojan Griha in a restored Rana-era mansion, with folk music kept low.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Patan (Lalitpur)
items.description: Artisan quarter with the finest Durbar Square; calm and cultured, the connoisseur's base.

items.name: Boudhanath
items.description: Around the great stupa; peaceful, Tibetan in feel, good for a contemplative stay.

items.name: Thamel
items.description: The backpacker and trekking-gear hub — convenient but loud; better for logistics than lodging.

events.name: Indra Jatra
events.note: Eight days of masked deity dances and the Kumari chariot procession around Kathmandu Durbar Square.

events.name: Dashain
events.note: Nepal's longest and most auspicious festival; the country empties home, so plan logistics carefully.

events.name: Tihar
events.note: The five-day festival of lights; homes and streets glow with oil lamps and marigold.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Land at Tribhuvan International (KTM); the airport is dated and busy, so a pre-arranged hotel representative to meet you airside and a private car for the short transfer into the valley make all the difference.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Move by private car and driver — the old city and Patan are best explored on foot with a guide, while the driver waits, as streets are narrow, unsigned and congested.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: An Ncell or NTC eSIM covers the valley well on 4G; wifi is fine in good hotels but assume patchy power and keep devices charged.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Nepalese rupee (NPR); cash is king outside top hotels, ATMs are plentiful in Thamel, and a small tip (5–10 percent) is appreciated but not assumed.

onGround.note: Stay in leafy Lazimpat or a heritage property in Patan rather than backpacker Thamel; the valley sits at 1,400 m so acclimatisation is minor, but if you continue to the mountains build in a rest day, and dress conservatively at temples and remove leather at Hindu shrines.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: October to November is the finest window, with clear skies and Himalayan views after the monsoon; March to April is a warm second-best with rhododendron bloom. Avoid the June to September monsoon (rain, cloud, obscured peaks) and the cold, hazy December-January.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi (~1h40m) on Air India, IndiGo and Nepal Airlines; from Mumbai and Bengaluru it is usually one-stop via Delhi. Air India and IndiGo carry business/premium cabins on the Delhi leg. It is a short hop, so private charter to remote lodges or Everest-view flights are the real luxury add-on.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations; routine jabs plus Hep A and Typhoid advised. The city sits at ~1,350m, so no altitude concern in Kathmandu itself, but treks above 2,500m need proper acclimatisation. Drink bottled water; air quality can be poor in winter. Safe with normal precautions.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Outstanding for vegetarians and very manageable for Jain travellers, given Nepal's own vegetarian traditions and a large Indian community. Excellent pure-veg and Indian at OR2K and Places Restaurant, and premium hotels handle Jain requests reliably.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Kathmandu, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Kochi — TripAgent
seo.description: Kochi, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Kochi
hero.tagline: Spice-trade port where colonial Kerala meets the sea.

ourTake.lede: Kochi is the most walkable and cosmopolitan corner of Kerala, and Fort Kochi deserves a slow two days on foot rather than a rushed stopover before the backwaters. Time your first evening for the Chinese fishing nets at sunset, but spend the days in the spice-trade lanes, the churches and synagogue, and the excellent contemporary art spaces. It is a good soft landing before or after the houseboats.
ourTake.comeIf: You want Kerala's history and harbour life as a gentle gateway to the backwaters.
ourTake.skipIf: You want nightlife or a beach holiday; this is a quiet, cultural port town.

firstLook.heroCaption: Modern pool villa with palms and umbrella

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: October to March is dry and pleasant, with the Biennale and Cochin Carnival crowning winter; avoid the heavy June-September monsoon downpours.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Kochi. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Brunton Boatyard
credentials: CGH Earth heritage hotel — leased from the Port Trust 1992, opened 1999
26 rooms, all harbour-facing, on the site of the original Brunton boatyard
History restaurant — dishes from the 32 communities of Fort Kochi
items.description: CGH Earth's heritage flagship on a 19th-century colonial boatyard — every one of its 26 rooms faces the harbour and the Chinese fishing nets.

items.name: The Malabar House
credentials: Relais & Châteaux — the first Indian member (accepted 1997)
Fort Kochi's original boutique heritage hotel
Home to The Malabar Junction, its Relais & Châteaux restaurant
items.description: The first Indian hotel accepted into Relais & Châteaux — an 18th-century mansion turned art-filled boutique of just 17 rooms.

items.name: Taj Malabar Resort & Spa, Cochin
credentials: Taj Hotels / IHCL — heritage wing built 1935, reopened after a year-long 2024 renovation
93 rooms and suites with waterfront views
Rice Boat — celebrated Kerala coastal-seafood restaurant
items.description: Cochin's grand harbour hotel since 1935 — a 2024-renovated Taj wrapping Ernakulam's waterfront, with an infinity pool over the backwaters.

items.name: Grand Hyatt Kochi Bolgatty
credentials: Hyatt — Grand Hyatt, 264 rooms including suites and four plunge-pool villas
Santata Spa — 1,000+ sq m, Ayurvedic and Western therapies
items.description: The city's largest luxury resort — 264 rooms on 26 waterfront acres of Bolgatty Island, with villas that have private plunge pools.

items.name: Old Harbour Hotel
credentials: Heritage mansion, ~300 years old — the first hotel of old Cochin
13 rooms, each named for a Fort Kochi street
Restaurant 1788 — seafood-led, with classical music at dinner
items.description: A 300-year-old Dutch-Portuguese mansion, Fort Kochi's first hotel — 13 characterful rooms around a garden and pool.

items.name: Xandari Harbour
credentials: Housed in two ~century-old wharf spice warehouses
16 rooms with harbour or garden views
Restaurant 51 — farm-to-table Malabar cuisine with a riverside balcony
items.description: Two century-old spice warehouses reborn as a 16-room boutique — an infinity pool and courtyard opening straight onto the water.

items.name: Forte Kochi
credentials: Paul John Resorts & Hotels — heritage boutique on Princess Street
Portuguese-Dutch-British mansion, once a Jewish family home
27 rooms; walking distance to the fishing nets and Mahatma Gandhi Beach
items.description: A Portuguese-era mansion on Princess Street, restored by Paul John into a 27-room heritage boutique in the heart of the fort.

items.name: Kayal Island Retreat
credentials: National Geographic — 'Around the World in 24 Hours' (the only Indian entry), for the Kakkathuruthu sunset
Condé Nast Traveller recognition — lakeside boutique
Four cottages on a private backwater island; reached by traditional rowboat
items.description: A four-cottage island hideaway on Vembanad Lake, reached only by rowboat — the sunset Nat Geo named one of the world's best.

items.name: The Chinese Fishing Nets (Cheena Vala)
items.description: The cantilevered shore-operated nets along the Fort Kochi waterfront are the city's signature image — teak-and-bamboo frames worked by teams of fishermen, thought to have arrived with traders from Kublai Khan's court centuries ago. Come at dusk when the light drops behind the harbour mouth and the silhouettes are at their most cinematic; the freshest catch is grilled to order at the stalls right beside them.

items.name: St Francis Church
items.description: The oldest European-built church in India, put up by Portuguese friars in the early 1500s, and the spot where Vasco da Gama was first buried before his remains were taken to Lisbon — his gravestone is still set in the floor. A cool, spare, whitewashed interior with old punkah cloth-fans overhead; a quiet ten minutes of deep history off Fort Kochi's main green.

items.name: Santa Cruz Cathedral Basilica
items.description: One of only a handful of basilicas in Kerala — twin white spires outside, and inside a ceiling of pastel frescoes and Gothic arches that feel more Iberian than Indian. It stands beside St Francis Church, so the two make a natural pairing on a slow morning walk through the old quarter.

items.name: A Fort Kochi Heritage Walk
items.description: The whole peninsula is really an open-air museum of Portuguese, Dutch and British layers — bungalows with wooden verandahs, godowns, cemeteries and coir-scented lanes. A guided morning walk (or an unhurried self-led wander from Vasco da Gama Square down the parade ground) is the best way to read the town; heritage stays like Malabar House and Brunton Boatyard sit right in the thick of it.

items.name: Vasco da Gama Square & the parade ground
items.description: The narrow seafront promenade beside the fishing nets, lined with fresh-catch stalls, tender-coconut carts and ice-cream sellers, opening onto the old colonial parade ground. It is where Fort Kochi comes out to watch the sunset — an easy, atmospheric stroll before dinner at one of the heritage-hotel terraces.

items.name: Princess Street & Loafer's Corner
items.description: One of the oldest streets in Fort Kochi, a run of bronze-plastered European houses now given over to curio shops, cafes and small galleries, meeting at Loafer's Corner where Princess, Peter Celli and Bastion Streets converge under a balconied heritage building. The most walkable, photogenic stretch for browsing and a slow coffee.

items.name: Indo-Portuguese Museum
items.description: Set in the grounds of the Bishop's House, this small, well-kept museum gathers altarpieces, vestments, carved wood and silver from Kerala's Latin Catholic churches — the clearest single account of the Portuguese imprint on the coast. Quiet, air-conditioned and rarely crowded, an easy hour between the churches.

items.name: The Mattancherry (Dutch) Palace & its murals
items.description: Built for the Kochi rajas in the mid-1500s and reworked by the Dutch, its plain exterior hides some of the finest temple murals in India — dense, glowing panels of the Ramayana and Mahabharata covering the royal chambers. Photography is barred inside, which only sharpens the attention; the coronation hall and palanquins evoke the old spice-port court.

items.name: The Paradesi Synagogue
items.description: India's oldest active synagogue, from 1568, its floor laid with hand-painted blue-and-white Chinese tiles no two of which are alike, hung with Belgian glass lamps and fronted by a Dutch clock tower whose four faces carry Hebrew, Roman, Malayalam and Arabic numerals. A moving relic of Kochi's near-vanished Malabari and Paradesi Jewish community. Closed Fridays, Saturdays and Jewish holidays.

items.name: Jew Town & the antiques quarter
items.description: The lanes leading to the synagogue are a treasure hunt of dealers — rosewood cabinets, brass and bronze, old maps, temple lamps, nautical instruments and colonial curios, alongside spice-scented cafes. Serious collectors ship home genuine restored pieces; browsers get one of the most characterful shopping walks in India.

items.name: The Mattancherry spice markets
items.description: The godowns and open shopfronts behind Jew Town still trade Kerala's pepper, cardamom, cloves, ginger and turmeric — the very commerce that drew the Portuguese and Dutch here five centuries ago. The air is thick with it; buy graded whole spices at source, far better than anything back home.

items.name: A Kathakali performance
items.description: Kerala's dance-drama of green-and-crimson painted faces, elaborate costume and a whole language of eye and hand gestures. The best centres let you arrive early to watch the hour-long make-up ritual, then narrate the story before the show so it never feels opaque — a genuinely spellbinding evening, and children are often riveted.

items.name: A Kalaripayattu demonstration
items.description: Kerala's ancient martial art — thought to be among the oldest in the world — all low stances, high leaps, and combat with staff, sword and shield, performed in a sunken earthen arena. Fast, athletic and thrilling to watch up close; several Fort Kochi venues stage an evening show alongside Kathakali.

items.name: The Kerala Folklore Museum
items.description: A private labour of love built by an antique dealer, its three floors reconstructed in Malabar, Kochi and Travancore styles from salvaged old buildings, holding thousands of masks, sculptures, jewellery, ritual objects and terracotta. The top-floor theatre, under an 18th-century carved wooden ceiling, is one of the most beautiful rooms in the city.

items.name: The Hill Palace Museum
items.description: The former seat of the Cochin royal family — a cluster of buildings across a wooded hilltop, now Kerala's largest archaeological museum, with the royal crowns, jewellery, palanquins, weapons, coins and a family tree of the maharajas. Deer park and gardens make it an easy, uncrowded half-day slightly out of town.

items.name: Marine Drive promenade
items.description: The mainland's breezy waterfront walkway facing the harbour and the islands, with the Rainbow and Chinese-net-shaped footbridges, ferry jetties and evening food carts. The go-to spot for sunset on the Ernakulam side and to catch a public ferry across to Fort Kochi or Vypin — cheap, breezy and local.

items.name: A Kochi harbour & backwater sunset cruise
items.description: A late-afternoon boat out across the harbour mouth, past Willingdon and Bolgatty islands, the naval ships and the fishing-net line, timed for the sun going down over the Arabian Sea. Public ferries do it for a few rupees; a chartered or houseboat sundowner does it in privacy with a drink in hand.

items.name: The Ernakulathappan (Ernakulam Shiva) Temple
items.description: The city temple that gives Ernakulam its name, on Durbar Hall Road near the waterfront, its Shiva idol held to be swayambhu (self-manifested). A working temple at the centre of town, especially alive during the eight-day Utsavam festival with its caparisoned elephants. (Traditional dress; non-Hindus should check entry etiquette.)

items.name: David Hall gallery & cafe
items.description: A restored 17th-century Dutch bungalow on the Parade Ground, run as a contemporary art gallery with a leafy garden cafe — one of the anchors of Kochi's living art scene and a recurring Biennale venue. A civilised place to pause over coffee between exhibitions.

items.name: Kashi Art Cafe & Gallery
items.description: The artsy heart of Fort Kochi since the 1990s — a Dutch-era house that is equal parts gallery and much-loved cafe, a hub for the town's painters, curators and the Biennale crowd. Come for the rotating shows and stay for the courtyard breakfast.

items.name: The Kochi-Muziris Biennale (seasonal)
items.description: India's largest contemporary-art event, held every couple of years across the old spice warehouses of Fort Kochi, Mattancherry and Willingdon Island — Aspinwall House, Pepper House, Anand Warehouse and more. The sixth edition, 'For The Time Being', runs December 2025 to March 2026; if your dates align it transforms the whole town into a walkable exhibition.

items.name: Aspinwall House
items.description: A sprawling waterfront former trading-company estate — coir godowns, a bungalow and a jetty right on the harbour — and the flagship venue of the Biennale. Even between editions the scale and the sea-facing grounds are worth the walk; in season it holds the headline installations.

items.name: Bolgatty Palace & island
items.description: A 1744 Dutch garden mansion on its own island in the harbour — reckoned among the oldest surviving Dutch palaces outside the Netherlands — now a KTDC heritage hotel with a small golf course, pool and lawns running to the water. A short ferry hop for a lunch or a drink with a straight view back to the city skyline.

items.name: Willingdon Island
items.description: A British-era man-made island built from harbour dredgings, named for a viceroy, and still home to the port, the Southern Naval Command and grand old dame hotels. More a texture of Kochi than a ticked sight — but the waterside setting and the Taj Malabar's harbour-facing terrace make a fine, quiet sundowner.

items.name: Vypin Island
items.description: One of the string of islands that make up Kochi, reached by a two-minute ferry from Fort Kochi and worth it for the drive out to Cherai, the old Portuguese Pallipuram Fort and the sea-and-backwater strip. Rural, breezy and a world away from the town in minutes.

items.name: Cherai Beach
items.description: A long, calm golden strand on the northern tip of Vypin where the Arabian Sea and the backwaters run almost side by side — palm-fringed, good for a swim, with dolphins sometimes offshore. About an hour from the centre; the least touristed easy beach day from Kochi and lovely at sundown.

items.name: Pallipuram Fort
credentials: Oldest surviving European fort in India (built 1503)
items.description: The oldest surviving European fort in India, a small hexagonal Portuguese watchtower from 1503 on the northern tip of Vypin. It is a modest, off-the-map stop, but for anyone tracing the coast's colonial history it is the literal starting point — and it pairs naturally with Cherai just down the road.

items.name: Mangalavanam Bird Sanctuary
items.description: A pocket of protected mangrove wetland tucked improbably behind the High Court in the middle of the city — the 'green lung of Kochi', with a walking trail and a watchtower for egrets, herons, cormorants and migratory waders. A surprising, cool, ten-minute escape from downtown for anyone who likes birds.

items.name: An Ayurveda treatment
items.description: Kerala is the home of Ayurveda, and Kochi is where most trips begin it — from a single restorative abhyanga oil massage or shirodhara at a Fort Kochi spa to a multi-day panchakarma programme at a dedicated centre. A natural, unforced way to slow the pace, especially at the start or end of a wider Kerala loop.

items.name: A spice-garden & plantation experience
items.description: Hands-on visits to working spice gardens and cooking sessions let you follow pepper, cardamom, cinnamon and vanilla from vine to kitchen, then cook a Kerala meal — the coastal vegetarian and seafood layers, from appam and stew to the Syrian-Christian and Mappila kitchens. A rich, tactile afternoon and easy to arrange for a family.

items.name: Fort Kochi's colonial cemeteries & Dutch Cemetery
items.description: The walled Dutch Cemetery near the beach — consecrated in 1724, among the oldest European cemeteries in India — with weathered tombs of the traders and soldiers who died far from home. A quiet, atmospheric ten minutes for anyone drawn to the human side of the town's layered history.

items.name: Munnar & the tea estates (day trip / overnight)
credentials: Western Ghats — UNESCO World Heritage Site (natural)
items.description: About four hours up into the hills, a sea of manicured tea gardens rolling over the ridges, with the old Tata tea museum, misty viewpoints and cool mountain air — a complete change of register from the coast. The high ranges here sit within the Western Ghats, and it rewards an overnight far more than a rushed day.

items.name: An Alleppey backwater houseboat
items.description: The classic Kerala experience — a converted kettuvallam rice barge drifting the palm-lined canals and lagoons of Vembanad, meals cooked aboard, the day slipping by from the deck. About 90 minutes south of Kochi; a private overnight houseboat is one of the most peaceful, self-contained luxuries in India, ideal for couples or a family who want the water to themselves.

items.name: Kumarakom backwaters & bird sanctuary
items.description: The quieter, more polished side of Lake Vembanad — a cluster of luxury backwater resorts and a small ornithological sanctuary on former estate land, with egrets, herons, darters and winter migrants. Calmer and greener than Alleppey; a fine base for a slow lakeside couple of days and a village canoe ride.

items.name: Athirappilly Falls (day trip)
items.description: Kerala's largest waterfall — a broad curtain plunging some 80 feet through rainforest, often called the 'Niagara of India' and a much-filmed backdrop. About two hours from Kochi, thunderous just after the monsoon; combine it with the smaller Vazhachal falls and the forest drive for a full day out.

items.name: Thattekad Bird Sanctuary (day trip)
items.description: Salim Ali's favourite birding ground, a lowland-forest sanctuary on the Periyar with an exceptional density of species — Malabar endemics, hornbills, owls and kingfishers among hundreds recorded. Around two hours out; a dawn walk with a local guide is the way to do it, a serious draw for keen birders.

items.name: The Muziris Heritage Trail
items.description: A cluster of sites around the lost 2,000-year-old Roman-trade port of Muziris — the Pattanam excavations, the Paravur synagogue and Jew Street, Kottappuram and Pallipuram forts, old churches and mosques, several turned into small museums. For the historically curious it is the deep back-story of the whole Malabar spice coast, an easy self-driven day north of the city.

items.name: Guruvayur Sri Krishna Temple (day trip)
items.description: One of the most revered Krishna temples in India, about 90 minutes to two hours north, a major Vaishnavite pilgrimage centre famous for its temple elephants and its steady flow of devotees. A meaningful stop for the observant; note it is open to Hindus only, with a traditional dress code.

items.name: Thrissur & the Vadakkunnathan Temple (day trip)
items.description: Kerala's cultural capital, about 75 km north, built around the ancient hilltop Vadakkunnathan Shiva temple — a superb example of Kerala's tiered wooden temple architecture — and home to the spectacular Thrissur Pooram elephant festival each spring. The temple interior is open to Hindus only, but the mound, the grounds and the town's museums reward the trip.

items.name: Chottanikkara Bhagavathy Temple (day trip)
items.description: A famous Devi temple about 20 km from the city where the goddess is worshipped in three forms across the day — Saraswati at dawn, Lakshmi at noon, Durga at dusk — drawing pilgrims from across the south. An atmospheric, deeply local temple visit close enough to fold into a half-day. (Traditional dress; open to Hindus.)

items.name: Broadway Market
items.description: Ernakulam's dense old bazaar street — spices, textiles, gold, provisions and Kerala snacks sold cheek by jowl, the mainland counterpoint to Fort Kochi's polish. A vivid, unvarnished slice of everyday Kochi commerce and the best place to pick up graded spices and coir on the city side.

items.name: A Kerala cooking & appam breakfast experience
items.description: Kochi is the gateway to Kerala's food — lace-edged appam with vegetable stew, Syrian-Christian and Mappila dishes, Fort Kochi's fish grilled fresh from the nets, and one of India's most vegetarian-friendly coastlines besides. A home-kitchen class or a guided food walk turns a meal into the trip's most memorable afternoon.

items.name: A country-boat village backwater trip
items.description: For the backwaters without the drive south, small dugout canoes thread the narrow canals and coir-making villages just outside the city — quieter and more intimate than a big houseboat, gliding under low palms past paddy and toddy shops. A gentle half-day, especially good with children or grandparents.

items.name: Cochin Club & the Fort Kochi green
items.description: The old British-era Cochin Club and the wide parade-ground green behind the seafront — cricket on the grass, rain trees, and the genteel bones of colonial club life still intact. Not a ticketed sight but the calmest corner of Fort Kochi for a stroll and a sense of how the town once lived.

items.name: The Malabar Junction
credentials: Relais & Châteaux restaurant, at The Malabar House
Carnatic / Hindustani music or classical dance at dinner (cooler months)
items.description: Fort Kochi's Relais & Châteaux table — Keralan produce and Mediterranean technique, served to courtyard music.

items.name: Rice Boat
credentials: Taj Malabar Resort & Spa — its signature restaurant
Long-renowned for Kerala coastal and seafood cooking
items.description: The Taj's celebrated Kerala seafood room, shaped like a traditional rice barge over the harbour water.

items.name: History
credentials: Signature restaurant at Brunton Boatyard (CGH Earth)
Menu built from the recipes of Fort Kochi's 32 historic communities
items.description: CGH Earth's storytelling kitchen — dishes drawn from the 32 communities who made Fort Kochi, from Syrian Christian to Jewish to Dutch.

items.name: Kashi Art Café
credentials: Established 1997 — a pioneering Kochi art-café institution
Kochi-Muziris Biennale patron, with a working front gallery
items.description: The café that launched Fort Kochi's art scene in 1997 — coffee, cake and a gallery, a Biennale patron since the start.

items.name: Fort House Restaurant
credentials: Waterfront pier-side restaurant on the Fort Kochi harbour
items.description: An open-air deck on the harbour pier — charcoal-grilled seafood with big ships passing on their way to sea.

items.name: Dal Roti
credentials: A long-standing Fort Kochi institution on Lily Street
items.description: A beloved heritage-house institution for North Indian rolls and thalis — Lonely Planet's Fort Kochi favourite.

items.name: Qissa Café
credentials: Artist-run in spirit — paintings on the walls, an unhurried room
items.description: A quiet, art-hung café in the fort — good coffee, breakfast and sandwiches, named for the Persian word for 'story'.

items.name: The bar at Brunton Boatyard
credentials: Inside Brunton Boatyard (CGH Earth), on the Fort Kochi harbourfront
Heritage-hotel setting overlooking the water and the fishing nets
items.description: A composed harbour-side drink at CGH Earth's heritage flagship — the most atmospheric evening in Fort Kochi.

items.name: Mattancherry Bar, Taj Malabar
credentials: Inside Taj Malabar Resort & Spa, Cochin
items.description: The city's most polished cocktail room — Taj standards and harbour views on Willingdon Island.

items.name: Fort Kochi rooftop cafés
credentials: Rooftop cafés across the Fort Kochi heritage quarter
The definitive Fort Kochi evening — sunset over the harbour and Chinese fishing nets
items.description: Not bars but the fort's real evening — coffee or a sundowner on a heritage rooftop as the light goes over the harbour and the nets.

items.title: Private heritage walk of Fort Kochi and Mattancherry
items.description: A historian-led morning through the Portuguese, Dutch and Jewish quarters, ending at the Paradesi Synagogue.

items.title: Private Kathakali or Kalaripayattu performance
items.description: An intimate viewing of Kerala's classical dance-drama or its ancient martial art, with the make-up ritual explained.

items.title: Chef's table of coastal Malabar and Syrian-Christian cuisine
items.description: A curated meal of the region's layered spice cooking, from meen curry to Nasrani specialities.

items.title: Private day into the backwaters from the city
items.description: A tailored houseboat or country-boat excursion into the quieter canals of the Vembanad system.
