plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Check into Brunton Boatyard on the harbour, then walk the Chinese fishing nets and St Francis Church before the day heats up.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Mattancherry Palace murals and the Paradesi Synagogue on Jew Town's Synagogue Lane, ending among the antique dealers.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A Kathakali performance at the Kerala Kathakali Centre, arriving early for the make-up, then dinner of Kerala prawns at the Rice Boat.

days.title: Spice history and the backwater edge

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The spice warehouses and pepper exchange of Mattancherry with a trader who knows the trade's history, then coffee at a colonial-era godown.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A private country-boat afternoon through the quieter Kumbalangi canals, seeing the coir-making and Chinese nets away from the crowds.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Sundowners on the Brunton Boatyard verandah over the harbour, then a seafood dinner cooked to your catch.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The galleries and installations of the Kochi-Muziris Biennale trail around Aspinwall House and Pepper House, unhurried.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Cross to Ernakulam for a tailored Kerala Sadhya lunch, then the boutiques and coffee of the newer town.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A quiet last dinner at Malabar Junction in the Malabar House courtyard.

items.name: Fort Kochi
items.description: The atmospheric heritage peninsula of boutique stays and cafes; best for walking and art.

items.name: Mattancherry
items.description: The spice-trade and antiques quarter next door; suits those who want texture and history.

items.name: Marine Drive / Ernakulam
items.description: The modern city across the water; for shopping, dining and transport links rather than heritage.

events.name: Cochin Carnival
events.note: A ten-day Fort Kochi street festival ending on New Year's Eve with the burning of the Pappanji effigy.

events.name: Kochi-Muziris Biennale
events.note: India's leading contemporary-art event, staged in warehouses and heritage buildings across the fort.

events.name: Onam
events.note: Kerala's grand harvest festival, with flower carpets, feasts and boat races across the region.

events.name: Thrissur Pooram (nearby)
events.note: The spectacular caparisoned-elephant temple festival is a short trip north, among India's grandest.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Cochin International Airport (COK), about an hour's chauffeured drive to Fort Kochi; the airport is solar-run and unhurried.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with driver for the mainland, and country-boat or ferry crossings between the islands and Fort Kochi, where walking suits the Dutch and Portuguese quarters.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Reliable Jio and Airtel 4G/5G throughout; a local SIM from the airport covers you across Kerala.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Indian rupee; cards are widely accepted in Fort Kochi and Ernakulam, with cash useful for spice markets and ferries; tipping is light.

onGround.note: Base yourself in a Fort Kochi heritage house rather than the commercial Ernakulam side; light linen and closed shoes suit the humidity, and the Chinese fishing nets are best at first light or sunset.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: November to February is the kind season, dry with 17-30C days; avoid June-September, when the southwest monsoon hits this windward coast hard, and the humid March-May heat.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Cochin International (COK) is well-connected: direct from Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru (about 3, 2 and 1.5 hrs), plus Gulf hubs. IndiGo, Air India and Akasa fly it; for business/first, route via a Gulf carrier (Emirates through Dubai) or use a flagship lounge at your metro origin, as COK's lounges are modest.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No special vaccinations beyond routine Hepatitis A/Typhoid; mosquito cover is sensible in the wet months. Safe, easy port city. Drink sealed or filtered water and be mindful of humidity.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Very easy for vegetarians, with Kerala sadya (banana-leaf thali) and abundant South Indian food; Jain is understood in the better hotels and restaurants. Kashi Art Cafe and the veg sadya at Fort Kochi's heritage tables are genuinely good.

seo.title: Kolkata — TripAgent
seo.description: Kolkata, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Kolkata
hero.tagline: Colonial grandeur, Bengali arts and unhurried intellectual soul.

ourTake.lede: Kolkata is India's most literary and soulful big city, and it rewards walking, conversation and coffee-house afternoons more than any monument checklist. Do the colonial core and the north-Kolkata lanes with a good guide, give real time to the food and the sweet shops, and, if you possibly can, time your visit to Durga Puja. Skip the rush; the city's pleasure is in lingering.
ourTake.comeIf: You want the most literary, coffee-house city in India and its extraordinary food.
ourTake.skipIf: You want polish, beaches or nightlife.

firstLook.heroCaption: Modern pool villa with palms and umbrella

Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: The cool, dry winter from November to February is the city at its finest, crowned by October's Durga Puja; sidestep the sticky summer and the July-to-September monsoon.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Kolkata. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: The Oberoi Grand, Kolkata
credentials: Forbes Traveler 400 — Best Hotels & Resorts in the World (2008, 2009)
INTACH Blue Cultural Plaque (2024) — heritage recognition as the 'Grande Dame of Chowringhee'
items.description: The 'Grande Dame of Chowringhee' — a colonnaded 1880s landmark and the definitive luxury address in the city for over a century.

items.name: Taj Bengal, Kolkata
credentials: National Tourism Award — Best Luxury Hotel, Eastern Region (1998)
IHCL / Taj Hotels — recognised at Condé Nast Traveller Readers' Travel Awards (group)
items.description: The Taj's leafy Alipore flagship since 1989 — a grand atrium house in the city's most gracious residential quarter.

items.name: ITC Royal Bengal, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Kolkata
credentials: BW Hotelier Indian Hospitality Awards 2025 — General Manager, Luxury (East)
items.description: A vast LEED-Platinum modern palace and the newest apex hotel in the city — Bengal grandeur at scale.

items.name: JW Marriott Hotel Kolkata
items.area: CBD-adjacent (JBS Haldane Avenue, near Science City)
credentials: Marriott JW Marriott brand — luxury tier
items.description: A polished contemporary JW with a striking infinity pool — the sharp business-and-wedding house on the eastern flank.

items.name: The Park Kolkata
credentials: Travel + Leisure India — Best Business Hotel in India (2020)
The Park Hotels — India's pioneering boutique-design group
items.description: India's original design hotel and the beating heart of Park Street nightlife — four bars and clubs under one roof.

items.name: ITC Sonar, Kolkata
credentials: Houses West View & Dum Pukht Kolkata — ITC signature dining
items.description: A garden-and-water resort within the city — lagoon-set lawns, a celebrated spa, and one of India's greenest luxury hotels.

items.name: Taj Taj City Centre New Town, Kolkata
items.area: New Town / Rajarhat (near the airport & IT corridor)
credentials: IHCL / Taj Hotels — luxury group standing
items.description: A crisp, contemporary Taj beside the New Town business district — the practical modern-Taj option near the airport.

items.name: Victoria Memorial Hall
items.description: The great white Makrana-marble monument the British raised to their Empress, its Indo-Saracenic dome floating above the Maidan's lawns. Twenty-five galleries hold the finest collection of Raj-era paintings and Kolkata's own history; come at dusk when it glows and the reflecting pools double it.

items.name: The Maidan
items.description: Kolkata's vast green lung, a mile of parkland running from Fort William to Park Street where the whole city comes to breathe, jog, play cricket and fly kites. A morning walk here, past grazing horses and hand-pulled tea sellers, is the truest way to feel the city's rhythm.

items.name: St Paul's Cathedral
items.description: The first purpose-built Anglican cathedral in Asia, all soaring Gothic Revival white and stained glass by Burne-Jones. A cool, hushed contrast a two-minute walk from the Victoria Memorial, and a lovely place to sit for a moment away from the heat.

items.name: Indian Museum
items.description: The oldest and largest museum in India, founded in 1814, a colonnaded treasure house of Gandhara sculpture, the Bharhut stupa railings, Egyptian mummies and Mughal miniatures. The building itself, wrapped around a grand courtyard, is worth the visit for architecture lovers travelling with children.

items.name: Howrah Bridge (Rabindra Setu)
items.description: The steel cantilever colossus that has carried Kolkata across the Hooghly since 1943, one of the busiest bridges on earth and the city's defining silhouette. Best seen at first light from the Mullick Ghat flower market beneath it, where garlands pile up in colour.

items.name: Hooghly River cruise
items.description: A slow boat down the Hooghly threads together the ghats, the two great bridges, Belur Math and the colonial river frontage in one unhurried afternoon. Sunset sailings with tea and Bengali snacks are the most civilised way to watch the city's skyline turn gold.

items.name: Marble Palace
items.description: A private 1835 mansion of a Bengali aristocrat, packed floor to ceiling with Italian marble, Belgian chandeliers, Rubens and Reynolds canvases and a menagerie in its garden. Still owned by the Mullick family; a permit and a guide are needed, which keeps it wonderfully untouristed.

items.name: Kumartuli idol-makers' quarter
items.description: The warren of riverside workshops where generations of sculptors shape the clay Durga and Kali idols for the whole city's festivals. In the weeks before Durga Puja the lanes are thick with straw armatures and wet earth; a photographer's dream and a living craft, not a museum.

items.name: Kalighat Kali Temple
items.description: The 19th-century shrine that gave Calcutta its name, one of the 51 Shakti Peethas and the spiritual heart of the city's devotion to the goddess. Intense, crowded and deeply alive; a guide will help you navigate the queues and understand what you are seeing.

items.name: Dakshineswar Kali Temple
items.description: Rani Rashmoni's grand nine-spired temple on the Hooghly, where the mystic Ramakrishna served as priest and had his visions. The riverside setting and the twelve Shiva shrines along the bank make it far more serene than Kalighat; note that phones and cameras are not allowed inside.

items.name: Belur Math
items.description: The riverside headquarters of the Ramakrishna Mission, whose extraordinary temple deliberately fuses Hindu, Islamic, Buddhist and Christian architecture into one form. The vast, calm gardens on the Hooghly are among the most peaceful spaces near the city; pair it by ferry with Dakshineswar opposite.

items.name: Mother House (Missionaries of Charity)
items.description: The simple headquarters of Mother Teresa's order, where her plain tomb and small museum room draw quiet pilgrims from across the world. An unadorned, moving stop that puts the city's charitable spirit in front of you.

items.name: College Street book bazaar (Boi Para)
items.description: A kilometre of pavement stacked with new, old and rare books, said to be the largest second-hand book market in the world and the intellectual soul of Bengal. Browse for a first edition, then do as the students do and disappear into the coffee house for adda.

items.name: Indian Coffee House, College Street
items.description: The high-ceilinged, faded hall where poets, filmmakers and revolutionaries have argued over infinite cups since the 1940s, the very cradle of Bengali adda. The coffee is ordinary and the conversation is the point; sit under the fans and let time slow.

items.name: Park Street
items.description: Kolkata's grand old boulevard of jazz, cabarets and legendary restaurants, still lined with institutions like Flurys, Trincas and Mocambo. It blazes with lights at Christmas and stays the city's most nostalgic address for a long, unhurried dinner.

items.name: South Park Street Cemetery
items.description: A hauntingly beautiful garden of 1,600 crumbling Georgian tombs, obelisks and pyramids overgrown with roots, one of the oldest non-church European cemeteries anywhere. An atmospheric, photogenic hour reading the epitaphs of the young Britons who never made it home.

items.name: BBD Bagh (Dalhousie Square) colonial core
items.description: The old imperial heart, where the East India Company ran an empire from a square of magnificent buildings around a central tank. Walk it slowly to read Kolkata as the second city of the British Empire, block by grand block.

items.name: Writers' Building
items.description: The long red pile that housed the clerks ('writers') of the East India Company and later the seat of Bengal's government, its facade one of the most recognisable in the city. Best admired from the square outside, a monument to Company rule.

items.name: General Post Office (GPO)
items.description: A soaring domed rotunda on the site of the original Fort William, marking the very spot of the infamous Black Hole of Calcutta. Its Corinthian columns and philatelic museum make it a rewarding pause on any Dalhousie heritage walk.

items.name: Town Hall (Kolkata)
items.description: A restored Roman-Doric grand hall of 1813, now home to an engaging museum on the city's own story told through light, sound and models. A polished, air-conditioned introduction to Kolkata's history for a first-time or multi-generation visit.

items.name: Prinsep Ghat
items.description: A graceful Palladian riverside pavilion of 1841 beneath the Vidyasagar Setu cable-stayed bridge, and the prettiest stretch of Kolkata's waterfront. Come for the sunset, a short boat ride, and the promenade that fills with families in the cool of the evening.

items.name: Eden Gardens & Test cricket
items.description: One of the oldest and most storied cricket grounds on earth, a cauldron of 65,000 voices when India play under lights. Even on a quiet day the ground carries the weight of legendary matches; catching a fixture here is a bucket-list experience for the cricket-loving family.

items.name: New Market (Hogg Market)
items.description: The rambling Victorian covered bazaar of 1874, a labyrinth of over 2,000 stalls selling everything from cheese and cold cuts to fabric, flowers and silver. Nahoum's, the century-old Jewish bakery inside, is the reason many still make the pilgrimage.

items.name: Tiretti Bazaar Chinese breakfast
items.description: At dawn on the lanes of old Chinatown, the last families of Kolkata's Chinese community sell momos, pork buns, fish-ball soup and rice-noodle rolls from steaming carts. A vanishing ritual worth setting an early alarm for; go on a Sunday when it is busiest.

items.name: Jorasanko Thakur Bari (Tagore House)
items.description: The rambling ancestral mansion where Rabindranath Tagore was born, wrote much of his work and died, now a beautifully kept museum to the family that shaped modern Bengal. Essential for anyone who loves literature and the Bengal Renaissance, set in an evocative old-city quarter.

items.name: Academy of Fine Arts
items.description: Kolkata's leading gallery and theatre complex beside the Rabindra Sadan cultural district, home to changing exhibitions and a permanent Tagore collection. The best single stop to take the pulse of the city's contemporary art and stage life.

items.name: Kolkata tram ride
items.description: Asia's oldest operating tram network, running since 1902, still trundles a handful of heritage routes through the old city at a gloriously unhurried pace. A joyride on a wooden-slatted carriage past Esplanade is a nostalgic pleasure that is slowly disappearing.

items.name: Durga Puja pandal-hopping
credentials: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity
items.description: For five days each autumn the whole city becomes an open-air gallery of themed pandals, some the size of cathedrals, each an artwork built to be dissolved in the river. It is Kolkata at its most joyous and unmissable; the festival is inscribed on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.

items.name: Kalighat Pat painting & patuas
items.description: The bold, quick-brushed folk paintings born in the temple bazaars of the 19th century, a distinctly Kolkata art form now prized by collectors. Seek them out near the temple and in city galleries; an original pat is a meaningful thing to take home.

items.name: Park Street kathi rolls & street food
items.description: The kathi roll, an egg-coated paratha wrapped around spiced kebab, was invented at Nizam's near New Market and is Kolkata's great gift to street food. Eating one hot off the griddle, then a phuchka from a roadside cart, is a rite of passage in this most food-obsessed of Indian cities.

items.name: Bengali sweets crawl
items.description: The city that gave the world the rosogolla still treats sweet-making as high art, from the syrup-soaked chhena of Balaram Mullick to the nolen gur mishti doi of winter. A morning tasting your way through the century-old sweet shops is pure, delicious Bengal.

items.name: Kolkata coffee-house adda
items.description: Adda, the unhurried art of conversation for its own sake, is Bengal's greatest institution, practised over endless cups in coffee houses and para rooftops. To be drawn into an adda is to be let into the real city; nowhere in India talks quite like Kolkata.

items.name: Nakhoda Masjid & Zakaria Street
items.description: The city's largest mosque, a red-sandstone echo of Akbar's tomb, presides over the fragrant Muslim quarter of Zakaria Street. In Ramadan the lanes below turn into one of India's great night food markets, heavy with haleem, kebabs and firni.

items.name: Paresnath Jain Temple (Shitalnath)
items.description: A dazzling 1867 Jain temple encrusted with mirrors, Belgian glass, Venetian mosaics and coloured stones set in a fountain garden. One of the most ornate and least-visited jewels in the city, and a serene surprise in the busy north.

items.name: Rabindra Sarobar & the Lakes
items.description: A tranquil man-made lake ringed by walking paths, rowing clubs and old trees, where south Kolkata comes to jog, row and do sunrise yoga. A green, breathable counterpoint to the crowded old city, and lovely early in the morning.

items.name: Victoria Memorial sound-and-light show
items.description: As night falls, the monument's own history and that of the city are narrated across its lit facade in an evening spectacle in the gardens. A gentle, atmospheric way to end a day, especially with children in tow.

items.name: Kumortuli to Sovabazar heritage walk
items.description: The lanes of old north Kolkata hide crumbling merchant mansions (rajbaris), hidden thakur-dalans and the courtyards where Durga Puja began. A guided morning walk here peels back the aristocratic Bengal that built the city, layer by layer.

items.name: Mullick Ghat flower market
items.description: One of Asia's largest wholesale flower markets sprawls under the Howrah Bridge, a riot of marigold garlands, lotus and roses from before dawn. Arrive at sunrise for extraordinary photographs of colour, chaos and the great steel bridge above.

items.name: Metropolitan Building & Esplanade colonial walk
items.description: The restored, cream-and-red Metropolitan (Whiteaway Laidlaw) building anchors a stretch of grand old department stores and colonial facades around Chowringhee. A rewarding architecture stroll that ends naturally at New Market or the Grand.

items.name: The Oberoi Grand high tea
items.description: The 'Grande Dame of Chowringhee', a colonial-era hotel whose colonnaded courtyard has hosted the city's grandest occasions for over a century. Even if you stay elsewhere, afternoon tea beneath its arches is a graceful way to touch old Calcutta.

items.name: Sundarbans day trip
items.description: The world's largest mangrove forest and the tiger-haunted delta where the Ganges meets the sea, best explored slowly by launch through its tidal creeks. A UNESCO World Heritage Site and biosphere reserve; a night on a boat is far better than a rushed day, but even a day gives you the wild edge of Bengal.

items.name: Shantiniketan day trip
items.description: Tagore's serene university town where classes are still held under the trees and the whole ethos is art, nature and simplicity. Visit the ashram, the Kala Bhavana art school and the Saturday tribal craft market; the winter Poush Mela is magical.

items.name: Bishnupur terracotta temples day trip
items.description: The old Malla capital is studded with 17th-century temples whose brick walls are carved edge to edge with terracotta scenes from the epics, unlike anything else in India. Pair the Rasmancha and Jor Bangla temples with a Baluchari silk saree bought at its source.

items.name: Chandannagar day trip
items.description: A former French colony on the Hooghly with a genuinely Gallic riverfront promenade, a domed church and the elegant Dupleix mansion museum. A charming half-day of European Bengal, at its most dazzling during its famous Jagaddhatri Puja illuminations.

items.name: Chinsurah & Bandel Church day trip
items.description: The Hooghly's old colonial river-towns layer Portuguese, Dutch and Danish history within an hour of the city, crowned by the 1599 Bandel Basilica, one of the oldest churches in Bengal. A quiet, offbeat outing for travellers who like their history undiscovered.

items.name: Bohemian
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India x Zomato Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 41 in India
items.description: Chef Joymalya Banerjee's modern-Bengali table — traditional spices and ingredients pushed into unexpected, playful territory.

items.name: Baan Thai
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India x Zomato Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 27 in India
items.description: The Oberoi Grand's long-loved Thai room — teak, silk and precise, refined cooking above Chowringhee.

items.name: 6 Ballygunge Place
credentials: Landmark Kolkata Bengali fine-dining institution — regarded among the city's best for authentic Bengali cuisine (Incredible India, Culture Trip)
items.description: Bengali fine dining in a restored 1930s mansion — slow-cooked royal-Bengal curries in the city's most gracious dining house.

items.name: Oh! Calcutta
credentials: Landmark restaurant credited with popularising Bengali fine dining nationally (Speciality Restaurants — recognised group)
items.description: The restaurant that carried Bengali cuisine across India — comforting fish curries and melt-in-the-mouth mutton in a warm room.

items.name: West View
credentials: Inside ITC Sonar — ITC Hotels signature dining
items.description: ITC Sonar's grill-and-fine-dining room — a polished western table for members who want a hotel-standard dinner near the CBD.

items.name: Kewpie's Kitchen
credentials: Legendary family-run Kolkata institution — regarded among the city's best for home-style Bengali cuisine (India.com, Culture Trip)
items.description: A family home turned dining room — authentic Bengali cooking from recipes handed down through the Dasgupta family.

items.name: Peter Cat
credentials: TasteAtlas — 150 Most Legendary Restaurants in the World (2023), ranked No. 17
items.description: The Park Street icon since 1975 — home of the Chelo Kebab, rice and kebabs under a poached egg, a Kolkata institution unto itself.

items.name: Mocambo
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India x Zomato Top Restaurant Awards 2024 — No. 37 in India
Kolkata heritage-restaurant status — Park Street institution
items.description: A 1956 continental time-capsule — Devil Crab, sizzlers and Anglo-Italian classics under the same neon since the fifties.

items.name: Kwality
items.area: Park Street area (17 Park Street / Free School Street)
credentials: Kolkata heritage-restaurant status — Park Street institution
items.description: One of Park Street's grand old continental-and-Mughlai rooms — chelo, kebabs and dal that have fed the city for generations.

items.name: Arsalan
credentials: Landmark Kolkata biryani institution — the city's best-known Kolkata biryani (est. 2002; Tripadvisor top-ranked biryani)
items.description: Kolkata's most famous biryani house — the fragrant, potato-and-egg Kolkata biryani that defines the city's Mughlai table.

items.name: Flurys
credentials: Heritage Park Street institution since 1927 — Kolkata's most storied tearoom
items.description: The 1927 Park Street tearoom — a Raj-era confectionery of pastries, rum balls and English breakfasts, unchanged in spirit.

items.name: Nizam's
credentials: Heritage institution — credited as the birthplace of the Kolkata Kathi Roll (est. 1930s)
items.description: The birthplace of the Kathi Roll — kebabs rolled in a paratha, invented here in the 1930s and still served hot to order.

items.name: Trincas
credentials: Historic Park Street live-music institution since 1959
The enduring heart of Kolkata's jazz-and-cabaret nightlife
items.description: Park Street's legendary listening room — live music every night since 1959, the stage that launched Usha Uthup.

items.name: The Chowringhee Bar
credentials: Named Best Bar/Pub — The Times Food Guide, The Times of India (2004)
Inside The Oberoi Grand — INTACH heritage-recognised (2024)
items.description: The Oberoi Grand's clubby colonial bar — dark wood, single malts and the quietest, most grown-up nightcap in the city.

items.name: Roxy
credentials: Inside The Park Kolkata — India's pioneering design-hotel group
items.description: A witty, design-led cocktail-and-wine bar channelling the swinging sixties — the most stylish drinking room on Park Street.

items.name: Someplace Else
credentials: Pioneering Indian live-music pub — the brand that took Kolkata nightlife national
Inside The Park Kolkata — Travel + Leisure India Best Business Hotel (2020)
items.description: India's original live-band pub — the loud, joyful rock room that has defined Kolkata's pub culture for three decades.

items.title: Durga Puja pandal-hopping with a local host
items.description: A curated night through the great artistic pandals, seeing the city's most extraordinary living festival from the inside.

items.title: Private heritage walk of colonial and north Kolkata
items.description: A historian-led morning through the old mansions, the ghats and the printing lanes of the original city.

items.title: Bengali fine-dining and sweet-shop trail
items.description: A curated meal of classic Bengali cuisine paired with a tour of the legendary sweet houses.

items.title: Sunrise on the Hooghly and the flower market
items.description: A dawn boat under the Howrah Bridge past the Mullick Ghat flower market, the city at its most cinematic.

plan.heading: 4 days in Kolkata, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Victoria Memorial and the Maidan in the morning, then St. Paul's Cathedral nearby.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Indian Museum and a slow walk down the colonnades of the old central business quarter.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at the Bengali table of 6 Ballygunge Place, or Kewpie's home-style thali.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The lanes of Kumartuli where the idol-makers work in clay, then Marble Palace.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Howrah bridge and a boat on the Hooghly past the ghats at dusk.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Kathi rolls at Nizam's, or a proper dinner at Oh! Calcutta.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: College Street's book market and the Indian Coffee House, then the Ashutosh museum.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Rabindra Bharati house-museum at Jorasanko, Tagore's family home.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A cultural evening, then dinner at The Bridge in the Taj Bengal.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A morning of Bengali sweets, sandesh and mishti doi from a century-old shop like Balaram Mullick.

slots.label: Afternoon

slots.label: Evening

items.description: The leafy, gracious residential south; for a quiet, upscale base among old bungalows.

events.name: Durga Puja
events.note: The city's defining festival, a UNESCO-recognised explosion of art, devotion and street life; the single best time to visit.

events.name: Kali Puja & Diwali
events.note: A dramatic night of goddess worship and lights following close on Durga Puja.

events.name: Kolkata International Film Festival
events.note: A major, long-running film festival that fills the city's cinemas and its intellectual life.

events.name: Poush Mela / Christmas season
events.note: Park Street's famous Christmas lights and the nearby Santiniketan Poush Mela make December especially lively.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose international airport and take a private chauffeur into town; the airport is in the north, roughly forty-five minutes to an hour from the central and south Kolkata hotels.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car and driver is the sensible way to navigate the traffic, though the colonial core around Park Street and the Maidan is a rewarding walk, and a heritage tram or river ferry makes a fine occasional detour.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Reliable 4G and 5G across the city on all networks; eSIMs and hotel wifi are dependable.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Indian rupee; cards and UPI are widely taken, with cash handy for old bookshops, sweet shops and markets; ten percent is a gracious tip.

onGround.note: Stay around Park Street, Alipore or the Victoria Memorial for the best of old Calcutta; the city is at its most beautiful and social during Durga Puja in autumn, though it books out early; the coffee houses, sweet shops and colonial architecture reward an unhurried pace.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: November–February is the kind season: dry, mild and at its cultural best around Durga Puja's aftermath and the winter calendar. Avoid April–June's punishing heat-and-humidity and the June–September monsoon, when the city floods.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi (~2h10m), Mumbai (~2h40m) and Bengaluru (~2h30m) into Kolkata (CCU); Air India flies business on the Delhi/Mumbai trunk, IndiGo carries the frequency. It is also the natural gateway on to Bhutan and the Northeast — use the premium lounge, and allow time as the city-side traffic is dense.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations beyond routine for a standard visit. A safe, walkable city with warm people; normal metro caution. No altitude. Humidity is heavy outside winter. Tap water is not potable — sealed bottled water, and be selective with street food despite the temptation.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Good for vegetarians and workable for Jain, though Bengali cuisine leans fish-forward. The city has a strong Marwari/Gujarati community, so pure-veg and Jain kitchens are genuinely easy to find. 6 Ballygunge Place and Bhojohori Manna do fine vegetarian Bengali; Kewpie's and the veg-Jain kitchens at the Taj/ITC properties handle strict requirements well.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Kolkata, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Krabi — TripAgent
seo.description: Krabi, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Krabi
hero.tagline: Towering karsts, jade waters and tranquil Andaman shores.

ourTake.lede: Krabi is the calmer, more scenic alternative to Phuket, and its best assets are offshore, so build the trip around the water. Base yourself on the quieter beaches or a private island rather than busy Ao Nang, and get onto the sea early to beat the crowds to Railay and the Hong islands. November to March is the dry, clear window; the monsoon months turn the sea rough and the boats unreliable.
ourTake.comeIf: You want limestone cliffs, calm water and a slower, more scenic side of the Thai coast.
ourTake.skipIf: You want nightlife and a busy scene; Krabi is quieter and more about the landscape.

firstLook.heroCaption: Woman in infinity pool facing limestone islands

grid.caption: Grand Palace golden spires and white temple courtyard
purple allium blooms in soft focus

whenToGo.blurb: November to March brings dry days, calm seas and clear rock; the May-October monsoon means heavy rain and rough water for island-hopping.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Krabi. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Rayavadee
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World — member
Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice Awards — Top Asia Resorts & World's Best Beach Resorts
UK Tatler Travel Guide — '101 Best Hotels in the World'
items.description: The Andaman icon — two-storey pavilions in a coconut grove ringed by three beaches and towering limestone, reachable only by boat.

items.name: Phulay Bay, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve
credentials: MICHELIN Three Keys (2025) — Krabi's only Three-Key hotel
Forbes Travel Guide — rated Krabi hotel
items.description: Krabi's most decorated address — 54 Moorish-Thai villas and pavilions, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve and the region's only Three-Key hotel.

items.name: Banyan Tree Krabi
credentials: MICHELIN Two Keys (2025 — retained for a second year)
items.description: An all-villa beachfront house on Tubkaak looking across the bay to the karsts — Banyan Tree's Krabi flagship.

items.name: Pimalai Resort & Spa
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World — member
MICHELIN Guide Hotels — Koh Lanta selection
items.description: A hundred acres of tropical forest above 900 metres of private Andaman beach — Koh Lanta's grandest resort.

items.name: The Tubkaak Krabi Boutique Resort
credentials: '1000 Places to See Before You Die' — listed
items.description: An intimate southern-Thai boutique on quiet Tubkaak sand, with karst-and-island views the strip resorts don't get.

items.name: Sofitel Krabi Phokeethra Golf & Spa Resort
credentials: Sofitel / Accor Luxury — maison group flagship in Krabi
Forbes-list class resort on Klong Muang Beach
items.description: A colonial-elegant Sofitel on Klong Muang with Thailand's largest lagoon pool and a 9-hole course — grand and family-scaled.

items.name: Dusit Thani Krabi Beach Resort
credentials: Dusit Thani — Thailand's flagship luxury hotel maison
Five Star Alliance — featured luxury resort, Krabi
items.description: A relaxed, gardens-and-sand Dusit Thani on Klong Muang — the group's warm Thai hospitality on a quiet beach.

items.name: Amari Vogue Krabi
credentials: Amari / ONYX Hospitality — maison group resort
Tubkaak Beach — among Krabi's most-recommended luxury addresses
items.description: Thai Lanna architecture and tiered infinity pools cascading to Tubkaak sand — polished value with the best view on the beach.

items.name: Railay Peninsula — arriving only by longtail boat
items.description: A tiny peninsula cut off from the mainland by sheer limestone walls, so there are no roads in — you step off a longtail boat straight onto the sand. That severance is the whole point: no cars, no through-traffic, just four beaches, climbers on the cliffs and the karsts glowing at dusk. The obvious base for a honeymoon or a family that wants Krabi's drama without Phuket's noise.

items.name: Railay West Beach
items.description: The postcard beach — a soft white crescent framed by towering karsts, where the longtails pull in and the sun sets straight down the water. It is where Rayavadee and the smart resorts sit, and where you gather at dusk with a drink to watch the cliffs turn amber. Calm, swimmable and the social heart of the peninsula.

items.name: Railay East Beach & the mangrove boardwalk
items.description: The quieter, mangrove-fringed side of the peninsula — muddy at low tide and not for swimming, but this is where the boats to Ao Nang and Krabi Town dock and where the cheaper bars and climbing shops cluster. A five-minute walk on the flat path links it to Railay West, so you can stay on the pretty side and pass through here to move around.

items.name: Phra Nang Cave Beach (Hat Tham Phra Nang)
items.description: Regularly rated one of the most beautiful beaches on earth — a short walk from Railay East past the Rayavadee grounds delivers you to a jewel of white sand tucked under a colossal overhang, with karst islets offshore and water the colour of glass. Longtails sell fresh fruit and cold beer off the water. Arrive early; by midday the day-trip boats crowd in.

items.name: Princess Cave (Tham Phra Nang Nok) & the fertility shrine
items.description: At the end of Phra Nang beach, a cave holds a shrine to a sea princess where local fishermen leave carved wooden phalluses as offerings for a good catch and fertility — an unmissable, slightly startling piece of living folklore. It takes two minutes to see and gives the beach its name and its spirit.

items.name: The Princess Lagoon (Sa Phra Nang) hike
items.description: A hidden emerald pool sunk deep inside the karst, reached only by a genuinely demanding scramble down ropes and mud from the viewpoint trail — around 45 minutes of rock-clinging descent to a still lagoon walled by cliffs. Strictly for the fit and sure-footed, but the reward is a secret world almost no day-tripper reaches.

items.name: Railay Viewpoint
items.description: A short but steep, rope-assisted climb off the East–Phra Nang trail opens onto the definitive photograph of Railay: both beaches, the whole peninsula and the Andaman laid out below. Ten to twenty sweaty minutes up; wear proper shoes and go at high tide for the full effect.

items.name: Rock climbing on the Railay & Ton Sai crags
items.description: Railay is one of the world's great climbing destinations — hundreds of bolted routes on sea-cliff limestone, from beginner walls above Railay East to overhanging test-pieces at Ton Sai. Reputable schools run half-day introductions with guides and gear, so a first-timer or a teenager can top out over the sea by lunch. Deep-water soloing off a boat is the adrenaline upgrade.

items.name: Ton Sai Beach
items.description: The rugged, bohemian neighbour of Railay — a rocky-at-low-tide bay backed by jungle and the climbing crowd, reached by a scramble over the headland or a short longtail hop. Rawer and cheaper than Railay proper; worth a wander for the climber-café atmosphere and the sense of Railay before the resorts.

items.name: Ao Nang — the mainland base and beach town
items.description: The busy beach town on the mainland that most trips run from: the pier for every island tour, a long promenade of restaurants (including reliable Indian and clearly-labelled vegetarian kitchens), dive shops and hotels. Not the prettiest beach in Krabi, but the logistics hub — the longtails to Railay leave from here, and it is where a family stocks up between excursions.

items.name: Nopparat Thara Beach & the Mu Ko Phi Phi–Nopparat Thara National Park
items.description: A long, quiet, casuarina-shaded beach just west of Ao Nang that most visitors overlook — at low tide a sandbar links out to a small island. It is the mainland gateway of the marine national park that also covers Phi Phi, and a calmer alternative to the Ao Nang strip for a slow local morning.

items.name: The Four Islands day trip
items.description: Krabi's signature outing — Phra Nang Cave Beach, Chicken Island, Tup Island and Poda Island in one loop of white sand, snorkelling and karst scenery. Charter a private longtail or speedboat and time it around the tide so you have the beaches before the crowds; the classic honeymoon and multi-gen day on the water.

items.name: The Tup Island sandbar (Koh Tup / Koh Mor)
items.description: At low tide a ribbon of white sand rises from the sea to link three islands, and you can walk from one to another across the ocean floor — Krabi's most photographed natural trick and a genuine delight for children. It appears only for a few hours a day, so a good boatman plans the whole trip around the tide table.

items.name: Chicken Island (Koh Kai) snorkelling
items.description: Named for a limestone spur that really does look like a chicken's head and neck, this island has the shallow, beginner-friendly reef of the Four Islands loop — soft coral and clouds of fish in warm, calm water. The easy snorkel stop for families and first-timers.

items.name: Poda Island (Koh Poda)
items.description: A near-perfect little island of powder sand and clear shallows with a lone karst pinnacle rising offshore — the quintessential Krabi beach for swimming, sunbathing and a picnic lunch. Charter your own boat to have it before the tour fleet arrives.

items.name: The Hong Islands (Mu Ko Hong) & the hidden lagoon
items.description: 'Hong' means 'room' — and the star island hides an enclosed emerald lagoon reached through a narrow gap in the cliffs, opening into a walled world of still turquoise water. Often quieter and arguably lovelier than Phi Phi; the private-longtail version, paddling in by kayak, is one of Krabi's most romantic mornings.

items.name: Sea-kayaking the Hong lagoon
items.description: The Hong lagoon is fully enclosed and sheltered, so even a complete novice can paddle in through the rock gate and drift under 100-metre cliffs reflected in glassy water. A gentle, photogenic activity that suits couples, grandparents and children alike — the calm counterpoint to the Ao Thalane mangroves.

items.name: The Phi Phi Islands day trip
items.description: The famous day out from Ao Nang or Railay — Phi Phi Leh's soaring cliffs and lagoons, the snorkelling, Monkey Beach and lunch on Phi Phi Don. Go by private speedboat at sunrise to reach Maya Bay and Pileh before the fleet; the difference between a magical morning and a floating traffic jam is entirely about timing.

items.name: Maya Bay — 'The Beach'
items.description: The cove made world-famous by the Leonardo DiCaprio film, a flawless bowl of white sand walled by cliffs — reopened under strict rules after years of recovery, with no swimming at the beach and a boardwalk approach from the back of the island. Note the seasonal closure: the bay shuts to visitors every 1 August–30 September (2026 included) to let the reef rest. First boat in, before 9am, is the only way to have it feel wild.

items.name: Pileh Lagoon
items.description: A long, narrow inlet almost slicing Phi Phi Leh in two, walled by 100-metre cliffs with unreal turquoise water and a soft white sand bottom — no coral, so it is safe to float and swim freely. Often the highlight of the whole Phi Phi day; arrive early and it can feel like a private cathedral of rock.

items.name: Viking Cave (Tham Phaya Nak)
items.description: A vast sea cave named for ancient wall paintings that resemble longships, and still worked by sea-gypsy collectors of prized swiftlet nests. The cave itself is closed to landings, so boats slow to let you look from the water — a brief but atmospheric stop on the Phi Phi loop.

items.name: Bamboo Island (Koh Phai)
items.description: A low, sandy island north of Phi Phi Don ringed by a wide curve of white beach and shallow reef in two to four metres of water — the best snorkelling stop of the Phi Phi day and a lovely place to simply lie on the sand. Part of the national park, so a fee applies and it can close in low season.

items.name: Koh Lanta — the slow island
items.description: A long, laid-back island south of Krabi reached by car ferry or road bridges, strung with a dozen quieter beaches that grow emptier the further south you drive. This is where you go to decompress after the island tours — think honeymoon stillness, sunset dinners and a pace that Ao Nang no longer has.

items.name: Lanta Old Town (Ban Si Raya)
items.description: A photogenic old Chinese-Thai fishing village of stilted wooden shophouses over the water on Lanta's east coast — seafood restaurants on the piers, small galleries and craft shops, and a gentle, unhurried afternoon of strolling. The most characterful town on the island and a window into its trading past.

items.name: Kantiang Bay
items.description: A gorgeous horseshoe of sand near Lanta's southern end, cradled by jungle-clad cliffs and home to the island's most upmarket resort — the drive over the hills to reach it is half the pleasure. One of the loveliest and least crowded beaches in the whole Krabi region for a couple seeking quiet.

items.name: Mu Ko Lanta National Park & the lighthouse (Laem Tanod)
items.description: At Lanta's southern tip, a national park headland crowned by a small lighthouse gives a sweeping panorama of sea, cliffs and islands, with a short jungle nature trail where you may meet resident monkeys. The end-of-the-island reward after a scenic coastal drive past Kantiang and Bamboo bays.

items.name: Tiger Cave Temple (Wat Tham Suea) — the 1,237-step climb
items.description: A working meditation temple wrapped around a cave where a monk once saw tigers, with a brutally steep staircase of over 1,200 steps rising 280-odd metres to a golden Buddha and a 360-degree view across Krabi to the Andaman. A serious 40–60 minute climb in the heat, best at dawn; profoundly worth it for the fit. Free to enter.

items.name: The Emerald Pool (Sa Morakot)
items.description: A natural spring-fed pool of impossibly clear, milky-jade water in the rainforest of the Khao Phra Bang Khram sanctuary — warm, swimmable and ringed by jungle, reached by an easy boardwalk. About an hour from Ao Nang and usually paired with the Blue Pool; go early before the tour buses. Small entry fee.

items.name: The Blue Pool (Sa Nam Phut)
items.description: A short jungle walk beyond the Emerald Pool, this geothermal spring glows an almost electric sapphire when the light hits — deep, hot and not for swimming, but mesmerising to stand over. Opens later than the Emerald Pool (from 10am); the two together make the definitive Krabi rainforest half-day.

items.name: The natural hot springs (Nam Tok Ron)
items.description: A cascade of smooth stone pools where warm mineral water tumbles down the rock into a cool stream — you soak in a natural jacuzzi in the jungle and then dip in the cold pool below. Usually combined with the Emerald and Blue Pools into one restorative inland day; soothing for grandparents and children alike.

items.name: Than Bok Khorani National Park
items.description: An easily-missed mainland park north of Krabi where an emerald pool fed by a limestone spring spreads through a small botanical forest of orchids, gingers and wild gardenias — swimmable, serene and blissfully untouristed. A gentle nature stop and the launch point for the Bor Thor cave-and-mangrove kayaking.

items.name: Khao Khanab Nam — the twin karst cliffs
items.description: The two limestone towers that guard the mouth of the Krabi River are the emblem of the town, a fifteen-minute longtail ride upstream from the pier. Land to explore the caves at their base, where stalactites and traces of prehistoric human habitation have been found. A short, evocative outing that doubles as a river cruise past the mangroves.

items.name: Sea-kayaking the Ao Thalane mangroves
items.description: Paddle silent channels through cathedral-like limestone canyons and mangrove tunnels, gliding past macaques, mudskippers, kingfishers and the occasional monkey trying to hitch a ride. Gentle enough for the whole family and, at the right tide, one of the most atmospheric wildlife experiences in Krabi — the wild counterpart to the polished Hong lagoon.

items.name: Kayaking Klong Root (Crystal Lagoon)
items.description: A freshwater lagoon fed by an underground spring, so clear you can watch fish and submerged trees beneath the kayak as you paddle through a green, silent, Jurassic-feeling jungle. Quieter and more surreal than the sea kayaking; a lovely, low-effort morning for couples and families who want stillness.

items.name: Tha Pom Khlong Song Nam — the 'two-water canal'
items.description: A short boardwalk trail follows a crystal stream where fresh spring water meets the Andaman's saltwater, turning the shallows a vivid emerald that shifts with the tide — you can cool off in the clear pool where the two waters mix. A quiet, easy nature walk near Ao Nang that most visitors never find.

items.name: Susan Hoi — the Fossil Shell Beach
items.description: One of only a handful of shell-fossil beaches on earth: a 200-metre shelf of grey rock made entirely of freshwater snail shells fused into stone over tens of millions of years, cracking off in great slabs at the sea's edge. A genuinely rare geological curiosity, quick to see and fascinating for children and curious travellers.

items.name: Krabi Town Walking Street night market
items.description: On weekend evenings the old town's Maharat Soi 8 fills with food stalls, a live stage and lantern-lit lanes — grilled seafood, mango sticky rice, southern curries and plenty of clearly-marked vegetarian and fruit stalls. The most authentic, unpolished evening in the area and an easy, atmospheric night out away from the resort strip.

items.name: Sunset dinner on Phra Nang beach at Rayavadee
items.description: Rayavadee's celebrated 'The Grotto' sets tables inside a limestone cave right on Phra Nang beach — cocktails and dinner under the karst as the sun drops, arguably the single most romantic table in Krabi. A private-yacht or longtail transfer turns dinner into an occasion for a honeymoon or anniversary.

items.name: Private-yacht island-hopping & sunset sailing
items.description: Charter a private yacht or luxury catamaran to trace the Four Islands, Hong and Phi Phi archipelagos at your own pace, with a chef, a swim platform and the karsts to yourselves at golden hour. The definitive way for an UHNI family to see Krabi — no crowds, your own tide plan, and a sundowner sail back into the cliffs.

items.name: Private longtail charter for the day
items.description: The most authentic — and surprisingly attainable — luxury here is your own long-tail boat and boatman for the day, so you land on beaches when they are empty and skip the group timetable entirely. The single best decision most Krabi visitors make; ask your advisor to time it to the tides for the sandbars and lagoons.

items.name: Scuba diving the Andaman reefs
items.description: Ao Nang is a full-service dive base for the local reefs and pinnacles around Phi Phi and the King Cruiser wreck, with leopard sharks, turtles and seasonal whale sharks and manta rays on the outer sites. Reputable centres run PADI courses and Discover Scuba dives, so a novice or a teenager can take a first breath underwater in warm, clear water.

items.name: Snorkelling day trips
items.description: For those who would rather stay on the surface, the shallow reefs off Bamboo, Chicken and the Phi Phi fringes deliver easy, colourful snorkelling straight off the boat. A private charter lets you reach the best patches at the quiet hours and keeps it gentle for children and non-swimmers with a guide.

items.name: Ao Nang / Ao Thalane deep-water soloing & cliff jumping
items.description: The purest thrill in Krabi: climbing unroped over the sea straight from a boat, then falling back into deep water when your grip gives — guided by the same climbing schools that run the Railay crags. For confident, adventurous travellers, an unforgettable half-day that only this coastline's overhanging karst makes possible.

items.name: Nui Bay & the hidden southern coves of Lanta
items.description: Beyond Kantiang, tiny bays like Nui and Bamboo tuck into the cliffs on the road to the national park — a string of near-private beaches for the traveller willing to drive to the island's wild southern end. The reward for renting a car on Lanta and chasing the emptiest sand in Krabi.

items.name: Phang Nga Bay / 'James Bond Island' day trip
items.area: Offshore (Phang Nga, via Krabi or Phuket)
items.description: The surreal drowned-karst seascape of Phang Nga Bay — sea caves, floating Muslim fishing village Koh Panyee and the needle-rock island from 'The Man with the Golden Gun' — is reachable from Krabi, though it sits closer to Phuket. A private long-tail or yacht charter through the hongs (tidal caves) is the memorable, crowd-free way to do it.

items.name: The Grotto
credentials: Rayavadee — The Leading Hotels of the World; the resort's signature cave restaurant
items.description: Dinner inside a limestone cave on the sand of Phra Nang — charbroiled Andaman lobster and day-boat seafood beneath the overhang, one of Thailand's most theatrical settings.

items.name: Krua Phranang
credentials: Rayavadee — The Leading Hotels of the World; the resort's principal Thai restaurant
items.description: Rayavadee's beachfront Thai kitchen — southern-Thai and royal-Thai cooking with the karsts as backdrop.

items.name: Chomtawan
items.area: Nong Thale (Phulay Bay, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve)
credentials: Phulay Bay, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve — MICHELIN Three Keys (2025), Forbes Travel Guide
items.description: Refined Thai dining inside Krabi's only Three-Key hotel — the region's most polished kitchen, on the water.

items.name: Saffron
credentials: Banyan Tree Krabi — MICHELIN Two Keys (2025); the group's flagship Saffron brand
items.description: Banyan Tree's signature Thai room, carried across the group's resorts — precise cooking with a karst-and-bay view.

items.name: Seafire
credentials: Pimalai Resort & Spa — MICHELIN Two Keys (2025), Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: Beachfront live-fire and Andaman seafood at Pimalai — grilled catch of the day with your feet near the sand.

items.name: Lae Lay Grill
credentials: Ao Nang's best-known destination seafood restaurant — a long-established local landmark with panoramic bay views
items.description: A long-running hillside seafood house above Ao Nang with a sweeping sunset view over the bay — the town's landmark table.

items.name: Carnivore Steak & Grill
credentials: Ao Nang's leading established steakhouse — a long-standing fixture on the town's dining strip
items.description: Ao Nang's serious steakhouse — proper cuts and a cellar for the member who wants beef done well after days of seafood.

items.name: The Grotto Bar
credentials: The bar of Rayavadee's cave restaurant (The Leading Hotels of the World) — Krabi's signature setting for a sunset drink
items.description: Cocktails on the sand inside a limestone cave as the light goes over Phra Nang — the most singular sundowner in the region.

items.name: Rock Bar / beach bar, Phulay Bay
items.area: Nong Thale (Phulay Bay, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve)
credentials: The signature bar of Phulay Bay, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve — MICHELIN Three Keys (2025), Forbes Travel Guide
items.description: An unhurried sundowner at Krabi's only Three-Key hotel — the most polished drink on the coast, on the water.

items.name: Rooftop bar, Ao Nang seafront
credentials: Ao Nang's seafront rooftop bars — the town's established sunset-drink circuit overlooking the bay and islands
items.description: The town's seafront rooftops catch the sunset over the islands — an easy elevated drink before dinner on the Ao Nang strip.

items.name: REEVE Beach Club
credentials: Ao Nang's established beachfront beach club — a recognised day-to-night venue on the main bay with a nightly fire show
items.description: Ao Nang's prime beachfront club on the best corner of the bay — café by day, cocktails and a nightly fire show by the water after dark.

items.title: Private long-tail to Railay at dawn
items.description: The cliff-backed peninsula reachable only by boat, walked before the day boats land and fill the sand.

items.title: Private island-hopping through the Hong Islands
items.description: The hidden lagoons and empty beaches of the Hong archipelago on a chartered boat, away from the tour convoys.

items.title: Rock-climbing or a via ferrata on the Railay karsts
items.description: The world-famous limestone cliffs, climbed with a private guide over the sea.

items.title: Sunset dinner on a private beach
items.description: A table set on an empty stretch of sand as the karsts turn gold, arranged through one of the peninsula's resorts.

plan.heading: 3 days in Krabi, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive at Rayavadee, tucked into Phranang beach and reachable only by boat, and settle among the limestone towers.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Walk to Phranang Cave beach and swim, then watch the rock climbers on the Railay walls from the sand.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at The Grotto, tables set inside a limestone cave at the water's edge.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private longtail to Hong Island's hidden lagoon early, before the tour boats reach it.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Snorkel the clear water off Poda and Chicken Island, with a quiet picnic lunch on an empty stretch of sand.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A seafood dinner back at the resort, then stars over the Andaman with no city glow.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A calm kayak through the Ao Thalane mangroves at high tide, watching for kingfishers and monitor lizards.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A last swim and a slow lunch of massaman curry.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: An early supper before the boat and road transfer out.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Railay
items.description: A cliff-ringed peninsula cut off by land and reached only by boat; for seclusion, climbing and dramatic scenery.

items.name: Ao Nang
items.description: The main beach hub with the boats, restaurants and shops; convenient and lively but the least quiet.

items.name: Koh Lanta
items.description: A longer, laid-back island south of Krabi with wide beaches; for travellers who want to slow right down.

events.name: Loy Krathong
events.note: The festival of lights, celebrated along Krabi's beaches with floating candlelit offerings at dusk.

events.name: Songkran
events.note: Thai New Year, marked with water-splashing and temple visits across the province at the height of the hot season.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: You land at Krabi International (KBV); a private car reaches Ao Nang in about thirty minutes, while Rayavadee and the Railay peninsula are reached only by a resort longtail or speedboat across the bay.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Use a private driver on the mainland and a chartered longtail or speedboat for Railay, Hong and the Phi Phi islands, since the finest spots have no road.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: An AIS or TrueMove eSIM holds 4G along the coast; signal thins on remote beaches, so lean on resort wifi.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Thai baht (THB); cards work at resorts but cash is essential for boatmen and village stops; small tips are welcomed, not expected.

onGround.note: Base yourself on Railay or at Rayavadee for the dramatic karst setting away from the Ao Nang crowds; November to March is the dry, calm window, and reef shoes help on the limestone shallows.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: December to March gives the clear skies and calm water Krabi is known for; avoid May to October, and September especially, when Andaman monsoon rain and swell shut down much of the island access.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No non-stop from India; route via Bangkok (about 4.5h) then a short 1h 15m domestic hop to Krabi, or via Phuket by road/boat. Thai Airways and Bangkok Airways cover the connection with lounge access at BKK. Plan on one connection and a half-day of travel.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations; keep routine jabs current, Hepatitis A and Typhoid sensible. Safe and quiet. Bottled water only. Monsoon-season sea and cliff conditions warrant caution.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian is manageable at resorts and beach restaurants; Jain needs clear briefing in advance. Indian food is limited compared with Phuket or Bangkok, so lean on your resort kitchen or arrange a private cook for anything specific.
