whenToGo.blurb: Spring and early autumn are ideal, April to June and September to October; avoid July and August when the city empties and bakes.
whenToGo.bestMonths: May, Jun, Jul and Aug

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental Ritz, Madrid
items.description: The capital's defining address — a Belle Époque palace beside the Prado, restored to its full 1910 grandeur.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Madrid
items.description: Seven heritage buildings woven into one grand house at Canalejas — Four Seasons' first Spanish address, between Sol and the Prado.

items.name: Rosewood Villa Magna
items.description: The Salamanca grande dame reborn — Rosewood's flagship on Madrid's most coveted boulevard, all calm and quiet polish.

items.name: BLESS Hotel Madrid
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A contemporary luxury house on the Golden Mile, in the former Gran Hotel Velázquez — bold, design-led, and gastronomically serious.

items.name: Santo Mauro, a Luxury Collection Hotel
items.description: A duke's 1894 neoclassical mansion turned intimate palace hotel — a marble staircase, a garden, and deep quiet off the Castellana.

items.name: Hotel Único Madrid
items.description: A restored 19th-century Salamanca townhouse turned intimate luxury hotel, on the city's smartest shopping street.

items.name: Gran Meliá Palacio de los Duques
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A 19th-century palace and former 13th-century convent by the Royal Palace, dressed with a Velázquez-inspired hand.

items.name: The Madrid EDITION
items.description: Ian Schrager's cool, light-filled house in the old centre — a rooftop, a pool and a lively scene under one modern roof.

items.name: URSO Hotel & Spa
items.description: A restored Belle Époque palace turned boutique house between Chamberí and Chueca — a Natura Bissé spa and quiet good taste.

items.name: The Principal Madrid
items.description: An early-20th-century building crowned by one of Madrid's great rooftops, at the head of Gran Vía.

items.name: The Westin Palace, Madrid
items.description: A 1912 grand hotel between the Prado and the Thyssen — its stained-glass rotunda one of the city's great rooms.

items.name: Gran Hotel Inglés
items.description: Madrid's oldest luxury hotel, reborn — a jewel-box in the literary quarter, restored with real depth of character.

items.name: Brach Madrid
items.description: Philippe Starck's exuberant, botanical Madrid house — a lush, design-forward stay near the Salamanca boutiques.

items.name: CoolRooms Palacio de Atocha
items.description: A restored palace near Atocha and the Reina Sofía, with a rooftop pool over the old town.

items.name: Only YOU Boutique Hotel Madrid
items.description: A design-led townhouse in the heart of Chueca — warm, sociable and well-placed for the city's most vibrant quarter.

items.name: Only YOU Hotel Atocha
items.description: A polished, contemporary house near Atocha station and the Retiro — easy connections and a rooftop terrace.

items.name: Museo Nacional del Prado
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Paseo del Prado and Buen Retiro, a landscape of Arts and Sciences (2021)
items.description: Spain's crown jewel of a picture gallery: Velázquez's Las Meninas, Goya's Black Paintings and the largest hoard of Bosch and Titian anywhere. Book a private out-of-hours or expert-led tour so a multi-generational family can stand alone before the masterpieces before the crowds arrive.

items.name: Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Paseo del Prado and Buen Retiro (2021)
items.description: Home to Picasso's Guernica, which commands its own hushed room, alongside the country's greatest collection of Dalí and Miró. A private guide makes the modern-art narrative land for teenagers and grandparents alike.

items.name: Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Paseo del Prado and Buen Retiro (2021)
items.description: The third point of the Golden Triangle, a former private aristocratic collection that fills the gaps the Prado and Reina Sofía leave — from early Italian gold-ground panels to Hopper and Impressionism. Its scale is human, ideal for a gentle, unhurried afternoon.

items.name: Palacio Real de Madrid (Royal Palace)
items.description: One of the largest palaces in Europe with over 3,000 rooms — grander than Versailles or Buckingham — where the Throne Room, Royal Armoury and Stradivarius collection dazzle. Private after-hours access can be arranged for discreet visits.

items.name: Catedral de la Almudena
items.description: Madrid's neo-Gothic cathedral faces the Royal Palace across the Plaza de la Armería, its brightly coloured modern ceiling a surprise inside a classical shell. Climb to the dome for a quiet rooftop panorama over the old town.

items.name: Parque del Buen Retiro (El Retiro)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Paseo del Prado and Buen Retiro (2021)
items.description: The city's green lung and former royal pleasure garden, made for rowing on the boating lake, strolling shaded avenues and letting children run free. Its rose garden and grand monuments reward a slow morning walk.

items.name: Palacio de Cristal del Retiro
items.description: A shimmering 1887 glass-and-iron pavilion set beside a pond in the Retiro, one of Madrid's most photographed structures. Note it is closed for restoration until around 2027, though its striking exterior — currently wrapped in Reina Sofía art interventions — is still worth the walk.

items.name: Plaza Mayor
items.description: The grand arcaded 17th-century square at the heart of Habsburg Madrid, ringed by frescoed facades and framed by nine stone archways. Best at early morning or evening when the day-trippers thin and the porticoes empty out.

items.name: Puerta del Sol
items.description: The symbolic centre of Spain, marked by the Kilometre Zero plaque from which all the country's roads are measured and the bear-and-strawberry-tree statue. A useful orienting point and the beating pulse of the city.

items.name: Gran Vía
items.description: Madrid's early-20th-century grand boulevard of belle-époque and art-deco towers, cinemas and rooftop bars — the 'Spanish Broadway'. Walk it at dusk when the facades light up, or catch a Spanish-language musical.

items.name: Mercado de San Miguel
items.description: A beautiful 1916 wrought-iron market turned gourmet food hall beside Plaza Mayor, where stalls run from Galician shellfish to Rodrigo de la Calle's Michelin-starred paella. Grazing here suits mixed groups and there are plenty of vegetable and cheese counters for veg-aware guests.

items.name: El Rastro
items.description: Spain's largest open-air flea market, spilling down La Latina's streets every Sunday morning with antiques, leather, prints and curios. Follow it with tapas and a vermouth in the surrounding taverns, a cherished local Sunday ritual.

items.name: Templo de Debod
items.description: A genuine 2nd-century-BC Egyptian temple, gifted to Spain and re-erected on a hill west of the centre, mirrored in a reflecting pool. It is Madrid's most romantic sunset spot, when the stones glow amber over the sierra.

items.name: Azotea del Círculo de Bellas Artes
items.description: The rooftop terrace of the century-old fine-arts club, 56 metres up, delivers a 360-degree sweep over Gran Vía, Cibeles and the tiled skyline. Come at golden hour with a cocktail for the most elegant view in the city.

items.name: Teatro Real (Royal Opera House)
items.description: Madrid's 1850 opera house, facing the Royal Palace, stages world-class opera and ballet under lavish gilt and superb acoustics. A private box turns an evening into an occasion for a family or a discreet party.

items.name: Corral de la Morería
credentials: MICHELIN Guide — Corral de la Morería Gastronómico, One Star
items.description: Widely regarded as the finest flamenco tablao in the world, hosting legendary dancers since 1956 in an intimate room where you dine as you watch. Its separate gastronomic space under chef David García holds a Michelin star — a rare pairing of art and haute cuisine.

items.name: Estadio Santiago Bernabéu
items.description: Real Madrid's newly rebuilt cathedral of football, where the Bernabéu Tour walks you onto the pitch, through the dressing room and past the trophy room. A thrill for children and lifelong fans; VIP and matchday hospitality can be arranged discreetly.

items.name: DiverXO
items.description: Chef Dabiz Muñoz's boundary-smashing tasting menu is the only three-Michelin-star table in Madrid and ranks among the world's top five restaurants. A theatrical, once-in-a-trip splurge; the kitchen accommodates dietary requests with advance notice.

items.name: Barrio de Salamanca — the Golden Mile
items.description: Madrid's most refined district, where Calle Serrano and Calle Ortega y Gasset line up Loewe, Chanel, Dior and Spain's finest ateliers amid grand 19th-century mansions. The natural base for luxury shopping and elegant, unhurried lunches.

items.name: Museo Sorolla
items.description: The preserved home, studio and Andalusian-inspired garden of Joaquín Sorolla, Spain's master of light, hung with over a thousand of his luminous canvases. A serene, intimate escape that feels worlds away from the tourist trail.

items.name: Museo Lázaro Galdiano
items.description: The former mansion of a financier-collector, four floors of Goya, El Greco, Zurbarán, jewellery and ivories displayed in opulent private-house rooms. One of Madrid's most rewarding hidden gems, rarely crowded.

items.name: Museo Cerralbo
items.description: A 19th-century aristocrat's palace frozen in time, its ballroom, chandeliers, tapestries and armour left exactly as the Marquis of Cerralbo arranged them. An intimate window into how Madrid's nobility once lived.

items.name: Real Jardín Botánico
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Paseo del Prado and Buen Retiro (2021)
items.description: An 18th-century royal botanical garden of some 5,000 plant species right beside the Prado, laid out in tranquil terraces and glasshouses. A calming green interval between museum visits, easy for elders and children.

items.name: Monasterio de las Descalzas Reales
items.description: A still-working convent of Franciscan nuns founded in 1559 in a former royal palace, concealing an astonishing hoard of tapestries, paintings and a frescoed grand staircase. Guided visits only, which keeps this treasure blissfully quiet.

items.name: Real Basílica de San Francisco el Grande
items.description: A neoclassical basilica crowned by one of the largest domes in Europe, its interior a gilded blaze of frescoes and canvases including an early Goya. Underrated and often near-empty despite its splendour.

items.name: Ermita de San Antonio de la Florida
items.description: A tiny hermitage whose dome Goya frescoed in 1798 — and beneath which the painter himself is buried. A jewel-box of a stop, moving for anyone who has just seen his work in the Prado.

items.name: CaixaForum Madrid & Vertical Garden
items.description: A Herzog & de Meuron arts centre appearing to float above the street, fronted by a living wall of 15,000 plants — the first vertical garden in Spain. Ambitious rotating exhibitions make it a reliable cultural draw beside the Golden Triangle.

items.name: Barrio de las Letras (Literary Quarter)
items.description: The old haunt of Cervantes, Lope de Vega and Spain's Golden Age writers, now a lattice of pedestrian lanes with literary quotes underfoot, wine bars and antique shops. A characterful stroll between the Prado and Puerta del Sol.

items.name: La Latina tapas crawl
items.description: Madrid's most atmospheric tapas district, its Cava Baja and Cava Alta streets packed with historic taverns pouring vermouth and plating croquetas and tortilla. Many kitchens do excellent vegetable and egg dishes, easy for veg-aware guests to graze happily.

items.name: Malasaña
items.description: The bohemian, design-forward barrio born of Madrid's 1980s countercultural Movida, now full of vintage boutiques, specialty coffee and independent galleries. A younger, creative counterpoint for teenagers and design lovers.

items.name: Chueca
items.description: Madrid's stylish, welcoming and famously vibrant quarter, dense with concept stores, terraces and some of the city's best modern restaurants around Mercado de San Antón. Lively yet easy, with rooftop dining that suits mixed groups.

items.name: Faro de Moncloa
items.description: A 92-metre observation tower with a glass-walled deck giving a clean, elevated panorama over the western parks, the sierra and the whole city grid. A quick, uncrowded way to grasp Madrid's layout on arrival.

items.name: Matadero Madrid
items.description: A vast former slaughterhouse reborn as a raw, buzzing contemporary-arts campus of cinemas, exhibition halls, design studios and theatre. A window into today's creative Madrid, and a striking piece of industrial reuse.

items.name: Madrid Río & Puente de Toledo
items.description: A riverside park reclaimed by burying the ring road, now a leafy ribbon of walkways, playgrounds and beach-fountains along the Manzanares. A relaxed, family-friendly counterpoint to the museums, best on foot or by bicycle.

items.name: Plaza de Cibeles & Palacio de Cibeles rooftop
items.description: The city's most iconic fountain and civic square, with the wedding-cake CentroCentro palace beside it offering a viewing terrace, Mirador Madrid, over the rooftops. The junction of the Paseo del Prado's grand ceremonial axis.

items.name: Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando
items.description: A superb, blessedly quiet picture gallery holding Goyas — including his own self-portraits — plus Zurbarán, Rubens and El Greco, where the great painter once served as director. The connoisseur's alternative to the Prado's crowds.

items.name: El Corte Inglés Gourmet Experience, Callao
items.description: A top-floor food hall and terrace with a head-on view of the Gran Vía's illuminated Schweppes building and rooftops. Casual, high-energy and easy for a mixed-age group wanting a drink with a view.

items.name: Museo Arqueológico Nacional
items.description: Spain's national archaeology museum, whose star is the enigmatic Iberian sculpture the Lady of Elche, alongside Roman mosaics and Visigothic treasures. Beautifully modernised and rarely overwhelming — good for curious children.

items.name: Toledo
items.area: Day trip — approx. 70 km / 35 min by high-speed train
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic City of Toledo
items.description: A medieval hilltop city encircled by the Tagus where Christian, Muslim and Jewish worlds fused, home to El Greco's greatest works and a soaring Gothic cathedral. A private guide and car make an unforgettable full day; its whole historic city is a UNESCO site.

items.name: Segovia
items.area: Day trip — approx. 90 km / 30 min by high-speed train
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Old Town of Segovia and its Aqueduct
items.description: A storybook town crowned by a Roman aqueduct of 20,000 mortar-free granite blocks and the turreted Alcázar that inspired Disney. Lunch on the region's famed roast — or lighter Castilian fare for veg-aware guests — before the drive back.

items.name: El Escorial (Real Monasterio de San Lorenzo)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Monastery and Site of the Escurial
items.description: Philip II's austere granite monastery-palace at the foot of the sierra, part royal mausoleum, part library, part basilica, and one of Spain's most powerful monuments. Cool mountain air and a grand setting make it an easy, rewarding half-day.

items.name: Aranjuez
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Aranjuez Cultural Landscape
items.description: A royal spring retreat of palaces and formal riverside gardens along the Tagus, all fountains, tree-lined avenues and 18th-century calm. Arrive on the vintage Strawberry Train in season for a gentle, multi-generational outing.

items.name: Alcalá de Henares
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — University and Historic Precinct of Alcalá de Henares
items.description: The world's first planned university city and Cervantes's birthplace, with a golden-stone historic quarter and Spain's most storied lecture halls. A cultured, easy escape that pairs literary heritage with excellent Castilian tapas.

items.name: Chinchón
items.description: A perfectly preserved medieval town built around a circular, galleried Plaza Mayor that doubles as a bullring, ringed by taverns pouring the local anís. A charming, off-the-beaten-track lunch stop far from the crowds.

items.name: DiverXO
items.description: Dabiz Muñoz's wild, world-beating three-star canvas — the most audacious tasting menu in Spain, and one of the greatest on earth.

items.name: Deessa
items.description: Quique Dacosta's Mediterranean haute cuisine in the Ritz's Belle Époque splendour — two stars beside the Prado.

items.name: Coque
items.description: The Sandoval brothers' theatre of a restaurant — a five-act journey from cellar to kitchen to table, held at two stars.

items.name: Paco Roncero Restaurante
items.description: Paco Roncero's avant-garde cooking inside the grand Casino de Madrid — technical, playful, two stars.

items.name: DSTAgE
items.description: Diego Guerrero's raw, industrial-chic room and free-thinking cooking — one of Madrid's most personal two-star tables.

items.name: Smoked Room
items.description: Dani García's fire-and-smoke haute cuisine — a small, intense counter built around the embers, at two stars.

items.name: Ramón Freixa Atelier
items.description: Ramón Freixa's signature cooking, back at two stars in an intimate new atelier — precise, considered, personal.

items.name: A'Barra
items.description: Product-driven cooking of real refinement, and a live-fire counter that is a show in itself.

items.name: El Invernadero
items.description: Rodrigo de la Calle's temple to the vegetable — 'gastrobotánica' cooking that puts produce centre-stage.

items.name: Saddle
items.description: Grand, gracious service and classical-contemporary cooking — a room that revived the art of the trolley and the table-side flourish.

items.name: Yugo the Bunker
items.area: Barrio de las Letras (Calle San Blas)
items.description: A Japanese-Spanish counter and a hidden 'bunker' below — Julián Mármol's cult sushi and kaiseki.

items.name: La Tasquería
items.description: Javi Estévez's ode to offal — the humblest cuts turned into something dazzling, and a star for the effort.

items.name: Clos Madrid
items.description: Marcos Granda's produce-led Mediterranean cooking and an exceptional cellar — a sommelier's restaurant.

items.name: Corral de la Morería Gastronómico
items.description: A tiny, four-table gastronomic room inside the world's great flamenco tablao — dinner and pure flamenco in one night.

items.name: Gaytán
items.description: Javier Aranda's minimalist room around an open kitchen — precise, seasonal cooking under a striking geometric ceiling.

items.name: Ricardo Sanz Wellington
items.description: The godfather of Spanish-Japanese fusion — Ricardo Sanz's nigiri and Mediterranean-inflected sushi at the Wellington.

items.name: RavioXO
items.description: Dabiz Muñoz's dumpling house — the DiverXO imagination poured into pasta and dumplings from around the world.

items.name: Ugo Chan
items.description: Hugo Muñoz's free-wheeling Spanish-Japanese cooking — one of the city's most exciting recent stars.

items.name: Desde 1911
items.description: A fish-house of extraordinary quality from a historic fishmonger — the finest seafood, treated with reverence.

items.name: Quimbaya
items.description: Edwin Rodríguez's refined Colombian cooking — the first star for a kitchen bringing South America to Madrid.

items.name: Cebo
items.area: Centro (Hotel Urban, Carrera de San Jerónimo)
items.description: Contemporary Spanish cooking with a Levantine hand, inside the design-led Hotel Urban.

items.name: Santerra
items.description: Miguel Carretero's cooking rooted in the Spanish countryside — game, croquetas and produce done seriously.

items.name: Gofio
items.area: Barrio de las Letras (Calle Lope de Vega)
items.description: Safe Cruz's tribute to Canary Islands cooking — a tiny room bringing the archipelago's produce and culture to Madrid.

items.name: OSA
items.description: A young couple's produce-led tasting menu by the river — tradition and innovation in a serene, out-of-the-way room.

items.name: Toki
items.description: Marcos Granda's intimate omakase counter — precise, seasonal Japanese cooking in a hushed, tiny room.

items.name: VelascoAbellá
items.description: Óscar Velasco and Montse Abellá's market-driven cooking — a first star for two of Spain's most respected hands.

items.name: La Tasquita de Enfrente
items.description: A beloved market-cuisine institution behind Gran Vía — Juanjo López's produce so good the menu changes by the morning.

items.name: Sobrino de Botín
credentials: Guinness World Record — world's oldest restaurant
items.description: The oldest restaurant on earth, open since 1725 — cochinillo and cordero from the original wood-fired oven.

items.name: Tripea
items.description: Roberto Martínez Foronda's tiny market stall doing vivid Asian-Peruvian fusion — one of Madrid's most joyful tables.

items.name: Bacira
items.description: A trio of chefs weaving Mediterranean, Japanese and Peruvian threads — creative, generous, always full.

items.name: Kappo
items.description: Mario Payán's Japanese counter — an honest, affordable omakase and one of the city's best sushi seats for the price.

items.name: Casa Macareno
items.description: An old-fashioned Madrid tavern reborn — traditional Spanish cooking and a bar, done with real care.

items.name: Tepic
items.description: Honest, vibrant Mexican cooking in the heart of Chueca — a Bib Gourmand favourite for good, affordable food.

items.name: Taberna Pedraza
items.description: Classic Spanish taberna cooking of the highest order — the tortilla and croquetas that locals argue are the city's best.

items.name: Lakasa
items.area: Chamberí (Plaza del Descubridor Diego de Ordás)
items.description: César Martín's warm, produce-led cooking — an inventive neighbourhood room that has kept its Bib for years.

items.name: Gin Bar, Santo Mauro
credentials: Inside a MICHELIN One-Key hotel — a bar of real standing
items.description: An Art Deco cocktail bar in a duke's mansion, channelling old New York — the most discreet drink in the city.

items.name: Charrada — Four Seasons Madrid
credentials: Inside a MICHELIN Two-Key, Forbes 5-Star hotel — a bar of international standing
items.description: A polished cocktail bar inside the Four Seasons at Canalejas — expert drinks in the city's finest new luxury house.

items.name: Salmón Gurú
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars 2025 (No. 37) — the highest-ranked bar in Madrid
items.description: Madrid's globally-ranked cocktail bar — Diego Cabrera's high-energy, comic-book den of bold, laboratory-made drinks.

items.name: Angelita Madrid
items.description: A dual wine bar and cocktail lab from the Villalón brothers — 500 labels upstairs, farm-to-glass drinks below.

items.name: Círculo de Bellas Artes — Azotea
credentials: Atop a Bien de Interés Cultural landmark — the city's most celebrated rooftop
items.description: The rooftop of Madrid's grand 1880s arts club — the definitive panorama over Gran Vía and the Metropolis dome.

items.name: Picalagartos Sky Bar
credentials: A landmark Gran Vía rooftop, atop the NH Collection Gran Vía
items.description: A sleek rooftop over the theatre-lit canyon of Gran Vía — cocktails with the city's grandest avenue at your feet.

items.name: Ginkgo Sky Bar
credentials: A landmark rooftop, atop the VP Plaza España Design hotel
items.description: A twelfth-floor rooftop and pool over Plaza de España — cocktails with the Royal Palace and Sierra beyond.

items.name: Palosanto — The Madrid EDITION
credentials: Atop a MICHELIN One-Key hotel — a destination rooftop
items.description: The EDITION's buzzy rooftop over the old centre — a pool, a scene and a considered drink under the Madrid sky.

items.title: The Prado at opening or in the last free hours
items.description: Go straight to the Velázquez and Goya rooms before the crowds thicken, then stop when you tire rather than forcing the whole collection.

items.title: A proper tablao flamenco in the old quarter
items.description: Book an intimate room such as Corral de la Morería rather than a tourist dinner-show, and sit close.

items.title: Sunday morning at El Rastro and the tapas that follow
items.description: Work the flea market early, then settle into the bars around La Latina for vermouth and small plates as the neighbourhood fills.

items.title: An afternoon in the Retiro and the Crystal Palace
items.description: Row on the lake, then walk to the glass Palacio de Cristal for whatever installation is showing inside it.

plan.heading: 3 days in Madrid, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private tour of the Prado at opening, focused on Velazquez, Goya and Bosch.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Reina Sofia for Picasso's Guernica, then a walk in the Retiro to the Crystal Palace.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at DiverXO, Dabiz Munoz's three-Michelin room, booked well ahead.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Royal Palace and its armoury, then the gardens and the neighbouring cathedral.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The lanes of the Barrio de Las Letras and Plaza Mayor, then jamon and sherry at a classic taberna.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Aperitivo on the rooftop of the Hotel Riu or the Four Seasons Dani, then dinner at Santceloni or DSTAgE.

days.title: Toledo and the tables of Madrid

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive to Toledo for the Cathedral, El Greco's Burial of the Count of Orgaz, and the old Jewish quarter.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Return via lunch, then the Thyssen-Bornemisza to complete the Golden Triangle.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A final dinner at Coque, the Sandoval brothers' Michelin room, ending in its cellar.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Barrio de las Letras / Huertas
items.description: Literary, walkable and central, close to the Prado triangle; suits first-time visitors who want everything on foot.

items.name: Salamanca
items.description: The city's polished, moneyed grid of flagship boutiques and quiet streets; suits those who want calm and good shopping.

items.name: Malasaña / Chueca
items.description: Younger, design-led and lively after dark; suits travellers who want the bars and the buzz on their doorstep.

events.name: Fiestas de San Isidro
events.note: Madrid's patron-saint festival brings open-air verbenas, chotis dancing and concerts across the old city.

events.name: Mad Cool Festival
events.note: The city's major international music festival, held over four days at the Iberdrola Music grounds in Villaverde.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Madrid Barajas (MAD), where a chauffeured car collects you and reaches the centre in around twenty-five minutes.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The centre is walkable and the metro excellent; a discerning traveller keeps a private driver for the museums, evenings and day trips to Toledo or Segovia.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Strong 5G citywide; a Spain or EU eSIM works instantly and hotel wifi is reliable.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Euro; cards and contactless are standard, carry a little cash for tapas bars and taxis, and tipping is light with rounding up considered generous.

onGround.note: The Barrio de Salamanca and the streets around the Prado are the refined places to stay; the city dines late, so reserve for 9:30pm or later, and reserve the Prado and Reina Sofia in advance.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: April-June and September-October are ideal: warm, dry, clear. Avoid July-August, when the high plateau bakes past 35 C and locals leave the city, and the coldest snaps of January.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No non-stop from India. Air India flies Delhi-Madrid one-stop; cleaner premium routings are one-stop via Gulf hubs (Qatar via Doha, Emirates via Dubai, Etihad via Abu Dhabi) or via European hubs into Madrid Barajas (~12-14h total). Qatar Qsuite via Doha is the strongest business cabin; Barajas Terminal 4S handles most one-world/Iberia arrivals, so match your hub to your onward cabin.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required; routine EU standards. One of Europe's safer capitals; ordinary big-city pickpocketing on the metro and around Sol/Gran Via is the main caution. Tap water is excellent and safe to drink.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Workable for vegetarians though Spanish cuisine is meat-heavy, so choose venues deliberately; Jain needs clear briefing (garlic, jamon and fish stock are pervasive). Good Indian options, e.g. Benares and Swagat, plus dedicated vegetarian spots like Vega and El Huerto de Lucas.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Madrid, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Mahé — TripAgent
seo.description: Mahé, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Mahé
hero.tagline: Granite-boulder beaches and jungle peaks on the Indian Ocean.

ourTake.lede: Mahé is where you land and where you should linger a day or two, but the Seychelles reveal themselves on Praslin and La Digue — plan the inter-island hops in. On Mahé itself, trade Beau Vallon's crowds for the harder-to-reach south — Anse Intendance and Petite Anse are the beaches you'll remember. Rent a car and do the cross-island mountain road; the Morne Seychellois forest is the island's overlooked half.
ourTake.comeIf: You want granite-boulder beaches and rare seclusion, visa-free, with Mumbai close.
ourTake.skipIf: You want nightlife or sightseeing; the islands reward stillness and swimming.

firstLook.heroCaption: seychelles destination

grid.caption: Modern pool villa with palms and umbrella
purple allium blooms in soft focus

whenToGo.blurb: April-May and October-November bring the calmest seas and clearest skies between the trade winds; expect windier water and swell at the height of each monsoon.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Sep, Oct, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Mahé. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: North Island, a Luxury Collection Resort
items.area: North Island (private island, ~30 km off Mahé; access by helicopter or boat)
credentials: Marriott's The Luxury Collection — the marque's Seychelles flagship
Named among the world's most beautiful hotels; World Luxury Hotel Awards winner
items.description: The icon of the Seychelles — a barefoot private island of just eleven hand-built villas, where the whole island is yours and the price of entry buys near-total seclusion.

items.name: Six Senses Zil Pasyon
items.area: Félicité (private island, near La Digue; boat or helicopter transfer)
credentials: Condé Nast Traveler — Triple Crown Award; Hot List on opening
items.description: Thirty pool villas scattered across a granite-boulder island — the most complete expression of Six Senses wellness in the Indian Ocean, with a spa carved into the rocks.

items.name: Fregate Island Private
items.area: Frégate Island (private island, easternmost of the granitic Seychelles; helicopter transfer)
credentials: Oetker Collection — the group's Indian Ocean private island
Anse Victorin named among the world's best beaches (The Times; CNN Travel)
items.description: An Oetker Collection private island of sixteen clifftop villas above Anse Victorin — a beach repeatedly called one of the world's best — run as much as a conservation estate as a resort.

items.name: Four Seasons Resort Seychelles
items.area: Mahé (Petite Anse / Baie Lazare, southwest coast)
credentials: MICHELIN Guide hotel selection (a hotel listing, not a dining star)
items.description: The benchmark for polished, family-capable luxury on the main island — treehouse-style villas terraced down a jungle hillside to a private horseshoe bay.

items.name: Anantara Maia Seychelles Villas
credentials: Anantara / Minor Hotels flagship — award-winning gardens and spa
Recognised across the luxury travel trade for its all-villa, butler-led model
items.description: Thirty villas on a private peninsula wrapped in thirty acres of jungle — a butler-for-every-villa, all-inclusive sanctuary designed by Bill Bensley.

items.name: Raffles Seychelles
items.area: Praslin (Anse Volbert / Baie Sainte Anne, north coast)
credentials: World Travel Awards — Indian Ocean's Leading Luxury Resort and Leading Honeymoon Resort (multiple years)
Forbes Travel Guide-recognised; Condé Nast Traveller Hot List (opening)
items.description: Praslin's grande dame — 86 hillside pool villas above the beach, with the storied Raffles service and easy reach of the Vallée de Mai and La Digue.

items.name: Constance Ephélia
items.area: Mahé (Port Launay, northwest coast, on the Port Launay Marine Park)
credentials: Constance Hotels flagship — Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice Awards nominee
Award-winning Spa de Constance (one of the region's largest)
items.description: A sprawling estate across two beaches and 120 hectares, home to one of the largest spas in the Indian Ocean — the most versatile big resort on Mahé.

items.name: Mango House Seychelles, LXR Hotels & Resorts
items.area: Mahé (Anse aux Poules Bleues, Baie Lazare, southwest coast)
credentials: Hilton's LXR Hotels & Resorts — the group's Seychelles property
MICHELIN Guide hotel selection (a hotel listing, not a dining star)
items.description: The former home of Italian photographer Gian Paolo Barbieri reborn as a design-led boutique retreat — the most stylish, character-rich address on Mahé.

items.name: Vallée de Mai, the primeval palm forest
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Vallée de Mai Nature Reserve (inscribed 1983)
items.description: A UNESCO-listed valley where you walk through a forest almost unchanged since prehistory — the world's last great stand of the coco de mer palm, whose 20kg double-lobed nut is the largest seed on Earth and whose suggestive shape once fed legends that this was the original Garden of Eden. Go early with a naturalist guide, listen for the rare Seychelles black parrot found nowhere else, and let the cathedral hush of the primeval forest do the rest.

items.name: Anse Source d'Argent, the granite-boulder beach
items.description: The most photographed beach in the world — a string of shallow, glass-clear coves screened by sculpted pink granite boulders 750 million years old, reached on foot through the L'Union Estate coconut plantation. Come at low tide in the soft late-afternoon light, ideally by bicycle from the jetty, for the barefoot, camera-in-hand honeymoon picture the Seychelles is famous for.

items.name: Anse Lazio, Praslin's crescent
credentials: Repeatedly ranked among the world's best beaches (TripAdvisor Travellers' Choice; CNN)
items.description: A wide arc of powder sand framed by takamaka trees and warm granite, repeatedly ranked among the best beaches on the planet by CNN and TripAdvisor and calm enough for a long swim off the rocks at either end. Arrive mid-morning before the day-trippers, take lunch at one of the two beach restaurants, and treat the whole afternoon as the definition of unhurried.

items.name: Anse Georgette, the hidden gem
credentials: Ranked among the world's 50 best beaches (World's 50 Beaches)
items.description: A perfect, near-empty white bay inside the grounds of Constance Lémuria — access is free but must be arranged in advance if you are not a resort guest, which keeps the crowds away and the sand pristine. For couples chasing the barefoot-billionaire seclusion the Seychelles promises, this is the quiet counterpoint to busier Anse Lazio.

items.name: Curieuse Island giant-tortoise day trip
items.description: A twenty-minute boat hop lands you on a russet-earthed island where some 300 free-roaming Aldabra giant tortoises graze among the mangroves and a boardwalk threads a rare coco-de-mer-and-mangrove landscape. Pair it with a Creole barbecue lunch on the sand and a snorkel stop; a private charter turns a good excursion into an unhurried, uncrowded one.

items.name: St Pierre islet snorkelling
items.description: A picture-book cluster of granite boulders crowned with palms, ringed by some of Praslin's clearest water and busiest reef fish — the classic snorkel stop on a Curieuse day trip. Charter a private boat to arrive before the group excursions and you may have the whole jewel-like islet to yourselves.

items.name: Cousin Island seabird sanctuary
items.description: A strictly protected conservation island reached only on a guided landing, where thousands of nesting seabirds, hawksbill turtles and the once-vanishing Seychelles magpie-robin have been brought back from the brink. Visitor numbers are capped and mornings only — a rare, deeply intimate wildlife encounter for travellers who value pristine nature over crowds.

items.name: Aride Island, the northernmost bird island
items.description: The Seychelles' most important seabird island — over a million birds and the largest colonies of some species on Earth — landing on a wild, roadless nature reserve open only a few days a week and closed in the roughest season. A private boat and a calm-sea day make it one of the archipelago's great, little-seen natural spectacles.

items.name: Beau Vallon beach
items.description: Mahé's long, easy, palm-backed north-coast bay — the most reliable place on the island for a proper year-round swim, with sunset paddleboarding, a Wednesday-evening bazaar and casual Creole grills a short stroll away. An unfussy home base for a family who want the sea on the doorstep rather than a trek to a wild cove.

items.name: Anse Intendance, the wild south beach
items.description: A broad, undeveloped stretch of white sand and rolling surf in Mahé's untamed south, framed by granite headlands and backed only by takamaka trees — the beach beside Banyan Tree and among the most dramatic on the island. Magnificent for a long walk and a photograph; the currents are strong when the trade winds blow, so it's for watching the ocean's power more than swimming.

items.name: Anse Takamaka
items.description: A gently curving south-coast bay of pale sand and clear water named for the shade trees that line it, famous for its sunsets and, on calm days, its snorkelling. Chez Batista on the sand serves grilled fish with your toes in the sand — the essence of a slow Mahé afternoon.

items.name: Petite Anse
items.description: A flawless, sheltered cove within the Four Seasons estate but open to the public — reached down a short forest path, with soft powdery sand and gentle water that make it one of the south coast's most swimmable beaches. A discreet, resort-tended stretch of sand for couples who want beauty without the trek.

items.name: Anse Soleil & Anse Soleil beach
items.description: A tiny, boulder-flanked south-western cove at the end of a steep road, with excellent snorkelling straight off the sand and a beloved barefoot Creole café above it. Small, sheltered and gloriously out of the way — the reward for a driver who knows the back lanes of Baie Lazare.

items.name: Sir Selwyn Selwyn-Clarke Market
items.description: The beating heart of the tiny capital since 1840 — a covered market piled with tropical fruit, vanilla pods, cinnamon bark, chilli and the morning's reef catch, best at 8am when the fishmongers set out. A short, sensory, grounding stop between beaches, and the place to understand how Creole, African, Indian and French flavours met on these islands.

items.name: The Clock Tower (Little Big Ben)
items.description: The silver Victorian clock tower erected in 1903 at the crossroads of the capital, modelled on a London original and the postcard symbol of Victoria — one of the smallest capital cities in the world. A five-minute stroll takes in the tower, the market and the Hindu temple; a gentle way to feel the island's colonial layer.

items.name: Arul Mihu Navasakthi Vinayagar Temple
items.description: The only Hindu temple in the Seychelles — a vividly painted gopuram on Quincy Street, built in 1992 and dedicated to Lord Vinayagar (Ganesha), serving the island's small Tamil-descended community. A moment of the familiar for Indian travellers, and a reminder of how far the diaspora and its gods have travelled across the Indian Ocean.

items.name: Seychelles National Botanical Gardens
items.description: A century-old garden on the edge of the capital with 200-plus species — coco de mer palms, a spice grove, orchids, a colony of fruit bats and a paddock of feedable Aldabra giant tortoises. A cool, shaded, easy hour for grandparents and children alike, a short drive from the harbour.

items.name: The National Museum of History
items.description: The capital's museum of Seychelles history housed in a restored colonial building — the Stone of Possession that claimed the islands for France, pirate lore, and the Creole story of settlement, slavery and independence. A short, well-curated context stop for travellers who like to understand a place before they lie on its beaches.

items.name: Morne Seychellois National Park
items.description: The mist-forested spine of Mahé — a protected mountain wilderness of cloud forest, endemic pitcher plants and hidden trails climbing to the island's 905m high point. The wild green heart behind the beaches, best explored on foot with a guide who can read the endemic flora.

items.name: The Copolia Trail
items.description: The island's most rewarding short hike — an hour through shaded palm forest to a bald granite dome at nearly 500m, with an eagle's-eye sweep over Victoria, the Sainte Anne islands and, on a clear day, Praslin and La Digue. Manageable for most fitness levels and the single best view on Mahé for the effort.

items.name: Morne Blanc & the Tea Factory
items.description: A steep, short nature trail climbing to a sheer-drop lookout over Mahé's west coast, beginning near the little hillside tea plantation that has grown Seychelles tea since 1962. Combine the walk with a stop at the tea factory shop for vanilla and citronella teas — a fragrant, cool interlude high above the sea.

items.name: Sauzier Waterfall (Port Launay)
items.description: A ten-minute walk through a private garden brings you to a jungle waterfall tumbling into a cool freshwater pool you can swim in — a rare, refreshing counterpoint to the salt and the sun. Easy enough for children, quiet enough for couples, and a lovely hidden gem near the west-coast beaches.

items.name: Mission Lodge (Venn's Town) viewpoint
items.description: The ruins of a 19th-century school for the children of freed slaves, high on the Sans Souci road, with a hilltop gazebo built for Queen Elizabeth II's 1972 visit that frames a sweeping view of Mahé's forested west. A poignant piece of history and one of the island's most cinematic viewpoints in a single easy stop.

items.name: Takamaka Rum Distillery, La Plaine St André
items.description: The island's craft rum distillery set in a restored 1792 plantation house, with guided tours, tastings, resident giant tortoises named Taka and Maka, a garden restaurant and Friday-night cocktails and live music. A relaxed, characterful half-day and the obvious place to taste — and take home — the Seychelles' signature spirit.

items.name: Domaine de Val des Prés craft village
items.description: A cluster of traditional wooden Creole houses restored as artisan workshops — model boat-builders, jewellers, potters and a plantation-house restaurant serving classic island cooking. The most tangible taste of old Creole life and craft on Mahé, and a good place to buy something genuinely local.

items.name: Baie Lazare & the south-western coves
items.description: A sleepy fishing village that gives its name to the loveliest tangle of coves in Mahé's south-west — the gateway to Anse Soleil, Petite Anse and Anse Gaulette, with a hilltop church and Creole eateries. The area to base a day of unhurried cove-hopping with a private driver.

items.name: Anse Royale
items.description: A long, reef-protected east-coast beach with calm, shallow water ideal for family swimming and snorkelling at the little offshore island, backed by a friendly village and casual takeaways. An easygoing, local-feeling stretch that balances Mahé's wilder south beaches.

items.name: Eden Island
items.description: A modern marina-and-residence development off Victoria with waterfront restaurants, a small mall and the archipelago's main yacht berths — the practical launch point for many private charters and a pleasant evening stroll and dinner by the boats. Useful and comfortable rather than wild, and where a chartered yacht will likely meet you.

items.name: Grand Anse & Petite Anse, La Digue
items.description: La Digue's dramatic south-east coast — Grand Anse a wide, powerful surf beach and, over the headland on foot, the quieter, more sheltered Petite Anse and Anse Cocos. A beautiful, breezy bicycle-and-walking loop through the island's wild side, best when the sea is calm from October to April.

items.name: The ox-cart & bicycle island life of La Digue
items.description: An island with almost no cars, where the traditional way to travel is by bicycle or ox-cart along sandy lanes past pastel Creole houses and vanilla plantations. Renting a good bike for the day is the whole point of La Digue — the slowest, most charming pace in the Seychelles.

items.name: Nid d'Aigle viewpoint
items.description: The 'Eagle's Nest' — La Digue's 333m high point, reached by a steep track (best by hired local transport for part of the way, then on foot) to a panorama over the island's granite peaks and the turquoise channel to Praslin. The reward for the effort is the finest view in the inner islands.

items.name: L'Union Estate, La Digue
items.description: The historic coconut-and-vanilla plantation you pass through to reach Anse Source d'Argent — an old copra mill turned by an ox, a colonial plantation house, a vanilla plot and a pen of giant tortoises. A living slice of 19th-century island life that adds depth to the world's most photographed beach.

items.name: Sainte Anne Marine National Park
items.description: The Indian Ocean's first marine park — six islands just off Victoria, with over 150 species in the clear channels, easy snorkelling among hawksbill turtles and reef fish, and glass-bottom-boat trips for those who prefer to stay dry. A gentle, family-friendly introduction to the underwater Seychelles, minutes from the capital.

items.name: Diving the inner islands
items.description: Warm, clear water over granite drop-offs, wrecks and reefs alive with turtles, rays, whale sharks in season and the occasional reef shark — with reputable dive centres on Mahé and Praslin catering to first dives and log-book veterans alike. The archipelago's granite topography makes for some of the Indian Ocean's most atmospheric diving.

items.name: Whale-shark encounters (seasonal)
items.description: Between roughly August and October the world's largest fish gathers off Mahé's coast, and licensed operators run respectful swim-alongside snorkel trips to meet these gentle giants. A once-in-a-lifetime, strictly seasonal experience — worth timing a trip around for wildlife-minded travellers.

items.name: Turtle nesting & hatching (seasonal)
items.description: Hawksbill turtles nest by day on Seychelles beaches from roughly October to February, and on conservation-minded islands and resorts guests can quietly watch a female lay or, weeks later, hatchlings scramble to the sea. A tender, protected wildlife moment that the best luxury islands build guided programmes around.

items.name: Deep-sea game fishing
items.description: The drop-offs and banks off the Seychelles hold sailfish, marlin, wahoo, dogtooth tuna and giant trevally — some of the Indian Ocean's finest big-game and fly-fishing, from half-day trolls to serious blue-water charters. A private boat with a seasoned skipper turns it into a bespoke day at sea.

items.name: Private yacht & catamaran charter
items.description: The most luxurious way to see the Seychelles is to sail it — a crewed catamaran or motor yacht out of Eden Island, anchoring off empty beaches, snorkelling deserted reefs and dining on deck as the sun goes down. Complete privacy, your own itinerary, and the barefoot seclusion the islands are made for.

items.name: Island-hopping by helicopter
items.description: Zil Air's air-conditioned helicopters connect Mahé, Praslin, La Digue and the private-island resorts in minutes, with scenic flights that reveal the archipelago's turquoise lagoons and granite peaks from above. The fastest, most spectacular way for time-short travellers to string the best of the islands together — or to arrive at a private island in style.

items.name: A day at a private-island resort
items.description: The Seychelles' defining ultra-luxury experience — a whole island to a handful of guests, whether North Island's barefoot villas, Six Senses Zil Pasyon on Félicité, Frégate with its wild tortoise colonies or Cousine's conservation reserve. The pinnacle of the private-island escape, reached by boat or helicopter, where the beach outside your villa may be entirely your own.

items.name: Fond Ferdinand Nature Reserve
items.description: A less-visited, guided alternative to the Vallée de Mai — a steep-sided reserve with an even larger stand of coco de mer palms and, from its ridge, a rare panoramic view over Praslin and out to the neighbouring islands. Quieter and more strenuous, it rewards travellers who want the coco de mer forest with fewer people.

items.name: Côte d'Or (Anse Volbert)
items.description: Praslin's long, calm, palm-lined main beach — safe for swimming, dotted with beach restaurants and dive shops, and the departure point for boats to Curieuse, St Pierre and the bird islands. The convenient, easygoing base for a Praslin stay, with plenty for families.

items.name: Creole cuisine & a spice-trail lunch
items.description: Seychellois cooking is a fragrant crossroads — grilled bourgeois and job-fish, octopus curry, coconut and breadfruit, tamarind and chilli — and Indian palates find the spicing gloriously familiar, with good vegetarian and Indian options at the larger resorts. A long lunch at a beachside Creole table is as much a highlight here as any view.

items.name: A signature island spa ritual
items.description: The luxury resorts — Four Seasons, Constance, Six Senses, Raffles, North Island — build spas around treetop pavilions and clifftop decks, using local coconut, vanilla and frangipani in barefoot rituals to the sound of the sea. The unhurried, restorative core of a Seychelles honeymoon or escape.

items.name: '20 Degrees Sud'
items.description: Anantara Maia's signature table — a hilltop or intimate wine-cellar setting for Creole-Mediterranean cooking and hard-to-find wines, the most refined dining experience on the main island.

items.name: ZEZ
items.area: Four Seasons Resort Seychelles, Mahé (Petite Anse)
credentials: Four Seasons Resort Seychelles' signature dinner venue (Forbes Four-Star resort)
items.description: Four Seasons' hilltop restaurant, high above the bay — an inventive sharing menu at night with one of the best ocean views on the island.

items.name: Kannel
items.area: Four Seasons Resort Seychelles, Mahé (Petite Anse)
credentials: Four Seasons Resort Seychelles restaurant (Forbes Four-Star resort)
items.description: Beachside all-day dining at the Four Seasons, marrying Mediterranean flavours with Creole tradition — ceviches and salads by day, seafood and pasta by night.

items.name: Marie Antoinette
items.area: Mahé (Serret Road, St Louis, above Victoria)
credentials: One of the oldest and most celebrated Creole restaurants in the Seychelles (est. 1972); a long-standing press and guidebook fixture
items.description: The islands' most storied Creole table — a set feast of parrotfish, tuna, aubergine fritters and chicken curry served in a colonial planter's house since 1972.

items.name: Del Place
credentials: A long-running west-coast Creole seafood institution, widely recommended in Seychelles dining guides
items.description: A seafront Creole seafood house on the quiet west coast, tables almost in the water, with sunsets over the neighbouring islands.

items.name: La Plage
credentials: A landmark restaurant on Beau Vallon, the Seychelles' best-known beach, and a fixture of local dining guides
items.description: Feet-in-the-sand Italian-Creole cooking on the island's most famous beach — the archetypal Beau Vallon sundowner-and-dinner.

items.name: Boardwalk Bar & Grill
credentials: The marquee bar-and-grill on Eden Island, the Seychelles' upmarket marina development
items.description: The marina-side gathering point on Eden Island — waterfront tables, live music and a late bar, the most reliable evening scene outside the resorts.

items.name: Boat House
credentials: A long-established Beau Vallon dining-and-bar landmark
items.description: A Beau Vallon institution pairing a Creole buffet with a lively bar and live music — the beach's social anchor after dark.

items.name: The resort bars
credentials: Credentialed by the resorts themselves — see the Forbes, Condé Nast and maison hotels listed above
items.description: The honest truth of Seychelles nights: the best-made drink you'll have is almost always at your own resort — a sunset villa deck, a spa-hotel bar or an island long bar.

items.name: Katiolo
items.area: Mahé (Anse Faure, east coast, near the airport)
credentials: The Seychelles' longest-running and best-known nightclub — the only beachside disco in the country
items.description: The Seychelles' oldest and most iconic nightclub — an open-air dancefloor by the sea, and about as close as the islands get to a genuine late night out.

items.title: Anse Intendance at dawn
items.description: A wild, unprotected south-coast beach with big surf and almost no one on it early.

items.title: Sainte Anne Marine Park by boat
items.description: Snorkelling and glass-bottom drifting among six islands just off Victoria, rich with turtles and rays.

items.title: Morne Seychellois cross-island hike
items.description: Trails through cloud forest and cinnamon to the highest point in the archipelago.

items.title: Day hop to La Digue's Anse Source d'Argent
items.description: The granite-boulder beach reached by ferry and bicycle — the image the whole country is known for.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Land at Seychelles International (SEZ) on Mahé; a private car transfer reaches most of the island within 30–45 minutes, while a helicopter or short Air Seychelles hop connects you to Praslin, La Digue or a private-island resort.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver suits Mahé's winding coast roads; for island-hopping use scheduled helicopters, the Cat Cocos fast ferry, or your resort's boat.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: An Airtel or Cable & Wireless eSIM gives good 4G on the main islands; resort wifi is reliable, coverage thins on remote islets.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Seychellois rupee (SCR); cards are widely accepted and euros often quoted at resorts, with a 5–10 percent tip appreciated where service isn't added.

onGround.note: Stay in the northwest around Beau Vallon for beaches and dining or a private-island resort for total seclusion; it's low-key and barefoot-luxury in tone, the sun is fierce so plan water and shade, and the granite beaches (Anse Source d'Argent, Anse Intendance) are the ones worth the effort.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: April-May and October-November are the calm, in-between sweet spots with light winds and clear water. The May to September southeast trade winds bring breezier seas and seaweed on some beaches, while December to March is hotter, wetter and humid.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Mumbai (~4h30m) on Air India a few times weekly; otherwise connect via Colombo on SriLankan/Air Seychelles (~4h Colombo-Mahé) or via the Gulf on Emirates/Etihad/Qatar in first or business. The Gulf carriers offer the finest premium cabins, and a Colombo routing pairs naturally with a Sri Lanka stopover.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations from India (yellow-fever certificate only if transiting an endemic country); routine jabs sufficient. Tap water on Mahé is generally safe, bottled is easy to find. Very safe and private, a favoured discreet escape; no altitude concerns.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Manageable but less abundant than Mauritius; Creole cuisine is fish-forward, so vegetarians should lean on hotels, which cater well. Strict Jain travellers should arrange menus in advance with the resort (North Island, Four Seasons, Six Senses Zil Pasyon all accommodate), and Indian options exist but are limited off-property.

seo.title: Malé & the Atolls — TripAgent
seo.description: Malé & the Atolls, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Malé & the Atolls
hero.tagline: Overwater villas and luminous lagoons across scattered coral atolls.

ourTake.lede: Skip Malé itself beyond a half-day for the fish market and Hukuru Miskiy; the reason you come is the water, so spend on the atolls, not the capital. Choose one resort island and stay put rather than hopping — the seaplane transfer is half the magic, and a good house reef beats any excursion. The quiet play is a liveaboard through the Baa or Ari atolls if you actually want the diving, not just the pool.
ourTake.comeIf: You want an overwater villa, a private house reef and nothing on the agenda but each other.
ourTake.skipIf: You need a city, a night scene or things to do beyond the resort's shoreline.

items.name: Hukuru Miskiy — the Old Friday Mosque
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List — Coral Stone Mosques of the Maldives
items.description: The Maldives' oldest and most ornate mosque, built in 1658 from interlocking coral-stone blocks, every surface hand-carved — Quranic inscriptions, lacquered woodwork, and a 13th-century panel that records the arrival of Islam here. A quiet, moving half-hour that grounds a resort trip in the country's real history.

items.name: The coral-stone Munnaaru (minaret) & royal cemetery
items.description: Beside the Old Friday Mosque stands the squat, banded 17th-century minaret and a walled graveyard of intricately carved coral tombstones and sultans' mausoleums — rounded tops for women, pointed for men. It reads like an open-air museum of Maldivian craft, and it takes only minutes to see.

items.name: The Islamic Centre & Grand Friday Mosque
items.description: The gold-domed Grand Friday Mosque is Malé's landmark, holding several thousand worshippers, its interior finished in Maldivian wood-carving and Arabic calligraphy. Non-Muslim visitors can usually enter outside prayer times with modest dress — a striking counterpoint to the tiny old mosque nearby.

items.name: The National Museum, Sultan Park
items.description: Set in the last surviving building of the old royal palace, it holds sultans' thrones, lacquerware, royal parasols and pre-Islamic Buddhist coral relics — the deepest single window into the archipelago's past. A cool, calm hour for multi-generational groups between beach days.

items.name: Sultan Park
items.description: The green heart of the capital, once the grounds of the sultan's palace, now shaded gardens of tropical trees and flowering shrubs. A rare patch of quiet in dense Malé, pleasant for a stroll before or after the museum next door.

items.name: The Malé fish market
items.description: Late afternoon, dhonis unload the day's tuna and reef fish onto the harbourfront and the market fills with the theatre of the catch — the truest slice of working Maldivian life. A vivid, photogenic stop on a capital walk (busiest and best around late afternoon).

items.name: A Malé local-life walk
items.description: One of the most densely populated capitals on earth, packed onto a two-square-kilometre island — colourful lanes, tea shops (hotaa) serving short eats, the produce market and the harbour crammed with dhonis. An hour here shows the human Maldives most resort guests never glimpse.

items.name: The Artificial Beach
items.description: A man-made swimming beach on Malé's eastern seafront where the capital's families gather at sunset — food stalls, evening football, and the only place locals swim in the city. Not a resort beach, but a genuine, easy taste of everyday island leisure.

items.name: Staying in an overwater villa
items.description: The signature Maldivian experience: your own timber villa perched over a lagoon, glass floor to the reef, private deck and steps straight into warm turquoise water. For an Indian honeymoon or a milestone family trip it is the whole point of coming — barely a four-hour flight from home, and dining that top resorts tailor to vegetarian and Jain needs without fuss.

items.name: Snorkelling your resort's house reef
items.description: Many luxury islands sit on their own living reef, so world-class snorkelling begins a few fin-kicks from your villa steps — parrotfish, turtles, blacktip reef sharks and soft coral, no boat required. The gentlest way for children and first-timers to meet the ocean.

items.name: Hanifaru Bay — swimming with feeding mantas & whale sharks
items.description: In season, wind and tide funnel plankton into this small bay and hundreds of reef mantas — sometimes whale sharks too — gather to feed in a slow, cyclonic swirl, the largest known manta aggregation on earth. Snorkel-only and permit-controlled, it is one of the great wildlife spectacles anywhere, reached from Baa Atoll resorts.

items.name: Whale-shark snorkelling in South Ari Atoll
items.description: South Ari's Marine Protected Area holds the world's only documented year-round resident population of whale sharks, cruising the shallow reef shelf where you slip in and swim alongside the ocean's largest fish. Unlike everywhere else on earth there is no season to wait for — a bucket-list encounter within snorkel reach.

items.name: Diving Fish Head (Mushimasmingili Thila)
items.description: A protected pinnacle famous as one of the Maldives' finest shark dives — grey reef sharks patrol the current-swept reef by the dozen, over walls of soft coral and clouds of fusiliers. A classic on any serious diver's Maldives list.

items.name: Night-diving Maaya Thila
items.description: This coral pinnacle is a top day dive but comes alive after dark, when white-tip reef sharks hunt in packs around the lights in a genuine feeding frenzy, joined by turtles, nurse sharks and rays. One of the most electrifying night dives in the country.

items.name: Diving Banana Reef
items.description: One of the very first dive sites explored in the Maldives, a banana-shaped reef of overhangs, caves and coral gardens that's as rich at three metres as at thirty. Calm enough for newer divers yet loved by veterans — a fitting first Maldivian dive.

items.name: Diving Kandooma Thila
items.description: A long teardrop pinnacle raked by current, drawing schooling trevally and jacks, eagle rays and reef sharks around dramatic overhangs and soft-coral 'Jack's Corner'. A thrilling drift dive for the experienced.

items.name: Manta cleaning-station dives & snorkels
items.description: At coral bommies that act as manta 'cleaning stations', reef mantas queue to have parasites picked off by wrasse, hovering motionless an arm's length away. Hypnotic and reliable in season — one of the calmest, most magical wildlife encounters in the Maldives.

items.name: Night snorkelling with mantas under the lights
items.description: Several resorts rig lights off a jetty or boat at night to draw plankton — and the reef mantas that feed on it — so you float above them as they barrel-roll and somersault through the glow. A more intimate, dreamlike cousin of the daytime encounter.

items.name: The 'Sea of Stars' — bioluminescence at Vaadhoo
items.description: On dark nights the shoreline glows electric blue as disturbed plankton light up with every wave and footstep, a natural phenomenon Vaadhoo made famous. Many atolls see it seasonally; it needs no booking, just a moonless night and a walk along the water's edge.

items.name: A private sandbank picnic
items.description: Your resort ferries you to a bare crescent of white sand in the middle of the ocean — a table, a parasol, chilled champagne and nothing else for miles. The definitive Maldivian castaway moment, and a favourite for proposals and honeymoons.

items.name: A deserted-island day
items.description: A step beyond the sandbank: a full day marooned on an uninhabited palm island with a picnic, snorkel gear and a hammock, collected by dhoni at dusk. Robinson Crusoe with a private chef — pure, unhurried escape.

items.name: Sunset dolphin-watching cruise
items.description: Pods of spinner dolphins ride the bow wave of a traditional dhoni as the sky turns gold — dozens at a time, leaping and spinning clear of the water. Easy, uplifting and perfect for children and grandparents alike.

items.name: A seaplane scenic flight over the atolls
items.description: The transfer to many resorts is itself a spectacle — a barefoot-pilot Twin Otter skimming low over a mosaic of turquoise lagoons, coral rings and sandbanks. Charter a scenic loop and the aerial view of the archipelago becomes an experience in its own right.

items.name: Surfing the North Malé Atoll breaks
items.description: Consistent, warm, uncrowded reef waves — Sultans, Honky's, Chickens, Cokes and Jailbreaks all within a short boat ride, from mellow long walls to hollow barrels. The Maldives is a world-class surf destination for those who want more than a lounger, best from March to October.

items.name: Sunset fishing & traditional line-fishing
items.description: Head out on a dhoni at dusk to hand-line for snapper and grouper the old Maldivian way, then have the resort kitchen grill your catch for dinner. A gentle, sociable evening on the water that connects you to the islands' fishing soul.

items.name: Big-game & fly fishing
items.description: Beyond the reef the drop-offs hold sailfish, wahoo, dogtooth tuna and giant trevally, and the flats offer world-class saltwater fly fishing for GTs and bonefish. A serious pursuit for the angler in the family, arranged through the top resorts.

items.name: Dining at Ithaa Undersea Restaurant
items.area: Conrad Maldives Rangali Island, South Ari Atoll
items.description: The world's first all-glass undersea restaurant, five metres down with a 270-degree acrylic view of the reef swimming past over dinner. It seats just fourteen — a once-in-a-lifetime meal that has topped 'world's most extraordinary restaurants' lists for two decades.

items.name: An underwater spa treatment
items.description: A handful of resorts have built glass-walled treatment rooms below the waterline, so reef fish drift past as you're massaged. A quintessentially Maldivian indulgence — wellness with a coral-garden view.

items.name: A local-island day on Maafushi
items.description: The busiest of the inhabited 'local islands', Maafushi shows the Maldives beyond the resort bubble — a working village, a bikini beach, cafes serving Maldivian short eats, and cheap boat trips to nearby reefs. A grounding half-day contrast to five-star seclusion.

items.name: Dhigurah — the two-kilometre sandbar island
items.description: A long, slender local island fringed by what many call the finest beach in the Maldives — a powder-white spit running out to sea — and sitting right on the whale-shark protected area. Laid-back guesthouse island life with world-class snorkelling on the doorstep.

items.name: Thoddoo — the fruit island
items.description: Unusually green and flat-farmed, Thoddoo is the Maldives' watermelon and papaya basket, ringed by quiet beaches and famous for meals cooked from produce picked that morning. A gentle, agricultural side of the islands few travellers see.

items.name: The Whale Submarine dive off Malé
items.description: A real passenger submarine descends around 45 metres to a sunken reef, so non-divers — grandparents, small children — can watch snappers, reef sharks and coral through the portholes in air-conditioned comfort. A rare way to reach the deep reef without getting wet (check current operating status when planning).

items.name: A stargazing observatory night
items.description: With near-zero light pollution, the atoll skies are extraordinary — and Soneva's resident astronomers open a rooftop observatory to point a research-grade telescope at Saturn's rings and distant galaxies. Romance and wonder rolled into one after-dark experience.

items.name: Cinema Paradiso — open-air film under the stars
items.description: Soneva Fushi's over-water cinema screens classics on a giant screen while you recline on daybeds with popcorn and the lagoon lapping below. A charming, only-here evening that delights children and film-lovers alike.

items.name: Coral-restoration & marine-biology sessions
items.description: Many luxury resorts run in-house marine labs where a resident biologist takes guests out to plant coral fragments on reef frames and adopt a nursery colony. Meaningful, hands-on and genuinely educational — a highlight for older children and conscientious travellers.

items.name: Turtle snorkel safaris
items.description: Green and hawksbill turtles graze the seagrass and reef flats across the atolls, and resort guides know the spots where you can reliably swim alongside them. Slow, serene and a guaranteed thrill for first-time snorkellers.

items.name: Snorkelling a night reef with reef sharks & rays
items.description: After dark the reef changes shift — hunting moray eels, parrotfish asleep in mucus cocoons, rays gliding the sand and blacktips on the prowl, all under torchlight. A safe, guided adrenaline hit off the house reef.

items.name: A private yacht or luxury liveaboard charter
items.description: Charter a crewed yacht or dhoni to island-hop the atolls on your own schedule — remote dive sites, empty sandbanks and sunset anchorages with the family. The most flexible, private way to see a country that is 99 percent water.

items.name: Parasailing & jet-ski over the lagoon
items.description: From up under a parasail the reef structure and the resort's ring of turquoise reveal themselves in full colour, while jet-skis put the lagoon at speed. Easy, high-energy fun for teenagers and thrill-seeking multi-gen groups.

items.name: A traditional Bodu Beru drumming & dance evening
items.description: The Maldives' folk music — big-drum Bodu Beru, chanting and quickening dance — is performed on many resort and local-island beaches, often around a bonfire. A warm, rhythmic window into island culture after dinner.

items.name: Kayaking, paddleboarding & lagoon time
items.description: The glassy, waist-deep lagoons around most islands are ideal for gentle kayaking and stand-up paddleboarding, often over rays and baby sharks. Complimentary at most resorts and perfect for a slow morning with children.

items.name: A sunset champagne dhoni cruise
items.description: A curved-prow Maldivian dhoni sets out as the sun drops, the crew pouring champagne while dolphins often join the wake and the sky burns over the water. A quietly romantic ritual — the classic Maldives honeymoon evening.

items.name: A floating breakfast in your villa pool
items.description: A tray of tropical fruit, pastries and juices set afloat on your private pool or lagoon — the most photographed indulgence in the Maldives, and easily arranged veg or Jain by top resorts. Pure, playful honeymoon theatre.

items.name: A destination dinner on the beach or sandbank
items.description: Resorts stage private candle-lit dinners on a stretch of beach, a sandbank or your own deck, with a dedicated chef and butler and the menu built around you. The setting for anniversaries, proposals and quiet milestone celebrations.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Arrive at Velana International (MLE); your resort's seaplane or a private speedboat completes the transfer to the atoll, arranged and timed to your flight by the resort.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Within a private-island resort everything is walked, cycled or reached by buggy; between islands it is speedboat or seaplane, all resort-managed.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: An eSIM covers Malé and transfers, but resorts provide fast villa wifi and often a local SIM on arrival.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The rufiyaa is local but resorts bill in US dollars; cards settle everything and a 10 percent service charge is standard, with discreet extra tipping welcomed.

onGround.note: Choose a seaplane atoll for seclusion or a nearby speedboat island for shorter transfers; the country is dry outside resorts and modest dress applies in Malé, so keep alcohol and beachwear to the resort.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: The dry northeast monsoon, roughly December–April, brings sun, calm seas and the best diving visibility. May–November is the wet season with more rain and rougher water; avoid June–August for a fixed beach itinerary.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Nonstop from Mumbai (about 2.5–3 hours) and Delhi (about 4–4.5 hours) on IndiGo and Air India to Malé (MLE). Fly the daytime departures so the onward seaplane to the atoll runs in daylight, as seaplanes are visual-flight only and do not operate after dark.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations; the Maldives is very safe and resort-isolated. Do not drink tap water — resorts provide desalinated/bottled water; sun and marine stings are the real risks, so pack accordingly. Indians get free visa on arrival.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian and Jain are easily handled at any resort with advance notice, and most flagship resorts run a dedicated Indian kitchen with a chef on request. Signal Jain or veg needs at booking so the island stocks accordingly, given supply runs are by boat and seaplane.

seo.description: Manali, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Manali
hero.tagline: Snow peaks, apple orchards and the rushing Beas river.

ourTake.lede: Manali splits sharply between the overrun main town and the quiet, beautiful Old Manali and the villages up the valley, so stay in the latter. Use it as a base for the high passes and the Spiti or Sissu side rather than the town's tourist strip. Timing is everything: the Rohtang and Atal Tunnel access, the snow, and the road to Spiti all depend on season, so plan around what's open.
ourTake.comeIf: You want mountains, orchards and river valleys a short hop from Delhi.
ourTake.skipIf: You want to avoid crowds in peak season, or want a beach.
