whenToGo.blurb: Autumn and spring are kindest, bookended by the Australian Open in January and the Spring Racing Carnival in November; the city is famous for four seasons in a day.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Melbourne. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Park Hyatt Melbourne
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide 4-Star (2025) — Melbourne's only Four-Star house
items.description: A low, calm grande dame beside St Patrick's Cathedral and Fitzroy Gardens — the surest luxury in the city.

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton, Melbourne
credentials: MICHELIN One Key (2025) — inaugural Australian Keys
items.description: The top seventeen floors of Australia's tallest hotel — the city and Port Phillip Bay laid out beneath the glass.

items.name: Crown Towers Melbourne
credentials: A landmark luxury hotel of Melbourne — Crown Riverside
Home to Nobu and Yu Su — flagship dining
items.description: The riverside landmark of Melbourne luxury — grand suites, a serious spa and the city's marquee dining under one roof.

items.name: Grand Hyatt Melbourne
credentials: A landmark luxury hotel of Collins Street
items.description: Melbourne's original grand hotel on the smart end of Collins Street — a polished city house for three decades.

items.name: The Langham, Melbourne
credentials: Chuan Spa — a landmark Melbourne hotel spa
items.description: A gracious riverside grande dame on Southbank — afternoon tea, a celebrated spa and the city skyline across the Yarra.

items.name: Lyall Hotel & Spa
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World
A landmark boutique hotel of South Yarra
items.description: An all-suite boutique house in leafy South Yarra — hushed, residential and quietly indulgent.

items.name: 1 Hotel Melbourne
credentials: MICHELIN One Key (2025) — inaugural Australian Keys
items.description: A biophilic, greenery-draped tower on the river — sustainable luxury with a rooftop pool over the city.

items.name: Hyde Melbourne Place
credentials: MICHELIN One Key (2025) — inaugural Australian Keys
items.description: A design-led tower above the theatre district — warm, contemporary rooms and a rooftop bar over the city.

items.name: United Places Botanic Gardens
items.description: Twelve suites facing the Royal Botanic Gardens — a private residence in all but name.

items.name: Jackalope Hotel
credentials: A landmark design hotel of the Mornington Peninsula
Doot Doot Doot — an acclaimed regional dining room
items.description: A dramatic art-and-wine hotel set among the vines of the Mornington Peninsula — surreal, sculptural, one of a kind.

items.name: The Como Melbourne, MGallery
credentials: MGallery Collection — a landmark South Yarra hotel
items.description: A long-loved all-suite hotel in the heart of chic South Yarra — the address for Chapel Street and the boutiques.

items.name: Hotel Windsor
credentials: A landmark grand hotel of Melbourne
items.description: Australia's grand Victorian hotel, opposite Parliament since 1883 — old-world grandeur and a legendary afternoon tea.

items.name: W Melbourne
credentials: A landmark contemporary design hotel of Flinders Lane
items.description: A bold, laneway-inspired design tower on Flinders Lane — colour, energy and a buzzing bar scene.

items.name: Next Hotel Melbourne
credentials: Handwritten Collection (Accor) — a design-led CBD hotel
items.description: A sleek, art-filled hotel tucked into a heritage Collins Street arcade — central, contemporary and well-run.

items.name: QT Melbourne
credentials: A landmark QT design hotel of the CBD
items.description: A playful, fashion-forward design hotel with one of the city's liveliest rooftop bars.

items.name: Ovolo South Yarra
credentials: A landmark Ovolo design hotel of South Yarra
items.description: A bright, art-splashed design hotel on Chapel Street — colour, fun and generous inclusions.

items.name: Federation Square
items.description: Melbourne's angular civic heart, facing Flinders Street Station across the river — a good first anchor for orienting the city, with the Ian Potter Centre and ACMI opening off the plaza. A private guide can start you here and walk you into the laneways within minutes.

items.name: Hosier Lane street art
items.description: The most famous of Melbourne's graffiti bluestone lanes, a wall-to-wall canvas that changes weekly and runs off Flinders Lane opposite Fed Square. Even a short walk-through gives the family the city's counter-culture in ten minutes; nearby Rutledge Lane extends it.

items.name: Degraves Street
items.description: A narrow cobbled lane packed with awning-shaded cafe tables — the postcard of Melbourne's coffee culture. Order a flat white standing at a hole-in-the-wall roaster and watch the city's obsession up close.

items.name: The Block Arcade & Royal Arcade
items.description: Two exquisitely preserved Victorian-era shopping arcades: the Block with its mosaic-tiled floor and the historic Hopetoun Tea Rooms, and Royal Arcade with its Gog and Magog figures. Genteel, unhurried and a lovely stop between laneways for tea and chocolate.

items.name: National Gallery of Victoria — International (NGV)
items.description: Australia's oldest and most-visited public gallery, whose St Kilda Road building holds the international collection behind a famous water-wall entrance. The blockbuster summer exhibitions and the stained-glass Great Hall ceiling are worth timed tickets; entry to the permanent collection is free.

items.name: NGV Australia — Ian Potter Centre
items.description: The Fed Square site of the NGV devoted entirely to Australian art, including the country's most significant collection of Indigenous art. A shorter, focused visit that pairs naturally with Federation Square for a multi-generation morning.

items.name: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria
items.description: Thirty-eight hectares of lakes, lawns and rare plantings sweeping down toward the river — Melbourne's green lungs and an easy, buggy-friendly wander for elders and children alike. Take the Aboriginal Heritage Walk or an Punt Road picnic; the Tan track circles it.

items.name: Shrine of Remembrance
items.description: Melbourne's grand war memorial on a rise above the Botanic Gardens, its ceremonial forecourt and city views making it one of the CBD's most dignified vantage points. Climb to the balcony for the sightline straight down Swanston Street to the city.

items.name: Queen Victoria Market
items.description: A sprawling 19th-century open-air market — delis, produce, seafood and the Winter/Summer Night Markets — and the best single place to graze the city's food cultures in one visit. A guided Ultimate Foodie tour lets the family taste widely without the crush.

items.name: Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG)
items.description: The spiritual home of Australian sport and one of the world's great stadiums, holding 100,000 for AFL and cricket. A behind-the-scenes tour of the members' rooms and the arena thrills any sports-loving traveller; a Boxing Day Test or an AFL final is a bucket-list day.

items.name: National Sports Museum
items.description: Inside the MCG, an immersive museum of Australian sport — cricket, AFL, the Olympics and the Australian Open — with interactive galleries the children will not want to leave. Combine it with the stadium tour.

items.name: Melbourne Skydeck (Eureka Tower)
items.description: The Southern Hemisphere's highest public viewing platform, on the 88th floor at 285m, with 360-degree views and 'The Edge' glass cube that slides out over the city. Best at dusk to catch daylight then the lit skyline; the recently rebranded Eureka Skydeck.

items.name: State Library Victoria
items.description: One of the world's most beautiful reading rooms — the domed octagonal La Trobe Reading Room — free to enter and quietly spectacular from the upper galleries. A serene pause from the CBD, and home to the Ned Kelly armour.

items.name: Immigration Museum
items.description: Housed in the old Customs House, it tells the story of the peoples who built Melbourne — a resonant stop for Indian families, tracing the migration threads that make the city so plural today.

items.name: Royal Exhibition Building & Carlton Gardens
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Royal Exhibition Building and Carlton Gardens
items.description: Australia's first UNESCO-listed building, a soaring 1880 exhibition palace set in formal Victorian gardens beside Melbourne Museum. Time a dome-promenade tour; the gardens are a lovely picnic setting for elders and children.

items.name: Melbourne Museum
items.description: A modern natural-history and cultural museum beside the Exhibition Building, with the Bunjilaka Aboriginal Cultural Centre, a living rainforest gallery and the beloved racehorse Phar Lap. Genuinely absorbing across three generations, and there is an IMAX alongside.

items.name: Fitzroy — Brunswick Street & Gertrude Street
items.description: Melbourne's original bohemian quarter and still its most characterful — independent boutiques, record shops, wine bars and some of the city's best small dining. The neighbourhood to walk slowly with a coffee and let the family drift.

items.name: Collingwood & Smith Street
items.description: Once industrial, now the city's hottest strip — Smith Street runs from cult roasters to natural-wine bars and the rooftop of the old Foy & Gibson warehouses. A cool-hunter's afternoon for younger travellers.

items.name: Brunswick — Sydney Road & Lygon Street north
items.description: A multicultural strip of Middle Eastern grocers, live-music rooms and third-wave cafes, north of the centre and refreshingly un-touristed. Good for a driver to loop through for a taste of the real, everyday Melbourne.

items.name: Lygon Street, Carlton — Little Italy
items.description: The historic Italian quarter where Melbourne's espresso culture began, lined with trattorias and gelaterie. An easy, crowd-pleasing dinner street a short hop from the Exhibition Building and museum.

items.name: St Kilda Pier & the little-penguin colony
items.description: A newly rebuilt pier reaching into Port Phillip Bay, where around 1,400 wild little penguins come ashore at dusk on the breakwater — free to view from the boardwalk. A magical, gentle evening for children; go at sunset and keep torches off.

items.name: Luna Park Melbourne
items.description: The 1912 amusement park behind its famous grinning Mr Moon face on the Esplanade, home to one of the world's oldest continually operating roller-coasters (the Scenic Railway). Nostalgic and photogenic; open weekends and holidays.

items.name: The Esplanade & St Kilda foreshore
items.description: Melbourne's bayside promenade — palm-lined beach, Sunday art market, and the grand old Espy hotel — an easy seaside afternoon 15 minutes from the CBD. Cakes on Acland Street's continental-cake row are a ritual.

items.name: Southbank & the Yarra promenade
items.description: The riverside arts-and-dining precinct across from Flinders Street — Arts Centre spire, restaurants along the water, and the launch point for river cruises. A pleasant sundown stroll with the skyline reflected in the Yarra.

items.name: Yarra River cruise
items.description: A relaxed way to read the city from the water — sightseeing cruises run upriver toward the gardens and downriver to Docklands and the port. Charter a private vessel for a multi-gen group; a slow, low-effort highlight for elders.

items.name: Docklands & The District
items.description: A modern waterfront quarter of marinas, waterside dining and public art west of the CBD, reached by the free City Circle tram. Calmer than the centre and good for a harbourside lunch; the Melbourne Star wheel here is undergoing a planned reopening.

items.name: Arts Centre Melbourne
items.description: Under its lattice spire, the city's flagship performing-arts complex — ballet, opera, theatre and the Melbourne Symphony at Hamer Hall. Worth a night out; the Sunday market of makers runs along its forecourt.

items.name: Abbotsford Convent
items.description: A 19th-century convent turned rambling arts precinct on the riverbank — galleries, artist studios, gardens and the excellent Lentil As Anything and Convent Bakery. Free to wander, deeply atmospheric, and next to Collingwood Children's Farm for the little ones.

items.name: Fitzroy Gardens & Cooks' Cottage
items.description: A grand formal park on the CBD's edge, with elm avenues, a fairy tree and the transplanted stone cottage of Captain Cook's family, shipped brick-by-brick from England. A short, shaded green stop for elders between sights.

items.name: Chinatown & Little Bourke Street
items.description: One of the oldest continuous Chinatowns in the Western world, its arches spanning Little Bourke Street, with the Chinese Museum tucked among the restaurants. The address for late dumplings and the setting of Flower Drum.

items.name: Flower Drum
items.description: Melbourne's legendary Cantonese fine-diner, quietly running for over forty years on Market Lane — Peking duck, aromatic baked crab, and discreet, faultless service. The special-occasion dinner for a discerning family; book well ahead.

items.name: Chin Chin
items.description: The buzzing, all-day Southeast Asian diner on Flinders Lane that has drawn queues since 2011 — hawker-style shared plates built for a table of many. Lively, generous and easy for a mixed group; the 'Feed Me' menu takes the decisions away.

items.name: Vue de Monde
items.description: Melbourne's landmark fine-dining room on the 55th floor of the Rialto, a native-ingredient degustation with the whole city at your feet. The city's dress-up dinner; request a window and let the sommelier lead.

items.name: Attica
items.description: Ben Shewry's celebrated suburban restaurant, long ranked among the world's best, serving a deeply personal tasting menu of native Australian ingredients. A pilgrimage table for serious food travellers; reservations open in advance and go fast.

items.name: Flinders Lane dining
items.description: The single best street to eat in Melbourne — a dense run of hatted restaurants and wine bars from Movida's tapas to Cumulus Inc. Let a concierge match the room to your group; walkable end to end.

items.name: Melbourne coffee crawl
items.description: Coffee is a genuine civic craft here — a private roaster-hopping morning through hole-in-the-wall bars and single-origin cafes reveals the culture better than any sight. Ask for a barista-led tasting; the flat white is the local benchmark.

items.name: Yarra Valley wineries (day trip)
items.description: An hour east, Victoria's premier cool-climate wine region — cellar doors from Domaine Chandon's French sparkling house to acclaimed Pinot and Chardonnay estates, with long lunches among the vines. Ideal as a chauffeured day; several estates cater beautifully to non-drinkers and families.

items.name: Great Ocean Road & the Twelve Apostles (day trip)
items.description: One of the world's great coastal drives, curling past surf beaches and rainforest to the limestone stacks of the Twelve Apostles rising from the Southern Ocean. A long but unforgettable full day; a private car and a helicopter add-on over the Apostles turn it into a highlight of the whole trip.

items.name: Mornington Peninsula & Peninsula Hot Springs (day trip)
items.description: Ninety minutes south, a coast of vineyards, beach boxes and Australia's largest natural hot-springs bathing complex — geothermal pools and a hilltop bath with bay views. A restorative day for elders and couples; pair the springs with a peninsula winery lunch.

items.name: Phillip Island Penguin Parade (day trip)
items.description: Around two hours south-east, the nightly spectacle of hundreds of little penguins waddling ashore after dusk, watched from boardwalks and tiered stands. Book premium or underground-viewing tickets for the family; the island also offers koalas and the Nobbies coast.

items.name: Dandenong Ranges & Puffing Billy (day trip)
items.description: An hour east into fern-gullied mountain forest, riding the century-old Puffing Billy steam train with legs dangling from open carriages — pure delight for children and grandparents alike. Add the William Ricketts sanctuary and a Sassafras tea room.

items.name: Sovereign Hill, Ballarat (day trip)
items.description: A vast, living re-creation of a 1850s gold-rush town about 90 minutes west — costumed streets, gold panning, and a nightly sound-and-light show. Immersive and hands-on for multi-generation groups curious about how Victoria's wealth was made.

items.name: Werribee Park Mansion & Shadowfax (day trip)
items.description: A grand 1870s Italianate mansion in formal gardens 30 minutes south-west, beside Shadowfax winery and the Werribee Open Range Zoo. A gentle, elegant half-day that combines heritage, wine and a safari-style drive for children.

items.name: Melbourne's parks & gardens promenade
items.description: The linked chain of parkland ringing the CBD — Kings Domain, Alexandra Gardens and the riverbank — makes for a long, level walk or a hired-bike loop past the Shrine and the rowing sheds. An easy way to see the city's famed green ring.

items.name: Australian Open (seasonal — January)
items.description: The year's first tennis Grand Slam, drawing the world to Melbourne Park each January — night sessions under lights at Rod Laver Arena are electric. Corporate suites and premium hospitality make it a marquee outing; book the season far ahead.

items.name: Australian Grand Prix (seasonal — March)
items.description: Formula 1 returns to the parkland circuit around Albert Park Lake each autumn, a fast street-style track minutes from the CBD. Trackside paddock and grandstand packages suit a group of enthusiasts; the city hums all weekend.

items.name: Melbourne Cup Carnival (seasonal — November)
items.description: 'The race that stops a nation' — the first Tuesday of November at Flemington, the centrepiece of a spring carnival of fashion, marquees and champagne. The Birdcage enclosure is the ticket for a memorable, dressed-up day.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Arrive at Tullamarine (MEL), a 30 to 40-minute chauffeured drive into the centre; a private car is the right call as there is no rail link from the airport.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The compact grid is made for walking, and the free City Circle trams cover the centre; keep a private driver for the wineries and the coast.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM (Telstra or Optus) delivers strong 5G citywide; wifi is everywhere.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Currency is the Australian dollar; cards and contactless are universal and cash is seldom needed; tipping is modest, around 10 percent when you wish.

onGround.note: Melbourne rewards the curious: its best bars, cafes and restaurants hide down unmarked laneways, so a good local guide is worth it; day-trip to the Yarra Valley wineries or the Great Ocean Road, and pack layers as the weather turns in an afternoon.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Famous for 'four seasons in a day'; Mar-Apr (autumn) and Oct-Nov (spring) are the most settled, Dec-Feb is warm but can spike to sudden heat, and Jun-Aug is cold, grey and wet.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No nonstop from India in the standard schedule; route via Singapore (Singapore Airlines) or via Delhi/Sydney on Air India. Qantas runs a seasonal Delhi-Melbourne service 26 Oct 2026 to late Mar 2027. Fly Singapore Airlines business via Changi for the cleanest connection; pack layers, Melbourne weather turns fast.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations; the same strict biosecurity applies — declare all food on arrival. Tap water is safe and healthcare is world-class. Melbourne is very safe. Weather swings are the main practical planning point.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Outstanding for vegetarians and Jain diets; a deep Indian community, superb pure-veg and South Indian restaurants, and a cafe culture that treats vegetarian and vegan as standard. Indian food along Sydney Road and in the eastern suburbs is genuinely good.

seo.title: Mexico City — TripAgent
seo.description: Mexico City, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Mexico City
hero.tagline: A high-altitude capital of grand boulevards and world-class kitchens.

ourTake.lede: Mexico City is one of the world's great food and art capitals and deserves more than a stopover — base in Roma or Condesa and walk. Reserve the big restaurants weeks ahead; the wait for Pujol or Quintonil is real. Go to Teotihuacán early to beat the heat and crowds, and don't miss the Frida Kahlo house — but book its timed ticket in advance.
ourTake.comeIf: You are a serious food and culture traveller who holds a US visa and wants the real thing.
ourTake.skipIf: You want an easy, short-haul trip or you are nervous about a big city.

items.description: Two 1940s mansions woven into one 19-room house facing Lincoln Park — the only Two-Key hotel in the city, and its most refined address.

items.name: Sofitel Mexico City Reforma
items.description: A sleek French-accented tower on Reforma, crowned by the 38th-floor Cityzen rooftop — grand views and a lively social scene under one roof.

items.name: Pug Seal Allan Poe
items.description: A colour-drenched, art-filled boutique house on a quiet Polanco street — bold design, 24-hour pantry and a temazcal ritual on site.

items.name: Brick Hotel Mexico City
items.description: An early-20th-century mansion turned intimate hotel in the heart of Roma Norte — Belle Époque bones, a courtyard and a good restaurant.

items.name: La Valise Mexico City
items.description: A three-suite townhouse of theatrical, one-of-a-kind rooms — a bed that rolls onto the balcony is the signature — pure Roma romance.

items.name: Octavia Casa
items.description: A serene, minimalist house by fashion designer Roberta Maceda in leafy Condesa — natural materials, calm light and quiet good taste.

items.name: Ignacia Guest House
items.description: A restored 1913 house of just five rooms around a courtyard — warm, personal and among the most charming small stays in Roma.

items.name: The Zócalo (Plaza de la Constitución)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco
items.description: One of the largest city squares on earth, laid over the sacred heart of Aztec Tenochtitlán, where a vast national flag is raised and lowered by the army each day. A private guide reads the layered history for the whole family before the crowds and the altitude tell on anyone.

items.name: Metropolitan Cathedral (Catedral Metropolitana)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco
items.description: The largest and oldest cathedral in Latin America, a 250-year Spanish Baroque masterpiece slowly sinking into the old lakebed — you feel the floor tilt as you walk toward the altar. Cool, quiet and shaded, a gentle first stop for elders on a busy day.

items.name: Templo Mayor & Museum
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco
items.description: The excavated main temple of Tenochtitlán, unearthed beside the cathedral, with a superb museum holding the great stone disc of the goddess Coyolxauhqui. A guide brings the ruins alive for children who might otherwise see only rubble.

items.name: Palacio Nacional & Diego Rivera Murals
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco
items.description: Rivera's monumental staircase murals — sixteen years of work sweeping across all of Mexican history — line a working seat of government on the Zócalo's east side. Entry is free with photo ID; a guide is essential to decode the crowded, political panels.

items.name: Palacio de Bellas Artes
items.description: A dazzling white-marble Art Nouveau and Art Deco palace crowned with a Tiffany glass stage curtain, holding murals by Rivera, Siqueiros and Orozco. The evening Ballet Folklórico de México here — pre- and post-Hispanic dance staged since 1952 — is a beautiful, wordless family night.

items.name: Ballet Folklórico de México
items.description: Amalia Hernández's legendary company performs its riot of regional Mexican dance under the Tiffany curtain of Bellas Artes twice weekly. No language needed, so grandparents and children share the same spectacle; private box seats can be arranged.

items.name: Torre Latinoamericana Observation Deck
items.description: The 1956 skyscraper that survived every great earthquake gives a 44th-floor panorama of the endless valley city, best at dusk with a drink in the sky-lounge below. A quick, easy way to grasp the sheer scale before diving into the streets.

items.name: Museo Nacional de Antropología
items.description: The world's greatest museum of Mesoamerican civilisation — 22 vast halls holding the Aztec Sun Stone, colossal Olmec heads and Maya treasures under a soaring stone-and-water canopy. Too big to see whole; a private guide curates a two-hour path so no one tires.

items.name: Chapultepec Castle (Museo Nacional de Historia)
items.description: The only true royal castle in the Americas, crowning the forested hill where Emperor Maximilian once lived, now a history museum with hilltop gardens and city views. A gentle uphill or short shuttle; the terraces reward the climb.

items.name: Museo Tamayo
items.description: Rufino Tamayo's own gift to the city, a striking concrete pavilion in Chapultepec woods showing international and Mexican contemporary art. Calm, uncrowded and air-conditioned — a refined counterpoint to the grand anthropology halls next door.

items.name: Museo de Arte Moderno (MAM)
items.description: Home to icons of 20th-century Mexican art, including Frida Kahlo's famous 'The Two Fridas' and works by Rivera, Siqueiros and Remedios Varo. A compact, digestible collection set in a sculpture garden, easy to pair with the surrounding park.

items.name: Bosque de Chapultepec
items.description: One of the largest urban parks in the Western Hemisphere, twice the size of Central Park, its lakes, forests and museums lending the whole family room to breathe at altitude. A private guide and driver make its scattered sights effortless in a day.

items.name: Museo Frida Kahlo (Casa Azul)
items.description: The cobalt-blue house where Frida was born, lived with Diego and died — her studio, wheelchair, corsets and garden left as they were, deeply moving even to those who know little of her art. Timed tickets sell out; a concierge secures a quiet slot in advance.

items.name: Museo Casa de León Trotsky
items.description: The fortified house where the exiled revolutionary lived under Frida and Diego's protection and was assassinated in 1940, his study frozen at the moment of the ice-axe blow. A short walk from Casa Azul; a compelling, sombre stop for older travellers with a taste for history.

items.name: Museo Diego Rivera Anahuacalli
items.description: Rivera's black-volcanic-stone 'temple of the arts', a pyramid-like fortress he built to house his immense collection of pre-Columbian pieces, set in an ecological reserve. Included with the Casa Azul ticket and blessedly serene — a hidden gem few tourists reach.

items.name: Coyoacán Historic Centre & Market
items.description: Cobbled colonial squares, twin plazas, fountains and a lively covered market of textiles, crafts and tostadas make this the city's most enchanting village-within-a-city. Leafy and walkable, it suits a slow multi-generational afternoon with plenty of shaded benches.

items.name: Bazar Sábado & San Ángel
items.description: Every Saturday this cobbled colonial quarter fills with a genteel art-and-artisan bazaar around Plaza San Jacinto, from fine silver to painting. Compact and refined shopping with courtyard restaurants — a graceful morning for shoppers of all ages.

items.name: Museo Casa Estudio Diego Rivera y Frida Kahlo
items.description: The pair of bold functionalist studio-houses — one pink, one blue, linked by a rooftop bridge — designed by Juan O'Gorman for the artists, a landmark of Mexican modernism. Quiet and architectural, a fine companion to a San Ángel stroll.

items.name: Museo Soumaya
items.description: Carlos Slim's free museum, a shimmering twist of 16,000 mirrored steel tiles, holds the largest Rodin collection outside France alongside old masters and Mexican art. Architecturally jaw-dropping and easily woven into a Polanco shopping day.

items.name: Museo Jumex
items.description: David Chipperfield's crisp travertine gallery next to the Soumaya houses Latin America's finest private contemporary-art collection. A cool, curated hour for serious collectors, with a good café — a refined pause between boutiques.

items.name: Avenida Presidente Masaryk Luxury Shopping
items.description: Mexico's most expensive avenue, a leafy boulevard of Louis Vuitton, Hermès, Cartier, Bulgari and Tiffany showrooms alongside acclaimed restaurants. Discreet, tree-lined and easy for a driver to shadow — the natural base for luxury travellers.

items.name: Casa Luis Barragán (Casa Estudio)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Luis Barragán House and Studio
items.description: The Pritzker laureate's own house and studio, a serene interplay of light, colour and volume that is the touchstone of modern Mexican architecture. Strictly small guided groups by reservation only — a quiet, unmissable pilgrimage for design lovers.

items.name: Xochimilco Trajineras
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco
items.description: The last living remnant of the Aztec lake, where flower-painted trajinera barges glide through canals and floating chinampa gardens, mariachis drifting alongside. A private boat with catered food and mezcal turns it into a joyful, safe family afternoon.

items.name: Teotihuacán Pyramids (Day Trip)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Pre-Hispanic City of Teotihuacan
items.description: An hour from the city rise the vast Pyramids of the Sun and Moon along the Avenue of the Dead, a metropolis older and grander than the Aztecs who revered it. Go early with a private guide and driver, or float above it all at dawn in a hot-air balloon.

items.name: Arena México — Lucha Libre
items.description: The 'Cathedral of Lucha Libre', where masked luchadores fly from the ropes to roaring, family-friendly crowds — pure, joyful Mexican theatre. A curated evening with ringside seats and a guide (skip the rougher streets outside) is a memory kids never forget.

items.name: Mercado de San Juan
items.description: The gourmet market of the city, famed for exotic ingredients, fine cheeses, jamón and stalls where chefs shop — a feast for food-curious travellers. A guide can steer vegetarians to the produce, cheese and prepared-food counters that suit.

items.name: Mercado de Artesanías La Ciudadela
items.description: The city's best one-stop craft market, aisles of Talavera pottery, Oaxacan textiles, silver, alebrijes and Day-of-the-Dead art under one roof. Fixed and calm enough for relaxed, unhurried gift-buying with the family.

items.name: Parque México & Parque España
items.description: Two lush Art Deco parks at the heart of leafy Condesa, ringed by 1920s architecture, dog-walkers and pavement cafés. A gentle, green stroll that lets multi-gen groups slow down and simply feel the city's most liveable neighbourhood.

items.name: Roma Norte Galleries & Dining
items.description: Belle Époque mansions now hold design shops, art galleries and some of the city's finest restaurants along tree-lined Álvaro Obregón. Walkable, stylish and full of tasting menus that thoughtfully accommodate vegetarians on request.

items.name: Museo Nacional de Arte (MUNAL)
items.description: A palatial Beaux-Arts building housing four centuries of Mexican painting and sculpture, from colonial altarpieces to the great landscapes of José María Velasco. Grand, uncrowded and beautifully told by a private guide.

items.name: Museo del Templo de la Enseñanza & Calle Madero Walk
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco
items.description: The pedestrian Madero street links Bellas Artes to the Zócalo past the tiled Casa de los Azulejos and ornate churches — the finest colonial promenade in the city. Flat, car-free and easy for elders, threading the Centro's greatest hits in one walk.

items.name: Museo del Objeto del Objeto (MODO)
items.description: A witty, one-of-a-kind design museum of everyday Mexican objects and advertising, set in an Art Nouveau townhouse. Small, playful and unexpected — a light, charming stop that amuses children and grown-ups alike.

items.name: Biblioteca Vasconcelos
items.description: A soaring 'megalibrary' of suspended glass floors and a whale skeleton hovering in the void, one of the world's most photographed modern libraries. A quick, awe-inducing detour that thrills teenagers and architecture buffs.

items.name: Monumento a la Revolución & Mirador
items.description: A colossal Art Deco arch, tomb of revolutionary heroes, with a glass lift rising to a rooftop viewing deck above Reforma. Fast and striking, with a fine panorama and a plaza that dances with fountains at night.

items.name: Ángel de la Independencia & Paseo de la Reforma
items.description: The golden Angel of Independence presides over Mexico's grand Haussmann-style boulevard, lined with monuments, hotels and Sunday cyclists. A driver's slow cruise here orients the family to the modern city's spine.

items.name: Basílica de Santa María de Guadalupe
items.description: Mexico's most sacred shrine, where the miraculous image of the Virgin of Guadalupe draws millions, its modern circular basilica beside the old sinking one. A moving, deeply human place; a guide navigates the vast pilgrim crowds respectfully.

items.name: Jardín Centenario & Coyoacán Churches
items.description: The garden square framed by the 16th-century San Juan Bautista church and the coyote fountain is the soul of old Coyoacán, alive with musicians and ice-cream sellers. Shaded, sociable and endlessly photogenic for an easy family hour.

items.name: Mercado Roma
items.description: A multi-storey gourmet food hall with rooftop terrace gathering the city's best artisan producers, taquerías and mezcal bars under one stylish roof. Curated and comfortable, with clearly labelled options for vegetarian members of the party.

items.name: Cineteca Nacional & Mezcal Tasting
items.description: Mexico's cinematheque is a sleek cultural campus of open-air screens and cafés, and the surrounding south is dotted with refined mezcalerías. A private tasting flight — smoky espadín to rare tobalá — reveals Mexico's soul in a glass, guided and unhurried.

items.name: Puebla (Day Trip)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Puebla
items.description: Two hours east, a UNESCO colonial jewel of Talavera-tiled facades, gilded churches and mole poblano beneath the Popocatépetl volcano. A private car makes it a gracious full day of architecture, cuisine and artisan ceramics.

items.name: Tepoztlán (Day Trip)
items.description: A magical mountain 'Pueblo Mágico' an hour south, crowned by the cliff-top Tepozteco pyramid, ringed by mystic peaks, market stalls and a warmer climate. A relaxed day for wellness and nature, with the pyramid hike optional for the fitter.

items.name: Museo Kaluz
items.description: A refined newer museum in a restored colonial hospice by the Alameda, showing Mexican art across five centuries, with a rooftop terrace over Bellas Artes. Elegant, calm and rarely crowded — a connoisseur's stop with a fine view.

items.name: Museo Nacional de las Culturas del Mundo & Moneda Street
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco
items.description: Behind the cathedral, this world-cultures museum sits on a beautiful colonial street of Rivera murals in the old Mint. A quiet, free-flowing detour a step off the Zócalo's bustle.

items.name: Jardín Botánico & Chapultepec Zoo
items.description: Within the great park, a serene botanical garden and a free zoo home to giant pandas make a gentle, green interlude. Ideal for younger children in the multi-gen group when the museums have run long.

items.name: Templo de San Francisco & Casa de los Azulejos
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco
items.description: On Madero, a graceful old Franciscan church faces the House of Tiles, a blue-and-white Talavera-clad palace now a landmark café. A quick, atmospheric pairing of church and courtyard in the heart of the walk.

items.name: Mercado de Coyoacán Antojitos
items.description: The covered market's food aisles serve legendary tostadas, quesadillas and aguas frescas in a festive, colourful setting. A guide can point vegetarians to the many meat-free antojitos so no one misses out on the fun.

items.name: Six Flags & Bosque de Tlalpan (Southern Green Escape)
items.description: For families with children, the forested Bosque de Tlalpan offers easy trails and clean mountain air on the city's southern edge, a calm antidote to museum days. Peaceful, safe and green — the local families' weekend refuge.

items.name: Quintonil
credentials: The World's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 — No. 3 (Best in North America)
items.description: Jorge Vallejo and Alejandra Flores' temple to Mexican produce — herbs, heirloom corn and native ingredients at the very peak of world dining.

items.name: Pujol
items.description: Enrique Olvera's landmark — the mole madre, aged for years and served in a ring beside a fresh mole, remains one of gastronomy's great dishes.

items.name: Máximo Bistrot
items.description: Eduardo 'Lalo' García's bright, produce-driven room — French technique and Mexican soul, cooked from the day's market.

items.name: Rosetta
items.description: Elena Reygadas' cooking in a romantic Roma townhouse — Italian roots and Mexican produce from the World's Best Female Chef.

items.name: Sud 777
items.description: Edgar Núñez's garden-driven cooking in the leafy south — much of the produce grown in the restaurant's own beds.

items.name: Em
items.description: Lucho Martínez's intimate counter — a personal, fire-led tasting menu that was among the guide's most talked-about stars.

items.name: Esquina Común
items.description: A young, produce-obsessed kitchen turning Mexican ingredients into a precise, evolving tasting menu — a quiet critical favourite.

items.name: Masala y Maíz
items.description: Norma Listman and Saqib Keval's dialogue between Mexican, Indian and East African kitchens — one of the city's most original tables.

items.name: Contramar
items.description: Gabriela Cámara's sunlit seafood institution — the tuna tostada and the split-colour pescado a la talla are city rituals.

items.name: Vigneron
items.description: A wine-led French bistro from a serious sommelier team — precise cooking built around an exceptional cellar.

items.name: Expendio de Maíz
items.description: A tiny, counter-only corn kitchen with no fixed menu — cooking is dictated by what the market gives, heirloom masa at its centre.

items.name: Comedor Jacinta
items.description: Chef Edgar Núñez's warm ode to Mexican home cooking — grandmother's recipes plated with real care, in a bright Polanco room.

items.name: Galanga Thai House
items.description: Vivid, genuinely spicy Thai cooking in a small Roma house — a Bib favourite and a welcome change of register.

items.name: Molino El Pujol
items.description: Enrique Olvera's neighbourhood mill and kitchen — heirloom corn ground on site, turned into tortillas, tamales and simple, brilliant plates.

items.name: Comal Oculto
items.description: A produce-led, comal-driven kitchen turning market vegetables and heirloom corn into a considered, good-value menu.

items.name: Filigrana
items.description: A refined-yet-relaxed kitchen doing modern Mexican cooking with real polish, at genuine value.

items.name: Taquería El Califa de León
credentials: MICHELIN ★ (2025) — the first taquería in the world to earn a star
items.description: A stand-up taquería the size of a garage, awarded a Michelin star for a single thing done to perfection — the gaonera taco.

items.name: Taquería Los Cocuyos
items.description: A round-the-clock street stand in the old centre — slow-cooked meats and the suadero taco that locals swear by.

items.name: El Vilsito
items.description: A mechanic's garage by day, a legendary al pastor taquería by night — one of the city's benchmark trompos.

items.name: Handshake Speakeasy
credentials: North America's 50 Best Bars 2025 — No. 1 (Best Bar in North America)
items.description: Eric van Beek's precision cocktail temple, now in grander premises in Juárez — technique-driven, theatrical drinks at the very top of the craft.

items.name: Licorería Limantour
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars 2025 — No. 52 (extended list)
items.description: The bar that lit the fuse of Mexico City's cocktail renaissance — polished, inventive drinks and a benchmark for the whole scene.

items.name: Baltra Bar
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars 2025 — No. 78 (extended list)
items.description: A tiny, Galápagos-themed Condesa bar of quiet obsession — one of the city's most respected rooms for the seriously made classic.

items.name: Rayo
items.description: An agave-devoted bar built around the myth of Mayahuel — mezcal, tequila and pulque woven into story-driven, thoughtful cocktails.

items.name: Kaito del Valle
items.description: A Japanese-leaning cocktail bar of real precision — omakase-style drinks and a hushed, considered room away from the tourist trail.

items.name: Bijou Drinkery Room
items.description: A small, jewel-like bar with a sharp, spirit-forward list — a critics' favourite that punches far above its size.

items.name: Ticuchi
credentials: North America's 50 Best Bars 2025 — No. 82 (extended list)
items.description: Enrique Olvera's agave bar beside Pujol — a dark, atmospheric room devoted to mezcal and its cousins, with cooking to match.

items.name: Cityzen — Sofitel Mexico City Reforma
credentials: Atop a MICHELIN One-Key hotel — the city's premier skyline rooftop
items.description: The Sofitel's 38th-floor rooftop bar — the definitive high-altitude drink over Reforma and the Angel of Independence.

items.name: Hanky Panky
items.description: A hidden speakeasy behind an unmarked door — one of the city's original cocktail dens, still buzzing late into the night.

items.title: Hot-air balloon over Teotihuacán
items.description: A dawn flight over the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon before the site opens to visitors.

items.title: Chef's table at Pujol or Quintonil
items.description: A tasting menu at two of the world's fifty best restaurants, booked far ahead.

items.title: Private trajinera on the Xochimilco canals
items.description: A decorated boat with a mariachi and a chef-prepared lunch, away from the party crowds.

items.title: After-hours at a great museum
items.description: A private walk through the Anthropology Museum or a Kahlo/Rivera collection with a curator.

plan.heading: 4 days in Mexico City, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Check into the Ritz-Carlton or a Roma townhouse, then coffee and a slow walk through Condesa's leafy streets.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The design shops and galleries of Roma Norte at an unhurried pace.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Rosetta in a restored Roma mansion, then mezcal nearby.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Zócalo, the Templo Mayor, and the murals of the Palacio Nacional at opening.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Palacio de Bellas Artes and lunch at Azul Histórico in a colonial courtyard.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Quintonil, among the world's fifty best, in Polanco.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Casa Azul (Frida Kahlo Museum), booked ahead, and Coyoacán's cobbled plazas.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Anahuacalli or the Dolores Olmedo collection, then the Coyoacán market.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Pujol, Enrique Olvera's flagship, with the mole madre.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: An early private drive to Teotihuacán, walking the Avenue of the Dead before the sun climbs.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A cave lunch at La Gruta, then back to the city to rest.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A final table at Contramar for its tuna tostadas and pescado a la talla.

items.name: Polanco
items.description: Luxury retail and the best hotels near Chapultepec — polished and safe.

items.name: Roma / Condesa
items.description: Tree-lined art-deco streets, cafés and restaurants — the walkable creative heart.

items.name: San Ángel / Coyoacán
items.description: Cobbled colonial villages with Kahlo's house — for old-world charm.

events.name: Día de Muertos parade
events.note: A grand parade down Paseo de la Reforma into the Zócalo — 2025's runs on the weekend of 1–2 November.

events.name: Zona Maco
events.note: Latin America's leading contemporary art fair, filling the city with openings.

events.name: Grito de Independencia
events.note: Independence night, when the Zócalo fills for the president's cry and fireworks.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Arrive into Mexico City International (MEX), roughly 30–45 minutes from the smart neighbourhoods; a vetted private car and driver should meet you, which is the discreet norm here.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Always a trusted private driver rather than street taxis or ride-hailing pickups; within Polanco, Roma and Condesa the tree-lined streets are lovely to walk by day.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Mexican eSIMs (Telcel via Airalo) work well; wifi is reliable in good hotels and restaurants.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Mexican pesos; cards are widely accepted but carry some cash for markets and tips; tip around 10–15 percent in restaurants.

onGround.note: Stay in Polanco for the grandest hotels and dining or Roma/Condesa for atmosphere; the altitude (2,240m) can mildly affect the first day, and reserve tables at the marquee restaurants weeks ahead.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: The city sits at 2,240m, so it is temperate year-round; March to May is warm and dry — the sweet spot — while June to September brings near-daily late-afternoon thunderstorms that clear by evening.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No direct service from India; cleanest routings are one stop via Europe — KLM (Amsterdam), Air France (Paris), Lufthansa (Frankfurt) — or via the Gulf and a US or European hub, typically 20-24 hours. Book the transatlantic leg on a carrier strong in business; a long European layover is best spent in a flagship lounge.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: Routine vaccinations plus Hepatitis A and typhoid are sensible; do not drink the tap water — bottled or filtered only, and take it easy on day one for the altitude. Safe in Polanco, Roma, Condesa and the historic centre with normal precautions; use hotel cars and vetted transport rather than street hails.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian dining is genuinely good and growing; Jain-strict needs take a little briefing but are workable, especially at hotels. Indian restaurants exist in Polanco and Roma though the scene is modest — worth arranging Jain meals in advance with your hotel or advisor.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Mexico City, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Miami — TripAgent
seo.description: Miami, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Miami
hero.tagline: Tropical Art Deco glamour where Latin America meets the sea.

ourTake.lede: Miami is two cities — the beach and the mainland — and the interesting one is increasingly the mainland: the Design District, Wynwood, and the Cuban weight of Little Havana. Use South Beach for the Art Deco architecture and a swim, but base yourself with intent rather than defaulting to the ocean-front strip. The heat and humidity are real; the season that matters runs roughly November to April.
ourTake.comeIf: You want art-deco beaches, Latin energy and a serious nightlife.
ourTake.skipIf: You want culture, quiet or a manageable flight.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel at The Surf Club
items.description: A restored 1930s beach club turned Richard Meier landmark — the most complete luxury address on the Miami sand.

items.name: The Setai, Miami Beach
items.description: A serene Art Deco-meets-Asian sanctuary on Collins Avenue — the quietest true luxury on the beach.

items.name: Faena Hotel Miami Beach
items.description: Alan Faena's theatrical red-and-gold fantasy — a Damien Hirst gilded mammoth and a cabaret theatre on the sand.

items.name: Acqualina Resort & Residences on the Beach
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide 5-Star Hotel & Spa (2026, 14th consecutive year)
The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A Mediterranean palazzo on the Sunny Isles sand — Forbes Five-Star for hotel and spa, fourteen years running.

items.name: The St. Regis Bal Harbour Resort
items.description: The grand oceanfront St. Regis beside Bal Harbour Shops — butler service and a rarefied, moneyed calm.

items.name: 1 Hotel South Beach
items.description: A living-green, reclaimed-wood sanctuary on Collins — sustainable luxury with four pools and the beach at the door.

items.name: Nobu Hotel Miami Beach
credentials: Part of the Nobu Hospitality maison (Robert De Niro & Nobu Matsuhisa)
Home to the flagship Nobu Miami restaurant
items.description: The Nobu world made a hotel inside the Eden Roc — Japanese-minimalist rooms above the flagship restaurant.

items.name: The Miami Beach EDITION
items.description: Ian Schrager's polished, playful oceanfront tower — a skating rink and bowling alley beneath quiet-luxury rooms.

items.name: Mr. C Miami – Coconut Grove
items.description: The Cipriani family's intimate Italian-styled tower over the Grove — old-world Venetian service in leafy Miami.

items.name: The Betsy – South Beach
items.description: A colonial-white Ocean Drive landmark with a literary soul — the most cultured small hotel in South Beach.

items.name: Ocean Drive & the Art Deco Historic District
credentials: Miami Beach Architectural District — U.S. National Register of Historic Places
items.description: A mile of pastel 1920s–30s hotels in candy colours, neon and porthole windows — the largest concentration of Art Deco architecture in the world. Walk it early morning before the heat, camera in hand; the multi-gen crowd loves it and the light on the facades is best just after sunrise.

items.name: Art Deco walking tour (Miami Design Preservation League)
items.description: The definitive 90-minute guided walk from the 1001 Ocean Drive welcome centre, decoding the streamline-moderne facades, the theming, and how a preservation battle in the 1980s saved the district. A cultured, easy outing for parents and grandparents who want the story, not just the photo.

items.name: Wynwood Walls
items.description: The world's largest outdoor street-art museum — a curated open-air courtyard of monumental murals by 120-plus artists from 25-plus countries, rotated regularly. Entry is now timed and ticketed through the welcome centre, so pre-book; the surrounding streets are free to roam.

items.name: Wynwood Arts District galleries & mural streets
items.description: Beyond the Walls, the whole neighbourhood is a canvas — galleries, warehouses, breweries and cafes wrapped in ever-changing murals. Come on a Second Saturday Art Walk when studios open late; a relaxed evening for design-minded families before dinner.

items.name: Miami Design District
items.description: A walkable open-air quarter where flagship maisons — Louis Vuitton, Dior, Hermès, Cartier, Bulgari — sit among public art, Buckminster Fuller's Fly's Eye Dome and sculpture-lined plazas. Serious shopping paired with architecture and art, valet-easy and unhurried.

items.name: Institute of Contemporary Art (ICA Miami)
items.description: A sharp, free-admission contemporary-art museum with a sculpture garden, set right in the Design District so you can pair it with the boutiques. A quick, refined cultural stop that never feels like homework.

items.name: Vizcaya Museum & Gardens
items.description: James Deering's 1916 Italian-Renaissance villa on Biscayne Bay, with formal gardens, a stone barge breakwater and antique-filled rooms — the most romantic estate in Miami. A multi-generational favourite; go on a weekday morning and linger in the gardens before the tour crowds.

items.name: Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM)
items.description: Herzog & de Meuron's hanging-garden pavilion on the downtown bayfront holds 20th- and 21st-century international art, with terraces over Biscayne Bay. The cafe and shaded verandah make it easy with elders and children in tow.

items.name: Phillip & Patricia Frost Museum of Science
items.description: A planetarium, a three-level aquarium and hands-on galleries share the bayfront park with PAMM — the two sell a combo pass. The most reliable half-day for grandchildren, with plenty of air-conditioned space when the sun is fierce.

items.name: The Bass
items.description: Miami Beach's contemporary-art museum in a restored 1930s Art Deco building by Russell Pancoast — the first public exhibition space in South Florida. Compact and beautifully curated, a short walk from Collins Avenue and easy to fold into a beach day.

items.name: Rubell Museum
items.description: One of the largest private contemporary-art collections in the U.S., shown across a converted warehouse complex with a courtyard, garden and excellent restaurant. A quieter, connoisseur's alternative to the marquee museums — ideal for collectors.

items.name: Superblue Miami
items.description: An experiential-art destination built for immersive installations — mirrored infinity rooms and light works you walk through. Genuinely wondrous for children and grown-ups alike; book a timed slot and pair it with the Rubell nearby.

items.name: Little Havana & Calle Ocho
items.description: The heart of Cuban Miami — cigar rollers, fruit stands, rum bars, galleries and the aroma of cafecito along SW 8th Street. Come for the walk, the music and a guava pastry; the veg-aware will find plenty in the fruit shakes and rice-and-plantain plates.

items.name: Máximo Gómez (Domino) Park
items.description: A tiny corner park where elders have gathered over dominoes and heated debate for four decades — pure, unstaged neighbourhood life. Open daily; stand at the rail and watch, a memorable few minutes for grandparents who recognise the ritual.

items.name: Ball & Chain
items.description: A live-music landmark on Calle Ocho since 1935, with indoor and courtyard stages, salsa and no cover charge. An authentic Havana-style evening — free salsa lessons on Thursdays if the younger set wants to try.

items.name: The Biltmore Hotel
items.description: A 1926 Mediterranean-revival landmark with a soaring lobby, a Donald Ross golf course and the largest hotel pool on the U.S. East Coast, set in 150 acres. Take afternoon tea or a heritage tour even if you're not staying — grand, hushed, old-world luxury.

items.name: Venetian Pool
credentials: U.S. National Register of Historic Places
items.description: A 1923 swimming grotto carved from a coral-rock quarry, fed by spring water, with caves, waterfalls and Venetian bridges. A one-of-a-kind, storybook swim for the whole family on a hot afternoon.

items.name: Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden
items.description: 83 acres of palms, cycads, flowering trees and a butterfly conservatory, with a tram if walking is tiring. Serene and shaded — a gentle morning for elders and a wonder for children, especially during the seasonal art and orchid shows.

items.name: Miracle Mile & downtown Coral Gables
items.description: A leafy, Mediterranean-styled main street of boutiques, galleries and fine restaurants, with fountains and canopy trees. A civilised, low-key afternoon of strolling and shopping away from the beach crowds.

items.name: Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park & Lighthouse
credentials: Cape Florida Light — U.S. National Register of Historic Places
items.description: The tip of Key Biscayne, with the 1825 Cape Florida Light — the oldest standing structure in Miami-Dade — and a calm, palm-backed beach 15 minutes from downtown. Climb the 109 steps for views over Stiltsville and the skyline; two Cuban-food cafes on site make an easy family day.

items.name: Crandon Park Beach
items.description: A two-mile crescent of soft sand with shallow, gentle water and cabanas — one of the calmest, most family-friendly beaches near the city. Quieter than South Beach; good for grandparents and small children who want the sea without the scene.

items.name: South Beach (Lummus Park beachfront)
items.description: The iconic wide white-sand beach backed by pastel lifeguard stands and the Art Deco skyline. Rent a private cabana for shade and service; the promenade behind is perfect for an evening stroll with the family.

items.name: Bal Harbour Beach & boardwalk
items.description: A refined, low-rise stretch of sand fronting the luxury enclave, linked by a shaded oceanfront boardwalk toward Surfside. Calm and discreet — the beach of choice if you want quiet luxury over spectacle.

items.name: Sunny Isles Beach
items.description: A broad, uncrowded beach lined with gleaming towers — favoured by international families for space and its easy villa-and-condo stays. Wide sand, warm water and a relaxed pace for a multi-day base.

items.name: Bal Harbour Shops
items.description: The most exclusive open-air mall in America — Chanel, Dior, Prada, Cartier and an expanded Tiffany among koi ponds and tropical greenery, anchored by Neiman Marcus and Saks. A major 2026 expansion is nearly doubling its size; peerless, unhurried luxury shopping with valet and fine dining.

items.name: Aventura Mall
items.description: The largest mall in South Florida — 300-plus stores balancing Hermès, Gucci and Louis Vuitton with everyday favourites and Nordstrom and Bloomingdale's anchors. Fully covered and cool, with a play area and slide tower for children; the practical choice for big family shopping.

items.name: Star Island celebrity-homes boat cruise
items.description: A 90-minute sightseeing cruise from Bayside past the waterfront mansions of Star, Palm and Hibiscus Islands and the downtown skyline. Charter a private yacht instead for a bespoke sunset run — the classic way to see Miami's wealth from the water.

items.name: Bayside Marketplace & Bayfront Park
items.description: A waterfront marketplace of shops, cafes and live music beside the marina where most bay cruises depart, next to the green sweep of Bayfront Park. An easy, walkable staging point before a boat tour, with the skyline as backdrop.

items.name: Coconut Grove village & waterfront
items.description: Miami's oldest neighbourhood — leafy, bohemian and bayfront, with sidewalk cafes, sailing marinas and the CocoWalk arcade. A gentle, tree-shaded afternoon; pair it with Vizcaya just up the road.

items.name: Brickell & Brickell City Centre
items.description: Miami's glossy financial district, with a climate-controlled open-air shopping and dining complex, rooftop bars and river-mouth views. Sleek and cosmopolitan — good for an evening of dining and skyline drinks.

items.name: Little Haiti Cultural Complex
items.description: A Caribbean-styled arts centre with a gallery, dance and a marketplace, hosting Konpa concerts and guided neighbourhood tours through the culture and food of Haitian Miami. An off-the-beaten-path cultural afternoon most visitors miss.

items.name: Everglades day-trip: Shark Valley
credentials: Everglades National Park — UNESCO World Heritage Site
items.description: The northern gateway to the Everglades, where a 15-mile paved loop — by tram, bike or foot — puts alligators and wading birds within arm's reach, ending at a lookout tower over the sawgrass. A genuine wilderness half-day, naturalist-guided and gentle enough for all ages.

items.name: Everglades airboat safari
items.description: A fast, exhilarating glide across the wetlands with a wildlife show and gators up close, at parks along the Tamiami Trail west of the city. Book a private boat for a calmer, unhurried run; a thrill the grandchildren will talk about for years.

items.name: Key West & the Florida Keys day-trip
items.description: A scenic drive down the Overseas Highway across turquoise water to Florida's southernmost city — Duval Street, Hemingway's house, Mallory Square sunsets and reef snorkelling. Long but rewarding; consider a chauffeur or a stay overnight to do it at leisure.

items.name: Islamorada & the Upper Keys
items.description: The gentler, closer Keys escape — sport-fishing capital, sandbar picnics, tarpon feeding and waterfront seafood, an hour and a half south. A relaxed alternative to the full Key West haul, easy as a private half-day charter.

items.name: Lincoln Road Mall
items.description: A pedestrian promenade of shops, cafes and galleries designed by Morris Lapidus, lined with fountains and shaded seating a block from the beach. An easy, car-free evening stroll for browsing and people-watching.

items.name: Faena District & the Faena Forum
items.description: A theatrical enclave of Alan Faena's making — a gilded Damien Hirst mammoth, a Rem Koolhaas-designed cultural forum and a hotel dripping in Baz Luhrmann drama. Come for a drink and the spectacle even if you stay elsewhere; unabashed, cinematic luxury.

items.name: Holocaust Memorial of Miami Beach
items.description: Kenneth Treister's powerful sculptural memorial — a giant bronze hand rising amid figures, set in a contemplative garden. A quiet, moving stop of real gravity a short walk from the Convention Center and Botanical Garden.

items.name: Miami Beach Botanical Garden
items.description: A serene 2.6-acre green pocket of palms, orchids, a Japanese garden and lily ponds in the middle of the city — and free to enter. A cool, shaded pause between the beach and the Convention Center.

items.name: The Wolfsonian–FIU
items.description: A design-and-decorative-arts museum in a striking 1927 building, exploring how design shaped the modern age — propaganda, industry, Art Deco objects. A thoughtful, air-conditioned hour for design-minded visitors on Washington Avenue.

items.name: Zoo Miami
items.description: A vast cage-free, walk-and-tram safari park with Asian and African habitats and a Florida section — one of the country's largest zoos. A full, gentle family day; go early to beat the heat, and use the tram to spare tired legs.

items.name: Deering Estate
credentials: U.S. National Register of Historic Places
items.description: Charles Deering's bayfront estate — historic houses, a fossil-rich hammock, mangrove shoreline and canoe access, quieter than its famous sibling Vizcaya. A tranquil nature-and-history morning for those who like their culture uncrowded.

items.name: Matheson Hammock Park & atoll pool
items.description: A man-made tidal atoll pool ringed by sand and palms beside Biscayne Bay, calm and shallow with the skyline in the distance. One of the safest, prettiest swims for small children, with a marina and cafe alongside.

items.name: Española Way
items.description: A pretty pedestrian lane of Mediterranean-revival buildings, string lights, tapas terraces and buskers a block off Ocean Drive. A charming spot for an early-evening aperitivo before dinner.

items.name: Pérez-area sunset sail / private yacht charter
items.description: Beyond the group cruises, Biscayne Bay is made for a private catamaran or motor-yacht charter — a captain, a chef, veg-friendly catering and a swim stop off a sandbar. The most memorable evening on the water, tailored entirely to your family.

items.name: Nightlife on Washington Avenue & the rooftops
items.description: Miami's after-dark reputation is earned — from South Beach clubs to rooftop lounges over Brickell and the Design District's sleeker bars. For UHNI guests, a host or table-service arrangement smooths the night; the concierge can curate a discreet, easy evening.

items.name: L'Atelier de Joël Robuchon
items.description: The Robuchon counter in the Design District — the only two-star table in Florida, for a third year running.

items.name: The Surf Club Restaurant
items.description: Thomas Keller's continental grand room inside the Four Seasons Surf Club — old-glamour Miami at its most refined.

items.name: Cote Miami
items.description: The Michelin-starred Korean steakhouse from New York — smokeless grills, dry-aged beef and endless Champagne.

items.name: Elcielo Miami
items.description: Juan Manuel Barrientos's multisensory Colombian tasting menu — theatre, memory and Andean flavour in Brickell.

items.name: Shingo
items.description: Shingo Akikuni's fourteen-seat omakase in the Gables — pristine edomae sushi of great precision.

items.name: Hiden
items.description: An eight-seat omakase behind a hidden door in Wynwood — Seijun Okano's singular, secret counter.

items.name: Ogawa
items.description: Refined Edomae-style omakase paired with rare Japanese whiskies — quiet mastery north of the city centre.

items.name: Tambourine Room by Tristan Brandt
items.description: Tristan Brandt's French cooking with Asian notes inside the Carillon — a jewel-box tasting-menu room.

items.name: Ariete
items.description: Michael Beltran's New-American-meets-Cuban cooking in the Grove — personal, Miami-rooted and quietly excellent.

items.name: Boia De
items.description: A tiny, cult Italian-American counter in a strip mall — outsized cooking, no ceremony, a real find.

items.name: Le Jardinier Miami
items.description: Alain Verzeroli's garden-driven French room in the Design District — seasonal, light and beautifully composed.

items.name: Los Félix
items.description: Masa-driven modern Mexican in the Grove — a Green Star kitchen built on heirloom corn and local produce.

items.name: Stubborn Seed
items.description: Top Chef winner Jeremy Ford's refined, ingredient-led room — a Green Star for its sustainable kitchen.

items.name: EntreNos
items.description: A twelve-seat counter from Evan Burgess and Osmel Gonzalez — hyper-local, sustainable, deeply personal.

items.name: Mutra
items.description: The world's first kosher restaurant to earn a Michelin star — Raz Shabtai's inventive seasonal Middle Eastern.

items.name: Ghee Indian Kitchen
items.description: Chef Niven Patel's farm-driven Indian cooking — coastal curries and roasted vegetables from his own fields.

items.name: Phuc Yea
items.description: Vietnamese-Cajun cooking with real swagger — a beloved, boldly flavoured MiMo institution.

items.name: Lucali
items.description: The Brooklyn pizza legend's Miami outpost — thin-crust pies made one at a time, worth the wait.

items.name: Sanguich de Miami
items.description: The definitive Cuban sandwich, made from scratch — house-cured meats and pressed medianoche on Calle Ocho.

items.name: Broken Shaker
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars (multiple years; first Miami bar to make the list)
Tales of the Cocktail Spirited Award — Best American High Volume Cocktail Bar
items.description: The garden bar that put Miami on the world cocktail map — herb-driven, barefoot-glamour drinking by the pool.

items.name: The Living Room, Faena Hotel
credentials: Inside a MICHELIN Two-Key, Forbes 5-Star hotel — a Miami Beach landmark
items.description: A drink amid Faena's gilded, red-velvet theatre — the most glamorous hotel bar in Miami Beach.

items.name: The Bar at The Surf Club
credentials: Inside a MICHELIN Two-Key, Forbes 5-Star hotel (Four Seasons Surf Club)
items.description: A jewel-box bar in a restored 1930s beach club — Winston Churchill drank here; the glamour is real.

items.name: Café La Trova
items.description: Julio Cabrera's Havana-style cantina — the finest Cuban cocktails in America, poured by master cantineros.

items.name: ViceVersa
items.description: A refined, ingredient-driven cocktail room that broke into the region's very best — Miami's newest star bar.

items.name: Sweet Liberty Drinks & Supply Co.
credentials: Tales of the Cocktail Spirited Award — Best American Cocktail Bar (Best New, 2016)
items.description: John Lermayer's warm, all-day neighbourhood bar — serious cocktails without a shred of pretension.

items.name: Sugar, EAST Miami
credentials: Widely rated among Miami's best rooftop bars
items.description: A Balinese-styled rooftop garden on the 40th floor — the highest bar in the city, with 360° bay-and-skyline views.

items.title: Vizcaya at opening
items.description: The Gilded-Age villa and Italianate gardens on the bay are best in the first cool hour before the day heats up.

items.title: Everglades airboat and private naturalist
items.description: An hour west, a private guide gets you past the tourist airboat circuit into genuine wetland and wildlife.

items.title: Design District art and architecture walk
items.description: The Institute of Contemporary Art, the De la Cruz collection and the architecture make a serious cultural afternoon.

items.title: Day sail to the Biscayne sandbars
items.description: A private boat out to Stiltsville and the sandbars is the way locals actually enjoy the water.

plan.heading: 3 days in Miami, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle into a cabana suite at The Setai, then a slow walk through the Art Deco district off Ocean Drive before the crowds gather.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A private charter out of Miami Beach Marina to sandbars and a quiet swim, back for a late afternoon on the sand.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Carbone Miami in the Design District, then a nightcap at Sweet Liberty.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Institute of Contemporary Art and the Design District's flagship maisons before lunch at MC Kitchen.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Rubell Museum and Wynwood's serious galleries and studios, at your own pace.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Omakase at Ogawa, then Espanola Way for a quiet drink.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The gardens and villa at Vizcaya Museum before the heat, with time along Biscayne Bay.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Coconut Grove and a table at Cote or a long lunch at the Biltmore in Coral Gables.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Sunset dinner at Stubborn Seed in South Beach to close.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: South Beach
items.description: Art Deco, ocean and nightlife — iconic but busy; ideal for a couple of nights, less so for a whole stay.

items.name: Design District / Midtown
items.description: Galleries, flagship boutiques and the best new restaurants — the tasteful, walkable base on the mainland.

items.name: Coconut Grove
items.description: Leafy, low-rise and family-old-money; bayfront calm for travellers who want green over glitz.

events.name: Art Basel Miami Beach
events.note: The city's marquee week; the fair anchors dozens of satellite shows and the design world descends.

events.name: Ultra Music Festival
events.note: Electronic-music weekend at Bayfront Park that headlines Miami Music Week.

events.name: Miami International Boat Show
events.note: One of the world's largest boat shows, a fixture of the city's on-water calendar over Presidents' Day weekend.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Arrive into Miami International (MIA), roughly 20 minutes from the coast; a chauffeured car meets you planeside where arranged, or a private car from arrivals to Miami Beach, Bal Harbour or Brickell.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car and driver is the way to move between the beach, the Design District and Coconut Grove; distances are short but the heat and valet-only culture make walking impractical.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: US eSIMs (Airalo, T-Mobile) activate instantly and coverage is universal; every good hotel and restaurant has fast wifi.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: US dollars; cards are used for everything and contactless is standard; tip 18–20 percent in restaurants and a few dollars for valet and bellhops.

onGround.note: Stay in Bal Harbour or the South-of-Fifth end of South Beach for quiet and space away from the party strip; dress is relaxed but polished, and reserve beachfront restaurants well ahead in season (December–April).

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: December to April is dry, warm and clear — the reason to come; June to October is hot, humid and inside Atlantic hurricane season, with September and October the wettest and riskiest.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No direct service from India; the clean routing is one stop through the Gulf — Qatar (Doha) or Emirates (Dubai) — at roughly 19-22 hours door to door, both strong in business and first. Doha's Al Mourjan and Dubai's Emirates lounge make the layover restful; European hubs (BA via London, Lufthansa via Frankfurt) work but add time.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required beyond routine; tap water is safe. Safe for the traveller staying in Brickell, South Beach, Coral Gables or Bal Harbour; ordinary big-city caution at night. Sun and heat are the real hazards in summer.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian dining is effortless — the city runs on it, and Jain-friendly meals are readily adapted. Strong Indian options in and around the metro; the sizeable Gujarati and South Indian community means authentic thalis and dosas are close at hand.

seo.title: Milan — TripAgent
seo.description: Milan, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Milan
hero.tagline: Italy's capital of fashion, design and quiet wealth.

ourTake.lede: Milan is a working luxury city, not an open-air museum — its pleasures are the shops, the aperitivo hour and one or two great sights done properly. Book Leonardo's Last Supper weeks ahead; it is the one thing you cannot walk up to. Skip the crowded Duomo rooftop queue at midday and go at opening, then spend the evening in the Brera lanes.
ourTake.comeIf: You want fashion, design and aperitivo, and Lake Como an hour up the road.
ourTake.skipIf: You want ruins and postcard Italy over style and shopping.
