guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Bvlgari Hotel Milano
items.description: The jeweller's Milanese house — a hidden 18th-century palazzo with a vast private garden, a cul-de-sac from Via Montenapoleone.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Milano
items.description: A serene former Renaissance convent in the heart of the fashion quarter — cloistered gardens and the surest hands in Milan.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental, Milan
items.description: Four linked 18th-century palazzi on a discreet backstreet beside La Scala — the city's only Forbes Five-Star.

items.name: Portrait Milano
items.description: A Ferragamo-family house built around Milan's oldest Baroque seminary courtyard — the address of the moment.

items.name: Armani Hotel Milano
items.description: Mr Armani's own vision of stay — greige calm and 'stay with Armani' service on Via Manzoni.

items.name: Hotel Principe di Savoia, Dorchester Collection
items.description: A neoclassical grand dame on Piazza della Repubblica — old-Milan splendour on a generous scale.

items.name: Grand Hotel et de Milan
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: Milan's historic grand hotel since 1863 — Verdi's home for decades, steps from La Scala.

items.name: Casa Cipriani Milano
items.description: A members'-club-style house of quiet exclusivity — the Cipriani sense of ease, brought to central Milan.

items.name: Palazzo Parigi Hotel & Grand Spa
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A light-filled palazzo on the edge of Brera — marble, French windows and one of Milan's largest hotel spas.

items.name: Excelsior Hotel Gallia, a Luxury Collection Hotel
items.description: A 1932 Art Deco landmark by Centrale station — Milan's largest hotel spa and a celebrated rooftop over the city.

items.name: Bulgari, Château Monfort
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A fairy-tale Art Nouveau castle near the Giardini — theatrical, romantic and a little out of the ordinary.

items.name: Vico Milano
items.description: A sleek, design-led newcomer in the towers of Porta Nuova — contemporary Milan at its most current.

items.name: Milano Verticale | UNA Esperienze
items.description: A sleek vertical hotel in the towers of Porta Nuova — contemporary Milan, with a Michelin-starred kitchen inside.

items.name: Senato Hotel Milano
items.description: A serene, all-white design boutique built around a courtyard — 43 rooms of quiet Milanese taste.

items.name: Rosa Grand Milano — Starhotels Collezione
items.description: A polished, well-run house a minute from the Duomo — location above all.

items.name: Room Mate Giulia
items.description: A design hotel tucked right beside the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II — you cannot stay more central.

items.name: The Yard Milano
items.description: A quirky, sport-and-vintage-themed townhouse hotel with real personality, near Porta Romana.

items.name: Maison Borella
items.description: A restored canal-side house on the Naviglio Grande — a rare pocket of calm on the water.

items.name: Duomo di Milano (Milan Cathedral)
credentials: MICHELIN Green Guide ★★★ — worth a special journey
One of the largest cathedrals in the world
items.description: The vast pink-Candoglia-marble Gothic cathedral that took nearly six centuries to build is the emotional centre of Milan and the natural first stop for a multi-generational family. Book a skip-the-line entry so grandparents move straight in from the piazza rather than queueing in the sun.

items.name: Duomo Rooftop Terraces
credentials: MICHELIN Green Guide ★★★ — worth a special journey
items.description: You walk among 3,400 statues, spires and flying buttresses in Candoglia marble, with the Alps on the horizon on a clear day and the golden Madonnina overhead. Take the lift rather than the 251 steps for older relatives and small children, and go late afternoon for the light.

items.name: The Last Supper (Il Cenacolo), Santa Maria delle Grazie
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Church and Dominican Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie with 'The Last Supper' by Leonardo da Vinci (inscribed 1980)
MICHELIN Green Guide ★★★ — worth a special journey
items.description: Leonardo da Vinci's fragile 1490s mural survives on the refectory wall of a Dominican convent, seen by only small timed groups for 15 minutes at a time. Tickets vanish months ahead, so this is exactly the sort of unlock a concierge should secure well before you travel.

items.name: Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II
credentials: One of the world's oldest active shopping arcades (opened 1877)
items.description: The soaring 1877 glass-and-iron arcade linking the Duomo to La Scala is both a monument and the world's oldest luxury shopping mall, home to the original Prada boutique, Louis Vuitton, and the historic Camparino bar. Spin your heel on the mosaic bull for luck, then let the family browse in cool shade.

items.name: Teatro alla Scala (La Scala)
credentials: MICHELIN Green Guide ★★ — worth a detour
One of the world's leading opera houses
items.description: Opened in 1778, La Scala is the most storied opera house on earth, where Verdi and Puccini premiered and where a box for the season opener is one of Milan's true social currencies. Pair a performance with the adjoining museum for the daytime members of a multi-gen group.

items.name: Quadrilatero della Moda (Fashion Quadrilateral)
credentials: Among the most expensive and prestigious luxury shopping districts in the world
items.description: The grid of Via Montenapoleone, Via della Spiga, Via Sant'Andrea and Via Manzoni is the densest concentration of maison flagships in the world — Armani, Prada, Versace, Dolce & Gabbana, Bottega, Hermes. Ask for private appointments and after-hours boutique openings; this is the reason many UHNI travellers come to Milan at all.

items.name: Castello Sforzesco (Sforza Castle)
credentials: MICHELIN Green Guide ★★ — worth a detour
items.description: The vast 15th-century Sforza fortress holds a cluster of civic museums including Michelangelo's unfinished final work, the Rondanini Pietà. The scale and open courtyards make it easy for children and grandparents to wander at their own pace before Parco Sempione behind it.

items.name: Pinacoteca di Brera
credentials: MICHELIN Green Guide ★★★ — worth a special journey
One of Italy's foremost art collections
items.description: Milan's greatest picture gallery, with Raphael's Marriage of the Virgin, Mantegna's foreshortened Dead Christ and Piero della Francesca's Montefeltro Altarpiece. Compact enough for one focused visit, and set inside the atmospheric artists' quarter for lunch afterwards.

items.name: Brera District
items.description: The cobbled bohemian quarter around the Pinacoteca, with its botanical garden, art shops, antiques and candlelit trattorias, is the most romantic part of central Milan to stroll after dark. Quiet, walkable and discreet — ideal for an evening away from the crowds.

items.name: Museo Poldi Pezzoli
credentials: MICHELIN Green Guide ★★ — worth a detour
items.description: A perfectly preserved 19th-century aristocrat's house-museum steps from the fashion streets, its most famous piece Pollaiuolo's Portrait of a Young Woman. Intimate and rarely crowded — a refined pause between boutique appointments.

items.name: Museo Bagatti Valsecchi
items.description: The Bagatti Valsecchi brothers built a lavish neo-Renaissance home in the 1880s and filled it with genuine 15th- and 16th-century art and furniture, then lived in it. One of Europe's best-preserved historic house-museums, and a hidden gem in the middle of the Quadrilatero.

items.name: Museo del Novecento
items.description: Milan's museum of 20th-century Italian art sits inside the Palazzo dell'Arengario on Piazza del Duomo, its spiral ramp opening onto Futurist masterpieces and a fourth-floor window framing the cathedral. The rooftop restaurant Giacomo Arengario has cathedral views for lunch.

items.name: Gallerie d'Italia — Piazza Scala
items.description: Three interconnected palazzi facing La Scala hold a superb collection of 19th- and 20th-century Italian art, from Canova bas-reliefs to Boccioni. Beautifully restored, air-conditioned and calm — a civilised refuge in the very centre.

items.name: Fondazione Prada
items.description: Rem Koolhaas/OMA transformed a 1910s distillery into a striking contemporary art campus, complete with a gold-leaf-clad 'Haunted House' and Wes Anderson's jewel-box Bar Luce. A design pilgrimage that appeals to the younger generation as much as serious collectors.

items.name: Pirelli HangarBicocca
items.description: A colossal former industrial hangar showing ambitious contemporary art, anchored by Anselm Kiefer's permanent 'The Seven Heavenly Palaces' — seven leaning concrete towers up to 19 metres tall. Free to enter and genuinely awe-inspiring for all ages.

items.name: Navigli Canals
items.description: The Naviglio Grande and Naviglio Pavese canals, part of a system Leonardo helped engineer, are now a lively waterside quarter of aperitivo bars, vintage shops and the monthly antiques market. Charming to walk by day; for UHNI travellers a private canal-side dinner or a quiet aperitivo away from the student crowd works best.

items.name: Porta Nuova & Bosco Verticale
credentials: Bosco Verticale — International Highrise Award winner (2014) and CTBUH Best Tall Building Worldwide (2015)
items.description: Milan's gleaming business district around Piazza Gae Aulenti is crowned by the Bosco Verticale, Stefano Boeri's award-winning 'vertical forest' towers dressed in thousands of trees. A striking counterpoint to old Milan and a favourite with design-minded younger travellers.

items.name: Cimitero Monumentale
items.description: This vast 19th-century cemetery is an open-air museum of Italian funerary sculpture, with extravagant Art Nouveau and Art Deco tombs of Milan's great industrial families. Solemn, uncrowded and photographically extraordinary — a quietly moving hidden gem.

items.name: Corso Como & 10 Corso Como
items.description: The pedestrian Corso Como is home to the legendary concept store 10 Corso Como, founded by Carla Sozzani — a pioneering blend of fashion, design, gallery, bookshop and courtyard café. A one-stop distillation of Milanese taste for the shopping-focused.

items.name: Triennale Milano
items.description: Italy's leading museum of design and architecture, set in the elegant Palazzo dell'Arte on the edge of Parco Sempione, with the permanent Italian Design Museum and a rooftop restaurant. Essential for anyone who cares about how Milan became the world's design capital.

items.name: Fuorisalone & Salone del Mobile (in season)
credentials: Salone del Mobile — the world's largest furniture and design fair
items.description: Each April the world's design elite descends on Milan for the Salone del Mobile furniture fair and the citywide Fuorisalone installations across Brera, Tortona and 5vie. In season it is the single best week to be in Milan — book everything, hotels included, far in advance.

items.name: Basilica di Sant'Ambrogio
credentials: MICHELIN Green Guide ★★ — worth a detour
One of the most ancient churches in Milan (consecrated 379–386 AD)
items.description: One of the oldest churches in Milan, founded by the city's patron Saint Ambrose in the 4th century, its austere Romanesque form a world away from the Gothic Duomo. A serene, deeply historic stop with beautiful golden mosaics.

items.name: Basilica di San Lorenzo Maggiore & Colonne di San Lorenzo
items.description: An early-Christian basilica fronted by 16 Roman columns — the finest surviving ancient Roman ruin in Milan — with the exquisite Cappella di Sant'Aquilino and its 4th-century mosaics inside. The colonnade square is a lively evening gathering spot in the Ticinese.

items.name: Villa Necchi Campiglio
credentials: Managed by FAI — Fondo per l'Ambiente Italiano
items.description: A 1930s rationalist villa with pool and tennis court, restored by the FAI and used as a film set (I Am Love, House of Gucci), offering a rare glimpse into moneyed Milanese domestic life between the wars. Its garden café is a discreet, elegant lunch.

items.name: Pinacoteca Ambrosiana
credentials: MICHELIN Green Guide ★★ — worth a detour
Holds Leonardo da Vinci's Codex Atlanticus
items.description: Founded by Cardinal Federico Borromeo in 1618, this gallery holds Caravaggio's Basket of Fruit, Raphael's cartoon for the School of Athens, and pages of Leonardo's Codex Atlanticus. A serious, uncrowded collection a short walk from the Duomo.

items.name: Museo Nazionale Scienza e Tecnologia Leonardo da Vinci
credentials: Italy's largest science and technology museum
items.description: Italy's largest science and technology museum, with galleries of machines built from Leonardo's drawings plus a real submarine and vintage aircraft. The most reliable crowd-pleaser in the city for children and teenagers.

items.name: Parco Sempione & Arco della Pace
items.description: Milan's grand central park unfurls behind the Sforza Castle to the Napoleonic Arch of Peace, with the Torre Branca observation tower for aerial views. Green, walkable space for grandparents and children between the museums.

items.name: QC Termemilano (Spa)
items.description: A refined day-spa set in a historic building beside a stretch of the old Spanish city walls, with pools, saunas and a tram-carriage relaxation room. A restorative half-day for the adults while the family shops or sightsees.

items.name: Chiesa di San Maurizio al Monastero Maggiore
items.description: Nicknamed the 'Sistine Chapel of Milan', this modest 16th-century church interior is entirely covered in luminous frescoes by Bernardino Luini and his school. Free, uncrowded and utterly unexpected — a true hidden gem near the Last Supper.

items.name: Corso Vittorio Emanuele II & San Babila
items.description: The pedestrian high street running from the Duomo to Piazza San Babila is Milan's mainstream shopping spine — Italian and international brands, department stores and cafes. Useful for the family's everyday buys while serious shopping happens in the Quadrilatero next door.

items.name: Excelsior Milano & La Rinascente (rooftop)
items.description: La Rinascente, Italy's landmark department store beside the Duomo, has a seventh-floor terrace of food counters and bars looking straight onto the cathedral spires. A convenient, glamorous perch for a break with unbeatable views.

items.name: Fondazione Nicola Trussardi & Palazzo Marino (Piazza della Scala)
items.description: The elegant Piazza della Scala, anchored by the 16th-century Palazzo Marino (Milan's city hall) and a Leonardo monument, is one of the city's most photogenic squares. A graceful pause between La Scala and the shopping streets.

items.name: Chiostri dell'Umanitaria & Rotonda della Besana
items.description: The Rotonda della Besana is a serene 18th-century circular arcaded courtyard, once a cemetery, now a tranquil green enclosure with a baroque chapel. A calm, little-known spot for a quiet stroll away from any crowd.

items.name: Isola Neighbourhood
items.description: Once a working-class 'island' cut off by the railway, Isola is now Milan's coolest quarter — independent boutiques, natural-wine bars and design studios in the shadow of the Bosco Verticale. Best explored on foot for a feel of contemporary Milanese life.

items.name: Porta Venezia & Corso Venezia palazzi
items.description: Corso Venezia is lined with grand Liberty-style (Italian Art Nouveau) palaces and leads to the leafy Giardini Pubblici Indro Montanelli. An elegant residential quarter with fine dining and the city's Natural History Museum for children.

items.name: Aperitivo in Milan
items.description: The pre-dinner ritual of a Negroni or Milano-Torino with generous snacks was effectively invented here — Campari was born in Milan. For UHNI travellers, a reserved table at a rooftop bar such as Terrazza Aperol or a hotel bar beats the crowded street scene.

items.name: Historic Cafes: Camparino & Cova
credentials: Cova — one of Milan's oldest pastry shops (founded 1817)
items.description: Camparino in Galleria (1915) is the birthplace of the Campari ritual, while Pasticceria Cova on Via Montenapoleone has served Milanese society since 1817. Both are elegant, vegetarian-friendly stops for coffee, pastries and people-watching.

items.name: Lake Como (Bellagio, Como, Varenna)
credentials: MICHELIN Green Guide ★★★ — worth a special journey
Villa del Balbianello and Villa Carlotta are among Italy's most celebrated lake villas
items.description: Under an hour by train or car, Lake Como delivers the classic Italian lakes fantasy — Bellagio's terraced gardens, Villa del Balbianello, Villa Carlotta and George Clooney's Laglio. Arrange a private boat and a villa lunch; this is the single most requested escape from Milan.

items.name: Bergamo Alta (Upper Town)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Venetian Walls of Bergamo (part of 'Venetian Works of Defence between the 16th and 17th Centuries', inscribed 2017)
items.description: Less than an hour away, Bergamo's walled Città Alta is a beautifully intact medieval-Renaissance hill town reached by an 1887 funicular, crowned by the Piazza Vecchia and the Colleoni Chapel. Its Venetian walls are UNESCO-listed and its restaurants excellent and unhurried.

items.name: Lake Maggiore & the Borromean Islands
credentials: MICHELIN Green Guide ★★★ — worth a special journey
Isola Bella — Palazzo Borromeo and its baroque garden
items.description: Around 90 minutes away, Lake Maggiore's Borromean Islands hold the baroque Palazzo Borromeo on Isola Bella, its terraced gardens roamed by white peacocks, and the fishing village of Isola dei Pescatori. Grander and quieter than Como, ideal for a private-boat day.

items.name: Certosa di Pavia
credentials: MICHELIN Green Guide ★★★ — worth a special journey
One of the largest monasteries in Italy
items.description: Less than an hour south, this Carthusian charterhouse commissioned in 1396 by the Visconti dukes is one of the great masterpieces of Italian Gothic-Renaissance architecture, its facade a riot of marble sculpture. Serene, still a working monastery, and beautifully off the mainstream tourist trail.

items.name: Franciacorta Wine Country
credentials: Franciacorta DOCG — Italy's premier traditional-method sparkling wine region
items.description: About an hour east toward Lake Iseo, Franciacorta is Italy's answer to Champagne — rolling vineyards producing traditional-method sparkling wine, with elegant cellars offering private tastings and lunches. A refined, adult day out for oenophiles.

items.name: Pavia (Old University Town)
credentials: Home to the University of Pavia (founded 1361)
items.description: The medieval city on the Ticino river has one of Europe's oldest universities (1361), a distinctive covered bridge and towered skyline. Easily paired with the Certosa for a full, unhurried day away from Milan's bustle.

items.name: Enrico Bartolini al MUDEC
items.description: Milan's only three-star — Italy's most-decorated chef, on the top floor of the MUDEC museum.

items.name: Seta by Antonio Guida
items.description: Antonio Guida's two-star room at the Mandarin Oriental — Mediterranean precision, faultlessly served.

items.name: Andrea Aprea
items.area: Porta Venezia (Fondazione Luigi Rovati, Corso Venezia)
items.description: Aprea's elegant two-star atop the Rovati foundation — contemporary Italian with a Neapolitan soul.

items.name: Il Luogo di Aimo e Nadia
items.description: A Milanese institution — Negrini and Pisani carrying forward one of Italy's great kitchens.

items.name: Verso
items.description: The Capitaneo brothers' assured two-star — refined, personal cooking near the Duomo.

items.name: Cracco in Galleria
items.description: Carlo Cracco's grand dining room inside the Galleria itself — the most glamorous address in Milan.

items.name: IYO Aalto
items.description: Takeshi Iwai's ambitious Japanese-European tasting room in the Porta Nuova towers.

items.name: Langosteria
items.description: Milan's glamorous seafood temple — oysters, crustaceans and the catch of the day, done with real flair.

items.name: Contraste
items.description: Matias Perdomo's playful, boundary-pushing tasting menu in an intimate townhouse room.

items.name: Berton
items.description: Andrea Berton's clean, modern cooking in the glass towers of Porta Nuova — broths and clarity are his signature.

items.name: Sadler
items.description: Claudio Sadler's long-held star — classical technique and Milanese elegance, quietly enduring.

items.name: Viva Viviana Varese
items.description: Viviana Varese's bold, sustainability-minded cooking — one of the city's most personal kitchens.

items.name: IYO
items.description: Italy's first starred Japanese restaurant — the room that proved sushi could be haute in Milan.

items.name: Horto
items.description: Norbert Niederkofler's radically seasonal 'Cook the Mountain' ethos, on a rooftop above the centre.

items.name: Joia
items.description: Europe's first vegetarian restaurant to win a star — Pietro Leemann's meditative, plant-led cooking.

items.name: L'Alchimia
items.description: A polished modern-Milanese room with a cocktail-bar heart — refined cooking, easy warmth.

items.name: Anima
items.description: A confident hotel-restaurant star in Porta Nuova — contemporary Italian with technical polish.

items.name: Sine by Di Pinto
items.description: Roberto Di Pinto's personal, southern-rooted cooking — one of the city's warmest starred rooms.

items.name: Procaccini
items.description: A newly-starred room of very personal cooking and live piano each evening — raw material, technique, hospitality.

items.name: Abba
items.description: Fabio Abbattista's 2024 debut, starred within a year — precise, well-travelled contemporary cooking.

items.name: Ratanà
items.description: Cesare Battisti's love letter to Lombard cooking — the yellow risotto alla milanese, done properly.

items.name: Trattoria Trippa
items.description: Diego Rossi's cult trattoria — offal, Milanese classics and Italian regional cooking, done with real conviction.

items.name: Dongiò
items.description: A beloved family-run Calabrian trattoria — 'nduja, fresh pasta and southern warmth, unchanged for decades.

items.name: L'Angolo d'Abruzzo
items.description: Generous, homely Abruzzese cooking in enormous portions — a great-value Milan institution.

items.name: Serendib
items.description: Milan's long-loved Sri Lankan and Indian table — the name means 'happy land', and it delivers.

items.name: La Cucina dei Frigoriferi Milanesi
items.description: Modern Italian cooking in the revived Palazzo del Ghiaccio complex — creative and good value.

items.name: Le Nove Scodelle
items.description: Serious, fiery Sichuan cooking — a reminder that some of Milan's best value is well beyond the centre.

items.name: Confine
credentials: 50 Top Pizza Italy 2025 — No. 2 in Italy
items.description: The best pizza in Milan — Neapolitan rounds, fried, padellino and gourmet slices, with a wine list to match.

items.name: Dry Milano
credentials: 50 Top Pizza Italy 2025 — No. 7 in Italy
items.description: The pizza-and-cocktails original that redefined the Milanese evening — great pies, better drinks.

items.name: Marghe
items.description: Honest, well-made Neapolitan pizza across the city — a dependable, everyday favourite.

items.name: Pasticceria Marchesi 1824
items.description: Milan's most elegant historic pasticceria — a Prada-owned jewel-box for coffee and pastries under the Galleria.

items.name: Pavé
items.description: A modern Milanese bakery beloved for its brioche and pastries — the city's best morning ritual.

items.name: Camparino in Galleria
items.description: The birthplace of the Milanese aperitivo — a Liberty-style bar under the Galleria, where Campari itself was born.

items.name: Bar Basso
credentials: Where the Negroni Sbagliato was invented (1972)
items.description: The birthplace of the Negroni Sbagliato — an unchanging 1960s institution and the temple of Milanese aperitivo.

items.name: Moebius Milano
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars — best in Italy on the list
items.description: Milan's highest-ranked bar — a food-music-and-cocktails concept of rare coherence, and the world's Highest Climber of its year.
A password-and-membership speakeasy of quiet excellence — one of Italy's most consistently ranked bars.

items.name: Nottingham Forest
items.description: A tiny, cult tiki-and-molecular bar that has long featured among the world's best — theatre in a glass.

items.name: Terrazza Aperol
credentials: A landmark aperitivo terrace overlooking the Duomo
items.description: An aperitivo terrace looking straight onto the Duomo — the most Milanese spritz there is.

items.name: Ceresio 7
credentials: A landmark rooftop bar atop a Dsquared2-designed building
items.description: Dsquared2's rooftop bar and pools above the old Enel building — glamour, a spritz and a sweep over the skyline.

items.name: Dry Milano
items.description: The pizza-and-cocktails original — a Brera room where the drinks are as serious as the pies.

items.title: Private viewing of The Last Supper
items.description: A reserved slot with an art historian for Leonardo's fresco, limited to a handful of visitors at a time.

items.title: Backstage during Fashion Week
items.description: Seats at a runway show and showroom access during the men's or women's collections.

items.title: Box at La Scala
items.description: A night at the world's most storied opera house, ideally for a premiere in the winter season.

items.title: Private tour of a maison's atelier
items.description: Behind-the-scenes at a Milanese fashion or design house not open to the public.

plan.heading: 3 days in Milan, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

days.title: The Duomo and the Last Supper

slots.text: The Montenapoleone quarter and the maison flagships, then aperitivo in Brera.

slots.label: Evening

slots.label: Evening

items.name: Brera
items.description: Cobbled artists' quarter with galleries and the best strolling — the romantic base.

items.name: Quadrilatero della Moda
items.description: The luxury shopping grid around Montenapoleone — for the serious shopper.

items.name: Navigli
items.description: Canalside bars and aperitivo — for a livelier, younger evening scene.

events.name: Milan Fashion Week
events.note: The women's shows twice a year turn the city into fashion's world capital.

events.name: Salone del Mobile (Design Week)
events.note: The world's biggest furniture and design fair, spilling into installations across every district.

events.name: Sant'Ambrogio & La Scala opening night
events.note: The city's patron-saint feast and the opera season's gala premiere on the same night.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Malpensa or the closer Linate; a chauffeured car handles the transfer, with Linate only about 15 minutes from the centre.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver for the city and the lakes, while the fashion quarter and centre around the Duomo are best walked.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Strong everywhere; a TIM or Vodafone eSIM works well, with fast wifi in hotels.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Euro; cards are accepted throughout and cash is rarely needed; service is generally included, so tipping is minimal.

onGround.note: Stay in the Quadrilatero della Moda or Brera for the best of the city; Milan dresses sharply, so an elegant wardrobe is expected, and Como, the lakes and the Alps are an easy day's drive with a car.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: May-June and September-October are best: mild, clear and comfortable for the city and lakes. Avoid humid, hazy July-August and the cold, fog-prone damp of December-January.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Air India flies nonstop Delhi-Milan Malpensa, about 9.5 hours on a Boeing 787 Dreamliner, roughly four times weekly; Mumbai and Bengaluru connect neatly via a Gulf hub. Malpensa is calmer than Fiumicino; pre-arrange a car for the 50-minute run into the city or on to Lake Como.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations beyond routine; safe, with ordinary care against pickpocketing around the Duomo, Centrale station and on the metro. Tap water is safe to drink.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian dining is straightforward; Jain and strict no-onion-garlic want advance notice. A fair Indian presence exists, but Milan's strength is refined vegetarian Italian; the advisor should brief fine-dining kitchens, which accommodate readily.

seo.title: Mumbai — TripAgent
seo.description: Mumbai, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Mumbai
hero.tagline: India's restless maximum city of sea, cinema and commerce.

ourTake.lede: Mumbai is a night-and-morning city; do the sea-facing walks and the dabbawala-era south at dawn, then let the evening belong to its restaurants and bars, which are among the best in the country. Don't waste a day on the crowded 'Bollywood tour' circuit; the real texture is in the Fort district's architecture and the fishing-village edges. Base yourself in the south, not the suburbs, unless you have a specific reason.
ourTake.comeIf: You want India's most cosmopolitan city — colonial architecture, serious restaurants, a real night out and sea-facing suites at the Taj or Four Seasons.
ourTake.skipIf: You are after quiet, nature or a slow escape; Mumbai is dense, loud and relentless.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Mumbai. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: The Taj Mahal Palace, Mumbai
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide 2025 Star Awards — recognised
Taj / part of IHCL's Taj palaces
items.description: India's most storied hotel, facing the Gateway of India since 1903 — the address every visiting family knows by name.

items.name: The Oberoi, Mumbai
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide 2025 Star Awards — recognised
The Oberoi Group / member, The Leading Hotels of the World (historic)
items.description: Serene, glass-walled and faultless on Marine Drive — Oberoi service at the southern tip of the city.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Mumbai
items.description: A polished uptown tower crowned by AER, the 34th-floor rooftop — the Four Seasons standard, in the middle of the city.

items.name: The St. Regis Mumbai
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide 2025 Star Awards — recognised
items.description: A soaring tower over Lower Parel with the theatrical Asilo rooftop — St. Regis butler service above the mills.

items.name: Taj Mahal Tower, Mumbai
items.description: The modern tower alongside the Palace — the same Gateway views and Taj address, at a lighter tariff.

items.name: The Leela Mumbai
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide 2025 Star Awards — recognised
The Leela Palaces, Hotels and Resorts
items.description: A lush, art-filled garden hotel by the international airport — the calm landing pad for arrivals and departures.

items.name: ITC Maratha, a Luxury Collection Hotel
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide 2025 Star Awards — recognised
items.description: An ITC grande dame near the airport — Maratha-inspired grandeur and ITC's celebrated kitchens.

items.name: ITC Grand Central, a Luxury Collection Hotel
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide 2025 Star Awards — recognised
items.description: A colonial-modern ITC house in Parel — well-run, central, and close to the Lower Parel dining scene.

items.name: InterContinental Marine Drive, Mumbai
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide 2025 Star Awards — recognised
items.description: A compact boutique tower on Marine Drive with a rooftop over the Queen's Necklace — the small-hotel sea view.

items.name: Gateway of India
items.description: The basalt triumphal arch on the harbour is where the city gathers at dawn and dusk, with Elephanta ferries pulling away and the Taj rising behind you. Step out of a Taj suite, cross the road, and the whole postcard of Bombay is at your feet.

items.name: The Taj Mahal Palace, Mumbai
items.description: Jamsetji Tata's 1903 landmark is still the grand dame of the city, its Florentine dome and cantilever staircase as much a Bombay institution as a hotel. Even if you are staying at the Oberoi, come for high tea at the Sea Lounge or a night at Harbour Bar, India's first licensed bar.

items.name: Elephanta Caves
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Elephanta Caves
items.description: An hour by ferry from the Gateway, these 5th–6th-century rock-cut Shiva temples on a green island are crowned by the colossal three-headed Trimurti, one of the great sculptures of India. Charter a private launch, go early, and have the caves nearly to yourself before the day crowds land.

items.name: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus
items.description: F.W. Stevens' 1887 Victorian Gothic railway cathedral, a working station moving millions daily, blends stone gargoyles and stained glass with Indian palace forms. Book the heritage tour to climb behind the façade into the boardroom and the star-chamber dome.

items.name: Fort & Kala Ghoda heritage precinct
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai
items.description: The tight grid around Kala Ghoda holds the densest concentration of Bombay's Victorian Gothic and Indo-Deco architecture, best walked slowly with a coffee and an eye for detail. This is the heart of the ensemble that earned the city its 2018 UNESCO listing.

items.name: Marine Drive & the Queen's Necklace
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai
items.description: The great Art Deco arc along the Arabian Sea glows into a curve of lights after dark, hence its nickname, and its curving parade of 1930s buildings is part of the UNESCO ensemble. A slow evening walk to Nariman Point, or a drive with the windows down, is the city's oldest ritual.

items.name: Chowpatty Beach
items.description: The city beach at the northern end of Marine Drive where Bombay comes to eat bhelpuri, watch the sunset, and mark Ganesh Visarjan every year. Come at dusk for the sea breeze and the theatre of the crowd, not for a swim.

items.name: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya (CSMVS)
items.description: The former Prince of Wales Museum, a domed Indo-Saracenic masterpiece by George Wittet, holds Indus seals, Gupta bronzes, Mughal miniatures and Chola sculpture across 60,000 objects. Ask about a curator-led private morning walk through the Indian sculpture and miniature galleries.

items.name: Jehangir Art Gallery
items.description: Since 1952 the city's most storied gallery, where Husain, Souza and the Progressives showed and where the pavement outside still doubles as an open-air art bazaar. It anchors a five-minute cluster of the country's best contemporary galleries.

items.name: Kala Ghoda galleries (Chatterjee & Lal, Galerie Mirchandani + Steinruecke, Project 88)
items.description: Within a few walkable blocks sit the galleries that define Indian contemporary art, from blue-chip names to the sharpest young programmes. A morning here is how serious collectors take the temperature of the market.

items.name: Prince of Wales Museum garden & the Kala Ghoda Arts Festival
items.description: Each February the precinct becomes a nine-day open-air festival of art, installations, music and design that fills the streets of the heritage district. The rest of the year the leafy quarter rewards an unhurried wander between galleries and cafés.

items.name: University of Mumbai Fort Campus & Rajabai Clock Tower
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai
items.description: Gilbert Scott's Venetian-Gothic library and its 85-metre Rajabai Tower, modelled on Big Ben and funded by a Jain merchant in his mother's name, look straight across the Oval Maidan. The interiors, when open, hold soaring stained glass and carved teak.

items.name: Bombay High Court & the Oval Maidan
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai
items.description: One of the grandest colonial Gothic courts in the country faces a wide green maidan flanked by Marine Drive's Deco towers, the Gothic-versus-Deco face-off that is the whole point of the UNESCO citation. Cricket on the grass, robed advocates on the steps, pure Bombay.

items.name: Asiatic Society of Mumbai (Town Hall)
items.description: Behind thirty steps and eight Doric columns, this 1833 neoclassical library holds a quarter-million books and rare manuscripts, including one of only two original copies of Dante's Divine Comedy. The reading room feels frozen in another century, and few tourists ever climb the steps.

items.name: Horniman Circle Gardens
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai
items.description: A perfect ring of gardens ringed by grand arcaded Victorian buildings, laid out on the site of the old Bombay Green, and a favourite for evening concerts and design pop-ups. The colonnade around it is the most elegant address in the old town.

items.name: Flora Fountain & Hutatma Chowk
items.description: The 1864 Portland-stone fountain of Flora at the crossroads of the Fort district marks the ceremonial centre of business Bombay. Around it radiate the banks, bookshops and Irani cafés of the old commercial city.

items.name: David Sassoon Library & Reading Room
items.description: A Venetian-Gothic gem of 1870 with a first-floor verandah of cane chairs shaded by trees, one of the loveliest quiet spaces in the city. Members read newspapers here as they have for 150 years, unhurried by the traffic below.

items.name: Colaba Causeway
items.description: The city's most famous shopping street, from silver and antiques to street stalls, cotton kaftans and the legendary Leopold and Café Mondegar. Have your driver drop you at one end and browse your way to a coffee at the other.

items.name: Sassoon Docks
items.description: Bombay's oldest wet dock, from 1875, comes alive before dawn as Koli fisherwomen auction the night's catch in a riot of colour and salt. Since the 2017 St+art project its walls carry striking murals and portraits of the fishing community.

items.name: Crawford Market (Mahatma Jyotiba Phule Mandai)
items.description: A Norman-Gothic market hall of 1869 whose entrance friezes were designed by Rudyard Kipling's father, still trading in fruit, flowers, spices and imported foods. Go for the architecture and the theatre; the wholesale spice lanes behind are a sensory education.

items.name: Chor Bazaar & Mutton Street antiques
items.description: The famous 'thieves' market' is the city's great hunting ground for colonial furniture, vintage Bollywood posters, gramophones, brass and genuine bric-a-brac. Bring an eye and patience; the best pieces sit above the shopfronts, brought out for serious buyers.

items.name: Haji Ali Dargah
items.description: A white marble tomb and mosque set on an islet, reached by a causeway that vanishes at high tide, floating on the Arabian Sea off Worli. The walk out at low tide, past qawwali singers and the open water on both sides, is one of the city's great atmospheres.

items.name: Shree Siddhivinayak Temple
items.description: Mumbai's most beloved Ganesh temple, its inner sanctum gleaming with gold, draws everyone from film stars to industrialists on Tuesday mornings. Arrange a VIP darshan to bypass the queues and enter with calm at first light.

items.name: Mahalaxmi Temple
items.description: A seaside temple to the goddess of wealth perched above the rocks near Haji Ali, garlanded and thronged, especially during Navratri. The short causeway between the two shrines is one of the more spiritual walks in the city.

items.name: Banganga Tank & Walkeshwar Temple
items.description: A sacred spring-fed stone tank from AD 1127, ringed by temples, ghats and old dharamshalas, hidden in a fold of the city's most exclusive hill. It hosts an intimate classical music festival and feels a thousand miles, not a few streets, from the towers of Malabar Hill.

items.name: Hanging Gardens & Kamala Nehru Park
items.description: Terraced gardens atop Malabar Hill with topiary hedges and a sweeping view down over the Marine Drive arc and Chowpatty. The 'old woman's shoe' at the children's park is a nostalgic Bombay landmark for multi-generational visits.

items.name: Dhobi Ghat viewpoint (Mahalaxmi)
items.description: From the bridge above Mahalaxmi station you look down on the world's largest open-air laundry, hundreds of concrete washing pens worked by hand exactly as they have been for over a century. A ten-minute stop that captures the city's engine of labour in one frame.

items.name: Dr Bhau Daji Lad Mumbai City Museum
items.description: The city's oldest museum, a jewel-box of restored Victorian interiors telling the story of Bombay through models, maps and decorative arts. Its exquisite gilt-and-colour restoration won a UNESCO Asia-Pacific award and is a joy for anyone who loves design.

items.name: Veermata Jijabai Bhosale Udyan & Zoo (Byculla / Rani Baug)
items.description: The city's oldest public garden, from 1861, a leafy 50-acre botanical garden and zoo that also guards the original stone elephant that gave Elephanta its name. A gentle green outing with children away from the heat and horns.

items.name: Sanjay Gandhi National Park
items.description: A genuine tropical forest of 100-plus square kilometres inside the city limits, home to leopards, birdlife, a lion-and-tiger safari and quiet walking trails. A morning here is the surprising green lung of a megacity of twenty million.

items.name: Kanheri Caves
items.description: More than a hundred Buddhist rock-cut caves carved into a basalt ridge in the forest, dating from the 1st to 10th centuries, with a magnificent chaitya prayer hall. Combine with the national park for a half-day of forest, history and stillness.

items.name: Global Vipassana Pagoda
items.description: A gilded Burmese-style pagoda near Gorai crowned by the world's largest pillarless stone dome, seating 8,000 meditators and enshrining relics of the Buddha. Reached by a short ferry, it offers ten-day courses and drop-in guided meditation in serene surrounds.

items.name: Bandra Bandstand & the Promenade
items.description: A rocky seafront promenade where the young suburb comes to walk, court and watch the sea, past the walls of Bollywood's biggest homes, including Shah Rukh Khan's Mannat. Sunset here is Bandra's answer to Marine Drive, breezier and more bohemian.

items.name: Bandra street art & Chapel Road murals
items.description: The old East Indian village lanes around Chapel Road, Ranwar and Waroda Road are a living gallery of murals, cottages and cross-shrines. A morning walking tour reveals the Portuguese-Catholic soul beneath the city's coolest neighbourhood.

items.name: Mount Mary Basilica
items.description: A hilltop basilica above Bandstand whose September Bandra Fair draws lakhs of the faithful of every religion. The view over the bay and the quiet candle-lit interior reward a short climb through the old village.

items.name: Bandra–Worli Sea Link
items.description: A cable-stayed bridge sweeping across Mahim Bay, best experienced at speed with the skyline of the western seafront laid out ahead. The view back from the Worli side at dusk is the modern city's most cinematic frame.

items.name: Worli Village & Worli Fort
items.description: A tiny Koli fishing village and crumbling 17th-century watch-fort survive at the tip of Worli, surrounded by the gleaming new skyline. The lanes, boats and sea-facing bastion are a photographer's secret and a reminder of the original seven islands.

items.name: Nehru Centre & Nehru Planetarium
items.description: A striking modernist dome housing a science-and-culture centre, art gallery and planetarium, a good rainy-day or multi-generational stop. Its cultural programming brings some of the city's better classical concerts and talks.

items.name: Juhu Beach
items.description: The long suburban beach lined with film-star bungalows and the grand old JW Marriott and Sun-n-Sand hotels, famous for its evening chaat stalls. Come for the promenade, the pav bhaji and the sunset, not the swim.

items.name: ISKCON Sri Sri Radha Rasabihari Temple
items.description: A serene marble Krishna temple with beautifully carved interiors, tucked just off Juhu beach, with an excellent pure-vegetarian Govinda's restaurant attached. A calm and easy stop for a family darshan and a sattvic thali.

items.name: Film City (Dadasaheb Phalke Chitranagari)
items.description: The sprawling studio complex in the hills of Goregaon where much of Bollywood is shot, with sets, gardens and hilltop lookouts. A guided studio tour, or a fixer arranging a live shoot visit, is a rare window into the world's largest film industry.

items.name: Nita Mukesh Ambani Cultural Centre (NMACC)
items.description: The city's spectacular new performing-arts complex, with a grand theatre, an art house and the crystal-lotus Great Hall, presenting world-class opera, theatre and blockbuster exhibitions. The most glamorous cultural night out in India right now, dress code and all.

items.name: Irani café crawl (Britannia, Kyani, Yazdani, Merwan)
items.description: The bentwood-chaired Parsi-Irani cafés are a vanishing Bombay institution, from Britannia's famous berry pulao to Kyani's bun-maska and Yazdani's brun. A slow morning across a few of them is the tastiest way to read the city's cosmopolitan history.

items.name: Art Deco Marine Drive & Oval walking trail
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai
items.description: The stretch of streamlined 1930s apartment blocks along the Oval and Marine Drive is the second-largest Art Deco ensemble in the world after Miami. A guided walk decodes the sunbursts, ships' rails and 'Indo-Deco' motifs that put this cityscape on the UNESCO list.

items.name: Khotachiwadi heritage village
items.description: A pocket of nineteenth-century East Indian and Portuguese-style timber cottages, brightly painted and threaded with narrow lanes, hidden in the heart of the old city. Designer James Ferreira's home and the annual open-house bring this fragile gem to life.

items.name: Mani Bhavan (Gandhi Museum)
items.description: The modest Malabar Hill house where Gandhi stayed on his Bombay visits from 1917 to 1934, now a moving museum and library with his room preserved. A quiet, humbling hour on the freedom struggle a short drive from Chowpatty.

items.name: Dharavi social-enterprise walk
items.description: A guided walk through one of Asia's largest informal settlements reveals a staggering economy of leather, recycling, pottery and textiles, run responsibly with local social enterprises. Confronting and clarifying, it upends every assumption about how the city actually works.

items.name: Mumbai heritage & food walk (Fort / Bhuleshwar / Khau Galli)
items.description: A curated walking tour, whether Fort's architecture, Bhuleshwar's temple-and-flower lanes or the vegetarian street food of the Gujarati quarters, is the best way into the city's layers. Private guides can tailor a Jain-friendly, entirely vegetarian route with ease.

items.name: Alibaug & Mandwa
items.description: A fifty-minute ferry from the Gateway to Mandwa reaches the coast of second homes, Kihim's casuarina-fringed beaches and the sea-fort of Kolaba. This is where Mumbai's families keep their weekend villas; charter a speedboat and make a lazy day of it.

items.name: Madh Island & Erangal
items.description: A quiet peninsula of Koli villages, palm groves, an old Portuguese fort and beach shacks, reached by a short vehicle ferry from Versova. A low-key escape for a seafood lunch and empty sands within the city's own limits.

items.name: Masque
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 — No. 19; The Best Restaurant in India
items.description: India's most decorated tasting menu — a ten-course journey through the country's produce in a former textile mill.

items.name: Papa's
items.description: A twelve-seat chef's counter above a sandwich shop — the most exciting fine-dining ticket in Bandra.

items.name: Wasabi by Morimoto
credentials: Inside The Taj Mahal Palace — MICHELIN One Key hotel (2025)
items.description: Masaharu Morimoto's Japanese room inside the Taj Palace — the city's benchmark for sushi and omakase.

items.name: Ziya
items.description: Contemporary Indian by Vineet Bhatia — the first Indian chef to win a Michelin star (in London) — with the sea at your feet.

items.name: Americano
items.description: A chic, low-lit Kala Ghoda room where sharp cooking meets some of the best cocktails in the city.

items.name: The Table
items.description: A Colaba institution for fifteen years, back on form — eclectic, produce-led global cooking to share.

items.name: The Bombay Canteen
items.description: The modern-Indian restaurant that changed how the city eats — regional dishes, reimagined, ten years on.

items.name: Ekaa
items.description: Niyati Rao's ingredient-led kitchen in a historic Fort building — produce-driven cooking that ignores the rulebook.

items.name: Trishna
items.description: The back-alley seafood legend of South Mumbai — the butter-pepper-garlic crab is a rite of passage.

items.name: Yauatcha
credentials: Part of the Hakkasan Group (London Yauatcha holds a Michelin star)
items.description: The Mumbai outpost of the London dim sum house — glossy, precise and reliably excellent.

items.name: Hakkasan Mumbai
credentials: Part of the Hakkasan Group (London Hakkasan holds a Michelin star)
items.description: Dark, glamorous modern Cantonese in Bandra — the international Hakkasan name, brought to the suburbs.

items.name: Bastian at the Top
items.description: Mumbai's most glamorous seafood-and-scene restaurant — big flavours, bigger crowd, sea breeze on the terrace.

items.name: Bombay Sweet Shop
credentials: By Hunger Inc (of Asia's 50 Best-listed The Bombay Canteen)
items.description: A joyful reinvention of the Indian mithai shop — traditional sweets made brilliantly, by the Bombay Canteen team.

items.name: Britannia & Co.
items.description: A century-old Parsi cafe famous for berry pulav — a living piece of old Bombay you eat lunch inside.

items.name: Swati Snacks
items.description: The city's beloved home of Gujarati and Mumbai street food, served clean and impeccable in a bright canteen.

items.name: Harbour Bar
credentials: Inside The Taj Mahal Palace — MICHELIN One Key hotel (2025)
items.description: India's oldest licensed bar, facing the Gateway of India — the most storied nightcap in the city.

items.name: The Bombay Canteen
items.description: A bar that mines the Indian pantry for its drinks the way its kitchen does for food — one of the country's most-awarded.

items.name: Americano
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 — No. 71 (the room is celebrated as much for its bar)
items.description: Some of the sharpest cocktails in the city, in a chic low-lit Kala Ghoda room that doubles as a fine kitchen.

items.name: AER
credentials: Inside Four Seasons Hotel Mumbai — MICHELIN Guide Hotel
items.description: The 34th-floor open-air lounge over Worli and the sea — for years the definitive Mumbai rooftop.

items.name: Asilo
credentials: Inside The St. Regis Mumbai — Forbes Travel Guide 2025 recognised
items.description: A theatrical rooftop above Lower Parel — cocktails, city lights and a scene, at the top of the St. Regis tower.

items.name: Dome
credentials: Inside InterContinental Marine Drive — Forbes Travel Guide 2025 recognised
items.description: An all-white rooftop lounge over the Queen's Necklace — the classic Marine Drive sundowner.

items.title: Private sunrise at the Gateway and a chartered boat to Elephanta
items.description: Reach the rock-cut caves before the ferries, with a private guide to the Shiva sculptures.

items.title: Heritage architecture walk through the Fort and Kala Ghoda
items.description: A curator-led morning among the Gothic and Art Deco facades, a UNESCO-listed ensemble most visitors rush past.

items.title: Chef's table at Masque
items.description: Mumbai's most ambitious ingredient-led tasting menu, sourced from small Indian farms and best reserved weeks ahead.

items.title: Private tabla or classical evening with a leading musician
items.description: An intimate baithak-style recital arranged in a private home or heritage space.

plan.heading: 3 days in Mumbai, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

days.title: The old city by the sea

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Check into a sea-facing suite at The Taj Mahal Palace, beside the Gateway of India.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Walk the Kala Ghoda art district and Fort's Gothic and Art Deco streets with a heritage guide.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Wasabi by Morimoto within the Taj, then a nightcap at the Harbour Bar.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Private launch to the Elephanta Caves and their rock-cut Shiva sculptures across the harbour.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Return for the Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj museum, then the galleries of Colaba.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dine at The Table or Masque in Byculla, the tasting-menu room sourcing from its own farm.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Dawn at the Sassoon Docks fish market, then Banganga Tank and the quiet lanes of Walkeshwar.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A drive along Marine Drive and Chowpatty, tea at the Willingdon Club or a Malabar Hill garden.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Sundowners at Ling's Pavilion or a final dinner at Trishna for its butter-pepper-garlic crab.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Colaba / Apollo Bunder
items.description: The historic south by the harbour; best for first-timers who want the landmarks and grand hotels on the doorstep.

items.name: Marine Drive / Churchgate
items.description: The Art Deco seafront; suits those who want morning sea walks and central calm.

items.name: Bandra West
items.description: The stylish, creative suburb of cafes and boutiques; for repeat visitors who want the contemporary side.

events.name: Ganesh Chaturthi
events.note: The city's biggest festival, ending in vast processions to the sea; thrilling but expect road closures and dense crowds.

events.name: Kala Ghoda Arts Festival
events.note: A well-run nine-day street arts festival in the Fort district, good for design, film and installations.

events.name: Diwali
events.note: The seafront and homes light up; a fine time for the food and shopping but book restaurants early.

events.name: Mumbai Film / NMACC cultural season
events.note: The Nita Mukesh Ambani Centre and the film calendar bring major stage and screen events through the cooler months.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Land at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (BOM) Terminal 2, met by a chauffeured car for the drive to South Mumbai along the Sea Link.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with driver is the only sensible way through Mumbai's traffic; keep destinations clustered and travel outside peak hours.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Reliable 5G and hotel wifi throughout; an Indian eSIM or Jio/Airtel SIM activates in minutes.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Indian rupee (INR); cards are widely accepted, small cash is useful, and tipping around ten percent is the norm.

onGround.note: Base yourself in South Mumbai (The Taj Mahal Palace or The Oberoi at Nariman Point) for the sea, the clubs and the galleries; allow generous time for any airport run.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Nov-Feb is the pleasant, dry and breezy stretch along the sea; Mar-May turns hot and sticky. Avoid Jun-Sep, when the monsoon is intense and can flood low-lying roads.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Home hub: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International (BOM) is a primary origin, so no connection needed from Mumbai and a 2-2.5 hour hop from Delhi or Bengaluru on Vistara or IndiGo. Terminal 2 is world-class; use the GVK or Air India lounges and arrange a private car, as taxi queues and traffic to South Mumbai can be long.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: Routine vaccines plus Hepatitis A and typhoid advised; stick to sealed or filtered water. Mumbai is among India's safer big cities and comfortable to move around with normal care; monsoon flooding (Jun-Sep) is the main seasonal disruption.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Very easy for vegetarian and Jain diets, with widely available Jain menus and a strong local Gujarati vegetarian tradition. For notable dining, Masque offers a modern tasting approach and Swati Snacks or Soam serve refined regional vegetarian fare.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Mumbai, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Munich — TripAgent
seo.description: Munich, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Munich
hero.tagline: Bavarian capital of beer gardens, baroque and effortless wealth

ourTake.lede: Munich is Germany at its most comfortable — green, prosperous and easygoing — and it works best as a base for both the city and the Alps an hour south. Give the beer halls a night but don't stop there; the real pleasures are the Englischer Garten, the museum quarter and the food markets. If you come for Oktoberfest, book everything far ahead and know the city is fuller and pricier; for a truer sense of the place, the strong-beer season in Lent or a bright autumn week is more rewarding.
ourTake.comeIf: You want an orderly, handsome city as a base for the Alps, the beer halls, and the castles beyond.
ourTake.skipIf: You want sun and sea, or a city that feels loose and improvised; this one runs on precision.

firstLook.heroCaption: Classical hotel facade with flags and cars
