seo.title: Muscat — TripAgent
seo.description: Muscat, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Muscat
hero.tagline: Serene Arabian coast of forts, wadis and white minarets.

ourTake.lede: Muscat is the antidote to the Gulf's glass towers — low white buildings, a real corniche, and mountains that fall straight into the sea. Don't treat it as a one-night stop; base here and drive out to the wadis and Nizwa. Skip the beach-resort bubble and spend a night in the Hajar mountains instead.
ourTake.comeIf: You want Arabia with its dignity intact - forts, wadis and empty coast rather than glass towers.
ourTake.skipIf: You want nightlife, big shopping and constant motion; Oman is deliberately gentle.

firstLook.heroCaption: Modern pool villa with palms and umbrella

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: Come October to March, mild and pleasant, and time it to the January Muscat Festival; for the green Khareef monsoon head south to Salalah July-August, and avoid Muscat's May-to-September heat.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Muscat. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: The Chedi Muscat
items.area: Al Ghubra North, Shatti Al Qurum
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller Readers' Choice Awards — #4 Hotel in the Middle East (2025); #1 Hotel in the Middle East (2024)
World Travel Awards — World's Leading Luxury Beach Resort & Spa (2022, 2023, 2024, 2025)
items.description: GHM's serene, minimalist beachfront sanctuary — the hotel that defined understated luxury in the Gulf, and Oman's one true icon.

items.name: Al Bustan Palace, a Ritz-Carlton Hotel
items.area: Al Bustan, between the Hajar mountains and the sea
credentials: World Travel Awards — World's Leading Palace Hotel (2018)
Condé Nast Traveller Readers' Choice — Top-5 Hotel in the Middle East (2018)
items.description: A former royal-guest palace turned seaside grand hotel — a soaring 38-metre atrium, private beach and mountains at its back.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental, Muscat
credentials: Mandarin Oriental Hotel Group (Leading maison group; Forbes Travel Guide inspected — 'soon to be rated')
Opened June 2024, the brand's first hotel in Oman
items.description: The group's Oman debut — a bright-white beachfront house where Omani craft meets Mandarin Oriental's quiet precision.

items.name: Anantara Al Jabal Al Akhdar Resort
items.area: Jebal Akhdar (Green Mountain) — ~2hr drive from Muscat
credentials: World Travel Awards — Oman's Leading Luxury Resort (2020, 2021, 2022)
items.description: One of the highest resorts on earth, perched 2,000m on a canyon rim where Princess Diana once stood — a genuine mountain escape.

items.name: Al Husn, a Waldorf Astoria Hotel
credentials: Waldorf Astoria Hotels & Resorts — Oman debut of the brand (rebranded from Shangri-La Al Husn, 1 Jan 2026; Forbes Travel Guide 4-Star as Shangri-La Al Husn)
Part of the landmark Barr Al Jissah resort complex
items.description: An adults-oriented clifftop 'castle' above a private turquoise cove — the crown of the Barr Al Jissah headland, now under the Waldorf Astoria flag.

items.name: Alila Jabal Akhdar
items.area: Jebal Akhdar (Green Mountain) — ~2hr drive from Muscat
credentials: World Travel Awards — Oman's Leading Resort (2023, 2024); Middle East's Leading Boutique Hotel (multiple years)
Condé Nast Traveler Hot List (2015, on opening); first LEED-certified hotel in Oman
items.description: A stone-clad, low-slung Hyatt-luxury retreat woven into the mountainside — Oman's first LEED-certified hotel, all quiet and view.

items.name: The St. Regis Al Mouj Muscat Resort
credentials: World Travel Awards — World's Leading New Resort (2025); Oman's Leading Luxury Resort (2025)
items.description: A polished beachfront newcomer beside Muscat's smartest marina-and-golf community — St. Regis butler service and a long private beach.

items.name: Kempinski Hotel Muscat
credentials: Kempinski Hotels — recognised in Condé Nast Traveller Readers' Choice Awards (2025)
World Travel Awards — Oman's Leading Beach Resort; Business Traveller Middle East — Best Business Hotel in Muscat
items.description: A vast six-kilometre-beachfront European grande-dame resort — eleven dining venues and a private stretch of sand at Al Mouj.

items.name: W Muscat
credentials: Marriott W Hotels (design-forward luxury brand); W Muscat is the brand's Oman debut
Luxury Lifestyle Awards — Luxury Lifestyle Hotel, Oman (2024)
items.description: The brand's beachfront 'W Escape' — high-design, high-energy and unabashedly scene-y, right on Shatti Al Qurum.

items.name: Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque
items.description: Oman's grandest mosque and the one unmissable landmark of Muscat — 300,000 tonnes of Indian sandstone, a single hand-woven Persian carpet that took years to make, and a Swarovski chandelier hanging under the main dome. Non-Muslim visitors are welcome between 8 and 11 in the morning (not Fridays); entry is free, dress is modest, and abayas are lent at the gate. Serene and spotless — an easy, moving stop for all generations.

items.name: Royal Opera House Muscat
items.description: The Gulf's leading opera house — Omani stone and marble outside, Islamic, Mughal and European craftsmanship within. Either take a daytime house tour of the auditorium and its inlaid detail, or book an evening of opera, ballet or orchestral music from the October–May season. A refined, dressy night out that families and culture-minded couples both love.

items.name: Mutrah Corniche
items.description: The great curving seafront of old Muscat — whitewashed merchant houses on one side, dhows and the Sultan's harbour on the other, the Hajar hills behind. Walk it late afternoon into golden hour when the light softens and the mosque minarets glow. The gentle, unhurried heart of the city.

items.name: Mutrah Souq
items.description: One of the oldest markets in the Arab world, a warren of covered lanes trading frankincense, silver khanjars, pashminas, antique silver and Omani halwa. Prices are gentle by Dubai standards and the traders are warm, not pushy — good for unhurried, multi-generation browsing. Best late afternoon into the evening when it reopens and comes alive.

items.name: Mutrah Fish Market
items.description: A working morning market under a striking wave-form roof on the harbour, where Omani fishermen land and sell the day's catch. Come at dawn for the full theatre of it — kingfish, tuna and hammour changing hands amid the calls of the auction. Vivid, authentic, and a photographer's delight.

items.name: Al Alam Palace
items.description: The Sultan's ceremonial palace — flamboyant gold-and-blue flared columns framed by manicured avenues, designed by Mumbai's Shapoorji Pallonji firm. You cannot go inside, but the grand approach and the palace flanked by two Portuguese forts is the classic Muscat photograph. A short, easy stop paired with Old Muscat's museums.

items.name: Al Jalali & Al Mirani Forts
items.description: Two 16th-century Portuguese forts guarding the natural harbour on either side of Al Alam Palace. Neither is generally open to the public, but they crown the rocky headlands and give Old Muscat its dramatic, defensible silhouette. Best seen from the palace forecourt or the corniche, especially at dusk.

items.name: National Museum of Oman
items.description: Oman's flagship museum, opposite Al Alam Palace — beautifully lit galleries of the ruling dynasty, Omani silver, frankincense trade, arms and maritime heritage, with Arabic Braille throughout. Cool, calm and well-curated: the single best hour for understanding the country before you explore it. Excellent for curious teenagers.

items.name: Bait Al Zubair Museum
items.description: A private family museum in a cluster of traditional houses — the finest privately held collection of Omani khanjars, jewellery, costume and household life, plus a garden, café and art gallery. Intimate and personal where the National Museum is grand; the two together tell the whole story. On Al Saidiya Street in Old Muscat.

items.name: Ghalya's Museum of Modern Art
items.description: A quiet gem on the Mutrah corniche — a reconstructed Omani house recreating daily life from 1950 to 1975, room by room, with a small modern-art gallery upstairs. Founded by a member of the royal family, it is warm, unhurried and rarely crowded. A tender, human counterpoint to the big state museums.

items.name: Old Muscat walking circuit
items.description: The walled original town behind the corniche — palace, forts, museums, the old Muscat Gate and quiet lanes, all within a compact, walkable radius. A morning here, with a private guide to unlock the history, gives you the founding story of the whole city in a couple of unhurried hours. Shaded stops and easy pacing suit all ages.

items.name: Amouage Perfume Factory & Visitor Centre
items.description: The home of Oman's luxury house of perfume, built on frankincense, myrrh and Omani rose. A complimentary guided tour walks you from raw ingredient to finished bottle, ending in a boutique where you can sample and buy the full collection. A civilised, air-conditioned hour and a genuinely Omani luxury souvenir. Sunday to Thursday, mornings and afternoons.

items.name: Dolphin watching by boat
items.description: Morning boats slip out of the marina to meet wild spinner and common dolphins that ride the bow and leap in their hundreds along this coast. A short, easy two-hour trip — thrilling for children and grandparents alike, with the fort-studded shoreline as backdrop. Best in the calm, cool morning sea.

items.name: Sunset dhow cruise
items.description: Sail the coast at dusk aboard a traditional wooden dhow, past cliffs, coves and the lights of Muscat coming on. Private charters can be arranged with Omani coffee, dates and dinner aboard — a discreet, romantic way to end a day. The gentlest luxury on the water.

items.name: Bandar Khayran
items.description: A hidden labyrinth of turquoise inlets, cliffs and mangroves southeast of the city — 'the blue lagoons' — reached by boat or the coast road. Kayak or snorkel the sheltered bays by day, or take a sunset paddle through bioluminescent plankton in winter, when each stroke lights the water. Wild, unspoilt and private-feeling.

items.name: Daymaniyat Islands
items.description: A protected archipelago of nine uninhabited islands about 40km offshore — Oman's finest snorkelling and diving, with clear water, turtles, rays and, in season, whale sharks. Reached by licensed boat with a reserve permit; open roughly October to April. A blue-water day out to rival the Maldives, but a short flight from India. Charter privately for a family.

items.name: Qurum Beach
items.description: A long, clean city beach backed by luxury hotels and the corniche — easy walking, calm swimming and a string of cafés and restaurants. The relaxed everyday beach of Muscat, good for an early stroll or a sunset with the family. Between the Chedi and the Crowne Plaza cliff.

items.name: Qurum Natural Park
items.description: The city's largest green park — lakes, lawns, shaded walks, playgrounds and a rose garden set behind the beach. A cool, family-friendly escape for an evening, popular with local families. Simple, safe and easy with young children or grandparents.

items.name: Afternoon tea at The Chedi Muscat
items.description: Oman's most stylish resort — long reflecting pools, minimalist Omani-Zen design and a serene Lobby Lounge that serves an exquisite afternoon tea. Even non-residents can book in for tea or dinner and soak up the calm. Discreet luxury of exactly the kind that beats Dubai's glitz. Vegetarian and dietary requests handled with ease.

items.name: Al Bustan Palace, a Ritz-Carlton Hotel
items.description: A landmark hotel set between mountains and a private bay, with a soaring 38-metre domed atrium lobby. Come for afternoon tea beneath the dome or a beachfront dinner even if you stay elsewhere — one of Muscat's grand, gracious dining experiences. The setting alone is worth the drive.

items.name: Nizwa Fort & Souq
items.description: The old imamate capital, 90 minutes inland — a massive 17th-century round-towered fort you can climb for sweeping views, beside a restored souq trading silver, dates, pottery and frankincense. The cultural heart of Oman's interior, and an easy, rewarding day trip with a private car. Best paired with the Friday goat market.

items.name: Nizwa Friday Goat Market
items.description: Every Friday from around 6am, traders parade goats and cattle in a shouting, bargaining ring beside Nizwa Souq while deals are sealed over Omani coffee. Raw, theatrical and utterly authentic — a slice of living Oman found nowhere in Dubai. Come early; it is over by mid-morning.

items.name: Jabreen Castle
items.description: The most beautiful of Oman's castles — a 1670 palace-fort with painted wooden ceilings, hidden chambers, date-store rooms and a canal running through it. Small, intimate and gorgeously preserved, it rewards a slow wander. An easy pairing with Bahla Fort just up the road.

items.name: Bahla Fort
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Bahla Fort
items.description: Oman's only UNESCO-listed fort — a vast 13th-century mud-brick citadel with a 12km oasis wall, steeped in local legend. Recently restored, it is monumental and atmospheric, the great fortress of the interior. Combine with neighbouring Jabreen Castle and Nizwa for a full interior day.

items.name: Jebel Akhdar rose terraces
items.area: Al Jabal Al Akhdar (day trip / overnight)
items.description: The 'Green Mountain' — stepped villages clinging to slopes above 2,000m where Damask roses bloom each March–April and are distilled into Oman's famous rosewater. Walk the terraced village trail, visit an old distillery, and stay high at Alila or Anantara for cool air and canyon-edge infinity pools. Cooler, greener and utterly different from the coast.

items.name: Alila Jabal Akhdar
items.description: A serene stone-built retreat perched on the mountain plateau, all clean lines, big views and a spa above the clouds. The mountain base of choice for couples and families wanting quiet luxury, mountain walks and cool nights. Stay a night to feel Oman's other, alpine self.

items.name: Anantara Al Jabal Al Akhdar
items.description: The highest five-star resort in the Middle East, on the very lip of a canyon with a dramatic cliff-edge pool and rose-ritual spa. Refined, warm and spectacular — guided rose-farm and mountain-guru walks included. A destination in its own right for a multi-generation stay.

items.name: Jebel Shams — the Balcony Walk
items.description: Oman's highest peak overlooks Wadi Ghul, a 1,000m-deep gorge known as the Grand Canyon of Arabia. The Balcony Walk hugs the rim to an abandoned village, with a rustic canyon-edge café just minutes along for those who want only the view. Cool clear air and vast panoramas; go October to April. Best with a guide and a 4x4.

items.name: Wahiba Sands (Sharqiya Sands)
items.description: A sea of amber dunes over 100m tall, home to the Bedu. Ride the crests by 4x4, meet a Bedouin family, then sleep in a luxury desert camp under a spread of stars with dinner over the fire. The classic Arabian desert night — thrilling for children, magical for all. Book a tented camp with private, comfortable suites.

items.name: Wadi Bani Khalid
items.description: The most accessible of Oman's great wadis — emerald spring-fed pools among palms and smooth boulders, a five-minute walk from the car park, with a café overlooking the water. Swim in the warm rock pools or stroll the gorge; there is even a cave for the adventurous. Family-easy and gorgeous. Pairs with a Wahiba desert night.

items.name: Wadi Shab
items.description: Oman's most celebrated wadi hike — a short boat across the mouth, then an easy trail past turquoise pools to a hidden cave waterfall you swim to reach. About two hours from Muscat and doable in a day. Bring water shoes; the reward at the end is unforgettable. Best for active families and couples.

items.name: Bimmah Sinkhole
items.description: A turquoise limestone sinkhole, 20m deep and fed by mixed sea and fresh water, that locals call the 'falling star'. Steps lead down to a swim, and tiny fish nibble your feet. A quick, delightful stop on the coastal road to Wadi Shab or Sur — easy for everyone.

items.name: Wadi Tiwi
items.description: The 'Wadi of Nine Villages' — a narrower, greener gorge than neighbouring Wadi Shab, with terraced plantations, falaj channels and turquoise pools between towering walls. Quieter and lush, best explored by 4x4 and on foot. A serene pairing with Wadi Shab on the Sur road.

items.name: Ras Al Jinz Turtle Reserve
items.description: One of the Indian Ocean's most important green-turtle nesting beaches, where thousands return each year. On a ranger-led night or dawn walk you watch a female haul ashore, dig and lay by moonlight — a hushed, once-in-a-lifetime moment. Stay at the reserve's eco-lodge to be first on the beach. Peak nesting summer, but turtles come year-round.

items.name: Sur — dhow shipyard & Ayjah
items.description: A coastal town two hours south where master craftsmen still build wooden dhows by eye, without plans. Watch the shipwrights, cross to the whitewashed fishing village of Ayjah and its Portuguese-era lighthouse over the lagoon. A living slice of Oman's great seafaring past. Good base for Ras Al Jinz.

items.name: Al Hamra & Bait Al Safah
items.description: One of Oman's best-preserved old towns, with three-century-old mud-brick houses stacked below the Hajar. At Bait Al Safah, a 400-year-old house turned living museum, local women grind coffee, bake bread and press oil the old way. Warm, hands-on heritage the whole family enjoys. Combine with Misfat and Jebel Shams.

items.name: Misfat al Abriyeen
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Aflaj Irrigation Systems of Oman
items.description: A tumbling mountain village of mud-brick homes and shaded date terraces fed by ancient falaj channels, 1,000m up. Wander the lanes and green plantations, or stay in a restored guesthouse to feel the quiet. One of Oman's most photogenic villages, and gloriously unspoilt. Reached on the Al Hamra road.

items.name: Nakhal Fort & A'Thowarah Hot Springs
items.description: A dramatic fort built onto a rock outcrop above date plantations and the Hajar foothills — impossible to photograph badly — with warm mineral springs running through palm groves a short drive on. A gentle, scenic half-day loop from Muscat. Easy and rewarding for all ages.

items.name: Rustaq Fort
items.description: One of Oman's largest forts in a former capital, with towering walls, a mosque and its own hot spring within. Less visited than Nizwa, so often quiet, and paired naturally with Nakhal on the Batinah loop. A grand, uncrowded fort day for history-lovers.

items.name: Archaeological Sites of Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Archaeological Sites of Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn
items.description: A 5,000-year-old Bronze Age necropolis of stone beehive tombs and towers near Ibri — the most complete such ensemble in Arabia, from the age when Omani copper reached Mesopotamia. Remote, atmospheric and rarely crowded; a private guide brings the ancient trade world alive. For travellers who want the deep past. Combine with Bahla.

items.name: Jebel Sifah
items.description: A resort marina town on the coast south of Muscat, ringed by mountains and a long sandy beach with calm swimming and a golf course. An easy, laid-back seaside escape — kayaking, boat trips and quiet sand within an hour of the city. Good for a relaxed family day by the water.

items.name: Yiti Beach
items.description: A wild, quiet cove reached over the coastal hills from Muscat, with a hidden stretch that feels like a private beach. Big skies, few people and mountains meeting the sea — a favourite for a peaceful picnic or sunset drive. Best with a 4x4 and no fixed plans.

items.name: Wadi Al Arbeieen
items.description: A dramatic mountain wadi of blue-green pools among palms, less trodden than the famous names, about 1hr45 from the city. The scenic mountain drive in is half the pleasure; the pools reward those who make the effort. A 4x4 and a guide are recommended — a proper off-the-map day.

items.name: Muscat Gate & city viewpoints
items.description: The old ceremonial gate marking the entrance to Old Muscat, near the giant Riyam incense-burner monument on its hill. Climb for a panorama over the corniche, harbour and forts — a quick, free stop that frames the whole old city. Lovely near sunset.

items.name: Private guide & 4x4 grand tour
items.description: The best way to see Oman: a licensed private driver-guide and a comfortable 4x4 to link the forts, wadis, mountains and desert at your own pace, with the history unlocked and the logistics handled. Dietary needs — including Jain and pure-vegetarian — are easily arranged ahead. Discreet, flexible and ideal for a multi-generation family.

items.name: The Beach Restaurant, The Chedi Muscat
items.area: The Chedi Muscat, Shatti Al Qurum
credentials: Within The Chedi Muscat (Forbes 4-Star; World Travel Awards World's Leading Luxury Beach Resort & Spa)
items.description: Sand-underfoot seafood by the Gulf — Iranian and Caspian caviar, freshly shucked oysters and the line-caught catch of the day.

items.name: Diana's Point, Anantara Al Jabal Al Akhdar
items.area: Jebal Akhdar (Green Mountain) — ~2hr drive from Muscat
credentials: Within Anantara Al Jabal Al Akhdar (Condé Nast Traveler Gold List; World Travel Awards Oman's Leading Luxury Resort)
items.description: Private canyon-edge dining on the promontory where Princess Diana once stood — the most dramatic table in the country.

items.name: The Restaurant, The Chedi Muscat
items.area: The Chedi Muscat, Shatti Al Qurum
credentials: Within The Chedi Muscat (Forbes 4-Star; World Travel Awards World's Leading Luxury Beach Resort & Spa)
items.description: Four open kitchens — Arabic, Indian, Asian and Mediterranean — under one high, chandeliered ceiling; the Chedi's flagship all-day room.

items.name: Al Angham
items.area: Royal Opera House Muscat, Shatti Al Qurum
credentials: Set within the Royal Opera House Muscat cultural complex — Oman's flagship dedicated fine-dining Omani restaurant
items.description: The finest room dedicated to Omani cuisine — carved-plaster grandeur beside the Opera House, serving the sultanate's own dishes with real ceremony.

items.name: Bukhara, Kempinski Hotel Muscat
credentials: Within Kempinski Hotel Muscat (Condé Nast Traveller Readers' Choice 2025; World Travel Awards Oman's Leading Beach Resort)
items.description: Robust North Indian cooking from the clay tandoor, inside the city's largest beach resort — familiar flavours, done with polish.

items.name: Shahi Darbar (fine Indian dining)
credentials: Established Muscat Indian restaurant with a consistent local reputation
items.description: Long-standing, well-regarded North Indian kitchen with a devoted local following — generous, familiar, unfussy.

items.name: Ubhar
items.area: Bareeq Al Shatti, Shatti Al Qurum
credentials: Widely cited (Time Out Muscat and others) as Muscat's leading modern Omani restaurant
items.description: Modern Omani-and-Arabian cooking that treats the sultanate's home dishes seriously — shuwa, harees, camel, done with pride.

items.name: Kargeen Café
credentials: An enduring Muscat institution, widely recommended for atmosphere and authentic mezze
items.description: Lantern-lit garden courtyards and generous Omani-Levantine mezze — the city's most-loved relaxed table, buzzing past midnight.

items.name: Bin Ateeq
credentials: Long-established local institution for authentic traditional Omani cuisine
items.description: Floor-seated, private-room dining on Omani classics — shuwa and majboos served the old way, with no ceremony and real honesty.

items.name: The bar at Al Husn, a Waldorf Astoria Hotel
credentials: Within Al Husn, a Waldorf Astoria Hotel (Barr Al Jissah landmark; former Forbes 4-Star Shangri-La Al Husn)
items.description: Clifftop sundowners above a private cove at the crown of the Barr Al Jissah headland — the classic Muscat sunset drink, now under the Waldorf Astoria flag.

items.name: Duke's Bar, Al Bustan Palace, a Ritz-Carlton Hotel
credentials: Within Al Bustan Palace, a Ritz-Carlton Hotel (Forbes Recommended; World Travel Awards World's Leading Palace Hotel)
items.description: A classic hotel bar beneath the palace's soaring atrium — the grande-dame address for a measured evening drink in Muscat.

items.name: The Long Bar, The Chedi Muscat
items.area: The Chedi Muscat, Shatti Al Qurum
credentials: Within The Chedi Muscat (Forbes 4-Star; World Travel Awards World's Leading Luxury Beach Resort & Spa)
items.description: A hushed, low-lit lounge inside Oman's design icon — considered cocktails and a fireside calm, the most refined drink in the city.

items.name: Al Burj cocktail bar, Anantara Al Jabal Al Akhdar
items.area: Jebal Akhdar (Green Mountain) — ~2hr drive from Muscat
credentials: Within Anantara Al Jabal Al Akhdar (Condé Nast Traveler Gold List; World Travel Awards Oman's Leading Luxury Resort)
items.description: A Moroccan-style bar set in the tower of the resort's fort, cocktails 2,000m up with the canyon falling away below — a drink you don't forget.

items.title: Private dawn at the Sheikh Qaboos Grand Mosque
items.description: The vast Persian carpet and chandelier are best seen quietly, early, before the day's visitors.

items.title: Turtle nesting at Ras Al Jinz
items.description: A guided night on the beach to watch green turtles come ashore to lay, at the reserve east of the capital.

items.title: A dhow cruise into the Musandam fjords
items.description: Oman's dramatic 'Norway of Arabia' — sheer cliffs, dolphins and swimming stops, a flight or drive north.

items.title: Sunset at Jebel Akhdar
items.description: Stay on the canyon rim in the Hajar mountains, terraced with rose gardens and pomegranates, cool even in summer.

plan.heading: 3 days in Muscat, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque at opening, its single carpet and chandelier, then the Royal Opera House exterior.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Check into the Chedi Muscat, lunch by the long pool, then an afternoon in Muttrah Souq and along the corniche.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at The Restaurant at the Chedi, then the sea from the beach terrace.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive into the Hajar mountains to Nizwa's round fort and the Friday livestock market.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at the Alila Jabal Akhdar on the canyon rim, then the terraced rose villages of Saiq.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner on the escarpment as the light drops into Wadi Ghul.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A morning at Wadi Shab, walking to the hidden pool and swimming where few reach.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Drive the coast to Bimmah, then a late lunch of fresh hammour by the water.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A quiet last dinner back at the Chedi, and mint tea under the frankincense trees.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Mutrah
items.description: For the old corniche and the atmospheric souk — the most characterful place to walk at dusk.

items.name: Shatti Al Qurum
items.description: For beachfront hotels and easy dining, close to the museums and the city's centre of gravity.

items.name: Al Mouj
items.description: For a marina base with a golf course and newer restaurants, quieter and a little removed.

events.name: Muscat Festival
events.note: A month of crafts, culture and food across the city's parks during the cool season.

events.name: Salalah Khareef
events.note: In Oman's far south, the monsoon turns the hills green — a summer escape unlike anywhere else in Arabia.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Muscat International (MCT), a calm modern airport, where a meet-and-assist and a chauffeured car take you along the coast to Shatti Al Qurum or the Al Mouj marina.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver is essential — the sights spread along the coast and into the mountains — and Muttrah's corniche and souq are made for an unhurried evening walk.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: An eSIM from Omantel or Ooredoo covers the city and main roads on 4G/5G; signal thins in the interior wadis and dunes, so download maps ahead.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Omani rial (OMR) is one of the world's highest-valued currencies; cards work in hotels and cities, but keep cash for souqs and rural stops, and tipping is modest and welcomed.

onGround.note: Oman is quietly conservative and exceptionally courteous; dress modestly, cover shoulders and knees, and women should carry a scarf for the Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque. The Chedi and the Al Bustan Palace are the reference addresses; pair the city with a night in the Hajar mountains or the Wahiba Sands.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: November to March is the sweet spot: pleasant 20-30C days for the coast, forts and wadis. Avoid May-September, when heat climbs to 38-40C and travel becomes exhausting; June is the peak of it.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi (about 3.5 hours) and Mumbai (about 2h 45m, the shortest hop), also from Bengaluru. Oman Air flies it best in business, an understated and gracious product. Muscat's compact airport makes it an easy, calm arrival with none of the mega-hub scramble.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No special vaccinations; routine plus hepatitis A and typhoid is prudent. Oman is exceptionally safe and among the most courteous countries in the region. Tap water is treated and considered safe, though bottled is widely preferred. Heat, not crime, is the risk.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Comfortable for vegetarian and Jain travellers. A large Indian community means Indian food is genuinely good and everywhere; pure-veg is well understood. Gujarati and South Indian kitchens across Ruwi and Al Khuwair are reliable, and resort hotels prepare Jain on request.

closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Mykonos — TripAgent
seo.description: Mykonos, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Mykonos
hero.tagline: Cycladic glamour, windmills and the Aegean's liveliest shores.

ourTake.lede: Mykonos is two islands at once: the polished beach-club and party circuit, and a quieter Cycladic island of white lanes, windmills and little churches that most visitors barely see. Decide which one you came for. If it's the scene, base near town and book the beach clubs ahead; if it's the calm, take a boat to Delos, eat at the far tavernas, and treat the crowds in Little Venice as a sunset ritual to visit once, not live in.
ourTake.comeIf: You want polished Cycladic glamour, beach clubs and a yacht day, with dinners that run late.
ourTake.skipIf: You are travelling with young children or want quiet, unspoilt island life away from the scene.

firstLook.heroCaption: Modern pool villa with palms and umbrella

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: This is a scene, not a calendar: come late May to September when the beach clubs and dinners run at full tilt, peaking July-August; the island all but closes in winter.
whenToGo.bestMonths: May, Jun, Jul, Aug and Sep

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Mykonos. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Cali Mykonos
credentials: WELL Certified — Gold (health & wellbeing building standard)
Condé Nast Traveller — featured; 'one of the most luxurious hotels in the Cyclades'
items.description: The island's most talked-about newer address — a serene stone-and-marble retreat on Mykonos's calmer side, built for privacy rather than the party.

items.name: Belvedere Mykonos
items.area: Chora (School of Fine Arts district, above town)
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
Home to Matsuhisa Mykonos (Nobu Matsuhisa) and Six Senses Spa
items.description: The cosmopolitan heart of Mykonos glamour — a sun-bleached Cycladic labyrinth walking distance from town, home to the island's landmark Matsuhisa restaurant and a Six Senses spa.

items.name: Santa Marina, a Luxury Collection Resort
credentials: Home to Mykonos Social by Jason Atherton and Buddha-Bar Beach
items.description: A full private-peninsula resort on Ornos Bay with its own curve of sand — Marriott's Luxury Collection flagship on the island, and home to Jason Atherton's Mykonos Social.

items.name: Katikies Mykonos
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: An adults-only cliffside hideaway above Agios Ioannis beach, facing the island's best sunsets — all-white, serene, and almost every suite with its own plunge pool or jetted tub.

items.name: Kalesma Mykonos
credentials: MICHELIN One Key (2025) — inaugural Greece selection
Home to Pere Ubu fine dining
items.description: A hilltop village of Cycladic suites and villas overlooking the Aegean — nothing smaller than a one-bedroom suite, each with its own heated infinity pool. One of Greece's first MICHELIN Key hotels.

items.name: Bill&Coo Mykonos
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: An intimate, adults-only design hotel on the water at Megali Ammos, a short walk from town — polished, romantic, and known for one of the island's more serious kitchens.

items.name: Cavo Tagoo Mykonos
items.description: The island's original design landmark — carved white into the cliff above the sea just north of Chora, with a saltwater infinity pool and Kiku, its long-running Japanese restaurant.

items.name: Mykonos Blu, a Grecotel Resort
items.description: A Cycladic resort strung above glamorous Psarou beach — bungalows and villas cascading to the sand, steps from the island's most famous beach-club stretch.

items.name: Kensho Ornos
credentials: BIG SEE Design Award — architecture & interiors
items.description: A boutique house of understated, natural-material luxury above Ornos Bay — small, design-forward and calm, with a rooftop restaurant over the water.

items.name: Mykonos Town (Chora)
items.description: The whitewashed labyrinth of Mykonos — bougainvillea-draped lanes deliberately built to confuse pirates, now lined with boutiques, cafes and blue-shuttered doorways at every turn. Wander with no map; late afternoon light and early morning (before the cruise crowds) are the honeymoon-photo hours.

items.name: Little Venice (Alefkandra)
items.description: A row of 18th-century sea-captains' houses with wooden balconies leaning straight over the Aegean, so the waves lap at the walls. The most romantic sundowner in Mykonos — book a waterfront table and let the sky change colour with a glass in hand.

items.name: The Windmills of Kato Mili
items.description: Five white 16th-century windmills on the hill above Little Venice — the single most iconic image of Mykonos, catching the meltemi winds that once ground the island's grain. Time it for sunset when the whole ridge glows gold.

items.name: Panagia Paraportiani Church
items.description: A sculptural white cluster of five chapels melted into one form, begun in the 15th century — one of the most photographed churches in all Greece. Pure Cycladic minimalism; catch it against a blue sky or the last pink of dusk.

items.name: Aegean Maritime Museum
items.description: A quiet, beautifully-kept museum of Greek seafaring in a traditional Chora mansion, with model ships, old maps and a leafy garden holding the restored 19th-century lantern of the Armenistis lighthouse. A cool, cultured half-hour away from the sun and the crowds.

items.name: Lena's House
items.description: A perfectly preserved 19th-century middle-class Mykonian home — furniture, embroidery, framed photographs and all — kept exactly as it was lived in. A small, intimate window into island life before the glamour, right beside the Maritime Museum.

items.name: Matoyianni Street
items.description: The main artery of Chora and the island's luxury shopping spine — Louis Vuitton, Dior and Greek designers between the whitewashed walls, alive until well past midnight. The place to see and be seen while browsing.

items.name: Rarity Gallery
items.description: Greece's leading contemporary art gallery since 1994, on Kalogera Street, showing international names and hyperrealist sculpture that stops passers-by in their tracks. A serious, collectable stop for art-minded travellers between beach and dinner.

items.name: Dio Horia Gallery
items.description: A three-floor contemporary art platform in a converted Mykonian house, with an atmospheric rooftop bar looking over the town's rooftops. Cutting-edge exhibitions and a cocktail with a view, in one address.

items.name: Panagia Tourliani Monastery
items.description: The island's most important monastery, founded in 1542 in the inland village of Ano Mera, with a spectacular gilded Baroque altarpiece carved by Florentine artists in 1775. A serene, devotional counterpoint to the coast, and a genuine glimpse of local faith.

items.name: Ano Mera Village
items.description: The one real inland village on Mykonos — a tree-shaded square with tavernas serving unhurried, authentic island cooking, far from the port glamour. Where families and multi-gen groups go for a slow, honest Greek lunch.

items.name: Armenistis Lighthouse
items.description: An 1891 stone lighthouse on the island's north-western tip, built after a shipwreck, looking across the strait to Tinos. One of the least-crowded, most cinematic sunset perches on Mykonos — pack a picnic and arrive early.

items.name: 180° Sunset Bar
items.description: Perched on the walls of the old Castle Panigirakis at the highest point above town, this bar delivers the full panoramic sweep over Chora, the windmills and the sea as the sun drops. A polished spot for a celebratory sundown cocktail.

items.name: Caprice Bar, Little Venice
items.description: The classic waterfront sunset bar of Little Venice, where the Aegean laps at the terrace and the whole crowd turns to watch the sky. Get there before sunset to claim a table right at the water's edge.

items.name: Psarou Beach
items.description: The glamour beach of Mykonos — a sheltered golden crescent of turquoise water fronted by Nammos, where yachts anchor offshore and the jet-set sunbathe. Chic, family-friendly and firmly see-and-be-seen; book a lounger well ahead in season.

items.name: Ornos Beach
items.description: The most family-friendly beach on the island — a calm, shallow south-coast bay with good hotels, restaurants and water taxis at its doorstep. Easygoing and central, ideal for multi-generation trips with young children.

items.name: Platis Gialos Beach
items.description: The best all-round beach on Mykonos — a long stretch of golden sand, clear water and a good range of tavernas and beach bars, plus the hub for the south-coast water taxi that hops between every beach. Wonderfully practical for a full, easy beach day.

items.name: Paradise Beach
items.description: The legendary party beach — golden sand by day that turns into open-air dance floors as the sun sets, home to the famous Cavo Paradiso club on the cliff above. Framed here as the scene: go for the spectacle, or skip it if you want quiet.

items.name: Super Paradise Beach
items.description: The other half of the party legend — a stunning cove with brilliant water, beach clubs and daytime dancing that runs late into the afternoon. Iconic, hedonistic and inclusive; best appreciated by those who want the full Mykonos energy.

items.name: Elia Beach
items.description: The longest and most sophisticated of the organised south-coast beaches — broad, sandy, with space to breathe, good clubs and watersports at one end. A smart choice for a relaxed but well-serviced beach day.

items.name: Kalo Livadi Beach
items.description: Golden sand and clear water without the south-coast party machine — longer than Psarou, less crowded than Platis Gialos, with excellent beachfront restaurants. The sweet spot for couples and families who want style without the crush.

items.name: Agios Sostis Beach
items.description: A completely undeveloped north-coast beach — no sunbeds, no bars, no buses, just raw Cycladic coastline reached on foot. For a day of true privacy, with Kiki's Tavern hidden on the hill above for lunch.

items.name: Fokos Beach
items.description: One of the last wild, unspoilt beaches on Mykonos — remote, wind-brushed and gloriously empty, with a single well-loved taverna at the back. The island's answer to those who've had enough of the scene and want silence.

items.name: Panormos Beach
items.description: A long, handsome north-coast bay that mixes an undeveloped stretch with the stylish Principote beach club at one end. Fewer crowds than the south coast, with an effortless bohemian-chic mood by day.

items.name: Nammos Beach Club
items.description: The most famous beach club in the Mediterranean, on Psarou sand — a legendary scene of magnums, designer boutiques and celebrity-watching, with genuinely excellent seafood. The apex of Mykonos see-and-be-seen; reserve weeks ahead in high summer.

items.name: Scorpios
items.description: The island's most-referenced beach club, on a headland at Paraga — less about wild partying and more about a curated 'music, movement and community' ritual that builds into a sunset ceremony. Bohemian-luxe and unforgettable; book day beds far ahead.

items.name: Principote
items.description: The chic beach club on Panormos, striking a balance between glamour and relaxed comfort away from the south-coast intensity. Stylish loungers, good food and a calmer, more elegant scene — a fine choice for couples.

items.name: Delos Archaeological Site
items.description: The sacred birthplace of Apollo and Artemis, a uninhabited island 30 minutes by boat — an entire Greco-Roman city frozen in stone, from the Terrace of the Lions to the mosaic-floored House of Dionysos. The essential half-day of Mykonos; hire a private guide and go early before the heat.

items.name: Archaeological Museum of Delos
items.description: The on-site museum housing the finest sculpture and mosaics recovered from Delos, including the original Naxian lions moved indoors for protection. A cool, essential stop that brings the ruins outside back to life.

items.name: Private Catamaran Day Cruise
items.description: The definitive Mykonos indulgence — a full day on a private catamaran or motor yacht, sailing past Delos to swim in the aquamarine coves of Rhenia, with a chef, a crew and no one else aboard. Perfect for a honeymoon, a milestone or a family day at sea; veg and dietary menus arranged on request.

items.name: Rhenia Island
items.description: The uninhabited sister-island beside Delos, ringed with empty white-sand coves and impossibly clear water — reachable only by boat. The reward at the heart of a private cruise: swimming and snorkelling in near-total solitude.

items.name: Watersports & Diving
items.description: The organised south-coast beaches — Platis Gialos, Elia, Paradise — offer everything from jet-skis and paddleboards to scuba diving over clear reefs. Easy, well-run fun for active families and teenagers between the sunbathing.

items.name: Kiki's Tavern, Agios Sostis
items.description: A cult taverna above quiet Agios Sostis with no electricity, no phone and no reservations — everything grilled over charcoal, the salads famous, the queue part of the ritual. A gloriously unpretentious island lunch that money genuinely can't fast-track.

items.name: Kounelas Fish Tavern
items.description: A long-standing family fish taverna in the back lanes of Chora, where the day's catch is chosen at the counter and the louza and grilled seafood are the real thing. The kind of honest, atmospheric table locals still keep for themselves.

items.name: M-eating Restaurant
items.description: A refined Chora restaurant championing Greek produce done with modern polish — a strong place to taste island specialities like kopanisti cheese in an elegant setting. Intimate and well-suited to a quieter celebration dinner.

items.name: Interni Restaurant
items.description: A design-led courtyard restaurant in the old town, mixing Mediterranean and Asian technique with Greek produce, that turns into a buzzing scene as the night goes on. Dinner and glamour in one; the tuna tartare and lobster are the signatures.

items.name: Bill & Coo Fine Dining
items.description: The acclaimed dining rooms of the Relais & Chateaux Bill & Coo hotel, from the refined YEVO tasting menu to Beefbar on the coast — some of the most polished cooking on the island. A destination dinner for a special occasion, overlooking the bay.

items.name: Local Flavours — Kopanisti & Louza
items.description: Two things to eat before you leave: kopanisti, the peppery, tangy Mykonian cheese spread on rusk, and louza, the island's cinnamon-and-pepper cured pork, Mykonos's answer to prosciutto. Ask any good taverna — they are the true taste of the island beneath the glamour.

items.name: Cavo Paradiso
items.description: The clifftop superclub above Paradise Beach that brings the world's top DJs to Mykonos every summer, dancing under the stars until dawn. The pinnacle of the island's legendary nightlife — framed here as the scene for those who want it.

items.name: Fokos & the Wild North Tavernas
items.description: The rugged, taverna-dotted north coast — Fokos, Ftelia, Agios Sostis — where a rough drive rewards you with empty beaches and slow, sea-facing lunches. The antidote to the port: this is where Mykonos still feels like a real Cycladic island.

items.name: Day Trip to Tinos
items.description: The neighbouring island 20-30 minutes by ferry — its famous pilgrimage church, marble-carving villages, wild artichokes and its own louza make it the best-value escape in the Cyclades. A quiet, devotional, deeply Greek counterpoint to Mykonos's shine.

items.name: Matsuhisa Mykonos
credentials: At Belvedere Mykonos — The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: Nobu Matsuhisa's Mykonos table at the Belvedere — the island's landmark restaurant for two decades, and the world's original poolside Matsuhisa, serving the signature black cod miso and new-style sashimi.

items.name: Mykonos Social by Jason Atherton
credentials: Jason Atherton (MICHELIN-starred chef, London — Social group)
At Santa Marina, a Luxury Collection Resort
items.description: British chef Jason Atherton's Mediterranean table above Ornos Bay — inventive small plates and grilled seafood on a terrace made for long sunset dinners.

items.name: Pere Ubu at Kalesma
credentials: At Kalesma Mykonos — MICHELIN One Key (2025)
items.description: The hilltop dining room at Kalesma — refined Cycladic-Mediterranean cooking with produce-led menus, on a terrace with one of the island's finest Aegean panoramas.

items.name: Interni Restaurant
credentials: Long-running Chora landmark (est. 2000) — the original dinner-to-party destination in Mykonos Town
items.description: A secret-garden institution in the heart of Chora since 2000 — refined Mediterranean cooking, serious cocktails and the island's original dinner-into-party evening.

items.name: Kiku at Cavo Tagoo
credentials: At Cavo Tagoo Mykonos — Design Hotels member
items.description: The long-established Japanese kitchen at Cavo Tagoo — sushi, sashimi and modern rolls served against the hotel's cliffside cave-pool setting.

items.name: Beefbar Mykonos
credentials: At Bill&Coo The Coast, Agios Ioannis bay
items.description: The Mykonos outpost of the international Beefbar group — premium cuts and world grills on a beachfront terrace at Agios Ioannis, run by the Giraudi family.

items.name: M-eating
items.description: Chef Panagiotis Menardos's contemporary take on Cycladic and Greek recipes, in a restored early-1900s townhouse in the heart of town — the island's most respected Greek fine-dining room.

items.name: Bakalo
credentials: Established Chora favourite (est. 2010); expanded internationally (Miami Beach outpost)
items.description: A warm, unpretentious Greek eatery in the Lakka quarter of old town — honest regional recipes done well, long a favourite of visiting names for its lack of fuss.

items.name: Kastro's
credentials: Little Venice landmark since 1976 — among the island's most established and photographed tables
items.description: On the water's edge in 18th-century Little Venice since 1976 — one of the most photographed rooms on the island, its balcony tables set between old stone walls and the splashing Aegean.

items.name: Kadena
credentials: Established waterfront restaurant on Gialos, Mykonos Town
items.description: An all-day room on the Gialos waterfront in town — Mediterranean cooking of pasta, seafood and grills with the harbour and fishing boats in view.

items.name: Alemagou
credentials: Star Wine List — recognised wine programme
items.description: A bohemian beach taverna on windswept Ftelia — Aegean-fusion cooking, a serious wine list and a laid-back, barefoot afternoon-into-evening mood far from the glossy clubs.

items.name: Scorpios
credentials: Operated by Soho House / Soho Roc House — the island's defining beach-club-to-party institution
items.description: The island's most influential day-to-night beach club — a Soho House-run temple of long lunches, ritual sunsets and world-class DJs on the rocks above Paraga, part beach club, part cultural marketplace.

items.name: Nammos
credentials: Internationally renowned Psarou beach club — the island's most famous; a global luxury-lifestyle brand
items.description: The global byword for Mykonos beach glamour — a Psarou institution since 2003 that grew from a beach taverna into one of the most famous, and most expensive, beach clubs in the world.

items.name: Principote
credentials: Renowned Panormos beach club — among the most prestigious in the Cyclades
items.description: A bohemian-luxe beach club on quieter Panormos — hand-crafted design, Mediterranean cooking and DJ-led afternoons that build into celebratory sunset parties.

items.name: SantAnna Mykonos
credentials: The largest beach club on Mykonos; home to Europe's largest saltwater pool
items.description: The island's largest beach club — built around the biggest saltwater pool in Europe, an amphitheatre of daybeds, restaurants and stage shows on Paraga.

items.name: Bar at Cavo Tagoo
credentials: At Cavo Tagoo Mykonos — Design Hotels member
items.description: The cliffside pool bar of the island's original design hotel — cocktails beside the cave-cut saltwater pool as the sun drops behind the Aegean.

items.name: Cavo Paradiso
credentials: DJ Mag Top 100 Clubs — ranked worldwide (2024, 2025, 2026)
items.description: Mykonos's legendary open-air superclub — a clifftop dancefloor above the Aegean that has hosted the world's biggest electronic names since 1993, and the island's one internationally ranked club.

items.name: Bonbonniere
credentials: Sister club to Bonbonniere London — a leading Mykonos Town nightclub
items.description: The glossy town nightclub of the Mykonos jet set — sister to London's Bonbonniere, a small, high-energy room known for star DJs, celebrity nights and theatrical champagne service.

items.name: VOID Mykonos
credentials: One of the largest nightclubs in Mykonos Town — a leading house/techno venue
items.description: A three-level house-and-techno club in town — one of the island's largest indoor clubs, with a music-first programme that draws a serious dance crowd.

items.title: A private boat to the ruins of Delos
items.description: The sacred ancient island is a short crossing away and near-empty by late afternoon, a complete counterpoint to the beach clubs.

items.title: Sunset from Little Venice, then dinner in the back lanes
items.description: Watch the light drop behind the windmills with a drink, then slip inland to a quieter table away from the front.

items.title: A day at a marquee beach club
items.description: Book a bed at a name like Scorpios or Nammos and let the day drift from long lunch into music.

items.title: A traditional panigiri feast in a village
items.description: If your dates align with a church's saint's day, the communal food, wine and dancing are the real island.

plan.heading: 3 days in Mykonos, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The old town lanes at first light, Little Venice and the windmills before the day fills.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A slow lunch and the water at Scorpios or the calmer Kalo Livadi end of the island.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at the Belvedere's Nobu terrace or the tables of Bill & Coo above the bay.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private boat to Delos, the sacred island of Apollo, with a guide among the ruins.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: On to a quiet cove for the afternoon, the caïque anchored for swimming and lunch aboard.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Greek seafood at Kiki's-style simplicity, then a late table at Spilia carved into the rock.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A late start, then the fine sand and clear water of Agios Sostis or Fokos, away from the clubs.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at Alemagou on Ftelia, feet in the sand, then the drive back over the hills.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Sunset drinks at 180° Sunset Bar by the old castle, then dinner at M-eating in town.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Chora (Mykonos Town)
items.description: The whitewashed maze of shops, bars and nightlife; suits those who want to walk everywhere and be in the thick of it.

items.name: Psarou / Platis Gialos
items.description: The polished south-coast beach strip with the marquee clubs and calm swimming; suits sun-and-scene travellers.

items.name: Ano Mera
items.description: The quiet inland village around its monastery, away from the crowds; suits those wanting local calm and space.

events.name: XLSIOR Festival
events.note: One of the world's largest LGBTQ+ dance festivals, taking over the island's clubs and beach venues for five to six days.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Mykonos (JMK), fifteen minutes from town, or arrive by private yacht; a chauffeur meets the flight and drives you to the villa or hotel.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car and driver for the beaches and coast; the old town is pedestrian-only, a deliberate maze best explored on foot.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Networks are strong and an eSIM activates on arrival; wifi is standard, though beach clubs can be patchy at peak hours.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The euro; cards are taken everywhere, cash is handy at the smaller beach tavernas, and tipping around ten percent is welcomed at the busier venues.

onGround.note: Stay in the old town or Agios Lazaros for calm, away from the party beaches; the best clubs and beach restaurants require a reservation and a deposit in high summer, so arrange these before you land.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: June and September are the sweet spot — warm, swimmable, sociable without August saturation; July-August is peak crowd and price, and the summer meltemi wind can whip the beaches and disrupt ferries.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Via Athens — no India nonstop. Fly Athens (IndiGo direct, or Gulf/Turkish carrier in business), then a 40-minute Aegean/Sky Express flight to Mykonos (JMK) or a high-speed ferry from Rafina. Direct seasonal European flights to Mykonos exist but connections are simpler through Athens; secure summer legs well ahead.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required; tap water is desalinated and brackish — use bottled. Safe and relaxed; main cautions are scooter/quad-bike risk and slippery Chora lanes at night. No altitude concern.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Fine for vegetarians — Greek meze, salads and grilled vegetables are everywhere, though Jain needs explicit instruction. Indian dining is limited; a private chef suits a longer stay, and Nice n Easy or Bill & Coo handle refined vegetarian requests well.
