guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Hôtel du Cap-Eden-Roc
items.description: The legend of the Riviera since 1870 — a white palace on its own cape, with the sea-cut Eden-Roc pool the coast's most famous set piece.

items.name: Grand-Hôtel du Cap-Ferrat, A Four Seasons Hotel
items.description: A Belle Époque palace on seven hectares at the tip of the coast's most exclusive cape — private, forested and utterly serene.

items.name: Château de la Chèvre d'Or
items.description: A medieval eyrie clinging to the cliff of Èze village, 400m above the sea — the Riviera's most romantic address, with two-starred dining in-house.

items.name: La Réserve de Beaulieu & Spa
items.description: A rose-pink Italianate villa on its own harbour since 1880 — a hushed, aristocratic grande dame between Nice and Monaco.

items.name: Hôtel de Paris Monte-Carlo
items.description: The 1864 palace of the Place du Casino — the founding grand hotel of Monte-Carlo, home to Ducasse's three-star Le Louis XV.

items.name: Cap Estel
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A private peninsula of five acres between Nice and Monaco — a villa hotel wrapped by the sea on three sides, screened from the world.

items.name: Le Negresco
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: Nice's own pink-domed palace on the Promenade des Anglais — a private, family-owned house of art and theatre, a national monument since 1974.

items.name: Anantara Plaza Nice Hotel
items.description: An 1848 Belle Époque landmark off the Promenade, reborn by Anantara — Nice's most polished contemporary luxury, with a rooftop over the old town.

items.name: Hôtel Martinez, Cannes (Hyatt Unbound Collection)
items.description: The Art Deco grande dame of the Croisette — the address of the Film Festival, with the largest private beach in Cannes and a starred kitchen.

items.name: Hôtel Barrière Le Majestic Cannes
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A white 1926 palace at the head of the Croisette — grand, gracious and at the very centre of Cannes' glamour.

items.name: Promenade des Anglais
credentials: Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site — Nice, Winter Resort Town of the Riviera
items.description: The seven-kilometre Belle Époque seafront curving along the Baie des Anges, its blue chairs facing the water and the ochre Négresco dome behind. An unhurried morning stroll here, ice-cream in hand, is the Riviera at its most effortless — perfect for three generations moving at their own pace.

items.name: Vieux Nice (Old Town)
credentials: Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site — Nice, Winter Resort Town of the Riviera
items.description: A warren of ochre-and-terracotta lanes, baroque churches and shaded piazzas where laundry strings hang above artisan gelato shops. This is the emotional heart of Nice — small enough to wander with children, layered enough to reward a return each evening for aperitivo.

items.name: Cours Saleya Market
items.description: The famous flower-and-produce market — cut peonies, Menton lemons, tapenade, socca fresh off the copper pan — with a Monday antiques market in place of flowers. A vivid morning for the family, and a generous window into Niçoise produce for veg-leaning palates.

items.name: Colline du Château (Castle Hill)
credentials: Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site — Nice, Winter Resort Town of the Riviera
items.description: The green headland between the old town and the port, crowned by a man-made waterfall and the definitive view down over the terracotta rooftops and the sweep of the Baie des Anges. Reachable by a discreet free lift for those who prefer not to climb.

items.name: Musée Matisse
items.description: A red-ochre Genoese villa set in an olive grove, holding one of the world's most complete Matisse collections — the artist lived and died in Nice and is buried nearby. Intimate, sunlit and rarely crowded, it pairs naturally with a picnic under the Cimiez olive trees.

items.name: Musée National Marc Chagall
items.description: Purpose-built to hold Chagall's luminous Biblical Message cycle — seventeen large canvases glowing in a calm, light-filled space he helped design. A short, deeply moving visit that lands equally with art lovers and first-timers.

items.name: MAMAC — Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art
items.description: A striking marble-clad building holding Nice's own School (Yves Klein, Arman, the Nouveaux Réalistes) plus Warhol and Lichtenstein, with a rooftop terrace looking over the city. The contemporary counterweight to the city's Belle Époque grandeur.

items.name: Cimiez Quarter & Roman Ruins
credentials: Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site — Nice, Winter Resort Town of the Riviera
items.description: The genteel hill district of grand winter-palace hotels turned apartments, with Roman baths, an amphitheatre and a Franciscan monastery garden overlooking the coast. The refined, residential Nice the aristocracy chose — best explored slowly.

items.name: Port Lympia (Old Port)
credentials: Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site — Nice, Winter Resort Town of the Riviera
items.description: The photogenic old harbour framed by tall Italianate façades, where fishing boats sit beside superyachts and the seafood restaurants of the quai spill onto the water. The natural place to board a private charter or dine facing the masts at dusk.

items.name: Place Masséna & Promenade du Paillon
items.description: The grand red-arcaded square with its checkerboard paving and mirror-fountain, opening onto a long green park of water jets and lawns that runs to the sea. A cooling, kid-friendly spine through the city on hot afternoons.

items.name: Monaco & Monte-Carlo
items.description: The gilded sovereign city-state fifteen minutes along the coast — palace, harbour of superyachts, Belle Époque casino and grand hotels stacked on a rock over the sea. The Riviera's concentrated shot of glamour, best done by private driver for a day.

items.name: Casino de Monte-Carlo
items.description: Charles Garnier's Belle Époque temple of gaming, all gilt, marble and painted ceilings, facing the manicured casino gardens. Even without a chip on the table, the salons and the Café de Paris terrace opposite are pure theatre — jacket and passport advised.

items.name: Prince's Palace of Monaco
items.description: The Grimaldi family's residence high on the Rock, with lavish State Apartments open in season and the daily changing of the guard at 11:55 in the square outside. History and pageantry with one of the best harbour views in the principality.

items.name: Oceanographic Museum of Monaco
items.description: A monumental institution founded by Prince Albert I, clinging to the cliff eighty-five metres above the sea, with grand aquaria, a shark lagoon and a rooftop terrace. Genuinely spellbinding for children and a serene stop for adults.

items.name: The Monaco Grand Prix Circuit
items.description: The legendary street circuit runs through the everyday town — the Casino square, the Fairmont hairpin, the tunnel, the harbour chicane. Trace it on foot any day of the year, or watch it come alive over the late-May race weekend from a harbourside berth.

items.name: Èze Village
items.description: A medieval eagle's-nest village of stone lanes coiling up to a garden balcony 400 metres above the sea, entirely pedestrian and full of artisans' ateliers. One of the Riviera's most romantic vantage points — and a natural lunch stop between Nice and Monaco.

items.name: Jardin Exotique d'Èze
items.description: A cascade of cacti and succulents crowning the ruined castle at the very top of Èze, opening onto a dizzying panorama that on clear days reaches to Corsica. Small, sculptural and quietly the finest view in the village.

items.name: Sentier Nietzsche
items.description: The steep zig-zag path linking the seaside to the perched village, walked by the philosopher who is said to have drawn inspiration here. A vigorous, scented climb for the energetic — or an easy downhill after a private car drops you at the top.

items.name: Villefranche-sur-Mer
items.description: A jewel-box fishing port on one of the Mediterranean's deepest natural harbours, with a rose-and-ochre old town, a Cocteau-painted chapel and a sheltered beach. Ten minutes from Nice yet a world softer — a favourite anchorage for private yachts.

items.name: Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat
items.description: The discreet green peninsula of billionaires' villas and pine-shaded coastal paths, with a low-key port and some of the most exclusive addresses on the coast. Precisely the kind of quiet, moneyed seclusion the Riviera's oldest fortunes prize.

items.name: Villa Ephrussi de Rothschild
items.description: Baroness Béatrice de Rothschild's rose-pink palace on the crest of Cap Ferrat, ringed by nine themed gardens — French, Spanish, Florentine, Japanese — around a musical fountain. The Riviera's most exquisite house-and-garden day, and candlelit on summer evenings.

items.name: Villa Kérylos
items.description: A faithful recreation of an ancient Greek villa built on a rocky point over the sea by archaeologist Théodore Reinach, complete with mosaics, frescoes and Antiquity-inspired furniture. A serene, scholarly counterpoint to the coast's Belle Époque excess.

items.name: Antibes Old Town & Marché Provençal
items.description: Ramparts against the sea, cobbled lanes and a superb covered Provençal market of cheeses, olives, flowers and produce. Antibes wears its history lightly and dines beautifully — an easy, atmospheric half-day with the family.

items.name: Musée Picasso, Antibes
items.description: Set in the seafront Château Grimaldi where Picasso worked for a joyous few months in 1946, holding the paintings and ceramics he left behind. Compact, sunlit and looking straight onto the Mediterranean that fills the canvases.

items.name: Cap d'Antibes & Sentier du Littoral
items.description: The legendary green cape of grand villas and the fabled Eden-Roc, ringed by a coastal footpath past secret coves and the so-called Billionaires' Bay. Old-money glamour at its most photographed — walk the path, then a private lunch behind the pines.

items.name: Port Vauban & the Superyacht Quay
items.description: One of the Mediterranean's largest marinas, its 'Quai des Milliardaires' berthing the world's most extraordinary superyachts beneath the old fort. A striking evening walk, and the practical launch point for a day at sea.

items.name: Cannes — La Croisette
items.description: The palm-lined boulevard of palace hotels, designer flagships and private beach clubs where the film festival unfurls its red carpet each May. Glamour worn openly — dress the part and take an evening promenade past the Carlton and Martinez.

items.name: Le Suquet — Old Cannes
items.description: The steep original village above the port, its stepped lanes climbing to a watchtower and a panorama over the bay. A far quieter, more soulful Cannes than the Croisette — best at golden hour before dinner on the Rue Saint-Antoine.

items.name: Île Sainte-Marguerite
items.description: A short boat hop from Cannes to a pine-and-eucalyptus island of turquoise coves, ringed by the Fort Royal that once held the Man in the Iron Mask. Swim, walk and picnic where the crowds thin — bring a private tender for the finest anchorages.

items.name: Île Saint-Honorat & Lérins Abbey
items.description: A tiny monastic island farmed by Cistercian monks who make the celebrated Lérins wines and liqueurs among the vines and chapels. A rare, contemplative escape ten minutes from the glitz — tastings and a fortified monastery to explore.

items.name: Saint-Paul-de-Vence
items.description: A ravishing fortified hill village of galleries and stone ramparts that drew Chagall, Signac and half of mid-century Paris; Chagall is buried in its cemetery. Wander the lanes, then lunch at the storied La Colombe d'Or among its Picassos and Mirós.

items.name: Fondation Maeght
items.description: One of Europe's great private art foundations, a modernist building set in pine woods with a Giacometti courtyard, a Miró labyrinth and Braque pools — freshly expanded for its 60th anniversary. A pilgrimage for anyone serious about 20th-century art.

items.name: Grasse — Perfume Capital
items.description: The inland town that has scented the world for centuries, where the historic houses of Fragonard, Galimard and Molinard open their workshops. Compose your own bespoke fragrance in a private atelier — an intimate, memorable family afternoon.

items.name: Menton
items.description: The last town before Italy, a pastel amphitheatre of lemon groves and gardens basking in the Riviera's mildest microclimate, host to the famous February Lemon Festival. Softly Italianate and blissfully unhurried — a gentle day for all generations.

items.name: Jardin Serre de la Madone & Menton's Gardens
items.description: Menton's exceptional climate nurtures a constellation of botanical gardens — the terraced Serre de la Madone, the exotic Val Rahmeh, the Fontana Rosa. A tranquil, fragrant counterpoint for garden lovers away from the beach crowds.

items.name: The Three Corniches Drive
items.description: Three tiered clifftop roads — Basse, Moyenne and the vertiginous Grande Corniche — thread between Nice and Menton past Èze and Roquebrune with staggering sea views. The Riviera's definitive drive, best savoured slowly from the back of a private car.

items.name: Gorges du Verdon
items.description: Europe's grandest canyon, where turquoise water winds between limestone walls hundreds of metres deep, opening onto the emerald Lac de Sainte-Croix. A dramatic full-day inland expedition of clifftop drives, kayaking and the lavender plateaux beyond.

items.name: Roquebrune-Cap-Martin
items.description: A medieval hill village crowned by one of France's oldest castle keeps, with a coastal cape below of villas, pines and Le Corbusier's tiny Cabanon. Quiet, storied and perched between Monaco and Menton — a graceful hour or two off the main track.

items.name: Beaches & Private Beach Clubs of Nice
items.description: Along the Baie des Anges, a run of managed beach clubs offer loungers, umbrellas and service on the famous pebble shore, from Blue Beach to the hotel-run establishments. Reserve a front-row set — the discreet way to enjoy the sea in comfort.

items.name: Plage de Paloma & Cap Ferrat Coves
items.description: The elegant crescent of Paloma Beach on the tip of Cap Ferrat, with its long-loved beach restaurant and clear, sheltered water. The insiders' choice for a refined, uncrowded swim reached by coastal path or private tender.

items.name: Pampelonne-style Days at Juan-les-Pins
items.description: The lively pine-fringed bay next to Cap d'Antibes, birthplace of Riviera beach glamour in the Jazz Age and still lined with sandy beach clubs and evening bars. A more animated, youthful counterpoint for the family's beach day.

items.name: Private Yacht Charter along the Coast
items.description: The truest way to experience the Côte d'Azur — cast off from Nice, Antibes or Cannes to anchor off Cap Ferrat, the Lérins islands and the coves of Cap d'Antibes for a swim and lunch aboard. Privacy, freedom and the coast seen from its best angle.

items.name: Socca & Niçoise Table
items.description: Nice has its own cuisine — chickpea socca hot off the griddle, pan bagnat, ratatouille, tender-veg tians and pissaladière — much of it naturally vegetable-led. Graze the old town's institutions, or arrange a private Niçoise tasting for the family.

items.name: Vence & the Chapelle du Rosaire (Matisse Chapel)
items.description: A walled town near Saint-Paul whose true treasure is the little Rosary Chapel that Matisse designed and considered his masterpiece — pure white walls lit by cobalt-and-gold glass. A quiet, luminous stop for those who love him.

items.name: Mougins — Hilltop Village of Gastronomy
items.description: A pristine spiral village above Cannes where Picasso spent his last years, now a haven of galleries and celebrated tables. A polished, art-and-food afternoon away from the coast, easily paired with Grasse.

items.name: Musée Jean Cocteau, Menton
items.description: Menton's tribute to the poet-artist Jean Cocteau, spanning the little seafront Bastion he decorated himself and the collection he left the town. A charming, human-scaled museum to close a slow day near the Italian border.

items.name: Mirazur
items.description: Mauro Colagreco's cliff-garden temple above the Italian border — seed-to-plate cooking from twelve acres of biodynamic terraces, once the best restaurant on earth.

items.name: Le Louis XV-Alain Ducasse
items.description: Ducasse's landmark of Mediterranean 'naturalité' in the Hôtel de Paris — a founding three-star of the modern Riviera.

items.name: La Chèvre d'Or
items.description: Two-starred cooking suspended on the cliff of Èze village, the whole coast falling away below — chef Tom Meyer, Meilleur Ouvrier de France.

items.name: Flaveur
items.description: The Tourteaux brothers' two-star in central Nice — bold, spice-laced Mediterranean cooking, with Indian notes woven through local seafood.

items.name: La Palme d'Or
items.description: The Art Deco fine-dining room of the Hôtel Martinez, relaunched under Jean Imbert — the star table of the Croisette.

items.name: Le Restaurant des Rois
items.description: Julien Roucheteau's gastronomic room at La Réserve de Beaulieu — haute cuisine in a sumptuous seafront salon.

items.name: Le Chantecler
items.description: The starred dining room of Le Negresco — Virginie Basselot, Meilleur Ouvrier de France, cooking Mediterranean haute gastronomie in a wood-panelled salon.

items.name: Louroc
items.description: The starred restaurant of Hôtel du Cap-Eden-Roc — sea-facing Mediterranean cooking at the Riviera's most legendary address.

items.name: JAN
items.description: Jan Hendrik van der Westhuizen's intimate 20-seater near the port — French technique threaded with a South African soul.

items.name: Pure & V
items.description: Chef Pinja Paakkonen's Nordic-inflected kitchen in central Nice, with one of the coast's most characterful natural-wine lists.

items.name: Racines - Bruno Cirino
items.description: Bruno Cirino's 'kitchen-garden cuisine' — a single set menu of perfectly-ripe Mediterranean produce, largely vegetarian and farm-driven.

items.name: L'Aromate
items.description: Mickaël Gracieux's refined, produce-driven cooking in the heart of Nice — a quietly serious one-star.

items.name: Peixes
items.description: Fish and seafood served tapas-style in a blue-and-white tiled bistro near the opera — vibrant, Mediterranean-meets-South-American, and much loved.

items.name: Le Bistrot de Jan
items.description: The relaxed sibling of starred JAN — the same South African-French spirit at an easier, everyday pitch.

items.name: Maison Barale
items.description: A century-old Niçois family kitchen in Vieux Nice — the real ravioli, daube and socca of the old town.

items.name: La Merenda
credentials: A celebrated Niçois institution — chef Dominique Le Stanc (ex-Le Chantecler ★★)
items.description: Dominique Le Stanc's tiny, cash-only Niçoise counter — a former two-star chef cooking the humble classics of Nice by hand.

items.name: Le Relais
credentials: Within Le Negresco — Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: Le Negresco's walnut-panelled bar since 1913 — a century of Riviera legend from Delon to the Beatles, hushed by day, jazz-lit by night.

items.name: Le Bar Américain, Hôtel de Paris Monte-Carlo
credentials: Within Hôtel de Paris Monte-Carlo — Société des Bains de Mer
items.description: A wood-and-brass grand-hotel bar off the Place du Casino — live piano and the old glamour of Monte-Carlo.

items.name: Le Bar Churchill, Hôtel du Cap-Eden-Roc
credentials: Within Hôtel du Cap-Eden-Roc — MICHELIN Key (2025), Oetker Collection
items.description: The clubby bar of the Riviera's most legendary hotel — a Negroni among the pines, where the coast's glamour has gathered for a century.

items.name: Bar du Cap, Grand-Hôtel du Cap-Ferrat
credentials: Within Grand-Hôtel du Cap-Ferrat, A Four Seasons Hotel — MICHELIN Key (2025)
items.description: An elegant, low-lit bar in a Four Seasons palace on the cape — quiet, grown-up and framed by seven hectares of garden.

items.name: Le Bar du Ciel, Anantara Plaza Nice
credentials: Within Anantara Plaza Nice — MICHELIN Guide Hotel (Selected)
items.description: A rooftop bar over the old town and the sea — cocktails at golden hour above the centre of Nice.

items.name: Buddha-Bar Monte-Carlo
credentials: Part of the global Buddha-Bar name
items.description: A former concert hall turned Asian-themed temple of DJs and late nights — the loud, glamorous centre of Monaco's after-dark.

items.name: Movida / Vieux Nice bar quarter
items.description: The lanes around the Cours Saleya and Rue de la Préfecture — where Nice's own late night gathers, spilling from bar to bar.

items.title: Corniche drive to Èze and Monaco
items.description: The clifftop Grande Corniche is one of Europe's great coastal roads, with Èze's eagle-nest village en route.

items.title: Lunch at La Colombe d'Or, Saint-Paul-de-Vence
items.description: The hilltop inn hung with Picasso and Matisse, paid in art by the artists who stayed.

items.title: Sunset from Colline du Château
items.description: The old castle hill above Vieux Nice, with the whole sweep of the Baie des Anges below.

items.title: Day on the water off Villefranche
items.description: One of the deepest natural harbours on the coast, best seen from a small chartered boat.

plan.heading: 5 days on the Riviera, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Evening

slots.label: Afternoon

slots.label: Evening

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive the Grande Corniche to the perched village of Èze and its exotic garden.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Down to Monaco for the old town and the Oceanographic Museum.

slots.label: Evening

slots.label: Afternoon

slots.label: Evening

slots.label: Evening

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Vieux Nice
items.description: The atmospheric old town of markets and narrow lanes; lively and central, best for first visits.

items.name: Cimiez
items.description: Leafy hillside of Belle Époque villas and Roman ruins; quiet and residential, for a calmer stay.

items.name: Le Port / Riquier
items.description: Around the harbour, with the best local dining and fewer tourists; for those who want neighbourhood life.

events.name: Nice Carnival
events.note: One of the world's great carnivals, with flower battles and huge floats along the Promenade des Anglais.

events.name: Fête du Citron (Menton Lemon Festival)
events.note: Giant sculptures built from citrus fruit in nearby Menton — a short train ride east.

events.name: Nice Jazz Fest
events.note: A summer institution of over 70 years, staged in the heart of the city.

events.name: Jazz à Juan (Juan-les-Pins)
events.note: The legendary seaside jazz festival along the coast at Antibes.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Nice Cote d'Azur; a seven-minute helicopter transfer reaches Monaco, or a chauffeured car runs the coast road to Cap-Ferrat, Antibes or Saint-Tropez.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver for the corniches and coastal villages, with a chartered yacht or tender the natural way to move along the water in season.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Strong along the coast; a French eSIM covers the whole Riviera, and villas and hotels offer good wifi.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Euro (Monaco uses it too); cards are universal and service is included, so tipping is modest and optional.

onGround.note: Cap-Ferrat and Cap d'Antibes are the discreet places to stay; July and August are crowded and yachts and villas are reserved months ahead, and evenings on the coast run late and relaxed rather than formal.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: May-June and September give warm sea, calm light and the coast before and after the crush. July-August is beautiful but crowded and hot; November-March is quiet and many finer addresses close.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No nonstop from India; cleanest routing is direct to Paris on Air France, then a 1.5-hour hop to Nice, or via a Gulf hub (Emirates, Qatar Qsuite) or London. For a seamless arrival, hold business through to Nice on one ticket and pre-arrange a car from the terminal along the Basse Corniche.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required; very safe. Normal care with valuables in Nice old town and Cannes at events. Tap water is potable across the Riviera.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian is manageable but not a regional strength; Jain and no-onion-garlic need advance notice at most kitchens. Indian food is limited outside Nice and Monaco, so a villa chef briefed on veg/Jain is the reliable route; Monte-Carlo's hotel dining will cater on request.

seo.title: Osaka — TripAgent
seo.description: Osaka, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Osaka
hero.tagline: Japan's exuberant kitchen, neon-lit and warm-hearted.

ourTake.lede: Osaka is where you come to eat, so plan around meals rather than monuments and let the castle be a morning aside, not the point. Dotonbori is worth seeing once for the spectacle, but the better food is a street or two back in Shinsekai and the covered arcades, and the standing counters reward anyone willing to point and sit. Use it as a base for Kyoto and Nara by day and give the evenings entirely to the kitchens.
ourTake.comeIf: You want Japan's kitchen, a lively city and an easy hop to Kyoto and Nara.
ourTake.skipIf: You are strictly vegetarian and inflexible; dashi and seafood run through the cuisine.

whenToGo.blurb: Cherry blossom in early April and crisp maples in November are finest; time a July visit to Tenjin Matsuri, but skip the hot, humid deep summer.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Mar, Apr, May, Sep, Oct and Nov

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Osaka
items.description: Four Seasons' Osaka debut, opened August 2024 — including Gensui, the city's first modern-ryokan floor, tatami and all, inside a luxury tower.

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton, Osaka
items.description: The grande dame of Osaka luxury — a European-manor interior of antiques and oil paintings, above the Umeda business district.

items.name: Conrad Osaka
items.description: The top ten floors of the Nakanoshima Festival Tower — floor-to-ceiling glass over the Dojima River, and one of the great skyline bars in the city.

items.name: The St. Regis Osaka
items.description: A discreet, art-filled house on the Midosuji boulevard, with the signature St. Regis butler on every floor.

items.name: InterContinental Osaka
items.description: A polished flagship inside Grand Front Osaka, steps from the station — the practical luxury base for arriving and moving on by rail.

items.name: Waldorf Astoria Osaka
items.description: The Waldorf Astoria's first house in Japan, opened 2025, crowning the new Grand Green Osaka park quarter beside the station.

items.name: W Osaka
items.description: Tadao Ando's monolithic black tower on Midosuji — the boldest design hotel in the city, at the heart of the shopping and nightlife.

items.name: Patina Osaka
items.description: The first city hotel from Capella's Patina brand, opened 2025 — quiet, contemporary luxury with a strong wellness focus near Umeda.

items.name: Imperial Hotel, Osaka
items.description: The Osaka house of Japan's most storied hotel name, set on the cherry-lined Okawa river away from the crowds.

items.name: Hilton Osaka
items.description: A large, capable and reliably run Hilton facing Osaka Station — easy, central and generous for a family on the move.

items.name: Osaka Castle (Osaka-jo)
items.description: Toyotomi Hideyoshi's golden fortress rises on colossal cut-stone ramparts above a moat, the reconstructed keep now a museum climbing to a top-floor view over the whole city. A private guide can walk multi-generational families through the history at their own pace, with the keep's lift making the upper floors easy for grandparents.

items.name: Nishinomaru Garden
items.description: The manicured lawn garden inside the castle grounds frames the finest single view of the keep, with roughly 300 cherry trees that turn it into one of Osaka's great hanami spots and glow under illumination each spring. Quiet, flat and ticketed, so it stays calmer than the free parkland outside.

items.name: Dotonbori & the Glico Sign
items.description: Osaka's neon canyon of running-man billboards, giant mechanical crabs and canal-side food stalls, glowing since 1935 and best seen at dusk when the reflections hit the water. The full theatre of Osaka's kuidaore ('eat till you drop') spirit; a guide can steer veg and Jain travellers past the meat skewers to okonomiyaki and vegetable tempura options.

items.name: Ebisu Bridge
items.description: The little arched bridge over the Dotonbori canal is the classic photo spot, looking straight up at the Glico sign as crowds mill and pleasure boats slide beneath. Come early morning for the shot without the throng, or ride the Tombori River Cruise for a low-water view of the signboards.

items.name: Kuromon Ichiba Market
items.description: A 600-metre covered arcade of some 150 stalls, 'Osaka's Kitchen' since 1902, where chefs shop at dawn and visitors graze on grilled scallops, uni and fatty tuna by late morning. Seafood-heavy, so veg travellers should aim for the fruit, tamagoyaki and tempura vendors; a guide can pre-arrange stalls that plate to order.

items.name: Shinsekai & Tsutenkaku Tower
items.description: A gloriously retro 'New World' district of 1950s neon and hand-painted signboards under the 108-metre Tsutenkaku, an Eiffel-inspired tower crowned by the lucky Billiken statue whose feet you rub for fortune. This is the birthplace of kushikatsu deep-fried skewers, so flag ahead for vegetable-only sets.

items.name: Umeda Sky Building — Floating Garden Observatory
items.description: Two 173-metre towers bridged at the summit by a doughnut-shaped rooftop deck (the Kuchu Teien), reached by a glass escalator suspended in mid-air and modelled on the Hanging Gardens of Babylon. The open-air ring gives a 360-degree Osaka panorama that is unforgettable at sunset.

items.name: Abeno Harukas 300 Observatory
items.description: At 300 metres, Abeno Harukas was Japan's tallest building until 2023, and its three-floor Harukas 300 deck wraps the top in floor-to-ceiling glass with a wooden inner courtyard and sky cafe. On a clear day the view runs to Awaji Island and Kobe; the tower sits atop a Kintetsu station and department store for effortless access.

items.name: Sumiyoshi Taisha
items.description: One of Japan's oldest and most important shrines, said to date to the 3rd century, built in a pure native Sumiyoshi-zukuri style untouched by mainland influence and approached over the steep vermilion Sorihashi drum bridge. Serene and free of crowds, it rewards an early, unhurried visit with a private guide to read its rituals.

items.name: Shitenno-ji
items.description: Japan's first state-built Buddhist temple, founded in 593 by Prince Shotoku, its five-storey pagoda and central halls faithfully rebuilt to the original 6th-century layout. A calm, spacious complex with a fine treasure house and garden, and one of the most historically significant sites in the country.

items.name: Osaka Museum of Housing and Living
items.description: On the ninth floor sits a full life-size street of 1830s Osaka, faithfully rebuilt with tenement houses, shops and shifting day-to-night lighting, complete with a rooftop cat and the sound of rain. Children can dress in kimono and wander the lanes; the one place in Japan that recreates a whole Edo townscape indoors.

items.name: teamLab Botanical Garden Osaka
items.description: After dark, the trees, ponds and ecosystems of Nagai Botanical Garden become a vast open-air digital artwork that responds to wind, rain and the movement of visitors. An interactive night wander that lands with every generation; book timed entry and pair it with an early dinner.

items.name: Osaka Aquarium Kaiyukan
items.description: One of the world's largest aquariums, built as a descending spiral around a nine-metre-deep Pacific Ocean tank home to whale sharks, with 620 species across the Pacific Rim. The gentle downward ramp is stroller- and wheelchair-friendly, making it a reliable multi-gen half-day.

items.name: Tempozan & the Giant Ferris Wheel
items.description: The harbourside quarter beside the aquarium, crowned by a 112-metre Ferris wheel whose night lighting forecasts tomorrow's weather. Air-conditioned gondolas make a smooth 15-minute loop over Osaka Bay; a soft, scenic add-on for families with young children.

items.name: Universal Studios Japan
items.description: The blockbuster theme park anchored by the playable, full-scale Super Nintendo World and the atmospheric Wizarding World of Harry Potter, with an expansion widening the magic. Express Passes and a VIP guided tour let a family skip the long queues and see the headline rides in a single day.

items.name: Nakanoshima Museum of Art, Osaka
items.description: A striking black cube opened in 2022 holding over 6,000 works of modern and contemporary art and design, from Modigliani to Yayoi Kusama's pumpkin at the entrance. The cultural heart of Nakanoshima island, walkable between two rivers and paired easily with the neighbouring museums.

items.name: The Museum of Oriental Ceramics, Osaka
items.description: Reopened in 2024 after renovation, this hushed museum holds the Sumitomo-gifted Ataka Collection of Chinese and Korean ceramics, including two National Treasures lit by natural light. A quiet, refined hour for connoisseurs, steps from the Nakanoshima rose garden.

items.name: Nakanoshima Rose Garden
items.description: At the eastern tip of Nakanoshima Park, riverside beds hold some 3,700 rose bushes across roughly 310 varieties, best in mid-spring and autumn against the old bridges and modern skyline. A free, flat, pretty stroll that stitches the island's museums together.

items.name: Amerikamura
items.description: Osaka's youth-culture quarter of vintage stores, streetwear boutiques, murals and Triangle Park, born from 1970s warehouses filled with imported American goods. A lively, offbeat counterpoint to the luxury malls, best for an afternoon of thrifting and people-watching.

items.name: Horie & Orange Street
items.description: A calmer, more design-led neighbour to Amerikamura, where Tachibana-dori (Orange Street) lines up interiors showrooms, curated vintage, specialty coffee and quiet cafes. The place to slow down between shopping runs, with a grown-up sense of Osaka style.

items.name: Namba Yasaka Shrine
items.description: A small city shrine dominated by a 12-metre lion-head stage built in 1975, its huge open mouth said to swallow bad luck and grant success in study and business. A quick, striking stop near Namba and a favourite for a good-fortune photograph.

items.name: Shinsaibashi-suji
items.description: Osaka's premier shopping spine, a long covered arcade running from the luxury flagships and the Daimaru department store down toward Dotonbori. Everything from global maisons to Japanese labels under one weatherproof roof; a personal shopper can arrange after-hours access at the top houses.

items.name: Namba Parks
items.description: A shopping and office complex whose real draw is an eight-level rooftop garden of 100,000 plants that rises like a terraced canyon above the city, open late and free to enter. A surprising pocket of green over Namba, lovely at golden hour.

items.name: HEP Five Ferris Wheel
items.description: A bright-red wheel bolted to the roof of a Umeda shopping centre, its air-conditioned gondolas climbing to 106 metres for a quick, central skyline loop with Bluetooth to play your own soundtrack. A fun, low-commitment lift right in the heart of the Kita district.

items.name: Grand Front Osaka & Umekita
items.description: The glossy twin-tower complex above Osaka Station, packed with design flagships, restaurants and the new Umekita greenspace that has transformed the north side of the station into a walkable urban park. The natural base for shopping, dining and easy transfers across the region.

items.name: Tenjinbashi-suji Shopping Street
items.description: Japan's longest covered shopping street runs some 2.6 kilometres through the old merchant quarter, lined with local shops, standing bars and unpretentious eateries far from the tourist crush. A genuine slice of everyday Osaka; pair it with the neighbouring Museum of Housing and Living.

items.name: Tenmangu Shrine & Tenjin Matsuri
items.description: Dedicated to the deity of learning, this shrine at the head of Tenjinbashi-suji hosts the Tenjin Matsuri each July, one of Japan's three great festivals, with a river procession of lantern-lit boats and fireworks. A discreet advisor can secure prime riverside vantage for the summer spectacle.

items.name: Expo '70 Commemorative Park & Tower of the Sun
items.description: The vast park left behind by the 1970 World Expo, still watched over by Taro Okamoto's monumental Tower of the Sun, whose restored interior you can now tour by reservation. Wide lawns, gardens and the fine national ethnology museum make it an easy green escape north of the city.

items.name: Cup Noodles Museum, Ikeda
items.description: On the very spot where Momofuku Ando invented instant ramen in 1958, this free museum lets you design and package your own original Cup Noodle to carry home. A genuinely charming, hands-on hour for children and adults; a short hop from Umeda on the Hankyu line.

items.name: Nintoku-tenno-ryo Kofun (Daisen Kofun)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Mozu-Furuichi Kofun Group
items.description: The keyhole-shaped mausoleum attributed to Emperor Nintoku is the largest tomb in Japan at 486 metres long, its scale rivalling the Great Pyramid and best grasped from the Sakai City observation deck or by air. The heart of the Mozu-Furuichi tomb cluster inscribed by UNESCO in 2019, it makes a thoughtful, uncrowded half-day.

items.name: Minoo Park & Falls
items.description: A paved 2.8-kilometre forest trail leads to the 33-metre Minoo waterfall, famed for its blazing autumn maples and for momiji tempura, batter-fried maple leaves sold along the path. Thirty minutes from Umeda yet feeling deep in the mountains, an easy nature day for all ages.

items.name: Katsuo-ji
items.description: A mountain 'temple of winner's luck' whose grounds are strewn with thousands of red daruma dolls tucked into every nook by pilgrims seeking success, framed by cherry blossom, hydrangea and autumn colour by season. Serene and photogenic; best reached by private car with the Minoo hills.

items.name: Day Trip — Kyoto
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto
items.description: Just 15 minutes by Shinkansen from Shin-Osaka, Japan's imperial capital lays out golden pavilions, torii tunnels, geisha lanes and Zen gardens across a single day. A private car and guide let a family cover Kinkaku-ji, Fushimi Inari and Gion without touching a crowded platform.

items.name: Day Trip — Nara
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara
items.description: Under 40 minutes from Osaka, Japan's first permanent capital offers Todai-ji's 15-metre bronze Great Buddha, the lantern corridors of Kasuga Taisha and over a thousand bowing sika deer roaming Nara Park. Flat, walkable and gentle; the biscuits sold for the deer delight children and grandparents alike.

items.name: Day Trip — Himeji Castle
items.description: The 'White Heron Castle' is Japan's finest surviving feudal fortress, a dazzling white hilltop keep of interlocking baileys reachable in under an hour by Shinkansen from Shin-Osaka. Pair the climb with the adjacent Koko-en gardens; one of Japan's first UNESCO inscriptions and its most complete original castle.

items.name: Day Trip — Koyasan (Mount Koya)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range
items.description: About two hours south by Nankai train and cablecar, this sacred mountain of Shingon Buddhism holds Okunoin, Japan's largest cemetery, cedar-shaded and lined with 200,000 tombs to Kobo Daishi's mausoleum, plus Kongobu-ji and the Danjo Garan temple complex. A temple-lodging shojin-ryori lunch is naturally vegan, ideal for veg and Jain travellers.

items.name: Day Trip — Kobe
items.description: Barely 20 minutes by rapid train, this elegant port city offers the world-famous Kobe beef, the Western merchant mansions of Kitano-cho, the Nunobiki herb garden ropeway and, close by, the hot springs of Arima Onsen. A refined, easygoing day that mixes cuisine, views and heritage.

items.name: Takoyaki — the octopus dumpling
items.description: Osaka's signature street snack, molten balls of batter with a piece of octopus, brushed with sauce and dancing bonito flakes and invented in this city in the 1930s. Watching the swift turning of the griddles is half the fun; a guide can point veg travellers to cheese or plain-vegetable versions where offered.

items.name: Okonomiyaki — the savoury pancake
items.description: The 'grill what you like' cabbage pancake cooked on a hotplate at your table is Osaka soul food, endlessly customisable and one of the easier local dishes to keep vegetarian. Book a private teppan counter for a hands-on family dinner where everyone cooks their own.

items.name: Kushikatsu — the deep-fried skewer
items.description: Breadcrumbed skewers of vegetables, meat and seafood fried to order and dipped once (never twice) in communal sauce, born in the working-class Shinsekai district. A fun, informal Osaka ritual; vegetable-forward sets are easy to request at the better houses.

items.name: Kappo & Kaiseki Fine Dining
items.description: Osaka's discreet Kitashinchi district hides intimate kappo counters and Michelin-starred kaiseki rooms where a chef cooks a seasonal procession before your eyes. A concierge can secure the near-impossible reservations and brief chefs in advance on veg, Jain or dietary needs.

items.name: Nakanoshima Central Public Hall
items.description: A red-brick neo-Renaissance landmark of 1918 on the river island, its grand hall a rare survivor of Osaka's early-modern civic architecture, floodlit beautifully at night. Worth a slow exterior circuit as part of a Nakanoshima museum walk.

items.name: Isshinji Temple
items.description: Near Shitenno-ji, this temple is known for its avant-garde black gate guarded by muscular modern Nio statues and, more soberly, for its okotsubutsu, Buddha images made from the cremated remains of the faithful. A striking, little-visited counterpoint to the classical temples nearby.

items.name: Nakazakicho
items.description: A pocket of old wooden houses that survived the war, now quietly reborn as a warren of independent cafes, vintage shops and tiny galleries a short walk from Umeda's towers. The most atmospheric slow-morning neighbourhood in northern Osaka.

items.name: Tombori River Cruise
items.description: A 20-minute open-boat glide along the Dotonbori canal delivers the neon signboards and the Glico man at eye level from the water, with a lively guide. A restful way to see the district's spectacle without the crowded bridge, and a hit with children.

items.name: La Cime
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Restaurants 2026 (No. 13, Best Restaurant in Japan)
items.description: Yusuke Takada's modern French read through Japanese ingredients — the finest table in Osaka, and among the very best in Asia.

items.name: Hajime
items.description: A former engineer's cosmos-on-a-plate — three stars won in a record 17 months, and the signature 'Chikyu' built from over a hundred ingredients.

items.name: Taian
items.description: Exacting, restrained kaiseki that has held three stars for over fifteen years — mastery expressed as quiet.

items.name: Kashiwaya Osaka Senriyama
items.description: A three-star kaiseki house in a serene garden setting on the city's northern edge — seasonal Japanese cooking of the highest order.

items.name: Kahala
items.description: Four decades of idiosyncratic, boundary-crossing kaiseki — a chef cooking exactly as he pleases, and celebrated for it.

items.name: Koryu
items.description: Pure, unshowy kaiseki devoted to tradition — one of Osaka's quiet two-star greats, relocated to a calm Kitahama room.

items.name: Fujiya 1935
items.description: A former udon shop turned two-star temple of contemporary cuisine — inventive, vegetable-forward and deeply personal.

items.name: Sushi Harasho
items.description: One of Osaka's most exacting sushi counters — classical technique and top fish, two stars in the guide.

items.name: Yugen
items.description: Refined, seasonal Japanese cooking of great poise — a two-star kaiseki room away from the Kitashinchi crush.

items.name: Tenjinbashi Aoki
items.description: Precise, seasonal Japanese cuisine on Osaka's great old shopping street — quiet excellence, two stars.

items.name: Numata
items.description: A serene two-star tempura counter — course after course of impossibly light, precise frying.

items.name: Shunsai Ten Tsuchiya
items.description: A two-star tempura house on the city's edge, worth the short trip for the lightness of the frying alone.

items.name: Hiraishi
items.description: A refined one-star tempura counter that has held its star for years running — classical, exact and warmly run.

items.name: Tenmabashi Fujikawa
items.description: A long-standing one-star tempura kitchen — seasonal, unhurried, and a benchmark of the Osaka style.

items.name: Mizuno
items.description: A 1945-founded okonomiyaki griddle that turned Osaka's soul food into a credentialed pilgrimage — the yamaimo-yaki is the order.

items.name: Takohachi
items.description: A beloved 1945 Dotonbori institution for octopus and okonomiyaki, honoured by the guide for years running.

items.name: Udondokoro Shigemi
items.description: Kansai-style udon done exactly right — the hiyakake, with its clear dashi and Kagawa-trained noodles, is the bowl to have.

items.name: Bar K
credentials: A cornerstone of Osaka's classic cocktail and whisky scene; alma mater of Craftroom's Ryu Fujii
items.description: A revered Kitashinchi institution with one of Japan's deepest whisky backbars and the classical, ice-carving craft Osaka is known for.

items.name: Bar Nakanoshima
credentials: An established name in Osaka's traditional Kitashinchi bar quarter
items.description: A long-standing Kitashinchi cocktail room in the exacting Osaka tradition — hand-carved ice, flawless classics, quiet mastery.

items.name: Craftroom
items.description: Ryu Fujii's six-seat counter tucked into a station building — seasonal twists on the classics, freshly baked pies, and a jazz soundtrack.

items.name: Bar Nayuta
items.description: A whimsical, no-menu speakeasy behind a hidden door near Triangle Park — bespoke cocktails built to each guest's spirit and mood.

items.name: Atmos
credentials: Conrad Osaka signature bar; MICHELIN One Key hotel
items.description: The Conrad's 40th-floor lounge — the Dojima River and the whole lit city through floor-to-ceiling glass.

items.name: Shinsekai & the kushikatsu alleys
credentials: Shinsekai — a historic Osaka entertainment quarter dating to 1912
items.description: Under the glow of Tsutenkaku, a warren of loud, cheap, gloriously unpretentious kushikatsu and highball joints that run late.

items.title: Kappo counter dinner at a chef's table
items.description: Osaka's kappo tradition puts you an arm's length from the knife; the great counters serve a running, improvised menu shaped by what came in that morning.

items.title: Private kuidaore food crawl with a local guide
items.description: A well-connected guide gets you past the queues at the takoyaki and kushikatsu institutions that tourists never find.

items.title: Bunraku puppet theatre at the National Bunraku Theatre
items.description: Osaka is the home of this UNESCO-listed puppet art; a single act with commentary is a rare, intimate performance.

items.title: After-hours Osaka Castle grounds walk
items.description: A guided early or late visit to the keep and its moats sidesteps the daytime crush around the tower.

plan.heading: 3 days in Osaka, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle into the Conrad Osaka high above Nakanoshima, then walk the canalside quiet of the island's rose garden and the Museum of Oriental Ceramics.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Cross into Chuo-ku for Osaka Castle and its keep, then wander the covered arcades toward Dotonbori as the crowds thin.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Hajime, the three-Michelin room where Yoshiaki Takasu plates a single composed narrative of Japan.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Breakfast among the traders at Kuromon Ichiba market, then an unhurried morning at the tea houses of Sumiyoshi Taisha.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A knife-shopping hour on Doguyasuji, then coffee and the city's design shops around Minami-Semba.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Counter kappo at Koryu, one of Osaka's most quietly revered kaiseki tables, booked well in advance.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The forty-minute train to Nara for Todai-ji's Great Buddha before the coaches arrive, deer and moss underfoot.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The lantern paths of Kasuga Taisha, then a light lunch of kakinoha-zushi in the old town.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Back in Osaka, a final counter of kushikatsu done well, and a nightcap at the Conrad's 40 Sky Bar over the river.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Kitashinchi / Umeda
items.description: Osaka's polished business and dining quarter; suits those who want quiet high-end restaurants and easy rail connections.

items.name: Namba / Minami
items.description: The neon heart around Dotonbori; loud, late, and central, best for travellers who want the food and nightlife at the door.

items.name: Nakanoshima
items.description: A calm river island of museums and grand architecture; ideal for a more grown-up, low-key base.

events.name: Tenjin Matsuri
events.note: One of Japan's three great festivals, ending with a river procession of boats and fireworks over the Okawa.

events.name: Kishiwada Danjiri Matsuri
events.note: Teams race four-tonne wooden floats through the streets of Kishiwada, cornering them at speed in one of the country's most thrilling festivals.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Kansai International (KIX) on Osaka Bay; a pre-booked black-car service or the hotel's chauffeur clears the roughly 50-minute run into the city, avoiding the crowded airport express.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with an English-speaking driver for day trips to Kyoto and Nara, with unhurried walking through Namba and Kita for dining and boutiques.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Buy a Japan eSIM (Ubigi, Airalo) before landing; coverage is excellent everywhere and most hotels offer strong free wifi.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Japanese yen; cards are widely accepted in hotels and fine dining but keep cash for smaller kaiseki and craft shops, and note that tipping is not practised and can cause discomfort.

onGround.note: Stay in Kita (Umeda) for polish or Namba for the food scene; the finest sushi and kappo counters seat only a handful and require a concierge introduction weeks ahead.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Late March–early April brings the cherry blossom and clear, cool days; June is the plum rain, and July–August is heavy, humid heat best avoided. Autumn (late Oct–Nov) is dry and mild with the maple colour.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Nonstop from Delhi on Air India and Japan Airlines to Kansai (KIX), roughly 7.5–8 hours; from Mumbai it is typically one stop via a Southeast Asian hub. Fly JAL or ANA business for the reliable service, and use the KIX-hub JAL Sakura Lounge on transit.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations; Japan is exceptionally safe and orderly, with tap water safe to drink. Standard routine vaccines are enough; carry a copy of prescriptions as some common Indian medicines are restricted.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian and especially Jain eating needs care, as dashi (fish stock) is in most broths, so name it clearly; the Indian community around Namba/Nishihonmachi supports good vegetarian Indian tables. Book a kaiseki that can do shojin (Buddhist vegetarian) in advance, and Ashoka and Mumbai Kitchen serve reliable Indian.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Osaka, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Paris — TripAgent
seo.description: Paris, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Paris
hero.tagline: Light on the Seine, a table for every hour, elegance worn lightly.

ourTake.lede: Give Paris more mornings than you think you need — the Louvre before ten, the Marais before the shops open, a café before the city fills. The great mistake is treating it as a checklist of monuments; the real pleasure is a single arrondissement walked slowly, one long lunch, and the light going gold over the rooftops around seven. Skip the Champs-Élysées entirely and eat where the waiters don't speak English.
ourTake.comeIf: You want grand museums, three-star tables and quiet luxury within walking distance of each other.
ourTake.skipIf: You are chasing beaches, wilderness or an unhurried resort week doing nothing.
