whenToGo.blurb: Come late May through June for long light, Roland-Garros and the couture calendar, or September into October for the art season; skip a shuttered, sweltering August and grey January.
whenToGo.bestMonths: May, Jun, Jul and Aug

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Le Bristol Paris
items.description: The grande dame of them all — a courtyard garden hidden behind the city's most powerful street.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel George V
items.description: The Four Seasons standard our members already trust, wrapped in legendary flowers.

items.name: Le Meurice, Dorchester Collection
items.description: Starck's hand over an 18th-century bones, looking straight onto the gardens.

items.name: Hôtel Plaza Athénée, Dorchester Collection
items.description: The couture address — Dior at the door and the red awnings on the avenue.

items.name: Cheval Blanc Paris
items.area: 1st arr. / La Samaritaine, by the Seine
items.description: LVMH's newest icon — river light, a Dior spa, and a pool most hotels can only envy.

items.name: Hôtel de Crillon, A Rosewood Hotel
items.description: An 18th-century palace on the grandest square, restored without losing its nerve.

items.name: Le Royal Monceau – Raffles Paris
items.area: 8th arr. / near the Arc de Triomphe
items.description: The artist's palace — Starck design, its own gallery and cinema, a long quiet pool.

items.name: La Réserve Paris
items.area: 8th arr. / Avenue Gabriel, by the Élysée
items.description: A forty-key mansion that feels less like a hotel and more like a private house.

items.name: Shangri-La Paris
items.description: A Bonaparte prince's palace, with the Eiffel Tower filling many of the windows.

items.name: The Peninsula Paris
items.area: 16th arr. / near the Arc de Triomphe
items.description: Peninsula precision and a rooftop that trades on the finest view in Paris.

items.name: Bulgari Hotel Paris
items.description: Italian glamour dropped onto the smartest corner, with one of the city's largest hotel spas.

items.name: Hôtel Lutetia
items.description: The only Palace on the Left Bank — literary Saint-Germain in an Art Deco landmark.

items.name: Hôtel Fouquet's Paris, Barrière
items.description: Family-owned Barrière glamour above the most famous brasserie on the avenue.

items.name: The Ritz Paris
items.description: The most famous hotel name in the world, still keeping the promise on Place Vendôme.

items.name: Maison Villeroy
items.description: A discreet townhouse near the Élysée for members who prefer to be unseen.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental, Paris
items.description: A garden courtyard hidden off the smartest shopping street, run to the group's quiet precision.

items.name: Saint James Paris, Relais & Châteaux
items.area: 16th arr. / near the Bois de Boulogne
items.description: The only château-hotel in Paris, set behind its own gardens.

items.name: Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme
items.description: Refined and understated, a calm base a step from the jewellers of Vendôme.

items.name: J.K. Place Paris
items.description: Italian-run, jewel-box luxury on the Left Bank — warm where the palaces can be grand.

items.name: Nolinski Paris, Evok Collection
items.description: A chic forty-five-key house between the Louvre and the Palais Royal.

items.name: Brach Paris, Evok Collection
items.description: Starck-designed and buzzing, with a rooftop garden and a fashionable crowd.

items.name: Grand Powers
items.description: Elegant, intimate and perfectly placed for a day among the maisons.

items.name: Le Burgundy Paris
items.description: Refined and central, with a spa and a Michelin-recognised kitchen of its own.

items.name: Château Voltaire
items.description: A fashion-crowd design hotel that hides its glamour behind a plain door.

items.name: Maison Proust
items.description: Belle Époque opulence and a La Mer spa, tucked into the Marais.

items.name: Le Grand Mazarin
items.description: Joyful maximalism and one of the liveliest hotel restaurants in town.

items.name: La Fantaisie
items.description: A garden-inspired newcomer with a rooftop and a light-hearted spirit.

items.name: Maison Delano Paris
items.description: Sleek and discreet, arranged around a quiet courtyard.

items.name: Le Pavillon de la Reine
items.description: Hidden behind the loveliest square in Paris — romantic and quiet.

items.name: Monsieur George
items.description: A warm, well-placed boutique with more soul than its size suggests.

items.name: Grand Hôtel du Palais Royal
items.area: 1st arr. / by the Palais Royal gardens
items.description: Elegant and superbly placed, a step from the arcades of the Palais Royal.

items.name: Relais Christine
items.description: A hushed Left Bank townhouse built around its own courtyard.

items.name: Eiffel Tower
credentials: most-visited paid monument in the world
items.description: The city's iron heart; go to the summit at dusk and catch the on-the-hour sparkle, or dine at the Jules Verne on the second floor for a table above Paris.

items.name: Arc de Triomphe
items.description: Climb the 284 steps to a rooftop where twelve avenues fan out like a star, with the Champs-Élysées running straight to the Louvre.

items.name: Notre-Dame Cathedral
items.description: Reopened December 2024 after the 2019 fire, the restored nave gleams brighter than in living memory; entry is free, and the bell towers reopened in September 2025 for the climb to the gargoyles.

items.name: Sainte-Chapelle
credentials: finest medieval stained glass in the world
items.description: A jewel-box royal chapel where fifteen soaring windows of 13th-century stained glass wrap you in coloured light — go on a bright morning for the full effect.

items.name: Sacré-Cœur Basilica
items.description: The white domed basilica crowns the highest point in Paris; the steps below give one of the great free panoramas, and the dome climb rewards with a 360° sweep.

items.name: Panthéon
items.description: A neoclassical temple where France buries its greats — Voltaire, Curie, Hugo — with Foucault's pendulum swinging under the dome and a colonnade viewpoint above.

items.name: Les Invalides & Napoleon's Tomb
items.description: Under the gilded dome lies Napoleon in six nested coffins; the complex also holds the Army Museum, strong on the family history-of-France angle.

items.name: Palais Garnier (Opéra)
credentials: inspiration for Phantom of the Opera
items.description: The most opulent theatre in Europe — grand staircase, gilded foyer, and a Chagall-painted ceiling; tour it by day or take an advisor-booked box for a ballet.

items.name: The Louvre
items.description: The world's largest art museum; ask us to arrange an early-access or after-hours private hour so you meet the Mona Lisa and Venus de Milo without the crush.

items.name: Musée d'Orsay
credentials: Finest Impressionist collection in the world
items.description: A grand Beaux-Arts railway station turned temple of Impressionism — Monet, Renoir, Van Gogh, Degas — best from the giant golden clock window on the top floor.

items.name: Musée de l'Orangerie
items.description: Two oval rooms hold Monet's monumental Water Lilies, wrapping you in eight curved panels designed by the painter himself — a meditative, unhurried half-hour.

items.name: Musée Rodin
items.description: The sculptor's mansion and rose garden, where The Thinker and The Kiss sit among clipped hedges — one of the loveliest, calmest museums in the city, ideal with children.

items.name: Musée Picasso
items.description: A restored 17th-century mansion in the Marais holding the world's greatest Picasso collection, drawn from the artist's own estate.

items.name: Centre Pompidou
items.description: The inside-out building of coloured pipes houses Europe's biggest modern-art museum; note it is closing for a multi-year renovation, so confirm access with us before you plan.

items.name: Bourse de Commerce — Pinault Collection
items.description: François Pinault's contemporary art inside a domed former grain exchange reimagined by Tadao Ando — a concrete cylinder within a historic rotunda; the 2026 show 'Clair-obscur' runs into late August.

items.name: Musée Marmottan Monet
items.description: The world's largest Monet holding, including 'Impression, Sunrise' — the painting that named the movement — in an intimate townhouse well off the tourist track.

items.name: Musée du Quai Branly — Jacques Chirac
items.description: Jean Nouvel's museum of the arts of Africa, Asia, Oceania and the Americas, wrapped in a living green wall — a thoughtful, less-obvious stop near the Eiffel Tower.

items.name: Petit Palais
items.description: The city's fine-arts museum in a jewel of a 1900 building — free entry, a gilded interior, and a serene garden café most visitors walk right past.

items.name: Grand Palais
items.description: Reopened in 2024 after a sweeping restoration, its vast glass-and-iron nave is Paris's grandest exhibition hall — check what blockbuster show is on.

items.name: Musée Nissim de Camondo
credentials: House museum of the Camondo family
items.description: A perfectly preserved aristocratic mansion of 18th-century French decorative arts, with a moving family history — a quiet gem beside Parc Monceau.

items.name: Musée Jacquemart-André
items.description: A collector couple's opulent townhouse hung with Italian and French masters; take tea in the frescoed dining room under a Tiepolo ceiling.

items.name: Le Marais
items.description: The best-preserved old quarter — Renaissance mansions, the arcaded Place des Vosges, designer boutiques and falafel lanes; wander with no plan, it rewards it.

items.name: Saint-Germain-des-Prés
items.description: Literary Left Bank of Café de Flore and Les Deux Magots, antique galleries and the city's oldest church — the neighbourhood for a slow morning and good browsing.

items.name: Montmartre
items.description: The village on the hill — cobbled lanes, the last working vineyard in Paris, artists in Place du Tertre, and hidden squares away from the crowds if you climb early.

items.name: Île Saint-Louis
items.description: A serene 17th-century island in the Seine, one main street of mansions and small shops — stroll the quays with a Berthillon ice cream, a Paris rite.

items.name: Canal Saint-Martin
items.description: Iron footbridges, plane trees and locks lined with young Paris; walk the canal to Bassin de la Villette, or take a slow boat cruise through the underground vaults.

items.name: Latin Quarter & Rue Mouffetard
items.description: Student Paris around the Sorbonne, plus the sloping market street of Rue Mouffetard — one of the oldest in the city, lined with cheese, wine and produce stalls.

items.name: Jardin du Luxembourg
items.description: The most beloved park in Paris — sail a toy boat on the fountain, watch a puppet show, and sit in the green chairs among statues and orchards; children adore it.

items.name: Jardin des Tuileries
items.description: The grand formal garden linking the Louvre to Place de la Concorde; ponds, statues and, in summer, a fairground with a big wheel over the treetops.

items.name: Palais-Royal Gardens
items.description: A hidden arcaded courtyard behind the Louvre — Buren's striped columns, lime-tree walks and old-world boutiques; one of the quietest lovely corners in the centre.

items.name: Parc des Buttes-Chaumont
items.description: The most dramatic park in Paris — cliffs, a lake, a temple on a crag and a suspension bridge; a local, family-filled escape far from the tourist centre.

items.name: Bois de Boulogne & Fondation Louis Vuitton
items.description: Paris's great western woodland for boating and gardens, now anchored by Frank Gehry's glass-sail Fondation Louis Vuitton — a landmark of art and architecture in itself.

items.name: Père Lachaise Cemetery
items.description: A hilly garden-necropolis of cobbled avenues and grand tombs — Chopin, Wilde, Piaf, Jim Morrison; strangely peaceful and beautiful, especially in autumn.

items.name: Galeries Lafayette Rooftop
items.description: Under the great stained-glass dome of the flagship store, then up to the free rooftop terrace for one of the best open-air views of the Opéra and Eiffel Tower.

items.name: Montparnasse Tower Observation Deck
credentials: Tallest observation deck in central Paris
items.description: The one skyline view that includes the Eiffel Tower — the 56th-floor deck and open rooftop give the finest sunset panorama in the city, minus the queues of the tower itself.

items.name: The Covered Passages
items.description: Glass-roofed 19th-century arcades — Galerie Vivienne, Passage des Panoramas, Passage Jouffroy — full of mosaic floors, old bookshops and tearooms; a rainy-day treasure hunt.

items.name: Marché d'Aligre
items.description: One of the liveliest, most authentic markets — a covered hall of fine cheese and produce plus an open-air flea market; go with us for a chef-led tasting stroll.

items.name: Rue Cler Market Street
items.description: A pretty pedestrian market street of cheesemongers, bakeries and florists near the Eiffel Tower — the classic spot to assemble a picnic for the Champ de Mars.

items.name: Marché aux Puces de Saint-Ouen
credentials: World's largest antiques and flea market
items.description: The world's largest antiques market — a sprawling maze of dealer stands in vintage furniture, art and curiosities; an advisor guide makes the labyrinth worthwhile.

items.name: Bouquinistes of the Seine
items.description: The green riverside book boxes are a UNESCO-listed Paris institution — browse antique prints, posters and old books along the quays between the bridges.

items.name: Seine Dinner Cruise
items.description: Glide past the floodlit monuments over a fine dinner; we book the private or premium boats — and can arrange a fully vegetarian or Jain-aware menu on board.

items.name: Avenue Montaigne
items.description: The couture spine of Paris — Dior, Chanel, Louis Vuitton, Valentino — flagship after flagship; we can arrange private in-store appointments and after-hours access.

items.name: Rue Saint-Honoré & Place Vendôme
items.description: From Colette concept-store cool to the high-jewellery houses of Place Vendôme — Cartier, Van Cleef, Boucheron — set around the Ritz; the address for jewels and watches.

items.name: Le Bon Marché
items.description: The world's first department store and still the most refined — with La Grande Épicerie next door for one of the great food halls in Paris.

items.name: Atelier des Lumières
items.description: A former foundry turned immersive digital art hall where masterpieces sweep across the walls and floor to music — a hit with children and the whole family.

items.name: Promenade Plantée (Coulée Verte)
items.description: The elevated garden walkway on a disused railway viaduct — the inspiration for New York's High Line — running above the arch-shops of the Viaduc des Arts.

items.name: Philharmonie de Paris
items.description: Jean Nouvel's silver concert hall with world-class acoustics; we secure seats for an evening of the Orchestre de Paris or a visiting name.

items.name: A Jazz Cave in Saint-Germain
items.description: Descend into a vaulted stone cellar like Caveau de la Huchette or Le Duc des Lombards for late live jazz — an intimate, only-in-Paris night out.

items.name: Perfume or Patisserie Atelier
items.description: Compose your own scent with a Grasse-trained perfumer, or spend a morning making macarons and éclairs with a pastry chef — a hands-on experience we tailor to the family.

items.name: Palace of Versailles
items.description: The supreme royal palace — Hall of Mirrors, the State Apartments, and vast formal gardens with the musical fountain shows; ask us for a private guide and skip-the-line timing.

items.name: Giverny — Monet's Garden
items.description: The painter's own water-lily pond, Japanese bridge and flower gardens, exactly as in the canvases — an unforgettable day trip in spring and summer bloom.

items.name: Château de Chantilly
items.description: A fairytale château in a moat, holding the finest old-master collection outside the Louvre, plus the Great Stables and a Le Nôtre park — quieter than Versailles.

items.name: Château de Fontainebleau
items.description: A royal residence for eight centuries, from Francis I to Napoleon — sumptuous, uncrowded, and set in a vast forest ideal for a family walk or ride.

items.name: Champagne Day Trip — Reims & Épernay
items.description: Cellar tours in the great houses along the Avenue de Champagne, chalk caves and tastings, plus Reims' Gothic coronation cathedral — a first-class day out we arrange end to end.

items.name: Kei
items.description: A Japanese hand on French cooking, exact to the millimetre — one of the city's nine three-stars.

items.name: Plénitude – Cheval Blanc Paris
items.area: 1st arr. / La Samaritaine, by the Seine
items.description: Sauces treated as the whole point, in a room that looks out over the river.

items.name: Arpège
items.description: The garden on the plate — Passard's near-vegan turn is the finest veg-friendly table at this height.

items.name: Le Cinq
items.description: Classical French haute in a palace dining room — the grand occasion, done properly.

items.name: Épicure – Le Bristol
items.description: French haute cuisine facing Le Bristol's garden — serene, precise, timeless.

items.name: Pierre Gagnaire
items.area: 8th arr. / Rue Balzac, near the Champs-Élysées
items.description: The avant-garde of modern French cooking, three stars held since 1996.

items.name: Le Gabriel – La Réserve Paris
items.description: Intimate three-star cooking inside one of the city's most private houses.

items.name: Alléno Paris au Pavillon Ledoyen
items.description: A pavilion in the Champs-Élysées gardens, and Alléno's modern French at full stretch.

items.name: Le Pré Catelan
items.description: A belle-époque pavilion set deep in the park — one of the loveliest tables in Paris.

items.name: Restaurant Guy Savoy – Monnaie de Paris
items.area: 6th arr. / on the Seine, the former Mint
items.description: The most-decorated name in the city by La Liste, in a riverside palace.

items.name: Table by Bruno Verjus
items.description: The international ticket of the moment — produce-led cooking from the counter.

items.name: L'Ambroisie
items.description: Old-guard grandeur on the most beautiful square in Paris.

items.name: Le Clarence
items.description: A private mansion, a Bordeaux cellar to match, and cooking of real depth.

items.name: La Scène
items.description: Stéphanie Le Quellec's precise modern French — one of the city's top kitchens.

items.name: David Toutain
items.description: Vegetable-forward modern French, curious and quietly brilliant.

items.name: Le Taillevent
items.description: A grande-maison institution, classical to its bones.

items.name: Le Grand Restaurant – Jean-François Piège
items.description: A jewel-box room and Piège's exacting modern French.

items.name: L'Orangerie – Four Seasons George V
items.description: The George V's lighter, luminous second table — no less serious for it.

items.name: L'Abysse au Pavillon Ledoyen
items.description: A sushi counter of rare finesse, within Alléno's pavilion.

items.name: L'Oiseau Blanc – The Peninsula Paris
items.description: French cooking on the rooftop, with the Eiffel Tower for company.

items.name: Le Jules Verne
items.description: Dinner inside the Eiffel Tower itself — the view every first visit wants.

items.name: Maison Rostang
items.description: Old-school luxury and classical French in Art Nouveau rooms.

items.name: Sushi Yoshinaga
items.description: An omakase counter working with fish of exceptional quality.

items.name: Alliance
items.area: 5th arr. / Left Bank, near the Seine
items.description: Restrained, precise modern French with none of the theatre.

items.name: Septime
items.description: The most coveted mid-price reservation in Paris — seasonal, confident, warm.

items.name: Frenchie
items.description: Greg Marchand's intimate, buzzing bistronomy — small room, big following.

items.name: Benoit
items.description: The only Michelin-starred bistro in Paris — Belle Époque, and run by Ducasse.

items.name: Allard
items.description: Escargots, sole meunière and a 1900s room — the Paris bistro, preserved.

items.name: Sharma Ji
items.description: The one genuinely Michelin-listed Indian in Paris — refined, and never a cliché.

items.name: Le Bon Georges
items.description: Produce and wine of unusual seriousness, in a warm neighbourhood room.

items.name: Desi Road
items.area: 6th arr. / Rue Dauphine, near Pont Neuf
items.description: A glamorous Indian bistro on the Left Bank with real vegetarian breadth.

items.name: Le Comptoir du Relais
items.description: The cult bistronomy address — a small counter that shaped a whole movement.

items.name: Chez L'Ami Jean
items.description: A lively Basque institution — generous cooking and a legendary riz au lait.

items.name: Le Baratin
items.description: The birthplace of bistronomy, still personal, still priced with restraint.

items.name: Pierre Sang in Oberkampf
items.description: Surprise tasting menus at an open kitchen — French technique, Korean soul.

items.name: Bistrot Paul Bert
items.description: The bistro of the imagination — steak-frites, soufflé, a wall of wine.

items.name: Clamato
items.description: Septime's seafood sibling — small plates, natural wine, no reservations.

items.name: Double Dragon
items.description: The Levha sisters' playful pan-Asian — bright, fun, generous.

items.name: Le Radis Beurre
items.description: Warm bistronomy and a blackboard menu, at a price that flatters the cooking.

items.name: Le Grand Bain
items.description: Creative small plates and natural wine in an easy, buzzy room.

items.name: Les Canailles
items.description: Simple French cooking done exactly right — the food a French grandmother would make.

items.name: Le Pantruche
items.description: A 1940s bistro mood and a short, seasonal menu that rarely misses.

items.name: Au Bon Accueil
items.description: Seasonal bistro cooking and a terrace that looks straight at the tower.

items.name: Mensae
items.description: French comfort cooking with real value — a neighbourhood room worth the trip.

items.name: Kokoro
items.description: A Franco-Japanese couple's regional French, touched lightly by Japan.

items.name: Chez Michel
items.description: A 1939 institution of Breton-leaning bistronomy, in a Japanese chef's careful hands.

items.name: Lao Siam
items.description: A flavour tour of Laos and Thailand, credentialed and unpretentious.

items.name: Impérial Choisy
items.description: Cantonese cooking done cleanly and well, in the heart of Paris's Chinatown.

items.name: Mandoobar
items.description: A tiny counter given over to Korean dumplings, made with real care.

items.name: Bar Hemingway — The Ritz Paris
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — 50 Best Discovery
items.description: Twenty-five seats, a legend at the shaker, and the most storied cocktail room in Paris.

items.name: Bar Nouveau
items.description: The highest-ranked bar in Paris right now — Art Nouveau brought to life, drink by drink.

items.name: The Cambridge Public House
items.description: A British pub reimagined by serious bartenders — warm, unpretentious, world-class.

items.name: Danico
items.description: Velvet and gold in a covered arcade — precise cocktails behind Daniele Dalla Pola's counter.

items.name: Little Red Door
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — No. 6 (2023); 51–100 list (No. 59, 2024)
items.description: For a decade one of the world's most decorated bars — conceptual menus, faultless execution.

items.name: Candelaria
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — repeat listee (peak No. 9, 2013); Top 500 Bars 2025
items.description: The bar that began the Paris speakeasy era — a taqueria out front, a hidden room behind.

items.name: Le Syndicat
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — recent listee (No. 68, 2023)
items.description: French spirits only — Cognac, Calvados, Armagnac — behind a deliberately shabby door.

items.name: Cravan
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — 50 Best Discovery; Difford's Guide top-50 bar
items.description: Franck Audoux's study of pre-1930s French cocktails, in a listed Art Nouveau corner house.

items.name: Combat
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — 50 Best Discovery
items.description: A female-led room, light and green, from alumni of the Experimental Cocktail Club.

items.name: Le Tout-Paris — Cheval Blanc Paris
items.area: 1st arr. / La Samaritaine, by the Seine
credentials: Inside Cheval Blanc Paris (French Palace distinction)
items.description: The seventh-floor terrace of an LVMH palace, from Notre-Dame to the Eiffel Tower.

items.name: Les Ombres
items.description: A glass rooftop under Jean Nouvel's roof, with the Eiffel Tower almost close enough to touch.

items.title: Private evening at the Musée d'Orsay
items.description: An after-hours walk-through of the Impressionist floors with a curator, the galleries emptied of the day's crowds.

items.title: Dinner at a three-star table booked months ahead
items.description: Le Cinq, Guy Savoy or Plénitude — the kind of meal you plan a trip around, not squeeze between sights.

items.title: Dawn at Versailles before the gates open
items.description: The Hall of Mirrors and the gardens to yourself on a private early access, before the coaches arrive.

items.title: A tasting in a grande maison cellar in Champagne
items.description: A car out to Reims or Épernay for a private cellar visit at a house that doesn't take walk-ins.

plan.heading: 4 days in Paris, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive at Le Bristol, then the Musée de l'Orangerie for Monet's Water Lilies in the round.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Tuileries and Place Vendôme on foot, a stop at the historic jewellers.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Le Cinq at the Four Seasons George V, three stars and impeccable service.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Louvre from opening, guided, keeping to the Italian galleries and the Egyptian wing.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Sainte-Chapelle for the glass, then a slow walk across Île Saint-Louis for Berthillon.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Guy Savoy on the Quai de Conti, overlooking the Seine.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Musée d'Orsay early for the Impressionists under the great clock.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Saint-Germain-des-Prés and the galleries of the Rue de Seine, coffee at Café de Flore.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Arpège, Alain Passard's vegetable garden on the plate.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A car to Versailles for a private morning in the State Apartments and the Hall of Mirrors.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The gardens and the Grand Trianon at a walk, returning by mid-afternoon.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A final dinner at L'Ambroisie on Place des Vosges, classical and restrained.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Saint-Germain-des-Prés (6th)
items.description: Left Bank at its most literary and moneyed — for those who want galleries, old cafés and quiet luxury within walking distance.

items.name: Le Marais (3rd/4th)
items.description: Medieval lanes, the best small shops and a young energy — for repeat visitors who'd rather live in the city than tour it.

items.name: Rue Saint-Honoré / 1st
items.description: Palace hotels, the Louvre and the Tuileries at the doorstep — for a first visit where the icons should be close.

events.name: Roland-Garros (French Open)
events.note: The clay-court Grand Slam; the toughest ticket in Paris and worth timing a spring trip around.

location.address: Stade Roland-Garros, 2 Av. Gordon Bennett, 75016 Paris

events.name: Fête de la Musique
events.note: The whole city becomes a free stage on the solstice — every square and street corner has live music until late.

events.name: Nuit Blanche
events.note: An all-night contemporary-art takeover of the city, museums and monuments open through the small hours.

events.name: Fête des Vendanges de Montmartre
events.note: The Montmartre vineyard's harvest festival — parades, tastings and an old-Paris village mood above the city.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Charles de Gaulle; a chauffeured car handles the 45-minute run into the centre, or a helicopter transfer to a heliport shortens it when time matters.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver for the city and day trips, though the Right Bank between the Louvre and the Champs-Elysees is a pleasure on foot.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Reliable throughout; an Orange or SFR eSIM is simplest, with fast wifi in hotels and most cafes.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Euro; cards are taken everywhere and cash is seldom necessary; service is included, so only a few euros are left for exceptional service.

onGround.note: Base yourself in the 1st, 7th or 8th for the finest addresses; the best tables and couture appointments are booked well in advance, and a little effort with 'bonjour' before any request is always noticed.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Late May-June and September offer warm, dry days and open terraces without August's heat. Avoid a shuttered, humid August when Parisians leave, and the wet chill of December-February.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Nonstop from Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru in about 9.5-10 hours. Air France (La Premiere and its refreshed business) and Air India serve it directly; Vistara-era product now under Air India. Air France's La Premiere ground service at CDG, with private car to the aircraft, is the finest connection touch on this route.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations beyond routine; safe, with normal vigilance for pickpocketing around tourist landmarks and the Metro. Tap water is safe to drink.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian dining is easy at the high end; strict Jain needs a quiet word ahead. Excellent Indian at Michelin-recognised places, and the Little Jaffna / La Chapelle quarter has authentic South Indian; ask the advisor to pre-brief kitchens on onion-garlic.

seo.title: Paro & Thimphu — TripAgent
seo.description: Paro & Thimphu, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Paro & Thimphu
hero.tagline: Himalayan valleys of dzongs, prayer flags and cliffside monasteries.

ourTake.lede: Don't rush Bhutan — the tariff means every day costs, so linger rather than cramming dzongs. Paro and Thimphu are the gentle entry; save your legs and lungs for the climb to Tiger's Nest and do it early, ideally acclimatised after a day or two. Time a trip to a tshechu if you can, but even outside festival season the valley walks and farmhouse dinners are the real Bhutan.
ourTake.comeIf: You want the Tiger's Nest, empty valleys and Aman-grade calm.
ourTake.skipIf: You want nightlife, shopping or a beach.

whenToGo.blurb: Spring and autumn are clear and mild; late September to November offers the crispest Himalayan views. A daily sustainable-tourism fee applies year-round.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Mar, Apr, May, Jun, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Paro & Thimphu. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Amankora
credentials: MICHELIN Key 2025 — Two Keys (Bhutan's top tier)
Aman — the group's flagship Bhutan collection
items.description: Aman's circuit of five intimate lodges across Bhutan's valleys — you journey lodge to lodge like a pilgrimage, and it remains the country's defining luxury experience.

items.name: Six Senses Bhutan
credentials: Prix Versailles World Award — Best Hotel Design
items.description: Five architecturally distinct lodges — the Thimphu hilltop, Paro's 'stone ruins', Punakha's flying farmhouse — bound into one wellness-led circuit.

items.name: Gangtey Lodge
items.description: Twelve farmhouse suites above the Gangtey monastery and the black-necked-crane valley — Bhutan's most decorated single lodge, and its most romantic.

items.name: COMO Uma Paro
credentials: Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice Awards 2018 — among the world's best hotels
items.description: COMO's serene hillside house over the Paro valley — ten minutes from the airport, and home to Bukhari, the country's best-known table.

items.name: Pemako Punakha
credentials: Condé Nast Traveler Hot List 2024 — best new hotels in the world
items.description: Bill Bensley's theatrical tented palace on the Mo Chhu — twenty-one pool villas, five dining venues, pure Punakha extravagance.

items.name: andBeyond Punakha River Lodge
credentials: DestinAsian Luxe List 2024 — best new hotels & resorts in Asia
items.description: andBeyond's first owned lodge in Asia — six canvas-and-timber tented suites on the banks of the Mo Chhu, light-footprint safari luxury brought to the Himalaya.

items.name: Zhiwa Ling Heritage
credentials: Genuine standing — Bhutan's landmark locally-owned heritage hotel, one of the few five-stars in Bhutanese hands
items.description: An owner-built Bhutanese heritage house — hand-carved timber, painted murals, and a shrine of 450-year-old restored monastery wood, with Tiger's Nest in view.

items.name: COMO Uma Punakha
credentials: Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice Awards 2018 — voted the best hotel in Asia
items.description: COMO's small, calm eleven-room lodge above the Punakha valley — intimate, unhurried, with the river valley laid out below.

items.name: Paro Taktsang (Tiger's Nest)
credentials: Bhutan's most iconic pilgrimage and hike
items.description: Bhutan's defining image: a 17th-century monastery clinging to a sheer cliff 900 metres above the Paro valley, reached by a 4-to-5-hour round-trip climb through pine and prayer flags. Guru Rinpoche is said to have flown here on the back of a tigress; the ascent is the emotional centre of any Bhutan trip and doable at a gentle multi-generational pace with horses to the halfway teahouse.

items.name: Rinpung Dzong (Paro Dzong)
credentials: On Bhutan's UNESCO Tentative List (Bhutanese dzongs)
items.description: The 'Fortress on a Heap of Jewels' rises in whitewashed tiers above the Paro river, a working seat of monks and district administration and the stage for the springtime Paro Tshechu. The covered cantilever bridge below is one of the most photographed sights in the kingdom.

items.name: Ta Dzong (National Museum of Bhutan)
items.description: A round former watchtower above Paro Dzong, now holding over 3,000 works spanning 1,500 years of Bhutanese art, thangkas, bronzes and ritual objects. It gives multi-gen travellers the cultural grounding that makes the rest of the trip legible.

items.name: Kyichu Lhakhang
items.description: One of the oldest and most sacred temples in Bhutan, said to be among 108 built by a Tibetan king in the 7th century to pin down a demoness across the Himalayas. Small, deeply atmospheric and still living, with two ancient orange trees that fruit year-round in the courtyard.

items.name: Drukgyel Dzong
credentials: On Bhutan's UNESCO Tentative List (Bhutanese dzongs)
items.description: The romantic ruin at the head of the Paro valley, built in 1649 to mark victory over Tibetan invaders and now being carefully reconstructed. On a clear morning the sacred peak of Jomolhari fills the horizon behind it.

items.name: Paro town & weekend market
items.description: A single handsome main street of traditional painted shopfronts, easy to stroll for textiles, thangkas and hand-woven kira. The riverside market brings in valley farmers with red rice, dried chillies, cheese and wild honey.

items.name: Chele La Pass
items.description: Bhutan's highest motorable pass at 3,988 metres, an hour's spectacular drive from Paro through spruce and larch to a ridge draped in thousands of prayer flags. On a clear day the sacred Jomolhari and Jichu Drake stand out to the northwest; short walks lead to higher viewpoints.

items.name: Kila Nunnery
items.description: One of Bhutan's oldest nunneries, a cluster of retreat houses tucked into the cliffs just below Chele La and reached on a serene forest walk. The 20-odd nuns keeping it feel a world away from the tourist circuit.

items.name: Traditional farmhouse visit & hot-stone bath
items.description: Tea, ara and a home-cooked meal inside a rammed-earth Bhutanese farmhouse, followed by the classic dotsho: soaking in river water heated by fire-roasted stones and infused with artemisia. A quiet, deeply local evening that the Aman and COMO lodges also stage beautifully.

items.name: Archery (datse) demonstration
items.description: Watch or try Bhutan's national sport, where teams loose arrows at a target a improbable 145 metres away and celebrate each hit with song and dance. Many guides can arrange a friendly local match near Paro.

items.name: Dumtse Lhakhang
items.description: A rare chorten-shaped temple near Paro, built in 1421 by the iron-bridge saint Thangtong Gyalpo and, by legend, once chained down so it would not fly to heaven. Inside are some of the finest and most complete Buddhist wall paintings in the country.

items.name: Zuri Dzong hike
items.description: A gentle 1.5-hour walk to Bhutan's oldest dzong, past a cave where Guru Rinpoche is said to have meditated, ending on a ridge with a full bird's-eye sweep of the Paro valley. The rewarding alternative for those who want a view without the Tiger's Nest climb.

items.name: Jomolhari base-camp trek (start point)
credentials: One of Bhutan's classic high-Himalayan treks
items.description: The classic Himalayan trek to the foot of Bhutan's most sacred 7,326-metre peak begins in the upper Paro valley, threading yak pastures and remote hamlets. For the fit traveller it is one of the great multi-day walks of the eastern Himalaya.

items.name: Buddha Dordenma
credentials: Among the largest Buddha statues in the world
items.description: A 51-metre gilded-bronze Shakyamuni Buddha seated above the capital, housing more than 100,000 smaller Buddhas within. The terrace commands the whole Thimphu valley and is especially moving at first light.

items.name: Tashichho Dzong
credentials: Seat of Bhutan's government and central monastic body
items.description: The gleaming white fortress-monastery on the Thimphu river that houses the throne room, government ministries and the central monk body. Its scale and craftsmanship set the standard for Bhutanese architecture, and it glows under floodlight at night.

items.name: National Memorial Chorten
items.description: The most-visited religious landmark in central Thimphu, built in 1974 in memory of the third king. From dawn, elderly locals circle it clockwise turning prayer wheels; it is the most human, living portrait of Bhutanese faith you can witness.

items.name: Motithang Takin Preserve
credentials: Home to Bhutan's national animal, the takin
items.description: A forested reserve on the edge of the capital devoted to the takin, Bhutan's improbable national animal, a creature that looks assembled from a goat and a cow. A short, easy, kid-friendly stop with real curiosity value.

items.name: Folk Heritage Museum
items.description: A restored three-storey rammed-earth farmhouse that recreates rural Bhutanese life of a century ago, room by room. The most tangible way to understand how most Bhutanese still live outside the towns.

items.name: Royal Textile Academy & National Textile Museum
items.description: Bhutan's finest showcase of weaving, where the extraordinarily intricate kira and gho fabrics that clothe the nation are displayed and demonstrated on the loom. Essential for anyone who values craft, and a discreet place to acquire heirloom-grade textiles.

items.name: Changangkha Lhakhang
credentials: Oldest temple in the Thimphu valley
items.description: A 12th-century fortress-temple on a ridge above Thimphu, the oldest in the valley, where local families bring newborns to be named and blessed. The ramparts give a lovely panorama over the capital.

items.name: Thimphu weekend market
items.description: A riverside pavilion that fills Thursday to Sunday with farmers from across the country: red rice, fiery dried chillies, discs of fresh datshi cheese, ferns, pickles and southern wild honey, plus a handicraft section across the footbridge. The best single window onto everyday Bhutan.

items.name: The giant prayer wheel at Memorial Chorten & Zilukha
items.description: Enormous copper-and-gold mani wheels, each packed with millions of printed mantras, that pilgrims turn to release blessings with every rotation. Spinning one in the flow of chanting elders is a small, grounding ritual you will remember.

items.name: Simply Bhutan living museum
items.description: A hands-on 'living museum' where you try the national dress, archery, butter-tea and folk song in a recreated village setting. Touristic but genuinely fun and a gentle, engaging option for children and grandparents.

items.name: Sangaygang viewpoint
items.description: A short drive to a hillside at 2,685 metres below the telecom tower, giving the classic full-valley view of Thimphu framed in prayer flags. A ten-minute stop that reorients the whole capital for you.

items.name: Cheri Monastery hike
credentials: Site of Bhutan's first monastic community (1620)
items.description: A steep, quiet hour's climb across a covered bridge to the 1620 monastery where Bhutan's unifier established the first monastic body. Deeply peaceful, often shared only with monks and grazing goral on the slopes.

items.name: Tango Monastery hike
items.description: A 90-minute forest walk to a serene 13th-century Buddhist college north of Thimphu, still a place of retreat and study. Pairs naturally with Cheri for a full, unhurried day in the upper valley away from the crowds.

items.name: Dochula Pass & the 108 chortens
items.description: The 3,100-metre pass on the road east from Thimphu, crowned by 108 Druk Wangyal chortens built by the Queen Mother and, on a clear morning, a jaw-dropping line-up of the eastern Himalayan snow peaks. The mountainside cafe here is the classic tea stop en route to Punakha.

items.name: Punakha Dzong
credentials: On Bhutan's UNESCO Tentative List (Bhutanese dzongs)
Often called Bhutan's most beautiful dzong
items.description: Widely held to be the most beautiful dzong in Bhutan, standing at the confluence of the 'father' and 'mother' rivers and blazing purple with jacaranda in spring. Built in 1638, it was the old capital and remains the winter home of the central monk body; the coronation and royal wedding were held here.

items.name: Chimi Lhakhang (the fertility temple)
items.description: A small 1499 hilltop temple reached on a gentle walk through rice terraces and a village painted with phalluses, dedicated to the irreverent 'Divine Madman' saint Drukpa Kunley. Couples come from across Bhutan and abroad for a fertility blessing; the walk itself is one of the loveliest in the west.

items.name: Punakha suspension bridge
items.description: At around 160 metres, one of the longest suspension bridges in Bhutan, swaying gently over the Po Chhu river and hung with prayer flags. A short, exhilarating crossing with dzong and river views, and a fine spot for photographs.

items.name: Khamsum Yulley Namgyal Chorten walk
items.description: A beautiful 45-minute walk across the valley floor and up through pine forest to an elaborately painted royal chorten completed in 1999. The rooftop gives the finest panorama over the terraced Punakha valley and its winding rivers.

items.name: Punakha valley & river
items.description: At around 1,200 metres, warm, low and green, this is where Bhutan slows down: rice paddies, riverside luxury camps and gentle raft floats on the Mo Chhu past the great dzong. The most relaxed leg of a western Bhutan trip, ideal for multi-gen travellers.

items.name: Mo Chhu river rafting
items.description: A gentle scenic float down the Mo Chhu, passing the Punakha Dzong from the water with kingfishers and the occasional heron along the banks. Soft-adventure that suits families and non-paddlers alike.

items.name: A tshechu festival
items.description: The great annual masked-dance festivals, held in dzong courtyards, where monks in brocade and carved masks enact the triumph of dharma over chaos before the whole valley in its finest dress. The Paro Tshechu (spring) and Thimphu Tshechu (autumn, the country's largest) are the most spectacular; dates follow the lunar calendar, so plan the trip around them.

items.name: A monk's blessing
items.description: A private audience or blessing from a lama in a working temple, the thread of blessed cord tied at the neck and butter lamps lit for one's family. In a country where faith is woven into daily life, it is often the moment travellers remember most.

items.name: Guided meditation & mindfulness
items.description: Sunrise meditation in a monastery or lodge shrine room, led by a monk or the resident wellness team at Amankora, Six Senses or COMO. In the last Himalayan Buddhist kingdom this is the natural centrepiece of a slow, restorative trip.

items.name: Ema datshi & Bhutanese cuisine
credentials: Ema datshi is Bhutan's national dish
items.description: The national dish is ema datshi, whole chillies stewed in soft cheese, eaten with nutty red rice, and the wider table is unusually kind to vegetarians, with cheese, ferns, buckwheat and mushrooms everywhere. A cooking demonstration or farmhouse lunch turns a meal into an experience.

items.name: Haa Valley
items.description: One of Bhutan's least-visited valleys, reached over Chele La, where the pace slows, homestays and farmhouses replace hotels and the twin white-and-black temples of Lhakhang Karpo and Lhakhang Nagpo anchor the valley floor. For travellers who have seen the icons and want the road less travelled.

items.name: Blue poppy & rhododendron season
credentials: Blue poppy is Bhutan's national flower
items.description: In late spring the high slopes around Chele La and the passes blaze with rhododendron, and the elusive blue poppy, Bhutan's national flower, appears above the treeline. A quiet draw for keen walkers and photographers timing the trip to May and June.

items.name: Amankora circuit
items.description: Aman's five intimate lodges in Paro, Thimphu, Punakha, Gangtey and Bumthang let you travel valley to valley without leaving the brand, with private guides, farmhouse dinners and hot-stone baths arranged throughout. The benchmark for a seamless ultra-luxury Bhutan journey.

items.name: Six Senses Bhutan lodges
items.description: A parallel five-lodge route across the west, each property designed around a distinct valley theme, with standout spas and dramatic architecture at Thimphu ('flying farmhouse') and Punakha. A strong choice for wellness-led, design-conscious travellers.

items.name: COMO Uma Paro & Punakha
items.description: COMO's two hilltop retreats above Paro and in the Punakha valley pair the group's celebrated wellness and cuisine with a warmer, more relaxed feel than the grander houses. Often the best value at the top of the market and excellent for families.

items.name: Punakha to Gangtey (Phobjikha) extension
credentials: Winter roost of the endangered black-necked crane
items.description: A day's drive east of Punakha opens the glacial Phobjikha valley, the winter home of the rare black-necked cranes that arrive from Tibet each November and the graceful Gangtey Goenpa monastery above the wetlands. The natural next step for those extending beyond the west.

items.name: Bukhari
credentials: COMO Uma Paro — Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice Awards 2018
items.description: Named for the Himalayan wood-burning stove at its heart, this circular pavilion at COMO Uma Paro is Bhutan's best-known table — local produce, elegant technique, the valley all around.

items.name: Amankora dining
items.description: Quiet, seasonal Bhutanese and Western cooking within the Aman lodges — private, unhurried, and part of the journey rather than a separate outing.

items.name: Six Senses lodge dining
credentials: Six Senses Bhutan — MICHELIN Key 2025 (One Key)
items.description: Wellness-led 'Eat With Six Senses' cooking across the lodges — garden produce, Bhutanese flavours, and a sustainability ethos that runs to the plate.

items.name: Babesa Village Restaurant
credentials: World Culinary Awards 2024 — Bhutan's Best Restaurant
items.description: Traditional Bhutanese home cooking in a 500-year-old rammed-earth farmhouse — ema datsi, red rice, the real thing, loved by locals.

items.name: Amankora & lodge bars
credentials: Genuine standing — the bars of Amankora (MICHELIN Key, Two Keys) and the other grand lodges; the considered heart of a Bhutan evening
items.description: In Bhutan the evening happens at the lodge — a fireside single malt, local Bumthang wine or an ara nightcap, in perfect stillness, is the country's idea of a night out.

items.name: Bukhari bar, COMO Uma Paro
credentials: Genuine standing — the bar at COMO Uma Paro (Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice 2018)
items.description: A quiet, elegant drink beside the wood-burning stove that gives Bukhari its name — the most polished bar setting in the Paro valley.

items.name: Mojo Park
credentials: Genuine standing — Thimphu's best-known live-music venue, on Chang Lam
items.description: Thimphu's live-music institution since 2011 — local and visiting bands, an easy crowd of Bhutanese and expats, and the closest the capital comes to a real night out.

items.title: Hike to Tiger's Nest (Taktsang)
items.description: The cliffside monastery clinging above Paro valley — a steep half-day climb that earns its reputation.

items.title: Traditional hot-stone bath
items.description: River stones heated in a fire and dropped into a wooden tub of artemisia-infused water after a day's walking.

items.title: Private audience with a lama
items.description: A blessing and butter-lamp offering at a working monastery, arranged through a good operator.

items.title: Punakha Dzong by the river
items.description: Bhutan's most beautiful dzort at the confluence of two rivers, worth the drive over Dochula Pass.

plan.heading: 5 days in Paro & Thimphu, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The mountain landing into Paro, then a slow settling-in and lunch at your lodge in the valley.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Rinpung Dzong and the old cantilever bridge, then the National Museum in the round watchtower above.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Como Uma Paro or Six Senses, quiet ema datshi and red rice by the fire.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The long walk up to Taktsang, the Tiger's Nest monastery on its cliff, paced with rests and a mid-way tea house.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Descend and rest, then a hot-stone bath to ease the legs.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: An early, restorative dinner at the lodge with an early night.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive to the capital, stopping at Simtokha Dzong, then the great seated Buddha Dordenma above the city.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The weekend market or the National Textile Museum, and the memorial chorten among the prayer wheels.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Six Senses Thimphu overlooking the valley, or a chef's table at Babesa village restaurant.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Up to the Dochula pass and its 108 chortens, the Himalayan range laid out on a clear morning.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Back in Thimphu, the painting school and a papermaking workshop, choosing pieces slowly.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A quiet dinner and an early rest before the return.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Return to Paro for the Kyichu Lhakhang, one of Bhutan's oldest temples, walked in the morning calm.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A farmhouse lunch and a short walk through terraced fields before packing.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A final dinner at the lodge, the valley darkening, before the morning flight.

items.name: Paro Valley
items.description: Airport, Tiger's Nest and rice fields; scenic and calm, the classic first base.

items.name: Thimphu
items.description: The capital — Bhutan's only city, for markets, the dzong and a night of dinner and craft shopping.

items.name: Punakha
items.description: Lower, warmer valley beyond the pass; suits an extra day for the dzong and river walks.

events.name: Paro Tshechu
events.note: Masked dances at Rinpung Dzong, closing with the dawn unfurling of the giant Guru Thongdrel tapestry.

events.name: Thimphu Tshechu
events.note: The capital's grand festival in the courtyard of Tashichho Dzong; dates follow the lunar calendar.

events.name: Punakha Drubchen & Tshechu
events.note: A dramatic re-enactment of a 17th-century battle precedes the tshechu at Punakha Dzong.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Paro (PBH) — one of the world's most demanding approaches, flown only in daylight by Drukair or Bhutan Airlines — where your licensed guide and private vehicle meet you, as all visits are pre-arranged through a local operator.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private vehicle with driver and your assigned guide accompany you throughout by law; the hour's drive between Paro and Thimphu is straightforward and scenic.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: TashiCell or B-Mobile eSIMs give workable 4G in Paro and Thimphu; wifi is reliable in the better lodges, thinner in the valleys and on trekking routes.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Ngultrum (BTN), pegged one-to-one with the Indian rupee, which is accepted directly; cards work at high-end lodges but carry cash, and tipping your guide and driver at the end is customary.

onGround.note: Thimphu sits near 2,300 m and Paro's Tiger's Nest hike climbs higher, so pace the first day for altitude; dress is modest with covered shoulders and knees for dzongs and temples, and Bhutan levies a daily Sustainable Development Fee handled within your arrangement.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: March to May brings spring blooms and clear valleys, and September to November offers crisp air and the best mountain views; both are the kind seasons. Avoid the June to August monsoon (rain, cloud, flight delays) and the deep cold of December to February.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Paro (PBH) is served only by Drukair and Bhutan Airlines, with daily direct flights from Delhi (~2h30m) and Kolkata; from Mumbai/Bengaluru connect via Delhi or Kolkata. Both carry a business cabin. Seats are limited and the mountain approach is spectacular, so book early and request a left-side window for Everest views inbound.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations; routine jabs plus Hep A advisable. Paro sits at ~2,200m and Thimphu ~2,320m, so mild altitude effects are possible on arrival, take the first day gently. Very safe and low-crime. Drink bottled water; a Sustainable Development Fee applies per day.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Straightforward for vegetarians; Bhutanese cuisine is chilli-and-cheese heavy but every hotel offers Indian and vegetarian options, and the Indian community is well served. Jain travellers should notify lodges in advance, as onion/garlic-free cooking needs prior arrangement; luxury lodges (Amankora, Six Senses) accommodate readily.

seo.title: Phuket — TripAgent
seo.description: Phuket, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Phuket
hero.tagline: Andaman beaches, limestone bays and barefoot luxury.

ourTake.lede: Phuket splits sharply between the built-up west-coast beaches and the quieter north and east, and where you stay decides your entire trip, so choose carefully. Skip Patong unless nightlife is the point; the discreet resorts sit around Mai Khao, Cape Panwa and the headlands. Come November to April for the calm sea, and give Phuket Old Town a proper afternoon for its Sino-Portuguese streets and food.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a beach week with world-class resorts, island-hopping and quiet coves within reach.
ourTake.skipIf: You want an untouched, undiscovered shore; Phuket's coast is developed and busy in parts.

whenToGo.blurb: November to March is dry, calm and radiant; the May-October monsoon brings rain and rough seas, though October's Vegetarian Festival is a spectacle worth the weather.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Amanpuri
credentials: MICHELIN Three Keys (2025) — Phuket's only Three-Key hotel
items.description: The house that began Aman — Lanna pavilions above a private coconut headland, still the island's benchmark for calm.

items.name: Trisara
credentials: Condé Nast Traveler Gold List 2024 & 2025 (only Thai resort listed)
items.description: Thirty-nine private-pool villas folded into a protected bay — extreme privacy, and the island's most decorated kitchens.

items.name: Rosewood Phuket
credentials: Travel + Leisure Luxury Awards Asia Pacific 2025 — Top Beach & Island Resort in Thailand
items.description: A 600-metre private beach and 71 pavilions that dissolve into the hillside — Rosewood's Andaman idyll.

items.name: Six Senses Yao Noi
items.area: Koh Yao Noi, Phang Nga Bay
credentials: Condé Nast Traveler Gold List (world's best places to stay)
items.description: Fifty-six clifftop pool villas facing the limestone karsts of Phang Nga Bay — the island beyond the island.

items.name: Iniala Beach House
items.description: Ten designer villas and residences on a wild beach north of the bridge — a private art-house of a hotel.

items.name: COMO Point Yamu
items.description: A Paola Navone-designed headland looking across Phang Nga Bay — cool, contemporary and gloriously away from the strip.

items.name: Anantara Layan Phuket Resort
items.description: A secluded palm-shaded bay of pool villas and hillside residences — Anantara at its most private.

items.name: InterContinental Phuket Resort
items.description: Seven Thai-inspired houses running from jungle to sand, with a private yacht and five pools.

items.name: Keemala
items.description: Thirty-eight clay cottages, tree-pool houses and tented villas woven into a rainforest hillside — pure fantasy, quietly done.

items.name: The Nai Harn Phuket
items.description: A crisp white headland hotel above one of the island's best beaches — polished and unfussy.

items.name: Andara Resort & Villas
items.description: Hillside suites and freestanding villas above Kamala Bay — space, privacy and a private chef if you want one.

items.name: The Slate
items.description: A tin-mining heritage turned into industrial-chic design — characterful, arty and close to the airport.

items.name: The Naka Island, a Luxury Collection Resort & Spa
items.description: A private-island retreat of pool villas a short boat ride from Phuket — barefoot seclusion within easy reach.

items.name: The Pavilions Phuket
items.description: Adults-only pool villas on a hillside above Layan — intimate, private and made for two.

items.name: The Racha
items.description: White-on-white minimalism on a clear-water island — the Andaman at its most postcard-blue.

items.name: Aleenta Phuket–Phang Nga Resort & Spa
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: Thirty beachfront villas and suites, every one facing the sea on a near-empty stretch of sand.

items.name: Banyan Tree Phuket
items.description: The resort that invented the private-pool villa in 1994 — mature gardens, lagoons and a serious spa.

items.name: Angsana Laguna Phuket
items.description: A big, buzzy lagoon resort at the heart of Laguna — one of the island's longest free-form pools.

items.name: SALA Phuket Mai Khao Beach Resort
items.description: Sino-Portuguese pool villas on the island's longest, quietest beach — an easy, private escape.

items.name: Renaissance Phuket Resort & Spa
items.description: A relaxed low-rise beach resort on Mai Khao — pool villas and gardens without the crowds.

items.name: The Big Buddha (Ming Mongkol Buddha) on Nakkerd Hill
items.description: A 45-metre white-marble Buddha crowning the hill between Chalong, Kata and Rawai, with a 360-degree panorama that lets the whole family take in half the island at once. Dress modestly (shawls provided), come at golden hour, and have your driver hold at the quieter lower terrace while grandparents rest.

items.name: Wat Chalong (Wat Chaithararam)
items.description: Phuket's grandest and most revered temple, a serene complex of gilded pavilions culminating in a 60-metre pagoda that houses a fragment of the Buddha's bone. Fifteen minutes from the Big Buddha, it pairs naturally into a calm, multi-generational morning of merit-making before the heat.

items.name: Promthep Cape at sunset
items.description: The island's southernmost headland, where crowds gather each evening as the sun drops into the Andaman behind rocky islets. Skip the car park scrum: charter a sunset catamaran or have your villa's chef pack a chilled hamper for the grassy point just above the lighthouse.

items.name: Old Phuket Town's Sino-Portuguese quarter
items.description: A photogenic grid of restored tin-baron shophouses in sherbet colours, best explored on a slow, cool-of-the-morning walk with a private heritage guide. The pace and history suit older travellers; the cafes and boutiques keep younger ones happy.

items.name: Thalang Road
items.description: The old town's 350-metre historic artery, lined with the best-preserved Sino-Portuguese facades on the island and the first street here to bury its power lines underground. It threads together tea houses, textile shops and gold-leaf shrines in one strollable ribbon.

items.name: Soi Romanee
items.description: A once-notorious lane now reborn as the town's prettiest, its pastel two-storey shophouses spilling with bougainvillea, artisan coffee and ice-cream parlours. It is the single most-photographed street in Phuket and a gentle five-minute stroll off Thalang Road.

items.name: Sunday Walking Street (Lard Yai)
items.description: Every Sunday from 4pm, Thalang Road closes to traffic and fills with hawker carts, live music and Hokkien-Thai street food beneath the lantern-lit shophouses. Ask your guide to steer the family to the vegetarian and fresh-fruit stalls, plentiful here thanks to Phuket's own veg-food tradition.

items.name: Patong Beach
items.description: Phuket's most famous and most energetic beach, a broad two-kilometre curve backed by every convenience. Base here only if you want buzz; otherwise it makes a lively half-day of jet-skis and beach clubs before retreating to a quieter west-coast villa.

items.name: Kata Beach and Kata Noi
items.description: Two gently curving, palm-fringed bays that are calmer and more polished than Patong, with reliable swimming and easy surf lessons for teens in the green season. The stretch is a favourite of families who want beach days without the noise.

items.name: Karon Beach
items.description: A wide, quieter three-kilometre run of squeaky white sand that stays uncrowded even in season, backed by low-key resorts and lagoon parkland. Long enough for a proper morning walk before the sun turns fierce.

items.name: Surin Beach
items.description: Once nicknamed 'Millionaire's Row', a compact golden bay flanked by Phuket's smartest beach resorts and clubs. The most discreet-luxury stretch on the coast, ideal if you want a chic sundowner without the mainstream crowds.

items.name: Kamala Beach
items.description: A relaxed, family-friendly bay just south of Surin with a genuine village feel and calm swimming water. It anchors the low-key luxury enclave of Phuket's northwest, within easy reach of the island's headline beach clubs.

items.name: Nai Harn Beach
items.description: A postcard cove in the island's south, backed by a lagoon and monastery and consistently rated among Phuket's most beautiful. Sheltered and swimmable, it draws a quieter, in-the-know crowd and sits minutes from Promthep Cape.

items.name: Freedom Beach
items.description: A secluded 300-metre ribbon of powder sand reachable only by boat or a steep jungle path, which keeps it blissfully empty. Charter a longtail or speedboat from Patong for a private half-day; it is the island's most accessible 'hidden' beach.

items.name: Karon Viewpoint (Three Beaches Hill)
items.description: The island's classic postcard lookout, framing the three arcs of Kata Noi, Kata and Karon in one turquoise sweep. An easy roadside stop between beaches and the south, best in clear morning light.

items.name: Windmill Viewpoint
items.description: A cliff-edge lookout just south of Karon Viewpoint, above Ya Nui and Nai Harn, with sweeping views over Rawai and the offshore islands. Quieter than its famous neighbour and a fine spot to pause on the coastal drive south.

items.name: Phang Nga Bay by private boat
items.description: A dreamscape of sheer limestone karsts rising from emerald water an hour north of Phuket, best seen away from the day-boat crowds. A private yacht or speedboat charter lets the family set its own pace through the caves and hidden lagoons, with a chef and shade on board.

items.name: James Bond Island (Khao Phing Kan / Koh Tapu)
items.description: The needle-thin islet made famous by 'The Man with the Golden Gun', still one of the bay's signature sights. Time a private charter for early morning or late afternoon to have the viewpoint largely to yourselves before the tour armada arrives.

items.name: Sea-cave canoeing in Phang Nga Bay
items.description: The quiet highlight of any bay trip: a skilled paddler steers you through low sea caves into secret 'hong' lagoons ringed by jungle cliffs, in near silence. Gentle enough for grandparents and children alike, and unforgettable at dusk when the bats emerge.

items.name: Koh Panyee floating village
items.description: A Muslim fishing community of about 1,600 built entirely on stilts at the foot of a towering cliff, complete with a mosque, seafood restaurants and a famous floating football pitch. A vivid, humane counterpoint to the bay's natural drama.

items.name: Phi Phi Islands day trip
items.description: The Andaman's most celebrated islands, ringed by jade water, karst walls and coral gardens roughly 45 minutes by speedboat from Phuket. Charter privately and start at dawn to reach the snorkelling coves and viewpoints before the fleets, then lunch quietly offshore.

items.name: Maya Bay
items.description: The luminous cliff-ringed cove made globally famous by 'The Beach', now carefully rationed to protect its recovering reef. Landings are via the Loh Samah back beach with timed slots and no swimming inside the bay; note it closes each 1 August to 30 September for regeneration.

items.name: Similan Islands (seasonal)
items.description: A national-park archipelago of glass-clear water, granite boulders and world-class reefs, open only 15 October to 15 May each year. A long but spectacular day out from Phuket, best on a fast private catamaran; among Southeast Asia's finest snorkelling and diving.

items.name: Racha Yai (Raya) Island
items.description: A calm, clear-water island south of Phuket prized for easy snorkelling and swimming off soft white sand, reachable in under an hour. Its sheltered bays and single luxury resort make it a serene private-charter day escape.

items.name: Coral Island (Koh Hae)
items.description: A close, family-friendly island just fifteen minutes off Chalong pier, with two gentle beaches and shallow reef ideal for first-time snorkellers and children. Perfect for a half-day charter when you want sea and coral without a long crossing.

items.name: Naka Island (Naka Yai)
items.description: A tranquil island a short hop off Phuket's northeast, home to a serene luxury resort and a quiet Saturday-Sunday morning market. It suits couples and families wanting seclusion and spa time rather than crowds.

items.name: Phuket Elephant Sanctuary
items.description: Phuket's first true ethical sanctuary, where rescued elephants roam free with no riding and, from April 2026, no feeding interactions at all: you observe from a canopy walkway and learn at the on-site hospital. Endorsed by National Geographic and World Animal Protection, it is the responsible choice for multi-generational visits.

items.name: Wat Phra Thong (the half-buried Buddha)
items.description: A quietly atmospheric temple built around a gilded Buddha that, by legend, cannot be fully dug out of the earth, so only its head and shoulders show. An offbeat, uncrowded stop north of the airport for those drawn to Phuket's older spiritual life.

items.name: Jui Tui Shrine and Bang Neow Shrine
items.description: The two great Chinese Taoist shrines at the heart of the old town and the ceremonial core of Phuket's famous Vegetarian Festival each autumn. Richly decorated and incense-filled, they add depth to any old-town walk.

items.name: Thai Hua Museum
items.description: A beautifully restored former Chinese-language school that tells the story of Phuket's tin-mining Peranakan heritage in an elegant Sino-Portuguese mansion. A cool, air-conditioned hour that gives the old town's streets their context.

items.name: Phuket Vegetarian Festival
items.description: A dramatic nine-day Taoist festival each September or October when devotees observe a strict plant-based diet and perform intense street processions. The rigorous vegetarian offerings citywide make this a rare and comfortable time for Jain and vegetarian travellers.

items.name: Muay Thai training or a ringside night
items.description: Thailand's national fighting art, available either as a private morning session at a serious camp or as an electric evening at a stadium like Bangla or Patong Boxing Stadium. A private coach can tailor a fun, safe session for energetic teenagers.

items.name: A traditional Thai spa afternoon
items.description: Phuket's marquee resorts and standalone maisons offer some of Asia's finest spa rituals, from herbal-compress massage to hammam-style scrubs. Arrange a private couples' or family suite for an unhurried afternoon of quiet luxury.

items.name: Simon Cabaret
items.description: Phuket's long-running, lavishly costumed transgender cabaret, a polished hour of feathers, sequins and lip-synced spectacle that has become a Southeast Asian institution. Family-friendly and easy to book into a private box; three nightly show times.

items.name: Bangla Road
items.description: Patong's neon-lit pedestrian strip, the loud, unfiltered epicentre of Phuket nightlife, worth a brief look-in for its sheer spectacle rather than a long stay. Most discerning travellers prefer a single curious walk-through before retiring to a quiet rooftop bar.

items.name: Sunday sundowners at a west-coast beach club
items.description: The Kamala-Surin coast holds Phuket's most stylish beach clubs, where infinity pools meet the Andaman and DJs play as the sun drops. Reserve a daybed or cabana for a relaxed, grown-up afternoon that still works for older children.

items.name: Chillva Market
items.description: A hip, local-favourite night market of repurposed shipping-container stalls, street food and live music, busiest Wednesday to Saturday evenings. A younger, more contemporary scene than the heritage Sunday market, and refreshingly free of tourist mark-ups.

items.name: Private yacht charter around the southern islands
items.description: The definitive way to see Phuket's waters: a crewed motor yacht or catamaran for the day, threading between Coral, Racha and the Phi Phi group with a chef, water toys and shade on board. The itinerary bends to your family, dietary needs included.

items.name: Ao Sane and Ya Nui beaches
items.description: Two tiny, boulder-framed coves near Promthep Cape with the best shore snorkelling on the island and a fraction of the crowds. Bring your own masks for a quiet morning in clear, fish-filled water before the day-trippers arrive.

items.name: Laem Singh Beach
items.description: A jewel-like cove tucked below the coastal road, now reached via a private beach-club path or by boat, with calm water and a genuine hidden-gem feel. Best arranged through a resort concierge for the smoothest access.

items.name: Rang Hill (Khao Rang) viewpoint
items.description: A leafy, breezy hill just above the old town with a sweeping view over the rooftops to Chalong Bay and a couple of relaxed cafes. An easy, uncrowded sunset alternative close to town when you don't want to drive to the coast.

items.name: Ban Bang Rong and the northeast mangroves
items.description: A peaceful Muslim fishing community on the quiet east coast where you can kayak or take a longtail through mangrove channels and eat fresh seafood over the water. A gentle, authentic half-day far from the beach resorts.

items.name: Khao Phra Thaeo rainforest and Bang Pae Waterfall
items.description: Phuket's last virgin rainforest, home to a modest waterfall and a gibbon rehabilitation project you can visit responsibly. A green, cooler counterpoint to the beaches for families who want a short jungle walk.

items.name: Cape Panwa and the far southeast
items.description: A quiet, wooded headland of luxury villas and calm coves with an aquarium at its tip, well away from the west-coast bustle. A serene base or half-day drive when you want the island's gentler, more residential side.

items.name: PRU
items.description: Chef Jimmy Ophorst's 'Plant. Raise. Understand.' — the island's first star, built entirely on its own farm and coast.

items.name: Aulis Phuket by Simon Rogan
items.description: Simon Rogan's fifteen-seat chef's table — his farm-to-table philosophy transplanted to the Andaman coast.

items.name: Jampa
items.description: A zero-waste, live-fire kitchen in the middle of its own organic farm — sustainability as the whole point.

items.name: Jaras
items.description: Chef 'Nui' Srivorakul's photogenic modern southern Thai — the first Thai kitchen to partner with WWF Thailand.

items.name: hom
items.description: A fermentation-led modern Thai room exploring the depth of the island's larder.

items.name: Suay Cherngtalay
items.description: Chef Noi Tammasak's creative modern Thai — one of Phuket's most-loved kitchens for years.

items.name: Samut
items.description: Modern Thai and Andaman seafood in the quiet south — precise, coastal, of-the-island.

items.name: Royd
items.description: A modern southern-Thai kitchen giving Phuket's own recipes a fine-dining voice in the old town.

items.name: Blue Elephant Phuket
items.description: Royal Thai cuisine in a grand Sino-Portuguese mansion — the old town's most theatrical dining room.

items.name: L'Arome by the Sea
items.description: Contemporary French with an Andaman view — polished, romantic and quietly ambitious.

items.name: Bisou Phuket
items.description: A modern French room on the Bang Tao strip — refined cooking amid the beach-club energy.

items.name: Acqua
items.description: A long-standing modern-Italian fixture with a serious cellar above Patong.

items.name: Five Olives
items.description: Contemporary Italian cooking done with care on the Bang Tao coast.

items.name: La Gaetana
items.description: A tiny, personal Italian trattoria that has long outpunched its size in the old town.

items.name: Tambu
items.description: Modern Indian cooking with real ambition — a rare fine-dining Indian voice on the island.

items.name: The Smokaccia Laboratory
items.description: A modern, smoke-and-fire-driven kitchen doing some of Surin's most inventive cooking.

items.name: Wagyu Steakhouse
items.description: A precise, cuts-led steakhouse for the member who wants marbled beef done properly.

items.name: Ta Khai
items.description: A recreated fishing-village kitchen inside Rosewood — southern Thai recipes cooked the old way.

items.name: Talung Thai
items.description: Long-running southern-Thai home cooking with a devoted following.

items.name: Bucha Gallery & Restaurant
items.description: Southern-Thai cooking in a gallery-like room away from the beaches.

items.name: HEH Restaurant
items.description: A modern Thai-and-seafood room bringing a young energy to the old town.

items.name: One Chun
items.description: The old town's most beloved kitchen for Phuket-Hokkien home cooking — moo hong, crab curry, and heritage.

items.name: The Charm
items.description: Refined Phuket and southern-Thai cooking in a handsome old-town setting.

items.name: Chom Chan
items.description: Phuket and southern-Thai flavours cooked with real depth — a Bib favourite in town.

items.name: Raya
items.description: A grand old Sino-Portuguese mansion serving classic Phuket dishes — crab curry and heritage in equal measure.

items.name: Naam Yoi
items.description: Generations-old local and southern-Thai cooking, prized for its balanced, honest flavours.

items.name: Mor Mu Dong
items.description: A stilted seafood shack over the mangroves — southern-Thai fishing-village cooking at its most authentic.

items.name: Salaloy Seafood
items.description: A long-loved beachside seafood house on the southern shore — fresh, simple, unpretentious.

items.name: Go Benz
items.description: The island's cult stop for noodle soup and rice porridge — a decades-old institution.

items.name: Khao Tom Thanon Dibuk
items.description: Late-night rice soup and southern-Thai comfort food on Dibuk Road — a local ritual.

items.name: Niyom Salt Grilled Duck
items.description: Thirty-odd charcoal-roasted ducks a day, tender and salt-crisp — a single-dish master.

items.name: Krua Baan Platong
items.description: Intensely flavoured Phuket home cooking from local ingredients — the essence of the island on a plate.

items.name: Kin Kub Ei
items.description: Southern-Thai family recipes passed down the generations, balanced and quietly excellent.

items.name: Pathongko Mae Pranee
items.description: A morning institution for pathongko and hot soy milk — breakfast the Phuket way.

items.name: A Pong Mae Sunee
items.description: Crisp-edged coconut a-pong griddle cakes from a stall the Michelin inspectors sought out.

items.name: Roti Thaew Nam
items.description: Flaky roti and Thai-Muslim curries on an old-town lane — a cult breakfast and lunch stop.

items.name: Go La Hokkien Fried Noodles
items.description: A single-wok master turning out the island's definitive Hokkien fried noodles.

items.name: Prawn Noodle Ao Ke
items.description: A specialist doing one thing — rich Hokkien prawn noodles — better than anyone on the island.

items.name: Catch Beach Club
credentials: Phuket's original beach club (opened Surin, 2012) — the venue credited with launching the island's beach-club scene, by Twinpalms
items.description: Twinpalms' beachfront original — the club that started Phuket's whole beach-club culture, still the name against which the rest are measured.

items.name: Rock Salt
