credentials: The signature beachfront bar-restaurant of The Nai Harn (MICHELIN One Key hotel), on Nai Harn Beach
items.description: The Nai Harn's beachfront terrace above one of the island's finest bays — an unhurried sundowner in the quiet south.

items.name: The Fool Speakeasy
credentials: Best Bar in Phuket/Samui — Bangkok Bar Show Awards 2025
items.description: A tarot-themed hideaway in an old shophouse — twenty-two Major Arcana cocktails and the most serious mixing on the island.

items.name: Baba Nest
credentials: Named among the world's best beach/rooftop bars by CNN; voted a global top-three beach bar (CNNgo)
items.description: A rooftop deck 60 metres above the sea, ringed by its own infinity moat — a 360-degree sunset the world has decided is among the best anywhere.

items.name: Vanilla Sky
credentials: Long-standing rooftop bar atop Cape Sienna Gourmet Hotel — a recognised fixture on Phuket's rooftop-bar circuit, 180-degree Kamala Bay view
items.description: Cape Sienna's clifftop rooftop with a full sweep of Kamala Bay — cocktails as the light goes over the Andaman.

items.name: XANA Beach Club
credentials: The beach club of Angsana Laguna Phuket — one of Bang Tao's established day-to-night party venues
items.description: Angsana Laguna's beachfront pool club — day-to-night DJs and a young, lively crowd on the Bang Tao sand.

items.title: Private yacht day through Phang Nga Bay
items.description: The limestone karsts and hidden lagoons reached at first light, before the day-tripper flotillas, with lunch aboard.

items.title: Seaplane or helicopter to a private island
items.description: A short flight to one of the quieter islands off Phuket for a day the ferries can't deliver.

items.title: Private chef's table on a headland at sunset
items.description: A reserved table at one of the cliffside resorts, timed for the light over the Andaman.

items.title: Guided Old Town heritage and food walk
items.description: The Sino-Portuguese shophouses, temples and Hokkien food explained by a local who grew up there.

plan.heading: 3 days in Phuket, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Check in at Amanpuri on Pansea headland or Trisara, then a slow morning by your private pool as the day settles.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A guided walk through Old Phuket Town's Sino-Portuguese shophouses on Thalang Road, ending with kopi at a Peranakan café.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Sunset and dinner at PRU, the island's Michelin-starred farm-to-table room at Trisara.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private yacht from the resort marina out to Phang Nga Bay, threading the limestone karsts and sea caves by kayak.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Anchor for a quiet swim and a fresh seafood lunch aboard, away from the day-tripper flotillas.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Back on land, dinner at Suay by Chef Noi or a beach barbecue laid out privately on the sand.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A long spa morning and a swim, the island at its slowest.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A final lunch of southern Thai curries, then unhurried packing.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: An early sundowner at Baba Nest before the transfer to the airport.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Mai Khao / Natai
items.description: The quiet northern beaches with the discreet luxury resorts and long empty sand; for privacy over nightlife.

items.name: Cape Panwa / Ao Yon
items.description: A calm southeastern headland of secluded resorts and marinas; suits couples and yacht days.

items.name: Phuket Old Town
items.description: The colourful Sino-Portuguese quarter with the best local food and cafés; a cultural counterpoint to the beaches.

events.name: Phuket Vegetarian Festival
events.note: The nine-day Nine Emperor Gods festival, with white-clad devotees, temple processions and dramatic firewalking rituals.

events.name: Loy Krathong
events.note: The festival of lights, marked along the island's beaches with floating candlelit krathong at dusk.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: You arrive at Phuket International (HKT); a private car reaches most west-coast resorts in thirty to sixty minutes, and a resort-arranged speedboat or seaplane is the elegant line to the islands.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Take a private car with driver — the island is large and taxis are inconsistent — and switch to a chartered longtail or yacht for Phang Nga Bay and the surrounding islands.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: An AIS or TrueMove eSIM gives solid 4G/5G along the coasts; villa and resort wifi is dependable.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Thai baht (THB); resorts and restaurants take cards, but carry cash for boatmen, markets and beach vendors; tipping is modest and discretionary.

onGround.note: The quiet luxury sits on the west coast — Amanpuri and the Cape Panwa headland over busy Patong; November to April is dry and calm, while the May–October monsoon brings strong currents and closed beaches on some days.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: December to March is the dry, calm-sea season for the beaches and island-hopping; avoid the Andaman monsoon from May to October, worst in September when seas are rough and ferries are routinely cancelled.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No non-stop from India; the clean routing is via Bangkok on Thai Airways or Air India (about 4.5h to BKK, then roughly 1h 20m south). Bangkok Airways serves Phuket well on the domestic leg with its own lounges. Overall door-to-door is a half-day with one connection.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations; routine jabs plus Hepatitis A and Typhoid advised. Safe and relaxed. Bottled water only; sea conditions in monsoon months can be genuinely dangerous, so heed red flags.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian is easy at resorts and better restaurants; Jain is possible with advance notice. Indian food is available in the tourist belts (Patong, Bang Tao) though less refined than Bangkok. Best handled through your resort or a private chef for consistency.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Phuket, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Porto — TripAgent
seo.description: Porto, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Porto
hero.tagline: Granite, port wine and the river Douro's working banks.

ourTake.lede: Porto is smaller and moodier than Lisbon, and better for it: the pleasure here is the river, the granite streets and the port lodges across the water in Gaia. Do one serious cellar visit and a tasting rather than three, walk the Ribeira at golden hour, and don't over-schedule; the city is compact enough to be enjoyed by drifting. The Douro valley is the reward for an extra day or two.
ourTake.comeIf: You love port cellars, riverside tiles and unhurried food-and-wine days.
ourTake.skipIf: You want beaches, big-ticket sights or a fast-moving metropolis.

firstLook.heroCaption: Hillside hotel amid greenery above the sea

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Dappled forest path with wooden railings

whenToGo.blurb: Late spring and early autumn are warm and dry, with São João's midsummer madness on June 23rd; winters are wet and summers busy.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Mar, Apr, May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep and Oct

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: The Yeatman
items.area: Vila Nova de Gaia (across the Douro)
credentials: Home to The Yeatman restaurant — MICHELIN ★★ (2026)
items.description: Porto's defining luxury address — a wine hotel terraced into the Gaia hillside, every room facing the old city and the river below.

items.name: Maison Albar — Le Monumental Palace
items.description: A restored Belle Époque palace on the grand avenue — Parisian glamour and marble, in the ceremonial heart of the city.

items.name: Pestana Palácio do Freixo
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
Palácio do Freixo — a classified National Monument (1910)
items.description: A UNESCO-listed baroque palace by Nasoni on the banks of the Douro — a national monument turned pousada, with gardens to the water.

items.name: Vila Foz Hotel & Spa
credentials: Home to Vila Foz restaurant — MICHELIN ★ (2026)
items.description: A 19th-century mansion on the ocean edge, reimagined by designer Nini Andrade Silva — sea, spa and a starred table where the Douro meets the Atlantic.

items.name: Torel Avantgarde
items.description: A design-led house tumbling down the hill toward the river — art-forward rooms, each themed to an artist, with some of the best views in the old town.

items.name: Torel Palace Porto
items.description: Two restored 19th-century palacetes near the Casa da Música — quiet grandeur, a garden and a pool, a step back from the tourist core.

items.name: GA Palace Hotel & Spa
items.description: A restored 19th-century villa near the river's mouth — a small, polished house with a spa and a considered, contemporary hand.

items.name: Torel 1884
items.description: A boutique house on a Ribeira square themed to the great Age of Discoveries — richly detailed rooms steps from the riverfront.

items.name: PortoBay Flores
items.description: A restored 16th-century palace on Porto's prettiest shopping street — a heritage courtyard hotel in the centre of the old town.

items.name: The Ribeira & Cais da Ribeira riverfront
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Oporto, Luiz I Bridge and Monastery of Serra do Pilar
items.description: Porto's soul: a tumble of medieval houses in ochre, terracotta and blue stacked above the Douro, with the arcaded quay below full of cafes and river light. Walk it in the late afternoon when the sun turns the far bank gold, then have a private guide unpick the two-thousand-year history behind the facades. The heart of the UNESCO-listed old town.

items.name: Dom Luís I Bridge
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Oporto, Luiz I Bridge and Monastery of Serra do Pilar
items.description: The double-deck iron bridge (1881-86) that frames every postcard of Porto, linking the old town to the port lodges across the river. Walk the upper deck alongside the metro for the finest view in the city — the whole Ribeira falling to the water on one side, Gaia's cellars on the other. Best at dusk when both banks light up.

items.name: Monastery of Serra do Pilar
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Oporto, Luiz I Bridge and Monastery of Serra do Pilar
items.description: The circular 16th-century church and cloister crowning the Gaia hilltop, and the single best viewpoint over Porto, the Dom Luís I bridge and the river bend. Reached in a moment from the bridge's upper deck; go at golden hour for the panorama, then let a guide explain its role in the siege of Porto.

items.name: Taylor's Port cellars
items.description: One of the oldest port houses (founded 1692) and still independently family-run, with historic lodges, a beautiful audio-guided cellar walk and a hilltop terrace looking back at Porto. The tawny flight and the Barão Fladgate restaurant reward an unhurried afternoon; easy to arrange a private tasting for a small group.

items.name: Graham's Port lodge
items.description: The most polished of the lodge experiences, high on the hill above Gaia since 1890, with cellars of some 3,000 casks and vintage bottles back to the 1890s. The private vintage tastings and the acclaimed Vinum restaurant, with sweeping river views, suit a discreet, high-end afternoon for a couple or family.

items.name: Sandeman cellars
items.description: The house of the black-caped Don, right on the Gaia riverfront and the liveliest of the big-name tours, its guides in the famous cape. A good, accessible introduction to how port is made and aged; combine the classic tawny and vintage tastings for a first port lesson before moving to the smaller houses.

items.name: WOW — World of Wine cultural district
items.description: A whole hilltop quarter of museums, restaurants and shops carved from converted port cellars — wine and cork museums, a chocolate story, a fashion collection — with terraces over the river. Genuinely multi-generational: children and teenagers have as much to do as the adults, and there are veg-friendly restaurants throughout.

items.name: Ferreira Port lodge
items.description: The great Portuguese-owned house, tied to the legendary Dona Antónia Ferreira who shaped the Douro in the 19th century. A quieter, more historically rich tasting than the tourist-heavy lodges, with a strong story to tell — an elegant stop for those who want depth over spectacle.

items.name: Six Bridges Douro river cruise
items.description: A 50-minute sail in a traditional rabelo boat from the Ribeira quay, gliding under all six bridges that span the river — Dom Luís I, Arrábida, Maria Pia, Infante, São João and Freixo. For an unhurried version, charter a private boat or yacht for sunset with champagne rather than the shared hourly departures.

items.name: Livraria Lello
items.description: The 1906 neo-Gothic bookshop with a scarlet swooping staircase and stained-glass skylight, often called the most beautiful in the world and a muse for Harry Potter lore. Timed tickets are essential and the crowds are real; a private out-of-hours slot, arranged ahead, lets you take it in calm. A short walk from Clérigos.

items.name: Clérigos Tower & church
items.description: Nicolau Nasoni's baroque masterpiece, a 75m granite bell tower visible from across the city. Climb the 225 steps for a 360-degree view over the terracotta roofs to the river; late-evening openings let you see Porto lit at night. The linked church and the Passeio dos Clérigos below are worth the pause.

items.name: São Bento railway station azulejos
items.description: A working train station whose entrance hall is lined with some 20,000 blue-and-white azulejo tiles depicting Portugal's history — battles, royal weddings, the coming of the railway. Free to walk in; ten minutes with a guide turns a photo stop into a lesson in the country's founding myths. Steps from the cathedral and Lello.

items.name: Porto Cathedral (Sé)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Oporto, Luiz I Bridge and Monastery of Serra do Pilar
items.description: The fortress-like Romanesque cathedral on the hill above the old town, with a Gothic cloister of blue-and-white tiles and a silver altarpiece. The terrace out front is one of the great free viewpoints over the river and the Gaia lodges. A cornerstone of the UNESCO historic centre.

items.name: Palácio da Bolsa & the Arab Room
items.description: The 19th-century Stock Exchange Palace built on the old St Francis convent, its show-stopper the Moorish-revival Arab Room modelled on the Alhambra and finished with some 18 kilos of gold. Visits are by guided tour only; a private tour for a small group is the discreet way to see the state rooms without the queue.

items.name: Church of São Francisco
items.description: Behind a plain Gothic shell lies Porto's most astonishing interior — nearly every surface carved and gilded in some 400kg of Brazilian gold, a riot of baroque wood. The eerie catacombs below add a second, sombre note. Small and easy to overwhelm, so go early; a short, unforgettable stop beside the Bolsa.

items.name: Igreja do Carmo azulejo facade
items.description: The 18th-century church whose whole side wall is a vast blue-and-white tile panel (added 1912) showing the founding of the Carmelite order. Next to it stands one of the narrowest houses in the world, squeezed between Carmo and Carmelitas. A five-minute photo and history stop near Lello.

items.name: Capela das Almas (Chapel of Souls)
items.description: A small chapel on the corner of the main shopping street entirely sheathed in some 15,000 blue-and-white tiles depicting the lives of St Francis and St Catherine — a wall of azulejos hiding in plain sight amid the shops. A quick, rewarding detour beside the Bolhão market.

items.name: Crystal Palace Gardens (Jardins do Palácio de Cristal)
items.description: Romantic terraced gardens above the Douro with rose beds, fountains, resident peacocks and one of the finest free views over the river and Gaia. A calm green escape from the old-town crowds; lovely for a slow morning walk or a picnic with a private guide who knows the quiet corners.

items.name: Serralves — museum, villa & park
items.description: Portugal's leading contemporary-art institution: Álvaro Siza's white minimalist museum, the pink Art Deco Serralves Villa, and 18 hectares of gardens and woodland with a treetop walkway. A cultured half-day for families — art for the adults, the park and treetop trail for children. Veg-friendly cafe on site.

items.name: Casa da Música
items.description: Rem Koolhaas's bold, faceted concert hall — a landmark of modern architecture and Porto's finest room for classical, jazz and fado. Take the guided architecture tour by day, or, better, book seats for an evening concert; a striking contrast to the baroque old town.

items.name: Foz do Douro seafront
items.description: Where the river meets the Atlantic — a genteel seaside district of villas, the Pergola da Foz promenade, lighthouses and rock pools. Drive or walk the coastal road at sunset and dine at one of the smart seafood restaurants; the most relaxed, moneyed corner of Porto, away from the tour crowds.

items.name: Mercado do Bolhão
items.description: Porto's grand covered market, trading since 1839 and reopened after a careful restoration — two tiers of iron galleries around an open courtyard, full of flowers, cheese, cured meats, produce and tascas. A vivid sense of daily Porto; go with a guide for tastings and the best stalls, veg options included.

items.name: Rua de Santa Catarina & Café Majestic
items.description: Porto's main pedestrian shopping street, and on it the Majestic — a 1921 Belle Époque cafe of mirrors, carved wood and Art Nouveau flourish, all leather and marble. Take morning coffee and a pastel de nata in its gilded room, then browse the boutiques. Reserve ahead; it is deservedly busy.

items.name: Miragaia quarter
items.description: The old riverside neighbourhood just west of the Ribeira, quieter and more lived-in — laundry on balconies, tiny squares, locals about their day. A rewarding wander for those who have seen the headline sights and want the real, unpolished Porto; lovely on a private walking tour at a slow pace.

items.name: Jardim do Morro
items.description: A small hillside garden at the Gaia end of the upper bridge deck, and the classic sunset perch — the Douro turning to gold below and Porto's roofs glowing across the water. Arrive early evening; pair it with a walk down to the port lodges afterwards.

items.name: Igreja de Santo Ildefonso
items.description: The twin-towered 18th-century church at the top of Santa Catarina, its whole facade wrapped in a huge blue-and-white tile panel from 1932. One of the city's great azulejo set-pieces, and an easy stop between the Majestic cafe and the Bolhão market.

items.name: Miradouro da Vitória
items.description: A tucked-away terrace in the old Jewish quarter with a sweeping, crowd-free view across the tiled roofs to the cathedral and the river. Locals' favourite for a quiet sundowner; a short climb rewards you with the view everyone else queues for elsewhere.

items.name: Funicular dos Guindais
items.description: A short, steep funicular that spares you the climb between the riverside Ribeira and the upper town near the bridge, with fine views of the Douro on the way up. A charming, practical ride that doubles as a viewpoint — useful with children or older travellers.

items.name: Igreja de Santa Clara
items.description: A modest Gothic exterior hiding one of the most lavish gilded baroque interiors in Portugal, recently restored to full glory. Far less visited than São Francisco and all the more rewarding for it — a quiet, dazzling stop near the old city walls.

items.name: Douro Valley wine day-trip (Pinhão & the quintas)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Alto Douro Wine Region
items.description: The world's oldest demarcated wine region and one of the most beautiful — river-carved terraces of vines climbing impossibly steep slopes to Pinhão. Do it privately: two or three great quintas (Quinta do Crasto, Quinta do Noval, Quinta da Pacheca) for tastings and lunch, and a rabelo cruise from Pinhão. Veg lunches on request.

items.name: Quinta do Noval
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Alto Douro Wine Region
items.description: One of the Douro's most storied estates, source of the legendary Nacional vintage ports, with a beautiful terraced vineyard above the Pinhão river. A private visit and vertical tasting here is a pilgrimage for serious port lovers — arrange ahead through the estate.

items.name: Pinhão village & railway station
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Alto Douro Wine Region
items.description: The pretty heart of the Douro wine country, its tiny station famous for azulejo panels of the harvest and river life. The jumping-off point for quinta visits and rabelo cruises; a scenic train from Porto hugs the river the whole way for those who prefer the rails to the road.

items.name: Guimarães day-trip
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Guimarães
items.description: The birthplace of Portugal and of its first king, Afonso Henriques — a beautifully preserved medieval old town of cobbled lanes and squares, crowned by a 10th-century castle and the Dukes' Palace. Under an hour from Porto; an easy, atmospheric half-day, ideally with a private guide for the history.

items.name: Braga & Bom Jesus do Monte day-trip
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Sanctuary of Bom Jesus do Monte, Braga
items.description: Portugal's religious capital, with its ancient cathedral and grand baroque churches, and just outside it the sanctuary of Bom Jesus do Monte — a theatrical zig-zag baroque stairway of 573 steps climbing to the church, with a water-powered funicular for those who would rather ride. Often paired with Guimarães in one day.

items.name: Aveiro day-trip
items.description: The 'Portuguese Venice', an hour south — a lagoon town of canals plied by colourful moliceiro boats, Art Nouveau facades and salt pans. Add the striped fishermen's houses of nearby Costa Nova for the photographs. A gentle, pretty contrast to Porto's granite intensity.

items.name: Igreja dos Grilos & the old city walls
items.description: A handsome Mannerist church beside the cathedral hill, with a surviving stretch of Porto's medieval Fernandine walls nearby offering river views. A quieter counterpoint to the crowded Sé terrace for those exploring the upper old town on foot.

items.name: Rua das Flores & the artisan quarter
items.description: The elegant pedestrian street linking São Bento to the river, lined with restored merchant houses, boutique jewellers, specialty coffee and small galleries. The most refined browsing street in the old town; slot it between the station azulejos and the Bolsa.

items.name: Casa do Infante
items.description: A medieval customs house on the riverfront, said to be the birthplace of Henry the Navigator, now a small museum over Roman mosaics uncovered beneath. A compact, worthwhile stop for the history behind Porto's age-of-discoveries wealth, moments from the São Francisco church.

items.name: Palácio das Cardosas & Avenida dos Aliados
items.description: Porto's grand civic boulevard, a sweep of Beaux-Arts facades rising to the ornate City Hall, with the Cardosas palace (now a luxury hotel) anchoring the lower end by São Bento. The city's most monumental space; walk it at night when the buildings are lit.

items.name: Fundação de Serralves Treetop Walk
items.description: A raised timber walkway threading through the crowns of the Serralves park's oldest trees, with viewpoints over the gardens and villa. A gentle, novel highlight for children and grandparents alike within the wider Serralves visit.

items.name: Praia da Luz & the coastal beaches
items.description: Porto's own city beaches strung along the Atlantic promenade at Foz — Praia da Luz, Praia dos Ingleses — with beach-club cafes and sunset bars on the rocks. A relaxed afternoon of sea air after the old-town sightseeing; the water is bracing, the terraces are the draw.

items.name: Vintage tram & the tram museum
items.description: Line 1's restored wooden tram trundles along the river from the Ribeira out to Foz — a slow, scenic ride past the water, ending near the Electric Tram Museum in an old power station. A characterful way to reach the coast, and a treat for children and rail enthusiasts.

items.name: Palacete Pinto Leite / Casa da Companhia gardens
items.description: Restored 19th-century merchant mansions and their gardens now open as boutique venues and tea rooms in the elegant Boavista and Cedofeita districts — a glimpse of the gilded-age Porto that port wealth built. A refined, low-key stop between Serralves and the centre.

items.name: Bolsa do Café / specialty coffee & pastelaria trail
items.description: Porto takes its coffee and cakes seriously — from the historic cafes to the wave of specialty roasters around Rua das Flores and Cedofeita. A morning tasting trail of pastéis de nata, francesinha (in a veg version too) and single-origin coffee, easily arranged with a food guide.

items.name: Igreja de São Lourenço (dos Grilos) viewpoint & Passeio das Virtudes
items.description: A grassy garden terrace tumbling down the hillside above Miragaia, beloved by locals for picnics and one of the finest sunset spots facing west over the river mouth. Uncrowded and unhurried — bring a bottle of Douro white and watch the light go.

items.name: The Yeatman
items.area: Vila Nova de Gaia (across the Douro)
items.description: Ricardo Costa's two-star room high above the river — the region's most celebrated table, matched to one of Portugal's great cellars.

items.name: Casa de Chá da Boa Nova
items.description: Rui Paula's two-star seafood kitchen inside Álvaro Siza's landmark tea house — cooking with the Atlantic breaking on the rocks below.

items.name: Antiqvvm
items.description: Vítor Matos's two-star room in a 19th-century mansion above the Crystal Palace gardens — bold, layered reinterpretations of Portuguese flavour.

items.name: Pedro Lemos
items.description: A long-held star in a stone townhouse near the river's mouth — precise, produce-led cooking and a lovely rooftop terrace.

items.name: Euskalduna Studio
items.description: Vasco Coelho Santos's eight-seat counter facing the open kitchen — the most personal, exacting chef's-counter experience in northern Portugal.

items.name: Le Monument
items.description: Julien Montbabut's star inside the Monumental Palace — French technique and Portuguese produce, in a Belle Époque room on the grand avenue.

items.name: Blind
items.description: Vítor Matos's second Porto star — a playful, contemporary tasting menu that sends the diner into the kitchen's imagination.

items.name: Vinha
items.area: Vila Nova de Gaia (across the Douro)
items.description: Henrique Sá Pessoa's Gaia star — assured contemporary cooking over the river, from one of Portugal's most respected chefs.

items.name: DOP
items.description: Rui Paula's city-centre star — refined, generous Portuguese cooking in a handsome downtown palace of the arts.

items.name: ÉON
items.description: Tiago Bonito's star in a restored palacete — precise, seasonal cooking from one of the north's quiet talents.

items.name: Gastro by Elemento
items.description: Ricardo Dias Ferreira's fire-led star — wood, embers and smoke at the centre of an intense, produce-driven menu.

items.name: IN Diferente
items.description: Angélica Salvador's star near the coast — a personal, contemporary kitchen and one of Porto's newer one-star rooms.

items.name: Cozinha das Flores
items.description: Nuno Mendes's return to Portugal — fire, local produce and tradition, in an intimate room off the old town's prettiest street.

items.name: OMA
items.description: A young, well-travelled team turning out a considered tasting menu at real value — Michelin's pick for quality without ceremony.

items.name: Prova
credentials: A respected Porto wine bar led by sommelier Diogo Amado
items.description: Sommelier Diogo Amado's wine room near the river — some fifty Portuguese wines by the glass, poured with real knowledge.

items.name: Port-lodge tastings, Vila Nova de Gaia
items.area: Vila Nova de Gaia (across the Douro)
credentials: Historic port houses — Graham's, Taylor's, Ferreira and others across the river
items.description: An evening tasting at a historic port house — vintage and tawny flights in the candlelit cellars that made the city famous.

items.name: Aduela
credentials: A landmark of Porto's Baixa bar scene, on the lively Rua das Oliveiras / Rua do Almada
items.description: A cult neighbourhood bar in a former haberdashery — laid-back, characterful and the anchor of Porto's most social drinking street.

items.name: The Royal Cocktail Club
items.description: Porto's most serious cocktail room — velvet, chandeliers and a precise, inventive list; the benchmark for a grown-up drink in the city.

items.name: Base
credentials: A well-known Porto open-air garden bar, in the Cordoaria beside Clérigos
items.description: An open-air garden bar under the pines beside the Clérigos tower — daytime-into-night drinks and DJs in the heart of town.

items.name: Terrace at The Yeatman
items.area: Vila Nova de Gaia (across the Douro)
credentials: Terrace of The Yeatman — MICHELIN One Key hotel, Relais & Châteaux
items.description: A glass of port or a cocktail on the terrace of Porto's grandest hotel — the whole old city and river spread out below.

items.title: A port tasting in a historic Gaia lodge
items.description: Cross the Dom Luís bridge and sit down at a name like Graham's or Taylor's for tawnies and vintages with the river below.

items.title: A Douro valley river cruise or drive
items.description: Take the train or boat upriver to the terraced vineyards and lunch at a working quinta.

items.title: Livraria Lello, early and ticketed
items.description: Book the first slot to see the curling staircase before the crowds, then move on quickly.

items.title: A francesinha and a fine at a proper old café
items.description: Order the city's outrageous stacked sandwich where locals do, not on the tourist strip.

plan.heading: 3 days in Porto, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

days.title: The old city and the river

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Livraria Lello at opening, then the Sé and the tiled nave of São Bento station.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Down through Ribeira to the quay, crossing the Dom Luís I bridge on foot to Gaia.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Antiqvvm, Vítor Matos's Michelin room above the Douro.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private tasting and cellar walk at Taylor's, followed by the terrace view over the city.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The trams and gardens of the Foz do Douro, where the river meets the sea.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Grilled fish and vinho verde at Pedro Lemos in the Foz, one star, quiet and precise.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A driver up the Douro to Quinta do Crasto for a vineyard walk and the infinity pool view.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch and tasting at The Yeatman's terrace or a riverside quinta among the terraced vines.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Back in Porto, a nightcap of aged tawny at the Vintage House bar.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Ribeira
items.description: The postcard riverfront of tiled houses and terraces; atmospheric but busy, best for those who want to be in the middle of it.

items.name: Baixa / Aliados
items.description: The grand civic centre with the best hotels and squares; suits travellers who want polish and everything walkable.

items.name: Cedofeita / Miguel Bombarda
items.description: The arts and galleries quarter, quieter and more local; suits those after independent shops and a slower pace.

events.name: Festa de São João do Porto
events.note: The city's exuberant midsummer festival of bonfires, grilled sardines, plastic hammers and a midnight fireworks display over the river.

events.name: NOS Primavera Sound
events.note: A three-day international indie and electronic festival in the Parque da Cidade, an offshoot of the Barcelona original.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Francisco Sá Carneiro Airport (OPO), a twenty-five-minute drive from the river, with a private car waiting on arrival.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver for the port lodges across the Douro and day trips into the wine valley; the Ribeira and downtown are compact and made for walking.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Coverage is strong across the city; an eSIM activates instantly and wifi is dependable in hotels and lodges.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The euro; cards are universal, cash is rarely needed, and a small rounding-up gesture suffices for tips.

onGround.note: Base yourself in the Ribeira or near the Bolhão; arrange a private tasting at one of the family port houses in Vila Nova de Gaia, and consider a day on the Douro by boat or by the vineyard estates upriver.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: May-June and September deliver warm days and cool Douro evenings; July-August is busy and hot, and the winter months are notably wet — Porto is one of the rainier corners of Iberia.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No nonstop from India; connect via a European hub — Lufthansa/SWISS through Frankfurt or Zurich, or Air France via Paris, in business, around 14-16 hours total. TAP Air Portugal or the hub carrier flies the final leg into Porto (OPO); pre-clear Schengen at the European hub and use the Star Alliance lounge there, as Porto's own premium facilities are modest.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No special vaccinations; tap water is potable. Low crime, calm and walkable; standard care with valuables in the Ribeira crowds. No altitude issue.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Straightforward for vegetarians, though the city's tradition is meat-forward; good plant-based spots and some Indian dining exist. Try daTerra (vegetarian buffet) or Essência for refined meat-free plates.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Porto, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Prague — TripAgent
seo.description: Prague, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Prague
hero.tagline: City of a hundred spires above the winding Vltava

ourTake.lede: Prague is a walking city that punishes you for sleeping in — cross the Charles Bridge at dawn and you get it almost to yourself, by ten it's shoulder to shoulder. Give the castle a full morning and go beyond the courtyards into the smaller palaces. Skip the Old Town Square restaurants and eat in Vinohrady or Karlín where locals actually go.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a walkable old city of spires, castles and easy charm.
ourTake.skipIf: You need a beach, big luxury names or warm weather.

firstLook.heroCaption: Manicured garden facing historic hotel facade

grid.caption: Modern pool villa with palms and umbrella
purple allium blooms in soft focus

whenToGo.blurb: Late spring and early autumn are mild and golden; December glows with Christmas markets. Avoid the packed midsummer heat and grey deep winter.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Apr, May, Jun, Jul and Aug

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Prague
items.area: Staré Město (Old Town), on the Vltava riverbank
items.description: Three linked historic houses — Baroque, Renaissance and neo-Classical — on the river, with the finest Castle-and-bridge view in the city.

items.name: Fairmont Golden Prague
items.area: Staré Město (Old Town), by the river near the Jewish Quarter
items.description: A landmark riverfront grande dame reborn under Fairmont — the only hotel in Prague to earn two MICHELIN Keys.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental, Prague
items.area: Malá Strana (Lesser Town), below the Castle
items.description: A former 14th-century monastery turned serene Mandarin Oriental house, quietly hidden in the cobbled lanes beneath the Castle.

items.name: Augustine, a Luxury Collection Hotel
items.area: Malá Strana (Lesser Town), by the Augustinian monastery
items.description: Woven around a still-working 13th-century Augustinian monastery — cloisters, a monk's brewery, and Cubist-inspired design.

items.name: Andaz Prague
items.description: Set in the restored 1916 Sugar Palace — a design-led Hyatt house threading 1920s retro-futurist Czech art through the historic centre.

items.name: Almanac X Alcron Prague
items.area: Nové Město (New Town), near Wenceslas Square
items.description: A restored 1932 Art Deco landmark — the storied Alcron reborn, with its glamorous heritage dining room, Brasserie 1932.

items.name: The Grand Mark Prague
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A former Baroque palace with one of the largest private hotel gardens in the Old Town — classical grandeur, quietly kept.

items.name: Aria Hotel Prague
items.area: Malá Strana (Lesser Town), by St Nicholas Church
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A music-themed boutique below the Castle, each floor devoted to a genre — with a rooftop terrace over the red rooftops of the Lesser Town.

items.name: Alchymist Grand Hotel & Spa
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A cluster of Renaissance and Baroque townhouses restored with gilded, theatrical opulence — an ornate, old-world hideaway.

items.name: The Emblem Prague Hotel
items.description: A discreet contemporary design hotel a few steps from the Old Town Square — a rooftop lounge, a library, and a quietly modern hand.

items.name: Prague Castle (Pražský hrad)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Prague
Guinness World Records — largest ancient castle complex in the world
items.description: The largest coherent castle complex in the world by Guinness reckoning, a thousand years of palaces, courtyards and cathedral spires crowning the skyline above the river. A private early-access tour before the gates open lets a multi-generational family have the courtyards almost to themselves.

items.name: St Vitus Cathedral (Katedrála sv. Víta)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Prague
items.description: Nearly six centuries in the building, this soaring Gothic cathedral inside the castle walls holds the Bohemian crown jewels, royal tombs and the shimmering Art Nouveau windows Alfons Mucha designed. The 287-step climb of the Great South Tower rewards with the finest close view over the whole city.

items.name: Charles Bridge (Karlův most)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Prague
items.description: The 14th-century stone bridge lined with thirty Baroque saints, linking the Old Town to the castle side across the Vltava. Cross at dawn — before the crowds and buskers arrive — for the postcard light on the water and the towers, an unhurried moment that suits early-rising elders and children alike.

items.name: Old Town Square (Staroměstské náměstí)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Prague
items.description: The medieval heart of Prague, ringed by pastel Gothic and Baroque facades, the twin spires of Týn Church and pavement cafes. A grand, walkable stage for the whole family, with the Astronomical Clock chiming on the hour.

items.name: Prague Astronomical Clock & Old Town Hall (Orloj)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Prague
items.description: One of the oldest working astronomical clocks in the world, dating to 1410, with a procession of the Twelve Apostles that draws a crowd every hour. Climb the Old Town Hall tower for a bird's-eye sweep of the square and its rooftops — a lift makes it easy for less mobile travellers.

items.name: Josefov — the Jewish Quarter
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Prague
items.description: The most complete surviving complex of Jewish monuments in Europe, its historic synagogues and cemetery woven into the Old Town. A guided walk through seven centuries of Prague's Jewish story is one of the city's most moving and reflective experiences for a family.

items.name: Old-New Synagogue (Staronová synagoga)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Prague
items.description: The oldest active synagogue in Europe, in continuous use since around 1270, and the legendary home of the Golem myth. Its austere early-Gothic hall is unlike anything else in the city — small, atmospheric and still a living house of prayer.

items.name: Spanish Synagogue (Španělská synagoga)
items.description: A dazzling Moorish-Revival interior of gilded arabesques, stained glass and a starry domed ceiling — the most sumptuous of all Prague's synagogues, part of the Jewish Museum. Intimate evening chamber concerts here are a discreet, refined way to spend an hour.

items.name: Old Jewish Cemetery (Starý židovský hřbitov)
items.description: Twelve thousand weathered headstones tilting against each other in layered rows, one of the most evocative burial grounds in the world, used from the 15th to the 18th century. A quiet, thought-provoking stop within the Jewish Museum circuit.

items.name: Malá Strana (Lesser Town)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Prague
items.description: Prague's Baroque quarter beneath the castle, its noble palaces, hidden courtyards and cobbled lanes barely changed since the 18th century. The perfect district for an unhurried private walk, with quiet corner cafes and garden restaurants for a mid-stroll pause.

items.name: St Nicholas Church, Malá Strana (Kostel sv. Mikuláše)
items.description: The supreme masterpiece of Prague Baroque, a vast green dome and a ceiling fresco so grand it seems to open the roof to heaven. Time a visit to one of the frequent organ or chamber concerts held beneath the dome.

items.name: Church of Our Lady before Týn (Chrám Matky Boží před Týnem)
items.description: The twin black Gothic spires rising over Old Town Square are the defining silhouette of medieval Prague, each crowned with a crown of mini-spires. The astronomer Tycho Brahe lies buried inside this soaring, dimly lit interior.

items.name: Loreta (Loreta Praha)
items.description: A jewel-box Baroque pilgrimage shrine near the castle, built around a replica of the Holy House, with a famous treasury of monstrances glittering with thousands of diamonds. Its cloister and carillon of bells make it a peaceful counterpoint to the busier castle.

items.name: Strahov Monastery & Library (Strahovský klášter)
items.description: Two of the most beautiful Baroque library halls on earth — the Theological and Philosophical Halls — with painted ceilings, antique globes and a cabinet of curiosities. The hilltop terrace outside offers one of the best panoramas of the spired city below.

items.name: Klementinum — Baroque Library & Astronomical Tower
items.description: A jaw-dropping 1727 Jesuit library hall of frescoed ceilings and historic globes, reached only by guided tour, plus a climb up the Astronomical Tower for a wraparound view over the Old Town rooftops. The small-group entry keeps it calm and civilised.

items.name: Golden Lane (Zlatá ulička)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Prague
items.description: A row of tiny brightly-painted 16th-century cottages tucked inside the castle walls, once home to castle marksmen and later, briefly, to Franz Kafka at No. 22. A charming, storybook lane that delights children and grandparents alike.

items.name: Municipal House (Obecní dům)
items.description: The finest Art Nouveau building in Prague, a 1912 confection of mosaics, stained glass and interiors decorated by Mucha and his peers, wrapped around the grand Smetana concert hall. A guided tour of the salons, then dinner in the opulent French restaurant, makes an elegant evening.

items.name: Mucha Museum
items.description: The world's first museum devoted to Alfons Mucha, the Czech master whose sinuous posters of flowing-haired Slavic women defined Art Nouveau. A compact, intimate collection a short walk from Wenceslas Square — an easy, rewarding hour for art lovers of any age.

items.name: The Slav Epic by Alfons Mucha (at the Municipal House)
items.description: Mucha's monumental twenty-canvas cycle telling the saga of the Slavic peoples, some panels the size of a cinema screen, now on show inside the Municipal House. A single, awe-inspiring encounter with a national masterpiece.

items.name: Petřín Hill & Lookout Tower (Petřínská rozhledna)
items.description: A wooded 327-metre hill of orchards and rose gardens crowned by a miniature Eiffel-style tower with a 360-degree view of Prague. A gentle, green escape from the streets below, with a mirror maze and observatory that keep younger travellers happy.

items.name: Letná Park & Metronome (Letenské sady)
items.description: A wooded plateau above the river where a giant metronome now stands on the old plinth that once held a Stalin statue, and where you can count seven of Prague's bridges in one sweep. The seasonal beer garden with its Old Town view is a beloved local sunset spot.

items.name: Vltava River Cruise
items.description: The classic way to see the castle, Charles Bridge and the National Theatre reflected in the water, from a leisurely daytime glide to a candlelit dinner cruise at night. A private charter with a chef briefed on vegetarian and Jain preferences is easily arranged.

items.name: Kampa Island & the Lennon Wall
items.description: Nicknamed 'Prague's Venice' for its little canal and waterwheel, this leafy island beneath Charles Bridge holds a riverside park and the ever-changing John Lennon Wall of painted messages. A relaxed, romantic wander with the Kampa modern-art museum alongside.

items.name: Kampa Museum (Museum Kampa)
items.description: A converted riverside mill housing a fine collection of Central European modern art, strong on František Kupka and the Cubist sculptor Otto Gutfreund. A calm, well-curated space with a terrace café looking straight across the Vltava.

items.name: Wallenstein Garden (Valdštejnská zahrada)
items.description: A grand early-Baroque garden of clipped hedges, a dramatic frescoed grotto and bronze statues, hidden behind the walls of a palace that is now the Czech Senate — and free to enter. Peacocks roam the lawns, delighting children, and it is blissfully quiet.

items.name: Vrtba Garden (Vrtbovská zahrada)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Prague
items.description: One of the most beautiful terraced Baroque gardens in Central Europe, climbing in ornamental tiers up the hillside with statues and a view over the red roofs of the Lesser Town. A serene, little-known hideaway ideal for a private moment.

items.name: Estates Theatre (Stavovské divadlo)
items.description: The exquisite 1783 Classical theatre where Mozart himself conducted the world premiere of Don Giovanni in 1787, still staging the opera today in near-original surroundings. To hear Mozart in the very room he wrote it for is one of Europe's great cultural experiences.

items.name: National Theatre (Národní divadlo)
items.description: The gilded neo-Renaissance temple of Czech culture on the riverbank, its golden roof a landmark, staging opera, ballet and drama beneath a ceiling of allegorical paintings. A box for an evening performance is a grand, memorable night out.

items.name: Rudolfinum & the Czech Philharmonic
items.description: One of the finest 19th-century concert halls on the continent, whose Dvořák Hall is home to the world-class Czech Philharmonic. A ticket here is the connoisseur's choice for classical music in Prague, in a riverside setting of real grandeur.

items.name: State Opera (Státní opera)
items.description: A sumptuously restored neo-Rococo opera house near the top of Wenceslas Square, staging grand opera and ballet under a lavishly painted auditorium. The recent renovation returned it to full jewel-box splendour.

items.name: Black-Light Theatre Ta Fantastika
items.description: Prague's distinctive black-light theatre, where UV-lit figures float and transform against a black stage in wordless, dreamlike shows. Because it needs no language, it is a genuinely fun, all-ages evening for multi-generational groups.

items.name: Vyšehrad Fortress
items.description: A cliff-top fortress above the Vltava, wrapped around the neo-Gothic Church of Sts Peter and Paul, ancient ramparts and the Slavín cemetery where Dvořák, Smetana and Mucha lie. Far quieter than the castle, with sweeping river views and space for children to run.

items.name: National Gallery — Trade Fair Palace (Veletržní palác)
items.description: Prague's great museum of modern and contemporary art, in a landmark 1928 Functionalist building, with works by Picasso, Klimt, Van Gogh and Mucha's Slav Epic hall. The single most important art collection in the country, and rarely crowded.

items.name: DOX Centre for Contemporary Art
items.description: A sharp, converted-factory space for cutting-edge contemporary art, architecture and design, crowned by the Gulliver airship — a huge wooden zeppelin on the roof. The most forward-looking cultural stop in the city, with a good design shop and café.

items.name: Wenceslas Square & the National Museum (Václavské náměstí)
items.description: The grand boulevard-square at the heart of modern Prague, scene of the 1989 Velvet Revolution, closed at its top by the newly restored, palatial National Museum. History, shopping and grand architecture in one broad sweep.

items.name: Vinohrady
items.description: A stately residential quarter of Art Nouveau apartment blocks, leafy squares and the city's best independent restaurants and wine bars — regularly named among the world's coolest neighbourhoods. The relaxed, refined district in which discerning travellers actually want to spend an evening.

items.name: Riegrovy sady (Rieger Gardens)
items.description: A rolling park in Vinohrady whose grassy slope offers a classic view of the castle and spires at sunset, home to one of Prague's largest and most beloved beer gardens. A local, easygoing way to end a warm day.

items.name: Žižkov TV Tower (Žižkovská televizní věž)
items.description: Prague's tallest structure and its most divisive landmark, a 216-metre space-age tower with crawling giant baby sculptures by David Černý and a 360-degree observation deck. There's a one-room luxury suite and a restaurant near the top for a memorable, offbeat treat.

items.name: Karlín
items.description: A once-industrial district reborn after the 2002 floods into one of Prague's leading quarters for design, cuisine and cafés, anchored by the grand neo-Romanesque Church of Sts Cyril and Methodius. The place to see contemporary, creative Prague away from the tourist core.

items.name: Náplavka Riverbank & Farmers' Market
items.description: The revived Vltava embankment of vaulted cellar bars and moored boats, with a lively Saturday farmers' market of Czech produce, cheeses and street food. A genuinely local scene with castle-and-bridge views, and plenty of vegetarian-friendly stalls.

items.name: Havelské tržiště (Havel's Market)
items.description: The last surviving open-air market in the historic core, trading since 1232, with stalls of fruit, flowers, wooden toys and Czech crafts. A quick, atmospheric stop between the Old Town Square and the river.

items.name: Powder Tower (Prašná brána)
items.description: A soaring blackened-Gothic gate tower marking the start of the medieval coronation route to the castle, standing beside the Art Nouveau Municipal House in a striking clash of eras. A short climb gives a fine view down the Royal Way.

items.name: Kutná Hora & the Sedlec Ossuary
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Kutná Hora with the Church of St Barbara and the Cathedral of Our Lady at Sedlec
items.description: A former silver-mining boomtown an hour east, home to the soaring Gothic St Barbara's Cathedral and the extraordinary Sedlec Ossuary, a chapel decorated with the bones of tens of thousands. An unforgettable, easily private half- or full-day excursion.

items.name: Karlštejn Castle (Hrad Karlštejn)
items.description: Charles IV's fairy-tale Gothic fortress crowning a wooded hill just west of the city, once the treasury for the imperial crown jewels and the jewel-encrusted Chapel of the Holy Cross. The closest and easiest of the great castle day trips, lovely for a multi-generational outing.

items.name: Český Krumlov
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Historic Centre of Český Krumlov
items.description: A storybook medieval town cradled in a bend of the Vltava, all pastel houses, cobbled lanes and a vast hilltop castle with its own Baroque theatre. Worth an overnight rather than a rush; a private car and guide turn the long drive into an unhurried pleasure.

items.name: Karlovy Vary
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Great Spa Towns of Europe
items.description: The grand 19th-century spa town of colonnades, thermal springs and pastel promenades where emperors and composers once took the cure, and the home of Becherovka liqueur and Moser crystal. A refined day of mineral springs, café society and a spa treatment for the whole party.

items.name: La Degustation Bohême Bourgeoise
items.description: The first restaurant devoted to Czech cuisine to win a MICHELIN star — a long tasting menu reviving 19th-century Bohemian cookbooks.

items.name: Field
items.description: Radek Kašpárek's playful, farm-driven modern cooking — Prague's most consistently celebrated star, and a MICHELIN Service Award winner.

items.name: Casa de Carli
items.description: Chef Matteo de Carli cooking the food of his Italian homeland — handmade pasta at the counter, and Prague's newest MICHELIN star.

items.name: Levitate
items.description: Christian Chu's Nordic technique laced with Asian spice — an inventive, individual tasting menu that won a star in 2025.

items.name: Štangl
items.description: Martin Štangl's manifesto for modern Czech cooking — foraged herbs and forgotten ingredients, and both a MICHELIN Star and Green Star.

items.name: Leaf
items.description: Barbora Šimůnková's sustainability-led kitchen — a MICHELIN Green Star for produce-forward, low-waste cooking.

items.name: Terasa U Zlaté Studně
items.area: Malá Strana (Lesser Town), below the Castle
items.description: A rooftop dining terrace with one of the great Prague views — the Castle and the red rooftops laid out below.

items.name: Alma
items.area: Nové Město (New Town), V Jirchářích, near the National Theatre
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — 50 Best Discovery (the bar)
items.description: A day-to-night gastronomic complex — café, restaurant and one of Europe's most acclaimed bars — with a MICHELIN Bib Gourmand kitchen.

items.name: The Eatery
items.description: Confident, generous modern Czech cooking that has held its Bib Gourmand — a favourite of the local dining crowd.

items.name: Dejvická 34
items.description: A polished neighbourhood restaurant with Italian leanings — reliably good, and a long-standing Bib Gourmand.

items.name: Na Kopci
items.description: Czech and French cooking on a quiet hill in Smíchov — a warm, well-priced Bib Gourmand off the tourist map.

items.name: Výčep
items.description: Modern Czech cooking with a serious approach to Czech beer — a fresh Bib Gourmand doing the classics properly.

items.name: U Kalendů
items.description: An assured, ingredient-led kitchen that earned a Bib Gourmand in the guide's first Czechia edition.

items.name: U Matěje
items.description: A refined take on Czech classics in a smart neighbourhood room — a new Bib Gourmand for 2025.

items.name: Eska
items.description: A bakery-and-restaurant landmark of the Karlín revival — modern Czech cooking, wood-fired bread, and a MICHELIN listing.

items.name: Black Angel's Bar
items.area: Staré Město (Old Town), beneath the U Prince Hotel on Old Town Square
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — 50 Best Discovery
items.description: A Prohibition-era cocktail cellar in a Gothic vault right on the Old Town Square — barrel-aged classics served on hand-made Moser glass.

items.name: Hemingway Bar
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — 50 Best Discovery
items.description: A dark, intimate cocktail den devoted to Hemingway — rare rums, an absinthe fountain, and some of the most inventive drinks in the city.

items.name: L'Fleur
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — 50 Best Discovery
items.description: Cocktails and Champagne given equal billing — exposed brick, chandeliers, candlelight, and one of the largest Champagne lists in the world.

items.name: Alma
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — 50 Best Discovery
items.description: Prague's most decorated bar — wild herbs, foraged ingredients and pickled pine cones in the glass, in a converted former cinema.

items.name: Cloud 9 Sky Bar & Lounge
items.area: Nové Město (New Town), atop the Hilton Prague
credentials: Atop the Hilton Prague — a landmark high-level bar
items.description: A glass-walled sky bar and terrace over the Vltava — one of the few genuine high-level views in a city of low rooftops.

items.name: Terasa U Zlaté Studně
items.area: Malá Strana (Lesser Town), below the Castle
credentials: Atop the U Zlaté Studně hotel — a MICHELIN Guide dining address
items.description: A rooftop terrace tucked beneath Prague Castle — the Baroque rooftops and spires of the Lesser Town laid out at your feet.

items.title: Private dawn on the Charles Bridge
items.description: The statues and river mist to yourself with a guide, before the crowds and buskers arrive.

items.title: Private concert in a baroque hall or church
items.description: A chamber recital in one of the city's historic halls, arranged for a small party.

items.title: After-hours at Prague Castle
items.description: A curator-led evening walk through the castle complex and St Vitus after the gates close.

items.title: Private tasting at a historic brewery cellar
items.description: A guided cellar tasting of Czech beer and Moravian wine most visitors never see.

plan.heading: 3 days in Prague, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Prague Castle and St Vitus Cathedral at opening, then the Golden Lane before the day tours arrive.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Descend through the Lesser Town to the Wallenstein Garden, then coffee at the Augustine cloister.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at La Degustation Bohême Bourgeoise, the Michelin room reworking old Czech recipes on Haštalská.

days.title: The old town and the river

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Cross the Charles Bridge at first light, then the Old Town Square and the Astronomical Clock before ten.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Jewish Quarter — the Old-New Synagogue and the Spanish Synagogue — at an unhurried pace.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Field, the Michelin-starred room near the river, then Hemingway Bar for a late drink.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Mucha Museum and the Municipal House, then a private viewing of the Slav Epic if it is on show.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at the Café Savoy, then browse the Pařížská maison houses before packing up.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at the Alcron, the restored Art Deco room off Wenceslas Square.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Malá Strana
items.description: Baroque lanes below the castle — the most atmospheric, romantic base.

items.name: Vinohrady
items.description: Leafy residential streets and the best restaurants — for a local stay.

items.name: Josefov / Old Town
items.description: Central and historic but busy — for those who want everything on foot.

events.name: Prague Spring International Music Festival
events.note: The country's premier classical festival, opening with Smetana's Má vlast.

events.name: Signal Festival
events.note: A festival of light installations that transforms the historic centre after dark.

events.name: Christmas markets
events.note: The Old Town and Wenceslas squares fill with wooden stalls and mulled wine.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: You arrive at Václav Havel Airport (PRG), about 30 minutes by private car into the centre, with a chauffeur handling the approach through the cobbled quarters.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The historic core is compact and walkable but the cobblestones are unforgiving, so keep a private driver for evenings and anything beyond the old town.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Connectivity is strong; an eSIM works instantly and wifi is dependable, though the EU roaming zone covers Czechia as well.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Czech koruna, not the euro; cards are widely taken but keep some koruna for taxis and cafés, and a 10 percent tip is customary at restaurants.

onGround.note: Stay in Malá Strana or on the quieter side of the Old Town away from the tourist crush; taxis are best pre-booked through your hotel to avoid overcharging, and the city rewards early mornings before the crowds reach the Charles Bridge.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: May, June and September give warm days and long light over the Old Town without August's heat; December has atmospheric markets but short, cold days. Avoid January-February for grey cold and July-August for peak crowds.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No non-stop from India; cleanest routing is via Munich or Frankfurt on Lufthansa (about 10h40m total), or via Zurich on SWISS, all with fine business cabins. A single European hub connection keeps it simple; the Baku routing on Azerbaijan Airlines is marginally faster but weaker in premium.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations needed; tap water is safe to drink. Prague is safe; the main nuisances are pickpockets and overcharging taxis around tourist squares, so use booked cars.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian food is straightforward and Indian options are good. Govinda and Dhaba Beas are dependable pure-veg spots; Jain requests are best pre-arranged as local menus lean onion-garlic.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Prague, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Queenstown — TripAgent
seo.description: Queenstown, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Queenstown
hero.tagline: Alpine adventure capital on a glacial mountain lake.

ourTake.lede: Queenstown is an adrenaline town that quietly does luxury very well — the trick is to balance one big adventure day against slower time on the lake and in the wine country next door. Base in or near the centre for the first night, then consider decamping to the quieter side of the lake. Central Otago's wineries are half the reason to come and most people underrate them; don't.
ourTake.comeIf: You want mountains and lakes with adventure or fine wine at the doorstep.
ourTake.skipIf: You want a short-haul trip; New Zealand is a long way for anything under a week.

firstLook.heroCaption: Modern pool villa with palms and umbrella

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: December to March delivers warm, long-lit days for the lake and hikes; June to August is ski season with the Winter Festival, and April brings Arrowtown's gold - there is no truly bad time.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Sep, Oct, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Queenstown. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Rosewood Matakauri
credentials: Travel + Leisure World's Best Awards 2024 — Top 100 Hotels in the World (No. 45)
Condé Nast Traveler Gold List / Readers' Choice
items.description: A tiny Rosewood lodge above Lake Wakatipu — three suites and four villas in the beech forest, service to rival any city house.

items.name: Blanket Bay
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: A great stone-and-timber lodge on the shore of Lake Wakatipu beneath the Humboldt range — the archetype of the New Zealand high-country lodge.

items.name: The Lindis
items.description: An architectural marvel under a slatted timber roof in a remote high-country valley — pods and suites dissolving into the landscape.

items.name: Eichardt's Private Hotel
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: The best few rooms in town — an 1861 lakefront landmark on Marine Parade, run as an intimate private hotel.

items.name: Gibbston Valley Lodge & Spa
items.description: Standalone villas set among organic Pinot Noir vines, beside the region's original wine cave and its landmark winery.

items.name: Azur Lodge
items.description: Nine private hilltop villas with floor-to-ceiling glass framing Lake Wakatipu and the Remarkables — seclusion two miles from town.

items.name: Whare Kea Lodge & Chalet
items.description: A six-room lakeside lodge on the shore of Lake Wanaka, with its own alpine chalet high in the Buchanan range for heli-guests.

items.name: Sofitel Queenstown Hotel & Spa
items.description: French polish in the heart of the village — the most refined full-service city hotel in Queenstown proper.

items.name: Hulbert House
items.description: A restored 1888 Victorian villa turned eight-room boutique hotel — the grand private-residence feel, above the village.

items.name: Stoneridge Estate
items.description: An alpine retreat and vineyard on the shores of Lake Hayes — five-star calm between Queenstown and Arrowtown.

items.name: QT Queenstown
items.description: A design-led, playful house near the lakefront — style and a good bar at a gentler price.

items.name: Skyline Gondola & Bob's Peak
items.description: The steepest cable-car lift in the Southern Hemisphere climbs 480m in about ten minutes to a glass-fronted eyrie over Lake Wakatipu, with The Remarkables and Cecil and Walter Peaks laid out across the water. Ride up for a leisurely buffet at the Stratosfare Restaurant, or simply for the sundowner view — gentle enough for the grandparents, spectacular for everyone.

items.name: The Skyline Luge
items.description: At the top of the gondola, gravity carts wind down banked, tunnelled tracks with 220-degree views of the lake and mountains — the Blue Track a gentle cruise, the Red Track steeper and faster. It is the rare thrill that a nine-year-old and a grandfather can both take on, at their own pace, side by side.

items.name: TSS Earnslaw Steamship Cruise to Walter Peak
items.description: The 1912 'Lady of the Lake' is the only hand-fired coal steamship still carrying passengers in the Southern Hemisphere — a 90-minute glide across the water to Walter Peak High Country Farm, engine room open to wander and a pianist on deck. At the farm, a gourmet barbecue and a sheep-shearing show delight children while elders relax by the fire; ask for the vegetarian menu in advance.

items.name: Queenstown Gardens & Lakefront Peninsula
items.description: A leafy peninsula reaching into Lake Wakatipu, threaded with rose gardens, giant sequoias, a frisbee-golf course and easy flat paths right on the water — five minutes' stroll from the town centre. It is the gentle, unhurried heart of Queenstown: a picnic, a slow lakeside walk, and the mountains reflected on still mornings.

items.name: The Queenstown Lakefront & Steamer Wharf
items.description: The waterfront promenade is the town's living room — jetties, the historic Steamer Wharf, lakeside restaurants and the famous Fergburger queue just up the hill. Take an evening walk as the peaks turn pink, or hand the family a lakeside table for dinner with the water at your feet.

items.name: Shotover Jet
items.description: The only operator licensed inside the sheer Shotover Canyons, these red jet boats skim inches from rock walls at 85kph and spin the signature 360s down a river no other boat can run. A thrilling but accessible half-hour — the kind of adrenaline the teenagers demand and the parents secretly love.

items.name: Kawarau Bridge Bungy — the World's First
items.description: AJ Hackett opened commercial bungy jumping here in 1988; the 43m leap off the historic suspension bridge into the Kawarau River is where the whole sport began. Even if no one in the family jumps, the viewing decks and cantilevered platform make it a genuine pilgrimage — watch, cheer, and photograph the leap.

items.name: The Nevis Bungy & Swing
items.description: Reached by 4WD across private farmland, the Nevis is New Zealand's highest bungy — a 134m plunge from a pod slung over a canyon — plus the world's biggest swing, which arcs a vast 300m and can be ridden tandem. This is the serious adventurer's badge; for the rest, the drive and the canyon setting alone are extraordinary.

items.name: Shotover Canyon Swing & Canyon Fox
items.description: A 60m freefall from a 109m clifftop platform before a giant 200m swing sweeps you over the river — jumped forwards, backwards or in one of dozens of theatrical release styles. It sits in the sweet spot between bungy and pure fun, with the milder Canyon Fox zipline alongside for those who prefer to watch.

items.name: Skydive Over The Remarkables (NZONE)
items.description: Tandem jumps from 9,000, 12,000 or 15,000 feet fall over an almost unfair panorama — the lake, the alps and the fjords all at once. It is the once-in-a-lifetime photograph; and for family members staying on the ground, the drop zone viewing is part of the theatre.

items.name: White-Water Rafting the Shotover & Kawarau Rivers
items.description: The Shotover delivers grade 3–5 rapids down the legendary Skippers Canyon Road and through the dark Oxenbridge Tunnel; the Kawarau runs a gentler grade 2–3 for families and first-timers. A guided, full-day wilderness outing — choose the river to match your nerve.

items.name: Onsen Hot Pools & Day Spa
items.area: Arthurs Point, above the Shotover River
items.description: Private cedar-lined hot tubs perched over the Shotover gorge, where a garage-style wall slides open so you soak half-inside, half under the open alpine sky. Booked room by room, it is the discreet, restorative counterpoint to a day of adventure — a couples' soak, or the whole family unwinding with the mountains in view.

items.name: Gibbston Valley Wine Tour
items.description: Twenty-five minutes from town, Central Otago's 'Valley of the Vines' is world-famous for cool-climate Pinot Noir, its cellar doors strung along the Kawarau Gorge. A private-driver tour lets everyone taste freely — seated fireside at Amisfield, or deep inside the country's largest wine cave at Gibbston Valley — over a long, unhurried lunch.

items.name: Gibbston Valley Winery, Wine Cave & Cheesery
items.description: The region's oldest vineyard, first vintage 1987, is now a small estate in itself — a candlelit tasting in New Zealand's largest wine cave, an on-site cheesery, a bistro and a luxury lodge and spa. A single, elegant stop that satisfies serious wine lovers and casual visitors alike.

items.name: Amisfield Cellar Door & Restaurant
items.description: A rustic converted woolshed turned into one of the country's most acclaimed dining rooms, where the celebrated 'Trust the Kitchen' tasting menu is paired with the estate's own Pinot. Reserve well ahead; it is the definitive long lunch, and the kitchen handles vegetarian and dietary requests with real care.

items.name: Arrowtown — Historic Gold-Rush Village
items.description: A jewel of a settlement on the gold-bearing Arrow River, its 1860s Buckingham Street lined with more than sixty preserved miners' cottages, boutiques and cafés. A gentle, walkable day of history and browsing — with the excellent Lakes District Museum for the curious and gold-panning in the river for the children.

items.name: Arrowtown Chinese Settlement
items.description: At the edge of town along Bush Creek stand the restored stone huts and Ah Lum's store of the Chinese gold-miners who arrived from 1866 — a quiet, moving record of a community that was pushed to the town's margins. A short, thoughtful walk that gives Arrowtown's prettiness real depth.

items.name: Arrowtown in Autumn
items.description: For a few weeks in April and May the town's avenues of oaks, poplars and sycamores blaze gold and amber — one of the most photographed sights in the South Island, crowned by the Arrowtown Autumn Festival. Time a visit here and the whole family walks through a painting.

items.name: Glenorchy & Paradise
items.area: Head of Lake Wakatipu, 45km from Queenstown
items.description: The road to Glenorchy is itself one of the world's great drives, hugging the lake to a tiny township at the gateway of Mt Aspiring National Park and the valley literally named Paradise. Base a serene day here among braided rivers and beech forest — the setting for Lord of the Rings' Misty Mountains and Isengard.

items.name: Dart River Wilderness Jet Safari
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Te Wāhipounamu / Mt Aspiring National Park
items.description: A jet boat threads the braided, glacier-fed Dart through the heart of a UNESCO wilderness, with 360-degree spins and a guided walk through ancient beech forest and film locations. Faster than the TSS Earnslaw but far gentler than the Shotover — a scenic thrill that spans the generations.

items.name: High-Country Horse Riding at Glenorchy
items.description: Guided treks cross glacial rivers and open flats beneath towering peaks, from gentle walking-pace rides for beginners to longer back-country trails. It is a soft, cinematic way into landscapes most visitors only see from a boat — well suited to a mixed-ability family group.

items.name: Lord of the Rings 4WD Film-Location Safari (Nomad Safaris)
items.description: A half-day 4WD tour to the real Middle-earth — the Kawarau Gorge that became the Pillars of the Kings, Deer Park Heights and The Remarkables that stood in for the Misty Mountains — with gold-panning along the way. Minimal walking and small Land Cruiser groups make it easy for every age.

items.name: Lake Hayes Loop Walk
items.description: A flat, beautiful 8km circuit around a mirror-still lake famous for its reflections of the surrounding hills — about two to three easy hours, or a gentle e-bike. One of the district's most relaxing outings, and a lovely stop paired with an Amisfield lunch nearby.

items.name: Moke Lake
items.description: A hidden, horseshoe-shaped lake ringed by hills down a short gravel road, gloriously quiet and framed for still-water reflections at dawn and dusk. A peaceful picnic, an easy loop walk or a paddle — the local's antidote to the town's bustle.

items.name: Milford Sound Day Trip
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Te Wāhipounamu / Fiordland National Park
items.description: Rudyard Kipling's 'eighth wonder of the world' — sheer cliffs, Mitre Peak and thundering waterfalls plunging into a dark fjord, cruised on a nature boat with dolphins, seals and penguins alongside. The classic full-day trip pairs a scenic coach through the UNESCO wilderness with the cruise; a private guide or a fly-cruise-fly upgrade turns the long day gracious.

items.name: Doubtful Sound Wilderness Cruise
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Te Wāhipounamu / Fiordland National Park
items.description: Deeper, wilder and far quieter than Milford — reached by boat across Lake Manapouri and a mountain pass, or by Air Milford's exclusive scenic flight — and famed for its 'Sound of Silence'. The connoisseur's fjord, for travellers who want the untouched over the iconic.

items.name: Milford Sound Scenic Flight (Fly-Cruise-Fly)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Te Wāhipounamu / Fiordland National Park
items.description: A 45-minute flight over the Southern Alps and glaciers to land at Milford, cruise the fjord, and fly home — often called the world's finest scenic flight, and a fraction of the driving day. The private, elevated way to see Fiordland when time and comfort matter.

items.name: Heli-Picnic on a Glacier
items.description: A helicopter tracks over Skippers Canyon and the edge of Mt Aspiring National Park to touch down on an ancient glacier or a secluded alpine spot such as Earnslaw Burn, where a fresh-produce picnic is laid out amid waterfalls and blue ice. The most private, discreet luxury Queenstown offers — bespoke catering, including vegetarian, arranged on request.

items.name: Scenic Helicopter Flight & Alpine Landing
items.description: Shorter flights sweep over the lake, The Remarkables and Cecil and Walter Peaks with a snow or summit landing — a gentle taste of the high country for those not ready for a full heli-picnic. A superb way to give elders the alpine grandeur without a hike.

items.name: Routeburn Track Guided Walk (Ultimate Hikes)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Te Wāhipounamu / Mt Aspiring & Fiordland National Parks
items.description: One of the world's ten classic hikes, a 32km alpine crossing of beech forest, high passes and hanging valleys — done as a guided full-day taste or a three-day lodge-based journey with all meals, packs carried and warm beds each night. The soft, curated way to walk a Great Walk.

items.name: Guided & Heli Fly-Fishing for Trout
items.description: Gin-clear high-country rivers hold sight-fishable brown trout that can top ten pounds; a private guide walks you to spring creeks, or a helicopter drops you into pristine backcountry water no road reaches. A meditative, world-class pursuit for the angler in the family — bespoke and unhurried.

items.name: Coronet Peak Ski Field
items.description: The closest field to town on a fully sealed road, with wide open runs, a strong learners' area and New Zealand's only floodlit night skiing followed by après.
