guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Signiel Seoul
credentials: MICHELIN Two Keys (2025) — Korea's only Two-Key hotel, with Signiel Busan
items.description: The city crowned from above — the upper floors of Korea's tallest tower, and its most decorated hotel.

items.name: The Shilla Seoul
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide 5-Star (2025, 7th consecutive year — Korea's first)
items.description: The grande dame of Korean hospitality — poised against Mount Namsan, and the country's benchmark for service.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Seoul
items.description: The surest hands in Seoul — a glass tower beside the palaces, where nothing is left to chance.

items.name: Josun Palace, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Seoul Gangnam
items.description: Heritage reborn in the heart of Gangnam — Korean motifs threaded through European modernism.

items.name: Fairmont Ambassador Seoul
items.description: Glass walls over the Han River, inside Sir Richard Rogers' landmark Parc.1 — understated new-Seoul glamour.

items.name: Park Hyatt Seoul
items.description: Minimalist, boutique-scaled calm above Gangnam — the quiet-luxury choice for those who prefer discretion.

items.name: Conrad Seoul
items.description: A sleek glass tower in the financial district, with the river laid out below.

items.name: Lotte Hotel Seoul
items.description: A long-cherished city classic in the middle of Myeongdong — grand, dependable, endlessly convenient.

items.name: Grand Hyatt Seoul
items.description: A hillside resort in the middle of the city — nine dining venues, and Seoul's most complete fitness and pool complex.

items.name: Banyan Tree Club & Spa Seoul
items.description: A self-contained spa resort at the foot of Namsan — a pool in nearly every room, ten minutes from downtown.

items.name: The Westin Josun Seoul
items.description: The oldest luxury name in the city, refreshed — a downtown classic with a walled garden of its own.

items.name: Andaz Seoul Gangnam
items.description: Hyatt's lifestyle house in Gangnam — design-led and plugged into Apgujeong's fashion energy.

items.name: RYSE, Autograph Collection
items.description: An art-and-design hotel in creative Hongdae — the base for members who want the city's cultural pulse.

items.name: L7 Myeongdong by Lotte
items.description: A bright, contemporary lifestyle tower in the thick of Myeongdong's shopping and street food.

items.name: Grand InterContinental Seoul Parnas
items.description: A large, capable Gangnam house wired straight into the COEX complex.

items.name: Mondrian Seoul Itaewon
items.description: The brand's first Asian house — a design-led lifestyle hotel in the thick of Itaewon.

items.name: Sofitel Ambassador Seoul
items.description: French spirit on the shore of Seokchon Lake, in the shadow of Lotte World Tower.

items.name: JW Marriott Dongdaemun Square Seoul
items.description: A polished house overlooking the old city gate, at the heart of Seoul's night-market district.

items.name: Gyeongbokgung Palace
items.description: The grandest of the Joseon dynasty's five palaces, its throne hall and lotus-pond pavilion framed by the peaks of Bugaksan behind. Time your morning for the changing-of-the-guard ceremony at Gwanghwamun Gate, and rent hanbok nearby so the whole family enters free — a photograph the grandparents will keep.

items.name: Changdeokgung Palace & Secret Garden (Huwon)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Changdeokgung Palace Complex
items.description: The best-preserved royal palace, and the only one where kings let the landscape lead rather than the geometry. The Secret Garden — five centuries of private royal retreat, lotus ponds and pavilions — is entered by timed guided tour only, so book the English slot in advance for a quieter, unhurried walk.

items.name: Bukchon Hanok Village
items.description: A living hillside of restored tile-roof hanok houses strung between the two great palaces, with lanes that suddenly open onto rooftop views over old Seoul. Residents still live here, so walk softly and early; the quiet upper alleys reward a slow, private wander far more than the crowded photo-spots.

items.name: Ikseon-dong Hanok Street
items.description: A 1930s hanok warren reborn as Seoul's most charming maze of tucked-away cafes, tea houses and tiny restaurants under glass-roofed alleys. Come for an afternoon of drifting between courtyards — an easy, atmospheric stop with plenty of dessert and tea for a multi-generational group.

items.name: Insadong
items.description: Seoul's traditional arts quarter — galleries, antique dealers, hanji paper shops and ceramics along a pedestrian spine, with the Ssamziegil spiral mall at its heart. The place to commission or buy serious Korean craft and celadon, and to find a calm vegetarian temple-food restaurant among the tea houses.

items.name: Samcheong-dong
items.description: The elegant lane rising from Gyeongbokgung's east wall, where hanok bones hold contemporary art galleries, design boutiques and refined cafes. Pair it with a Bukchon walk for the city's most graceful afternoon of browsing, with the wooded palace wall on one side.

items.name: National Museum of Korea
items.description: Korea's flagship museum and one of the largest in Asia, its vast halls tracing 5,000 years from gold crowns to the serene gilt-bronze Pensive Bodhisattva in its own darkened room. Entry to the permanent galleries is free, the scale is stroller- and elder-friendly, and half a day here anchors any first trip.

items.name: Leeum Museum of Art
items.description: Samsung's private museum: one building of Korean antiquities and celadon, another of modern and contemporary art, set in architecture by Mario Botta, Jean Nouvel and Rem Koolhaas. A concentrated, world-class collection — ask about private or docent-led viewing for a discreet, unhurried morning.

items.name: N Seoul Tower (Namsan Tower)
items.description: The city's classic panorama, reached by a wooded cable car up Namsan to an observation deck that takes in the whole basin and, on clear days, the mountains beyond. Go near sunset when Seoul lights up beneath you — an easy, crowd-pleasing outing for all ages.

items.name: Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP)
items.description: Zaha Hadid's silver, seamless neo-futurist landmark — Seoul's design and fashion hub, hosting major exhibitions and the after-dark LED rose garden. Wander the flowing halls, then dip into the surrounding 24-hour Dongdaemun wholesale fashion towers if the night is young.

items.name: Gwangjang Market
items.description: Korea's oldest continuously running market (1905), a roaring food alley of mung-bean bindaetteok, mayak gimbap and raw beef tartare eaten elbow-to-elbow with locals. For UHNI travellers it's the deliberate opposite of fine dining — visceral, real Seoul; go with a guide who can steer vegetarians to the right stalls.

items.name: Namdaemun Market
items.description: Seoul's oldest and largest market, its roots in the 15th century, now a sprawling maze of everything from kitchenware and hanbok fabric to ginseng and mountain gear. Beside the restored Sungnyemun (Namdaemun) gate — Korea's National Treasure No. 1 — it's a plunge into everyday commercial Seoul.

items.name: Jogyesa Temple
items.description: The chief temple of Korean Jogye-order Buddhism, right in the city centre, its main hall shaded by an ancient white pine and lantern-strung courtyard. Sit for a moment of calm between the palaces and Insadong; templestay and tea programmes can be arranged in advance for a deeper, quiet experience.

items.name: Bukhansan National Park
items.description: Granite spires and forested ridges rising straight out of the northern suburbs — one of the world's most-visited national parks, with trails from gentle temple walks to the scramble up Baegundae (836m). A guide and private car to the trailhead make a half-day summit or an easier valley hike simple for a family.

items.name: Seoul City Wall & Naksan Park
items.description: The Joseon-era fortress wall still ribbons across the city's inner hills; the Naksan stretch is the gentlest, an easy paved climb to a hilltop park with a wide sunset view over the rooftops. Combine it with the muraled Ihwa hillside village just below for a quiet, walkable evening.

items.name: Han River (Hangang) Parks
items.description: The broad river that splits Seoul is lined with a chain of riverside parks — cycle at Yeouido, picnic with fried chicken and a mat, or take a sunset dinner cruise past the illuminated bridges. Banpo's Moonlight Rainbow Fountain, the world's longest bridge fountain, puts on a nightly water-and-light show in warm months.

items.name: Seongsu-dong
items.description: Seoul's 'Brooklyn' — a former shoe-factory district now full of raw-concrete flagship stores, designer cafes and pop-up boutiques, and the epicentre of the city's craft and coffee culture. The most fashion-forward afternoon in town, and where luxury houses now stage their Seoul events.

items.name: Gangnam & Apgujeong Rodeo
items.description: South of the river: the polished district of luxury flagships, plastic-surgery clinics and K-pop agencies, with Apgujeong's Rodeo Street and the Cheongdam boutiques for serious high-end shopping. Base here for proximity to the grandest hotels, spas and Michelin-tier Korean fine dining.

items.name: Starfield Library, COEX Mall
items.description: A soaring 13-metre open library of 50,000 books inside Asia's largest underground mall — one of Seoul's most photographed indoor spaces. Easy, air-conditioned, and next to the COEX Aquarium and SMTOWN, it's a reliable rainy-day or with-children stop in Gangnam.

items.name: Bongeunsa Temple
items.description: A 1,200-year-old mountain temple marooned amid the glass towers of Gangnam, facing the COEX complex across the road — the serene counterpoint to the district's gleam. Its 23-metre standing Buddha and evening lantern courtyard make it a moving five-minute stop between meetings or shopping.

items.name: Hongdae
items.description: The university-fuelled arts and nightlife quarter — indie live-music clubs, street buskers, vintage shops and the youngest energy in Seoul. Come after dark for the buskers and the bars; a lively contrast to the palaces, best for the younger members of a travelling group.

items.name: Itaewon & Gyeongnidan-gil
items.description: Seoul's most international quarter, where the hillside Gyeongnidan and Haebangchon lanes hold the widest spread of global restaurants — including reliable halal and Indian options near the Seoul Central Mosque. Useful ground for travellers who want familiar or dietary-specific dining alongside the view down to Namsan.

items.name: Myeongdong
items.description: The dense downtown shopping grid — Korean cosmetics flagships, department stores, and after-dark street-food carts of egg bread and grilled lobster. Efficient for skincare and gifting hauls, with the Myeongdong Cathedral, Korea's mother church, for a quiet moment above the crush.

items.name: Deoksugung Palace & Stone Wall Road
items.description: The intimate downtown palace where Joseon met the modern world — traditional halls stand beside a Western-style stone hall, and its changing-of-the-guard is the most central. The tree-lined Deoksugung Doldam-gil stone-wall walk beside it is one of the city's loveliest strolls, especially in autumn.

items.name: Cheonggyecheon Stream
items.description: A once-buried stream reopened as a 10-kilometre sunken green corridor threading the heart of downtown — you descend from the traffic into a cool ribbon of water, stepping stones and evening light installations. An easy, level walk to break up a day of city sightseeing.

items.name: Changgyeonggung Palace
items.description: The quietest and most gardened of the royal palaces, built as a residence for dowager queens, with a large pond, a glass-and-iron botanical greenhouse from 1909, and far fewer crowds than its neighbours. Its rear connects to Changdeokgung, so the two can be walked together in one calm morning.

items.name: Jongmyo Shrine
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Jongmyo Shrine
items.description: The austere Confucian royal ancestral shrine where the spirit tablets of the Joseon kings are enshrined — a long, low, deeply solemn hall down a stone spirit-path through old forest. Its living ritual music and dance, the Jongmyo Jerye, is itself a recognised intangible heritage; visit by timed entry for the stillness.

items.name: Seoul Museum of Art (SeMA)
items.description: The city's principal contemporary art museum, behind the preserved facade of the former Supreme Court near Deoksugung, with a strong programme and a permanent Chun Kyung-ja gallery. Central, free to enter, and a graceful pairing with the Deoksugung stone-wall walk next door.

items.name: Seoul Museum of Craft Art (SeMoCA)
items.description: Korea's first public craft museum, opened 2021 on a historic school site between Bukchon and Insadong, tracing metalwork, ceramics, lacquer and textile across the centuries. A refined, uncrowded stop for anyone who buys craft seriously, with free admission.

items.name: Ttukseom / Seoul Forest
items.description: A large riverside park of woodland, a deer enclosure and open lawns beside the Han, adjoining the Seongsu boutiques — the city's most family-easy green space. Bring the children for the deer and the water play, then walk into Seongsu for coffee.

items.name: Lotte World Tower & Seoul Sky
items.description: At 555 metres, Korea's tallest building, with the Seoul Sky observatory near the top — glass-floor ledge, the world's highest, and a 360-degree view across the whole metropolis to the mountains. Fast lifts and clear timed entry make it an easy marquee outing; the tower also holds a Signiel luxury hotel and premium mall.

items.name: Lotte World
items.description: One of the world's largest indoor theme parks under a glass dome, plus the outdoor 'Magic Island' on a lake — a full, weatherproof day of rides for families with children. Right beside the tower, so a young group and an older one can split and reconvene.

items.name: War Memorial of Korea
items.description: A vast, moving museum and outdoor display tracing the Korean War and the peninsula's military history, with tanks, aircraft and a wall of the fallen. Free and thoughtfully told; it gives essential context for anyone heading to the DMZ.

items.name: Jjimjilbang & Korean Spa
items.description: The Korean bathhouse ritual — hot and cold pools, jade and salt saunas, scrubs and shared rest halls — is a cultural must; grand versions like Dragon Hill Spa run around the clock. For UHNI travellers wanting discretion, the top hotels and members' clubs offer private hammam-style suites and premium jade-room treatments.

items.name: Blue House (Cheong Wa Dae)
items.description: The former presidential residence behind Gyeongbokgung, opened to the public in 2022 — blue-tiled halls, formal gardens and a hillside path with a rare open view straight down over the main palace. Reserve a free entry slot in advance; it's a genuinely new thing to see in old Seoul.

items.name: Inwangsan & Suseongdong Valley
items.description: The granite mountain on the city's western edge, with a section of the old fortress wall, shamanist shrines among the boulders and a short valley trail that Joseon painters immortalised. Close to town and far quieter than Bukhansan — a soulful half-day for a walker who wants the folk-spiritual side of Seoul.

items.name: Gwanghwamun Square & Sejong Story
items.description: The great civic plaza on the palace axis, flanked by statues of King Sejong and Admiral Yi Sun-sin, with underground exhibition halls telling their stories. The ceremonial heart of the city and the natural starting point for a downtown day; grand at night when the palace gate is lit.

items.name: Ihwa Mural Village
items.description: A hillside of old alley-houses that artists covered in murals and installations, climbing beside the Naksan city wall with quiet cafes and long views back over the city. Steep but short, and best paired with the Naksan wall walk for a low-key, photogenic afternoon.

items.name: Garosu-gil
items.description: The ginkgo-lined 'tree-lined street' in Sinsa, dense with designer boutiques, flagship beauty stores and stylish cafes — Seoul's polished, tree-shaded shopping stroll. Golden in autumn, and an easy south-of-river counterpoint to Samcheong-dong's traditional lanes.

items.name: DMZ & Third Infiltration Tunnel
items.description: An hour north, the Demilitarized Zone at the world's most fortified border — the Dora Observatory looking into North Korea, the Third Tunnel dug by the North, and the Imjingak peace park. It must be visited on an authorised tour with passport; a private licensed guide makes it seamless and adds the deeper political context.

items.name: Suwon Hwaseong Fortress
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Hwaseong Fortress
items.description: A 40-minute train south, the magnificent late-18th-century fortress of King Jeongjo rings the old town of Suwon with 5.7 kilometres of gate-pierced walls you can walk in full. Pair it with the Haenggung temporary palace and, if travelling with children, the nearby Korean Folk Village of restored period houses.

items.name: Nami Island (Namiseom)
items.description: A crescent river island reached by ferry, its tree-lined avenues famous from Korean drama and gorgeous in every season — metasequoia and gingko lanes, cycling paths and lakeside cafes. Often combined with the Garden of Morning Calm and the Petite France village for a gentle countryside day out of the city.

items.name: Namsangol Hanok Village
items.description: Five aristocratic Joseon houses relocated to the foot of Namsan around a traditional garden and pond, with craft demonstrations, tea and a time capsule buried for 2394. A compact, central and uncrowded way to see hanok interiors when Bukchon feels too busy.

items.name: Noryangjin Fisheries Market
items.description: Seoul's great wholesale fish market — a cavernous hall of tanks where you choose your seafood and carry it upstairs to have it prepared and served on the spot. A vivid, non-touristy feast for adventurous eaters; a guide helps navigate the pricing and the raw-versus-cooked choices.

items.name: K-Pop & Hallyu Experience (HYBE Insight / SMTOWN)
items.description: For the K-culture obsessed, Seoul is the source — the entertainment districts around COEX and Yongsan hold agency stores, exhibition spaces and cafes tied to the biggest groups. A themed afternoon, or private studio and concert access via a fixer, turns a fan's dream into the trip's centrepiece.

items.name: Ttukseom Hangang / Banpo Bridge Cruise
items.description: An evening Han River cruise from Yeouido glides beneath the lit bridges to the Banpo Moonlight Rainbow Fountain show, with private and dining charters available. A relaxed, romantic way to see the skyline from the water — easily arranged as a discreet private booking.

items.name: Mingles
items.description: Korea's only three-star — Kang Min-goo's modern Korean, and the city's proudest table.

items.name: La Yeon
items.description: Korean haute cuisine at its most refined, high in The Shilla — hansik with the city at its feet.

items.name: Jungsik
items.description: The restaurant that redefined new Korean fine dining — and took the idea to the world.

items.name: Kwonsooksoo
items.description: Kwon Woo-joong's deeply seasonal Korean — royal-court refinement, quietly modernised.

items.name: Soigné
items.description: An inventive, globe-trotting kitchen that reads like a chef's private notebook.

items.name: Alla Prima
items.description: A precise, contemporary tasting counter — one of Gangnam's most assured two-stars.

items.name: Restaurant Allen
items.description: Chef Seo Hyun-min's contemporary cooking — technically dazzling, quietly personal.

items.name: Evett
items.description: Joseph Lidgerwood's fierce commitment to Korean produce and fermentation — newly two stars.

items.name: Kojima
items.description: A jewel-box Edomae counter of great purity — Seoul's finest sushi omakase.

items.name: Mitou
items.description: Twin-chef Japanese cooking of rare finesse — kaiseki instincts, Seoul ingredients.

items.name: Onjium
items.description: A research kitchen reviving Korea's royal-court cuisine — history you can taste.

items.name: Mosu Seoul
items.description: Sung Anh's international-Korean cooking — the chef whose pedigree spans the world's great kitchens.

items.name: 7th Door
items.description: Kim Dae-cheon's seven-course narrative of Korean flavour — cerebral, seasonal, singular.

items.name: Eatanic Garden
items.description: Inventive Korean cooking 36 floors up — the highest new entry on Asia's list that year.

items.name: Pierre Gagnaire à Séoul
items.description: The French master's Seoul outpost — grand, generous cooking high above the city.

items.name: Sushi Kanesaka
items.description: The revered Ginza name, transplanted — an exacting Edomae counter inside The Shilla.

items.name: Sosuheon
items.description: Park Kyung-jae's exacting sushi counter — a freshly-starred omakase of real poise.

items.name: Kojacha
items.description: A refined Korean kitchen that carries its star with unshowy confidence.

items.name: Hansikgonggan
items.description: Chef Cho Hee-sook's soulful, home-rooted Korean cooking — hansik with real heart.

items.name: Kang Minchul Restaurant
items.description: A chef-led contemporary kitchen with a quietly devoted following.

items.name: Bicena
items.description: Elevated Korean fine dining high in Signiel — refined hansik with the skyline for company.

items.name: Yu Yuan
items.description: Classic Cantonese cooking in a rarefied setting — the Four Seasons' newly-starred room.

items.name: Muni
items.description: A refined Japanese kitchen in a hanok setting — precision in a traditional Korean house.

items.name: Zero Complex
items.description: Lee Chung-hoo's quietly brilliant modern cooking — one of Seoul's understated stars.

items.name: Soigné's Y'east
items.description: A contemporary kitchen that climbed from selection to a star on its own ideas.

items.name: Légume
items.description: A vegan tasting menu that earned its star on merit — plant cooking taken entirely seriously.

items.name: Gigas
items.description: Jung Ha-wan's Mediterranean-leaning cooking — sunlit flavours, freshly starred.

items.name: Tutoiement
items.description: Kim Do-yoon's intimate French room — newly starred, and deeply personal.

items.name: Escondido
items.description: Jin Woo-bum's ambitious Mexican cooking — a first star for the genre in Seoul.

items.name: Solbam
items.description: A modern Korean kitchen holding its star with seasonal, ingredient-led cooking.

items.name: Soseoul Hannam
items.description: Eom Tae-chul's inventive Korean cooking in fashionable Hannam.

items.name: YUN Seoul
items.description: A meticulous beef-focused Korean kitchen — hanwoo treated with reverence.

items.name: Gomtang Lab
items.description: Beef-bone soup raised to an art — long-simmered gomtang, done properly.

items.name: Neungdong Minari
items.description: Water-celery and grilled pork, Korean home cooking with a cult following.

items.name: Myeon Seoul
items.description: Handmade noodles paired with traditional Korean liquor — quietly excellent.

items.name: Seoryung
items.description: Cold buckwheat noodles at their most refined — a naengmyeon specialist of long standing.

items.name: ALT.a
items.description: Plant-based Korean-Chinese cooking with a modern, knowing hand.

items.name: Youhan
items.description: A small Thai bistro punching well above its price — bright, fresh, precise.

items.name: Seokyonanmyunbang
items.description: An easy, inventive Korean-Italian room that quietly won its Bib.

items.name: Mipildam
items.description: North Korean-style dumpling soup done with real care — soulful and honest.

items.name: Nishimuramen
items.description: A serious Japanese ramen shop that earned its Bib on the bowl alone.

items.name: Zest
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Bars 2025 (No. 2) — Best Bar in Korea
items.description: Korea's best bar and one of Asia's finest — Korean ingredients, sustainability and craft, with not a bottle in sight.

items.name: Bar Cham
items.description: A deeply Korean cocktail bar behind a wooden door near Gyeongbokgung — omija, perilla and fermented grains, mixed with real feeling.

items.name: Alice
items.description: An Alice-in-Wonderland speakeasy that rose 33 places in a year — theatrical, precise, and great fun.

items.title: Private hanbok dawn at Gyeongbokgung
items.description: An early palace walk in period dress before the day-trippers, with the throne hall to yourself.

items.title: Temple stay at a mountain monastery
items.description: An overnight at a Bukhansan or nearby temple with monks — dawn chanting and templefood.

items.title: Chef's table at a three-star kitchen
items.description: A seat at Mingles or La Yeon for the refined edge of Korean fine dining, booked well ahead.

items.title: Private night market and pojangmacha crawl
items.description: A guided walk through Gwangjang's stalls and street tents where the city really eats.

plan.heading: 4 days in Seoul, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle into the Josun Palace in Gangnam, then Gyeongbokgung and the changing of the guard before the midday crowds.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The hanok lanes of Bukchon on foot, ending at the tea houses and craft shops of Insadong.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Mingles, Kang Min-goo's three-Michelin reinterpretation of Korean seasons, with its jang trolley.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Leeum Samsung Museum for its Korean antiquities and contemporary wing, in Hannam-dong.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A gentle hike or cable ride at Bukhansan, the granite mountain that frames the city.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Refined hanjeongsan at Onjium, run by a foundation preserving Korean court cuisine.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private morning to the DMZ and the third tunnel, an hour north, with a knowledgeable guide.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Return for the design shops of Seongsu-dong and coffee at a converted-warehouse roaster.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dry-aged Korean beef at Byeokje Galbi or a counter of hanwoo at Born and Bred, charcoal-grilled tableside.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A morning at Jogyesa temple, then the antiquarian book and brush shops nearby.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The department-store food halls of Shinsegae and a last walk of the Cheonggyecheon stream.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Tasting menu at Evett, Joseph Lidgerwood's Korean-terroir cooking, and a nightcap at Charles H. in the Four Seasons.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Bukchon / Samcheong
items.description: Hanok lanes, galleries and palaces — for the traditional, walkable Seoul.

items.name: Itaewon / Hannam
items.description: International, design-led, strong on dining — a cosmopolitan base.

items.name: Gangnam / Cheongdam
items.description: Glossy retail and flagship stores — for shopping and modern luxury.

events.name: Cherry blossom season
events.note: Yeouido and the palace grounds bloom for roughly a week — the city's prettiest, busiest moment.

events.name: Seoul Lantern Festival
events.note: Illuminated lanterns line the Cheonggyecheon stream through the heart of downtown.

events.name: Buddha's Birthday / Lotus Lantern Festival
events.note: A lantern parade through central Seoul and temples strung with color — dates follow the lunar calendar.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Land at Incheon (ICN), consistently rated among the world's finest airports; a pre-arranged private sedan covers the roughly hour-long drive into Gangnam or the palace district.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with driver for the sprawl, with walking through Bukchon, Hannam and the boutique lanes of Cheongdam.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM or airport SIM both work seamlessly; Korea has among the fastest mobile and wifi networks on earth.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Korean won; cards are accepted virtually everywhere and tipping is not customary or expected.

onGround.note: Stay in Hannam-dong or Gangnam for discretion and fashion; skincare and dermatology are world-class and best pre-booked, and the finest hanjeongsik and omakase seat few and reward advance introduction.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Late April–May and late September–October are the kind months: mild, dry, with blossom in spring and crisp foliage in autumn. Avoid the July monsoon rains and the deep January–February cold.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Nonstop from Delhi on Korean Air and Air India to Incheon (ICN), about 7–7.5 hours out; Mumbai is usually one stop. Fly Korean Air Prestige/First and use their Incheon lounge, and allow time as ICN is large but smooth.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations; South Korea is very safe with world-class medical care and safe tap water (locals often prefer filtered). Routine vaccines suffice; winter air quality can dip, worth noting for the sensitive.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian takes effort as fish sauce and anchovy stock are pervasive, and Jain is hard without clear briefing; temple cuisine (sachal eumsik) is the exception and is superb. Balwoo Gongyang (Michelin temple vegetarian) is outstanding, and Itaewon has decent Indian options.

seo.title: Shanghai — TripAgent
seo.description: Shanghai, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Shanghai
hero.tagline: Art-deco riverfront facing a skyline of tomorrow.

ourTake.lede: Shanghai's pleasure is the contrast between the two riverbanks: the 1920s Bund and French Concession on one side, the science-fiction Pudong skyline on the other, and the trick is to sleep on the old side and admire the new one from across the water. Walk the plane-tree lanes of the former French Concession in the afternoon rather than queuing for observation decks, and save the Bund for a night when it is lit. The city is very easy to over-programme; leave time to simply wander the lane houses.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a fast, cosmopolitan city break with world-class dining, skyline views and serious shopping.
ourTake.skipIf: You want nature, quiet or an unfiltered, budget-first experience.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Bvlgari Hotel Shanghai
items.description: The Roman maison's 48-storey jewel, set inside the restored 1920s Shanghai Chamber of Commerce — glamour with a Bulgari signature.

items.name: The Peninsula Shanghai
items.description: The last great building raised on the Bund — an Art Deco grande dame with celadon walls and the river at its feet.

items.name: Capella Shanghai, Jian Ye Li
items.description: Fifty-five restored shikumen lane houses turned into private villas — the most secluded luxury in the city.

items.name: Amanyangyun
items.description: An Aman built from a transplanted Ming forest and camphor-wood mansions — a serene estate an hour from the towers.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental Pudong, Shanghai
items.description: The group's riverside flagship — a calm, contemporary house looking straight across the Huangpu to the Bund.

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton Shanghai, Pudong
items.description: A modern Art Deco tower high in Lujiazui, with the legendary Flair rooftop and full-frontal Bund views.

items.name: Waldorf Astoria Shanghai on the Bund
items.description: The old Shanghai Club reborn — home of the Long Bar, all dark wood and colonial-era grandeur on the southern Bund.

items.name: The Middle House
items.description: Piero Lissoni's serene, design-led house from the Swire stable — the quietest luxury in central Shanghai.

items.name: The PuLi Hotel and Spa
items.description: An urban-resort sanctuary beside Jing'an Park — a long infinity pool, a great spa, and a genuinely tranquil city retreat.

items.name: InterContinental Shanghai Wonderland
items.description: The 'deep pit' hotel built into a flooded quarry cliff — 18 storeys, two of them underwater, and unlike anywhere else on earth.

items.name: The Bund (Waitan)
items.description: The mile-long riverfront promenade where 1920s European stone facades face the neon towers of Pudong across the water. Walk it at dusk when the whole skyline switches on, then let your driver collect you for dinner up on the strip.

items.name: Huangpu River Evening Cruise
items.description: The Bund and the Pudong skyline are best seen from the middle of the river, both lit and mirrored on the water at once. A private charter with dinner aboard turns forty minutes of glow into the evening's centrepiece for the whole family.

items.name: Shanghai Tower Observation Deck
items.description: China's tallest building and one of the highest observatories on earth, reached by a lift that climbs 118 floors in under a minute. On a clear day the city unrolls in every direction; the twisting glass skin softens the wind far below.

items.name: Shanghai World Financial Center Observatory
items.description: The 'bottle opener' tower whose 100th-floor Sky Walk is a glass-floored bridge suspended 474 metres over the city. Children and grandparents alike freeze at the edge before daring the transparent floor.

items.name: Oriental Pearl Tower
items.description: The pink-sphered TV tower that became Shanghai's postcard symbol, with a glass-floor walkway ringing one of its orbs. Dated but beloved, it is the shot every first-time visitor wants of themselves against the skyline.

items.name: Yu Garden (Yuyuan)
items.description: A Ming-dynasty scholar's garden of rockeries, koi ponds, dragon-topped walls and moon gates, laid out over four centuries ago. A private guide reads the hidden symbolism in each pavilion so the labyrinth becomes a story rather than a crowd.

items.name: Yuyuan Bazaar & City God Temple
items.description: The warren of upturned-eave shophouses around the garden, thick with silk, jade, tea and steaming dumpling stalls beside the working Taoist City God Temple. Loud, festive and photogenic; go early with a guide before the tour buses land.

items.name: Nanxiang Steamed Bun Restaurant (xiaolongbao)
items.description: The century-old teahouse in the Yu Garden bazaar that made Shanghai's soup dumplings famous, still folding them by hand. Ask for a private upstairs table and vegetable-filled baskets so vegetarian travellers share in the ritual.

items.name: Shanghai Museum (People's Square)
items.description: The bronze-ding-shaped building holding one of the world's great collections of Chinese bronzes, ceramics, jade, painting and calligraphy. A calm, air-conditioned afternoon of five thousand years of craft, ideal with a scholar-guide.

items.name: Shanghai Museum East
items.description: The vast new Pudong wing, opened in full in 2024 and nearly double the original in size, with eight galleries devoted mostly to ancient Chinese art. The showpiece is the panoramic top-floor view back across the river to the People's Square building.

items.name: Museum of Contemporary Art Shanghai (MoCA)
items.description: A glass pavilion set in People's Park showing rotating international and Chinese contemporary shows, a cool counterpoint to the antiquities nearby. Small enough to fold into a morning without tiring younger travellers.

items.name: West Bund Museum (Centre Pompidou x West Bund)
items.description: David Chipperfield's opalescent-glass museum on the riverside, home to the landmark exhibition partnership with Paris's Centre Pompidou. Modern-art masterpieces from the Pompidou's collection, rotated in a serene daylit setting.

items.name: Long Museum (West Bund)
items.description: A dramatic concrete gallery of vaulted 'umbrella' arches, holding one of China's most important private collections from imperial art to the contemporary. The architecture alone rewards the visit; the shows are consistently ambitious.

items.name: Yuz Museum
items.description: A converted aircraft hangar on the West Bund turned into a soaring space for large-scale contemporary and immersive installations. The scale suits the blockbuster shows that draw Shanghai's art crowd.

items.name: Power Station of Art
items.description: China's first state-run contemporary art museum, set in a former power plant with its old chimney still marking the riverside. Home to the Shanghai Biennale and cavernous, industrial-scale installations.

items.name: Wukang Road (Ferguson Lane area)
items.description: The most photographed corner of the old French Concession, anchored by the ship-prow Wukang Mansion and lined with plane trees and 1920s villas. Stroll slowly with a coffee; the whole street is a period film set.

items.name: Tianzifang
items.description: A maze of shikumen lane houses reworked into tiny galleries, design boutiques, tea rooms and cafes. Tight and buzzing; a guide keeps the family together and points you to the makers worth stopping for.

items.name: Xintiandi
items.description: Restored stone-gate lane houses turned into an upscale district of restaurants, wine bars and flagship boutiques. The polished, safe, evening-out heart of old Shanghai, walkable and easy for multi-generation groups.

items.name: The Plane-Tree Streets of the French Concession
items.description: Wuyuan Road, Anfu Road, Fuxing Road and their neighbours form a leafy grid of villas, independent cafes and boutiques under a canopy of century-old planes. The most walkable, human-scaled Shanghai, best explored on foot with no fixed plan.

items.name: Jing'an Temple
items.description: A gilded Buddhist temple whose gold roofs sit startlingly against glass office towers on Nanjing West Road. Small but sumptuous, with a giant silver Buddha and a camphor-wood hall, an easy pause between shopping streets.

items.name: Jade Buddha Temple
items.description: An active monastery housing two Buddhas carved from single blocks of white Burmese jade, brought from Myanmar in the 1880s. Incense, chanting and a vegetarian temple kitchen make it a serene, veg-friendly stop.

items.name: Nanjing Road (East & West)
items.description: China's most famous shopping street, from the pedestrian neon stretch near the Bund to the luxury flagships of Nanjing West. A guide and driver let you cherry-pick the maisons and skip the crush.

items.name: Shanghai Propaganda Poster Art Centre
items.description: A private collection of thousands of Maoist-era and Cultural Revolution posters, now shown in a tower on Yan'an West Road after years hidden in a basement. Vivid, strange and unexpectedly moving; a guide gives the political context.

items.name: M50 Art District (Moganshan Road)
items.description: A cluster of galleries and studios in old textile-mill warehouses along Suzhou Creek, long the hub of Shanghai's contemporary scene. Graffiti-lined and gritty; go with a guide who knows which galleries are showing.

items.name: Rockbund Art Museum
items.description: A jewel-box contemporary museum in a restored 1932 Art Deco building a block behind the Bund. Tightly curated, ambitious shows in an intimate, beautifully restored setting.

items.name: fu1015 / Historic Concession Villas
items.description: The grand garden mansions of the old concession, some now private clubs, restaurants and galleries behind their walls. A curated visit inside one of these villas reveals the East-meets-West glamour of 1930s Shanghai.

items.name: Rooftop Bars over the Bund
items.description: Terraces such as Bar Rouge, the Peninsula's Sir Elly's and the towers of Pudong put the whole lit skyline at eye level with a cocktail in hand. The definitive Shanghai sundowner, reserved ahead for the best rail-side tables.

items.name: Fuxing Park
items.description: A formal French-style park where locals practise tai chi, dance and play chess under the trees each morning. A gentle, authentic slice of daily Shanghai life, lovely for grandparents and children between grander sights.

items.name: People's Square & People's Park
items.description: The green civic heart of the city, ringed by the Shanghai Museum, MoCA and the grand theatre, with the famous weekend 'marriage market' of parents' handwritten notices. A convenient, central anchor between museums.

items.name: Suzhou Creek Waterfront Walk
items.description: The revived creekside promenade lined with Art Deco warehouses, the historic post office and quiet cafes, far calmer than the Bund. A slow morning walk that shows the city's older, industrial romance.

items.name: Shanghai Disneyland
items.description: Asia's largest Disney park, with the world's biggest Enchanted Storybook Castle and its own distinctly Chinese touches. A full family day; a VIP tour guide skips the queues and choreographs the rides for a multi-gen group.

items.name: Shanghai Ocean Aquarium
items.description: A large modern aquarium beside the Oriental Pearl, with one of the longest underwater viewing tunnels in the world. A reliable crowd-pleaser for younger travellers within the Pudong sightseeing cluster.

items.name: Tianzifang & Taikang Road Design Lanes
items.description: The wider Taikang Road creative quarter around Tianzifang, dense with independent designers, ceramicists and studio-shops. Good for unhurried, one-of-a-kind gift-hunting away from the flagship stores.

items.name: Longhua Temple & Pagoda
items.description: Shanghai's largest and oldest temple complex, its leaning tenth-century pagoda rising beside working halls and a peach orchard that blooms in spring. Quieter than the central temples, with a vegetarian dining hall.

items.name: Zhujiajiao Water Town
items.description: The best-preserved of Shanghai's own canal towns, seventeen hundred years old, with stone arch bridges, willow-lined waterways and a hand-poled boat ride. Just over an hour by car, it makes an easy half-day escape into old Jiangnan.

items.name: Qibao Old Town
items.description: A compact canal town reachable on the metro, with a short old street of snack stalls, a small temple and a scattering of bridges. The closest water-town taste to the city centre when time is short.

items.name: Classical Gardens of Suzhou (Day Trip)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Classical Gardens of Suzhou
items.description: The UNESCO-listed scholar gardens, the Ming-dynasty Humble Administrator's Garden chief among them, are barely half an hour away by bullet train. A private day of raked ponds, poetry pavilions and silk workshops, worlds from the neon.

items.name: West Lake, Hangzhou (Day Trip)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — West Lake Cultural Landscape of Hangzhou
items.description: The lake that has defined Chinese ideas of beauty for a thousand years, its causeways, pagodas and tea hills an hour south by train. A private boat, a Longjing tea garden and a lakeside lunch make a serene full day.

items.name: Wuzhen Water Town (Day Trip)
items.description: The most cinematic of the canal towns, its eastern and western scenic zones threaded with stone bridges, black-tiled roofs and lantern-lit night waterways. Stay for the evening lighting; the western zone is quietest after dark.

items.name: Tongli Water Town (Day Trip)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Classical Gardens of Suzhou (Retreat and Reflection Garden)
items.description: A serene town of fifteen canals, forty ancient bridges and its own UNESCO-listed classical garden, the Retreat and Reflection Garden. Combines beautifully with Suzhou for an unhurried Jiangnan day away from the crowds.

items.name: Zhouzhuang Water Town (Day Trip)
items.description: The most famous of the ancient water towns, nine hundred years old, with fourteen stone bridges and preserved Ming and Qing dwellings mirrored in the canals. Go early with a private guide to have the bridges before the tour groups.

items.name: Shanghai Grand Theatre / Symphony Hall
items.description: World-class ballet, opera and orchestral programming in two architecturally striking halls, the acoustically superb Symphony Hall among them. A refined evening; the concierge secures the best boxes for touring companies.

items.name: Bund Sightseeing & Waibaidu Bridge
items.description: The steel Waibaidu Bridge and riverside gardens at the Bund's northern end frame the classic view where Suzhou Creek meets the Huangpu. A quiet, photogenic bookend to the main promenade.

items.name: Qibao to Sheshan Excursion
items.description: Sheshan's forested hill carries the Basilica of Our Lady, an observatory and easy walking trails, a green half-day beyond the city. A gentle nature-and-history option for families wanting a break from pavements.

items.name: Bund Bull & Financial District Walk
items.description: The Lujiazui skyway loops the three super-towers past the bronze Bund Bull and glass plazas, giving vertigo-free views up at the giants. An easy stroll that stitches the observation decks together.

items.name: Shanghai History Museum (Shanghai Revolution Museum)
items.description: Set in the former Shanghai Race Club building, it traces the city's rise from fishing village to global port with rich period detail. A well-told introduction that gives context to everything else you'll see.

items.name: Cool Docks / South Bund Fabric & Antique Markets
items.description: The South Bund fabric market lets you commission tailored qipao, suits and shirts in a day, near the riverside Cool Docks dining quarter. A practical, memorable stop for made-to-measure keepsakes of the trip.

items.name: Ultraviolet by Paul Pairet
items.description: A single table for ten, a secret address, and a psycho-taste tour of sound, scent and vision — the most theatrical meal in Asia.

items.name: Taian Table
items.description: Chef Stefan Stiller's precise, produce-led modern European tasting menu at an open counter — three stars, quietly held.

items.name: 8½ Otto e Mezzo BOMBANA
items.description: Umberto Bombana's grand Italian on the Bund — white truffle in season and a room built for occasions.

items.name: Da Vittorio Shanghai
items.description: The Cerea family's Bergamo institution, transplanted to Shanghai — the paccheri Vittorio is worth the crossing.

items.name: Fu He Hui
items.description: Tony Lu's zen temple to Chinese vegetarian fine dining — meat-free courses of real depth across three hushed floors.

items.name: Bao Li Xuan
items.description: Elegant Cantonese inside the Bulgari — silk-lined rooms, creek views and cooking of real finesse.

items.name: Maison Lameloise
items.description: The Shanghai outpost of the storied three-star Burgundy house — classical French haute cuisine high over the river.

items.name: Canton 8 (Huangpu)
items.description: Chef Chan Yan Tak's protégé kitchen — pristine, classical Cantonese that has held two stars for years.

items.name: Imperial Treasure Fine Chinese Cuisine
items.description: Grand, classical Cantonese and Peking duck in a polished Bund-front room — a benchmark banquet address.

items.name: Ji Pin Court
items.description: Refined, restrained Cantonese cooking in a serene setting — two stars earned on precision, not spectacle.

items.name: Meet the Bund
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 (No. 14 — Best Restaurant on the Chinese Mainland)
items.description: Chef DeAille Tam's inventive Fujian-rooted cooking — named the best restaurant on the Chinese mainland.

items.name: Ling Long
items.description: Chef Jason Liu's set menu chases xian (umami) on a course-by-course journey across regional China — inventive and personal.

items.name: Il Ristorante – Niko Romito
items.description: Niko Romito's essential, pared-back Italian inside the Bulgari — deceptively simple, deeply exact.

items.name: Xin Rong Ji
items.description: The celebrated Taizhou seafood house — pristine yellow croaker and coastal Zhejiang cooking at its finest.

items.name: Fu 1088
items.description: Refined Shanghainese in a 1930s garden villa of private rooms — old-money Shanghai dining, room by room.

items.name: Yong Yi Ting
items.description: Elegant Jiangnan cooking — the delicate, sweet-savoury flavours of the Yangtze delta, beautifully rendered.

items.name: Da Dong (Jing'an)
items.description: The roast-duck maestro's Shanghai kitchen — lean, lacquered Peking duck and modern Chinese theatre.

items.name: Yong Fu (Maoming Road)
items.description: Genteel Ningbo cooking in a former French Concession mansion — seafood-led and quietly aristocratic.

items.name: Canton Table
items.description: Modern Cantonese and dim sum with a Bund view — an easy, polished lunch or relaxed dinner.

items.name: Cheng Long Hang
items.description: Homely, hearty Shanghainese done properly — red-braised pork and drunken crab in an unfussy neighbourhood room.

items.name: Long Bar
credentials: Waldorf Astoria Shanghai on the Bund (Forbes 4-Star hotel)
Restoration of the historic 1911 Shanghai Club Long Bar
items.description: The restored 34-metre bar of the old Shanghai Club — where the city's tai-pans drank a century ago, poured with proper polish.

items.name: Speak Low
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars — listed every year since 2016 (peak No. 10, 2017)
items.description: Shingo Gokan's hidden multi-floor temple of drinks — enter through a sliding bookshelf and climb toward the serious pours.

items.name: Sober Company
items.description: Shingo Gokan's all-day, all-night compound — café, izakaya and the Sober Society cocktail den built on Chinese ingredients.

items.name: Epic
items.description: A refined, spirit-forward bar with a Bund-side pedigree — precise classics and a long-standing place on the Asian list.

items.name: Coa Shanghai
items.description: The agave temple's Shanghai outpost — 200-plus tequilas and mezcals, and the hospitality that redefined the Asian bar.

items.name: Pony Up
items.description: An intimate, welcoming neighbourhood bar with real craft behind the counter — a fresh face on the Asian list.

items.name: Union Trading Company
credentials: Cornerstone of Shanghai's modern cocktail scene
items.description: Yao Lu's cornerstone of the modern Shanghai scene — the bar that defined what a great neighbourhood cocktail room could be.

items.name: Flair Rooftop
credentials: One of the city's highest rooftop bars
items.description: The Ritz-Carlton's 58th-floor terrace — the single most dramatic full-frontal view of the Bund with a drink in hand.

items.title: Rooftop dinner on the Bund facing Pudong
items.description: A table at one of the Bund's historic buildings, timed for the skyline lighting across the Huangpu, is Shanghai's signature evening.

items.title: Private tailoring at a South Bund fabric master
items.description: A made-to-measure commission with a trusted tailor, fitted over a few days, is a genuinely Shanghai souvenir.

items.title: Yu Garden and Old City before opening
items.description: A guided early walk through the Ming-dynasty garden and tea house avoids the daytime crush entirely.

items.title: Private jazz evening in a Concession-era club
items.description: Shanghai's old jazz tradition survives in a handful of clubs; a reserved table is the elegant late-night close.

plan.heading: 3 days in Shanghai, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Check into the Peninsula Shanghai at the head of the Bund, then walk the colonnade to the river at first light.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Yu Garden and the lanes of the old city, then the Shanghai Museum's bronzes on People's Square.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Ultraviolet by Paul Pairet, the single-table sensory room outside the city, booked months ahead.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The plane-tree streets of the former French Concession on foot, and the villas of Wukang Road.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Contemporary art at the Long Museum West Bund, then tea in a converted lane house.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Huaiyang cuisine at Fu He Hui, the vegetarian-leaning tasting menu in a serene courtyard house.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A morning to the canals of Zhujiajiao, the water town an hour from the city, by private car.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Return to Pudong for the Shanghai Tower observatory and a walk of the riverside promenade.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Cantonese fine dining at Yong Yi Ting, then cocktails high in the Ritz-Carlton's Flair over the Bund.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Former French Concession
items.description: Plane-tree lanes, boutiques, and lane houses; the most charming and walkable base for those who want atmosphere.

items.name: The Bund & Huangpu
items.description: Grand riverfront architecture and heritage hotels; suits travellers who want the classic skyline at the doorstep.

items.name: Jing'an
items.description: Central, polished, and well-connected around the temple and Nanjing Road West; ideal for shopping and easy metro access.

events.name: Longhua Temple Fair
events.note: One of Shanghai's oldest folk fairs fills the grounds of its most important temple with performances and craft stalls.

events.name: Shanghai International Film Festival
events.note: China's leading film festival brings hundreds of screenings and its Golden Goblet competition to cinemas across the city.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Arrive at Pudong (PVG) for international routes; a chauffeured car handles the transfer to the Bund or the former French Concession, as the maglev is fast but ends short of the centre.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver is essential given scale and traffic, with unhurried walking through the tree-lined French Concession lanes.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Bring a China-ready eSIM with a built-in VPN, as many Western sites and apps are blocked; hotel wifi works but the firewall applies.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Chinese yuan; the city runs on Alipay and WeChat Pay, so link an international card in advance and carry some cash as a fallback; tipping is not customary.

onGround.note: Stay on the Bund for the skyline or the French Concession for charm; set up Alipay before arrival, and a Mandarin-speaking guide smooths reservations and the near-cashless everyday.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: October–November is the clearest, most comfortable window, and late March–May is pleasant spring. Avoid July–August humidity and heat and the damp, raw January cold.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Nonstop service from Delhi resumed in 2026 on Air India and China Eastern to Pudong (PVG), about 6.5–7 hours; from Mumbai expect one stop. Fly Air India business (flat beds on the 787) or connect via Hong Kong on Cathay; note Indians need a China visa arranged in advance.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations, though hepatitis A and typhoon-season timing are worth noting; Shanghai is safe. Do not drink the tap water — use bottled or filtered — and expect that many Western apps and cards need a VPN or WeChat/Alipay workaround.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian is workable and Jain difficult unless briefed carefully, as stocks and lard appear even in vegetable dishes; Buddhist vegetarian restaurants are the safe route. Godly (Gongdelin), the classic Shanghainese vegetarian house, is excellent, and Indian tables cluster around Hongqiao.

closing.headingHtml: Shanghai, with someone who knows it.

seo.title: Shimla — TripAgent
seo.description: Shimla, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Shimla
hero.tagline: Colonial hill-station grandeur amid Himalayan cedar forests.

ourTake.lede: Shimla is at its best out of season and out of the town centre; the Mall Road crush is precisely what to avoid, so base yourself a little outside and use the town for its colonial architecture and walks. The toy-train up from Kalka is a genuine pleasure and worth building the trip around. Come in spring or autumn; peak summer and the snow-season weekends bring Delhi's traffic with them.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a colonial hill station, the toy train and cool pine air near Delhi.
ourTake.skipIf: You want to dodge peak-season crowds, or want a beach.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Shimla. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Wildflower Hall, An Oberoi Resort, Shimla
credentials: The Oberoi Group — flagship Himalayan resort
Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Travel Awards — ranked among Asia's best resorts
Travel + Leisure India — recognised luxury resort
Former residence of Lord Kitchener, Commander-in-Chief of the British Army in India
items.description: The former estate of Lord Kitchener, reborn as a cedar-forest Oberoi palace — the Himalayan icon of Indian luxury.

items.name: The Oberoi Cecil, Shimla
credentials: The Oberoi Group — heritage flagship in the city
Established 1884; the founding Oberoi property, reopened 1997 after full restoration
items.description: Shimla's most storied address since 1884 — the hotel where Mohan Singh Oberoi began, restored to hushed colonial grandeur.

items.name: The Oberoi Clarkes, Shimla
credentials: Built 1898; one of Shimla's oldest hotels and the first owned by the Oberoi group
Ministry of Tourism — upgraded to Heritage Grand classification (2012)
items.description: A grand colonial bungalow on the Mall since 1898 — the first hotel the Oberoi group ever owned, intimate and full of history.

items.name: The Chalets Naldehra
credentials: Set on the Naldehra golf estate — the golf course laid out in 1905 by Lord Curzon, among the oldest in Asia
Boutique alpine-chalet resort, ~19 rooms and cottages
items.description: A boutique estate of chalets at 7,000 feet, wrapped around Asia's oldest golf course among the deodars.

items.name: Koti Resort, Shimla — Radisson Individuals Retreats
credentials: Hilltop resort in the Mashobra hills near Shimla
items.description: A hilltop retreat in the Mashobra forest with colonial warmth, Himalayan views and Radisson-backed service.

items.name: The Koti Village Resort, Kufri
credentials: Luxury cottages with panoramic Himalayan and Shimla-city views
items.description: Luxe glamping-style cottages at 8,000 feet, with 180-degree Himalayan panoramas above Kufri.

items.name: The Ridge
items.description: The great open promenade at 2,200 metres where all of Shimla gathers, the snow peaks lined up beyond Christ Church and the timber gables. A gentle early-morning stroll here, before the day-trippers arrive, is the Queen of Hills at her most composed.

items.name: The Mall Road
items.description: The pedestrianised Raj-era spine of the town, its lamp-lit facades and colonnades running above the valley. A private guide turns the evening amble into a walk through Kipling's Simla; the antique jewellers and Kashmiri shawl merchants reward an unhurried browse.

items.name: Christ Church
items.description: The butter-yellow neo-Gothic church of 1844, one of the oldest in North India, its stained glass and clock tower the postcard image of Shimla. Step inside for the cool hush and the organ; the frescoes were designed by Rudyard Kipling's father, Lockwood.

items.name: The Gaiety Theatre
items.description: A jewel-box Victorian Gothic theatre of 1887 by Henry Irwin, restored to its plush red-and-gilt glory, where the Raj once staged its amateur dramatics. A guided visit lets you stand on the same boards trod by viceroys and, later, a young Prithviraj Kapoor.

items.name: Scandal Point
items.description: The open shoulder where the Mall meets the Ridge, named for the alleged elopement of a Patiala prince with a viceroy's daughter. The best free view in Shimla and the town's natural meeting place, framed against the peaks.

items.name: The Viceregal Lodge (Indian Institute of Advanced Study)
items.description: The vast Elizabethan-Jacobean stone palace of 1888 from which the British ruled India each summer, where the 1945 Simla Conference and the Partition talks unfolded. The guided tour of the panelled interiors and manicured lawns is the single grandest Raj experience in the hills.

items.name: Jakhoo Temple & the giant Hanuman
items.description: Shimla's highest point at 2,455 metres, crowned by a 108-foot saffron Hanuman visible from across the town, on the spot the Ramayana links to the god's rest. A serene, cedar-shaded pilgrimage above the bustle; watch your spectacles around the resident monkeys.

items.name: Jakhoo Ropeway
items.description: The glass-cabin aerial ropeway that lifts you from the Ridge to the Hanuman temple in minutes, sparing the steep forest climb and gifting a bird's-eye sweep of the ridgeline roofs. The dignified way up for elders and children in a multi-generation party.

items.name: Kalka–Shimla Toy Train
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site (Mountain Railways of India)
items.description: The narrow-gauge marvel of 1903 that climbs 96 km through 102 tunnels and over 800 bridges to the summer capital, best savoured in a chartered first-class or the glass-roofed dome car. A slow, cinematic ascent through the Shivaliks that no drive can rival.

items.name: Shimla State Museum
items.description: A colonial mansion on Mount Pleasant holding Pahari miniature paintings, Kangra bronzes, temple sculpture and Himachali textiles. A quiet, well-curated hour that gives the whole hill region its artistic context, away from the crowds.

items.name: Johnnie's Wax Museum
items.description: A small, playful wax gallery in the Willow Banks estate on the Mall, its London-made figures of film stars and cricketers a reliable hit with children. A light-hearted diversion to break up a heritage-heavy afternoon.

items.name: Kali Bari Temple
items.description: The 1845 Bengali temple to Goddess Shyamala, from whom Shimla takes its name, a five-minute walk off the Mall. A living shrine of quiet devotion and a fragrant, flower-strewn contrast to the promenade below.

items.name: Tara Devi Temple
items.description: A 250-year-old hilltop temple to the star goddess, brought from Bengal, ringed by deodar at 1,850 metres with long views back to Shimla. A peaceful, uncrowded stop on the road in, worth the short detour for the panorama alone.

items.name: Kamna Devi Temple, Prospect Hill
items.description: A short, pretty pine climb to a Kali shrine crowning Prospect Hill, rewarded with a 360-degree sweep over Shimla and the valleys. A gentle morning walk that locals prize far more than tourists do.

items.name: Annandale
items.description: A flat green saucer amid the hills, once the Raj's playground for polo, cricket and flower shows, now home to a golf course and the Army Heritage Museum. A rare piece of level ground in Shimla and a graceful, breezy afternoon.

items.name: Summer Hill
items.description: A leafy, quiet suburb where Mahatma Gandhi stayed at Georgian-style Rothney Castle's neighbourhood and where Himachal University now sits. A calm base for pine walks and a stop on the toy-train line, away from the Mall's crush.

items.name: Chadwick Falls
items.description: A 90-metre cascade plunging through deep deodar and oak forest, fullest and most dramatic just after the monsoon. A short trek through the Glen woods brings you to a cool, green amphitheatre far from the town noise.

items.name: The Glen Forest
items.description: A shaded stream-side hollow of dense pine below the Cecil, a favourite Raj-era picnic ground and gentle woodland ramble. Close enough to walk to, wild enough to feel a world away from the Mall.

items.name: Lakkar Bazaar
items.description: Shimla's old woodcraft market beside the Ridge, stacked with hand-carved walnut and deodar keepsakes, walking sticks and toys. The place to pick up an honest, made-in-the-hills souvenir rather than a factory trinket.

items.name: Green Valley
items.description: The photogenic saddle on the way to Kufri where the road opens onto rolling green slopes and, on clear days, distant snow. A classic pause for a chai and a photograph, deodars falling away on both sides.

items.name: Kufri
items.description: A high meadowed ridge at 2,720 metres with grandstand Himalayan views, pony rides up to Mahasu Peak and winter snow. Touristy at its heart but a soaring backdrop; go early, or ride above the crowds to the quieter tops.

items.name: Himalayan Nature Park, Kufri
items.description: A high-altitude wildlife park sheltering snow leopard, Himalayan black bear, musk deer and the state-bird Monal pheasant among the deodars. A gentle, shaded walk that turns Kufri into something the children will actually remember.

items.name: Naldehra Golf Course
items.description: A nine-hole (18-tee) course laid out by Lord Curzon in 1905 on a deodar-fringed ridge at 2,200 metres, so loved he named a daughter for it. Among the oldest and highest greens in India, and a rarefied morning even if you never lift a club.

items.name: Mashobra
items.description: A hushed forest village of apple orchards and cedar walks, home to the Presidential Retreat and to Shimla's most exclusive resort. The address to choose for quiet, orchard-scented seclusion within reach of the town.

items.name: Craignano
items.description: An Italianate villa and terraced garden on a knoll above Mashobra, built by an Italian craftsman in the 19th century, now a serene HPTDC nature spot. A little jewel of a picnic ground with wide valley views and almost no crowd.

items.name: Fagu
items.description: A tiny hamlet above Kufri wrapped in apple orchards and drifting mist, with long, uncluttered views over terraced valleys. A gentler, quieter alternative to Kufri for those who want the scenery without the ponies.

items.name: Chail Palace
items.description: The 1891 summer palace the Maharaja of Patiala built in pique after being barred from Shimla, set in cedar forest on its own hilltop. Stay or lunch amid the royal drawing rooms and lawns for a taste of princely, rather than viceregal, India.

items.name: Chail Cricket Ground
items.description: The world's highest cricket and polo ground at 2,444 metres, levelled from a hilltop in 1893 and now part of the Chail Military School. A remarkable, pine-ringed plateau in the sky, worth the drive for the sheer improbability of it.

items.name: Kali ka Tibba, Chail
items.description: A hilltop Kali temple crowning the ridge above Chail, reached through thick deodar and rewarded with a full-circle Himalayan panorama. The finest viewpoint in the Chail hills and blessedly uncommercial.

items.name: Chail Wildlife Sanctuary
items.description: A protected belt of pine, oak and deodar sheltering the Himalayan black bear, leopard, ghoral and cheer pheasant. A calm forest drive or guided birding walk for those who prefer nature to the tourist trail.

items.name: Tattapani Hot Springs
items.description: Sulphur-rich thermal springs on the banks of the Sutlej, long prized for easing aches and stiff joints, with riverside camps and riverbank massages. A restorative, off-beat day out that pairs a warm soak with dramatic gorge scenery.

items.name: Narkanda
items.description: A fir-forested town at 2,700 metres deep in the apple belt, a gateway to snow views and gentle winter skiing. The air turns crisp and the crowds thin here; it is Shimla's district as it was before the resorts arrived.

items.name: Hatu Peak
items.description: A 3,400-metre summit above Narkanda crowned by the old wooden Hatu Mata temple, with a huge sweep of snow ranges on a clear day. A short drive plus a walk to one of the most panoramic and least-visited tops near Shimla.

items.name: Kotgarh & Thanedar apple orchards
items.description: The cradle of Indian apple growing, where the American Satyanand Stokes planted the first commercial orchards in 1916, now heavy with blossom in spring and fruit in autumn. Stay in an orchard homestead and walk the terraces where the industry began.

items.name: Sangla Valley (Baspa Valley)
items.description: A green Kinnauri valley of apple and apricot orchards, timber-and-stone villages and the Baspa river, ringed by snow peaks. A farther, wilder day or two beyond Shimla, and the loveliest introduction to the Kinnaur hills.

items.name: Chitkul
items.description: The last inhabited village on the old Indo-Tibetan trade route, where the motorable road ends against the meadows and the roar of the young Baspa. Remote, elemental and unforgettable, best reached with a seasoned mountain driver.

items.name: Kalpa
items.description: An orchard village perched opposite the sacred 6,000-metre Kinner Kailash range, whose face turns gold at sunrise above the apple trees. A serene, high-altitude perch for those going deep into Kinnaur, rich in old wooden temples.

items.name: Kasauli
items.description: A tiny, unspoilt colonial hill town of cobbled lanes, timber cottages and Christ Church, cool and green year-round. A restful, low-key detour on the way up from the plains, entirely free of the Mall's bustle.

items.name: Barog
credentials: On the UNESCO Kalka–Shimla Railway line
items.description: A sleepy railway hamlet on the toy-train line, home to the line's longest tunnel and its famous ghost story, wrapped in pine. A quiet, storybook halt to alight at or lunch in on the slow ascent to Shimla.

items.name: Wildflower Hall, An Oberoi Resort
items.description: Once Lord Kitchener's forest retreat, now a grand cedar-clad Oberoi at 2,500 metres with an open-air spa whirlpool facing the snows. Shimla's most romantic address for a honeymoon or a multi-generation escape, run entirely on hydro power.

items.name: The Oberoi Cecil
items.description: The Mall's most storied hotel, a Heritage Grand where Raj society once danced in the ballroom, now all fireplaces, a soaring wood atrium and valley views. A stay that puts you inside old Simla itself, minutes from the Ridge.

items.name: Chapslee
items.description: The Kapurthala royal family's 1830s mansion, still lived-in and hosting guests among Gobelin tapestries, Murano chandeliers and Persian carpets, opened as one of India's first heritage hotels in 1976. Tea or a stay here is a private audience with the vanished aristocratic Simla.

items.name: Shaily Peak
items.description: A short pony ride or walk to a modest summit with sweeping views over apple slopes and, on a clear day, distant snow. An easy, rewarding leg-stretch for a family exploring the Kufri hills.

items.name: Kufri Fun World
items.description: A hilltop amusement park with a go-kart track and one of the world's highest rides, a burst of colour amid the deodars. An easy crowd-pleaser to keep children happy on a Kufri day.

items.name: The Restaurant at Wildflower Hall
items.area: Mashobra / Charabra (Wildflower Hall, An Oberoi Resort)
credentials: Inside Wildflower Hall, An Oberoi Resort — the region's defining hotel
items.description: Indian, Asian and Continental cooking in a glass conservatory over the deodar forest — the grandest table in the Himalayas here.

items.name: Dining at The Oberoi Cecil
credentials: Inside The Oberoi Cecil — Shimla's founding heritage hotel
items.description: All-day Indian and international cooking beneath the hotel's soaring wood-panelled atrium — heritage dining in the heart of Shimla.

items.name: Ashiana & Goofa
credentials: Run by Himachal Pradesh Tourism Development Corporation (HPTC)
Long-standing Ridge / Mall Road landmark — the twin Ashiana (upstairs) and Goofa (basement)
items.description: A Shimla institution run by Himachal Tourism — a landmark circular pavilion on the Ridge, with the cave-like Goofa below.

items.name: Baljees
credentials: Long-standing Mall Road institution — a multi-generational Shimla landmark
items.description: A Mall Road fixture for generations — the beloved bakery-restaurant famous for its sweets and unhurried Shimla mornings.

items.name: Wake & Bake Café
credentials: Long-standing Mall Road café — a Shimla favourite
items.description: The Mall's favourite all-day café — a balcony table over Shimla, from breakfast crêpes to late cake.

items.name: The Bar at Wildflower Hall
items.area: Mashobra / Charabra (Wildflower Hall, An Oberoi Resort)
credentials: Inside Wildflower Hall, An Oberoi Resort — the region's defining hotel
The Oberoi Group — signature Himalayan lounge and bar
items.description: A firelit lounge and bar in the old Kitchener estate — single malts and mountain quiet, the grandest nightcap in the hills.

items.name: The Big Dipper, Koti Resort
credentials: Inside Koti Resort, Shimla — Radisson Individuals Retreats
Fireside English-style bar with a craft-cocktail list
items.description: An English-style bar with a warm fireplace and craft cocktails, tucked into the Mashobra hills.

items.title: Heritage ride on the Kalka–Shimla toy train
items.description: The UNESCO-listed narrow-gauge line through 100-odd tunnels, ideally in a chartered or first-class carriage.

items.title: Private colonial-architecture walk
items.description: A guided morning among the Viceregal Lodge, Christ Church and the Raj-era buildings, with the history told well.

items.title: Estate stay and forest walk in the deodar hills
items.description: A heritage cottage among the cedar forests outside town, with private guided walks.

items.title: Sunrise drive to Kufri or Chharabra ridge
items.description: An early run to the high ridges for the first light on the snow ranges before the day crowds.

plan.heading: 3 days in Shimla, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive at Wildflower Hall, Oberoi in Chharabra — Lord Kitchener's old estate high above Shimla — and take in the cedar forest and the snow line from the terrace.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A guided walk of the Ridge, Christ Church and the old Gaiety Theatre, then the Scandal Point and Mall in the cool of late afternoon.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Wildflower Hall's restaurant, with Himachali dishes among the classics and the deodars floodlit outside.

days.title: The toy train and the Raj

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive down to board a heritage carriage on the Kalka–Shimla railway for a stretch of the UNESCO narrow-gauge line through its tunnels and curves.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Viceregal Lodge at Observatory Hill, seen properly with a historian, then the Himachal State Museum's miniatures.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A fireside dinner back at the hotel, with a Himalayan wine and the valley lights below.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A guided forest walk from Chharabra toward Kufri through the cedar and oak, with the high peaks opening up.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A private picnic lunch at a viewpoint over the Sutlej valley, then a spa afternoon at the Oberoi.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A quiet final dinner on the terrace before the descent to Kalka or Chandigarh.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Chharabra / Mashobra (above town)
items.description: Quiet forested ridges with the best heritage retreats; best for calm and views.

items.name: The Ridge / Mall (central Shimla)
items.description: The colonial heart with the church and promenade; convenient but crowded at peak times.

items.name: Chhota Shimla / Kasumpti
items.description: Residential and quieter, a short way from the centre; for a more local, less touristy base.

events.name: Summer Festival
events.note: A week of cultural performances and events on the Ridge, marking the start of the hill-station season.

events.name: Winter Carnival
events.note: A festive cold-season carnival with music and local culture as the snow sets in.

events.name: Sipi Fair
events.note: A traditional spring fair in nearby Mashobra, a window into local Pahari culture.

events.name: Peak snow season
events.note: The most reliable window for snowfall around Shimla and Kufri, though weekends draw heavy crowds.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Chandigarh (IXC), then a three-to-four-hour chauffeured drive up to Shimla; the toy train from Kalka is a charming, unhurried alternative for part of the route.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with driver to the edge of the town, then walking, as the Mall Road and the central ridge are pedestrian-only; hotels arrange porters and short transfers.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Jio and Airtel 4G is solid in town but drops on the surrounding hill roads; hotel wifi is the steadier option for work.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Indian rupee; cards work along the Mall and at hotels, with cash useful for the bazaar and porters; tipping is modest.

onGround.note: The old town centre is vehicle-free, so choose a hotel near the Ridge or Mall to avoid a steep uphill walk with luggage; evenings are cold at 2,200 metres, and the colonial-era Cecil or Wildflower Hall side offers the finest quiet above the crowds.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: March to June brings pleasant 15-30C days, and December-January delivers snow; avoid July-September, when heavy monsoon and landslide-prone roads disrupt travel.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Shimla's own airstrip is limited, so fly to Chandigarh (IXC), then a scenic 3-3.5 hour drive up (about 115 km). Chandigarh takes direct flights from Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru on IndiGo/Air India/Vistara; use the lounge at Delhi T3 or Mumbai before the short hop, and pre-book a car for the hill climb.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: Modest altitude of about 2,200m, no acclimatisation needed for most. No special vaccinations beyond routine cover. Safe hill town; the main caution is icy or landslide-prone roads in winter and monsoon. Drink sealed or filtered water.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Easy for vegetarians, with plentiful North Indian veg and Himachali dishes; Jain is understood at the heritage hotels if flagged. The Oberoi Cecil and Wildflower Hall do polished vegetarian menus, and the Mall Road cafes cover casual veg fare.
