seo.title: Siem Reap — TripAgent
seo.description: Siem Reap, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Siem Reap
hero.tagline: Gateway to Angkor's temples and Khmer artistry.

ourTake.lede: Siem Reap is Angkor, and Angkor rewards patience — a three-day temple pass and a good private guide beat a rushed single day every time. Everyone piles into Angkor Wat for sunrise; the light is often better and the crowds thinner at Ta Prohm mid-morning or at Bayon's faces late afternoon. Base yourself well and treat the town itself as somewhere to rest, not sightsee.
ourTake.comeIf: You want Angkor at dawn and a handful of genuinely fine hotels in a quiet, low-key town.
ourTake.skipIf: You need a beach, nightlife or a busy itinerary beyond the temples.

firstLook.heroCaption: Modern pool villa with palms and umbrella

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: November to February brings dry, temperate mornings ideal for Angkor at dawn and the river's boat races; time the March or September equinox for sunrise aligned to the central tower, and avoid the March-May heat and summer monsoon.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Siem Reap. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Amansara
credentials: Aman Resorts — the group's Cambodia flagship
items.description: The address of the town — King Norodom Sihanouk's own 1960s guesthouse, reborn as Aman's most intimate resort.

items.name: Shinta Mani Wild — a Bensley Collection Hotel
items.area: South Cardamom National Park (≈3 hrs from Siem Reap; day-trip or add-on)
credentials: National Geographic Unique Lodges of the World
items.description: Bill Bensley's tented wilderness camp — arrive by zipline over a waterfall, sleep in the forest he saved from poaching.

items.name: Raffles Grand Hotel d'Angkor
items.description: The grande dame since 1932 — the first luxury hotel in Siem Reap, and still its most storied address.

items.name: Park Hyatt Siem Reap
items.area: Central Siem Reap (near Pub Street / Old Market)
credentials: Bensley design (former Hotel de la Paix, 1957)
items.description: The heritage Hotel de la Paix, reimagined by Bill Bensley — the most central of the true luxury houses.

items.name: Shinta Mani Angkor — Bensley Collection Pool Villas
items.description: Bill Bensley's theatrical black-and-white boutique — serene, artful, and quietly one of the town's most beloved stays.

items.name: Zannier Hotels Phum Baitang
items.description: A 'green village' of stilted wooden villas across working rice paddies — the rural retreat, a few minutes from the temples.

items.name: Anantara Angkor Resort
items.area: Central Siem Reap (near the Royal Residence)
items.description: An intimate all-suite house — 39 suites, private courtyards, and a butler to each — steps from the town centre.

items.name: Angkor Wat at sunrise
items.description: The largest religious monument on earth — 162 hectares raised by Suryavarman II around 1150 and dedicated to Vishnu — mirrored in its own moat as the sun climbs behind the five lotus towers. For an Indian family the shock of recognition is total: the bas-relief galleries run for hundreds of metres of the Churning of the Ocean of Milk and scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata. A private guide and a pre-dawn car secure the still-dark walk across the causeway before the crowds arrive.

items.name: The bas-relief galleries of Angkor Wat
items.description: Beyond the sunrise photograph lies the real marvel: nearly 600 metres of continuous carved wall depicting the Battle of Kurukshetra, the Battle of Lanka, Suryavarman's own army, heaven and 32 hells, and the great Samudra Manthan where gods and demons churn the cosmic ocean. Indian visitors read these panels like a familiar epic; a good guide slows the pace so grandparents and children take them in without the mid-day heat.

items.name: The faces of the Bayon at Angkor Thom
items.description: At the exact centre of Jayavarman VII's walled capital stands the Bayon, its towers carrying more than 200 vast serene faces that watch you from every angle as you climb. The lower galleries carve everyday 12th-century Khmer life — markets, cockfights, childbirth, war with the Cham — a rare human counterpoint to all the gods. Best in the soft light of early morning, with a guide to trace the eye-lines.

items.name: Baphuon, the tower of bronze
items.description: An 11th-century Shiva temple-mountain reached by a long raised causeway inside Angkor Thom, painstakingly rebuilt stone by stone in one of the largest jigsaw restorations ever attempted. Climb the steep upper terrace for a quieter, higher view over the treetops, and look for the vast reclining Buddha fashioned into its western wall by later Buddhist hands.

items.name: The Terrace of the Elephants
items.description: A 350-metre royal viewing platform from which the god-king once watched his armies and festivals pass below, its outer wall a continuous parade of life-size elephants, mahouts and hunting scenes. Stand where Jayavarman VII stood and look out over the Royal Square — an easy, flat, shaded walk that suits every generation.

items.name: The Terrace of the Leper King
items.description: Just north of the elephants, this smaller platform hides its best secret: a narrow trench along the inner face reveals an earlier buried wall, so you walk between two carved surfaces crowded with kings, apsaras and multi-headed nagas at arm's length. A quiet, atmospheric detour most rushed tours skip.

items.name: Ta Prohm, the tree temple
items.description: The temple the jungle refused to give back — silk-cotton and strangler-fig roots pour over doorways and prise apart the galleries, left deliberately unrestored so you see Angkor as the first explorers found it. Made famous by 'Tomb Raider', it is genuinely spellbinding for children; go at opening or late afternoon with a guide who knows which courtyards clear of crowds.

items.name: Banteay Srei, the pink citadel of the women
items.description: A miniature 10th-century Shiva temple in rose-pink sandstone, carved so finely the reliefs look cut in ivory — scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata, and the demon-king Ravana shaking Mount Kailasa. Some 25 km out among rice fields, it rewards the drive with the single most exquisite carving at Angkor; pair it with Kbal Spean for a full day out of town.

items.name: Preah Khan, the sword of the god-king
items.description: A sprawling monastic city built by Jayavarman VII for his father, half-swallowed by forest like Ta Prohm but with a fraction of the crowds — long corridors of diminishing doorways, a curious two-storey pillared hall, and roots draped over the outer walls. Genuine calm and grandeur; a favourite of guides who want to give discerning families the temples to themselves.

items.name: Neak Pean, the island shrine
items.description: A tiny Buddhist temple on a circular island at the centre of a great baray, reached by a boardwalk over water that in the wet season shimmers with lilies and drowned trees. It was conceived as a healing hospital modelled on the mythical Himalayan lake Anavatapta — a serene, contemplative stop rather than a monument to climb.

items.name: Ta Som and its embracing tree gate
items.description: A small, intimate Bayon-style temple on the outer circuit, best known for its eastern gopura where a strangler fig has grown clean over the face-tower, roots framing the stone visage like fingers. Rarely busy, it offers the tree-temple magic of Ta Prohm in a pocket-sized, unhurried setting.

items.name: Pre Rup at sunset
items.description: A tall 10th-century laterite temple-mountain, once a royal cremation ground, whose warm brick glows at dusk. Climb the steep tiers for a broad view over forest and rice paddy as the light goes gold — a calmer, more atmospheric sunset than Phnom Bakheng, and easy for a private group to have space at the top.

items.name: East Mebon, the temple of the vanished lake
items.description: A 10th-century Shiva pyramid that once stood on an island in the middle of a vast reservoir, now marooned in dry land — guarded at each corner by beautifully preserved monolithic stone elephants. Quiet, uncrowded and often paired with nearby Pre Rup for a late-afternoon loop.

items.name: Phnom Bakheng at sunset
items.description: The oldest temple-mountain of the Angkor plain, set on a hill between Angkor Wat and Angkor Thom, giving a rare elevated view of Angkor Wat's towers rising from the forest as the sun drops. Numbers are now capped at the summit, so a guide who times the climb turns a famous scrum into a composed hour.

items.name: Banteay Kdei and the royal bath of Srah Srang
items.description: A rambling, low-slung monastery temple full of dancing-apsara pillars and toppled galleries, paired across the road with Srah Srang — the 'Royal Bath', a huge stone-lined reservoir with a small landing terrace that is one of the loveliest, least-crowded sunrise spots in the park. A gentle, contemplative pairing away from the marquee sites.

items.name: The Roluos group — Bakong, Preah Ko and Lolei
items.description: The cradle of Angkor: the late-9th-century temples of Hariharalaya, the Khmer capital before Angkor itself, where the temple-mountain form was first attempted at Bakong. Preah Ko's brick towers still wear their original stucco and fine lintels. For anyone who wants the story in order, this is where the whole thousand-year epic begins — and it sees almost no crowds.

items.name: Prasat Kravan and its brick Vishnu reliefs
items.description: A small, easily missed 10th-century tower unique for its interior — rare brick bas-reliefs of Vishnu striding across the cosmos in three steps, and of Lakshmi, carved into the inner walls. A quick, quiet stop that rewards Hindu travellers with imagery they will recognise instantly and find nowhere else at Angkor.

items.name: Kbal Spean, the river of a thousand lingas
items.description: A jungle stream where 11th-century hands carved hundreds of lingas and yonis, plus Vishnu reclining on the serpent Ananta and Brahma rising on a lotus, straight into the riverbed and boulders so the water flowing over them is sanctified before it feeds the Angkor plain. A shaded 45-minute walk uphill leads to a small waterfall — deeply resonant, and best in the wet season when the river runs.

items.name: Phnom Kulen — the sacred mountain, waterfall and reclining Buddha
items.description: The holy mountain where Jayavarman II declared the Khmer Empire and its devaraja cult in 802, now Cambodia's most revered pilgrimage hill. A two-tier waterfall draws local families to bathe, and atop the summit a colossal 16th-century reclining Buddha is carved from a single sandstone boulder. A full private day-trip with a picnic; the mountain is one-way traffic and best begun early.

items.name: Beng Mealea, the temple the jungle keeps
items.description: A vast 12th-century temple built to the same plan as Angkor Wat but left almost entirely to the forest — collapsed galleries, moss-cloaked blocks and wooden walkways threading through the ruin. It is the closest thing to being an explorer stumbling on a lost city, and its remoteness keeps it blissfully quiet; a natural stop en route to Koh Ker.

items.name: Koh Ker, the pyramid capital in the forest
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Koh Ker: Archaeological Site of Ancient Lingapura or Chok Gargyar
items.description: A brief, brilliant 10th-century capital deep in the northern jungle, crowned by Prasat Thom — a seven-tier sandstone pyramid unlike anything else in Khmer architecture, climbable for a view over unbroken canopy. Long isolated and now cleared of mines, it makes a serious, rewarding full-day expedition by private car for those who want Angkor without another soul in sight.

items.name: The Angkor National Museum
items.description: The essential prologue to the temples — eight themed galleries, a hall of a thousand Buddhas, and the finest recovered Khmer sculpture, all clearly explained. An air-conditioned morning here before you set out means grandparents and children arrive at Angkor understanding what they are looking at, not just photographing it.

items.name: Artisans Angkor — silk, stone and lacquer
items.description: A Cambodian social enterprise that revived Khmer crafts nearly lost under the Khmer Rouge, where you can watch stone and wood carvers, silk weavers and lacquer and silver artisans at work, then buy directly. The silk farm outside town — mulberry to loom — is a lovely, unhurried multi-generation visit and a source of genuine, ethical gifts.

items.name: Phare, the Cambodian Circus
items.description: Not a circus in the Western sense but a soaring hour of acrobatics, live music, theatre and painting that tells modern Cambodian stories — often the hard ones of the Khmer Rouge years — performed by graduates of a school that began with refugee children and art as therapy. The single most affecting evening in town, and one children and elders love equally.

items.name: A dawn blessing by Buddhist monks
items.description: At a working temple within the park, a saffron-robed monk chants a Pali blessing, sprinkles lotus-scented water and ties a red cotton thread at your wrist for protection and good fortune — a quiet, sincere ritual that resonates deeply with Indian travellers who know the gesture. Arranged privately, it turns a temple visit into a moment the whole family carries home.

items.name: Kampong Phluk stilted village on the Tonle Sap
items.description: A community of houses raised on twenty-foot stilts at the lake's edge, where in the dry season you walk beneath homes that in the monsoon stand knee-deep in water, then glide by boat into a flooded mangrove forest by paddled canoe. Far more authentic than the tourist-heavy Chong Kneas; a private boat and a responsible operator make an unforgettable half-day.

items.name: Kampong Khleang, the great floating town
items.description: The largest and most authentic of the lake communities, some 50 km out — a working town of six thousand people, towering stilt houses and floating homes that migrate with the water, with barely a souvenir stall in sight. Community-run tours put your visit into local hands; the drive through rice country is half the pleasure.

items.name: Sunrise hot-air balloon over the temples
items.description: In the dry season, a balloon lifts you above the plain at first light, laying out the moated square of Angkor Wat and the forest-buried temples in a single sweep no ground view can match. A rare aerial perspective on the sheer scale of the ancient city; best booked for a calm, clear December-to-March morning.

items.name: Helicopter flight over Angkor Wat
items.description: A short private flight that banks over Angkor Wat's five towers, the walled city of Angkor Thom and the shimmering barays, revealing the geometry of the empire from the air. The most effortless way to give elders and children the grand overview, then land and explore at ground level with a guide.

items.name: Quad-bike ride through the rice-country back-lanes
items.description: An escorted run on red-dirt tracks past working paddies, sugar-palm groves, water buffalo and village pagodas at sunset, ending as the sky turns pink over the fields. A lively counterpoint to a day of temples that older children and teenagers love; hotels arrange transfers to the base.

items.name: A private Khmer cooking class
items.description: Start at a local market choosing lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime and palm sugar, then cook fish amok and a fresh green mango salad in a hands-on kitchen. Classes readily go fully vegetarian and Jain-friendly on request, making this an easy, engaging afternoon for a food-minded Indian family.

items.name: The Old Market (Psar Chas) and Pub Street, framed
items.description: The lively heart of old Siem Reap — Psar Chas piled with silk, spices, silver and lacquerware by day, the lantern-lit lanes around it buzzing after dark. Best experienced as a curated hour: a guide steers you to the honest craft stalls and a good rooftop, so you catch the colour and skip the tout-heavy scrum.

items.name: Sunset cocktails at Raffles Grand Hotel d'Angkor
items.description: The 1932 grande dame of Siem Reap, where Jackie Kennedy and Charlie Chaplin once stayed, still pours the sharp, gin-based Airavata amid teak, ceiling fans and a colonnaded garden. An elegant, air-conditioned reset between temple days, and a graceful setting for a multi-generation evening drink.

items.name: An almsgiving and merit-making morning at a working pagoda
items.description: At dawn, offer rice and receive a chanted blessing from monks on their alms round at a living wat such as Wat Bo or Wat Damnak — a gentle, respectful window into everyday Cambodian Buddhism away from the ruins. Deeply familiar in spirit to Indian travellers, and a calm, meaningful start to a day.

items.name: Sunset drinks and dinner cruise on the Tonle Sap
items.description: As the day cools, a private boat carries you out onto the great lake for the fiery sunset over Southeast Asia's largest freshwater expanse, drinks in hand and the floating world drifting past. A serene, comfortable way for elders to experience the Tonle Sap without a bumpy village walk.

items.name: The Landmine Museum and its founder's story
items.description: Founded by a former child soldier turned de-miner, this small, sober museum explains Cambodia's landmine legacy and cares for children affected by it — sobering, honest and important context for the country you are enjoying. A short, worthwhile stop on the way to or from Banteay Srei; older children come away changed.

items.name: Apsara dance over a fine Khmer dinner
items.description: The slow, precise classical dance of the celestial apsara — the same dancers carved by the thousand across Angkor's walls — performed live as you dine on refined Cambodian cuisine. A cultural evening that connects the stone reliefs to living tradition; better hotels stage intimate versions with proper vegetarian menus.

items.name: A guided countryside cycle to the temples at dawn
items.description: For the fitter traveller, a private guided ride on quiet forest lanes reaches the outer temples in the cool of early morning, moving between Preah Khan and Ta Som at the pace of birdsong rather than engines. An immersive, low-crowd way to feel the scale of the park, with a support vehicle trailing for anyone who tires.

items.name: Preah Neak Pean and the Jayatataka baray by boardwalk at golden hour
items.description: Timed for late afternoon, the long boardwalk across the drowned forest to Neak Pean glows amber and the dead trees mirror in still water — one of the most photogenic, meditative walks in the whole park. Flat and easy, it suits every generation and rewards patience with near-solitude once the day-tour buses leave.

items.name: The West Baray and Mebon for an afternoon on the water
items.description: The largest surviving Khmer reservoir, an 8-km sheet of water where locals swim and picnic, with the ruined island temple of West Mebon at its centre reachable by boat. A relaxed, refreshingly un-touristy way to spend a hot afternoon and glimpse how ordinary Cambodians enjoy Angkor today.

items.name: Silk Island silk-weaving and a village lunch
items.description: Beyond the town, a working silk farm and weaving village shows the full journey from mulberry leaf and silkworm to the shimmering golden Khmer silk on the loom, followed by a home-cooked country lunch. A gentle, hands-on morning for those who prefer craft and countryside to more ruins, and a source of beautiful ethical buys.

items.name: Wat Preah Prom Rath riverside temple
items.description: A serene, richly gilded working pagoda on the riverbank in the heart of town, with a large reclining Buddha, a boat-shaped shrine and monks going about their day — an easy, uncrowded pocket of living faith minutes from the market. A quiet stroll-in between activities that costs nothing and rewards with genuine calm.

items.name: Angkor Wat's upper level and Bakan sanctuary
items.description: The steep climb to the third level of Angkor Wat reaches the Bakan, the temple's holiest heart, where the towers that fill every postcard surround you at close quarters and the whole plain falls away below. Access is timed and modest dress required; a guide books the slot so the family ascends together into the sanctum.

items.name: A blessing-thread and Baksei Chamkrong at first light
items.description: A compact, elegant 10th-century brick pyramid just south of Angkor Thom's south gate, almost always empty, whose steep single stair rewards an early climb with a clean view down the approach to Angkor. A perfect quiet inclusion for travellers who want a temple entirely to themselves before the day begins.

items.name: Miniature Replicas garden and a stone-carving master
items.description: At the workshop of a celebrated local sculptor sit hand-built miniatures of Angkor's great temples alongside a live carving studio where you can watch — or try — the chisel-work that built the empire. A charming, low-key stop that helps children grasp the scale and craft behind the monuments they have been climbing.

items.name: Cuisine Wat Damnak
items.description: The first Cambodian restaurant ever ranked on Asia's 50 Best — Khmer produce and French technique in a wooden house.

items.name: Embassy Restaurant
items.description: Gourmet Khmer from the 'Kimsan Twins' — an all-female kitchen reviving forgotten royal-court recipes.

items.name: Malis Siem Reap
credentials: Chef Luu Meng (Thalias group) — Cambodia's leading fine-Khmer restaurateur
Sibling of Malis Phnom Penh, the capital's first Cambodian fine-dining room (2004)
items.description: Chef Luu Meng's 'living Cambodian cuisine' — the country's most established fine-Khmer name, on the river.

items.name: Kroya by Shinta Mani
credentials: Shinta Mani Angkor — a Bensley Collection hotel dining room
items.description: Shinta Mani Angkor's signature dining room — 'time-honoured recipes and the Khmer dishes of tomorrow.'

items.name: Pou Restaurant & Bar
credentials: Among Siem Reap's top-rated restaurants on Tripadvisor
Chef Mengly Mork — modern Khmer home cooking
items.description: Siem Reap-born chef Mengly Mork's family-inspired Khmer cooking — rustic, personal, and much-loved.

items.name: Marum
credentials: TREE Alliance training restaurant (Friends International model)
items.description: A training restaurant with real cooking — inventive Cambodian tapas that give marginalised youth a future.

items.name: Elephant Bar, Raffles Grand Hotel d'Angkor
items.description: Cocktail hour at the grande dame since 1932 — the most storied room in town for a drink.

items.name: Miss Wong Cocktail Bar
items.description: A tiny 1920s-Shanghai drinking den behind a cherry-red lantern — Siem Reap's most characterful cocktail bar.

items.name: Kong Kea Bar, Amansara
items.description: A discreet nightcap inside Aman's town villa — the quietest, most private drink in Siem Reap.

items.name: Pub Street
items.description: The neon spine of the town's night — loud, packed and unmissable, the place everyone eventually walks through.

items.title: Private dawn inside Angkor Wat
items.description: A guide who knows exactly where to stand as the sun comes up behind the towers, before the tour buses.

items.title: Helicopter over the Angkor complex
items.description: A flight that reveals the full scale of the temple city and its ancient reservoirs from the air.

items.title: Remote temple picnic at Beng Mealea or Koh Ker
items.description: A day trip to the jungle-swallowed outer temples with a private lunch laid on.

items.title: Sunset floating over the Tonlé Sap
items.description: A private boat through the stilt villages of the great lake, timed for the light.

plan.heading: 3 days in Siem Reap, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle at Amansara, once King Sihanouk's guesthouse, and take the house tour of its retro-modern grounds.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A late-afternoon private visit to Angkor Wat with a resident guide, timed for the softening light.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Amansara — Khmer and Western menus — or a private table arranged in the gardens.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Dawn at Angkor Wat's causeway before the tour buses, then the Bayon's faces and the terraces of Angkor Thom.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Ta Prohm, where the silk-cotton roots hold the stone, then a shaded picnic lunch laid out by Amansara.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A quiet evening — the spa, then dinner at Cuisine Wat Damnak, chef Joannès Rivière's seasonal Cambodian tasting.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private boat to Banteay Srei's fine pink-sandstone carving, then the villages of the plain.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The floating world of Kampong Phluk on the Tonle Sap, reached by private launch at the right hour.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at Pou Restaurant or the intimate Embassy, championing Khmer produce and young Cambodian chefs.

neighbourhoods.heading: Where to base yourself

items.name: Wat Bo / riverside
items.description: Quiet, tree-lined and close to the best boutique hotels — the calm base.

items.name: Old French Quarter / Pub Street fringe
items.description: Central and lively — for those who want dinner and markets on foot.

items.name: Charles de Gaulle road
items.description: Where the grand resorts sit on the way to the temples — for full-service seclusion.

neighbourhoods.pairWith: Bangkok, Hoi An & Da Nang, Singapore

events.name: Angkor Sankranta (Khmer New Year)
events.note: Cambodia's biggest celebration, with games and blessings staged around the temples themselves.

events.name: Bon Om Touk (Water Festival)
events.note: Marks the reversal of the Tonlé Sap's flow, with boat races and river festivities.

events.name: Angkor Wat International Half Marathon
events.note: A charity run through the temple grounds at first light — a rare way to see them car-free.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into the new Siem Reap-Angkor International (SAI); a private car handles the 45-to-60-minute transfer into town, and a licensed guide can be arranged for the temples.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with driver and guide is essential for the sprawling Angkor complex; in town, the hotel can arrange a remork (tuk-tuk) for short, atmospheric hops.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM (Cellcard or Smart) gives dependable 4G; hotel wifi is good, though signal thins out among the temples.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The US dollar is used everywhere alongside the riel (change under a dollar comes in riel); cards work at hotels, cash is king elsewhere, and small tips for guides and drivers are customary.

onGround.note: Cover shoulders and knees to enter Angkor Wat's upper level; start temples at sunrise to beat heat and crowds, buy the Angkor pass in advance, and stay along the quiet Charles de Gaulle road or near the river rather than in the Pub Street bustle.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: November to April is the dry season and the time to go — clear skies for the temples, cooler air December to February. Avoid the June to September peak of the wet season and the March-May build-up, when heat and humidity turn oppressive.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No direct flight from India; connect via Bangkok or Singapore into the new Siem Reap-Angkor International Airport (SAI, opened 2023, about an hour from town). Singapore Airlines via Singapore and Thai Airways or Bangkok Airways via Bangkok are the polished business-class routings; a Bangkok or Singapore layover pairs a good lounge with a short onward hop.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations from India, but hepatitis A, typhoid and up-to-date routine shots are recommended; Angkor's temple areas are low but not zero for mosquito-borne illness, so cover up at dawn and dusk. Very safe town. Bottled water only, and pace temple days in the heat.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian is straightforward and Khmer cooking adapts well; several tourist-facing restaurants cater to Indian and vegetarian diets. For a reliable Indian meal, Curry Walla and Maharajah are the established names in town, and Jain no-onion-garlic requests are best flagged in advance.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

closing.headingHtml: Siem Reap, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Singapore — TripAgent
seo.description: Singapore, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Singapore
hero.tagline: A garden city of gleaming towers and hawker soul.

ourTake.lede: Singapore is best read as a food city with a skyline, not the other way round — spend as much time in a Tiong Bahru coffee shop as at Marina Bay. The Gardens by the Bay light show is worth it, but go into the Cloud Forest dome at opening before the tour groups. Everyone rushes the Sands SkyPark; the better view is a drink at a bar across the water looking at it.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a spotless, effortless city that families and first-timers navigate without friction.
ourTake.skipIf: You are looking for wilderness, spontaneity or a bargain.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Raffles Hotel Singapore
credentials: World's 50 Best Hotels 2025 (No. 5, highest in Singapore)
items.description: The white colonial grande dame the whole city is measured against — and still the finest room in it.

items.name: Capella Singapore
items.description: A Norman Foster-restored colonial estate in the rainforest — resort calm, minutes from the city.

items.name: The Fullerton Bay Hotel Singapore
items.description: A glass pavilion on the water, looking straight across the bay to the skyline.

items.name: The Paiza Collection at Marina Bay Sands
items.description: The private hotel-within-the-hotel at Marina Bay Sands — arrival by Rolls-Royce, a dedicated lift, total discretion.

items.name: Raffles Sentosa Singapore
items.description: Raffles' all-villa resort debut — private pools and hilltop calm, the marque's newest Singapore address.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Singapore
items.description: The surest hands off Orchard Road — quiet, art-filled, and effortless with families.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental, Singapore
items.description: A fan-shaped tower with the group's quiet precision and rooms that fan out over the bay.

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton, Millenia Singapore
items.description: A serious art collection and octagonal-window bathtubs framing the bay — grand, and quietly famous for it.

items.name: The St. Regis Singapore
items.description: Old-world St. Regis grandeur off Orchard — butler service and a museum's worth of art in the halls.

items.name: Conrad Singapore Orchard
items.description: A polished, freshly reimagined Orchard tower — central, capable, and easy on the shopper.

items.name: Marina Bay Sands
items.description: The three-towered icon crowned by the ship-shaped SkyPark — the photograph the whole world knows.

items.name: Conrad Centennial Singapore
items.description: A dependable, art-hung tower by the convention halls — spacious and unshowy.

items.name: Artyzen Singapore
items.description: A calm, design-led newcomer off Orchard — vertical greenery and quiet good taste.

items.name: PARKROYAL COLLECTION Pickering
items.description: The famous hotel-in-a-garden — cascading sky terraces of greenery over the old town.

items.name: The Fullerton Hotel Singapore
items.description: The grand old General Post Office, a neoclassical landmark reborn at the mouth of the river.

items.name: The Capitol Kempinski Hotel Singapore
items.description: Two restored 1930s landmarks turned into a small, characterful house in the civic heart.

items.name: InterContinental Singapore
items.description: Peranakan shophouse charm woven into a grand hotel, over the arts-and-heritage quarter.

items.name: Pan Pacific Singapore
items.description: A soaring atrium tower with wide bay views and a smooth, Asian-service ease.

items.name: Fairmont Singapore
items.description: A big, capable twin-tower house with one of the city's best spas attached.

items.name: Goodwood Park Hotel
items.description: A garden-set heritage landmark of 1900, long a favourite for its quiet lawns and durian pastries.

items.name: W Singapore, Sentosa Cove
items.description: A high-energy design resort by the marina — for members who want the music turned up.

items.name: Gardens by the Bay
credentials: Guinness World Record — Flower Dome, largest glass greenhouse
items.description: The Supertree Grove, the Cloud Forest with the world's tallest indoor waterfall, and the record-holding Flower Dome — a garden built like a city. Come at dusk to walk the OCBC Skyway between the Supertrees, then stay for the free Garden Rhapsody light-and-sound show at night. Wide, flat and pram-friendly, so it works well for a multi-generation group.

items.name: Marina Bay Sands SkyPark Observation Deck
items.description: The ship-shaped deck cantilevered 57 storeys up gives the definitive Singapore skyline view — the bay, the CBD towers and Gardens by the Bay laid out below. Go at golden hour; if you are staying at the hotel you get the famous 150m infinity pool, which non-guests cannot access.

items.name: Singapore Botanic Gardens & National Orchid Garden
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Singapore Botanic Gardens
items.description: Singapore's only UNESCO World Heritage Site and the world's first tropical botanic garden on the list — 82 hectares of rainforest, lakes and heritage trees in the middle of the city. The ticketed National Orchid Garden holds 1,000+ species, including the hybrids named for visiting heads of state. Free entry to the wider gardens; ideal for an unhurried morning walk.

items.name: ArtScience Museum
items.description: The lotus-shaped building beside Marina Bay Sands, best known for the permanent teamLab 'Future World' immersive digital installations that children and adults get equally lost in. It also runs serious travelling exhibitions on science, design and art.

items.name: National Gallery Singapore
items.description: The world's largest public collection of modern Southeast Asian art, housed in the beautifully restored former Supreme Court and City Hall. Worth it for the architecture alone; finish with a drink at the rooftop bar for a Padang-and-bay view. Strong for collectors and anyone who wants depth beyond the theme parks.

items.name: Merlion Park & the Marina Bay waterfront promenade
items.description: The half-lion, half-fish icon spouting water into the bay, with the classic straight-on view of Marina Bay Sands across the water. The best move is simply to walk the full bayfront loop — Merlion to Esplanade to the Helix Bridge to Sands — especially after dark when everything is lit.

items.name: Chinatown & Sri Mariamman Temple / Buddha Tooth Relic Temple
items.description: Restored shophouse lanes, the ornate Sri Mariamman (Singapore's oldest Hindu temple) and the grand red-and-gold Buddha Tooth Relic Temple within a few streets of each other. Wander Pagoda and Temple Streets, then eat at Chinatown Complex or Maxwell. Plenty of vegetarian and South Indian food nearby, which helps veg and Jain travellers.

items.name: Maxwell Food Centre
items.description: The most decorated hawker centre in the city — eight stalls landed in the 2025 Michelin Bib Gourmand list. Home of the legendary Tian Tian Hainanese chicken rice; go early, eat like a local, and understand why Singaporeans take food this seriously.

items.name: Kampong Glam & Sultan Mosque
items.description: The old Malay-Arab quarter — the golden-domed Sultan Mosque, textile and perfume shops on Arab Street, and Haji Lane, a narrow alley of boutiques, murals and rooftop bars. The most atmospheric quarter to wander on foot in the late afternoon.

items.name: Little India & Sri Veeramakaliamman Temple
items.description: The most sensory neighbourhood in Singapore — garland stalls, spice shops, the colourful Tan Teng Niah house and the vivid Sri Veeramakaliamman Temple. For Indian travellers it is both familiar and a revelation; some of the best vegetarian thalis and dosas in the city are here, and Tekka Centre downstairs is a proper wet-market-plus-hawker experience.

items.name: Universal Studios Singapore
items.description: Southeast Asia's Universal park, with zones themed to Jurassic World, Transformers, Sci-Fi City and more — the anchor family attraction on Sentosa. Book Express passes to skip the queues; combine with a Sentosa hotel night to avoid a rushed day.

items.name: S.E.A. Aquarium (Singapore Oceanarium)
items.description: One of the world's largest aquariums, with a vast Open Ocean tank you can sit in front of like a cinema, home to manta rays and sharks. Reliable, air-conditioned and genuinely calming — an easy win with young children or grandparents.

items.name: Night Safari
items.description: The world's first nocturnal wildlife park — you ride a tram through dimly lit habitats to see lions, tapirs and Asian elephants active after dark. A distinctive Singapore evening; opens at 6:30pm, so pair it with the neighbouring parks earlier in the day.

items.name: Singapore Zoo & River Wonders
items.description: Consistently rated among the world's best zoos for its open, moated 'rainforest' design — famous for the Breakfast with Orangutans experience. Adjoining River Wonders adds giant pandas and a huge freshwater collection. The strongest single day out for families with children.

items.name: Bird Paradise
items.description: Asia's largest bird park, with eight walk-through aviaries you can stroll through as free-flying birds swoop around you, and 3,500 birds across 400 species. The newest of the Mandai parks and beautifully designed — quieter and more contemplative than the zoo.

items.name: Tiong Bahru
items.description: Singapore's oldest housing estate — curved 1930s Art Deco blocks, an indie bookshop, third-wave cafés and the excellent Tiong Bahru Market for hawker breakfast. The city's most walkable, low-key morning: no ticket, just wander and eat.

items.name: Katong & Joo Chiat
credentials: UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Award — Joo Chiat conservation
items.description: The heart of Peranakan Singapore — rows of pastel shophouses with ornate ceramic tiles, and the celebrated Koon Seng Road terraces. Come for laksa and kaya toast, and to see a heritage quarter that won a UNESCO Asia-Pacific conservation award. Off the tourist trail and all the better for it.

items.name: Peranakan Museum
items.description: A jewel-box museum devoted to Straits-Chinese culture — beadwork, porcelain, jewellery and the material world of the Peranakans, recently reopened after a full revamp. The best primer before wandering Katong or Emerald Hill.

items.name: National Museum of Singapore
items.description: The country's oldest museum, telling the Singapore story from its trading-port origins through independence, in a grand colonial building with a striking glass rotunda. A good orientation on day one — note the History Gallery is under restoration until late 2026, but the rest remains open.

items.name: The Southern Ridges — Henderson Waves
items.description: A 9km chain of hilltop parks linked by walkways, crowned by Henderson Waves — Singapore's highest pedestrian bridge, a sculptural timber wave 36m up with harbour and skyline views. Do the shorter Mount Faber to HortPark stretch for the best of it; the bridge is lit at night.

items.name: MacRitchie Reservoir & TreeTop Walk
items.description: The city's green lung — boardwalks over the reservoir, monkeys and monitor lizards, and a 250m suspension bridge strung through the rainforest canopy. A proper jungle hike ten minutes from downtown; go early to beat the heat.

items.name: Fort Canning Park
items.description: A hilltop park layered with history — 14th-century royal grounds, WWII bunkers and the famous 'Tree Tunnel' spiral staircase that fills every Instagram feed. A shaded, central green break between museum visits.

items.name: Emerald Hill
items.description: A single, quiet cul-de-sac of exquisitely preserved Peranakan terrace houses tucked just off the Orchard Road shopping strip — a five-minute detour that most visitors miss. Have a drink at one of the old shophouse bars at the foot of the hill.

items.name: Orchard Road
items.description: Singapore's mile of malls — ION Orchard, Ngee Ann City / Takashimaya and Paragon carry the full luxury roster. Efficient, air-conditioned and comprehensive; the practical choice when you want the brands under one roof rather than a hunt.

items.name: The Shoppes at Marina Bay Sands
items.description: The waterfront luxury mall with 170+ premium brands, a canal you can ride a sampan on, and the Apple 'floating' store on the bay. High-end flagship shopping with the Sands spectacle attached — and a rain-proof link to the museum, casino and hotel.

items.name: Raffles Hotel & the Long Bar
items.description: The grand colonial hotel where the Singapore Sling was invented in 1915 — restored to full lustre, with an arcade of luxury boutiques and the Long Bar where you still drop peanut shells on the floor. Worth a walk-through and a cocktail even if you are not staying.

items.name: Chijmes
items.description: A restored 19th-century convent and Gothic chapel turned into a courtyard of restaurants and bars — one of the prettiest places in the city for a candlelit dinner. A polished, atmospheric evening away from the malls.

items.name: Clarke Quay & the Singapore River
items.description: The riverside strip of old godowns (warehouses) now full of restaurants and bars, and the departure point for the classic bumboat river cruise past the Merlion to Marina Bay. Do the cruise at dusk for the city lights; the nightlife here has just been refreshed.

items.name: Lau Pa Sat
items.description: A gorgeous Victorian cast-iron market hall — a national monument — packed with hawker stalls, where the neighbouring street closes each evening to become the smoky 'Satay Street'. The most convenient CBD hawker experience and a beautiful building in its own right.

items.name: Chinatown Complex Market & Food Centre
items.description: Singapore's largest hawker hub — 700+ stalls over several floors, including the stall that once held a Michelin star for soya-sauce chicken. Gritty, authentic and endlessly cheap; go with an empty stomach and no plan.

items.name: Haw Par Villa
items.description: A gloriously eccentric 1930s park of lurid dioramas illustrating Chinese mythology — most famously the graphic 'Ten Courts of Hell'. Free, strange and unforgettable; nothing else in the city is remotely like it.

items.name: Sri Mariamman Temple
items.description: Singapore's oldest Hindu temple, its rainbow gopuram tower crowded with painted deities rising incongruously out of Chinatown. During the annual Theemithi festival, devotees walk over hot coals in the courtyard. A moving, active place of worship — for Indian travellers, a piece of home in an unexpected setting.

items.name: Thian Hock Keng Temple
items.description: The city's oldest and most important Hokkien temple, built in 1839 by grateful immigrants where the sea once lapped the shore — an exquisite piece of southern-Chinese architecture on Telok Ayer Street. Pair it with the mosque and church on the same historic street of faiths.

items.name: Singapore Flyer
items.description: The giant observation wheel over the bay, with 30-minute rotations that reveal the skyline, the Formula 1 street circuit and, on a clear day, Malaysia and Indonesia. You can book a private capsule with dinner for a discreet celebration.

items.name: Jewel Changi Airport & the HSBC Rain Vortex
items.description: The world's tallest indoor waterfall thundering seven storeys through a glass dome ringed by rainforest — and it is inside the airport. Worth a deliberate visit even without a flight; a genuinely jaw-dropping arrival or departure, and a fine last few hours before you fly.

items.name: Pulau Ubin
items.description: A 15-minute bumboat from Changi Point drops you into Singapore of the 1960s — a rustic island of last-remaining kampong (village) life, mangroves and jungle you explore by rented bicycle. The Chek Jawa wetlands at low tide are extraordinary. The city's easiest escape into another era.

items.name: Palawan Beach & the Southern Ridges of Sentosa
items.description: Sentosa's family beach, with a rope suspension bridge out to the 'Southernmost Point of Continental Asia' and a lookout tower. Low-key, shaded and easy — a gentler counterpoint to the island's theme parks.

items.name: Esplanade — Theatres on the Bay
items.description: The 'durian'-domed performing arts centre on the bayfront — world-class concerts, theatre and a strong run of free performances on the outdoor stage most evenings. Check the programme; there is nearly always something on, much of it free.

items.name: Singapore Cable Car (Mount Faber to Sentosa)
items.description: A glass cabin gliding from a rainforest hilltop across the harbour to Sentosa, with the port, container ships and Southern Islands spread below. The most scenic way to reach the island; private-cabin dining is available for a special occasion.

items.name: Gillman Barracks
items.description: A cluster of restored 1930s colonial army barracks turned contemporary-art enclave — commercial galleries, artist studios and a relaxed café or two under old rain trees. The quiet, serious end of the Singapore art scene, and pleasantly uncrowded.

items.name: Fort Siloso
items.description: Singapore's only preserved coastal fort, with WWII gun emplacements and tunnels and a treetop 'Skywalk' out to the ramparts. A substantial, breezy history stop on Sentosa that balances out the theme-park day.

items.name: Coney Island (Pulau Serangoon)
items.description: A rugged, deliberately undeveloped nature park on the northeast coast — coastal forest, casuarina groves and quiet beaches, best explored on foot or by bike. One of the last genuinely wild-feeling corners of Singapore, and rarely busy.

items.name: Bintan Island day trip (Indonesia)
items.description: A one-hour ferry from Tanah Merah reaches Bintan's beach resorts and spas — the standard Singapore beach escape for a day or an overnight. A useful reset when the city gets intense; passport and visa-on-arrival apply, so plan the paperwork.

items.name: Johor Bahru & Legoland day trip (Malaysia)
items.description: Across the causeway lies Malaysia — cheaper spa days, seafood, and Legoland Malaysia for younger children, all doable as a day trip. Weekday mornings avoid the border crush; keep passports handy.

items.name: Marina Barrage
items.description: A dam-turned-park with a grassy rooftop that is the city's favourite kite-flying and sunset picnic spot — and a rare uncrowded, front-row view straight across the water to the Marina Bay skyline. Quietly one of the best free things to do at dusk.

items.name: Kranji countryside & Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve
credentials: ASEAN Heritage Park — Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve
items.description: The rural far northwest — mangrove boardwalks alive with migratory birds, mudskippers and the occasional estuarine crocodile, plus a scatter of hydroponic and goat farms. An unexpectedly wild, agricultural side of Singapore that almost no visitor sees.

items.name: Odette
items.description: Julien Royer's modern French inside the National Gallery — the city's most decorated table.

items.name: Les Amis
items.description: A French institution since 1994 — classical haute cuisine and one of Asia's great cellars.

items.name: Zén
items.description: Björn Frantzén's Singapore house — Scandinavian purity meets Japanese finesse across three floors of a shophouse.

items.name: Cloudstreet
items.description: Rishi Naleendra's precise, fermentation-led cooking — Sri Lankan soul, exacting technique.

items.name: Jaan by Kirk Westaway
items.description: 'Reinventing British' cooking on the 70th floor — technique and a view in equal measure.

items.name: Meta
items.description: Sun Kim's highwire act between Korea and Europe — inventive, assured, quietly thrilling.

items.name: Saint Pierre
items.description: Emmanuel Stroobant's French-Asian cooking, waterside, with the bay for a backdrop.

items.name: Shoukouwa
items.description: An eight-seat sushi counter flown daily from Toyosu — the quietest luxury in town.

items.name: Thevar
items.description: Spice-spiked modern Indian cooking that earned Singapore's most exciting two-star climb.

items.name: Sushi Sakuta
items.description: A serene Edomae counter, newly promoted — precise, unhurried, deeply traditional.

items.name: Waku Ghin
items.description: Tetsuya Wakuda's intimate multi-room dinner at Marina Bay Sands — Japanese-European, jewel-like.

items.name: Cut by Wolfgang Puck
items.description: Wolfgang Puck's modern steakhouse — the city's most polished room for a great cut.

items.name: Burnt Ends
items.description: Everything through the custom four-tonne ovens — the barbecue counter that became a pilgrimage.

items.name: Candlenut
items.description: The world's first Michelin-starred Peranakan kitchen — Malcolm Lee's refined Nyonya cooking.

items.name: Labyrinth
items.description: Han Liguang's 'new Singaporean' cooking — hawker memories reimagined with local farms.

items.name: Seroja
items.description: Kevin Wong's ode to Nusantara flavours — Malay-archipelago cooking with real elegance.

items.name: Euphoria
items.description: Jason Tan's 'gastro-botanica' — vegetable-led fine dining of great delicacy.

items.name: Summer Pavilion
items.description: Refined Cantonese in a garden-pavilion setting — the grand Chinese lunch, immaculately done.

items.name: Shisen Hanten by Chen Kentaro
items.description: Third-generation Szechuan mastery — mapo tofu the way it should be.

items.name: Iggy's
items.description: A long-running critical darling — European cooking with a wine list to match.

items.name: Nouri
items.description: Ivan Brehm's 'crossroads cooking' — a thoughtful blur of world cuisines under one star.

items.name: Nae:um
items.description: Louis Han's memory-led Korean cooking — seasonal, personal, quietly moving.

items.name: Buona Terra
items.description: A warm, family-run Italian doing quietly excellent contemporary cooking.

items.name: Alma by Juan Amador
items.description: European fine dining with a light, generous hand in a garden-hotel setting.

items.name: Summer Palace
items.description: Classic, exacting Cantonese — the grand hotel Chinese dinner at its most assured.

items.name: Imperial Treasure Fine Teochew Cuisine
items.description: Teochew cooking done with rare precision — braised goose and clear, clean flavours.

items.name: Lei Garden
items.description: A Cantonese stalwart in the Chijmes cloisters — dim sum and roast meats, done properly.

items.name: Whitegrass
items.description: Contemporary Australian-French cooking in a restored chapel-precinct room.

items.name: Araya
items.description: A refined Latin-American tasting menu — precise, warm and hard to book.

items.name: Pangium
items.description: Malcolm Lee's second act — Southeast-Asian heritage cooking with a green conscience.

items.name: Kotuwa
items.description: Modern Sri Lankan cooking with real fire and spice — hoppers and curries done with care.

items.name: Jungle
items.description: Bold, herb-driven Thai cooking that punches well above its price.

items.name: Jigger & Pony
items.description: Singapore's best bar, and among Asia's finest — a cocktail room the world flies in for.

items.name: Nutmeg & Clove
items.description: Cocktails that tell Singapore's own story — local flavours, world-class craft.

items.name: Analogue
items.description: A sustainability-minded bar in the Chijmes cloisters — inventive, and quietly conscientious.

items.name: Native
items.description: Regional Southeast-Asian spirits and foraged flavours — a bar with a real sense of place.

items.name: Hill Street Tai Hwa Pork Noodle
items.description: The bak chor mee that holds a Michelin star — proof a single hawker bowl can be world-class.

items.name: Boon Tong Kee
items.description: A legendary Hainanese chicken rice house, freshly promoted for doing the classic best.

items.name: Ji Ji Wanton Noodle Specialist
items.description: A Hong Lim hawker favourite, newly starred by the Bib for its wanton mee.

items.name: Nam Sing Hokkien Fried Mee
items.description: A famed hawker plate of Hokkien mee — smoky, wet, and quietly perfect.

items.name: Sin Heng Claypot Bak Koot Teh
items.description: Peppery pork-rib soup in a claypot — old-Singapore comfort, credentialed by the inspectors.

items.name: To-Ricos Kway Chap
items.description: A beloved kway chap stall — braised, soulful, and worth the queue.

items.name: Song Kee Teochew Fish Porridge
items.description: Clean, restorative Teochew fish porridge — the antidote to a heavy week.

items.name: Lao Fu Zi Fried Kway Teow
items.description: Char kway teow with real wok hei — the smoky char that defines the dish.

items.name: Kitchenman Nasi Lemak
items.description: Fragrant coconut-rice nasi lemak done with a cook's care — a Bib-listed favourite.

items.name: Jigger & Pony
items.description: The city's defining cocktail room — polished, unhurried, and among the best on earth.

items.name: Atlas
credentials: Rémy Martin Legend of the List Award (2024)
items.description: An Art Deco cathedral to gin — a 15-metre tower of 1,300 labels beneath a soaring 1930s ceiling.

items.name: Nutmeg & Clove
items.description: Cocktails that tell Singapore's own story — local flavours, world-class craft.

items.name: Native
items.description: Regional spirits and foraged flavours — a bar with a real, rooted sense of place.

items.name: Sago House
items.description: A hand-built shophouse bar of upcycled charm — six classics, remade weekly from the market.

items.name: Offtrack
items.description: Vinyl on the turntable, pan-Asian plates and drinks — the easy, low-lit end of world-class.

items.name: Cat Bite Club
items.description: An agave den hidden in plain sight — tequila and mezcal handled with real seriousness.

items.name: Analogue
items.description: A sustainability-minded bar in the Chijmes cloisters — inventive, and quietly conscientious.

items.name: Side Door
items.description: A new entrant that arrived straight into the ranks — precise, confident, worth the seat.

items.name: Origin Bar
items.description: A grand-hotel bar with real craft behind it — the polished nightcap done properly.

items.name: Smoke & Mirrors
credentials: Time Out World's 2nd Best Rooftop Bar (2024)
The World's 50 Best Bars Discovery listing
items.description: Above the National Gallery, staring down the Padang to the bay — the city's finest rooftop terrace.

items.name: CÉ LA VI
credentials: Landmark SkyPark rooftop atop Marina Bay Sands; internationally recognised
items.description: Fifty-seven floors up on the SkyPark — the definitive high-above-the-bay drink.

items.name: Lantern
credentials: Landmark bay-level rooftop of The Fullerton Bay Hotel; Forbes Travel Guide 5-Star hotel
items.description: A rooftop pool bar at the water's edge — the softer, quieter front-row seat to the skyline.

items.name: Employees Only
items.description: The New York speakeasy's Singapore outpost — showman bartending and a room that runs late.

items.title: Private night at the National Gallery
items.description: An after-hours curator-led walk through the region's largest Southeast Asian art collection in the old Supreme Court.

items.title: Chef's table at a two-star kitchen
items.description: A counter seat at Odette or Zén, both among Asia's most sought-after reservations.

items.title: Private junk into the southern islands
items.description: A chartered boat to Lazarus Island and the Sisters' Islands for a swim well away from the city.

items.title: Behind-the-scenes at Gardens by the Bay

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Land at Changi (SIN), the benchmark of modern airports, where fast immigration and a chauffeured car — or the hotel's own limousine — put you in Marina Bay or Orchard within twenty-five minutes.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The city is walkable, immaculate and easily covered by private car; the MRT is world-class if you ever wish to move like a local, and Sentosa is a short causeway away.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: An eSIM (Singtel or a global provider) gives instant 5G, though free wifi is everywhere and reliable; connectivity is never a concern here.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Singapore dollar (SGD); cards and contactless are near-universal, cash is seldom needed, and tipping is not customary as a service charge is already added.

onGround.note: Marina Bay suits first-timers who want the skyline; Orchard for shopping, the quieter Dempsey and Sentosa for calm. The city is famously strict — no littering, no chewing gum sales, no jaywalking — and impeccably safe. Book the tasting-menu tables well ahead, as the best fill weeks out.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: February to April is the kindest: drier, less humid, comfortable for a tropical city. It is warm and humid year-round; the November-January northeast monsoon brings the heaviest rain, and June-July can see afternoon showers, though July stays relatively dry.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi and Mumbai, both around 5.5-6 hours, and from Bengaluru. Singapore Airlines flies it best, with a superb business cabin (and first on select rotations). SilverKris and The Private Room lounges at Changi are among the world's finest, and Changi itself makes onward connections a pleasure rather than a chore.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required beyond routine; hepatitis A worth having. One of the safest cities in the world, with immaculate public order. Tap water is fully potable straight from the tap. No altitude or water concerns; the only note is heat and humidity.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Excellent for vegetarian and Jain travellers. Little India offers outstanding pure-veg and Jain-friendly dining, and hawker centres and hotels understand the requirements well. Komala Vilas and MTR are dependable South Indian names; fine-dining kitchens prepare Jain readily on notice.
