seo.title: Srinagar — TripAgent
seo.description: Srinagar, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Srinagar
hero.tagline: Mughal gardens, houseboats and the still mirror of Dal Lake.

ourTake.lede: Srinagar is a lake-and-garden city best taken gently, and the classic way in is a night or two on a well-kept houseboat on Dal or, better, the quieter Nigeen Lake. Do the shikara at dawn for the floating vegetable market and the Mughal gardens in the late afternoon light. Check the situation before you commit, and lean on a good local operator; conditions can change, and local knowledge matters here.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a shikara on Dal Lake, a heritage houseboat and Mughal gardens in bloom.
ourTake.skipIf: You want nightlife or guaranteed year-round access.

firstLook.heroCaption: Modern pool villa with palms and umbrella

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: Come for tulips and gardens in April, gardens and Dal Lake through summer, and chinar colour in autumn; winter is cold, snowbound and hushed.
whenToGo.bestMonths: May, Jun, Jul and Aug

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Srinagar. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: The Lalit Grand Palace Srinagar
items.area: Srinagar (Gupkar / palace grounds, above Dal Lake)
credentials: Former palace of Maharaja Pratap Singh (built 1910) — recognised heritage-palace hotel, The Lalit Hotels
Historic site of the Gandhi–Maharaja Hari Singh meeting; former host to Lord Mountbatten
items.description: The Maharaja's own palace, set in 101 acres of chinar-shaded gardens above the Dal — the grandest address in the valley.

items.name: Taj Dal View, Srinagar
items.area: Srinagar (Kralsangri, Brein — Zabarwan hillside above Dal Lake)
credentials: Taj Hotels / IHCL flagship luxury hotel in Srinagar (formerly Vivanta Dal View)
items.description: The Taj flagship of the valley, set high on the Zabarwan hills with the Dal, the Mughal gardens and the Pir Panjal laid out below.

items.name: The Khyber Himalayan Resort & Spa, Gulmarg
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India Readers' Travel Awards — Favourite Boutique Hotel (multiple years, 2014–2023)
Condé Nast Traveller India — among the top hotels in India for Favourite Indian Leisure Hotel & Favourite Spa in a Hotel
items.description: A timber-and-stone lodge at 8,825 ft in the Pir Panjal, facing the snows of Apharwat — the finest mountain address in Kashmir.

items.name: Butt's Clermont Houseboats
items.area: Srinagar (western Dal Lake, by the Mughal 'Garden of the Morning Breeze')
credentials: Iconic heritage houseboats est. 1947 — former host to Lord Mountbatten, Nelson Rockefeller, George Harrison and Ravi Shankar
Recognised J&K Tourism (TIH) registered heritage houseboats
items.description: The most storied houseboats on the Dal — moored under century-old chinars, where George Harrison learned sitar with Ravi Shankar.

items.name: Sukoon Houseboat
credentials: Featured by Condé Nast Traveller and Mr & Mrs Smith — leading luxury houseboat on Dal Lake
items.description: The Dal Lake houseboat reimagined — carved walnut and cream linen, a rooftop terrace and a level of service found nowhere else on the water.

items.name: Welcomhotel by ITC Hotels, Pine N Peak, Pahalgam
credentials: ITC Hotels / Welcomhotel — recognised luxury property, the leading luxury retreat in Pahalgam
items.description: A cedar-and-stone retreat on the Rajwas plateau above the Lidder — the one true luxury address in Pahalgam.

items.name: Vivanta Dal View — Boulevard heritage stays
credentials: Taj group (IHCL) standing on the Dal Lake Boulevard
items.description: The dependable, well-run polish of a global group on the Dal's edge, minutes from the gardens and the shikara ghats.

items.name: A Shikara Ride on Dal Lake
items.description: The slow, cushioned glide of a hand-paddled shikara through the still water at golden hour is the image of Kashmir every Indian carries in their head. Have a private boat held for the family at first light or last light, when the lake empties of day-trippers and the Zabarwan hills turn copper on the surface.

items.name: A Heritage Houseboat Stay
items.description: The carved-cedar houseboats moored on the Dal and the quieter Nagin are a living relic of the Raj, all fretwork panelling, Kashmiri carpets and a verandah that opens straight onto the water. Book a full boat for the family for a night or two as a set-piece, then move to a hotel like the Vivanta or Lalit for the comforts a longer stay wants.

items.name: The Floating Vegetable Market at Dawn
items.description: Before sunrise, growers from the lake's floating gardens gather in a knot of shikaras to trade lotus stems, greens and haakh, bargaining boat-to-boat on the black water. It is the one experience here that rewards an unglamorous alarm; a guide who knows the growers gets you into the ring rather than watching from the edge.

items.name: Char Chinar Island
items.description: A tiny island in the Dal marked by four great chinar trees at its corners, laid out by a Mughal prince and unchanged in feel for centuries. Paddle out by shikara for kahwa under the plane trees, with the whole amphitheatre of lake, houseboats and mountains around you.

items.name: Nagin Lake
items.description: The Dal's clearer, quieter sister, ringed by willows and the calmest houseboats in the valley. Families who want the Dal's romance without its bustle base themselves here; the swimming and the stillness make it the connoisseur's address in Srinagar.

items.name: Shalimar Bagh
credentials: On UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List as part of the serial 'Mughal Gardens in Kashmir' nomination
items.description: Jahangir's garden of love, built in 1619 for the empress Nur Jahan, its central water channel stepping down through terraces of chinar shade to the Dal below. It is the grandest of the Mughal gardens and the one that most fully explains why the emperors called Kashmir paradise.

items.name: Nishat Bagh
credentials: On UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List as part of the serial 'Mughal Gardens in Kashmir' nomination
items.description: The 'garden of gladness', a twelve-terraced sweep on the eastern shore of the Dal, laid out in 1633 with the Zabarwan range rising directly behind it and the lake spread out in front. The most dramatically sited of all the gardens; go late afternoon when the light rakes across the terraces.

items.name: Chashme Shahi
credentials: On UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List as part of the serial 'Mughal Gardens in Kashmir' nomination
items.description: The smallest and most intimate of the Mughal gardens, built around a natural spring whose cold, sweet water is still bottled and carried home by Kashmiris for its reputed purity. A short, gentle visit with a fine view down over the Dal, easily paired with the tulip garden and Pari Mahal just above.

items.name: Pari Mahal at Sunset
credentials: On UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List as part of the serial 'Mughal Gardens in Kashmir' nomination
items.description: The terraced 'palace of the fairies', a former Sufi library and observatory cut into the mountainside above Chashme Shahi, with the finest single view in Srinagar: the whole Dal, the city and the encircling hills laid out below. Come as the light goes and the lamps of the city begin to answer the last of the sun.

items.name: The Naseem Bagh Chinars
items.description: A grove of some 700 towering chinar trees planted by the Mughals on the Dal's shore, now within the university campus and largely free of crowds. Walking its cathedral of plane trees, especially when they burn red in autumn, is the quiet, knowing counterpoint to the famous gardens.

items.name: Hazratbal Shrine
items.description: Kashmir's holiest Muslim shrine, its white marble dome mirrored in the Dal on the lake's western shore, home to the Moi-e-Muqaddas relic revered across the valley. Even for non-Muslim visitors it is a moving, deeply local place; dress modestly and go with a guide who can read its significance.

items.name: Jamia Masjid, Old City
items.description: Srinagar's great congregational mosque, first built in the 14th century, its vast prayer hall carried on more than 370 deodar pillars around a still courtyard. The wooden Indo-Saracenic architecture is unlike any mosque elsewhere in India and the anchor of any walk through the old city.

items.name: Khanqah-e-Moula
items.description: The valley's oldest and most beautiful Sufi shrine, a river-side confection of carved and painted woodwork, papier-mache ceilings and hanging lamps built where Kashmir's Islam first took root. Non-Muslims view from the exterior and threshold; the craftsmanship alone justifies the stop.

items.name: Old City Heritage Walk
items.description: The lanes of Shehr-e-Khaas — Zaina Kadal, the bridges of the Jhelum, the balconied brick-and-timber houses, the copper bazaars and papier-mache workshops — hold the real, unpolished Srinagar. A knowledgeable private guide turns a maze into a legible thousand-year story of trade, craft and faith.

items.name: Shankaracharya Temple
items.description: An ancient Shiva temple crowning a hill above the city, reached by a long stair or a drive, and named for the philosopher Adi Shankara who is said to have meditated here. The 360-degree view over Srinagar and the Dal is the reward; go early before the haze and the crowds.

items.name: Hari Parbat Fort & Makhdoom Sahib
items.description: The Afghan-era fort crowns a hill sacred to all three of Kashmir's faiths, ringed by the Sharika Devi temple, the Makhdoom Sahib Sufi shrine and a gurudwara on its slopes. A short, layered pilgrimage that captures the syncretic soul of old Srinagar in one climb.

items.name: SPS Museum (Sri Pratap Singh Museum)
items.description: The valley's principal museum, founded in 1898, with tens of thousands of objects: Kashmiri shawls and papier-mache, ancient sculpture, coins and Gandhara-era pieces. An hour here gives the crafts you will see in the bazaars their proper historical depth.

items.name: A Wazwan Feast
items.description: The multi-course royal Kashmiri banquet — rista, rogan josh, gushtaba and the rest, traditionally up to thirty-six dishes served on the shared copper trami — is the region's great table ritual, honed over generations of master wazas. Arrange a proper hosted Wazwan (a substantial vegetarian version can be laid on) as the centrepiece meal of the trip.

items.name: Kahwa & the Bakery Culture
items.description: The saffron-and-almond green tea called kahwa, poured from a samovar against the cold, and the morning kandur bakeries with their salt-tea breads — girda, lavasa, sheermal — are the small daily rituals that define Kashmiri hospitality. A guide can walk you into a working bakery at dawn, tea glass in hand.

items.name: Pashmina & Kani Shawl Shopping
credentials: Kashmir Pashmina and Kani Shawl both hold India's Geographical Indication (GI) tag
items.description: The genuine article — hand-spun pashm woven on a Kashmiri loom, or the intricate Kani shawl worked stitch-by-stitch on wooden spokes — is one of the finest textiles on earth and an heirloom purchase. Buy only through a trusted, GI-verified house; a private guide keeps you clear of the machine-made pretenders that flood the market.

items.name: Kashmir Carpets & Crewel
credentials: Kashmir Carpet holds India's Geographical Indication (GI) tag
items.description: Hand-knotted silk and wool carpets in Persian-derived patterns, and the chain-stitched crewel and namda work that dresses Kashmiri homes, are among the valley's signature crafts. The best ateliers will show you the knot count and the design cards; a considered carpet is the trip's grandest souvenir.

items.name: Walnut Wood & Papier-Mache
credentials: Kashmir Walnut Wood Carving and Kashmir Papier Mache both hold India's Geographical Indication (GI) tag
items.description: Kashmir's dark, close-grained walnut is carved into furniture and screens by families who have done it for generations, while papier-mache is painted in fine gold-flecked florals on boxes and panels. Both are GI-protected crafts best bought at the workshop, where you can watch the making.

items.name: Indira Gandhi Memorial Tulip Garden (Seasonal)
credentials: The largest tulip garden in Asia
items.description: For a few weeks from mid-March to April, seven terraces below the Zabarwan range blaze with well over a million tulips in scores of colours, framed by the Dal below. It opens for the annual Tulip Festival; time a spring trip to it and little else in the valley compares.

items.name: Badamwari Almond Blossom (Seasonal)
items.description: In February and early March, before anything else in the valley stirs, this historic almond garden at the foot of Hari Parbat breaks into pink-and-white blossom — Kashmir's first sign of spring. A quiet, uncrowded pleasure that most itineraries miss entirely.

items.name: Royal Springs Golf Course
credentials: Rated the No.1 golf course in India by Golf Digest
items.description: A Robert Trent Jones Jr. course laid along the slopes above the Dal, consistently rated among India's very best and one of the most scenic in Asia. A round here, chinars and lake below and snow peaks beyond, is a rare thing to do on a Kashmir morning.

items.name: Gulmarg: The Gondola to Apharwat
credentials: Among the highest cable cars in the world (world's second-highest / Asia's highest passenger ropeway)
items.description: The two-stage cable car climbs from the Gulmarg meadow to nearly 4,000 metres on the shoulder of Apharwat Peak, one of the highest passenger ropeways in the world with a Himalayan panorama at the top. Do both phases on a clear morning; carry warm layers even in summer, as it is another world up there.

items.name: Gulmarg: The Meadow & Golf Course
credentials: Gulmarg Golf Course is the world's highest green golf course
items.description: The 'meadow of flowers' is a vast bowl of alpine grass ringed by the Pir Panjal, and in summer its greens make up the highest golf course in the world. An easy, glorious day-trip base from Srinagar for families, with pony rides, walks and views in every direction.

items.name: Gulmarg: Skiing & Snow (Winter)
items.description: In winter Gulmarg becomes one of Asia's serious ski destinations, with genuine high-altitude powder off Apharwat reached by the gondola, plus gentle nursery slopes for first-timers and children. Arrange instructors and gear in advance; the off-piste here draws skiers from around the world.

items.name: Pahalgam: The Lidder Valley
items.description: The 'valley of shepherds' sits where the glacier-fed Lidder river runs cold and clear through pine and meadow, the classic Kashmiri summer retreat two-and-a-half hours from Srinagar. It makes a superb overnight base — riverside luxury stays, gentle walks and cool air — for families escaping the plains' heat.

items.name: Pahalgam: Betaab Valley
items.description: A wide green bowl where pine forests meet the Lidder, named for the Bollywood film shot here and postcard-perfect in every direction. An easy, level, kid-friendly stop that delivers the archetypal Kashmir meadow with almost no walking.

items.name: Pahalgam: Aru Valley
items.description: A hushed hamlet and meadow upriver from Pahalgam, the trailhead for the Kolahoi glacier and the Tarsar–Marsar lakes and far quieter than the main town. The place to base for a day of gentle riverside walks or a serious trek with a private outfitter.

items.name: Pahalgam: Chandanwari
items.description: The end of the motorable road up the Lidder, where snow lingers into summer and the annual Amarnath pilgrimage traditionally sets off on foot. A scenic drive to a high, cold, dramatic spot with a taste of the sacred geography beyond.

items.name: Sonamarg: The Meadow of Gold
items.description: 'Meadow of gold', a high alpine bowl at around 2,700 metres on the road to Ladakh, where the Sindh river braids through grass under snow-streaked peaks. The most alpine-feeling of the valley's day-trips and the classic launch point for river rafting and pony rides.

items.name: Sonamarg: Thajiwas Glacier
items.description: A short pony ride or walk from Sonamarg brings you to the snout of the Thajiwas glacier, ringed by conifers and meadows and holding snow through much of the year. A rare chance to stand at a glacier with children in tow, no serious trekking required.

items.name: Yusmarg
items.description: A quiet, rolling meadow of pines and open grass south-west of Srinagar that the crowds still largely skip, its name meaning 'meadow of Jesus'. The hidden-gem alternative to Gulmarg for a family picnic day, all space and silence and horse rides.

items.name: Doodhpathri
items.description: The 'valley of milk', an emerald meadow laced by a shallow, milk-white stream about an hour and a half from Srinagar, still one of Kashmir's least-spoilt escapes. Come for a slow, uncrowded day on the grass — the antidote to the well-trodden circuit.

items.name: The Jhelum Riverfront & Seven Bridges
items.description: The Jhelum threads the heart of the old city under a chain of historic bridges — the kadals — with tall timber-and-brick houses leaning over the water. A walk or a boat along it reads the older, workaday Srinagar that the lakes politely hide.

items.name: Manasbal Lake
items.description: The deepest lake in Kashmir, an hour north of the city, quiet and mirror-still with lotus blooming across it in summer and a small Mughal garden on its shore. A serene, birdwatcher's day-trip almost no tourist itinerary bothers with.

items.name: Wular Lake & the Kashmir Backwaters
items.description: One of the largest freshwater lakes in Asia, fed by the Jhelum and fringed by the villages of north Kashmir, vast and thinly visited. A guided trip out here — birdlife, fishing hamlets, open water under the mountains — is for travellers who have already done the classics.

items.name: Verinag Spring
credentials: On UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List as part of the serial 'Mughal Gardens in Kashmir' nomination
items.description: The deep, octagonal Mughal-walled spring that is the chief source of the Jhelum, ringed by chinars and remarkably peaceful, south of Srinagar on the Pahalgam road. A worthwhile detour that completes the story of the Mughals' love affair with Kashmir's water.

items.name: Achabal Bagh
credentials: On UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List as part of the serial 'Mughal Gardens in Kashmir' nomination
items.description: A serene Mughal spring-garden laid out for Nur Jahan around a powerful natural spring, with cascades, chinar avenues and far fewer visitors than the Srinagar gardens. A graceful, unhurried stop that pairs naturally with a run down towards Pahalgam.

items.name: The Amarnath Pilgrim Context
items.description: Each summer hundreds of thousands make the high-altitude yatra to the Amarnath ice-lingam cave, staging from Pahalgam's Chandanwari or Sonamarg's Baltal — a sacred rhythm that shapes the valley's whole season. Even without doing the trek, understanding it, and perhaps a helicopter darshan for the devout, is part of reading Kashmir honestly.

items.name: Saffron Fields of Pampore (Seasonal)
credentials: Kashmir Saffron holds India's Geographical Indication (GI) tag
items.description: The plateau around Pampore, minutes outside Srinagar, grows the world-renowned Kashmiri saffron, and for a fortnight each late autumn the fields turn purple with crocus at harvest. A short, vivid seasonal detour — and the place to buy the real, GI-tagged spice at source.

items.name: Dachigam National Park
items.description: A protected valley half an hour from the city and the last refuge of the endangered hangul, the Kashmir stag, alongside black bears and leopards in wooded slopes above the Dal. A permitted, guided visit is a rare wildlife dimension to a trip most people spend entirely on lakes and gardens.

items.name: Kashmiri Cuisine Beyond Wazwan
items.description: Past the grand banquet lies an everyday table worth exploring — haakh greens, nadru (lotus stem), morel mushrooms, the sour-red mujj chetin, and the lake's own fish — much of it deeply vegetarian-friendly. A guided food morning, from bakery to tea-house to home kitchen, is its own small journey.

items.name: Autumn Chinar Season (Seasonal)
items.description: For a few weeks in late October and November the valley's chinars turn crimson and gold — Naseem Bagh, the Mughal gardens, the university, whole avenues ablaze — in what Kashmiris call the harud. The quietest, most photogenic and most underrated time to come.

items.name: The Chinar at The Lalit Grand Palace
credentials: Inside The Lalit Grand Palace — recognised heritage-palace hotel, former Maharaja's residence
Noted for introducing a full and a vegetarian Wazwan (Rista, Modur Pulav, Gushtaba)
items.description: The grand Wazwan, served in the Maharaja's palace with the gardens and Dal beyond — the most refined Kashmiri feast in the city.

items.name: Ahdoos
credentials: Legendary institution est. 1918 — widely regarded as the benchmark for authentic Kashmiri Wazwan
items.description: The century-old benchmark of Kashmiri cooking — Persian carpets, old Srinagar photographs, and Wazwan as it should be.

items.name: Mughal Darbar
credentials: Long-running recognised Srinagar institution — among the most-cited Wazwan houses in the city
items.description: A city institution for the full spread — Wazwan-e-Khas and the finest cuts, done with real skill and no fuss.

items.name: Shamyana
credentials: Recognised Boulevard-Road Wazwan restaurant, consistently cited among Srinagar's best for Kashmiri cuisine
items.description: Authentic Kashmiri cooking a step from the Dal — Tabak Maaz, seekh kebabs and Rogan Josh with the lake at the door.

items.name: Krishna Dhaba
credentials: Legendary institution est. 1937 — Srinagar's best-known pure-vegetarian address (Krishna Vaishno Dhaba)
items.description: The valley's beloved pure-vegetarian institution — jam-packed, unpretentious, and famous for its dal makhani.

items.name: Houseboat evening on the Dal
credentials: Signature Srinagar evening — heritage Dal Lake houseboats (Butt's Clermont est. 1947; Sukoon, Condé Nast Traveller / Mr & Mrs Smith)
items.description: The valley's true night out — kahwa and dinner on your own carved-walnut deck as the lake goes silent and the hills fade to dark.

items.name: Hotel lounge nightcap
items.area: Srinagar (The Lalit Grand Palace / Taj Dal View)
credentials: Inside recognised luxury hotels — The Lalit Grand Palace (former Maharaja's palace) and Taj Dal View (IHCL)
items.description: A quiet drink in a heritage-palace or hilltop-hotel lounge — the calmest, most civilised late hour in the city.

items.title: Dawn shikara to the floating market on Dal Lake
items.description: A first-light glide among the produce sellers and lotus gardens before the lake wakes.

items.title: Night on a heritage houseboat on Nigeen Lake
items.description: A carved-cedar houseboat on the quieter of the two lakes, away from the Dal crowds.

items.title: Private visit to the Mughal gardens at golden hour
items.description: Nishat and Shalimar Bagh in the low evening light, with a historian on the Mughal design.

items.title: Day into the meadows of Gulmarg or Pahalgam
items.description: A private drive up to the high pastures, with the Gulmarg gondola or a Pahalgam valley walk.

plan.heading: 4 days in Srinagar, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive and board a heritage houseboat on Nigeen lake, the quieter of the two waters.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A shikara at dusk across Dal, past the floating gardens and kingfishers.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Wazwan dinner aboard, or at Ahdoos in town for the classic Kashmiri table.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Nishat and Shalimar Bagh in the morning cool, the chinars and terraced water channels.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Pari Mahal above the lake and the Hazratbal shrine along the shore.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return to the houseboat; a quiet supper with the lake still.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Jamia Masjid with its deodar pillars and the Shah-e-Hamdan shrine in the old quarter.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Visit a trusted pashmina and carpet atelier to see the weaving and kani work first-hand.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Mughal Darbar or a private wazwan arranged through your host.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive out to Pahalgam and the Lidder valley, or Gulmarg for the gondola and the meadows.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A walk among the pines and a picnic lunch in the open.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return to Srinagar for a last night on the water, or fly out.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Nigeen Lake
items.description: The calmer, cleaner lake with the best houseboats; best for a serene base.

items.name: Dal Lake (Boulevard side)
items.description: The famous, busier lake with shikaras and gardens close by; suits first-timers wanting the classic view.

items.name: Old City / Downtown
items.description: The historic heart of shrines, mosques and craft workshops; for those wanting heritage and texture.

events.name: Tulip Festival
events.note: Asia's largest tulip garden below the Zabarwan hills blooms for a few weeks; the signature spring event.

events.name: Almond blossom season
events.note: The Badamwari garden's almond trees flower, marking the first sign of the Kashmiri spring.

events.name: Saffron harvest (Pampore, nearby)
events.note: The purple crocus fields around Pampore bloom for the world's most prized saffron; a rare sight.

events.name: Shikara Festival
events.note: A summer lake festival with decorated-boat races and cultural events on Dal Lake.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Srinagar international airport and be met by a private car for the short transfer to the Dal Lake; the elegant arrival is by shikara across the water to a heritage houseboat or lakeside property.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver covers the city and day trips to Gulmarg, Pahalgam and Sonamarg, while a shikara is the graceful way to move on Dal and Nigeen lakes.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Only postpaid Indian SIMs are permitted to work in Kashmir; prepaid and many eSIMs will not connect, so arrange a postpaid line or rely on hotel wifi.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Indian rupee; carry cash for shikaras, markets and craft purchases, though hotels and better shops take cards; modest tipping is appreciated.

onGround.note: Stay on the quieter Nigeen Lake rather than the busier Dal for privacy; dress is conservative given local custom; the finest pashmina and saffron are bought through your host to avoid the tourist markets, and the Chinar valley is loveliest in autumn.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: April–October is lovely: tulips and almond blossom in spring, gardens and Dal Lake in summer, chinar-gold in October. Avoid December–February unless you want deep cold and snow (beautiful, but flights and roads get unreliable).

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi to Srinagar (SXR) in about 90 minutes, and from Mumbai in ~2.5hrs; Air India and IndiGo fly it well, Air India offering a business cabin on some Delhi frequencies. Take a morning slot — afternoon weather closes the valley — and use the Delhi lounge, as SXR itself is functional, not plush.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations beyond routine. Honestly: the valley is open and safe for tourism in 2026, with record arrivals and a strong tourist-police presence on the Srinagar–Gulmarg–Pahalgam circuit — stay to established routes and a vetted local operator. Srinagar is low-altitude and gentle; water sealed/bottled only.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Easy for vegetarian, and Jain is manageable with notice. Kashmiri cuisine is meat-heavy (the Wazwan), but haak, nadru (lotus stem) and rich vegetarian dishes are excellent; pure-veg and Jain kitchens exist in the city and every good hotel/houseboat will cook to order. Ask your houseboat or property to prep Jain in advance rather than improvising out.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

seo.title: St. Moritz — TripAgent
seo.description: St. Moritz, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: St. Moritz
hero.tagline: Engadine glamour where alpine sport meets old-world luxury

ourTake.lede: St. Moritz is at its best in winter, when the frozen lake becomes the whole point — this is where high-altitude sport meets old-money leisure, and you should lean into that rather than treat it as just a ski resort. Base yourself for the events and long lunches, not the piste-bashing; the skiing at neighbouring Corviglia and Corvatsch is good but the town's real currency is the après and the people-watching. Come in late January or February; a summer visit is quieter and lovelier for walking but misses the theatre.
ourTake.comeIf: You want the Alps at their most polished — long lunches on the piste, cashmere afternoons, and a grand old hotel where the staff remember your name.
ourTake.skipIf: You are chasing a lively nightlife scene or an affordable ski week; this is a small, formal, expensive village that sleeps early.

firstLook.heroCaption: Modern pool villa with palms and umbrella

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: December to March for snow and the frozen-lake season of White Turf and Snow Polo; July and August for high-alpine hiking. Avoid the muddy shoulder weeks when much closes.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Sep, Oct, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Badrutt's Palace Hotel
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The turreted symbol of St. Moritz since 1896 — the address the whole resort is measured against.

items.name: Kulm Hotel St. Moritz
items.description: Where Alpine winter tourism was invented in 1864 — GaultMillau's Hotel of the Year, above the lake and the Cresta.

items.name: Suvretta House
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A fairytale castle on its own plateau — the only ski-in, ski-out house in St. Moritz, with a private lift to Corviglia.

items.name: Carlton Hotel St. Moritz
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A former tsar's residence turned all-suite house — every room faces the lake, and the finest Italian table in Switzerland is downstairs.

items.name: Kempinski Grand Hotel des Bains
items.description: A grand spa house on St. Moritz's mineral springs — the wellness address, at the foot of the Corviglia lift.

items.name: Grace La Margna St. Moritz
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: A listed 1906 façade reborn as the resort's freshest luxury house — most rooms over the lake, two minutes from the station.

items.name: Grand Hotel Kronenhof
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A neo-Baroque grande dame facing the Bernina glaciers — the Engadin's most beautiful historic hotel, a short drive from St. Moritz.

items.name: Nira Alpina
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: A design-led mountain hotel with the Corvatsch cable car in the building — ski from bed to the glacier.

items.name: Corviglia & the Piz Nair Cable Car
items.description: The funicular climbs from the village directly to Corviglia at 2,489m — Switzerland's first railway built straight to a ski slope, opened in 1928 — and a cable car floats the last 530m to the Piz Nair summit at 3,056m, where the whole Engadin lake plateau and the Albula Alps open below you. This is the home mountain of St. Moritz society, groomed to perfection and laced with sun terraces; ski it in winter or ride it up in summer for the view and lunch.

items.name: The Mountain-Restaurant Scene on Corviglia
items.description: Lunch on Corviglia is a St. Moritz institution — the long, champagne-fuelled midday table where the see-and-be-seen crowd gathers between runs. La Marmite at the top station is the legendary address for truffle and caviar, El Paradiso for its terrace and DJs, and Restaurant Piz Nair '10,000 Feet' the highest of them all. Book ahead; a private guide can arrange a table and a heli lift back.

items.name: Skiing Corviglia — 155km Above the Lakes
items.description: 155 kilometres of immaculately prepared pistes and 24 lifts spread across Corviglia's blues, reds and blacks, all facing the frozen chain of Engadin lakes — the birthplace of Alpine winter tourism still skiing at the top of the game. Private instructors and ski-in lunch reservations are the norm here, and the whole family can be matched to terrain, elders included.

items.name: Piz Nair Sunrise
items.description: On select winter mornings the Piz Nair cable car runs before dawn to carry a small group up to 3,056m for breakfast as the first light sets the Bernina peaks alight, followed by the first tracks down empty pistes. It is one of the Engadin's quietly magical private-feeling experiences, best arranged in advance with your hotel concierge.

items.name: Corvatsch — Cable Car to 3,303m
items.description: The Corvatsch is the highest point reachable by cable car in the whole of eastern Switzerland, rising from Surlej to a viewing platform at 3,303m that looks straight across the Bernina glaciers and down onto the string of turquoise Upper Engadin lakes. In winter it delivers long, high, snow-sure descents; in summer, glacier air and a terrace among the four-thousanders.

items.name: Corvatsch Snow Night & Hahnensee Run
items.description: Corvatsch runs Switzerland's longest floodlit night-skiing on Fridays, and its celebrated Hahnensee descent drops all the way from the glacier down to St. Moritz-Bad — a long, wild top-to-valley run that ends steps from an aprés-ski table. A memorable, slightly adventurous half-day for confident skiers in the family.

items.name: Diavolezza — The Glacier Panorama
items.description: The Diavolezza gondola lifts you to a terrace at 2,978m where Piz Bernina — the highest peak in the Eastern Alps at 4,049m — and the fluted ice of Piz Palü rise directly across the valley, with the Pers and Morteratsch glaciers spilling beneath your feet. The sun-terrace of the Berghaus here has one of the great glacier views in the Alps; go simply to look, or ski the powder.

items.name: The Morteratsch Glacier Hike & Glacier Trail
items.description: From Morteratsch station a gentle, well-marked trail follows the retreating tongue of the mighty Morteratsch glacier, with markers showing where the ice stood in past decades — a moving, easy walk suitable across generations. For the more adventurous, a guided glacier traverse descends from Diavolezza across the Pers and Morteratsch ice; take a certified mountain guide.

items.name: Muottas Muragl — The Funicular & the Sunset
items.description: A wonderfully old-fashioned funicular from 1907 climbs to a terrace at 2,454m that frames the classic Engadin postcard — the chain of lakes below, the Bernina massif beyond, painted gold at dusk. The funicular runs late into the evening precisely so you can stay for the alpenglow and dinner at the Romantik Hotel; the single best sunset in the valley.

items.name: The Muottas Muragl Philosophers' Path
items.description: From the mountain station a contemplative loop trail carries quotations from the great thinkers who summered in the Engadin, winding into the Val Muragl and back with the lakes always in view. It is a gentle, thoughtful walk — the Engadin's landscape has always drawn writers and philosophers, and this path makes that lineage tangible.

items.name: The Muottas Muragl Panorama Trail to Alp Languard
items.description: One of the Engadin's signature high-balcony walks traverses from Muottas Muragl toward Alp Languard, hung high above the valley the whole way with the lakes on one side and the Bernina glaciers on the other, through stone-pine forest. A chairlift down to Pontresina at the far end means you need only walk the beautiful part.

items.name: White Turf — Horse Racing on the Frozen Lake
items.description: Across three February Sundays the frozen lake becomes a racecourse and the definitive event of the St. Moritz winter season — thoroughbred flat and trotting races on snow, plus skijöring, the St. Moritz-exclusive discipline where skiers are hauled behind riderless horses at up to 50km/h. It is glamour, furs, champagne tents and society in full flourish; the hospitality marquees are the place to be.

items.name: The Snow Polo World Cup
items.description: Snow polo had its world premiere here in 1985, and St. Moritz still stages the only high-goal polo tournament played on snow — three days of thundering ponies on the frozen lake, VIP tents and end-of-day parties in late January. Among the most exclusive tickets of the European winter social calendar.

items.name: Cricket on Ice
items.description: First played on the frozen lake in 1988, Cricket on Ice is the delightfully improbable spectacle of a full match staged on the snow-covered surface of Lake St. Moritz in February — a natural draw for Indian visitors and a very St. Moritz blend of sport, eccentricity and lakeside hospitality.

items.name: The St. Moritz Gourmet Festival
items.description: Running since 1994, the region's landmark culinary festival brings guest chefs from around the world into the grand hotels for Four-Hands Dinners and the legendary Gourmet Safari that walks a small group through several palace kitchens in a single evening. The Engadin already carries eight Michelin stars; this is the week it shows off. (Note: repositioned to summer from 2026.)

items.name: The Segantini Museum
items.description: Built in 1908 as a memorial to the painter Giovanni Segantini, this domed stone rotunda holds the world's most important collection of his work, crowned by the monumental Alpine triptych 'La Vita — La Natura — La Morte'. Segantini reinvented how the high Alps were painted, and standing before the triptych with the real peaks outside is quietly extraordinary.

items.name: The Berry Museum
items.description: Set in the centuries-old Villa Arona in the heart of the village, this intimate house-museum shows the luminous, Belle Époque paintings of the physician-artist Peter Robert Berry — a warm, personal counterpoint to the grand hotels, and a window into the St. Moritz of a hundred years ago.

items.name: The Leaning Tower of St. Moritz
items.description: The last surviving fragment of the old church of St. Mauritius, this 12th-century tower leans at 5.5 degrees — a steeper tilt than Pisa's — above the village. A quick but characterful landmark, and a good anchor for a stroll through the old centre and up to Via Serlas.

items.name: Sils Maria & the Nietzsche House
items.description: The most serene of the Engadin villages sits between Lakes Sils and Silvaplana, and it was here, in a modest house from 1881 to 1888, that Friedrich Nietzsche spent seven summers and conceived much of his thought. The house is now a museum; the village itself — car-light, lake-bound, ringed by peaks — is the Engadin at its most contemplative.

items.name: Silvaplana — Windsurfing & Kitesurfing
items.description: The reliable afternoon 'Maloja wind' turns Lake Silvaplana into one of Europe's great high-altitude surfing arenas — from May to October the water fills with bright kites and sails against the Corvatsch backdrop. Even if you only watch from the shore over a lakeside lunch, it is one of the Engadin's most alive summer scenes; lessons and gear are on hand at the surf centre.

items.name: Zuoz — The Sgraffito Village
items.description: The best-preserved patrician village in the Upper Engadin, Zuoz is a picture-book ensemble of thick-walled Engadin houses with funnel windows, oriel bays and the incised, whitewashed wall-decoration called sgraffito. A guided village walk unlocks the stories behind the coats of arms and the fountains; unhurried, cultured, real.

items.name: S-chanf & the Upper Engadin Villages
items.description: Just beyond Zuoz, S-chanf marks the edge of the great flat river meadows and, with neighbouring Madulain and La Punt, offers the same sgraffito-fronted Engadin architecture without the crowds — plus the gateway to the Swiss National Park nearby. A quiet, authentic half-day for those who want the valley's soul, not its shop windows.

items.name: Pontresina — Belle Époque Village on the Bernina
items.description: A sunny, south-facing resort village of grand Belle Époque hotels and traditional sgraffito houses at the mouth of the Roseg and Morteratsch valleys — the walkers' and climbers' base of the Engadin, calmer than St. Moritz but with its own refined charm. The perfect launch point for the Bernina glaciers and valley hikes.

items.name: Celerina & the Chapel of San Gian
items.description: Celerina sits at the foot of Corviglia — where the Cresta Run and Olympia Bob Run finish — and is crowned by the landmark 15th-century chapel of San Gian with its twin (one roofless) towers on a low hill. A gentler, more village-scaled base than St. Moritz, minutes away by rail or road.

items.name: The Bernina Express
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Rhaetian Railway in the Albula/Bernina Landscapes
items.description: The most spectacular Alpine rail journey runs from the Engadin over the Bernina Pass and down to palm-fringed Tirano in Italy, climbing past glaciers and looping through the celebrated Brusio spiral viaduct without a single rack rail. Ride it in the panoramic carriages, or splurge on the exclusive first-class 'Excellence Class' with dining service.

items.name: The Glacier Express
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Rhaetian Railway in the Albula/Bernina Landscapes
items.description: Billed as the world's slowest express, the Glacier Express links St. Moritz to Zermatt over eight hours of viaducts, gorges and the Oberalp Pass, its Albula section part of the same UNESCO railway. The Excellence Class carriage — one seat per window, five-course lunch, a personal concierge — is the way HNI travellers do it.

items.name: The Landwasser Viaduct
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Rhaetian Railway in the Albula/Bernina Landscapes
items.description: The six-arched limestone viaduct that curves 65m above the Landwasser gorge straight into a tunnel mouth in the cliff is the single most photographed image of the Rhaetian Railway and the icon of the UNESCO line. Whether from a carriage window or the trackside viewpoint, it is the picture people come for.

items.name: The Val Roseg by Horse-Drawn Carriage
items.description: One of the most beautiful side valleys in the Engadin is reached the loveliest way — a horse-drawn carriage that clops from Pontresina station up the Rosegbach to the glacier-view Hotel Roseg, past larch woods and grazing meadows. Ride up, lunch on the terrace before the Bernina ice, and walk the gentle path back; a treat for all ages, and a sleigh ride in winter.

items.name: Val Fex — The Hidden Valley Above Sils
items.description: Car-free and impossibly pastoral, the Val Fex climbs behind Sils Maria to a scatter of hamlets, a frescoed mountain chapel and a small glacier at its head. Reached on foot or by horse-carriage (sleigh in winter), it is the Engadin's secret garden — a quiet, cultured escape favoured by those in the know.

items.name: The Engadin Lakes Hike
items.description: The classic valley-floor walk strings together the four Upper Engadin lakes — St. Moritz, Champfèr, Silvaplana and Sils — on easy, near-level paths, the water often mirror-still and the Bernina reflected in it. Flat enough for grandparents, beautiful enough for anyone; do it in sections and picnic at a shore of your choosing.

items.name: The Cresta Run
items.description: Built in 1884 and run by the storied St. Moritz Tobogganing Club, the Cresta is a 1.2km natural-ice skeleton track where riders hurl themselves head-first down a hand-built channel of snow and ice — one of only two natural-ice runs left in the world staging international competition. It used the same track for the skeleton event at both the 1928 and 1948 Winter Olympics; watching from Junction is a St. Moritz rite.

items.name: The Olympia Bob Run
items.description: The birthplace of bobsleigh — first raced here in 1904 — is the last naturally built ice track in the world still hosting sanctioned bob and skeleton races, hand-carved each winter from snow and water alone. You can watch the professionals, or book a guest run and rocket down beside a pilot; St. Moritz hosted the Winter Olympics twice, in 1928 and 1948, and this track carried both.

items.name: Engadin Golf — The Oldest in Switzerland
items.description: Founded in Samedan in 1893, Engadin Golf is the oldest golf club in Switzerland and among the oldest in continental Europe, its flat valley-floor course ringed by 3,000m peaks and nicknamed the 'Swiss St. Andrews'. With a second course at Zuoz-Madulain and the high Kulm course above the village, it is high-altitude golf with an unmatched backdrop.

items.name: The Kempinski Alpine Spa & the Mauritius Spring
items.description: The Grand Hotel des Bains Kempinski stands on St. Moritz's 3,500-year-old bathing tradition, its vast Alpine Spa fed by the mineral-rich, naturally carbonated Mauritius spring that first made the town famous as a cure resort. Pools, Kneipp streams and thermal circuits make it one of the finest wellness addresses in the Alps.

items.name: The Palace Wellness at Badrutt's Palace
items.description: The spa of the legendary Badrutt's Palace — the address of St. Moritz society since 1896 — offers ten treatment rooms, private spa suites, saunas and heated indoor-outdoor pools looking to the lake. Even non-residents can book treatments; it is discreet luxury at the beating heart of the resort.

items.name: The Kulm Spa & the Kulm Country Club
items.description: The Kulm Hotel — where Alpine winter tourism was famously invented on a bet in 1864 — pairs a serene thermal-and-sauna wellness world with the Norman Foster-restored Kulm Country Club and the natural ice rink where the world's first Olympic ice events were held. History, wellness and glamour on one estate.

items.name: Via Serlas — The Luxury Mile
items.description: Reputed to be the world's shortest luxury shopping street, Via Serlas packs Chanel, Louis Vuitton, Gucci, Prada, Hermès, Cartier and Bulgari into a few glittering metres beside Badrutt's Palace. Around it, small St. Moritz institutions sell caviar, rare teas, Engadin specialities and fine watches — the whole resort's see-and-be-seen promenade.

items.name: Two Michelin Stars at IGNIV by Andreas Caminada
items.description: Andreas Caminada's playful fine-dining-as-sharing concept inside Badrutt's Palace holds two Michelin stars — beautifully composed modern European plates brought to the table to share, with the lake beyond the windows. One of the most sought-after tables in the Alps; reserve well ahead.

items.name: Da Vittorio — Two-Star Italian at the Carlton
items.description: The Cerea family's St. Moritz outpost of the famed Da Vittorio holds two Michelin stars for hearty-yet-refined Italian cooking, served in an elegant room above Lake St. Moritz — a natural favourite for guests who want gastronomy without ceremony overload, and staff attuned to dietary needs.

items.name: Ecco St. Moritz — Two Stars at Giardino Mountain
items.description: In the calm of Champfèr just outside the resort, Ecco within the Giardino Mountain hotel carries two Michelin stars for cuisine rooted in French tradition — the winter fine-dining destination for those who prefer their gastronomy a step removed from the St. Moritz throng.

items.name: Chesa Veglia — Badrutt's 17th-Century Farmhouse
items.description: A 1658 Engadin farmhouse turned into Badrutt's Palace's most atmospheric dining rooms, where pizza and grill are served under low painted beams and the après crowd gathers at the Polo Bar. Beautiful, historic and unmistakably St. Moritz — the enjoyable, less-formal counterpoint to the Michelin tables.

items.name: Mountain Biking the Engadin Trails
items.description: Beyond skiing, the Engadin is a serious summer bike destination — from easy, near-level lakeshore loops the whole family can ride to lift-served flow trails and technical high-alpine singletrack off Corviglia and Corvatsch. E-bikes and guides are easily arranged; a fine active day between the lakes and the peaks.

items.name: St. Moritz-Bad & Lake Staz (Lej da Staz)
items.description: A short walk or gentle carriage ride from the resort, the little forest-ringed Lej da Staz is the locals' summer swimming lake — warmer and calmer than the big lakes, with a rustic restaurant on its shore. A relaxed, unshowy escape that balances the glamour of the Dorf; lovely with children and grandparents.

items.name: Sailing & Rowing on Lake Silvaplana and Lake Sils
items.description: Two of the largest Alpine lakes in Graubünden, Silvaplana and Sils are prime high-altitude sailing water thanks to the dependable Maloja wind, and a graceful old passenger boat still crosses Lake Sils in summer. Charter a boat, take a sailing lesson, or simply cruise the mirror-calm mornings before the wind rises.

items.name: Alp Languard & the Marmot Trails Above Pontresina
items.description: A short chairlift from Pontresina lifts you to Alp Languard, a sunny alp famous for its bold, whistling marmots and easy family walks with the Bernina glaciers laid out opposite. Gentle, wildlife-rich and scenic — one of the Engadin's most rewarding low-effort mountain outings.

items.name: Heli-Skiing & Private Glacier Flights
items.description: For those who want the mountains to themselves, helicopters lift skiers to remote glacier descents and carry sightseers over the Bernina ice fields for a landing in the eternal snow. Arranged discreetly through the grand hotels or private guides, it is the Engadin at its most exclusive — and a spectacular multi-generational scenic flight in summer.

items.name: The Mili Weber House
items.description: The enchanting former home of illustrator Mili Weber, kept exactly as she left it and hand-painted with fairy-tale murals from floor to ceiling — a hidden, tender little gem quite unlike anything else in glamorous St. Moritz, visited by guided tour. A delightful, unexpected stop, especially with children.

items.name: Da Vittorio – St. Moritz
items.description: The Cerea family's Alpine outpost of their three-star Lombardy temple — widely held to be the finest Italian table in Switzerland.

items.name: Ecco St. Moritz
items.description: Reto Brändli's French-rooted cooking — depth and finesse in equal measure, in the calm of the Giardino Mountain.

items.name: IGNIV by Andreas Caminada
items.description: Caminada's fine-dining-meets-sharing concept inside Badrutt's Palace — generous, playful and technically exact.

items.name: Talvo by Dalsass
items.description: Mediterranean cooking of pure, produce-led essence in a 1658 Engadine farmhouse — one star, richly deserved.

items.name: The K by Tim Raue
items.description: Tim Raue's precise Asian-accented cooking — Berlin's two-star hand, brought to the Kulm's mountain room.

items.name: Cà d'Oro
items.description: Matthias Schmidberger's refined kitchen at the Kempinski — polished, contemporary and quietly excellent.

items.name: Grand Restaurant, Suvretta House
items.description: Fabrizio Zanetti's cooking in a coffered, candle-lit dining hall — old-world grandeur, thoroughly modern plates.

items.name: Matsuhisa by Nobu, St. Moritz
credentials: Part of the Nobu / Matsuhisa global group, at a MICHELIN Two-Key hotel
items.description: Nobu Matsuhisa's signature Japanese-Peruvian cooking, in the theatrical setting of Badrutt's Palace.

items.name: Dal Mulin
items.description: An independent village room of real ambition — Luca Porro's precise, personal cooking, free of any hotel.

items.name: Chesa Veglia
credentials: A genuine St. Moritz landmark, run by Badrutt's Palace (MICHELIN Two Keys, 2025)
items.description: A 1658 Engadine farmhouse owned by the Palace — pizza, grill and Alpine classics under carved timber and lantern light.

items.name: King's Social House
credentials: A Jason Atherton (multi-Michelin restaurateur) venue, inside Badrutt's Palace
items.description: Jason Atherton's restaurant-bar-club revival of Switzerland's oldest nightclub — a considered kitchen with a late tempo.

items.name: La Scarpetta
items.description: Honest, tasty Italian at a price the grand rooms can't touch — refined yet accessible, and new to the guide.

items.name: Renaissance Bar, Badrutt's Palace
credentials: Inside Badrutt's Palace — MICHELIN Two Keys (2025), The Leading Hotels of the World; a bar of genuine standing
items.description: The definitive St. Moritz hotel bar — timeless cocktails, a fireplace and a cigar selection, beneath the Palace's grandeur.

items.name: Dracula Club
credentials: A genuine St. Moritz institution — Gunter Sachs's private club (est. 1974), host of the Festival da Jazz
items.description: The legendary members' club founded by Gunter Sachs in the 1970s — 150 seats, and the private soul of St. Moritz nightlife.

items.name: King's Social House
credentials: A Jason Atherton venue inside Badrutt's Palace (MICHELIN Two Keys, 2025); the resort's storied club since the 1960s
items.description: Switzerland's oldest nightclub, reborn by Jason Atherton — dinner, drinks and roaming international DJs under the Palace.

items.title: White Turf on the frozen lake
items.description: Thoroughbred racing and skijoring on the frozen Lake St. Moritz, run over three February Sundays since 1907.

items.title: Snow Polo World Cup
items.description: The only high-goal polo tournament played on snow, staged on the lake each January.

items.title: The Glacier Express to Zermatt
items.description: Board the panoramic train at St. Moritz for one of the great slow rail journeys across the Alps.

items.title: Cresta Run toboggan descent
items.description: The historic members' ice run at St. Moritz-Celerina where riders go head-first at speed — arrange access well ahead.

plan.heading: 3 days in St. Moritz, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Coffee at the Hanselmann konditorei, then a walk along the frozen or blue lake below the Leaning Tower.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Segantini Museum for the Alpine painter, then the boutiques of the Via Serlas.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Ecco St. Moritz in the Giardino Mountain at Champfèr, two Michelin stars, then a drink at Badrutt's Palace.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Bernina railway toward the Morteratsch glacier, one of the great Alpine rail lines.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at El Paradiso above the lake, then a walk through the larch woods to Pontresina.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: The Grand Restaurant at Badrutt's Palace, or the intimate King's Club for a later, livelier night.

days.title: Snow, sun, and the good life

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Corviglia by funicular for the runs or simply the terrace at La Marmite, the mountain restaurant above the town.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The thermal waters at the Kempinski or Kulm spa, unhurried.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A last dinner at IGNIV by Andreas Caminada in the Grand Hotel Kronenhof at Pontresina, the sharing table by candlelight.

items.name: St. Moritz Dorf
items.description: The upper village of grand hotels and boutiques — for those who want to be at the centre of it.

items.name: St. Moritz Bad
items.description: By the lake and spa springs, quieter and a shade more relaxed than Dorf.

items.name: Suvretta
items.description: A hushed, wooded pocket above town for people who want privacy and ski-in access.

events.name: Snow Polo World Cup St. Moritz
events.note: Three days of top-level polo on the frozen lake.

events.name: White Turf
events.note: Horse racing and skijoring across three Sundays on the lake.

events.name: St. Moritz Gourmet Festival
events.note: Visiting chefs cook across the town's hotels over a week.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Most arrive by private car or helicopter, or by the scenic Engadin rail line; the nearest airports are Zurich (about three hours by car) and Samedan for private jets, minutes away.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car and driver handles the valley in winter snow; the village and lakeside are walkable, and hotel cars run guests to the slopes.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Reliable across the resort and valley; an eSIM activates on arrival and hotel wifi is strong.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Swiss francs (CHF); cards are universal and tipping stays modest — round up or leave a little for good service.

onGround.note: At around 1,800m the air is thin and dry, so ease in; St. Moritz is a see-and-be-seen resort in high season, so book the Badrutt's Palace or Kulm well ahead and time a visit around the winter polo or White Turf if that appeals.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: December to March is the classic winter season with dependable snow and the frozen-lake events; July to September is bright and dry for hiking. April to May and November are quiet closure months best avoided.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Fly into Zurich (direct from Delhi on SWISS or Air India, ~8h45), then about 3.5-4 hours by rail via Chur, or arrive in style on the Glacier Express. No direct train, so the change at Chur is the norm; the final stretch is one of the finest alpine rail rides in Europe.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations needed; extremely safe and discreet. St. Moritz lies at ~1,800 m, high enough that some guests feel the thin air on day one, so pace yourself, hydrate, and go easy with alcohol at first. Tap water is excellent.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian food is well catered for in the grand hotels, which are used to international and Indian guests. For Jain specifics, give your hotel notice; standalone Indian restaurants are few, so plan meals through the property.

seo.title: Sydney — TripAgent
seo.description: Sydney, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Sydney
hero.tagline: Harbour city of sails, surf and golden light.

ourTake.lede: Sydney is a harbour town before it is a city, so organise everything around the water — the ferries are the best value in Australian travel and the finest way to see the place. Do the Opera House and the bridge, then get out to the eastern beaches and the northern coves where locals actually spend their weekends. Skip Darling Harbour; give that time to a Manly ferry and a coastal walk instead.
ourTake.comeIf: You want harbour, beaches and a polished city with excellent Indian food, direct from Delhi.
ourTake.skipIf: You want a short-haul trip; Australia is far and deserves more than a few days.
