whenToGo.blurb: Warm and bright in the Australian spring (Oct–Dec) and autumn (Mar–Apr); Vivid lights up June, but the summer holidays are hot and busy.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

note.label: On credentials
note.text: Michelin’s inspectors don’t yet come to Sydney. So we don’t pretend a star — we credential its tables the way we’d want to be told: World’s 50 Best, Condé Nast Traveller, and the houses we would send our own family to.

items.name: Capella Sydney
credentials: World's 50 Best Hotels 2025 (No. 12) — Best Hotel in Oceania
items.description: A restored Edwardian sandstone palace off Circular Quay — the finest hotel in the country, and it knows how to wear it lightly.

items.name: Park Hyatt Sydney
credentials: Travel+Leisure World's Best — perennial Sydney listee
items.description: On the harbour's edge between the Bridge and the Opera House — the most cinematic address in the city.

items.name: Crown Towers Sydney
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller Gold List — Barangaroo landmark
items.description: Sydney's tallest luxury tower — glass, light and altitude, with the harbour laid out far below.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Sydney
items.description: The surest hands on the harbour — a dress-circle view of the Opera House and service you never have to think about.

items.name: The Langham, Sydney
items.description: A quiet grande dame tucked into historic Millers Point — the calmest luxury in the city.

items.name: The Darling
credentials: The Darling Spa — Forbes Travel Guide 4-Star Spa (2025)
items.description: A polished, design-led tower above The Star — sleek rooms and one of Sydney's finest hotel spas.

items.name: Shangri-La Sydney
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller — recognised Sydney harbour-view hotel
Home to Altitude, a landmark harbour-view dining room
items.description: High above The Rocks with the broadest harbour panorama of any city hotel — the Bridge and the Opera House in one sweep.

items.name: InterContinental Sydney
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide — recognised Sydney luxury hotel
A landmark heritage hotel of Circular Quay
items.description: A grand 19th-century Treasury building at Circular Quay, reborn around a soaring heritage atrium.

items.name: W Sydney
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller Hot List — Sydney opening
A landmark contemporary hotel of Darling Harbour
items.description: A bold, design-forward tower over Darling Harbour — colour, energy and a spectacular rooftop pool.

items.name: Kimpton Margot Sydney
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller — recognised Sydney design hotel
A landmark Art Deco building of the CBD
items.description: A heritage Art Deco office block turned playful design hotel — one of the CBD's most characterful stays.

items.name: Pier One Sydney Harbour
credentials: A landmark heritage-wharf hotel of Sydney Harbour
Condé Nast Traveller — recognised harbour hotel
items.description: Built out over the water on a restored finger wharf — you sleep almost on the harbour, under the Bridge.

items.name: Ovolo Woolloomooloo
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller — recognised Sydney design hotel
A landmark heritage-wharf hotel of Woolloomooloo
items.description: A vast timber-and-steel heritage wharf turned bold design hotel — one of the most striking arrivals in the city.

items.name: The Old Clare Hotel
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller — recognised Sydney boutique hotel
A landmark design conversion of Chippendale
items.description: A former brewery and pub reborn as an industrial-chic hotel in the arty heart of Chippendale.

items.name: Establishment Hotel
credentials: A landmark hospitality address of the CBD
Condé Nast Traveller — recognised Sydney boutique hotel
items.description: A discreet, glamorous townhouse hotel above one of the city's great dining-and-drinking addresses.

items.name: Little National Hotel Sydney
credentials: A recognised contemporary Sydney design hotel
Condé Nast Traveller — noted value luxury
items.description: A clever, design-conscious business base with a soaring library lounge and a rooftop over the CBD.

items.name: Sydney Opera House
items.description: Jørn Utzon's sail-shells over the harbour are the reason the world pictures Sydney at all. Beyond the one-hour guided tour, an evening in the Concert Hall or a dinner at Bennelong turns the icon into an occasion the whole family remembers; ask for the backstage Access or private tour if you want it uncrowded.

items.name: Sydney Harbour BridgeClimb
items.description: You climb the steel arch of the 'Coathanger' to 134 metres above the water, harnessed and led in small groups, for a 360-degree sweep from the Heads to the Blue Mountains. Dawn and dusk climbs are the ones to book; there is a gentler Sampler climb for older or younger members of the party.

items.name: Sydney Harbour Bridge & Pylon Lookout
items.description: Even without climbing, the walk across the bridge's pedestrian path and the 200-step Pylon Lookout give you the classic Opera-House-and-harbour frame for a fraction of the effort. A calm, no-booking option for a multi-generational group that wants the view without the harness.

items.name: Circular Quay & a Manly Ferry Crossing
items.description: The 30-minute ferry from Circular Quay to Manly is the best-value harbour cruise in the world — Opera House, bridge, headlands and open sea, all for a transit fare. Sit on the top deck outdoors; grand-parents and children alike love it, and Manly's beach and Corso make a natural lunch stop.

items.name: The Rocks
items.description: Sydney's oldest quarter, where colonial sandstone lanes, the weekend market and harbourside pubs sit right under the bridge. Do a walking tour for the convict history, then let the family browse craft and food stalls; it is compact, atmospheric and easy on older legs.

items.name: Royal Botanic Garden Sydney
items.description: Thirty hectares of harbourside gardens wrapping around the Opera House, free to enter and blissfully green. The Aboriginal Heritage Tour and the calm lawns make it a gentle multi-generational morning; the Garden runs right into Mrs Macquarie's Chair.

items.name: Mrs Macquarie's Chair
items.description: A sandstone bench carved for a governor's wife in 1810, sitting on the point that gives you the single most famous view of Sydney — Opera House and Harbour Bridge together in one frame. Come at sunset; it is a five-minute stroll from the Botanic Garden.

items.name: Bondi to Coogee Coastal Walk
items.description: A 6km cliff-top path linking Bondi, Tamarama, Bronte, Clovelly and Coogee — arguably the most beautiful urban walk in Australia, with the Icebergs pool, sea, and (each October) the Sculpture by the Sea open-air gallery. Do a section rather than all of it with elders; the café stops at Bronte and Coogee are excellent.

items.name: Bondi Beach & Bondi Icebergs
items.description: The most famous crescent of sand in the country, with the photogenic Icebergs ocean pool cut into the rocks at its southern end. Lunch at Icebergs Dining Room with the pool and surf below is one of Sydney's set-piece meals — and the menu handles vegetarian requests with ease.

items.name: Bronte Beach
items.description: A smaller, family-favourite beach with a natural rock pool, grassy park and shaded picnic areas — calmer than Bondi and better for children and grand-parents. The café strip behind the sand does a relaxed breakfast before the coastal walk.

items.name: Taronga Zoo
items.description: A hillside zoo across the harbour with koalas, kangaroos and giraffes framed against the Opera House and city skyline — reached by a scenic ferry and cable car. Kids adore it; the Roar & Snore overnight and private keeper experiences are the premium way to do it.

items.name: Art Gallery of New South Wales & Sydney Modern (Naala Badu)
items.description: The state gallery pairs a grand 19th-century building with SANAA's Pritzker-winning Sydney Modern (Naala Badu), opened 2022 — Australia's finest Aboriginal art holdings alongside major international shows. Free general entry, world-class, and a serene indoor option on a hot or rainy day.

items.name: Australian Museum
items.description: The country's oldest museum, strong on natural history, dinosaurs and a deep First Nations gallery — engaging across every age in the family. Well air-conditioned and central, it is a reliable half-day when the weather turns.

items.name: Barangaroo Reserve & the Barangaroo precinct
items.description: A reclaimed headland turned into a native-planted harbour park, backed by a glossy waterfront of restaurants and the Crown Sydney tower. Walk the foreshore at golden hour, then dine — this is where much of Sydney's newest fine dining and vegetarian-friendly kitchens have clustered.

items.name: Queen Victoria Building
items.description: A restored 1898 Romanesque arcade — stained glass, tiled floors and a copper dome — housing boutiques over three levels. A refined, cool-in-summer place to shop and take tea; the architecture alone earns the visit.

items.name: Sydney Tower Eye & Skywalk
items.description: The city's tallest structure, with a glass observation deck 250 metres up and an open-air Skywalk for the brave. The clearest single overview of how harbour, beaches and bushland fit together — good for orienting the family on day one.

items.name: Darling Harbour
items.description: A pedestrian waterfront of museums, aquarium and restaurants built for families — everything walkable around the water. The hub for SEA LIFE, WILD LIFE and the maritime museum, with plenty of casual dining that caters to vegetarians.

items.name: SEA LIFE Sydney Aquarium
items.description: Walk-through ocean tunnels with sharks, rays and one of the world's largest Great Barrier Reef displays, plus dugongs found in only a handful of aquariums worldwide. A dependable, weather-proof crowd-pleaser for younger children.

items.name: Australian National Maritime Museum
items.description: Floating exhibits including a destroyer, a submarine and a replica of Cook's Endeavour, alongside migration and Indigenous seafaring stories. Hands-on and open-air enough to keep restless kids happy between the galleries.

items.name: Watsons Bay & South Head
items.description: A harbourside village at the mouth of the harbour, with the dramatic ocean cliffs of The Gap on one side and calm Camp Cove on the other. Take the ferry out, walk to the Hornby Lighthouse, then eat seafood by the water — a classic, unhurried Sydney afternoon.

items.name: Paddington
items.description: Leafy Victorian terraces with iron-lace balconies, the Saturday Paddington Markets, and Oxford Street's boutiques and galleries. The most elegant neighbourhood wander in the city, and where much of Sydney's independent designer shopping lives.

items.name: Surry Hills
items.description: Sydney's dining heartland — narrow streets packed with acclaimed restaurants, specialty coffee and wine bars. The place to send serious eaters in the family, with strong vegetarian and modern-Australian options at every price point.

items.name: Chinatown & Spice Alley
items.description: Paddy's Markets, dumpling houses and the laneway hawker stalls of Spice Alley make this the city's best-value, most vibrant eating quarter. A lively, affordable night out with plenty of vegetarian pan-Asian choices.

items.name: Chinese Garden of Friendship
items.description: A walled classical Chinese garden of pavilions, koi ponds and waterfalls, built as a gift from Guangzhou — an oasis of calm beside busy Darling Harbour. The tea house and quiet paths suit elders who want to sit and slow down.

items.name: Hyde Park & St Mary's Cathedral
items.description: The city's oldest public park, with a grand fig-tree avenue and the Archibald Fountain, facing the sandstone Gothic St Mary's Cathedral. A green, central spot to regroup between museums and shopping.

items.name: The Grounds of Alexandria
items.description: A former industrial site turned garden café, bakery and market with an ornate, Instagram-famous flower-filled setting. A relaxed, veg-friendly brunch destination that delights children and photographers alike.

items.name: Cockatoo Island (Wareamah)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Australian Convict Sites
items.description: The harbour's largest island — a UNESCO-listed former convict prison and shipyard, reached by ferry, now a heritage site you can walk and even stay overnight on. A quirky, atmospheric half-day away from the crowds.

items.name: Manly & the Manly to Spit Bridge Walk
items.description: Beyond the famous ferry and surf beach, the 10km Spit-to-Manly track threads secluded coves, Aboriginal rock engravings and bush — one of the finest coastal walks near the city. Do the ferry-and-beach version with elders, the full walk with the active.

items.name: Palm Beach & Barrenjoey Lighthouse
items.description: The glamorous tip of the Northern Beaches — long golden sand, the 1881 Barrenjoey Lighthouse headland, and the setting of TV's 'Home and Away'. A gorgeous day trip; arrive by seaplane from Rose Bay for the ultimate discreet flourish.

items.name: Rose Bay Seaplane Scenic Flight
items.description: Australia's oldest seaplane base, where a private floatplane lifts off the water for a sweep over the harbour, beaches and coast — and can drop you at a waterfront lunch at Palm Beach or Cottage Point. A private-charter treat that turns a meal into a memory.

items.name: Blue Mountains (Three Sisters, Katoomba & Scenic World)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Greater Blue Mountains Area
items.description: A vast wilderness of eucalypt-blue valleys, the iconic Three Sisters rock formation, and Scenic World's steepest-in-the-world railway and cliff-hugging cable cars. An easy full-day escape; charter a private guide and finish with high tea at the Hydro Majestic hotel.

items.name: Hunter Valley Wine Country
items.description: Australia's oldest wine region — 150-plus cellar doors famed for Semillon and Shiraz, set among rolling vineyards with fine dining and hot-air balloons at dawn. A private car and a curated cellar-door route, with a vegetarian-friendly long lunch, make a superb full day or overnight.

items.name: Royal National Park
items.description: The world's second-oldest national park — clifftop coast walks, the Instagram-famous Figure 8 Pools, Wattamolla lagoon and empty beaches, all an hour from the city. A wilder, quieter day out for a family that wants nature over crowds.

items.name: Featherdale Wildlife Park
items.description: A hands-on wildlife park where you can hand-feed kangaroos and stand beside koalas — the easiest close-up with Australian animals near the city, and a natural stop on the way to the Blue Mountains. Children love it; keeper encounters can be arranged privately.

items.name: Vaucluse House & Nielsen Park
items.description: A grand colonial Gothic estate with harbour gardens, beside the sheltered netted beach and shady lawns of Nielsen Park (Shark Beach). A refined, low-key eastern-suburbs afternoon combining history, a swim and a garden tea.

items.name: Cockle Bay & King Street Wharf dining
items.description: A curved harbour promenade of waterfront restaurants and bars overlooking the city lights. An easy, walkable place for an evening meal with the family, with plenty of choice for vegetarians and fussy young palates.

items.name: Carriageworks Farmers Market
items.description: Saturday's best food market — restored rail workshops filled with the region's growers, bakers and producers, alongside a leading contemporary arts venue. A genuinely local morning for food-lovers, with excellent produce and coffee.

items.name: Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park & West Head
items.description: Rugged bushland dropping to the Hawkesbury, with ancient Aboriginal rock engravings and the sweeping West Head lookout over Pittwater and Palm Beach. Combine with a Palm Beach seaplane or boat day for a spectacular, uncrowded north-of-the-city outing.

items.name: Luna Park Sydney
items.description: A heritage-listed 1935 amusement park under its famous grinning-face entrance, right beneath the Harbour Bridge with knockout city views. Old-fashioned fun for children and a nostalgic photo stop for everyone else.

items.name: Wendy Whiteley's Secret Garden
items.description: A lush, artist-created garden built by hand on former railway land, tumbling down to the harbour on the north shore — free, hidden and quietly magical. A serene detour few tourists find, lovely with grand-parents in tow.

items.name: Government House & the Domain
items.description: The Governor's grand Gothic Revival residence, its rooms open on guided tours and its gardens open daily, set in the parkland above the harbour. A stately, uncrowded window onto Sydney's colonial grandeur.

items.name: Newtown & King Street
items.description: Sydney's bohemian spine — street art, vintage boutiques, live music and one of the city's densest, most vegetarian-friendly eat streets. A change of pace from the harbour for older kids and food-curious adults.

items.name: Sydney Fish Market
items.description: One of the largest fish markets in the Southern Hemisphere, with a working auction, seafood counters and waterfront eating. Go early; a lively, no-fuss stop, though a family will want to pair it with vegetarian options elsewhere.

items.name: Cabramatta
items.description: The most authentic Vietnamese and South-East Asian quarter in Australia — pho, herb-heavy noodle bowls and market stalls at everyday prices. A rewarding culinary excursion for adventurous eaters, with abundant vegetarian choice.

items.name: Bradleys Head & the Mosman foreshore
items.description: A wooded harbour headland with a coastal track, a naval mast memorial and postcard views straight back to the city skyline. A quiet, leafy walk that pairs naturally with a visit to nearby Taronga Zoo.

items.name: Chippendale & White Rabbit Gallery
items.description: A regenerated inner-city pocket around the green-walled One Central Park building, home to White Rabbit — one of the world's finest collections of contemporary Chinese art, free to enter. A sharp, uncrowded cultural stop with a good tea house.

items.name: Oncore by Clare Smyth
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Three Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Clare Smyth's Sydney room — the three-star London chef's ode to Australian produce, high over the harbour.

items.name: Quay
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Three Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Peter Gilmore's harbourside icon — the Opera House framed in the window and cooking to match the view.

items.name: Saint Peter
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Three Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Josh Niland's fin-to-tail seafood — the most original fish cooking in the world, in a handsome pub dining room.

items.name: Sixpenny
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Three Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: A tiny, produce-obsessed inner-west room that quietly cooks at the very top of the national game.

items.name: Aria
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: A grand harbour-edge dining room staring straight at the Opera House — polished, celebratory, unmistakably Sydney.

items.name: Bennelong
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Peter Gilmore's kitchen inside the sails of the Opera House itself — you dine within a World Heritage landmark.

items.name: Yoshii's Omakase
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: A serene sushi counter of great purity — one of Sydney's finest omakase seats.

items.name: a'Mare
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Alessandro Pavoni's coastal Italian at Crown — pasta and seafood of real refinement, harbour at the window.

items.name: Bentley Restaurant + Bar
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Brent Savage and Nick Hildebrandt's progressive, wine-led cooking — one of Sydney's most quietly ambitious kitchens.

items.name: Firedoor
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Lennox Hastie cooks over live fire and nothing else — the most primal, precise wood-fire room in the country.

items.name: Ester
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: A wood-fired inner-west favourite of honest, seasonal cooking — one of Sydney's most-loved rooms for a decade.

items.name: Icebergs Dining Room and Bar
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Italian cooking above the Bondi Icebergs pool — the most glamorous beach view in Sydney over a long lunch.

items.name: Rockpool Bar & Grill
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Grand Art Deco steakhouse glamour — dry-aged beef and a legendary wine list in a soaring 1930s banking hall.

items.name: Bathers' Pavilion
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Serene modern cooking in a Mediterranean-white pavilion right on Balmoral Beach — a lovely harbour-beach escape.

items.name: Margaret
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Neil Perry's warm, produce-first neighbourhood room — generous cooking in the city's smartest suburb.

items.name: Shell House Dining Room & Terrace
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: A glamorous heritage-tower dining room and terrace — one of the CBD's most beautiful rooms to eat in.

items.name: Spice Temple
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Neil Perry's dark, sultry basement of regional Chinese heat — the antidote to polite Cantonese.

items.name: Ormeggio at The Spit
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Alessandro Pavoni's refined Italian on the water at The Spit — pasta and a marina view in equal measure.

items.name: Porteno
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Argentine live-fire asado in a buzzing Surry Hills room — whole animals over the coals, and a party every night.

items.name: Yellow
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: A pioneering vegetable-led tasting menu in a former artists' haunt — plant cooking at its most inventive.

items.name: Aalia
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Modern Middle Eastern cooking with real finesse — one of the CBD's most exciting recent tables.

items.name: King Clarence
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Live-fire and live-tank seafood cooked on a custom barbecue — bold, contemporary and hard to book.

items.name: Pilu at Freshwater
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Sardinian cooking in a heritage beach house above Freshwater — a serene northern-beaches lunch.

items.name: Cafe Paci
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Pasi Petanen's idiosyncratic, personality-filled cooking — a critical darling of the inner west.

items.name: LuMi Dining
credentials: The Good Food Guide — Two Hats (2025/2026)
items.description: Italian-Japanese cooking on a Pyrmont wharf — delicate, precise and quietly one of the city's best.

items.name: Otto Ristorante
credentials: The Good Food Guide — One Hat (2025/2026)
items.description: The glamorous waterfront Italian that has anchored Woolloomooloo wharf for years — see-and-be-seen dining.

items.name: Catalina
credentials: The Good Food Guide — One Hat (2025/2026)
items.description: Seafood and sparkling water views at Rose Bay — the seaplanes taking off past your table.

items.name: Clam Bar
credentials: The Good Food Guide — One Hat (2025/2026)
items.description: A glamorous martini-and-seafood room from the Swillhouse team — the CBD's most stylish new classic.

items.name: Kiln
credentials: The Good Food Guide — One Hat (2025/2026)
items.description: A rooftop room of live-fire, Korean-inflected cooking above the Ace Hotel — sharp food and a skyline view.

items.name: Cho Cho San
credentials: The Good Food Guide — One Hat (2025/2026)
items.description: Stylish modern Japanese in the heart of Potts Point — sharp cooking in a beautiful pale-timber room.

items.name: Continental Deli
credentials: The Good Food Guide — One Hat (2025/2026)
items.description: A playful deli-bar of tinned fish, martinis on tap and clever bistro plates — Newtown at its most fun.

items.name: Poly
credentials: The Good Food Guide — One Hat (2025/2026)
items.description: The relaxed all-day sibling to Ester — modern plates and natural wine in a stripped-back Surry Hills room.

items.name: Bar Copains
credentials: The Good Food Guide — One Hat (2025/2026)
items.description: A tiny, wine-soaked French bistro-bar — a short, perfect menu and a cult following.

items.name: Abhi's Indian Restaurant
credentials: The Good Food Guide — One Hat (2025/2026)
items.description: A long-running, genuinely hatted Indian kitchen — refined regional cooking well beyond the curry-house norm.

items.name: Ho Jiak Town Hall
credentials: The Good Food Guide — One Hat (2025/2026)
items.description: Punchy, generous Malaysian street cooking taken to a hatted level — one of the city's most exciting Asian rooms.

items.name: Pellegrino 2000
credentials: The Good Food Guide — One Hat (2025/2026)
items.description: A moody, red-lit Italian-American diner-bar — pasta, negronis and Surry Hills swagger.

items.name: McRae Bar, Capella Sydney
credentials: Inside Capella Sydney — World's 50 Best Hotels 2025 (No. 12)
items.description: A Victorian-era drinking den reborn inside the country's finest hotel — intimate cocktails under sandstone and low light.

items.name: Maybe Sammy
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars 2025 (No. 42) — the only Sydney bar on the list
World's 50 Best Bars — listed every year since 2019
items.description: Rat Pack glamour in a room of pastels and pink dinner jackets — Sydney's world-ranked cocktail bar, seven years running.

items.name: Cantina OK!
credentials: Australian Bar Awards 2025 — Tequila Bar of the Year
items.description: A standing-room-only agave den in a former garage — twenty drinkers, mezcal poured with real love, and a global reputation.

items.name: Bar Planet
credentials: Australian Bar Awards 2025 — Gin Bar of the Year
items.description: A slick, spirit-nerd gin bar with one of the deepest botanical lists in the country.

items.name: Kittyhawk
credentials: A celebrated Sydney cocktail bar, from the team behind The Lobo
items.description: A handsome bar imagining liberation-day Paris — rum, rye and ten versions of the Old Fashioned.

items.name: Dean & Nancy on 22
credentials: Australian Bar Awards 2025 — Hotel Bar of the Year
items.description: A soaring 22nd-floor hotel bar of Art Deco glamour and a whisky room — the finest hotel bar in the country.

items.name: Old Mate's Place
credentials: Australian Bar Awards 2025 — Bar of the Year
items.description: A hidden rooftop-and-library bar over the CBD — plants, an open fire and a garden terrace, named the country's best.

items.name: Altitude Bar, Shangri-La Sydney
credentials: A landmark harbour-view bar of The Rocks
items.description: A high-floor harbour bar with the Bridge and the Opera House laid out beneath the glass — the broadest view in the city over a drink.

items.name: Ramblin' Rascal Tavern
credentials: Australian Bar Awards 2025 — Best Bartenders' Bar
items.description: A cult basement tavern where the industry drinks — irreverent, expert and gloriously unpretentious.

items.title: Climb the Sydney Harbour Bridge at dawn
items.description: The first climb of the day tops out as the sun comes up over the harbour.

items.title: Seaplane to a Hawkesbury lunch
items.description: A floatplane from Rose Bay lands you at a waterfront restaurant north of the city.

items.title: Opera House performance and late supper
items.description: See a show in the concert hall, then eat at Bennelong beneath the sails.

items.title: Bondi-to-Coogee walk, done early
items.description: The clifftop coastal path is best at first light before the crowds arrive.

items.name: The Rocks / Circular Quay
items.description: Historic and central, on the harbour and the ferries; the obvious first-timer base.

items.name: Potts Point / Elizabeth Bay
items.description: Elegant, walkable and full of good tables; suits those who want charm near the centre.

items.name: Bondi
items.description: Beach-focused and social, a bus ride from town; for travellers who want sand over skyline.

events.name: Sydney New Year's Eve
events.note: The world's headline midnight fireworks, staged off the bridge and harbour.

events.name: Sydney Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras
events.note: Weeks of events building to the Oxford Street parade, one of the world's largest.

events.name: Vivid Sydney
events.note: The city lights up nightly with projections, music and ideas across the harbour.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Land at Kingsford Smith (SYD), a 20 to 30-minute chauffeured run to the harbour; for a memorable entrance, a seaplane from Rose Bay can deliver you along the coast.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The harbour city is best mixed: a private car for distance, walking the Rocks and Botanic Gardens, and the ferries, which are the loveliest way to see it from the water.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM (Telstra or Optus) gives excellent 5G everywhere; wifi is universal.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Currency is the Australian dollar; cards and phone payments are accepted everywhere and cash is rarely needed; tipping is modest and optional, around 10 percent for fine dining.

onGround.note: Indian passport holders need an ETA or visitor visa arranged before travel; stay around Circular Quay or the eastern beaches, and a concierge can arrange a private yacht on the harbour and tables at Quay or Bennelong.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Southern seasons flipped: Oct-Nov and Mar-Apr are warm, clear and uncrowded; Dec-Feb is hot, humid and peak-holiday, and Jun-Aug is cool and wetter though still mild.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Air India flies Delhi-Sydney nonstop on the 787, about 13.5h; from Mumbai or Bengaluru route via Singapore (Singapore Airlines) or Delhi. Qantas serves Bengaluru-Sydney but the route is suspended 8 Aug-24 Oct 2026, so confirm before booking. Fly Singapore Airlines business via Changi for the smoothest one-stop and use The Private Room / SilverKris lounge.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations; Australia has strict biosecurity, so declare all food including anything veg/Jain you carry. Tap water is safe. Sydney is very safe with excellent private healthcare. Sun is intense — factor UV protection.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Excellent for vegetarians and Jain travellers; large Indian community means abundant, genuine Indian food and pure-veg kitchens, and most fine dining does serious vegetarian menus. Harris Park is the Indian food hub, and the city's vegetarian and vegan options are extensive.

seo.title: Taipei — TripAgent
seo.description: Taipei, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Taipei
hero.tagline: Night-market warmth beneath a soaring green tower.

ourTake.lede: Taipei is warmer and more relaxed than its bigger East Asian neighbours, and the right way to take it is slowly, with the night markets, the hot springs, and the tea hills all in easy reach. Skip the obligatory tower-observation-deck routine and instead spend an afternoon in the mountain teahouses of Maokong, then come down for a proper night-market dinner. The food is the reason to come, and it is best eaten standing up, one stall at a time.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a warm, effortless Asian city where night markets, hot-spring retreats and mountain trails sit half an hour apart.
ourTake.skipIf: You are chasing beaches, big-brand luxury nightlife or a grand-monument bucket list.

grid.caption: purple allium blooms in soft focus
Leopard resting on rock beside tree trunk

whenToGo.blurb: Come in spring or autumn for mild, dry days and blossom or lantern light. Avoid the humid heat and typhoons of June to September.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Oct, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental, Taipei
items.description: The city's grandest address — a tree-lined boulevard house with Taipei's most spacious rooms and its most sought-after afternoon tea.

items.name: Capella Taipei
items.description: André Fu's 'modern mansion' — 86 rooms of quiet, residential grandeur along a European-style boulevard, opened 2025.

items.name: Regent Taipei
items.description: A stalwart of well-heeled Taipei since 1990 — grand, dependable, with its own boutique galleria beneath it.

items.name: Grand Hyatt Taipei
items.description: The first international house in the city, freshly renovated — and the closest grand hotel to Taipei 101.

items.name: Shangri-La's Far Eastern Plaza Hotel, Taipei
items.description: The tallest hotel in the city, after a US$50 million refresh — sweeping views and nine restaurants and bars.

items.name: W Taipei
items.description: The bright, high-energy beacon of the Xinyi business district — the largest luxury hotel in the city.

items.name: Kimpton Da An, Taipei
items.description: A design-led boutique house in leafy Da'an — intimate, culinary-minded, and quietly cool.

items.name: Taipei Marriott Hotel
items.description: A large, polished house near the Miramar district — one of the city's best hotel pools and a strong all-round base.

items.name: Palais de Chine Hotel
items.description: An East-meets-West palace of imported French furniture and antiques — home to the city's three-star Le Palais.

items.name: Taipei 101 Observatory
credentials: Was the world's tallest building from its 2004 opening until the Burj Khalifa (2010), at 508m to the spire
items.description: Ride one of the world's fastest passenger elevators to the 89th-floor observatory, then look down on the 660-tonne golden tuned-mass damper that keeps the tower steady through typhoons and quakes. The 91st-floor outdoor deck is the family photograph; a private guide can pre-book timed entry so multi-gen groups skip the queue entirely.

items.name: Taipei 101 Mall & Din Tai Fung
items.description: The tower's lower floors hold a serene luxury mall — the maisons, plus a basement food hall — and the branch of Din Tai Fung that many visitors combine with the observatory. Dumplings and shopping under one roof make an easy, air-conditioned afternoon when the family wants low effort and high polish.

items.name: National Palace Museum
credentials: Holds one of the world's largest collections of imperial Chinese artefacts (Song, Yuan, Ming and Qing collections)
items.description: One of the world's greatest collections of Chinese art — jade, bronzes, ceramics, painting and calligraphy carried from Beijing's Forbidden City in 1949. Come at opening on a weekday and take a private art-historian guide; with nearly 700,000 objects rotated in cycles, a curated two-hour route through the masterpieces is far richer than wandering.

items.name: Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall
items.description: A vast white-and-blue marble hall rising above formal gardens and the grand Liberty Square gateway, guarded by soldiers whose hourly changing-of-the-guard drill is a precise, photogenic ceremony. The flanking National Theater and Concert Hall make it a serene early-morning walk before the day's heat.

items.name: Longshan Temple
items.description: Taipei's most atmospheric working temple, founded in 1738 in the old Bangka quarter, thick with incense and the murmur of worshippers folding Taoist, Buddhist and folk deities into one courtyard. Visit at dusk when the lanterns glow and locals come to pray; a guide unlocks the etiquette and the meaning behind the offerings.

items.name: Dalongdong Bao'an Temple
credentials: Won a UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Award for Culture Heritage Conservation (2003) — the first such honour for Taiwan
items.description: A jewel of Taiwanese temple craftsmanship dedicated to the God of Medicine, its 19th-century woodcarving, stone dragons and door-god murals painstakingly restored to international acclaim. Quieter than Longshan and paired naturally with the Confucius Temple next door for a calm morning in old Taipei.

items.name: Taipei Confucius Temple
items.description: A restrained, elegant Confucian temple built in the southern Fujian style, its unadorned dignity a deliberate contrast to the exuberance of Bao'an across the lane. Interactive halls explain the rites and the imperial examination system; the autumn Confucius birthday ceremony with its ancient music and dance is the moment to aim for.

items.name: Shilin Night Market
items.description: Taipei's largest and most famous night market — a maze of stalls turning out oyster omelettes, pepper buns, giant fried chicken and shaved ice, plus a basement food court. Best experienced with a local guide who can navigate the veg-friendly and Buddhist-vegetarian stalls (Taiwan's meat-free scene is deep) and steer the family to the good vendors.

items.name: Raohe Street Night Market
items.description: A tighter, more walkable single-lane market anchored by the Ciyou Temple at one end and famous for its black-pepper pork buns baked in a clay oven. Many food-lovers prefer it to Shilin for its density and lower chaos — an easy evening after a day in the east of the city.

items.name: Ningxia Night Market
items.description: A compact, old-Taipei night market beloved for classic Taiwanese street food — taro balls, egg yolk taro, oyster omelette — with less of the crush of Shilin. It sits at the edge of Dadaocheng, so pair it with an afternoon on Dihua Street for a full old-town day into night.

items.name: Dihua Street & Dadaocheng
items.description: Taipei's oldest commercial street, a corridor of restored merchant shophouses trading in Chinese medicinal herbs, dried seafood, fabrics and fine Taiwanese tea since the 19th century. A tea master or private guide turns a stroll into a proper tasting and a lesson in the old town's history; it comes alive further at Lunar New Year.

items.name: Xiahai City God Temple
items.description: A tiny, jewel-box temple on Dihua Street packed with over six hundred deities — including Yue Lao, the God of Love, which draws pilgrims across Taiwan praying for marriage and relationships. Small enough for a fifteen-minute visit, rich enough to anchor a Dadaocheng walk.

items.name: Beitou Thermal Valley
items.description: A steaming, sulphur-green geothermal lake — one of the hottest springs feeding all of Beitou — wreathed in mineral vapour and ringed by a short lakeside path. Free to enter and the natural starting point for a hot-spring day in Taipei's thermal quarter.

items.name: Beitou Hot Springs (private onsen)
items.description: Taipei's thermal valley is lined with hot-spring hotels where families can book a private in-room or reserved bath rather than share a public pool — the discreet choice for multi-gen groups. The waters run from milky white sulphur to rare radium-bearing green springs; ask the concierge to arrange a private thermal suite.

items.name: Beitou Hot Spring Museum
items.description: A graceful 1913 brick-and-timber Japanese bathhouse — once the largest in East Asia — with its grand tiled soaking hall preserved intact and a tatami resting room upstairs. A gentle, free introduction to the town's spa heritage, a short walk from the Thermal Valley.

items.name: Beitou Public Library
credentials: Taiwan's first building to receive Green Building certification
items.description: A quietly beautiful timber library set in Beitou Park, all deep balconies and vertical wooden louvres, and a landmark of green design. A five-minute detour on the hot-spring circuit that architecture-minded travellers genuinely enjoy.

items.name: Yangmingshan National Park
items.description: A volcanic upland of steaming fumaroles, sulphur vents, grasslands and — in spring — cherry blossom and calla-lily fields, all within an hour of the city. A private car and driver make it an easy half-day escape from the heat; the Xiaoyoukeng vents and Qingtiangang meadow are the set-pieces.

items.name: Elephant Mountain (Xiangshan)
items.description: A short but steep stair-climb of about 20–30 minutes delivers the postcard view of Taipei 101 rising over the city, best at golden hour and into the blue-hour lights. It's the classic city hike; go with a guide who knows the quieter viewing rocks so the family isn't jostling for the shot.

items.name: Maokong Gondola & Tea Houses
items.description: A cable-car glide over forested tea hills to Maokong, where hillside tea houses serve locally grown Tieguanyin with the Taipei skyline below. Book the glass-floored Crystal Cabin for the drama, then settle into a teahouse for an unhurried afternoon — a serene, low-effort day the whole family enjoys.

items.name: Taipei Zoo
items.description: One of Asia's largest zoos and the lower station of the Maokong Gondola, home to giant pandas and a well-regarded Formosan-animal area. Genuinely engaging for younger members of a multi-gen group and easily combined with the gondola ride above it.

items.name: Huashan 1914 Creative Park
items.description: A converted 1914 wine-and-camphor factory now given over to design shops, galleries, indie cinema and rotating art-and-immersive exhibitions, with good cafes in the old brick halls. The most central of Taipei's creative parks — an easy, stylish afternoon between sights.

items.name: Songshan Cultural & Creative Park
items.description: A former 1937 tobacco factory reborn as a design campus around a tranquil reflecting pool, home to the Taiwan Design Museum and the striking Eslite Spectrum flagship. Calmer and greener than Huashan, and a short walk from Taipei 101.

items.name: Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall
items.description: A monumental hall honouring the founding father of the Republic, with its own hourly military honour-guard ceremony and, from the plaza, one of the cleanest framed views of Taipei 101. The surrounding park is a favourite for morning tai-chi and evening strolls.

items.name: Miramar Entertainment Park Ferris Wheel (Taipei Eye)
items.description: A rooftop Ferris wheel atop the Miramar mall in the Dazhi district, lit up at night with a gentle turn over the city and the Keelung River. A relaxed evening spin, easy to pair with dinner in the mall — pleasant for children and grandparents alike.

items.name: Tamsui (Danshui) Old Street & Riverside
items.description: The end of the red MRT line opens onto a breezy riverside promenade and a food-street of iron-egg, A-gei and fishball snacks, with Taiwan's most celebrated sunset over the Tamsui estuary. An easy half-day that ends with the Fisherman's Wharf Lover's Bridge lit against the dusk.

items.name: Fort San Domingo (Hongmao Cheng)
items.description: A red-brick fort begun by the Spanish in 1628, rebuilt by the Dutch and later leased as the British Consulate — a layered relic of Taiwan's colonial trade history above the Tamsui river. The former consular residence and its gardens make it more than a quick fort stop; combine with Tamsui Old Street.

items.name: The Red House (Ximen)
items.description: A striking 1908 octagonal red-brick market hall, now a heritage arts-and-crafts venue with a designers' market and a lively creative-district plaza behind it. A quick, characterful stop at the heart of the Ximending shopping quarter.

items.name: Ximending
items.description: Taipei's neon pedestrian shopping district — the city's youthful pulse of street fashion, snack stalls, cinemas and buskers, often called its Harajuku. Best after dark; a lively, easy evening for teenagers in the group, with the Red House at its edge.

items.name: Da'an Forest Park
items.description: Taipei's largest central park — a green lung of banyan groves, an egret-filled ecological pond and open lawns, ringed by the city's most walkable cafe-and-boutique neighbourhood. The place to slow down between sights; the surrounding Da'an lanes reward an unhurried wander.

items.name: Museum of Contemporary Art Taipei (MOCA)
items.description: Taiwan's leading contemporary-art museum, set in a handsome 1920s red-brick former city hall and city school, with sharp rotating shows of local and international work. Compact and central — a good hour for collectors and art-minded travellers.

items.name: National Taiwan Museum
items.description: Taiwan's oldest museum, in a neoclassical hall inside the leafy 228 Peace Memorial Park, covering the island's natural history and indigenous cultures. A gentle, air-conditioned stop near the station, good for a mixed-age group on a hot afternoon.

items.name: Bopiliao Historic Block
items.description: A restored Qing-and-Japanese-era street of arcaded shophouses beside Longshan Temple, its weathered brick facades a favourite film-set and a window into old Bangka life. Free, quick and photogenic — the natural companion to a Longshan Temple visit.

items.name: Xiangshan / Xinyi rooftop bars & city views
items.description: The Xinyi district around Taipei 101 holds the city's best sky-high lounges and hotel bars, where a discreet dinner or nightcap comes with the tower framed at eye level. The refined evening counterpart to the daytime observatory — ask the concierge to secure a window table.

items.name: Yongkang Street food quarter
items.description: A leafy lane synonymous with Taipei eating — beef noodles, mango shaved ice, the original Din Tai Fung nearby, and no end of tea and dessert houses. A stroll-and-graze afternoon; with a food guide it becomes a curated tasting through the city's signature dishes, veg options included.

items.name: Bubble tea & tea culture
items.description: Taiwan is the birthplace of bubble (boba) tea, and Taipei is where to taste it at its source alongside serious high-mountain oolong and Tieguanyin. A private tea-house session — in Maokong, Dadaocheng or a Da'an salon — is a calm, sensory ritual that suits every generation.

items.name: Xiaolongbao & the Din Tai Fung story
credentials: Din Tai Fung's Xinyi Road branch is a Michelin Bib Gourmand; the chain's soup dumplings began at its original Xinyi Road shop
items.description: The soup dumpling reached global fame from Din Tai Fung's original Xinyi Road shop — the pleated, 18-fold xiaolongbao is Taipei's edible signature. The Xinyi branch carries a Michelin Bib Gourmand; book ahead or let a guide manage the timing so the family isn't queuing.

items.name: Jiufen Old Street
items.description: A former gold-mining town of lantern-lit stone stairways and cliffside tea houses looking out to the Pacific, its misty lanes widely linked to the mood of Miyazaki's Spirited Away. Go with a private driver and arrive before the crowds; a teahouse balcony at dusk is the moment to hold.

items.name: Shifen & Pingxi Sky Lanterns
items.description: In the old railway town of Shifen you write wishes on a paper sky lantern and release it to drift over the valley — one of Taiwan's most cherished rituals — with the wide Shifen Waterfall a short walk on. A private tour pairs it neatly with Jiufen for a full northern-hills day.

items.name: Yehliu Geopark
items.description: A dramatic coastal cape of wind-and-sea-carved sandstone — the famous 'Queen's Head', mushroom rocks and sea candles strung along a north-coast headland. A striking, easy walk that combines with Jiufen and Shifen on a private northern day trip.

items.name: Wulai Hot Springs & Waterfall
items.description: An indigenous Atayal mountain village south of the city with riverside hot springs, a plunging waterfall reached by a little scenic train, and a gondola to a forest plateau. A greener, quieter thermal alternative to Beitou — a restful half-day with a driver.

items.name: Keelung & Heping Island
items.description: A working harbour city half an hour north, famed for the buzzing Miaokou Night Market and the wave-sculpted rock coast of Heping Island Park. A good add-on to a north-coast day, or a seafood-focused evening out of the city.

items.name: Houtong Cat Village
items.description: A former coal-mining hamlet on the Pingxi line reborn as a hillside village of resident cats, old railway relics and easy trails. A light, charming stop that slots into a Jiufen–Shifen railway day, especially with children in the group.

items.name: 228 Peace Memorial Park & Museum
items.description: A calm central park built around the memorial to the 1947 February 28 Incident, with a small museum that gives sober, essential context to modern Taiwan. A short, meaningful stop that deepens any first visit; it also holds the National Taiwan Museum.

items.name: Lin Family Mansion & Garden (Banqiao)
items.description: One of Taiwan's finest surviving classical Chinese gardens and merchant mansions, all moon gates, pavilions and reflecting ponds built by the 19th-century Lin family. A serene, cultured half-day for those who love garden architecture, away from the tourist core.

items.name: Jinguashi & the Gold Museum
items.description: Beside Jiufen, this restored Japanese-era gold-mining settlement lets you walk a real mine tunnel and lift a colossal gold ingot at the Gold Museum, set among quiet mountain temples. The substantive, less-crowded counterpart to touristy Jiufen next door.

items.name: Riverside cycling & Dadaocheng Wharf
items.description: Taipei's riverside parks link into hundreds of kilometres of flat, protected bike paths, with Dadaocheng Wharf offering sunset river views, container-bar dining and evening cruises. A relaxed, active way to see the city's water side; bikes and a guide are easily arranged.

items.name: Le Palais
items.description: Taipei's crown — Cantonese seafood and dim sum at the highest level, three stars for the eighth year running.

items.name: Taïrroir
items.description: Chef Kai Ho's 'taste of terroir' — modern Taiwanese cooking that put the island's fine dining on the world map.

items.name: L'Atelier de Joël Robuchon
items.description: The late master's counter-dining concept in Taipei — precise French cooking around the famous red-and-black bar.

items.name: logy
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Restaurants No. 26 (2025) — Best Restaurant in Taiwan
items.description: Ryogo Tahara's cross-Asian tasting menu down a Da'an alley — named the best restaurant in Taiwan.

items.name: Molino de Urdániz
items.description: A rare two-star Spanish kitchen in Asia — an offshoot of the Navarran original, deeply seasonal and precise.

items.name: Mudan
items.description: An exacting tempura counter of great purity — the ingredient, the oil, the moment, and nothing else.

items.name: Restaurant A
items.description: Chef Alain Huang's personal French-Taiwanese cooking — promoted to two stars in 2025.

items.name: Eika
items.description: A refined Japanese counter that climbed to two stars in 2025 — quiet, exacting, seasonal.

items.name: Yu Kapo
items.description: A meticulous Japanese kitchen newly raised to two stars — kappo cooking with real finesse.

items.name: La Vie by Thomas Bühner
items.description: The three-Michelin-star German chef's Taipei room, high in the city — European fine dining, newly starred.

items.name: Tien Hsiang Lo
items.description: Refined Hangzhou cuisine of long standing — one of Taipei's most gracious classical tables.

items.name: Shin Yeh Taiwanese Signature
items.description: The refined face of home-style Taiwanese cooking — heritage recipes served with quiet polish.

items.name: Ya Ge
items.description: Elegant Cantonese cooking inside the Mandarin Oriental — assured, classical, beautifully served.

items.name: Sushi Kajin
items.description: An intimate Edomae sushi counter newly awarded a star in 2025 — clean, exacting omakase.

items.name: FRASSI
items.description: Refined contemporary Italian cooking, freshly starred — a warm, ingredient-led kitchen.

items.name: Mountain and Sea House
items.description: A restored old mansion serving classic Taiwanese banquet cooking — recognised for its sustainable sourcing.

items.name: Din Tai Fung (Xinyi)
credentials: MICHELIN Guide Taiwan — Bib Gourmand pedigree; the original flagship
items.description: The world's most famous dumpling house, born on Taipei's Xinyi Road in 1972 — xiao long bao at their source.

items.name: Clavius
items.description: Plant-based Taiwanese whole-food cooking, elevated with delicate Asian flavour — a new Bib Gourmand in 2025.

items.name: Indulge Experimental Bistro
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Bars — Heering Legend of the List (2020); peaked No. 2 (2018)
items.description: The bar that built Taipei's cocktail reputation — Aki Wang's tea-and-terroir mixing, a fixture of Asia's best for a decade.

items.name: Bar Mood Taipei
items.description: A refined, ingredient-led cocktail bar — one of the city's most decorated rooms on the Asian stage.

items.name: Lab (Alchemist)
items.description: An experimental, technique-driven bar pushing Taipei's cocktail scene forward — the city's highest-ranked bar of the year.

items.name: Wu (Nothingness)
items.description: A minimalist, concept-led bar that earned its place among Asia's best — spare, considered, precise.

items.name: Under Lab
items.description: The intimate downstairs counter from the Lab team — a more personal, experimental drinking room.

items.name: Draft Land
items.description: Angus Zou's cocktails-on-tap concept — 'no garnish, no bullshit', casual and fast, and quietly revolutionary.

items.title: Private tea tasting in the Maokong or Pinglin hills
items.description: A grower-led session among the terraces above the city is the real education in Taiwanese oolong, gondola up and all.

items.title: Din Tai Fung's original with a behind-the-scenes look, or a private banquet
items.description: The birthplace of the xiaolongbao empire still sets the standard; a quiet reserved table skips the famous queue.

items.title: Sky-lantern release in Pingxi, arranged privately
items.description: Away from the festival crush, a private evening in the old railway town lets you write and release a lantern in near-solitude.

items.title: Private after-hours viewing at the National Palace Museum
items.description: One of the world's great collections of Chinese art, best seen on a curator-led visit outside the day crowds.

plan.heading: 3 days in Taipei, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle into the Mandarin Oriental Taipei, then a full unhurried morning at the National Palace Museum's Chinese treasures.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The temples and herbalists of Dadaocheng, then oolong at a traditional tea house on Dihua Street.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at RAW, André Chiang's celebrated room reading Taiwan's twenty-four micro-seasons.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The gondola to the tea plantations of Maokong, mist over the ridgelines.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: An afternoon soak at a private Beitou hot-spring house in the volcanic hills north of the city.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Refined Taiwanese cuisine at Mountain and Sea House, once a private banquet room for the island's elite.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The lantern-lined old street of Jiufen on the coast before the crowds, an hour out of the city.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Return for the Longshan Temple and the fabric and craft lanes of Wanhua.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A guided eating walk of Raohe or Tonghua night market, then cocktails at the discreet Ounce speakeasy.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Xinyi
items.description: Modern, glossy, and around Taipei 101; suits those who want flagship hotels and shopping at the base.

items.name: Da'an
items.description: Leafy, residential, and cafe-rich around the parks and universities; the most liveable central base.

items.name: Zhongshan
items.description: Old department stores, design hotels, and quiet lanes; ideal for walkers who want a calmer, characterful centre.

events.name: Pingxi & Taipei Lantern Festival
events.note: The lantern season peaks with sky-lantern releases in Pingxi and large illuminated displays across Taipei around the first full moon of the lunar year.

events.name: Dragon Boat Festival
events.note: Dragon-boat races on the Keelung and Dahan rivers mark one of Taiwan's oldest holidays, with zongzi eaten citywide.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Land at Taoyuan (TPE); a pre-booked private car covers the roughly 40-minute run into the city, more comfortable than the airport MRT.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver for Yangmingshan and the tea hills, with easy walking and the clean, efficient MRT within the compact centre.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM or a local SIM both work well; wifi is widespread and reliable.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: New Taiwan dollar; cards are accepted in hotels and better restaurants but carry cash for night markets and small tea houses, and tipping is not expected.

onGround.note: Stay in Xinyi for modern polish or Da'an for leafy calm and dining; the city is famously relaxed and safe, and a guide unlocks the finest tea houses and private-room banquets.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: October–November and March–April are the mild, drier windows worth the trip; May–June is the plum rain and July–September is hot with typhoon risk best avoided.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No nonstop from India at present; connect via Hong Kong (Cathay), Bangkok or Singapore, roughly 9.5–11 hours total. Route through Cathay via HKG for the best cabin and lounge, and note Indians need an online travel authorisation (or hold a valid US/Schengen/Japan visa) for Taiwan.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations; Taiwan is very safe with excellent, affordable healthcare. Tap water is officially safe but locals boil or filter it — stick to bottled or filtered to be sure.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian is genuinely easy given Taiwan's strong Buddhist vegetarian (su shi) culture, with clearly marked veg eateries everywhere; Jain still needs onion/garlic to be flagged. Yang Shin and the many su-shi buffets are excellent, and Indian food is available but limited.

closing.headingHtml: Taipei, with someone who knows it.
closing.lede: Your advisor arranges the flights, the rooms and the visa — the trip, handled.

seo.title: Tokyo — TripAgent
seo.description: Tokyo, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Tokyo
hero.tagline: Neon precision and quiet ritual in endless measure.

ourTake.lede: Tokyo rewards precision and punishes the scattershot — pick two or three neighbourhoods and go deep rather than sprinting across the map. Book the difficult tables the moment you have dates; the best counters seat eight and vanish months out. And spend at least one evening entirely off the tourist grid, in a six-seat basement bar in Golden Gai or a yokocho under the tracks, where no one is trying to sell you Tokyo.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a precise, endlessly layered city where three-Michelin dining, quiet temples and next-day fashion sit within a single afternoon.
ourTake.skipIf: You are after a slow beach reset or want a single unhurried base rather than a dense, fast-moving metropolis.
