whenToGo.blurb: January to March for snow-sure skiing under the Matterhorn, July to August for high-alpine hiking. Shoulder weeks bring quiet and some lift closures.
whenToGo.bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Sep, Oct, Nov and Dec

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Mont Cervin Palace
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The 1852 grande dame at the heart of the village — the address Zermatt is measured against.

items.name: Riffelalp Resort 2222m
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: Europe's highest five-star hotel — car-free, reached only by the Gornergrat railway, alone with the Matterhorn.

items.name: Grand Hotel Zermatterhof
items.description: A Belle Époque palace built by the villagers themselves in 1879 — old-world grandeur, impeccably kept.

items.name: The Omnia
items.description: A minimalist mountain lodge on the rock above the village, reached by a tunnel and lift cut into the mountainside.

items.name: CERVO Mountain Resort
items.description: A cluster of chalets at the foot of the Sunnegga slopes — sustainable, stylish and quietly modern.

items.name: Backstage Hotel Vernissage
credentials: Home of After Seven — 2 MICHELIN Stars
items.description: Artist Heinz Julen's avant-garde design hotel — sculptural, theatrical and unlike anything else in the Alps.

items.name: Gornergrat Railway
credentials: Highest open-air cogwheel railway in Europe
items.description: The cogwheel train that hauls you from the village up to 3,089m in about 33 minutes, and the whole way the Matterhorn hangs in the window over a fan of glaciers and 4,000m peaks. Book seats on the right for the best of it, and let the little ones and the grandparents ride effortlessly to a view most people only earn on foot. This is the single easiest, most magnificent multi-generation morning in the Alps.

items.name: Gornergrat summit & Kulmhotel observatory
credentials: Views of 29 peaks above 4,000m including Monte Rosa, the highest in Switzerland
items.description: The top station is a natural balcony ringed by 29 peaks over 4,000m and the vast Gorner Glacier, with the astronomical observatory domes of the Kulmhotel crowning the ridge. The air is thin and the silence total; a private guide can name every summit while you sip something warm. Come for the panorama, stay for the astonishing near-zero-light-pollution night sky.

items.name: Matterhorn Glacier Paradise
items.description: The highest cable-car station on the continent, where a viewing platform opens onto 38 four-thousanders and 14 glaciers spread across Switzerland, Italy and France. The lift does all the climbing; you simply step out into the roof of Europe. For an Indian family, it is the closest thing to standing on top of the Alps without a rope.

items.name: The Glacier Palace ice cave
credentials: World's highest glacier ice palace (inside the 3,883m station)
items.description: A tunnel carved fifteen metres into the living glacier, walls of blue ice, carved sculptures, and a small ice slide the children will beg to repeat. It sits inside the highest cable-car station in Europe, so you fold it into the summit visit. Wrap up warm; the cave holds a steady sub-zero even in a July heatwave.

items.name: The Cinema Lounge, Klein Matterhorn
items.description: A small cinema at nearly 3,900m showing short films on the mountains, the glacier and the flora, a gentle place to acclimatise and rest while the body adjusts to the altitude. It is an easy, warm interlude for grandparents between the ice cave and the platform. A quiet reminder that even the roof of Europe can be done in comfort.

items.name: Matterhorn Glacier Ride (3S cableway)
items.description: The tri-cable gondola that lifts you the final stretch to the summit station in nine minutes, crystal-studded 'Crystal ride' cabins with glass floors on select cabins that turn transparent over the glacier. It is a thrill in itself, engineering as spectacle. Ask about the crystal cabin for a set-piece the teenagers will film the whole way up.

items.name: Matterhorn Alpine Crossing to Cervinia
credentials: Highest cross-border cable-car crossing in the Alps
items.description: Since 2023 you can ride cable cars clear over the ridge from Zermatt into Italy, lunch in Breuil-Cervinia, and glide back, the highest year-round border crossing in the Alps done entirely by gondola, no climbing, no passports checked mid-air but carry yours. Two countries and a plate of pasta on the Italian sun-terrace, all in an afternoon. A brilliant, effortless multi-country day.

items.name: Riffelsee & the Matterhorn reflection
items.description: Step off the cogwheel train at Rotenboden and a short walk brings you to the Riffelsee, the small tarn that gives the picture-postcard mirror image of the Matterhorn on a still morning. It is the most photographed reflection in the Alps and the reason to catch the earliest train. A calm, windless dawn is everything, so time it with your guide.

items.name: Gornergrat sunrise & Riffelsee special train
items.description: On set dates the railway runs a dedicated pre-dawn service so you reach the ridge as the first light turns the Matterhorn's east face to fire and doubles it in the Riffelsee. Breakfast follows at the mountain restaurant while the crowds are still asleep in the valley. Pure honeymoon material, and worth the early alarm.

items.name: Five Lakes Walk (5-Seenweg)
items.description: A gentle high trail past five alpine lakes, Stellisee, Grindjisee, Grünsee, Moosjisee and Leisee, three of which mirror the Matterhorn on a calm day. No exposure, no scrambling, just larch forest, wildflowers and one perfect reflection after another over three to four hours. The most rewarding easy hike above Zermatt for a mixed-ability family.

items.name: Stellisee lake
items.description: The wind-sheltered jewel of the Five Lakes Walk and, for many, the finest Matterhorn reflection of all, an unbroken double of the peak on a still summer morning. The Fluhalp mountain restaurant sits a few minutes on for a leisurely lunch with the same view. Go early; by midday a breeze usually ruffles the mirror.

items.name: Sunnegga & Leisee
items.description: A three-minute underground funicular from the village lifts you to a sunny terrace and the shallow Leisee, a warm-ish swimming lake with the Matterhorn behind and a lakeside playground, the gentlest of the high viewpoints. Perfect for a family with young children or grandparents who want the view without the walk. The quickest route from village to a first Matterhorn panorama.

items.name: Rothorn viewpoint
items.description: The highest of the Sunnegga-side summits, reached by funicular and cable car, with a wide sweep of glaciers and a superb, less-crowded angle on the Matterhorn. It is a spectacular sunrise perch for those who want the golden peak without the Gornergrat crowds. A quiet counterpoint to the busier railway summit.

items.name: Matterhorn Museum – Zermatlantis
items.description: An underground reconstructed old village that tells how a poor farming hamlet became the world's most famous mountain, centred on the snapped rope from the 1865 first ascent that killed four of Edward Whymper's seven climbers. Whymper's ice-axe and boots, the church bells, the cobbled lanes, it is moving and beautifully done. The one indoor hour that makes the whole valley make sense.

items.name: The Hinterdorf old village
items.description: A cluster of black larch barns, stables and granaries from the 16th to 18th centuries, many raised on stilts topped with round flat 'mouse-stones' to keep rodents out of the grain. A five-minute wander back through Walliser mountain life, wedged among the boutiques. Loveliest in late light when the resinous timber glows almost black.

items.name: The Kirchbrücke (church bridge) view
items.description: The little bridge over the Matter Vispa where the whole village funnels the eye straight up to the Matterhorn, the classic street-level shot with chalets, church tower and peak all in one frame. It is a two-minute stroll from the grand hotels and best at first light or blue hour. The picture everyone comes home with.

items.name: Bahnhofstrasse & luxury shopping
items.description: The car-free main street lined with Swiss watch houses and jewellers, Bucherer for Rolex, Patek, Chopard and Cartier, alongside ski and cashmere boutiques and chocolatiers. No cars, no fumes, just electric taxis and the Matterhorn at the end of the road. An elegant, unhurried afternoon between mountain excursions.

items.name: The car-free village stroll
credentials: One of Europe's original car-free (combustion-free) resorts
items.description: Zermatt has banned petrol cars for decades; you arrive by train and move by foot, e-taxi or horse-drawn sleigh, and the air is clean and the streets quiet. That exclusivity, an entire luxury village without traffic, is a large part of its charm for a discerning traveller. Simply walking it in the evening, watching the peak turn pink, is an event in itself.

items.name: Gorner Gorge (Gornerschlucht)
items.description: A narrow slot canyon of 220-million-year-old green serpentine rock, threaded by a timber walkway first built by local guides in the 1880s, with turquoise meltwater roaring below. Fifteen minutes from the centre and blessedly cool on a hot day. A short, dramatic detour that suits a rainy morning or restless children.

items.name: Mountaineers' Cemetery
items.description: A small, sobering graveyard where climbers who died on the Matterhorn and Monte Rosa lie, including victims of the 1865 first ascent, headstones carved with ropes, axes and 'I chose to climb'. It is quiet and dignified, a few minutes from the busy street. A poignant counterweight to the glamour, and part of understanding this mountain.

items.name: Chez Vrony, Findeln
items.description: The most coveted mountain table above Zermatt, a century-old family farm-restaurant on a sun-terrace facing the Matterhorn, serving its own dry-cured meats, alpine cheese and a famous burger from cattle grazed on the slope. Book well ahead; the terrace at lunch is where Zermatt's regulars are. An unhurried, glorious high-altitude lunch with the peak for a backdrop.

items.name: Findeln hamlet & its restaurants
items.description: A scatter of old timber chalets, a tiny chapel and a run of celebrated mountain restaurants, Findlerhof, Adler and others, strung across a south-facing slope twenty minutes' walk below Sunnegga. Larch, cowbells and the Matterhorn framed between the barns. The prettiest lunch-walk in the resort, gentle enough for most.

items.name: Fondue & raclette in the village
items.description: This is the Valais, the home of raclette, and a bubbling caquelon of fondue or a scraped wheel of alpine cheese in a low-beamed stube is the evening ritual after a day on the heights. Ask ahead and the better kitchens will do a fine vegetarian spread, cheese, potatoes, pickles, rösti, that suits Indian tastes well. Warm, convivial and utterly of the place.

items.name: Zermatt–Cervinia international ski area
items.description: One of the largest linked ski areas in the Alps, spanning two countries, over 300km of pistes and lifts to 3,883m, so you can ski down to lunch in Italy and be back in Switzerland by tea. Long, sun-soaked, high-altitude runs with the Matterhorn always in view. A private ski guide and ski-in ski-out chalet make it seamless for a family.

items.name: Summer glacier skiing
credentials: Highest and largest summer ski area in the Alps
items.description: The Matterhorn Glacier Paradise pistes let you ski or snowboard on real snow through July and August, a novelty few places on earth can offer, then swap boots for sandals in the valley the same day. Ideal for a summer-visiting family who want their children to touch snow in high season. The highest, largest summer ski area in the Alps.

items.name: Heli-skiing with Air Zermatt
items.description: One of only a handful of legal heli-ski zones in Switzerland, where the storied Air Zermatt lifts you to untracked glacier faces such as the Monte Rosa for a guided descent through deep powder. It is the ultimate winter adrenaline day, private, exclusive and framed by the Matterhorn. For confident skiers, nothing here comes close.

items.name: Climbing the Matterhorn (guided)
credentials: First climbed 1865 by Edward Whymper's party; four of seven died on descent
items.description: The bucket-list ascent, a serious two-day climb via the Hörnli hut with a Zermatt IFMGA guide one-to-one, demanding real fitness and prior alpine experience. Even if you never rope up, standing at the Hörnli hut base and watching the dawn summit attempts is unforgettable. For the right guest, this is the summit of a lifetime; for the rest, its story is the soul of the village.

items.name: Schwarzsee & the Maria zum Schnee chapel
items.description: A cable car ride to a small dark lake with a lonely white pilgrimage chapel and the Matterhorn looming directly above, close enough to feel its scale. On a still day the chapel and peak double in the water. It is also the gateway to the Hörnli hut trail, so climbers and photographers cross paths here.

items.name: The Matterhorn Glacier Trail
items.description: A well-graded high path beneath the Matterhorn's east face, past glacial lakes, information panels on the 1865 ascent and the retreating ice, with the peak looming the whole way. Around two hours, moderate, and endlessly photogenic. A serious Matterhorn hike that stays within reach of most fit walkers.

items.name: Riffelalp Resort & Europe's highest tram
items.description: A five-star mountain resort on the Gornergrat line with a 35°C open-air pool facing the Matterhorn and a little red tram, the highest in Europe, trundling guests from the station to the door. Even non-residents can ride up for the terrace and the spa's altitude drama. A honeymoon set-piece and a rare high-altitude luxury address.

items.name: Paragliding over Zermatt
items.description: A tandem flight that floats you off the shoulder of the mountain and out in front of the Matterhorn itself, twenty minutes of silent, soaring perspective no cable car can give. First-timers are strapped to a seasoned pilot; the harder part is the view, not the flying. An exhilarating hour for an adventurous couple or teenager.

items.name: E-biking & mountain biking
items.description: Marked trails for every level, from a gentle e-bike Glacier Garden loop to the technical Rothorn descent, with lifts that carry your bike up so you only ride the good bits. The Flower Trail rolls through larch woods thick with edelweiss and gentian back to Sunnegga. A fresh, active way to see the high meadows in summer.

items.name: Ibex & chamois watching
items.description: The rocky ridges above Sunnegga are home to alpine ibex with their great curved horns and nimble chamois, often spotted early or late along the higher trails. A guide with a scope will find them and tell you the mountain's natural history. A quiet thrill for children and grandparents alike, wildlife against a Matterhorn backdrop.

items.name: Alpine flora & the Flower Trail
items.description: In high summer the meadows blaze with edelweiss, gentian, alpine rose and dozens more species along a signed flower trail that winds gently down through larch and stone pine to Sunnegga. Easy underfoot and quietly beautiful, a botanist's and a photographer's walk. A soft, unhurried counterpoint to the big summits.

items.name: The Glacier Express to St Moritz
credentials: Runs onto the UNESCO-listed Rhaetian Railway (Albula/Bernina) line
items.description: The famously slow panoramic train that threads eight hours of Alpine grandeur, 291 bridges and the Landwasser viaduct, from Zermatt to St Moritz through the UNESCO Rhaetian Railway landscape. Book the Excellence Class for a single-seat-at-the-window, five-course, sommelier-served journey. One of the world's great rail experiences, and a superb way to leave or arrive.

items.name: Sunset on the Matterhorn from the village
items.description: In the last minutes of the day the peak catches an alpenglow that runs from gold to deep rose while the valley falls into shadow, best watched from the church bridge or a south-facing hotel terrace with a drink in hand. It happens every clear evening and never tires. The most reliable free spectacle in the resort.

items.name: Mont Cervin Palace
items.description: The grande dame of Zermatt, open since 1852 and a Leading Hotel of the World, whose sun-terrace on the main street is the village's social heart and whose kitchens include a Michelin-starred Italian table. Even for a drink or afternoon tea it is worth stepping inside for the old-world grandeur. The classic address for a traveller who wants the establishment choice.

items.name: THE OMNIA design hotel
items.description: A glass-and-timber mountain lodge set on a rock 45m above the village, reached by a lift bored up through the cliff, all clean lines, fireplaces and a Michelin-recognised kitchen. Its terrace hangs over the rooftops with the Matterhorn dead ahead. The design-led, intimate alternative to the grand palace hotels, and a honeymooners' favourite.

items.name: CERVO Mountain Resort
items.area: Above the village, by the Sunnegga funicular
items.description: A cluster of chic alpine chalets with a buzzing après terrace, a superb spa and a pan-Asian and Mediterranean dining scene that draws a younger, stylish crowd. Ski-in ski-out in winter, a design-forward retreat in summer. The most fashionable stay in Zermatt for guests who want energy as well as views.

items.name: Private chalet stays
items.description: Zermatt has some of the Alps' finest catered chalets, staffed with private chef, driver and in-house spa, giving a large family or group total privacy with the Matterhorn from the hot tub. Many arrange guide, heli and restaurant bookings as part of the stay. The natural choice for multi-generational or celebration travel.

items.name: Riffelberg & its little chapel
items.description: A mid-station on the cogwheel railway with a broad terrace, a tiny chapel set perfectly beneath the peak for scale, and gentle walks down toward Riffelalp through the flowers. A relaxed, less-strenuous stop for those breaking the Gornergrat journey. The chapel-and-mountain composition is a quiet favourite of photographers.

items.name: Trockener Steg & the Theodul Glacier
items.description: The great glacier junction where the cable cars change for the summit, ringed by the Theodul Glacier and a small lake that mirrors the Matterhorn's western flank. It is the staging point for summer skiing and the Italy crossing, worth a pause for the raw glacial scale. A window on the ice for those who go no higher.

items.name: Zermatt in high summer wildflower season
items.description: July and August turn the alpine pastures into a carpet of colour under snow-streaked peaks, with long warm days, quiet trails and the mountains at their most inviting, ideal for Indian families travelling in the summer holidays. Snow up top, wildflowers below, and the Matterhorn clear against blue. The valley at its most generous.

items.name: A guided Monte Rosa excursion
credentials: Monte Rosa is the highest massif in Switzerland (Dufourspitze 4,634m)
items.description: For strong walkers, a guided crossing of the Gorner Glacier toward the striking crystalline Monte Rosa hut is a genuine high-alpine adventure without the technicality of the Matterhorn. Roped up, crampons on, you feel the scale of Switzerland's highest massif underfoot. A serious mountain day for the fit and curious, arranged privately.

items.name: Winter horse-drawn sleigh & village nights
items.description: With no cars, winter evenings belong to horse-drawn sleighs jingling through snow-lined lanes, lantern light on the old chalets and the peak silvered by the moon. A short ride to dinner or simply around the village is pure alpine romance. The car-free hush makes Zermatt's winter unlike anywhere else.

items.name: After Seven
items.description: Ivo Adam's surprise menu cooked in an open kitchen — bread baked at your table, and the village's brightest star.

items.name: The Omnia
items.description: Alpine ingredients with a global hand, in the design hotel's cool dining room on the rock above the village.

items.name: Brasserie Lusi
items.description: The Zermatterhof's confident brasserie — grand-hotel cooking without the ceremony.

items.name: Chez Vrony
items.description: A century-old family alp above the village, cooking its own organic beef with the Matterhorn full in the window.

items.name: Findlerhof
items.description: The other beloved Findeln kitchen — sun-terrace mountain cooking, refined and warmly run.

items.name: Marmo
items.description: A modern mountain kitchen at Furi — a serious table on the slopes, not just a hut.

items.name: Bazaar
items.description: Predominantly vegetarian world flavours — Arab to Chinese — at CERVO's lively base.

items.name: Aroleid Restaurant
items.description: Seasonal, honest cooking that quietly won the village's only Bib Gourmand — value done right.

items.name: Elsie's Bar
items.description: A tiny champagne-and-wine room opposite the church, in an 1879 house — the chic address since 1961.

items.name: CERVO Bar & Terrace
credentials: Within CERVO Mountain Resort — Design Hotels (Marriott Bonvoy)
items.description: A two-level slope-side terrace at the foot of Sunnegga — cocktails, DJ sets and the day's best après crowd.

items.name: Vernissage Bar
credentials: Within Backstage Hotel Vernissage — MICHELIN Guide Hotel
items.description: Heinz Julen's cinema-cum-gallery-cum-bar — sculptural, candlelit and unlike any other room in the Alps.

items.name: Hennu Stall
credentials: World Snow Awards — Zermatt named Best Après-Ski
items.description: The legendary slope-side après barn — Jägermeister on skis, Europop and fancy dress until the light goes.

items.title: Heli-flight around the Matterhorn
items.description: A scenic helicopter loop of the peak and surrounding four-thousanders, weather permitting.

items.title: Private dawn on the Gornergrat
items.description: A first-train ascent to watch the Matterhorn catch the sunrise before the day skiers arrive.

items.title: Off-piste day with a mountain guide
items.description: A private guide for the high runs and glacier terrain, tailored to conditions and ability.

items.title: Fondue dinner at a mountain hut
items.description: A private table at a slope-side chalet reached by snowcat, high above the village lights.

plan.heading: 3 days in Zermatt, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The train in from Täsch — cars stay behind — and a slow settle into the village, the mountain filling the end of every street.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The walk up to the Gornergrat cog railway, or simply the church square and the old Hinterdorf timber barns.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at the After Seven in the Backstage Hotel, Zermatt's Michelin-starred table, then a nightcap at the Vernissage bar.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: First lift to Gornergrat for the Monte Rosa and the glacier at sunrise, coffee at the summit.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Five Lakes walk down, the Matterhorn mirrored in the Stellisee.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A mountain dinner at Chez Vrony in Findeln, arriving on foot or by rail, then down as the peaks turn.

days.title: The glacier and a long lunch

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The cable car to the Matterhorn Glacier Paradise, Europe's highest, and the ice palace.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A long table at the Chetzeron restaurant or a spa afternoon at the Mont Cervin Palace.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A final dinner at the Restaurant Schäferstube for the lamb, close and warm before departure.

items.description: The car-free heart with the grand hotels and shops — everything on foot.

items.name: Winkelmatten
items.description: A quiet hamlet on the edge with Matterhorn views — for seclusion near the pistes.

items.name: Riffelalp
items.description: Up the mountain at 2,200m — for those who want to stay in the high alpine, above the crowds.

events.name: Zermatt Unplugged
events.note: An acoustic music festival across village and mountain stages — the 2026 edition runs 7–11 April.

events.name: Zermatt Marathon

events.name: Folklore Festival
events.note: Alpine traditions, yodelling and flag-throwing fill the car-free streets in high summer.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Zermatt is car-free, so you arrive by private car or helicopter to Täsch and transfer by the short cog railway or a resort electric shuttle up to the village beneath the Matterhorn.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Everything moves on foot or by silent electric taxi and hotel e-buggy; the mountain railways and cable cars carry you up to the slopes and viewpoints.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Village and valley coverage is strong; an eSIM works well, and hotel wifi is reliable though it thins high on the mountain.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Swiss francs (CHF); cards are accepted across the village, carry a little cash for small mountain huts, and tipping is modest.

onGround.note: The village sits at roughly 1,600m and peaks reach far higher, so pace the first day and hydrate; stay slopeside near the Matterhorn view — a room facing the peak is worth requesting specifically.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: December to March for reliable snow and skiing under the Matterhorn; July to September for clear hiking weather. Late April to May is the shoulder low, when many lifts and hotels close for maintenance.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Fly into Zurich (direct on SWISS or Air India from Delhi, ~8h45), then about 3.5 hours by rail with one easy change at Visp. Zermatt is car-free, so arrange the electric-taxi or hotel transfer from the station; private cars stop at Tasch, 7 km below.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required; the village is very safe. Zermatt sits at ~1,600 m and excursions like Gornergrat (3,089 m) and the Matterhorn Glacier Paradise (3,883 m) reach real altitude, so ascend gradually, hydrate, and rest on arrival. Tap water is pure.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: A resort village, so dedicated Indian dining is limited, but hotels and mountain restaurants readily handle vegetarian requests. For strict Jain meals, ask your hotel to prepare in advance or stock a few essentials before arrival.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.

seo.title: Zurich — TripAgent
seo.description: Zurich, in hand: where to stay, what to do, where to eat and where the night goes — the addresses worth knowing.

hero.name: Zurich
hero.tagline: Banking grandeur, lakeside calm and Alpine air in one

ourTake.lede: Zurich is easy to underrate as merely tidy and rich; give it a day or two and the lake, the swimmable river and a genuinely serious art scene reveal themselves. Prioritise the Kunsthaus and a slow afternoon on the water over ticking off the Bahnhofstrasse, and in summer swim where the locals do at the badis along the Limmat. It is compact, punctual and expensive, so plan fewer things and do them well.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a lakeside base, effortless trains and the Alps an hour away.
ourTake.skipIf: You are watching the budget or want warmth and a beach.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes — grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Baur au Lac
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The city's grande dame since 1844 — family-owned, lake-facing, and quietly the address that matters.

items.name: The Dolder Grand
items.description: A fairy-tale hillside resort above Zurich — a spa, an art collection and the whole lake laid out below.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental Savoy, Zurich
items.description: The city's oldest grand hotel, reborn — Mandarin Oriental precision on the Paradeplatz.

items.name: Widder Hotel
items.description: Nine medieval townhouses stitched into one — an art-and-design masterpiece in the heart of the Old Town.

items.name: La Réserve Eden au Lac Zurich
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A Philippe Starck-imagined 'yacht club' on the lake — playful, private and thoroughly of the moment.

items.name: Storchen Zürich
items.description: Six hundred years on the Limmat — a riverfront address woven into the fabric of the Old Town.

items.name: Park Hyatt Zurich
items.description: Cool, contemporary calm a step from Bahnhofstrasse — glass, art and space where the city is dense.

items.name: Marktgasse Hotel
items.description: A restored 15th-century house in the pedestrian Old Town — design-led, intimate, and full of history.

items.name: Alden Suite Hotel Splügenschloss Zürich
items.description: An all-suite mansion of 1895 — quiet, discreet, and among the most private addresses in the city.

items.name: Kameha Grand Zürich
items.description: A Marcel Wanders design spectacle on the city's edge — bold, playful, and unlike anything in the Old Town.

items.name: 25hours Hotel Zurich West
items.description: A witty, design-forward base in the reinvented industrial west — excellent value by Zurich standards.

items.name: Grossmünster & the tower climb
items.description: Zurich's twin-towered Romanesque landmark, where Huldrych Zwingli launched the Swiss-German Reformation in the 1520s. Inside are choir windows by Augusto Giacometti and side windows by Sigmar Polke; climb the 187 steps of the Karlsturm for a close panorama over the Old Town roofs, the lake and the Alps beyond. A private guide can bring the Reformation history alive for older children and grandparents.

items.name: Fraumünster & the Chagall windows
items.description: A former abbey church on the elegant Münsterhof square, holding five stained-glass chancel windows designed by Marc Chagall in 1970 plus a rose window — among the most important works of modern religious art in Switzerland. Best in morning light when the colours flood the choir. Quiet, unhurried, and moving even for those with no interest in churches.

items.name: St. Peter's Church & Europe's largest clock face
credentials: Largest church clock face in Europe
items.description: Zurich's oldest parish church, whose tower carries the largest church clock face in Europe at roughly 8.7 metres across. A short, atmospheric stop between Lindenhof and Fraumünster; the surrounding lanes hide serious patisseries and boutiques for an easy stroll.

items.name: Lindenhof
items.description: A leafy hilltop terrace on the site of a Roman fort and later imperial palace, shaded by century-old linden trees, with one of the loveliest free views over the Limmat, the Old Town spires and Grossmünster. Locals play boules and chess here; a calm, camera-ready pause on a private walking tour, and a favourite spot for a golden-hour photograph.

items.name: Niederdorf (Dörfli) lanes
items.description: The pedestrianised heart of the Old Town — cobbled alleys winding up toward the Grossmünster, lined with boutiques, chocolatiers, cafés and long-standing patisseries. Best explored slowly on foot, ideally early evening; a private guide can thread you past the Cabaret Voltaire, Spiegelgasse and the quieter courtyards the crowds miss.

items.name: Bahnhofstrasse — the luxury mile
items.description: One of the most expensive shopping streets in the world, running from the main station to the lake. This is where Zurich's watches and jewellery live — the maisons, the grandes marques, and the great multi-brand houses — alongside international fashion. Stroll it end to end, then reward the family at Sprüngli on Paradeplatz. A concierge can arrange private after-hours appointments at the watch houses.

items.name: Beyer Chronometrie, Bahnhofstrasse
items.description: One of the world's oldest watch and jewellery houses, family-run since 1760, and a serious address for Patek Philippe, Rolex and the finest independents. The ground-floor salon is discreet and unhurried; ask for a private consultation. Below it sits the Beyer Clock and Watch Museum for the horology-minded.

items.name: Beyer Clock and Watch Museum
items.description: A jewel-box basement museum beneath the Beyer store on Bahnhofstrasse, tracing timekeeping from around 1400 BC to the present across some 270 objects — sundials, tower clocks, pocket watches and the prototype of the first quartz wristwatch. A short, rich stop that gives context before any watch purchase; a natural pairing for collectors.

items.name: Confiserie Sprüngli, Paradeplatz
items.description: The house that has stood at Paradeplatz since 1859, celebrated for its featherlight Luxemburgerli macarons and truffles. The upstairs café is a Zurich institution for a mid-morning coffee and cake; the boutique makes elegant, packable gifts to carry home. Reliable vegetarian sweets and a favourite treat for children and grandparents alike.

items.name: Lake Zurich cruise (ZSG)
items.description: The Lake Zurich Navigation Company runs daily scheduled cruises from the Bürkliplatz quay, from short 1.5-hour loops to longer runs past the villa-lined 'Gold Coast' to Rapperswil, aboard motor vessels and classic paddle steamers. Book a Dream Boat dinner or brunch cruise for a private-feeling occasion; the calm water and Alpine backdrop suit multi-generation groups.

items.name: Lakeside promenades — Bürkliplatz to Zürichhorn
items.description: The right-bank promenade runs from Bürkliplatz along the Utoquai to the parks at Zürichhorn — swans, plane trees, the Chinese Garden and, on clear days, the Alps mirrored in the water. A gentle, level walk perfect for grandparents and an evening stroll after dinner. Stop at the Pavillon Le Corbusier along the way.

items.name: Summer swimming at the Badis (Seebad Enge & Utoquai)
items.description: Zurich swims in its own lake and rivers in summer. Seebad Enge is a stylish lakeside lido with a sauna and a bar; the historic wooden Seebad Utoquai has welcomed swimmers off its docks for over 120 years. Clean, cold, and quintessentially local — a refreshing morning dip before the day's sightseeing.

items.name: Kunsthaus Zürich
items.description: Switzerland's largest art museum, expanded by a luminous David Chipperfield extension. The collection runs from Old Masters and a deep Giacometti holding to Munch, the Impressionists and Pipilotti Rist's immersive installations. Admission to the permanent collection is free on Wednesdays; a private docent can tailor a focused hour for the family.

items.name: Swiss National Museum (Landesmuseum)
items.description: Housed in a fairy-tale château beside the station, this is the most-visited museum of cultural history in Switzerland — a clear, beautifully staged journey through Swiss history, craft and identity, watches and design included. Excellent for context on your first day, and engaging for older children.

items.name: Museum Rietberg
items.description: Switzerland's only major museum of non-European art, set in three historic villas in the emerald Rieterpark above the lake. Strong Indian, Chinese, Japanese, African and Himalayan collections — of particular resonance for Indian visitors — shown with real care. Combine with a stroll through the park for one of the city's calmest cultural afternoons.

items.name: FIFA Museum
items.description: Three floors of football history opposite Bahnhof Enge, with the original World Cup trophy on display, over 1,000 pieces of memorabilia and hands-on digital stations. A genuine highlight for football-mad teenagers and a fine rainy-day option; interactive enough to hold a mixed-age group.

items.name: Uetliberg — Zurich's home mountain
items.description: The 871-metre mountain rising over the city, reached in about 20 minutes on the S10 train from the main station. From the lookout tower the whole of Zurich, the lake and, on clear days, the Alps unfold below. Gentle ridge walks, a summit restaurant and easy access make it a relaxed half-day with sweeping photographs.

items.name: Zurich Zoo & Masoala Rainforest
items.description: One of Europe's most respected zoos, home to over 300 species, the vast Kaeng Krachan elephant park and the Lewa Savanna. Its showpiece is the Masoala Rainforest hall — a walk-through slice of Madagascar with free-flying birds, lemurs and dense green heat. A sure hit for children; reach it by tram or the funicular up the Zürichberg.

items.name: Lindt Home of Chocolate, Kilchberg
credentials: World's largest chocolate fountain (Guinness World Record)
items.description: The Lindt & Sprüngli chocolate experience just outside the city, built around the world's tallest chocolate fountain at over nine metres, an interactive museum and a generous free tasting zone. Book a chocolate-making workshop for the family, and stock the largest Lindt shop in the world with gifts to carry home. Reachable by a short train or lake boat.

items.name: Zürich West — the Viadukt
items.description: A restored 19th-century railway viaduct whose brick arches now hold design boutiques, a covered market hall and cafés — the beating heart of the city's reinvented industrial west. Graze the market hall for lunch, browse Swiss makers, and feel a grittier, more creative Zurich than Bahnhofstrasse.

items.name: Frau Gerolds Garten & Prime Tower
items.description: An urban garden of shipping-container shops, a summer beer garden and street food beneath the Prime Tower — at 126 metres one of Switzerland's tallest buildings. A relaxed, in-the-know spot for a sundowner; ride up to the Clouds restaurant and bar in the tower for a skyline view over the district.

items.name: Zurich Opera House (Opernhaus)
items.description: A grand 19th-century opera house on the lakefront, one of Europe's most respected houses for opera and ballet. Book a box for an evening in your finest; the neo-Baroque interior and the square outside make it an occasion in itself. A concierge can secure premium seats and pre-theatre dining nearby.

items.name: Tonhalle Zürich
items.description: The 1895 concert hall of the Tonhalle Orchester Zürich, its acoustics ranked among the finest in Europe and its gilded interior beautifully restored. An evening of world-class symphonic music in an intimate, ornate room — a refined alternative to a night at the opera.

items.name: Old Botanical Garden (Alter Botanischer Garten)
items.description: A small, romantic city-centre garden laid out on a former bastion, with a historic domed palm house and quiet terraced lawns. A green pause a few minutes from the shopping — pleasant for grandparents and children needing a breather between museums.

items.name: Pavillon Le Corbusier
items.description: The last building Le Corbusier designed — his only work in steel and glass — a jewel of primary-coloured panels set in the lakeside park at Zürichhorn. Open roughly May to November; a short, distinctive stop for design lovers, easily folded into a lake promenade walk.

items.name: Cabaret Voltaire
items.description: The tiny room at Spiegelgasse 1 where the Dada movement was born in 1916, now a café-bar and cultural space. A niche but genuine piece of art history tucked into the Old Town lanes — worth a coffee and a glance for the culturally curious.

items.name: James Joyce's grave, Fluntern Cemetery
items.description: In the leafy Fluntern cemetery on the Zürichberg lies James Joyce, who spent his final years in Zurich, marked by a seated bronze statue of the writer, book in hand. A quiet literary pilgrimage that pairs naturally with a visit to the nearby zoo.

items.name: Polybahn funicular & ETH terrace
items.description: A short, historic funicular climbs from Central up to the ETH university terrace, where one of the city's best free viewpoints looks back over the Old Town, the Limmat and the lake. A quick, characterful ride and a fine photo stop, especially at dusk.

items.name: Rhine Falls at Schaffhausen (day trip)
credentials: Largest waterfall in Europe by volume
items.description: The largest waterfall in Europe by volume, thundering over a 23-metre drop amid vineyards about 45 minutes north of the city. Boat trips carry you to the rock in the middle of the falls, and Schloss Laufen looks down from above. A dramatic, easy day out; pair it with medieval Stein am Rhein nearby.

items.name: Stein am Rhein (day trip)
items.description: A perfectly preserved medieval town on the Rhine, its main square ringed by half-timbered houses covered in vivid painted frescoes and oriel windows. Small, walkable and postcard-pretty — an easy, gentle addition to a Rhine Falls day, well suited to a relaxed pace with grandparents.

items.name: Lucerne & the Chapel Bridge (day trip)
credentials: Kapellbrücke — Europe's oldest surviving covered wooden bridge
items.description: Central Switzerland's loveliest lake town, under an hour by direct train, built around the Kapellbrücke — Europe's oldest covered wooden bridge, dating to the 14th century. Wander the old town, the frescoed bridge and the lakefront; an effortless, scenic day, and the gateway to Pilatus and Rigi.

items.name: Mount Pilatus 'Golden Round Trip' (day trip)
items.description: The classic mountain day from Zurich via Lucerne, combining a lake steamer, the world's steepest cogwheel railway, a rotating cable car and a panoramic gondola to a summit above the clouds. A thrilling, effortless Alpine experience for the whole family; a private driver-guide can smooth the connections.

items.name: Mount Rigi — 'Queen of the Mountains' (day trip)
items.description: A broad, gentle summit above Lake Lucerne reached by Europe's oldest mountain railway, with meadow walks, thermal baths at Rigi Kaltbad and 360-degree Alpine views. Softer and less vertiginous than Pilatus — ideal for a mixed-age group wanting mountains without the drama. Best on a clear day.

items.name: Mount Titlis & Engelberg (day trip)
credentials: World's first rotating cable car (Titlis Rotair)
items.description: Year-round glacier and snow at 3,000-plus metres, reached from the monastery village of Engelberg via the world's first rotating cable car, plus a cliff walk suspension bridge and a glacier cave. The most reliable place near Zurich to put the family in real Alpine snow whatever the season.

items.name: Zürichberg forest walk
items.description: The wooded ridge above the city, laced with easy trails, clearings and a wildlife park, reached by tram or funicular. A green, restorative morning away from the crowds, with occasional views down to the lake — pleasant for a slow family walk before a zoo or cemetery visit nearby.

items.name: Freitag Tower, Zürich West
items.description: A stack of 17 rusted shipping containers forming the flagship of Zurich's cult Freitag brand, whose bags are cut from used truck tarpaulins — climb to the top for a view over the western district. A quirky design pilgrimage and a distinctly Swiss, one-of-a-kind gift to take home.

items.name: Rapperswil — the 'town of roses' (lake day trip)
items.description: The pretty medieval town at the far end of Lake Zurich, crowned by a hilltop castle, famous for its rose gardens and a long wooden pilgrim's bridge across the water. Reach it languidly by boat and return by train — a gentle, scenic half-day at an unhurried pace.

items.name: Chinagarten (Chinese Garden)
items.description: A serene walled Chinese garden by the lake, a gift from Zurich's twin city Kunming, with pavilions, a koi pond and ornate gates. A small, tranquil detour on the lakeside promenade — a quiet, contemplative pause that reads well with grandparents.

items.name: Grossmünster to Fraumünster river walk
items.description: The short, storybook walk that ties the Old Town together — crossing the Limmat between the two great churches, past the guild houses, the Rathaus and the Wühre riverfront. Best at golden hour when the water glows; the ideal orientation stroll for a first evening in the city.

items.name: The Restaurant
items.description: Heiko Nieder's classical-modern cooking, laced with exotic accents — the city's benchmark table, high above the lake.

items.name: Widder Restaurant
items.description: Stefan Heilemann bridges classic haute cuisine and Thai-inflected modernity — the Old Town's two-star jewel.

items.name: The Counter
items.description: Mitja Birlo's surprise menu at a U-shaped counter beside the open kitchen — two stars from a standing start, inside the station.

items.name: IGNIV Zürich by Andreas Caminada
items.description: Caminada's fine-dining-meets-sharing concept — generous, playful and technically exact.

items.name: Orsini
items.description: Dario Moresco's creative modern Italian, guided by Milan's two-star Antonio Guida — bold contrasts, beautifully balanced.

items.name: La Rôtisserie
items.description: Refined cooking in a 14th-century riverside room — the Limmat gliding past the window.

items.name: Mesa
items.description: Sebastian Rösch's precise, light cooking — classical foundations with a bright, modern hand.

items.name: Kle
items.description: Entirely vegan fine dining with Moroccan and Mexican accents — creative, seasonal and quietly radical.

items.name: Neue Taverne
items.description: Nenad Mlinarevic's purely vegetarian, market-driven cooking in the heart of the Old Town.

items.name: Shin
items.description: An intimate Japanese counter — omakase sushi for a handful of guests, prepared before you.

items.name: Ornellaia
items.description: Modern Italian with a namesake cellar — Bolgheri's great wines beside a considered kitchen.

items.name: La Muña
items.description: Nikkei cooking — Peru meets Japan — on a lively rooftop above the shopping street.

items.name: Kronenhalle
credentials: A globally renowned historic dining room
items.description: A Zurich institution since 1924 — Swiss and Viennese classics served beneath Chagall, Picasso and Miró.

items.name: Marguita
items.description: The Baur au Lac's signature room — Mediterranean-leaning cooking with the hotel's long-held polish.

items.name: Baur's
credentials: Swiss Bar Awards — Best Hotel Bar (2025)
items.description: A deluxe brasserie of the classics — Zürcher Geschnetzeltes and sole done immaculately.

items.name: Sushi Shin
items.description: Masami Okamoto's exclusive omakase for a few guests a night — pure, exacting Japanese craft.

items.name: Rosi
items.description: Markus Stöckle's self-styled 'neo-Bavarian' room — vivid, warm and unexpectedly refined.

items.name: EquiTable
items.description: Julian Marti's small, values-led kitchen — food, wine and service in quiet, sustainable harmony.

items.name: Gaijin Izakaya
items.description: A modern izakaya of real quality — Japanese small plates and charcoal, at an honest price.

items.name: Gül
items.description: Contemporary Turkish over wood and charcoal — a bright surprise menu that punches far above its price.

items.name: Freilager La Trattoria
items.description: Antonio Colaianni's lively trattoria — vitello tonnato and tiramisù finished at your table.

items.name: AuGust
items.description: Honest Swiss cooking — sausage, rösti and beer done properly, without a shred of ceremony.

items.name: Kronenhalle Bar
credentials: A genuine Zurich institution; the bar of the historic Kronenhalle (1924), with original art on the walls and Diego Giacometti lighting
items.description: Cocktails mixed beneath real Miró, Klee and Chagall, under lamps Diego Giacometti made for the room — a Zurich rite since the 1960s.

items.name: Widder Bar
credentials: Widder Hotel bar; long regarded among the best bars in Europe, celebrated for its 1,000+ spirits and whisky selection
items.description: Over a thousand spirits and a legendary whisky wall, with live jazz some nights — one of Europe's most respected hotel bars.

items.name: Old Crow
credentials: One of Zurich's most acclaimed cocktail bars, renowned for a 1,600+ bottle back-bar of rare spirits
items.description: A spirits pilgrimage — 1,600-odd bottles, rare whiskies and forgotten liqueurs, mixed with quiet precision.

items.name: Clouds
credentials: The city's highest bar, atop the 126m Prime Tower; own award-winning CLOUDS gin
items.description: Zurich's highest bar — the 35th floor, the Limmat valley and the Alps through the glass, best caught at sunset.

items.name: Jules Verne Panorama Bar
credentials: A landmark panorama bar in the historic Urania tower, above Brasserie Lipp
items.description: A round bar in the old Urania observatory tower — the Old Town, the lake and the Alps wrapped around you.

items.title: The Kunsthaus and its Giacometti and modern rooms
items.description: One of Europe's strong collections, expanded with the Chipperfield extension; give it a proper half-day.

items.title: A summer swim and drift down the Limmat
items.description: Float the river from the Flussbad Oberer Letten, a ritual the whole city shares on warm days.

items.title: A lake cruise to the Alpine backdrop
items.description: Take a boat out on Lake Zurich in clear weather for the mountains rising beyond the shore.

items.title: Chocolate and coffee at the old confiseurs
items.description: Sit down at Sprüngli on Paradeplatz for a Luxemburgerli and treat it as an institution, not a snack.

plan.heading: 3 days in Zurich, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip — the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

days.title: The old town, at a walk

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Coffee at Confiserie Sprüngli on Paradeplatz, then a slow loop through the Niederdorf lanes to the Grossmünster and across to the Fraumünster for the Chagall windows.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Walk the Bahnhofstrasse for the watch houses — Beyer, Türler — then along the lake promenade to Bürkliplatz.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Kronenhalle, the old dining room hung with Picasso and Miró, over a Zürcher Geschnetzeltes and a bottle of Bordeaux.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Kunsthaus for the Giacometti and Munch rooms, unhurried, before the tour groups arrive.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The boat from Bürkliplatz down the Zürichsee to Rapperswil, lunch on the water, and back.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at IGNIV by Andreas Caminada in the Marktgasse Hotel — the sharing table, the Grand Restaurant of the Year.

days.title: The Uetliberg and the quiet side

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Train up the Uetliberg for the ridge walk and the whole city laid out below the Alps.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Rietberg Museum in Rieterpark for non-European art, then tea in the park's villa.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A last dinner at Rico's in Küsnacht along the lake, or the tavern room at Widder Hotel if you'd rather stay in town.

cta.label: Have your advisor arrange the stay

items.name: Altstadt (Old Town)
items.description: The medieval core around the Limmat with the churches and best hotels; suits those wanting to walk to everything.

items.name: Kreis 5 (Zürich West)
items.description: The reinvented industrial district of galleries, design and nightlife under the viaduct arches; suits a younger, design-minded stay.

items.name: Seefeld
items.description: The refined lakeside quarter of good restaurants and swimming spots; suits those who want calm near the water.

events.name: Sechseläuten
events.note: Zurich's guild spring festival, culminating in the burning of the Böögg snowman to predict the summer.

events.name: Street Parade
events.note: The world's largest techno street party, drawing hundreds of thousands along the lakefront.

events.name: Zurich Film Festival
events.note: The city's international film festival brings premieres and stars to venues across the centre.

onGround.heading: On the ground

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: You land at Zurich Airport (ZRH), a fast, orderly hub, where a chauffeured car meets you plane-side or at arrivals for the 20-minute run into the city.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The old town and lakefront are best walked; a private car and driver covers anything further, and the trams are immaculate if you ever wish to use them.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Coverage is total; an eSIM (Swisscom or Salt) activates on landing and hotel wifi is fast throughout.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Swiss francs (CHF); cards are accepted everywhere and contactless is standard, so cash is rarely needed and tipping is modest — rounding up or 5–10 percent for exceptional service.

onGround.note: Base yourself around the Baur au Lac or the lower Bahnhofstrasse for lake and old-town access; the Swiss run on punctuality, so a car arriving to the minute is expected, not exceptional.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: June to September is warm and clear, ideal for the lake and day-trips into the Alps; January and February are cold and grey with short days, better skipped unless you want the Christmas markets in December.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi on SWISS and Air India, about 8h45; from Mumbai and Bengaluru it is usually one stop via Zurich, Frankfurt, Munich or a Gulf hub. SWISS business is the natural choice; if connecting, the SWISS lounge at Zurich airport is a short, calm transfer with fast onward rail into the city.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required beyond routine; Switzerland is among the safest countries in the world, with negligible street crime. Tap water is excellent everywhere, so no bottled water needed.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian and Jain travel very easily. Zurich has Hiltl, the world's oldest vegetarian restaurant, plus South Indian veg at Saravanaa Bhavan; several Indian kitchens such as Delhi House will prepare Jain dishes on request.

collections.lede: Every place we send you appears here on merit — follow the thread to more like it.
